Segmental gain of chromosome 17q is the most common genetic aberration in high-risk neuroblastoma, but its role in disease progression is poorly understood. This study aims to address the contribution of 17q gain to neuroblastoma malignancy. We analyzed the genetic and transcriptional landscape of 417 neuroblastoma patients across various risk groups and clinical stages using multi-omic approaches. Single-cell RNA/DNA sequencing and SNP arrays were combined to characterize genomic aberrations, while evolutionary trajectories were mapped to explore the accumulation of genetic changes in patients with neuroblastoma. Additionally, DNA and RNA sequencing were used to assess mutational burden and gene expression patterns. Our findings suggest that chromosome 17 gain is an early genetic event acquired during neuroblastoma development, correlating with the accumulation of additional chromosomal aberrations and poor prognosis. Increased segmental gains of chromosome 17q were observed during clonal evolution, relapse disease and metastasis. We identified PPM1D , a p53-inducible Ser/Thr phosphatase located on chr17q22.3, as a key player activated by segmental 17q-gain, gene-fusion, or gain-of-function somatic and germline mutations, further promoting neuroblastoma development/progression. Gain of chromosome 17 is an early driver of genetic instability in neuroblastoma, with PPM1D  emerging as a potential candidate gene implicated in high-risk disease progression.   Keywords Neuroblastoma  Chromosome 17q  p53  WIP1  PPM1D     1 Introduction Chromosomal instability (CIN), caused by errors in DNA replication and chromosomal segregation during mitosis, is a hallmark of most human cancers [1 ]. CIN frequently results in structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities, leading to intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity, which disrupts key cancer pathways that give rise to phenotypic variations, posing challenges for therapeutic interventions [2 ]. Neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor of the sympathetic neural system, typically exhibits, like most childhood tumors, a low burden of somatic mutations [3 ]. Instead, CN alterations play a dominant role, where focal amplification of the MYCN  oncogene, re-arrangements within the TERT  locus on chromosome 5, segmental gains of chromosome 17q, and loss of chromosomes 1p36 and 11q all associated with high-risk disease and poor survival [4 ]. The most common cytogenetic abnormality in neuroblastoma is segmental or whole chromosomal gain of chromosome 17, detected in over 80 % of tumors [5 ]. Segmental gain of 17q21 extending to 17qter is observed in more than 60 % of tumors and is the most frequent genetic aberration linked to high-risk disease and poor prognosis of neuroblastoma patients [6 ]. Recent studies have added to the genomic complexity by revealing significant spatial genetic heterogeneity within neuroblastomas [7 ,8 ]. Furthermore, these tumors display distinct cell-type states, which may coexist within the same tumor [9 ]. While no genetic differences between these cell-type states have been reported, they are distinguished by variations in their transcriptional and epigenetic profiles [10 ]. Characterization of the genetic events during neuroblastoma evolution has shown that chromosomal gains crucial to disease pathogenesis typically occur early, within the first trimester of pregnancy [11 ]. This suggests that the intra-tumor heterogeneity may arise from the stepwise accumulation of genetic aberrations during embryonic development, with cells at different developmental maturation stages contributing to the heterogeneity observed in patient samples. Inactivating mutations of the tumor suppressor gene TP53  is a hallmark of adult cancers and lead to impaired DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoint arrest and apoptosis, ultimately resulting in accumulation of DNA mutations and CIN's [12 ]. Pediatric cancers, on the other hand, including neuroblastoma, rarely exhibit TP53  mutations [3 ]. Nevertheless, p53 activity is frequently compromised in neuroblastoma, particularly in relapsed tumors, where the incidence of TP53  mutations increases [13 ]. This suggests that inactivation of p53 remains critical for tumorigenesis, with alternative mechanisms likely contributing to its attenuation during early neuroblastoma development. One such mechanism may involve PPM1D , a gene located on chr17q22.3, which is frequently gained in high-risk neuroblastomas [5 ]. PPM1D  encodes the nuclear serine/threonine phosphatase WIP1 (wild-type p53 induced phosphatase 1), a key regulator of DNA damage response and cell cycle progression, controlling the activity of p53, ATM, CHK1/2 and other key molecules involved in DNA repair, cell cycle progression and apoptosis [14–18 ]. In concordance, PPM1D  mutations, amplifications and WIP1 overexpression have been identified in various cancers [19–27 ], and we recently demonstrated that overexpression of WIP1 in mice can drive tumor development, including neuroblastoma, by repressing p53 activity, promoting apoptotic escape, inducing genomic instability, and impairing growth arrest [28 ,29 ]. This suggests that PPM1D  might acts as an oncogene, facilitating malignant tumor development. In this study, we use multi-omics approaches to investigate the genetic development of neuroblastoma, focusing on the most common aberration, gain of chromosome 17q, and the oncogenic role of PPM1D  and the p53 regulating phosphatase WIP1. We demonstrate that gain of chromosome 17 is an early event in CIN during neuroblastoma development, with additional copies acquired through clonal evolution in aggressive and metastatic disease. Moreover, PPM1D  gene fusions resulting in high expression levels of PPM1D  as well as activating germline and somatic mutations were detected, suggesting a pivotal role of PPM1D  in neuroblastoma disease progression.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Patient-derived tumor material and clinical data The collection of neuroblastoma tissue samples from Swedish patients was performed after either written or verbal consent obtained from parents/guardians according to ethical permits approved by the local Ethics Committee (Karolinska Institutet and Karolinska University Hospital, registration number 03–736, 2009/1369-31/1 and 2022-07254-1. Fresh tumor tissue was collected at surgery and snap-frozen and stored at −80o C until analysis. All patients were diagnosed, managed and treated according to national and international guidelines and protocols.  2.2 Neuroblastoma tissue genomics and transcriptomics 2.2.1 Patient material for genetic analysis DNA was extracted from frozen tumors or blood using DNeasy blood and tissue kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to manufacturer's protocol and evaluated through absorbance measurements, fluorometric quantitation and DNA integrity assessment on Agilent Tapestation (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA). Demographic and genomic data of patients are outlined in Table S1 .  2.2.2 SNP-microarray analysis Microarray analysis was performed on a consecutive series of samples from an unselected cohort of 417 neuroblastoma patients using Affymetrix CytoScan HD SNP microarrays (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). These analyses include the majority of cases from Sweden whereof 362 had sufficient tumor content and quality for assessment of copy number aberrations. Some tumors were staged according to the International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) and INRG criteria. Handling of the microarrays has been described previously [6 ,30 ]. Primary data analysis was performed using GeneChip Command Console Software version 5.0.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) prior CN analysis using Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS v.3.3.0; Thermo Fisher Scientific). All cases of chromosomal gain, loss, or amplification or allelic imbalances were scored, both segmental and numerical aberrations, including detailed information about the breakpoint positions when applicable. For practical reasons, all notations of gain and loss were considered in relation to a nominal tumor karyotype and a chromosomal break in a tumor was defined as a clear change in gene dose level in the genomic profile. All genomic position annotations are stated based on the hg19 build (http://genome.ucsc.edu/ ) of the human genome.  2.2.3 Analysis of 17q clonal evolution Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays including the Oncoscan (formalin fixed paraffins embedded samples) and Cytoscan HD (fresh frozen samples) platforms (Affymetrix Inc.) were retrieved from and subjected to comparisons of 17q CN. Evolutionary trajectories were formalized as phylogenetic ideograms along the lines described in the original publication [7 ]. In all, 100 multiregional samples collected from 23 patients with neuroblastoma were analyzed. Each patient was assigned to one of three simplified clinical-genetic risk groups, including children <18 months of age with only numerical aberrations found in their tumor's phylogenetic stem by SNP array (low-risk patients), tumors with MYCN  amplification in the stem (high-risk patients), and tumors with structural rearrangements in the stem (high-risk patients). DNTR sequencing, processing of RNA and DNA and data analysis were done as described previously [31 ].  2.2.4 Genome sequencing In total, tumor material from 73 Swedish neuroblastoma patients was subjected to either whole genome sequencing (WGS) or exome sequencing with procedures for handling as described previously [32 ,33 ]. Exome sequencing was performed through paired-end sequencing on Illumina platforms (Illumina, San Diego, CA) after enrichment with Agilent SureSelect All Exome enrichment kit (Agilent technologies, Santa Clara, CA) on DNA for 18 tumor/normal pairs and additional 20 tumors lacking corresponding constitutional DNA. Alignment against human reference genome hg19 was performed using BWA with GATK local realignment followed by SNV calling using SNPeff. For tumors sequenced without constitutional DNA, filtering was performed by retention of only non-synonymous SNVs and removal of common variants, e.g. showing an allele frequency above 0.01 in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD v2.1.1). WGS was performed on tumor DNA and corresponding constitutional DNA (n = 50) also using paired-end sequencing on Illumina instrumentation (Illumina) at Clinical Genomics, SciLife Laboratories, Gothenburg/Stockholm, Sweden, while mapping to hg19 and variant calling were done using the Sentieon suite of bioinformatics tools (Sentieon Inc., Mountain View, CA, USA) (Sentieon version v.201808.03). Only high-quality called SNVs with a minimum of 10 % variant allele frequency and a total read coverage of ten were considered. All synonymous variants or variants in non-coding regions (except those affecting canonical splice sites) were discarded. Remaining SNVs were kept for further analysis and evaluation including manual assessment through the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) [34 ] for removal of calls due to mapping artifacts and paralogs. FusionCatcher was applied to discover PPM1D -containing fusion transcripts in the National Cancer Institute TARGET dataset comprising paired-end RNA sequenced neuroblastoma patient samples (dbGap Study Accession:phs000218.v16.p6).  2.2.5 Immunohistochemistry Twenty-seven neuroblastoma samples derived from children of different ages and all clinical stages, including different biological subsets, were analyzed. Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded human tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and graded alcohols, hydrated and washed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). After antigen retrieval in sodium citrate buffer (pH 6) in a microwave oven, the endogenous peroxidase was blocked by 0.3 % H2O2 for 15 min. Sections from human neuroblastoma were incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody against PPM1D (ab31270, Abcam). As a secondary antibody, the anti-rabbit-horseradish peroxidase (HRP) SignalStain Boost IHC detection kit was used (Cell Signal Technology; #8114). A matched isotype control was used as a control for nonspecific background staining (not shown). Case description, germline PPM1D mutation detection (see supplementary methods)   2.2.6 Gene expression analysis Patient cohort and methodology of RNA-seq data analysis pipeline are extensively described in Ref. [35 ]. We used gene expression data of 498 neuroblastoma patients from seven countries: Belgum (n = 1), Germany (n = 420), Israel (n = 11), Italy (n = 5), Spain (n = 14), United Kingdom (n = 5) and Unated States (n = 42). All patients were enrolled in their respective clinical trials after providing informed consent. Age at diagnosis ranged from birth to 295.5 months, with a median age of 14.6 months [35 ]. According to the Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification system [36 ] we classified patients with MYCN  amplifications and patients with a metastatic disease and older than 18 months at diagnosis as high-risk patients (n = 176). Events were defined according to a revised version of the International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria [37 ]. RNA-seq gene expression analyses have been done using the MAGIC-AceView pipeline as previously described [35 ]. CN data for PPM1D  was derived from array comparative hybridization (aCGH) [38 ], whole exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing analyses [39 ].  2.2.7 Statistical analyses Gene expression of PPM1D  was investigated displayed on the gene level (PPM1D ) or transcript level for two selected transcript variants (AceView annotation, as a result of the analysis, i.e. PPM1D.aAug10  and PPM1D.bAug10 , corresponding to transcripts ENST00000305921 and ENST00000392995 respectively). PPM1D  expression in defined NB subgroups (according to INRG high-risk status, INSS stage, amplification status of MYCN, age, CN status of PPM1D  on chromosome 17) was displayed in Tukey box-and-whisker plots (box range: inter-quartile range, whiskers: 1.5x IQR). Where appropriate, either Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon or Kruskal-Wallis tests were performed to investigate differences in expression of two or more analyzed groups, respectively. Pearson correlation analyses have been applied to investigate correlation between PPM1D  expression and CN. To investigate the prognostic value of PPM1D  expression, optimal cut-point expression values separating the cohort into PPM1D -high and PPM1D -low groups that correlate best with outcome in terms of event-free survival (EFS; recurrence, progression and death from disease were considered as events), and overall-survival (OS) were calculated by means of maximally selected rank statistics (maxstat package in R v3.4.3) [40 ,41 ] in training sets. Differences in survival of PPM1D  high and low-expressing subgroups according to dichotomization with the established cutpoints was then tested by Mantel-Cox (log-rank) tests in corresponding validation sets. For this procedure, equally sized training and validation subsets (n = 296) were randomly sampled from the entire cohort (n = 498). Resampling was done 1000 times and the mode of those established cutpoint values which passed p < 0.05 in maxstat [40 ,41 ] as well as in the log-rank test was eventually selected to define PPM1D -high and PPM1D -low expressing subgroups (this procedure was independently done for EFS and OS). Subsequently, Kaplan-Meier survival estimates for the entire cohort were calculated and displayed from the time of diagnosis and clinical outcome of respective subgroups was compared using the log-rank test.  2.2.8 Principal Components Analysis (PCA) on expression data Raw data expression: CEL-files (HU133A chips from Affymetrix) from 30 primary neuroblastoma cases from two published microarray studies [42–44 ] were pre-processed using gcRMA normalization in Bioconducter for R 2.9.2 (library BioC 2.4). For each gene, the mean expression level from probe-sets was calculated, resulting in 8105 genes/variables [42 ]. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was performed on the pre-processed McArdle/Wilzén expression data set using Omics Explorer 3.2 from Qlucore (www.qlucore.se ). Genes with the lowest variance were filtered out (variance cut-off = 0.4), displaying a PCA plot based on 716 genes/variables and 30 samples/cases according to the method previously described [42 ]. Samples/cases were joined to their nearest neighbor using Euclidean distances, and they subdivided into four separate groups. The differential expression of PPM1D  between molecular subgroups was calculated by fold change and change and significance by Student's t-test (2-sided comparison, unequal variance).    3 Results 3.1 Chromosome 17 gain is the most common genetic aberration in neuroblastoma To investigate the genetic aberrations in neuroblastoma, we performed array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) on tumor samples from 417 Swedish neuroblastoma patients collected between 1986 and 2020. The most common genetic anomaly identified was gain of chromosome arm 17q, detected in 76.5 % of the tumors, either as segmental gains of 17q (n = 192) or as whole chromosome 17 gains (n = 127) (Fig. 1  A). Segmental 17q gains were predominately observed in unfavorable neuroblastomas, whereas favorable neuroblastomas typically exhibited whole chromosome 17 gains, which includes TP53  on 17p13.1. Importantly, neuroblastoma patients with segmental 17q gain had significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to those without this aberration, with 5-year overall survival probability of 42.9 % versus 88.2 %, respectively (P  = 4.6x10−14 . Fig. 1 B). Children with neuroblastoma lacking both segmental 17q-gain and other high-risk features such as MYCN  amplification and/or 11q-deletion, showed favorable long-term survival (94.2 %) 8–20 years from diagnosis, in most cases without requiring any treatment. In contrast, children with 17q-gain, despite receiving active multimodal therapy, had poorer survival (50.2 %) and an increased risk of late sequelae (Figure S1A ). A poorer survival in children with 17q-gain as compared to those with whole chromosome 17 gain lack of aberration was seen in patients with MNA, 11q-deletion or among those with other structural variants or only numerical changes (Mantel-Cox, p = 8.9e-23) (Fig. S1B ), further confirming 17q gain as a robust prognostic marker in neuroblastoma [4–6 ]. Given the close propinquity to the proximal breakpoints commonly associated with 17q gain and their presence in all tumors with segmental 17q gain, we identified three prominent gene candidates with tumorigenic capacity within this region: RAD51C , PPM1D  and BRIP1  (Fig. 1 A). Among these, only PPM1D  has previously been proposed as an oncogene in neuroblastoma, highlighting its potential role in driving tumorigenesis in cases with 17q gain [28 ,29 ] (http://www.cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/mutation/ ).  3.2 Copy number gain of chromosome 17 is an early genetic event in neuroblastoma and additional gene copies are acquired through clonal evolution To further delineate the chromosomal aberrations involved in neuroblastoma development and progression, we employed evolutionary trajectory analysis [7 ]. We analyzed SNP array data from 100 multiregional tumor samples collected from 23 neuroblastoma patients [7 ], with a focus on chromosome 17. Most tumors (57 %, 13/23) were found to harbor gain of chromosome 17q in over 90 % of tumor cells in all samples, indicating that this aberration was present early in tumor evolution, persisting as a stable feature throughout disease progression. In these cases, no additional CN changes were observed (Fig. 2  A, I and Table S2 ). However, 30 % (7/23) of tumors showed a progressive accumulation of additional 17q copies as tumors evolved, either regionally or during the transition from primary tumor to metastasis or relapse. In four of these cases, gain of 17q occurred early in the phylogenetic stem, followed by further gains of additional copies of these genes as regional clones evolved (Fig. 2 A, II). In three cases, clones with 17q gain emerged in subset of samples and expanded through selective sweeps, eventually encompassing all tumor cells in the samples (Fig. 2 A, III). The remaining 13 % of patients (3/23) showed regional variation in CN, making conclusive evolutionary analysis difficult. Among the 20 patients with informative evolutionary data, the successive accumulation of 17q copies was observed in more than half of high-risk cases (7/13; Table S1 ). In contrast, additional changes in 17q CN were not found in any of the low-risk patients, i.e. children under 18 months with only numerical changes in the stem (0/7; P  = 0.0445; two-sided Fisher's exact test). In additional neuroblastoma cases with multiple tumor samples available for analysis, we confirmed that 17q gain is an early event in neuroblastoma development (Fig. 2 B–S2 ), observed in both a child without known predisposition and in a child with a germline PHOX2B  mutation [45 ]. Our recent single-cell RNA-sequencing data from neuroblastoma patient samples revealed the presence of pre-malignant Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like cells in addition to the previously described adrenergic phenotype tumor cells [31 ]. This suggests that SCP-like cells might be the cell-of-origin in some neuroblastoma cases. To dissect the genetic landscape of neuroblastoma at the single-cell level, we used the Numbat algorithm [46 ] to identify CN variations and DNTR-Seq (Direct Nuclear Tagmentation and RNA sequencing) [47 ] to investigate the subclonal structure of tumor cells at the single-cell level. SCP-like cells were identified using the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB3 as a specific marker, whereas adrenergic cells were identified by CD24 [31 ]. An example of striking intra-tumoral heterogeneity with early chromosome 17 gain was detected with DNTR-seq (single-cell whole-genome sequencing) which revealed five major tumor cell clones (Fig. 2 C). In one cluster of cells with a SCP-like signature (Clone B), gain of chromosome 17 was the only detected genomic aberrations. The remaining malignant clones (clone 1–4), which all had adrenergic transcriptional profiles, displayed multiple whole-chromosome gains which included chromosome 17. Clone 2 which showed further evolution, had acquired segmental chromosomal aberrations that included loss of chromosome 1p and gain of chromosome 2p. Clones 3 and 4 shared the same genomic aberration as clone 2, except that Clone 3 had acquired one additional copy of chromosome 17, while Clone 4 had retained a normal diploid chromosome 5 (Fig. 2 C). Importantly, the gain of chromosome 17 was the only genomic event, shared by all aberrant cell populations (Fig. 2 C). It is also worthy of note that this was gained independently in SCP-like and adrenergic cell populations.  3.3 PPM1D  is activated by gene fusions and, somatic- and germ-line mutations in neuroblastoma Whole exome sequencing (WES) or whole genome sequencing (WGS) of 73 neuroblastoma patient samples, revealed a somatic pathogenic truncating mutation in in exon 6 of PPM1D  (c.1344_1345insT; p.L450fs) in a MYCN -amplified tumor from an infant girl (Fig. S3A ). Her neuroblastoma rapidly progressed from localized INSS stage 1 to metastatic INSS stage 4, ultimately leading to a fatal clinical outcome despite aggressive treatment (Fig. 3  A and S2A ). Additionally, we identified a de novo  germline mutation located in exon 6 of PPM1D  l (c.1528C > T; p.Q510∗), resulting in a premature truncation of the protein (Fig. 3 A). This mutation was found in a 26-month-old boy diagnosed with metastatic stage 4 (INSS/stage M, INRGSS) neuroblastoma originating in the left adrenal gland with bone metastases. The patient exhibited clinical features resembling previously described cases of children with intellectual disabilities and dysmorphic features associated with PPM1D  germline mutations (Fig. S3B ). The tumor lacked MYCN  amplification, and the patient had a poor clinical outcome after relapse and disease progression, despite multimodal clinical therapy. A detailed clinical description of this patient can be found in the Supplementary Methods section. Hence, the neuroblastoma-associated PPM1D  mutations both resulted in C-terminal truncated variants of WIP1, similar to those gain-of-function variants identified in other cancers (Fig. 3 A) (http//:www.cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/mutation/ ). In addition, by FusionCatcher analysis of RNA-sequencing data from neuroblastoma tumors we identified a gene fusion between PPM1D  and the breast carcinoma amplified sequence 3 (BCAS3)  gene located on chromosome 17q23.2 in a tumor from a patient enrolled in the Therapeutically Applicable Research to Generate Effective Treatments (TARGET) neuroblastoma dataset. This fusion was associated with high expression of PPM1D  and a predicted WIP1 isoform with a truncated C-terminal (Fig. 3 B). These findings, together with the evidence that chromosome 17q gain is an early event in neuroblastoma tumorigenesis, suggest that genes within this chromosomal region, particularly PPM1D , play a key role in neuroblastoma progression. Given PPM1D 's known functions in DNA repair, cell cycle regulation, and apoptosis, it is a strong candidate for driving further genomic instability and tumor evolution.  3.4 Overexpression of PPM1D  in neuroblastoma correlates with unfavorable clinical and biological features Our data demonstrating that the PPM1D  gene is altered in CN and/or structure in the majority of 17q gained high-risk neuroblastomas, incited us to investigate the clinical prognostic and biological features of PPM1D  gene expression in neuroblastoma. Our results demonstrate that higher expression levels of PPM1D  was associated with several neuroblastoma risk factors, including metastatic stage 4 disease, older age at diagnosis (>18 months), MYCN -gene amplification and classification into the INRG high-risk (HR) group as defined by combined clinical and biological features associated with unfavorable clinical outcome [36 ] (Fig. 4  A). Notably, the highest PPM1D  expression was observed in non-MYCN  amplified HR-neuroblastoma tumors (nMN HR; Fig. 4 A), which predominantly correspond to cases with 11q-deletions, a group frequently harboring segmental 17q gains. Next, we correlated PPM1D  expression with CN alterations, using data from CGH arrays, WES and WGS. CN gains were separated into numerical gains that included whole chromosome 17 and segmental gains that included the sub-region containing PPM1D . Correlation analysis revealed a significant gene dosage effect, with PPM1D  expression increasing proportionally with the number of 17q copies (Fig. 4 A and B). Moreover, high PPM1D  expression was strongly linked to poor clinical outcome, with significantly lower overall survival (OS; 59 % vs. 83 % at five years, p < 0.001) and event-free survival (EFS; 47 % vs. 68 %, p < 0.001) in patients with PPM1D  high-expressing tumors (Fig. 4 C). For comparison, we also performed similar analysis of IGF2BP1, TBX and BIRC5 that previously have been suggested to be involved in neuroblastoma development or contributing to the aggressive nature of high-risk neuroblastoma [48–50 ] (Fig. S4A ). We also compared gene expression patterns across different neuroblastoma subtypes [51 ]. Using principal component analysis (PCA) on gene expression profiles from 30 primary neuroblastoma samples from two published microarray studies [43 ,44 ] we observed that high PPM1D  expression was associated with the more aggressive subtypes Type 2A (17q gain with 14q- and/or 11q-deletions) and Type 2B (1p-deletion and MYCN -amplification) neuroblastomas. In contrast, low PPM1D  expression was characteristic of low-risk, near-triploid tumors with high TrkA expression (Type 1) (Fig. S4B ). Additionally, immunohistochemical analysis confirmed consistent WIP1 expression in all 17q-gained neuroblastoma samples (Fig. S4C ). These findings underscore the role of PPM1D  in neuroblastoma aggressiveness and suggest that high WIP1-expressing tumors correlate with worse patient outcomes, further reinforcing the significance of 17q gain as a prognostic marker (Fig. 1 A and S1 ) and highlighting the strong association between PPM1D  expression and 17q gain (Figs. 1B, 2A and 4A, B and S4B ).   4 Discussion Neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor originating from the developing peripheral nervous system, remains challenging to treat despite intensified multimodal therapy, and survival rates are still comparatively poor compared to pediatric cancers in general. Advancing our molecular understanding of neuroblastoma is therefore crucial to improve the outcome for these children/patients. We therefore investigated common genetic aberrations in neuroblastoma, identifying chromosomal gain of 17q as an early genetic event in tumorigenesis. Segmental gain of chromosome17q is the most common chromosomal aberration and predictor of poor prognosis in neuroblastoma [5 ,52 ]. Also, gain of 17q is frequently found in tumors of epithelial, neural and hematopoietic origin, suggesting that 17q harbors key genes involved in oncogenesis [53–58 ]. Our findings indicate that chromosome 17 gain may occur independently in pre-malignant Schwann cell precursor-like cell populations and in adrenergic tumor clones, and that subsequent evolving malignant cell clones may acquire additional copies of chromosome 17. Evolutionary trajectory analysis revealed that 17q gain typically appears at the phylogenetic stem of neuroblastoma tumors, with subsequent gains accumulating as the tumor progresses, supporting its role as an initial driver of malignancy. Together, these observations align with a recent study using molecular clock analysis and population genetic modelling to time the genetic event of neuroblastoma evolution [11 ], suggesting that neuroblastoma pathogenesis may be initiated in the first trimester of pregnancy, when rapidly proliferating neuroblasts are susceptible to CIN and aneuploidy [11 ]. This is also supported by a study on evolutionary history of pediatric cancer showing that whole or segmental gain of chromosome 17 as well as MYCN gene amplification was identified as early chromosomal aberrations in neuroblastoma [59 ]. The frequent gain of 17q, as opposed to losses on the 17p arm where TP53  resides, may further favor the accumulation of genomic aberrations and mutations, driving tumorigenesis [60 ]. Several cancer-associated genes have been identified on chromosome 17q including BIRC5, BRCA1, BRIP1, EME1, ERBB2, IGF2BP1, ncRAN, NME1, NF1, PPM1D, RAD51C, TBX2  and TRIM37 . In our analysis of 417 Swedish neuroblastoma samples, RAD51C, PPM1D  and BRIP1  are the only genes that are included in the shortest region of overlap of 17q gains which is similar to observations made in breast cancer [24 ,61 ,62 ]. Notably, PPM1D  CN gains were more frequent in high-risk, metastatic, and relapsed neuroblastomas than low-risk tumors, indicating its potential role in clonal expansion and disease progression. In our patient cohort, we identified both a somatic PPM1D  mutation (p.L450fs) and one de novo  germline mutation (p.Gln510∗) in exon 6, both resulting in truncated, gain-of-function WIP1 proteins that exhibit enhanced stability and lead to increased suppression of the p53 pathway [24 ,61–64 ], previously reported in numerous other malignancies [65 ]. PPM1D de novo  germline mutations, predominantly in the 5th and 6th exons, have previously been reported in children with the neurodevelopmental disorder Jansen-de Vries syndrome and have not yet been described in the context of cancer. However, an identical c.1528C > T (p.Gln510∗) somatic mutation has been reported previously in a malignant melanoma [66 ]. We also detected a gene fusion of PPM1D  and BCAS3  expressed at high levels in a neuroblastoma patient. The fusion is predicted to generate a C-terminal truncation and cause augmented WIP1 protein levels. Similarly, a fusion between PPM1D and C1QTNF1 in an Ewing sarcoma patient has been reported to drive high WIP1 expression  (https://pecan.stjude.cloud ).  Additional PPM1D  fusions, such as an intragenic region of RPSK6B1  and a PPM1D-ZNS655 fusion,  have been described in patients with diffuse cerebellar glioma and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), although without further investigation on the effect on WIP1 protein stability and abundance  [67 ] (https://pecan.stjude.cloud ). Given that PPM1D gene amplifications and C-terminal mutations are frequently detected in a wide spectrum of cancers  [65 ] suggests that PPM1D  is a pivotal gene on 17q contributing to neuroblastoma pathogenesis by promoting CIN and allowing tumor cells to evade p53-mediated apoptosis. In primary neuroblastoma, mutations of genes in the p53 pathway are rare, occurring in only 1–2 % of primary cases [39 ], but they become more common in relapsed disease (15 %) [39 ], where p53 inactivation appears to be linked to therapy resistance [68 ,69 ]. Mechanisms that inactivate p53 in neuroblastoma include MDM2  gene amplification or overexpression mediated by MYCN  amplification, hypermethylation or deletion of CDKN2A , miR-380-5p-mediated repression of p53, or its inactivation by the methyltransferase SETD8 [13 ,70–73 ]. Under normal conditions, WIP1 attenuates p53 activation by inhibiting p53-mediated transactivation of promoters by dephosphorylating p53 at Ser15 [74 ]. Additionally, WIP1 indirectly inhibits p53 activity by dephosphorylating Mdm2 and upstream p53 activating kinases [14–18 ]. Amplification and gain-of-function mutations of PPM1D  are proposed to only partially inhibit p53 activity, given that p53 undergoes multiple post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation, acetylation and ubiquitination that mediate p53-dependent beyond WIP1's regulatory influence [75 ]. Our recent mouse studies support this, showing that transgenic mice overexpressing PPM1D  generate tumors phenotypically similar to Trp53  loss-of-function derived tumors29  rather than the spectra of tumors observed in Trp53  knock-out mice. The effects of this partial inhibition of p53 activity together with the WIP1-mediated delay in DNA repair processes [65 ] suggest that PPM1D  activating mutations and/or overexpression disrupt the fidelity of DNA repair and DNA replication, allowing for accumulation of mutations and chromosomal aberrations that eventually result in malignant transformation. Our study demonstrates that gain of chromosome 17 is an early event in neuroblastoma and that additional copies of 17q, harboring PPM1D  locus, are associated with high-risk, metastatic and relapsed disease. High WIP1 expression in neuroblastoma appears to allow for the accumulation of cells with SNV and CIN in neural crest cells during development, ultimately resulting in the emergence of neuroblastoma with increased tumor aggressiveness and resistance to treatment. Therefore, inhibiting WIP1 could be a valuable addition to neuroblastoma treatment, with potential benefits extending to other pediatric and adult cancers exhibiting WIP1 dysregulation. As segmental gain of chromosome 17q is the most common genetic aberration associated with high-risk neuroblastoma, other genes, in addition to PPM1D , located within the 17q21-17qter chromosomal region have been suggested to be involved in neuroblastoma initiation and/or development of high-risk disease [48–50 ]. Insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA binding protein-1 is encoded by the IGF2BP1  gene located on chromosome 17q21.32. IGF2BP1 is highly expressed in high-risk neuroblastoma and has been shown to induce neuroblastoma in transgenic mice where IGF2BP  expression is driven by the dopamine hydroxylase promoter (dbh ) expressed in sympathoadrenal cells during development. IGF2BP1 has been shown to interact with Mycn in a feed-forward manner in which MYCN acting as a transcription factor induce the expression of IGF2BP1  whereas IGF2BP1 acting as an RNA binding protein stabilizes MYCN mRNA leading to increased half-life of Mycn proteins promoting the expression of other oncogenes contributing to the aggressive nature of high-risk neuroblastoma [50 ]. The T-box 2 transcription factor (TBX2 ) located on chromosome 17q21.22 is also overexpressed in high-risk neuroblastoma. TBX2 has been described as a super-enhancer included in the core regulatory circuitry (CRC) of transcription factors that regulate the expression of genes important for keeping neuroblastoma cells in an undifferentiated cellular state [48 ]. BIRC5  located on chromosome 17q25.3 encoding the anti-apoptotic protein survivin has for more than 25 years been shown to be associated with neuroblastoma and poor patient survival [49 ]. Although pharmacological or genetic repression of survivin inhibit the growth of neuroblastoma cells, this growth suppression was shown to be independent on 17q gain [5 ]. Moreover, a recent study combining DNA CN profiles and systems biology applying protein-protein networks analysis in high-risk NB harboring Chr 11q deletions identified five regulatory nodes corresponding to BIRC5, BRCA1, PRKCA, SUMO2 , and GPS1 all located on Chr 17q  and that this may affect chromatin remodeling and DNA repair [76 ]. Although Chr 11q deletions has been considered to be a late chromosomal event in NB [59 ], this may contribute to the chromosomal heterogeneity observed in high-risk NB. In summary, our data position 17q gain as an early and possibly the initial event in neuroblastoma development, with PPM1D  emerging as a strong candidate oncogene driving tumor progression through p53 pathway modulation and CIN promotion. Targeting WIP1 in neuroblastoma in combinations with current treatment modalities may address the challenge of genetic instability and therapy resistance, representing an avenue for improving outcomes in high-risk and relapsed pediatric neuroblastoma as well as other PPM1D -driven cancers. title: T-2 toxin induces senescence in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells by regulating the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway
abstract: The mechanisms by which T-2 toxin induces senescence in neurons, along with the involvement of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), remain poorly understood. Using human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells as a model, T-2 toxin (6 nM, 1–48 h) induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells, leading to cell cycle arrest. This was mediated by the upregulation of proteins involved in cell cycle regulation and stimulation of IL-6 and NF-κB expression. T-2 toxin rapidly triggered the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, disrupted mitochondrial function, and altered the levels of Alzheimer’s disease-associated proteins (Tau, p-Tau, and APP). T-2 toxin also transiently elevated HIF-1α levels. Notably, HIF-1α regulated the expression of cell cycle inhibitory proteins (p16, p21, p53) and senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors (IL-8, IL-6, CCL2), along with the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, thereby exacerbating T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence. These findings underscore the vital role of HIF-1α in T-2 toxin-induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells.

Edited by Dr R Pereira The mechanisms by which T-2 toxin induces senescence in neurons, along with the involvement of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), remain poorly understood. Using human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells as a model, T-2 toxin (6 nM, 1–48 h) induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells, leading to cell cycle arrest. This was mediated by the upregulation of proteins involved in cell cycle regulation and stimulation of IL-6 and NF-κB expression. T-2 toxin rapidly triggered the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, disrupted mitochondrial function, and altered the levels of Alzheimer’s disease-associated proteins (Tau, p-Tau, and APP). T-2 toxin also transiently elevated HIF-1α levels. Notably, HIF-1α regulated the expression of cell cycle inhibitory proteins (p16, p21, p53) and senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors (IL-8, IL-6, CCL2), along with the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, thereby exacerbating T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence. These findings underscore the vital role of HIF-1α in T-2 toxin-induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells. T-2 toxin has diverse toxicological effects, raising concerns due to its potential to cross the blood-brain barrier, accumulate in the central nervous system, and invoke neurotoxic effects (Zhang et al., 2020 ). Its neurotoxic mechanisms are multifaceted, involving a series of interconnected pathways including inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and glial cell activation (Pei et al., 2021 ). The interplay of these pathways culminates in neuronal injury, which manifests in a spectrum of neurological dysfunctions and pathological alterations (Shahba et al., 2021 ). Cellular senescence represents a complex biological phenomenon that integrates various facets of cellular distress and numerous molecular pathways, encompassing persistent DNA damage responses, impairment of telomere integrity, and activation of oncogenes (Di Micco et al., 2021 ). Senescence research has yet to identify a universal or model-specific biomarker within culture medium or tissue specimen that is capable of reliably distinguishing senescent cells (Gorgoulis et al., 2019 ). At present, the identification of senescent cells is predicated on an array of markers, which include the enhanced expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), the buildup of lipofuscin, notably altered and flattened cellular morphology, and an increased cytoplasm-to-nucleus size ratio (Di Micco et al., 2021; Lopez-Otin et al., 2023 ). Moreover, a defining feature of cellular senescence is the notable upregulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (CDKNs), with p16 and p53 being the most important proteins that inhibit the cell cycle (Kandhaya-Pillai et al., 2023 ). The activation of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) unfolds as a dynamic sequence in tandem with cellular senescence. Expression of cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and CCL2, which constitute the SASP core, is observed in almost all senescent cell types cultured in vitro (Hawthorne et al., 2023 ). Certain mycotoxins, such as aflatoxin G1, can disrupt cellular metabolic activities and impinge upon NF-κB and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling cascades, precipitating anomalous cellular functions and expediting the onset of senescence (Li et al., 2023a ). In the field of cellular biology, the ramifications of hypoxic environments on intracellular dynamics have garnered considerable interest. The hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) emerged as a critical regulatory element, orchestrating the activation of a multitude of genes during periods of low oxygen within cells, a phenomenon that appears to be widespread across cellular systems (Hayashi et al., 2019 ). Emerging evidence indicates that HIF-1α plays a consequential role in various physiological and pathological contexts, such as cancer biology, inflammatory responses, and angiogenic processes (Brockmueller et al., 2023 ). Pertinent research has revealed a strong correlation between crop-associated mycotoxins, particularly T-2 toxin, and hypoxia (Wu et al., 2020 ). This connection extends to immunological implications where HIF-1α is implicated in facilitating “immune evasion” mechanisms through the activation of the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway in the context of T-2 toxin exposure (You et al., 2022 ). Moreover, exposure to deoxynivalenol, a type B trichothecene mycotoxin, upregulates HIF-1α via the STAT3 signaling pathway, designating HIF-1α as an essential mediator of deoxynivalenol-elicited immunosuppressive responses (Zhang et al., 2023 ). In addition, emerging evidence suggests a significant link between mycotoxins (including T-2 toxin) exposure and the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Pei et al., 2021 ). The neurotoxic effects of T-2 toxin, particularly its ability to induce oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, mirror the pathological hallmarks observed in AD, including amyloid-beta plaque formation and tau hyperphosphorylation (Zhao et al., 2024 ). This connection underscores the importance of understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying T-2 toxin-induced neurotoxicity to develop potential therapeutic strategies and mitigate the risk of neurodegenerative diseases associated with environmental toxins. Within this framework, the potential involvement of mycotoxins, especially T-2 toxin, in triggering cellular senescence and the specific role of HIF-1α in this process have not been thoroughly investigated. Notably, a growing body of both in vivo  and in vitro  evidence underscores the brain as highly susceptible to mycotoxin-induced neurotoxic effects. This susceptibility may be associated with neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) (Pei et al., 2021; Mateo et al., 2022 ). The SH-SY5Y cells exhibit stable characteristics and demonstrate similar properties to neuronal cells in terms of signal transduction, and have been widely used in neuroscience research, particularly in studies of NDs (Wang et al., 2022 ). In this study, we employed the human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y as an in vitro  model to conduct both experimental and analytical assessments of the potential involvement of T-2 toxin in the critical process of cellular senescence within SH-SY5Y and the underlying function of HIF-1α in this context. The findings are anticipated to enhance the comprehension of the neurotoxic effects exerted by T-2 toxin and to offer prospective targets for intervention and therapeutic strategies against T-2 toxin-induced cellular damage.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Chemicals T-2 toxin was acquired from Qifa Experimental Reagent, Shanghai, China. Minimum Essential Medium (MEM), Ham’s F-12 medium, non-essential amino acids, sodium pyruvate, and GlutaMAX-1 were all purchased from iCell Bioscience, Shanghai, China. Dimethyl sulfoxide and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) transfer membranes for western blotting were obtained from Merck. Trypsin was obtained from Hyclone, Logan, USA. YC-1, an inhibitor of HIF-1α, was obtained from Bidepharm, Shanghai, China. Propidium iodide (PI) staining solution was purchased from Servicebio, Wuhan, China. The Senescence β-Galactosidase Staining Kit and Cell Counting Kit-8 were obtained from Beyotime, Shanghai, China. All the chemicals utilized in our study possess exceptional purity levels (≥99%). The primary and secondary antibodies used for western blotting are summarized in Supplementary Table 1 .  2.2 Cell culture and treatments Human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells were obtained from iCell Biotechnology, Shanghai. Cells were grown in MEM/F12 medium added with 10% fetal bovine serum (Tianhang Bio-technology, Hangzhou, China), 1% non-essential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 1% GlutaMAX-1, and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Solarbio, Beijing, China), kept in a humidified incubator (Changjin, Changsha, China) at 37°C and 5% CO2 . Cultured SH-SY5Y cells were inoculated from T-25 culture flasks into six-well plates at a density of 1×106  cells/mL (Cell counting using the TC20; Bio-Rad Automatic Cell Counter, USA). Based on CCK-8 assay results, the experimental concentration of T-2 toxin was defined as 6 nM. SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to T-2 toxin (6 nM) for 1, 2, 6, 12, 24 and 48 h. Simultaneously, a negative control (NC) group was treated only with MEM/F12 complete medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum, whereas a positive control group was treated with 100 μM CoCl2  for comparison of HIF-1α expression levels. In certain experiments, cells were first treated with the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1 (10 μM) for 24 h (Hu et al., 2020 ) and then incubated with T-2 toxin (6 nM) for the indicated times.  2.3 Western blotting Cellular protein extraction was conducted on ice, with pre-cooled sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), EP tubes, and a centrifuge, all maintained at 4°C, to ensure optimal conditions. Treated cells were lysed at 4°C for 20 min in RIPA buffer (Servicebio) containing protease inhibitors. After centrifuging the lysate, the supernatant was collected. The protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay kit (Beyotime). The protein concentration was diluted to 20 μg/μL, and 40 μg protein sample was transferred to each western blot lane. Extracted cellular proteins were isolated using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis gels and moved to PVDF membranes, then left to incubate overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (1:2000) mixed in TBST containing 5% skimmed milk powder (Servicebio). After rinsing three times with TBST, the membrane was incubated with the secondary antibody (1:10000) for 1 h at room temperature (18–25°C). The PVDF membranes were developed with ECL luminescence reagent (Meilun Biotechnology, Dalian, China).  2.4 Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) For qPCR analysis, we referred to experimental methods previously described by our research group (You et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In brief, total RNA was isolated using an RNA Extraction Kit (Tiangen Biotech, Beijing, China). RNA was reverse-transcribed using cDNA synthesis premix reagent (Tiangen Biotech). The qPCR was performed using a CFX96 Thermal Cycler system (Bio-Rad, USA) as follows. The initial phase involved pre-denaturation at 95°C lasting 30 s, succeeded by a 15 s denaturation phase at the same temperature, and the subsequent phase encompassed a 30 s annealing and extension step at 60°C. After 40 cycles, the fluorescence signal was recorded. The sequences of the specific primers are presented in Supplementary Table 2 . Results were computed using the 2-ΔΔCT  method.  2.5 Flow cytometry The cultured cells were digested by trypsin, washed with pre-cooled PBS 1× at 4°C, and centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 min. The cells were fixed with pre-cooled 75% ethanol at −20°C and kept away from light overnight at 4°C. Subsequently, cells were rinsed with pre-cooled PBS. To remove RNA, RNaseA (1 mg/mL, 2 μL; Solarbio) was added to the solution kept in a 37°C water bath for 40 min. Fluorescence labeling was performed by staining with 100 µL of 100 µg/mL PI staining solution for 20 min protected from light. Flow cytometry was performed using an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength of 585±21 nm. The cell cycle distribution was analyzed with Modfit software (Modfit LT 5.0 software, USA).  2.6 SA-β-gal staining SA-β-gal activity was assessed using a Senescence-associated β-Galactosidase Staining Kit. SH-SY5Y cells, cultured in six-well plates at a density of approximately 1×106  cells/mL, were rinsed with PBS, followed by a 15 min fixation step and three wash steps. PBS was aspirated, each well was supplemented with 1 mL of SA-β-gal staining solution, the six-well plates were wrapped with parafilm to avoid evaporation, and the cells were plated overnight at 37°C with staining solution, protected from light. The cells were observed and photographed using an inverted microscope. ImageJ software (version 1.53q, National Institutes of Health, USA) was used for image analysis to assess the proportion of positive cells to the total cell count in each group. The experiment was performed three times.  2.7 Transmission electron microscopy The medium was discarded from the grouped cultured cells, trypsin was added, and the cells were gently blown and centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, electron microscope fixative (Servicebio) was added, and cell pellet was resuspended. After fixation for 30 min at room temperature away from light, the cells were kept at 4°C. Subsequently, the cells were embedded in agar, fixed in osmium acid, dehydrated in ethanol at room temperature gradient for 15 min, impregnated with acetone:812 embedding agent, and subsequently embedded in pure 812 embedding agent. The cells were sectioned with an ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems, Weztlar, Germany), stained, and observed under a transmission electron microscope (HT7800; Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan). The images captured for analysis.  2.8 Statistical analyses Each experiment was repeated three times. GraphPad Prism (version 9.0.0, San Diego, USA) software was used for analyzing the data and creating graphs. Values were summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and intergroup variations were evaluated using one-way analysis of variance (one-way ANOVA) to assess statistical significance. p -values <0.05 were regarded as significant.   3 Results 3.1 T-2 toxin induces HIF-1α expression in SH-SY5Y cells Human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells were maintained in cultures, the morphology of the adherent cells was epithelioid with short extensions, and the cells tended to grow in clusters (Supplementary Figure 1). Initially, to evaluate the cytotoxic effects of T-2 toxin on SH-SY5Y cells, the CCK-8 assay was employed, revealing that T-2 toxin decreases cell viability in a time- and concentration-dependent manner ( Fig. 1 A). To balance inducing measurable toxic effects with retaining survivable cell populations, a T-2 toxin concentration of 6 nM was selected for subsequent experiments. Subsequent assays were aimed at exploring whether exposure to T-2 toxin can increase HIF-1α levels in SH-SY5Y cells. qPCR and western blotting experiments were conducted to analyze the changes in HIF-1α expression levels across a time frame spanning 1–48 h (Fig. 1 B, C). CoCl2 , a chemical agent acknowledged as a hypoxia mimic capable of upregulating HIF-1α levels, was deployed at a 100 μM concentration to act as a positive control in these experiments (Nowak-Stepniowska et al., 2022 ). The HIF-1α expression levels in cells subjected to CoCl2  were markedly and significantly elevated (p <0.01). Intriguingly, the pattern of HIF1A  expression induced by T-2 toxin exposure fluctuated over time (Fig. 1 B). The overall protein expression results were consistent with the trends observed at the gene level—initially rising, subsequently diminishing, before ultimately rising again—with the apex of HIF-1α expression at 6 h (Fig. 1 C). Collectively, these observations substantiate the premise that T-2 toxin can upregulate HIF-1α expression in the human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y.  3.2 T-2 toxin activates the expression of senescence-associated regulators in SH-SY5Y cells To confirm the induction of senescence in SH-SY5Y cells by T-2 toxin, we quantified the expression levels of senescence-associated biomarkers, including proteins such as p16, p21, p53, IL-6, and NF-κB and lncRNAs such as TERC , PINT , and DINO . These biomarkers were measured at various time points using western blotting and qPCR ( Fig. 2 ). Compared to the NC group, the p16 expression was notably decreased upon the administration of T-2 toxin for 1 h. This was followed by a continuous increase from 2 to 12 h, culminating in the highest expression level at 12 h. In contrast, p21 levels rose steadily during T-2 toxin exposure, reaching significant increases of 3.58-fold and 6.94-fold after 24 and 48 h, respectively (both p <0.01). The p53 protein exhibited a marked elevation (p <0.01) between 2 and 12 h of T-2 treatment, with the zenith at 6 h. IL-6 levels were significantly upregulated starting 1 h post-treatment and remained elevated from 12 to 48 h. The apex of IL-6 expression occurred at 24 h with a 1.68 times higher level than that observed in the NC group (p <0.01). For NF-κB expression, an initial significant decrease after 1 h of T-2 toxin treatment was observed, followed by a pronounced upregulation from 2 to 48 h, peaking at 12 h to a level 1.19 times that of the NC group (p <0.01; Fig. 2 A, B). These findings suggest that T-2 toxin catalyzes the activation of pivotal cellular senescence-associated proteins in SH-SY5Y cells, prompting senescence. To further dissect the senescence induction in SH-SY5Y cells attributed to T-2 toxin, we assessed using qPCRs the expression of the lncRNAs TERC , PINT , and DINO —key telomerase components, integrally linked with cellular senescence—at 2, 6, 12, and 24 h after-T-2 toxin exposure. Administration of T-2 toxin resulted in a general downregulation of TERC  and PINT  levels. TERC  expression was decreased at 2 and 6 h relative to that of the NC group, hitting a low of 0.23-fold, and showed an increase at 12–24 h while remaining below the NC group benchmarks. PINT  showed reduced expression levels from 2 to 12 h, with its nadir at 0.47-fold that of the NC group, and an increase at 24 h not surpassing the NC group levels. Strikingly, DINO  levels were consistently upregulated from 2 to 24 h, reaching up to 3.77-fold those of the NC group at baseline (Fig. 2 C). These data signal that T-2 toxin exerts its effect by hindering the synthesis of the telomerase complex and instigating DNA damage within cells.  3.3 T-2 toxin induces senescence of SH-SY5Y cells by inducing cell cycle arrest and stimulating the expression of SA-β-gal Cellular senescence is characterized by a permanent cessation of the cell cycle, heightened activity of SA-β-gal, alterations in cell morphology, and mitochondrial dysfunction—all of which serve as indicators of the senescent state (Gorgoulis et al., 2019 ). This study identified senescent cells using flow cytometry and SA-β-gal staining assays. In addition, we noted the occurrence of ultrastructural damage in SH-SY5Y cells after exposure to T-2 toxin. While senescent cells retain metabolic functions for a limited time, they are insensitive to mitogenic signals, resulting in sustained cell cycle arrest (Di Micco et al., 2021 ). Flow cytometric analysis was employed to examine the cell cycle distribution. Supplementary Figure 2 demonstrates that the proportion of cells in the G1 phase relative to the whole population rose from 64.61% at 6 h after T-2 toxin treatment to 66.01% at 24 h. These findings suggest that the interruption of both pre- and post-DNA synthesis processes increased progressively with the duration of T-2 toxin exposure. SA-β-gal is a glycoside hydrolase, and X-gal can be hydrolyzed by β-gal at pH 6.0 to form a blue-green precipitate that accumulates in cells, serving as a hallmark of senescent cells ( Fig. 3 ). Analyses of SA-β-gal staining showed that the area ratio of SA-β-gal-positive cells in the NC group was 4.30±2.65%, which increased rapidly 2 h after T-2 toxin treatment to 43.69±33.77%, and the area ratios were 18.34±10.81% and 17.39±12.01% after 6 and 24 h, respectively. The administration of the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1 followed by T-2 toxin resulted in area ratios of 17.72±8.37% and 6.10±1.32% after 6 h and 24 h, respectively, whereas the area ratios were 1.07±1.14% for YC-1 administration alone (Fig. 3 ). These results showed a substantial increase in senescent markers in T-2 toxin-treated cells, suggesting that T-2 toxin rapidly upregulated the expression of cellular SA-β-gal in a short period of time, which manifested early senescence. HIF-1α appeared to modulate the expression of this enzyme during extended T-2 toxin exposure. Transmission electron microscopy analyses demonstrated that the morphology of NC SH-SY5Y cells was normal, with clear edges of the cell membrane. Moreover, the mitochondria were structurally intact, uniformly distributed, and numerous. After 24 h of T-2 treatment, the cells were abnormally enlarged and flattened, and the cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio was disproportionately increased. In the YC-1+T-2 toxin-treated group, the nucleus morphology showed irregular contractions. The NC group showed mitochondria with clear double membrane structures and a uniform distribution of mitochondrial cristae. The numbers of mitochondria in the T-2 and YC-1+T-2 groups were significantly decreased compared to that of the control group. Cellular morphology of the T-2 and YC-1+T-2 groups observed under a transmission electron microscope showed that the mitochondria had blurred cell membranes and sparse cristae; some mitochondrial inner membranes were broken with vacuole-like degeneration ( Fig. 4 ). The transmission electron microscopy results suggest that T-2 toxin can evoke the morphological features of substantial cellular senescence and induce senescence of SH-SY5Y cells by damaging mitochondria.  3.4 HIF-1α plays a crucial regulatory role in T-2-induced cellular senescence Having established that T-2 toxin upregulates HIF-1α expression and induces cellular senescence in SH-SY5Y cells, we hypothesized the crosstalk between HIF-1α and T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence. The HIF-1α-specific inhibitor YC-1 was used to confirm the regulatory role of HIF-1α in cellular senescence. Evaluating the levels of the CDKNs p16 and p21 is a way to detect cells in cell cycle arrest, and p53 can arrest cell cycle progression in several ways. After specifically blocking HIF-1α with 10 μM YC-1 before T-2 toxin treatment, the levels of the cell cycle arrest-relevant proteins p16, p21, and p53 were significantly inhibited (p <0.01) at 6 h compared to those of the toxin group ( Fig. 5 ). This suggests that HIF-1α increases the T-2 toxin-induced expression of p16, p21, and p53 to some extent, exacerbating their inhibitory effect on the cell cycle. Activation of SASP is a hallmark of senescence. After inhibiting HIF-1α during T-2 toxin treatment, IL-6 expression was increased relative to that of the toxin group. After the administration of YC-1 alone, IL-6 levels were remarkably elevated compared to those of the NC and toxin groups, suggesting that HIF-1α suppressed the expression of IL-6 to a certain extent. The overall expression trends of IL-8 and CCL2 were similar. Unlike IL-6, IL-8 and CCL2 were significantly downregulated after the addition of YC-1, suggesting that HIF-1α positively regulates IL-8 and CCL2 expression. NF-κB levels after T-2 toxin treatment were significantly increased (1.53-fold, p <0.01) compared to those of the NC group. After co-incubation with T-2 toxin and YC-1, the NF-κB levels did not exhibit as significant changes as observed in p16, p21, and p53 compared to the toxin group, suggesting that the inhibitory effect of HIF-1α on NF-κB was not as obvious as the inhibition of the cell cycle (Fig. 5 ). These results indicate that T-2 toxin-induced senescence occurs in SH-SY5Y cells, with HIF-1α being a pivotal mediator in the regulation of toxin-induced cellular senescence.  3.5 T-2 toxin changes the activation of Tau, p-Tau, and APP—Key proteins of Alzheimer’s disease T-2 toxin is recognized as a potent neurotoxin. Growing evidence suggests a link between mycotoxin metabolites and NDs (Nguyen et al., 2022a ), and an increasing interest exists in uncovering additional associations between T-2 toxin and AD. In this context, we investigated the effects of T-2 toxin on pivotal AD-related proteins—including Tau, phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), and amyloid precursor protein (APP)—and the expression of the lncRNA BACE1-AS , which is highly specific and transcribed in the brains of patients with AD (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Furthermore, our study delved into how HIF-1α modulates the expression of these proteins following T-2 toxin exposure ( Fig. 6 ). After 1 and 2 h of T-2 toxin treatment, p-Tau expression was suppressed, followed by a notable rise at 6–24 h (p <0.01) in comparison to that of the NC group. Tau levels were markedly increased (p <0.01) at 1 h of T-2 toxin treatment, then aligned gradually with those of the NC group at 2 and 6 h, and were significantly decreased (p <0.01) at 12–48 h. After the addition of YC-1 to T-2 toxin, p-Tau expression was markedly reduced relative to that of the toxin group (p <0.01), and Tau expression levels were considerably decreased compared with those of the NC and toxin groups (p <0.01; Fig. 6 A). Given that amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques in the brains of patients with AD predominantly result from APP cleavage by β- and γ-secretases, we also measured APP expression. APP levels were not significantly different from those of the NC group at 1 h; however, they were notably downregulated at 2, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h following T-2 toxin treatment. According to these results, 12 h was chosen as the time point to investigate the influence of HIF-1α on T-2 toxin-triggered APP expression. In line with the results of the time-dependent experiments, APP expression was markedly reduced after 12 h of T-2 toxin treatment. The addition of YC-1 to T-2 toxin treatment markedly reduced the APP levels compared to those of the NC group but markedly upregulated them compared to those of the toxin group (p <0.01). BACE1-AS  was significantly downregulated by T-2 toxin at 12 h (Fig. 6 B). These findings indicate that T-2 toxin may provoke alterations in the expression of crucial AD proteins, hinting at the possible involvement of HIF-1α in the pathogenesis of mycotoxin-induced NDs in humans.   4 Discussion T-2 toxin is associated with various adverse negative health effects, including neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates a potential link between mycotoxin exposure and cellular aging or senescence (Li et al., 2023b ). The effects of mycotoxin exposure, including T-2 toxin, on cell senescence is an area of active research, requiring further investigation to thoroughly comprehend the scope and mechanisms of mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence (Wu et al., 2022 ). In the current study, we investigated the possibility of T-2 toxins inducing cellular senescence, with a focus on the involvement of HIF-1α activation. Mycotoxins can induce hypoxia (Wu et al., 2020; You et al., 2022 ). Mycotoxins inhibits mitochondrial function, resulting in the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which further damages cellular components and impairs oxygen utilization (You et al., 2021 ). The stabilization and activation of HIF-1α under mycotoxin exposure suggest a cellular attempt to adapt to a hypoxic environment. We treated SH-SY5Y cells with CoCl2  to establish an in vitro  hypoxia model as a positive control. Our results showed that SH-SY5Y cells undergo intermittent hypoxia in response to T-2 toxin (Fig. 1 B, C). Similarly, in RAW264.7 cells, deoxynivalenol persistently activated Hif1a , displaying a similar intermittent upregulation (Zhang et al., 2023 ). We further showed that T-2 toxin induces senescence in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 2 ). CDKNs are negative regulators of cell cycle progression; p21 and p16 are known inducers of senescence, and p53 and pRb are critical for establishing cell-cycle arrest; prolonged overexpression of any of these elements is sufficient to induce senescence (Zarneshan et al., 2023 ). In our study, p16, p21, and p53 were activated, peaking at 12, 48, and 6 h after T-2 toxin treatment, respectively. When cells are subjected to DNA damage or other stress stimuli, p53 is usually activated, and its expression is increased compared to that of other proteins (Zhou and Liu, 2022 ). These findings suggest that T-2 toxin-induced cell cycle arrest may proceed through the p53/p21 pathway, and the p16/pRb pathway may also be involved. Nonetheless, the intricate interplay between the upstream and downstream components of the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway, as influenced by T-2 toxin, requires further validation through subsequent research. In our study, we observed a significant increase in NF-κB levels following T-2 toxin treatment. The increase in NF-κB levels suggests that T-2 toxin induces a cellular stress response, likely mediated by oxidative stress, DNA damage, and inflammatory signaling pathways, leading to the activation of NF-κB. lncRNAs play vital roles in diverse physiological and pathological conditions. T-2 toxin treatment inhibited the expression of the lncRNAs TERC  and PINT  but increased lncRNA DINO  expression (Fig. 2 C). The classical function of TERC , a core component of telomerase, is to provide a template for telomerase extension (Mao et al., 2016 ). Insufficient telomerase activity leads to diseases associated with senescence. In the presence of DNA damage, PINT , as a negative regulator of cell cycle arrest, negatively regulates the p53 pathway. DINO  is a p53-dependent gene for DNA damage in response to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Therefore, our findings suggest that T-2 toxin causes a DNA damage response that activates p53 and impairs the telomere balance by inhibiting the synthesis of the lncRNA TERC  telomerase complex, potentially contributing to cellular senescence through telomere shortening. Flow cytometry analysis (Supplementary Figure 2) showed a gradual increase in G1 and G2 phase arrests with T-2 toxin treatment duration. Cells undergoing senescence typically stall in the G0 or G1 phases, reducing proliferation capacity, similar to previous observations in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from amnestic mild cognitive impairment (Salech et al., 2022 ). SA-β-gal expression, a biomarker to detect and quantify cellular senescence, was enhanced after 2 h of T-2 toxin exposure (Fig. 3 ). In our study, we did not conduct a statistical analysis comparing the T-2 toxin and YC-1 co-treatment group with the T-2 toxin alone group to determine any significant effects on cellular SA-β-gal. However, this does not entirely eliminate the potential for differences between the two groups, particularly at the 2-h and 24-h marks. After 24 h of T-2 treatment, cells appeared to be wrinkled compared to cells at 6 h, which corresponded to the transmission electron microscopy results. Apart from cellular flattening and morphological abnormalities, we noted that T-2 toxin treatment resulted in increased cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratios, as well as changes in mitochondrial number and structure, in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 4 ). All these findings suggest that T-2 toxin induces the SH-SY5Y cell senescence. We further focused on the role of HIF-1α in mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence. Current research suggests that hypoxia might have a dual role in cellular senescence, acting both as a physiological regulator of stress-induced senescence and preventing cellular senescence processes (Otero-Albiol and Carnero, 2021; van Vliet et al., 2021 ). Our results showed that HIF-1α positively regulated p16, p21, p53, IL-8, and CCL2, suggesting HIF-1α is involved in the promotion of T-2 toxin-induced SH-SY5Y cell senescence (Fig. 5 ). In addition, inhibition of HIF-1α exacerbated in our study the damage to mitochondrial structures (Fig. 4 ), suggesting a protective effect of HIF-1α on mitochondria. Similarly, prior studies have shown that HIF-1α can attenuate mitochondrial damage by promoting energy metabolism (Zhuonan et al., 2015 ). Moreover, HIF-1α regulates mitochondrial function and reduces the production of reactive oxygen species, providing a protective effect (Li et al., 2019 ). Under hypoxic conditions, HIF-1α stabilizes and translocates to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of genes involved in glycolysis and reduces mitochondrial oxygen consumption by downregulating mitochondrial biogenesis and function (You et al., 2021 ). This shift in metabolic pathways reduces the production of ROS by limiting the electron transport chain's activity, thereby minimizing oxidative stress and potential cellular damage. In addition, we observed that T-2 toxin treatment led to HIF-1α activation and induced cellular senescence. This suggests that the role of HIF-1α in cellular stress response can lead to senescence through specific signaling. Even with normal mitochondrial function, mitochondrial DNA mutations and altered energy metabolism can exacerbate senescence (Atamna et al., 2018 ). Thus, HIF-1α may exhibit different biological effects and depend on the type of stress, cellular environment, and interactions with other pathways. Our findings highlight the dual protective and senescent roles of HIF-1α under specific conditions and stressors. In addition to the relationship between T-2 toxin and cellular senescence, we were also interested in the connection between T-2 toxin and key factors of AD. We showed that T-2 toxin consistently reduced APP expression, whereas HIF-1α negatively regulated APP. BACE1-AS  was downregulated 12 h after T-2 toxin exposure, could be indicative of a cellular response aimed at counteracting the toxic effects of T-2 Toxin. Considering that T-2 toxin induces cellular senescence through the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway, it is conceivable that the down-regulation of BACE1-AS  forms part of a comprehensive adaptive response to oxidative stress and DNA damage, designed to alleviate additional neuronal harm. Related studies demonstrated that BACE1-AS  expression is significantly upregulated in the brains of patients with AD and promotes Aβ production (Zhang et al., 2018 ). A study reported that chronic hypoxia favors NDs in a mouse model of Leigh’s syndrome, that normobaric respiration at 11% O2  protects against neurodegeneration in patients with Leigh’s syndrome, and that hypoxia prevents and even reverses brain damage in mice with late neuropathology (Ferrari et al., 2017 ). Moreover, intermittent hypoxic acclimation of transgenic AD mice protected against anxiety-like behaviors as well as memory and learning impairments, markedly decreased cortical Aβ levels, markedly elevated glucose levels in the cerebral cortex, and significantly improved cognition and recovery of mitochondrial bioenergetic profiles (Correia et al., 2021 ). Our findings suggest a potential additional link between mycotoxin T-2 toxin and NDs (Nguyen et al., 2022b ). Nevertheless, our study using one cell line is not sufficient to generalize pathway activation. Furthermore, although signaling pathways can be triggered in in vitro  cell models, it remains unclear whether they are activated in vivo . Our study has some limitations. Future research should test multiple cell lines or animal models, and additional molecules in autophagy-regulated signaling pathways should be analyzed to further validate and expand the breadth of our findings. In addition to HIF-1α, HIF-1β could also be explored to elucidate the mechanisms of T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence in cellular hypoxic microenvironments. Given that RNA interference exhibits potential immunostimulatory properties, we did not employ the HIF-1α knockdown methodology in our study. Nonetheless, in future studies, we can refine the knockdown experiments to more definitively ascertain the function of HIF-1α within the cellular senescence process.  5 Conclusion Our research elucidated that T-2 toxin induces cell senescence in SH-SY5Y cells by upregulating the expression of cellular senescence-associated factors, such as p16 (peaked 12 h), p21, and IL-6, and by increasing the activity of SA-β-gal (at 2 h), which leads to cell cycle arrest (G1 phase). Notably, HIF-1α is a critical target of T-2 toxin and participates in T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence by affecting the expression of CDKNs (p16, p21, p53) and SASP factors (IL-8, IL-6, CCL2), along with the expression of SA-β-gal. Furthermore, a link between T-2 toxin and NDs may exist, with HIF-1α being a target of T-2 toxin regulating key AD proteins, including Tau, p-Tau, and APP (Supplementary Figure 3). This study offers insights into the field of mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence and further elucidates the information on the interaction between HIF-1α and cellular senescence mechanisms. title: Differential chromatin accessibility response to retinoic acid in neuroblastoma with <ce:italic>ATRX</ce:italic> in-frame-deletions versus <ce:italic>ATRX</ce:italic> loss-of-function
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer, arising in the developing sympathetic nervous system. Differentiation therapy with 13-cis-retinoic acid (RA) is given to children with neuroblastoma to prevent relapse, however there is little understanding of which patients benefit. ATRX alterations are identified in 10 % of high-risk neuroblastomas and associated with poor outcomes. The commonest type of ATRX alterations in neuroblastoma are in-frame multi-exon deletions, followed by nonsense mutations predicted to result in loss-of-function (ATRX LoF). We treated paired ATRX wild-type and LoF neuroblastoma cell-lines with RA: cells with ATRX LoF fail to upregulate direct RA target genes and show reduced chromatin accessibility differentiation and development related genes following RA treatment. Conversely, neuroblastoma models with in-frame deletions mount an appropriate epigenetic response to RA. Taken together this shows that the mechanism of differentiation in ATRX-altered neuroblastoma depends on the type of ATRX alteration, with implications relating to both oncogenesis and therapeutic response.
