Cells from these adrenal tissues were analysed using droplet-based scRNA-seq [Jansky et al., 2021] . The presence of chromaffin cells and neuroblasts inside the analysed adrenal glands was confirmed by immunohistochemical staining for the neuroblast markers and chromaffin cell markers. The cells analysed by the scRNA-seq pipeline were assigned cell identities along the sympathoadrenal lineage using unsupervised clustering and manual annotation using cell type markers (for details, see Jansky et al., 2021 ). This yielded data about the proportions of the cell types that made up the healthy adrenal medulla tissues, at different time points. The time points at which proportions were determined included CD19, CS20, and CD23, which is shortly after the first neural crets-derived cells appear in the adrenal anlage and before maturation of adrenal medullar cells. In addition, samples from human paediatric neuroblastoma patients (n = 498   ) were obtained and analysed with the same pipeline. These patients were divided into different categories of the tumour based on their clinical histories, including: tumours with mesenchymal features, MYCN-amplified, and TERT/ALT amplified. In contrast to the data for healthy paediatric samples, the data for neuroblastoma patients only contains one time point, which results from a biopsy or tissue sample at the time of surgical resection. Like the data for healthy tissue, these data contain the proportion of the cell population that belongs to the different cell types. Importantly, the data of Jansky et al. show that the different neuroblastoma categories can be related to different proportions of cell types, which we will aim to relate to developmental dynamics in the model in the next sections.  2.3 ODE for proportions of cell types The aim of this section is to introduce a way to relate the observed differences in cell type heterogeneity among healthy tissues and the neuroblastoma tumours that span several disease categories to model outputs. To this end, note that the model introduced in Section 2.1  models absolute cell counts, whereas the dataset contains data about the proportions of cells of each type making up the tumour. For that reason, to fit the parameters describing the dynamics of the model in Eqs. (1) –(7)  one must adapt the model so that it accounts for cell type proportions, rather than absolute cell counts. Denoting the proportion of cell type i   in the total population by R i   , where R i  = T i  / N    and N = ∑ i = 1  n  T i    , we find thatd R i   d t   = N ( λ i  T i  + ∑ j = 1  n  k i j   T j  )  − T i  ∑ j = 1  n  λ j  T j   N 2   ,     so that(9) d R i   d t   = λ i  R i  + ∑ j = 1  n  k i j   R j  − R i  ∑ i = 1  n  λ j  R j  .     Therefore, we obtain a nonlinear system of equations where the unknown parameters are the same as those of the original system of ODEs. That is, the parameters to be estimated from the data are the entries of λ    and those of K  . We discuss the fitting of the parameters to experimental data in Section 2.4 .  2.4 MCMC implementation for parameter estimation Having formulated a model for the evolution of the cell type proportions in Eq. (9) , we now aim to calibrate the unknown model parameters to the available data using Bayesian inference. We first note that the interconversion of neuroblasts and cycling neuroblasts in the model as described in Fig. 1  can lead to possible sources of non-identifiability of parameter values, since the effective proliferation rate of the neuroblast population is controlled by the transition rate between neuroblasts and cycling neuroblasts, k 57   , as well as the rate at which cycling neuroblasts proliferate, k 77   . Since the parameter k 57    effectively controls the amount of time that neuroblasts on average spend in the cycling state, and there is no experimental data to inform this, we set this parameter to unity, leaving only the parameter for the proliferation rate of the cycling neuroblasts to be inferred. A detailed derivation showing that fixing k 57  = 1    entails no loss of generality is provided in Appendix E . That leaves the parameters k 11   , k 23   , k 25   , k 34   , k 44   , k 56   , k 77    to be identified from the data. We use Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with a standard Haario-Bardenet adaptive covariance and four chains under the assumption of a Gaussian error implemented in Python with the PINTS package [Clerx et al., 2019] . We assume a Gaussian distribution of the error with a standard deviation of 10  %    in the cell proportions. Using multiple MCMC chains, in this case four, allows one to assess the ability of the algorithm to converge to the region in parameter space with high posterior probability [Clerx et al., 2019] . As a metric of convergence we use the R ^    statistic [Clerx et al., 2019] , which is defined as the ratio of the between- and within-chain variances of the chains [Clerx et al., 2019] . The R ^    statistic summarises mixing and stationarity, with a value of R ^  = 1    showing perfect mixing and stationarity of the chains. We use the reference value of R ^  = 1.05    for four chains [Vehtarh et al., 2021]  and set a maximum number of MCMC iterations to 2 × 10 4    . This MCMC procedure yields a posterior distribution over the model parameters, with marginal and bivariate posterior distributions shown in Appendix A . The marginal posterior means are given in Table 2 . We discuss the interpretation of the posterior distributions in the next section.  2.5 Cell type distribution in healthy adrenal medulla tissues Having obtained a posterior probability distribution over the unknown model parameters, we simulate the model with the posterior means of this distribution. The resulting model simulations are shown in Fig. 2   , which shows the posterior mean together with a posterior predictive plot showing the 95 % confidence interval around the posterior mean. Overall, these model simulations recapitulate key features of cell differentiation in the healthy adrenal medulla. Chiefly, these are the timing and ordering of cell-state transitions, which consist of an early bridge-cell phase, a sharp rise-and-fall in chromaffin and late-chromaffin cells, and the later predominance of late neuroblasts, which are the critical determinants of lineage allocation. Being intentionally minimal and designed to reveal qualitative principles, we expect modest quantitative deviations which might come from the exclusion of some biologically relevant mechanisms. For example, the confidence intervals in Fig. 2  do not capture the full magnitude of the peak in chromaffin cell populations. However, the model convincingly recapitulates a transient bottleneck in chromaffin commitment, which occurs in healthy adrenal medulla development but is altered in neuroblastoma [Jansky et al., 2021] . Moreover, the very small proportion of cycling and bridge type cells in the simulation are key features of the model simulations with the posterior mean. The posterior distributions shown in Appendix A  suggest not all parameters in the model are practically identifiable [Komorowski et al., 2011] . The parameter k 25    has a broad posterior distribution with a maximum close to zero. This parameter, which we recall describes the transition rate between connecting progenitor cells and neuroblasts, is correlated with the death rate of late chromaffin cells, k 44   , and the proliferation rate of cycling neuroblasts, k 77   . These correlations are intuitive, given that these parameters jointly determine the relative abundances of the different cell types. Therefore, the parameter k 25    cannot be confidently determined from the cell type proportion data alone in the absence of data regarding the proliferation of individual cell types. Nevertheless, the posterior predictive check in Fig. 2  shows that the posterior predicted values are distributed tightly around the posterior mean, and form an excellent fit to the experimental data.  2.6 Cell type distribution in different classes of neuroblastoma Knowing that the model in Eq. (9)  can recapitulate the proportions of cell types in healthy adrenal gland tissues, we wonder if the model can be used to shed light on possible developmental dynamics leading to the proportions of cell types observed in neuroblastoma tumours. Jansky et al. [2021]  found that the proportion of cell types in neuroblastoma tumours is characteristic for different classes of neuroblastoma. Now, we want to understand which parameter combinations can lead to the different make-up of neuroblastoma in different conditions. Recalling that the data for these tumours is not time-varying, but only contains a snapshot at the time of biopsy or resection, we make the assumption that these cell proportion data represent steady states of the model in Eq. (9) , i.e., the data satisfy d R i  / d t = 0    for all i  . We motivate this by noting that the average age of diagnosis of neuroblastoma is several months after birth, which is on a much longer time scale than the simulations carried out in the previous section, which considered only the 10 weeks post-CS18. Furthermore, to simplify the parameter set, we also assume that there is no cell death of terminally differentiated cells to set k 44  = 0   , utilising the finding that there is no distinct set of cycling chromaffin cells [Jansky et al., 2021] . Before carrying out computations to infer parameter combinations from steady-state snapshots of the cell proportions in the different neuroblastoma categories, we undertake a study to understand which kinetic parameters (or combinations thereof) can be estimated. In other words, which (combinations of) model parameters are identifiable given a single snapshot value of the steady state. In Appendix F , we show that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the steady states of the cell proportions, R i   , and the eigenpairs of a matrix, A ( k )   . The matrix A ( k )   , which depends on the parameters k i j    , is such that the model in Eq. (8)  can be written as(10) T  ˙  = A ( k )  T .     In Appendix F  we prove that six dimensionless combinations of parameters,k 23  ρ  ,  k 34  ρ  ,  k 56  ρ  ,  k 57  k 77  + ρ   ,  k 25  k 77  + ρ   ,  k 12  ρ + k 23  + k 25    ,        are uniquely determined by the data. Here, ρ : = k 11  − k 12    , is the leading eigenvalue of the matrix A ( k )    (see Appendix F  for additional details). Two degrees of freedom are intrinsically unidentifiable from a snapshot alone. These are a global time-scale multiplier, s > 0   , that rescales every kinetic constant equally, and the ratio δ = k 77  / ( k 11  − k 12  )    , which partitions the net proliferative flux in the neuroblast block between symmetric self-renewal, k 77   , and the coupled asymmetric division, k 57   , bridge-exit, k 25   , and bridge-entry, k 12   , rates. In sum, modulo the two rescalings ( s , δ )    above, the kinetic parameters describing differentiation within the cell population can be appropriately determined by a single steady-state snapshot. To pin down ( s , δ )    one must incorporate at least one additional temporal observable, which is unavailable from the present data set. Now, in order to identify parameter values that give steady states of the model, we take the cell proportion data for each of the neuroblastoma categories by Jansky et al. and substitute them into the right-hand side of Eq. (9) . This yields a nonlinear system of equations that express the parameter values corresponding to each of the neuroblastoma categories in terms of the available data. However, this system cannot be solved algebraically. Instead, the nonlinear system of equations must be solved numerically to find parameter values that result in the observed data being steady states of the model. We solve the system numerically using a modified Powell method implemented in the scipy.optimize  package in Python [Virtanen et al., 2020] . For each of the computational routines, we provide the parameter set of the healthy adrenal medulla as the initial guess for the Powell method. This yielded a set of parameter combinations that, when simulated, converge to cell proportions at steady state that are equal to those in the different neuroblastoma categories (see Fig. 3  ). For transparency, the inferred parameter values are reported in Appendix G . Recall that our identifiability analysis demonstrated that only certain parameter ratios can be uniquely identified from the data. In Table 3  , we report those parameter combinations for each neuroblastoma category and for healthy adrenal medulla tissue. The identifiable parameter ratios listed in Table 3  show that the different neuroblastoma categories can be distinguished by a small subset of mechanisms. Four of the five ratios, corresponding to the transition rates of progenitor to chromaffin cells, chromaffin maturation, neuroblast to intermediate neuroblast and the fraction of dividing neuroblasts, are one to four orders of magnitude smaller in every tumour category than in healthy adrenal-medulla development. Conversely, the fraction of bridge cells that are redirected into the neuroblast lineage, is roughly two orders of magnitude larger in all three tumour categories. Taken together, these ratios point to a disease scenario in which bridge cells are preferentially channelled back into the neuroblast pool while both differentiation along the sympatho-adrenal trajectory and neuroblast division are suppressed, thereby shifting the cellular composition observed in patient samples. Our identifiability analysis showed that most individual rate constants remain non-identifiable, and the snapshot data constrain only the dimensionless ratios listed in Table 3 . At the same time, the inferred parameter sets in Appendix G  contain values for ρ   which cluster tightly across all datasets. This allows us to perform a rough exploratory analysis by assuming that all parameter sets therefore follow a similar global time scaling. We simulated the ODE system in Eq. (9)  with the parameter values in Appendix G . Because no category-specific measurements of the starting composition are available, we adopted the initial condition used for the healthy adrenal medulla, consistent with evidence that bridge, progenitor and chromaffin cells dominate the early developmental landscape in both normal and tumour tissues [Jansky et al., 2021] . We stress that this rescaling is purely exploratory: it roughly anchors the overall time-to-steady-state without implying that the detailed transient trajectories are uniquely determined. Plotting the resulting cell differentiation trajectories on a common axis, Fig. 3  reveals that each of the parameter sets found for the neuroblastoma categories results in ODE solutions that converge to a steady state that matches the experimental data. Moreover, the relative ordering of convergence speeds becomes clear. The mesenchymal-feature parameter set settles most rapidly, whereas the MYCN- and TERT/ALT-amplified sets evolve over a considerably longer time scale. That hierarchy mirrors the later median age-at-diagnosis in tumours harbouring MYCN or TERT/ALT alterations [Körber et al., 2023] , supporting the view that protracted developmental programmes give time for additional genetic lesions to accrue. In the next section we extend the model to incorporate high-risk clinical features and show how perturbing the progenitor programme can further shape malignant phenotypes.   3 Modelling neuroblastoma formation during cell differentiation Having understood that the heterogeneity in cell types found in healthy adrenal tissue, as well as in the different categories of neuroblastoma tumours, can be related to differences in the differentiation dynamics according to the model, we wish to explore how these dynamics might interplay with the development of malignancy in a developing neuroblastoma tumour. Previously, it has been shown that the time taken for neuroblastoma development as well as the resulting heterogeneity play a role in disease outcomes and progression [Körber et al., 2023] . We introduce a phenomenological, population structured model to express population malignancy in Section 3.1 , which we use to explore the evolution of malignant traits in a tumour in Section 3.2 . In Section 4  we use the model to understand the role of developmental dynamics upon disease progression. 3.1 A phenomenological, population structured model for malignant traits During neuroblastoma development, tumour cells randomly acquire a series of mutations before they become malignant [Körber et al., 2023] . The occurrence of such mutations in cells at early times in the development of the tumour leads various malignant traits to be distributed in the tumour population later on. This distribution can be modelled using a phenotypically structured model [Villa et al., 2024] . To start constructing such a phenomenological model, we consider malignant trait acquisition by individual cells by assigning each cell a phenotype, m ∈ [ 0 , 1 ]   , where m = 0    represents a completely benign cell and m = 1    represents a completely malignant cell. Biologically, cells acquire driver mutations stochastically, and can repair damage to DNA. As a result, mathematical models describing the evolution of phenotypic traits of malignant cells are commonly given as stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with a drift, b ∈ R   , which describes a deterministic trajectory leading cells to acquire or lose mutations, and random noise with variance σ > 0    in the Stratonovich sense, which describes the occurrence of random mutations. By simulating the individual behaviours of a population of cells as they divide, acquire, and lose mutations, one can gain insights into the development of malignant properties in the tumour. Since we are interested in understanding the overall behaviour of the tumour rather than properties of individual cells, we relate how the trajectories of individual cells follow a distribution that evolves over time. For each cell type, i  , we define the density, p i  ( m , t )    , which gives the density of cells that have malignancy m   at time t  . Conveniently, for an SDE with drift b   and variance σ  , and where each cell type i   proliferates at rate λ i  ≥ 0   , the evolution of p i    for each cell type i  , is given by a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation [Risken, 1996] ,(11) ∂ p i  ( m , t )   ∂ t    = λ i  p i  ( m , t )  + ∂ ∂ m   ( b ( m )  p i  ( m , t )  )  + ∂ ∂ m   ( σ ( m )  ∂ p i  ( m , t )   ∂ m   )       + ∑ j = 1  n  k i j   p j  ( m , t )  ,        subject to the boundary conditions(12) ∂ m  p i  ( 0 , t )  = ∂ m  p i  ( 1 , t )  = 0 ,     for all t > 0   . Recall that b ( m )    is a drift term corresponding to the rate at which cells become malignant, and σ ( m )    is a diffusion coefficient that represents the (nonlinear) rate at which cells acquire random driver mutations. As in Eq. (8) , λ i    represents the proliferation rate of cell type i  , and k i j     represents the transition rate of cell type i   to cell type j  . The PDE description in Eq. (11)  provides a useful framework to keep track of the distribution of phenotypic traits. However, solving the full Fokker-Planck is associated with high computational cost, as well as difficulty in interpreting the results of the population density. Such issues have prompted previous works in phenotypically structured models to reduce Fokker-Planck PDEs to more tractable systems of ODEs [Villa et al., 2024] . To make progress, and to simplify the following analysis, we further define terms in the model that allow us to reduce the PDE in Eq. (11)  to a system of ODEs that are straightforward to solve numerically. To that end, we observe first that the densities p i    do not define a probability density, because they are not normalised. Rather, as in other works, p i    can be used to express the total number of cells at time t  , which is given by(13) T i  ( t )  = ∫ 0 1  p i  ( m , t )  d m .     Furthermore, we define the functional forms of the drift and mutation rates, b   and σ  , so that they are biologically realistic, and can be used to reduce Eq. (11)  to a system of ODEs. To that end, let(14) b ( m )   = γ ( 1 − m ) ,        (15) σ ( m )   = μ m ( 1 − m ) .        Here, γ   represents the rate at which cells that have acquired a mutation acquire a new mutation, and the functional dependence of b   on m   is chosen to reflect the fact that the number of possible new driver mutations decreases as the number of malignant traits in a cell increases. Likewise, μ   represents the rate at which random mutations are acquired, and the functional dependence on the malignancy is chosen to reflect two key characteristics. On the one hand, cells with few malignant traits have intact cell cycle checkpoints and DNA repair mechanisms, implying σ ( m ) → 0    as m ↓ 0   . On the other hand, cells that have many malignant traits will preserve their malignant traits and will not lose them through repair, implying σ ( m ) → 0    as m ↑ 1   . Having defined the drift and diffusion coefficient, we seek to reduce the PDE in Eq. (11)  to an ODE. We define(16) M i  ( t )  = ∫ 0 1  m p i  ( m , t )  d m .     In Appendix B , we show that M i    is governed by the ODE,(17) d M i   d t   = ( λ i  − γ − 2 μ )  M i  + ( γ + μ )  T i  + ∑ j = 1  n  k i j   M j  .     Moreover, T i    as defined in Eq. (13)  indeed follows Eq. (8) , as can be seen by integrating Eq. (11)  over m   and using the boundary conditions in Eq. (12) . Since T i    and M i    can be thought of as the total number of cells of type i  , and the expected number of cells of type i   that are malignant, the reduction of the phenotypically structured model in Eq. (11)  yields a straightforward system of ODEs that can be used to probe cell population dynamics and how they interface with malignant traits across the population.  3.2 Modelling average malignancy Having established a way to describe the difference between the total number of cells of each cell type, and the total number of cells weighted by their malignant traits in Eq. (17) , we use this framework to express to what extent each of the different cell populations exhibits malignant traits. The reason for doing this is that knowing the extent to which a cell population is comprised of malignant cells is highly informative for treatment outcomes and the potential for post-treatment relapse [Gomez et al., 2022, Schmelz et al., 2021, Zeineldin et al., 2022] . For example, it has been suggested that the cycling population of bridge cells might be a reservoir of potential malignancy [Jansky et al., 2021, Zeineldin et al., 2022] . However, it is difficult assess the extent to which any of the cell populations express malignant traits by only looking at cell numbers, M i    and T i   . To directly analyse the malignant traits in each of the cell populations, we aim to quantify the average malignancy of the cells of a given cell type. To do this, we define the average malignancy as M i  = M i  / T i  ∈ [ 0 , 1 ]    . The benefit of analysing this quantity is that it is independent of cell count and can be compared between cell types with different cell counts. In Appendix C , we derive that(18) d M i   d t   = ( γ + μ )  − ( γ + 2 μ )  M i  + ∑ j = 1  n  R j  R i   k i j   ( M j  − M i  )  .      Note that this equation only depends on the malignancies and relative abundances, R i   , so that this system can be simulated for each of the healthy and neuroblastoma cases found previously, for the simulations in Figs. 2  and 3 , respectively. Using these parameters, and setting γ = μ = 5 × 10 − 2    weeks − 1     , we simulate the system defined by Eq. (18)  coupled with Eq. (9)  for each cell population in each of the different parameter regimes (i.e. for normal development, and for each of the different neuroblastoma categories). For the initial condition of the proportions, we set the same proportions as in Fig. 3 . For the initial mean malignancy, in all simulations, we use M i  = 0    in all cell types other than the bridge population, and M bri  = δ = 0.005    for the initial population of malignant bridge cells. We show the results of these simulations in Fig. 4  . For all conditions we simulate between t = 0    weeks post-CS18 and t = 52    weeks post-CS18. Fig. 4  shows several interesting things. Most strikingly, the average malignancy for all cell types during normal development rapidly diminishes and remains stably close to zero for all cell types. In contrast, for all of the neuroblastoma categories, the average malignancy rises rapidly in the first weeks post-CS18. This results in cell populations with appreciable numbers of cells with malignant traits. The conclusion that developmental dynamics are themselves protective of the accumulation of malignancies is consistent with the main findings of Körber et al., who find that the timing of mutations in neuroblastoma correlates with clinical outcomes: early mutations, i.e., those most likely to occur in a bridge cell population, are associated with worse outcomes [Körber et al., 2023] . In such a model, early mutations drive both abnormal development dynamics as well as initial malignancy, and our findings show that these can create a synergistic effect which allows for the establishment of tumours that are more resistant to treatment and with worse prognosis. While our model does not capture this explicitly, increasing numbers of cells with malignant traits is generally associated with higher risk of metastasis and cancer progression [Zeineldin et al., 2022, Cohn et al., 2009] . Noting that the only difference between the simulations in healthy development and neuroblastoma development in Fig. 4  is the development dynamics, our model findings suggest that not only do healthy developmental dynamics contribute to controlling the proportion of cells with malignant traits within the population, but also that perturbations of these can be associated with the rapid accumulation of malignant traits.   4 Insights into neuroblastoma tumour progression The findings in the previous section revealed that the average malignancy of the cell populations involved in neuroblastoma is strongly influenced by the rates at which cell differentiation occurs. To further understand under which conditions progression of a benign mass into a tumour is predicted by our model, we seek to further reduce the complexity of the system under investigation by analysing the total tumour volume relative to the cell population. Whereas this only gives a proxy for the relative proportion of cells within the population that are malignant, it does provide a means to investigate under which conditions a benign neoplasia can progress into a malignant tumour. This quantity will then be used to investigate which parameters in the model are most strongly associated with the progression of the neuroblastoma tumour, yielding insights into treatment response and relapse. 4.1 Modelling of neuroblastoma tumour volume As a proxy for the share of the total tissue mass that is cancerous, we introduce the quantity V  , which we define as(19) V = ∑ i = 1  n  V i  = ∑ i = 1  n  R i  M i  ,     i.e., it is the weighted tumour burden on the patient. Expressing this quantity using the governing equation for the cell proportions, R i   , Eq. (9) , and that of the average malignancy, M i   , Eq. (18) , we find that(20) d V  d t   = ( γ + μ )  ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  R i  − ( γ + 2 μ )  V + ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  V i  − V ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  R i  ,     subject to V ( 0 )  = V 0    . Note that Eq. (20)  is in the form(21) d f  d t   = a ( t )  − b ( t )  f ( t )  ,     and therefore admits a solution in the form(22) V ( t )  = exp ( ∫ 0 t  − b ( ξ )  d ξ )  ( ∫ 0 t  exp ( ∫ 0 ζ  b ( ξ )  d ξ )  a ( ζ )  d ζ + V 0  )  ,     witha  = ( γ + μ )  ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  R i  + ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  V i  ,    b  = γ + 2 μ − ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  R i  .         As an initial investigation of neuroblastoma tumour progression in the different parameter regimes studied in this paper, we simulate the tumour burden in the case of healthy development dynamics, and in the case of MYCN amplified neuroblastoma, as various of the system parameters are studied. For the healthy development dynamics we again take the posterior means identified in Table 2 , and for the MYCN amplified neuroblastoma we take the parameters given in Table 4 . We then simulate for a varying range of initial conditions: V 0  = 0.05 , 0.01 , 0.001   . We also use different values for the mutation parameters μ , γ   : keeping μ = γ   , we take the values 1 × 10 − 1     , 5 × 10 − 2     , 1 × 10 − 2     , 5 × 10 − 3     , 1 × 10 − 3     , 5 × 10 − 4     , and 1 × 10 − 4    weeks − 1     . The different simulation traces are given in Fig. 5  . The plots in Fig. 5  demonstrate that the tumour burden dynamics as modelled by Eq. (20)  vary greatly between healthy and neuroblastoma conditions, but also within these conditions as the critical parameters μ   and γ   are varied. In the case of healthy development, reminiscent of the malignancy profiles in Fig. 4 , the tumour burden very rapidly shrinks, across all initial conditions and values of μ   and γ  . On the other hand, in the case of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma there are clear differences between the different parameter regimes for γ   and μ  . When γ   and μ   are small enough, the tumour burden remains constant or decreases in a manner similar to that of healthy development, whereas when the parameters are increased, the tumour burden in MYCN amplified neuroblastoma rapidly increases and escapes. The finding that, under normal-like conditions, the modelled tumor burden quickly regresses, whereas under abnormal neuroblastoma developmental conditions the tumor can grow, is echoed by the clinical link between neuroblastoma cell-state composition and treatment outcomes. High-risk and relapsed neuroblastomas are often enriched in primitive, mesenchymal-like cells, which are more therapy resistant [Chen and Wei, 2025] . In fact, relapsed tumors consistently show upregulation of mesenchymal gene signatures, whereas tumors that maintain an adrenergic, more differentiated state are more therapy sensitive [Chen and Wei, 2025] . Put together, our model simulations suggest that whereas healthy development dynamics can provide protection against tumour burden escape across a wide range of initial conditions and rates of mutation, this is no longer the case when these dynamics are altered. For that reason, it is important to ascertain which model parameters have the most influence on tumour burden to understand under which conditions one might expect tumour progression, and relapse after treatment.  4.2 Global parameter sensitivity analysis So far, we have observed that varying the parameters of malignancy progression, μ   and γ  , and those describing cell differentiation, influences whether the tumour will be eliminated or grow. In what follows, we would like to understand which parameters most influence the tumour burden. Given that the parameter space contains nine free parameters, a combinatorial grid search is not feasible to explore the parameter space. Parameter sensitivity analysis is a valuable tool for identifying the parameters to which a model’s output of interest is most sensitive. One widely used and effective method for global parameter sensitivity analysis is the calculation of Sobol indices, which quantify the contributions to the variance of a scalar model output from different model parameters [Sobol, 2001] . In this section, we will use Sobol indices to establish the key model parameters influencing total tumour burden. To calculate the Sobol indices, we first define bounds for the model parameters and then sample using a quasi-random sequence as detailed in Homma and Saltelli [1996] , Sobol [2001]  to generate multiple parameter sets within these bounds. The parameters included in this sensitivity analysis are the same as those listed in Table 2 , along with mutation parameters μ   and γ  . For each parameter set, the tumour volume at week 52 was computed using Eq. (20) . First and total order Sobol indices were then calculated using the Salib  package [Herman and Usher, 2017] , and the results are shown in Fig. 6  . The sensitivity analysis reveals that the parameters with the greatest influence on tumour burden at week 52 are the growth rate of the bridge cell population, k 11   , as well as the mutation parameters μ   and γ  . This is in agreement with the idea that the bridge population is a reservoir for malignancy, and that its continued expansion after a normal development window might drive the development of neuroblastoma.  4.3 Conditions for spontaneous regression Having identified that the mutation rates, μ   and γ  , and the bridge cell proliferation rate, k 11   , are the three key parameters that most influence tumour burden at week 52, we can further explore the role of these three parameters in tumour escape or regression. As observed in Fig. 5 , μ  , γ  , and k 11    all play a role in tumour burden, and this role differs between the normal development and MYCN amplified neuroblastoma. Therefore, we take each of the neuroblastoma parameter sets corresponding to normal development, MYCN amplified, TERT/ALT amplified, and neuroblastoma with mesenchymal features, fix all parameters other than μ  , γ  , and k 11   , and vary these three critical parameters along the parameter space to compute the week 52 tumour burden. This yields the heat maps in Fig. 7  . As expected, changes in k 11   , μ   or γ   do not result in a significant tumour burden in the normal development scenario. However, for the three tumour types, the overall tumour burden increases with the bridge cell proliferation rate k 11   . When k 11  = 10 − 3     , no combination of γ   or μ   result in a substantial tumour burden. As k 11    increases, distinct regions emerge in the ( γ , μ )    plane that correspond to either tumour escape or control, with these regions becoming most pronounced when k 11  = 10 − 1     . Specifically, a high tumour burden occurs when either γ   (the rate at which cells that have acquired a mutation acquire new mutation), or μ  , the rate at which random mutations are acquired, is elevated. However, a larger tumour burden is observed when γ   is large. Alternatively. both the values of γ   and μ   need to remain low (≈ ≤ 10 − 2     ) to achieve minimal tumour burden. Put together, necessary conditions for tumour escape are a sufficiently large value of the bridge cell population proliferation rate, k 11   , and a large value of γ   and/or μ  . Alternatively, necessary conditions for tumour regression are a sufficiently small value of k 11    and small values for both mutation parameters μ   and γ  . Interestingly, the regions of parameter space that result in either tumour escape or regression are similar between different tumour types but different from the normal development dynamics, again lending credence to the idea that normal development dynamics only lead to transient populations that can result in harmful tumour development if allowed to expand.  4.4 Treatment relapse A major challenge in the treatment of neuroblastoma is the risk of relapse after surgical resection, which is believed to be related to tumour population heterogeneity [Cohn et al., 2009, Maris, 2010, Zeineldin et al., 2022, Gomez et al., 2022, Brodeur and Bagatell, 2014] . The reappearance of the tumour is believed to arise from the fact that during surgical resection not all malignant cells are removed, and that they can repopulate the original tumour site. In the previous section, we learnt that while normal development dynamics prevent tumour escape, the clinically abnormal development dynamics associated with various forms of neuroblastoma permit tumour escape when the mutation rates μ   and γ   are located in a given region of the parameter space. In this section, we extend the question to whether development dynamics might have an impact on tumour reappearance after surgical resection of the tumour. To answer this question, we simulated the tumour burden for the three different tumour types defined by the parameters in Table 2  until week 52, then reduced the tumour burden by 99 % by reducing each cell population to 1 % of its size, to mimic surgical resection assuming that the tumour population is spatially mixed. We then continued simulating tumour growth for another 52 weeks to identify the conditions under which relapse occurs. Fig. 8   displays the tumour burden at week 52 before treatment and at week 104 after treatment respectively. In Fig. 8 , we observe that prior to treatment, the mesenchymal features tumour type has the largest tumour burden compared to the other types, for sufficiently large γ   and μ  , consistent with the predictions from the previous section. Post-treatment, the MYCN amplification and TERT/ALT amplification tumour types respond well to surgical resection, showing no resurgence in tumour burden for any combination of γ   and μ  . However, the mesenchymal features tumour type shows potential for relapse for large γ   and/or μ  . To further tease apart the possible dynamics of treatment relapse in the mesenchymal type neuroblastoma, we compute the tumour burden trajectories across the three neuroblastoma types using different parameter combinations. We show the traces in Fig. 9  . To interrogate to what extent these results depend on the proportion of the tumour removed by resection, we include results corresponding to 95 % and 90 % resection in Appendix D . These new traces show identical qualitative behaviour to the case of 99 % resection shown in Fig. 8 . The traces in Fig. 9  underscore the potential for relapse in the mesenchymal features tumour type, as tumour volume increases over time when γ   and/or μ   are sufficiently large, while this does not occur in the other tumour types. This can be related to the fact that the mesenchymal type neuroblastoma tumour contains the largest share of bridge cells out of the different types of tumour (recall the simulations in Fig. 4 ). Hence, surgical resection in this tumour type leads to the retention of the largest share of proliferative cells that can develop maligancy, and thus is likeliest to relapse after surgical resection. Additional traces are shown in Appendix D  where more of the tumour is left after resection. Unsurprisingly, with a larger tumour burden post treatment, the tumour burden grows larger for all tumour types. Put together, we have found that this model predicts not just that abnormal differentiation dynamics increase the potential of developing sympathoadrenal tissues to form a tumour, but also that treatment outcomes can be different, depending on the differentiation dynamics within the tumour.   5 Discussion In this work, we have introduced a modelling framework to describe the dynamics of cell differentiation, proliferation, and death in the sympathoadrenal lineage during early embryonic development. The sympathoadrenal lineage contributes to many structures in the embryo, such as the adrenal medulla, and contains the precursor population for neuroblastoma, the most common paediatric extracranial solid cancer. By carefully calibrating our model to clinical data, we found that it can accurately recapitulate the main trends in the dynamic transients of cell type proportions in the adrenal medulla of healthy patients and those in different categories of neuroblastoma tumours. The calibrated model parameters suggest that key parameters, such as the proliferation rate of immature progenitor cells – as opposed to that of mature cycling neuroblasts – and the rate of cell differentiation from a progenitor state to a chromaffin cell state, can explain the vastly different cell type proportions in the different patient categories. These findings contribute to existing efforts in the field to suggest the cell type transitions that are most associated with neuroblastoma development [Gomez et al., 2022, Zeineldin et al., 2022] , and can be used as a starting point to understand the genetic programmes and extra-cellular environmental cues responsible for driving abnormal differentiation dynamics leading to neoplasia and eventually neuroblastoma. To relate abnormal differentiation dynamics during sympathetic nervous system development to cancer, we introduced a phenomenological and phenotypically structured model to describe how malignant traits accumulate in the developing cell population. Taking a moments-based approach, we derived a model to describe the average malignancy within each of the constituent cell populations, and used this to describe the evolution of malignant traits in the population during sympathoadrenal development. Strikingly, we found that, regardless of the speed at which cells with malignant traits acquire subsequent traits, or the rate at which cells randomly lose and acquire malignant traits, healthy differentiation dynamics led to control of malignant traits. On the other hand, each of the cell differentiation programmes that was calibrated for the neuroblastoma categories led to an increase of malignant traits, and in some parameter regimes, to tumour progression. Finally, the model proposed in this paper predicts not just that abnormal differentiation dynamics increase the potential of developing sympathoadrenal tissues to form a tumour, but also that treatment outcomes can be different, depending on the differentiation dynamics within the tumour. The findings arising from this model complement existing theories that the bridge cell population is a potential reservoir for malignant cells [Jansky et al., 2021] , and confirm the potential for possible treatments in inducing cell differentiation, such as retinoic acic (RA) in conjunction with other therapies for neuroblastoma [Matthay et al., 1999, Körber et al., 2023, Zeineldin et al., 2022] . Being a simplified representation of sympathetic nervous system development, our model can be further analysed and extended in several ways. First, one of the key complications arising from neuroblastoma is the potential of the tumour to form metastases [Cohn et al., 2009, Maris, 2010, Zeineldin et al., 2022, Gomez et al., 2022] . While not captured in our model, the ability of the tumour to establish metastases greatly increases the risk of mortality due to neuroblastoma. For this reason, our model can be used as a starting point for modelling efforts aimed to describe the process of neuroblastoma metastasis, or that of a developmental cancer, more generally. This can be done in several ways, although the most immediate extension of this work would be to include a spatial component describing the extra-tumoural environment. This would entail partial differential equation (PDE) models that can carefully recapitulate the ability of each cell type to proliferate, differentiate, and invade the extracellular space. By including further clinically relevant features, such as sources of potential chemoattractants, and angiogenesis, such a model can provide key insights into the cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic factors driving neuroblastoma development and progression. Furthermore, a central theme in current clinical neuroblastoma research is the ample availability of genetic sequencing data of primary neuroblastoma tumours [Jansky et al., 2021, Gomez et al., 2022, Zeineldin et al., 2022] . With the advent of spatial transcriptomics, one might use various thin tissue slices to reconstruct a three-dimensional distribution of cell types. Further, one of the novelties of calibrating our model to clinical data of neuroblastoma tumours was that, in the absence of time-resolved data, we identified steady states of the model that could be related to the cell type proportions found in neuroblastoma tumours. Having time-resolved patient data would increase the ability to calibrate existing models from data, and potentially learn new models from data [Martina-Perez et al., 2021] . However, practically speaking, these data are often lacking since patient biopsies are not often performed during the course of treatment. Rather, emerging three-dimensional human neuroblastoma patient-derived organoid models may offer a means to obtain time-resolved genomic data. Doing so would contribute to our understanding of the nature of cell type conversions in neuroblastoma, which, despite advances in scRNA sequencing, remain elusive in the context of treatment [Zeineldin et al., 2022] . Time-resolved patient data could also be used to draw closer connections between mathematical modelling and its use in clinical practice and individualised medicine. For example, if one could link patient characteristics, such as genetic signatures, age of diagnosis, and anatomical location of the tumour to model parameters, modelling approaches could aid as a prognostic tool in individual cancer therapy. Such progress will necessitate not only vast amounts of time-resolved patient data, but also careful model calibration and uncertainty quantification. title: Picropodophyllotoxin alters EMT in neuroblastoma via inhibition of surface receptors IGF1R and ALK
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is a type of paediatric cancer that originates from embryonic sympathoadrenal cells. Despite its paediatric origin, NB is mostly treated with strategy of non-small cell lung cancer like adults due to lack of specific therapeutic approach. To improve treatment outcome for NB patients, developing drugs that specifically target the genetic mutations or molecular pathways involved in neuroblastoma is necessary. Overexpression of the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) has been linked to various malignancies, including paediatric cancers. We hypothesized that inhibiting IGF1R with ALK (NB specific mutation) by phytochemical compound could effectively treat NB while avoiding undesirable cytotoxic effects. We evaluated the efficacy of Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) as IGF1R inhibitor, for treatment of NB. The IC50 value of PPP on SH-SY5Y, NB cells after 24 h of treatment was found to be 0.501 μM. Molecular docking studies revealed that PPP had a binding score of −7.5 kcal/mol with IGF1R and − 8.8 kcal/mol with ALK. This suggests that PPP not only binds to and inhibits IGF1R but also has a strong affinity for ALK. Gene expression studies, densitometric analysis, scratch assays, and AO/EtBr differential staining were used to evaluate the efficacy of PPP in NB cells. Transcript expression and densitometric analysis revealed that PPP could downregulate IGF1R and ALK in NB cells. Downregulation of SNAIL, a mesenchymal marker, and upregulation of E-cadherin, an epithelial marker, indicated a mesenchymal to epithelial transition in NB cells, suggesting that PPP treatment inhibited NB cell migration and proliferation. This was further supported by scratch assay results in our study. Furthermore, gene expression analysis of p53, BAX and BCL2 indicated that PPP induces apoptosis in NB cells. AO/EtBr differential staining revealed apoptotic phenomena in NB cells after 24 h of PPP treatment. Although further research is needed to explore the receptor targeting approach using PPP for IGF1R and ALK inhibition.

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a type of paediatric cancer that originates from embryonic sympathoadrenal cells. Despite its paediatric origin, NB is mostly treated with strategy of non-small cell lung cancer like adults due to lack of specific therapeutic approach. To improve treatment outcome for NB patients, developing drugs that specifically target the genetic mutations or molecular pathways involved in neuroblastoma is necessary. Overexpression of the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) has been linked to various malignancies, including paediatric cancers. We hypothesized that inhibiting IGF1R with ALK (NB specific mutation) by phytochemical compound could effectively treat NB while avoiding undesirable cytotoxic effects. We evaluated the efficacy of Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) as IGF1R inhibitor, for treatment of NB. The IC50  value of PPP on SH-SY5Y, NB cells after 24 h of treatment was found to be 0.501 μM. Molecular docking studies revealed that PPP had a binding score of −7.5 kcal/mol with IGF1R and − 8.8 kcal/mol with ALK. This suggests that PPP not only binds to and inhibits IGF1R but also has a strong affinity for ALK. Gene expression studies, densitometric analysis, scratch assays, and AO/EtBr differential staining were used to evaluate the efficacy of PPP in NB cells. Transcript expression and densitometric analysis revealed that PPP could downregulate IGF1R and ALK in NB cells. Downregulation of SNAIL , a mesenchymal marker, and upregulation of E-cadherin , an epithelial marker, indicated a mesenchymal to epithelial transition in NB cells, suggesting that PPP treatment inhibited NB cell migration and proliferation. This was further supported by scratch assay results in our study. Furthermore, gene expression analysis of p53 , BAX  and BCL2  indicated that PPP induces apoptosis in NB cells. AO/EtBr differential staining revealed apoptotic phenomena in NB cells after 24 h of PPP treatment. Although further research is needed to explore the receptor targeting approach using PPP for IGF1R and ALK inhibition. It accounts for 8–10 % of occurrence of malignant tumors in children [1 ]. The overall survival of children with high-risk NB is around 40–50 % despite the aggressive treatment protocols consisting of intensive chemotherapy, surgery, radiation therapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [2 ]. One of the most common phenomena associated with different cancers is sustained signaling by growth factors. During development, growth factors regulate cellular differentiation and division in a controlled manner to maintain cellular physiology, however, its uncontrolled signaling leads to cancer metastasis. The ligand-receptor interaction of Insulin-like growth factor (IFG) with Insulin-like growth factor 1 Receptor (IGF1R) plays a pivotal role in regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis [3 ,4 ]. Multiple studies have characterized the pro-oncogenic role of IGF1R in NB cells and tumor models [5–9 ]. Furthermore, overexpression of ALK gene and protein, another tyrosine kinase receptor has been firmly established over the last two decades in certain subsets of neuroblastoma [10–15 ]. Considering the complex nature of the cancer disease, its treatment has been a continuous hassle with relatively little success. In NB patients, the response to current standard treatments is highly heterogeneous, varying from total regression to the development of multi-drug resistance and severe toxicities [16 ]. A promising approach for the development of treatment strategies for neuroblastoma could involve the inhibition of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases and the signaling networks that they are connected to. Currently available specific IGF1R tyrosine kinase inhibitor and ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors are associated with adverse events which impairs patient's quality of life [17–19 ]. Better treatment options may be developed without the related negative effects of chemotherapy if both of these tyrosine kinases were inhibited by a single phytochemical medication. Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP), derived from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum , is a phytochemical tyrosine kinase inhibitor reported to inhibit IGF1R in different cancers such as hepatoma, non-small cell lung cancer rhabdomyosarcoma [20 ,21 ]. As IGF1R and ALK both are receptor tyrosine kinase, we predicted that PPP could be able to inhibit both of this receptor tyrosine kinases. We aimed to evaluate, if PPP possessed dual inhibitory nature on IGF1R and ALK in SH-SY5Y NB cells.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Compound Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) (5R,5aR,8aS,9R)-5-hydroxy-9-(3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl)-5a,6,8a,9-tetrahydro-5H-[2]benzofuro[5,6 f][1,3]benzodioxol-8-one, a known IGF1R inhibitor, with a molecular weight of 414.41 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (T9576).  2.2 Cell line SH-SY5Y, neuroblastoma cell line was obtained from NCCS, Pune. Cells were cultured in MEM media with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1× antibiotics (penicillin-streptomycin; Gibco, 15,140,122) in 5 % CO2  at 37 °C. (The known characteristic feature of SH-SY5Y cells is that the plasma membrane is strongly enriched for ALKWT  whereas both ALKWT  and ALKF1174L  are present in intracellular compartments) [22 ].  2.3 Molecular docking The binding affinity of PPP was checked with tyrosine kinase receptors: ALK and IGF1R. The 3D structure of Picropodophyllotoxin was obtained from PubChem (PubChem Id: 72435) in SDF format to analyses the binding affinity of PPP with ALK (PDB Id: 5FTO ) and IGF1R (PDB Id: 5FXQ ). Ligand in SDF format was retrieved into the workspace of AutoDock tools 1.5.7. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina 1.5.7. For 2D visualization of the docked file, BIOVIA Discovery Study Visualizer 2021 was used. For 3D visualization of the docked file, PyMOL 2.5 software was used.  2.4 Evaluation of cytotoxicity SH-SY5Y cells were seeded into 96-well plates at the density of 5 × 104  cells. Cells were treated with various concentrations of PPP (0.89, 0.68, 0.48, 0.20, and 0.068 μM) and incubated for 24 h to measure the cytotoxicity. After exposure to PPP, MTT treatment was given for 4 h. Formazan crystals were dissolved using 200μL of DMSO and the intensity of color was measured at 570 nm (nm) using a microplate reader (InfiniteM200pro, Nanoquant Multimode reader, Tecan).  2.5 Gene expression analysis Cells were exposed to PPP for 24 h and used for RNA isolation. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15,596,018). After assuring the quality and quantity of RNA, it was used for cDNA synthesis (Bio-Rad iScript cDNA, 1,708,891). qPCR was performed with triplicate assays using the SYBR Green mix (Bio-Rad iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix, 1,725,121). Primers for IGF1R, PI3KCB, AKT, BAX, BCL2, CDH1, SNAIL, NANOG, TWIST, TUBULIN, CDK8, p53, ALK, MYCN, NFKB and GAPDH  were designed using the Primer-BLAST tool NCBI. GAPDH  was used as an internal control. Data analysis was done by CT value and fold change expression was calculated by the 2-ΔΔC T  method.  2.6 Western blot analysis After 24 h of PPP treatment to SH-SY5Y, cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89,900). The protein concentration was estimated by Pierce BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23,227). After SDS-PAGE, protein was transferred onto PVDF membrane (Bio-Rad, 1,620,177). Blocking was performed with 5 % BSA (HiMedia, MB083) in TBS for 1 h followed by overnight incubation with primary antibody at 4 °C. The blot was washed thrice with TBS-T buffer and incubated with HRP conjugated Goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Invitrogen, 656,120) in bocking buffer (1:1000 dilution) for 2 h. The intensity of the bands was observed in iBright CL100 Chemidoc (Thermo Fischer) and densitometric analysis was carried out using ImageJ software.  2.7 Immunocytochemistry Cells were incubated on Poly-d -lysine (Gibco, 1108) coated coverslip in 6 well plate. After PPP treatment for 24 h, the cells were washed with cold PBS and permeabilized with 1 % Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min. Blocking was performed for 2 h in buffer containing 2 % BSA (HiMedia, MB083) in PBS with 0.1 % Tween-20 (HiMedia, MB067). Cells were washed in chilled PBS and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. After primary antibody incubation, cells were washed with PBS and incubated with secondary antibody (Alexa Fluor 488 antibody, Invitrogen, A32731) for 1 h at room temperature in dark. Cells were observed under confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM 710 Confocal Microscope). Captured images were analyzed by ImageJ software.  2.8 Scratch healing assay The monolayer of SH-SY5Y cells was wounded with 100 μL pipette tip. Cells were incubated for 24 h with PPP. The migrated distance of cells was measured and three randomly chosen fields were analyzed for each well to observe the anti-migratory and anti-proliferative potency of PPP.  2.9 Cell death analysis (morphological analysis) SH-SY5Y cells were treated with PPP at 50 % confluency for 24 h. Cells were fixed in methanol and stained with Acridine orange (AO) (HiMedia, TC262) and Ethidium bromide (EtBr) (HiMedia, MB071) stain (a mixture containing 100 μg/mL AO and 50 μg/mL EtBr) for 10 min at room temperature in dark. Cell morphology was examined under a fluorescent microscope (Zeiss Axio Observer A1 Fluorescence Inverted Microscope).  2.10 Statistical analysis All data is expressed as Mean ± SEM. Data was analyzed on GraphPad prism software using student's t -test. Statistical significance was set at p  < 0.05. * denotes p  ≤ 0.05, ** denotes p  ≤ 0.01, *** denotes p  ≤ 0.001 and **** denotes p  ≤ 0.0001.   3 Results 3.1 Molecular docking of PPP to IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases PPP is a phytochemical that is known to inhibit IGF IR, a receptor tyrosine kinase by binding to the ATP binding domain and reducing its phosphorylation. We had hypothesized that PPP could be able to inhibit ALK too, as it is a receptor tyrosine kinase and PPP is an ATP binding competitor. In order to evaluate our speculation, molecular docking was performed. Docking score/binding affinity of PPP with IGF1R is −7.5 kcal/mol, while the docking score/binding affinity of PPP with ALK is 8.8 kcal/mol (Fig. 1  ). Docking score of ALK when compared with IGF1R suggest that PPP could be a potent inhibitor of ALK as well.  3.2 Cytotoxic potential of PPP We assessed the cytotoxicity of PPP in neuroblastoma cell line upon exposure for 24 h by MTT assay. Our documented IC50  of PPP in SH-SY5Y cells is 0.501 μM (Fig. 2  ). Investigators have previously found the IC50  value of PPP in other IGF1R-positive tumor cells in the range of 0.05 μM – 0.5 μM (Menu et al., 2006; Tarnowski et al., 2017). Our results are in accordance with the findings of previously mentioned investigators. However, MTT assay serves as an indirect measurement of the cell viability, and not a specific test for apoptosis. For further experiments, a dose of 16 nM PPP was used, which upon morphological examination under microscope revealed that it induces only apoptosis while avoiding necrosis in the cells.  3.3 PPP as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK To evaluate our docking results, gene expression analysis and, post-translational analysis by western blotting was performed. Expression of IGF1R  gene was downregulated upon PPP treatment (p  ≤ 0.0001), which is also supported by the decreased expression of IGF1R protein in the densitometric analysis of blots (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 3  ). Immunocytochemistry was performed to further validate the IGF1R expression (Fig. 4  ). Image analysis revealed a significant downregulation in IGF1R expression (p  ≤ 0.001) in NB cells upon PPP treatment. Interaction of IGF1 and IGF1R results in autophosphorylation of IGF1R at specific tyrosine residues, which stimulates further downstream signaling [23 ]. We assessed, if PPP inhibited autophosphorylation of IGF1R. The protein expression level of phosphorylated IGF1R was significantly lower than that of the non-treated NB cells (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, downregulation of ALK was observed at translational (p  ≤ 0.01) and post-translational levels (p  ≤ 0.001) (Fig. 3 ). Downregulation of ALK was further evaluated through immunocytochemistry (Fig. 4 ). Image analysis revealed significant downregulation of ALK (p  ≤ 0.0001), which further supports the gene expression and densitometric analysis. Gene expression and post-translational results strongly suggest that PPP effectively inhibits IGF1R and ALK in NB cells, acting as a dual inhibitor.  3.4 PPP alters downstream signal cascade activated by IGF1R and ALK IGF1R and ALK autophosphorylation can result in activation of multiple downstream signaling cascades, one of the prominent being PI3K/AKT [24 ,25 ]. To evaluate if inhibition of IGF1R and ALK by PPP results in diminished expression of these downstream kinases, gene expression analysis of PI3K  and AKT  was carried out, which revealed their significant downregulation (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 A ). CDK is another kinase involved in cell cycle regulation [26 ]. Uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation occurs as a result of abnormal CDK activation. Hyperactive PI3K/AKT pathway could increase CDK expression via activation of Cyclin D1 [27 ,28 ]. CDK8 is a member of the CDK family, serving crucial role in cell cycle regulation and it has been identified as a key oncogenic driver in many cancers [29 ,30 ]. It could thus be speculated that perturbed PI3K/AKT pathway leads to diminished expression of CDK8. Downregulated expression of CDK8  gene (p  ≤ 0.0001) validates our speculation (Fig. 5 A). Furthermore, PI3K/AKT signaling enhances cell survival via NF-κB and MYCN [25 ,31 ]. Gene expression analysis implies suppression of MYCN  and NF-κB  gene was observed upon PPP treatment (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 B). Additionally, immunocytochemical localisation of NF-κB was performed which indicated its significant downregulation (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 C). Diminished MYCN  and NF-κB expression further supports the speculation of PI3K/AKT inhibition.  3.5 PPP inhibits migration of SH-SY5Y NB cells One of the fundamental abnormalities of neoplastic cell is its unregulated migration. Cancer cells lose their migratory ability upon perturbation of migratory and proliferative signals via mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET). The role of insulin-like growth factors as potent chemotactic agents stimulating cancer migration is evident from the literature [32 ,33 ]. Increasing number of studies report the involvement of IGF1R signaling in EMT mediated tumor metastasis and drug resistance [34 ]. We thus assessed, whether PPP induced IGF1R inhibition could impair cancer cell migration. Gene expression analysis in PPP treated SH-SY5Y cells, when compared to control cells showed downregulation of TUBULIN , SNAIL , TWIST  and NANOG  mesenchymal markers (p  ≤ 0.0001). While upregulation of E-cadherin (CDH1)  epithelial marker was observed (p  ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 6  ). These data implies that PPP induced IGF1R inhibition via Mesenchymal to Epithelial transition could impede metastatic ability of the NB cell. Furthermore, the in vivo ability of cancer cells to migrate in an uncontrolled manner is mimicked by their in vitro behavior. Scratch assay was performed on SH-SY5Y cells to validate the anti-migratory ability of PPP. We observed that after 24 h of exposure, PPP was indeed able to attenuate cell migration in NB cells (Fig. 7  ). The observed wound enclosure of NB cells in control condition was measured to be 1.45 mm, whereas upon PPP exposure it was measured to be 1.88 mm. PPP treatment was thus able to hamper the characteristic uncontrolled growth and migratory feature of SH-SY5Y cells to a certain degree.  3.6 PPP alters morphology and induces apoptosis in SH-SY5Y NB cells IGF1R is known to impart anti-apoptotic properties in different types of cells [35 ]. Furthermore, studies have reported that cancer cells undergo regression upon IGF1R inhibition [36 ,37 ]. Therefore, we investigated if PPP mediated inhibition of IGF1R is able to induce apoptosis in NB cells as well. Low level expression of p53 is a phenomenon common to cancer cells, enabling them to proliferate in an uncontrolled manner. We thus postulated that upon inhibition of mitogenic IGF1R signaling through PPP, p53 expression in NB cancer cells may increase, ultimately driving the neoplastic cells towards programmed cell death. Gene expression analysis of p53  found increase expression of its transcript by 5.625 ± 0.16 fold (p  ≤ 0.0001). In addition to the p53  gene, BAX  and BCL2  genes play a significant role in regulating apoptosis. Gene expression analysis of transcripts of BAX, pro-apoptotic marker and BCL2, anti-apoptotic marker revealed a significant upregulation of BAX  (p  ≤ 0.0001) and a significant downregulation of BCL2  (p  ≤ 0.0001) in the PPP treated SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 8 A ). Cell viability and apoptosis were further evaluated in SH-SY5Y cells via AO/EtBr differential staining (Fig. 8 B, C). Acridine orange stains viable cells which gives green fluorescence, but with early apoptotic cells it gives yellow fluorescence whereas with late apoptotic cells along with ethidium bromide its gives orange fluorescence. EtBr is only taken up by necrotic cells and it gives red fluorescence. Nuclear condensation and cell shrinkage are the characteristic features of apoptotic cells that was observed due to PPP treatment. We observed a greater number of cells in the apoptotic phase on treatment of IGF1R inhibitor. These results along with p53 , BAX  upregulation and BCL2  downregulation implies that PPP could inhibit growth and induce apoptosis in NB tumor cells.   4 Discussion Neuroblastoma, a highly aggressive childhood cancer, poses significant challenges due to its resistance to conventional chemotherapeutic approaches and limited success with surgical interventions. The current treatment options for neuroblastoma have yielded low cure rates, underscoring the urgent need for the development of more targeted and effective therapeutic strategies [38 ]. Altered expression of IGF1R and ALK resulting in oncogenic signaling which drives the Neuroblastoma has been very well established over last couple of decades [8–10 ,12 ]. Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP), an epimer of podophyllotoxin, derived from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum  is known to act as an inhibitor of IGF1R tyrosine kinase [39 ,40 ]. Furthermore, PPP has exhibited notable anti-tumor activity in ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL) cancer [41 ]. This study aims to demonstrate the potential of the phytochemical PPP as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma (NB) cells. Molecular docking analysis indicated favourable binding affinities of PPP to both IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases, suggesting its ability to competitively inhibit their ATP binding domains. Indeed, the findings of molecular docking analysis indicate the potential of the phytochemical PPP, as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases. To evaluate the cytotoxic potential of PPP, the MTT assay was performed in the SH-SY5Y NB cells. The obtained IC50  value of 0.501 μM is consistent with previous reports of PPP's efficacy against IGF1R-positive tumor cells [42 ,43 ]. As our docking results implied that PPP could be an inhibitor of ALK along with IGF1R, we validated this speculation by gene expression analysis, western blotting, and immunocytochemistry. The expression of IGF1R gene and protein was significantly downregulated upon PPP treatment, indicating effective inhibition at both transcriptional and translational levels. The inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation further confirmed the disruptive effect of PPP on IGF1R signaling in NB cells. Inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation by PPP has previously been also reported in 5 T33 multiple myeloma cells [42 ]. Similar downregulation was observed for ALK, supporting the speculation that PPP acts as a dual inhibitor of both tyrosine kinases. To gain insights into the molecular mechanism of PPP treatment, we investigated the downstream signaling cascades activated by IGF1R and ALK, including the PI3K/AKT pathway [24 ,25 ]. Through gene expression analysis, a significant downregulation of PI3K and AKT was observed, indicating the inhibition of this pro-survival pathway. The findings were further supported by the downregulation of CDK8, a critical regulator of cell cycle progression [44 ], confirming the disruption of cancer cell proliferation by PPP. Moreover, we observed the suppression of MYCN and NF-κB genes, both known to play pivotal roles in promoting cell survival [45 ,46 ]. These results highlight the potential of PPP to target multiple signaling pathways simultaneously, further emphasizing its promising therapeutic implications. Uncontrolled migration is a hallmark of cancer, and IGF1R and ALK signaling has been implicated in tumor metastasis [24 ,47 ]. We investigated the effect of PPP on the migratory ability of NB cells using gene expression analysis and scratch assay. Our findings revealed that treatment with PPP resulted in a significant downregulation of key mesenchymal markers including TUBULIN , SNAIL , TWIST , and NANOG . Concomitantly, there was a remarkable upregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin. These alterations in gene expression profiles strongly suggested a shift in the phenotype of NB cells towards a less migratory and more epithelial-like state. To further substantiate this effect, we performed scratch assay to evaluate cell migration. Scratch assay demonstrated attenuation of NB cell migration upon PPP treatment. These collective findings indicate the potential of PPP as a promising anti-metastatic agent in NB cancer. The induction of apoptosis represents a critical goal in the development of effective anticancer therapies [48 ]. Our investigations revealed a substantial upregulation of the transcript of tumor suppressor protein p53, a key regulator of apoptosis [49 ], upon PPP treatment. Additionally, the transcript expression of BAX, a pro-apoptotic protein [50 ], was significantly elevated, while the transcript expression of BCL2, an anti-apoptotic protein [51 ], was notably reduced. These alterations in gene expression patterns collectively indicate the activation of apoptotic pathways in NB cells following PPP treatment. To complement the gene expression analysis, we employed AO/EtBr staining, a well-established method for visualizing apoptotic cells [52 ]. PPP-treated cells exhibited characteristic features of apoptosis, including nuclear condensation and cell shrinkage, as observed through microscopic examination. These morphological changes further confirm the ability of PPP to induce apoptosis in NB cells.  5 Conclusion Neuroblastoma is an aggressive childhood cancer, often resistant to the most aggressive chemotherapeutic and surgical interventions. Since the current cure rate of NB is very low, there is a need to develop target specific treatment options. The findings of current study demonstrates that PPP exhibits dual inhibitory effects on IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases in NB cells. PPP effectively disrupts the downstream signaling pathways of these kinases which contribute to the suppression of cancer cell migration and induction of apoptosis. Although, further in vivo evaluations are necessary to support our study, through in vitro experiments on SH-SY5Y NB cells, we have demonstrated that PPP could effectively attenuate embryonic cancers such as NB, highlighting PPPs therapeutic potential. PPP is currently being used in clinical trials in other solid cancer under the name AXL1717 [53 ]. PPP, thus could be used to develop treatment strategies to remediate NB as well, which reflects the clinical significance of our study. title: The paracrine TAC1-TACR1 signaling promotes endothelial senescence and metastatic progression in neuroblastoma
abstract: Distal metastasis remains a major clinical challenge in neuroblastoma (NB), the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. However, the molecular mechanisms mediating tumor-endothelial crosstalk and NB metastasis remain incompletely understood. By integrating single-cell omics analyses of clinical NB samples with experimental validations, we established the molecular subtypes of NB and identified a C2 subtype marked by MYCN amplification and dual positivity for TWIST1 and TAC1 expressions. This aggressive tumor subpopulation exhibited enhanced secretion of the neuropeptide substance P (encoded by TAC1), which was regulated by the transcription factor TWIST1. TAC1 signaled to tumor-associated endothelial cells with elevated TACR1 expression, consequently leading to endothelial senescence and disrupted vascular integrity. Remarkably, TAC1 overexpression was sufficient to accelerate NB tumorigenesis, circulating tumor cell (CTC) generation and metastatic progression in vivo. Clinically, TWIST1+TAC+ CTCs were significantly enriched in the blood samples of metastatic NB patients compared to the non-metastatic group. As a proof-of-principle study, we further demonstrated that the TACR1 antagonist aprepitant could effectively suppress endothelial senescence, tumorigenesis, and CTC-mediated metastatic progression in vivo, presenting a potential therapeutic strategy for NB patients with TAC1-TACR1 activation.

Fig. 1 Single-cell omics reveal MYCN-amplified TWIST1+  TAC1+  NB subpopulation associated with adverse clinical outcomes.  (A).  UMAP plot showing the subtypes of neuroblast cell, each dot indicated a single cell. Color-coded for the cell type. (B).  Kaplan–Meier estimation of over survival (OS) time in NB patients from TARGET-NBL by the characteristic genes of each subpopulation based on single-cell RNA-seq. The classification of TARGET-NBL was calculated using the ‘ConsensuClusterPlus’ package. (C).  A pairwise Jaccard index heatmap to visualize the similarity of characteristic gene sets among subpopulations from single-cell RNA-Seq and subtypes from TARGET-NBL cohort. X-axis represents the neuroblastoma subpopulations from single-cell RNA-Seq; Y-axis represents the subtypes from TARGET-NBL cohort. (D).  Sankey plot showing representative TARGET-NBL data divided into three subtypes C1, C2 and C3 (Own molecular subtypes) and clinical molecular typing (COG risk, MYCN status and INSS stage). (E).  Bar graph showing the pathway enriched in the Neuroblast_TAC1 cluster. The x-axis indicates the -log10 P value.  (F).  Gene expression levels of neuropeptide across subpopulations of neuroblast cells. Dot size indicates the fraction of expressing cells and the color represents normalized expression levels. (G).  Kaplan-Meier estimation of overall survival time in NB patients according to the tachykinin precursor score. HRs and 95% CIs were calculated based on a Cox regression model (two-sided P value  by log-rank test). Tachykinin precursor score was calculated for each sample as the sum of normalized expression of TAC1 and TAC3. (H).  Differential expressed transcription factor genes between Neuroblast_TAC1 subpopulation, and the other cell subpopulations. Y axis indicates the log2foldchange, genes ordered by log2foldchange along the x-axis. (I).  Binding of TWIST1 to the TAC1 gene in 293 T and hESC derived neural crests cells. All peaks were called by MACS2 (P  < 0.05). (J).  ChIP-PCR assay was performed to detect the extent of TWIST1 binding to the TAC1 gene in SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y cells. (K).  Schematic illustration of the predicted TWIST1-binding motif within the human TAC1 promoter and the corresponding wild-type (WT) and motif-mutated (MUT) sequences used for reporter construction (top). Dual-luciferase reporter assays were performed in SK-N-BE (2) (left) and SH-SY5Y (right) cells transfected with WT or MUT TAC1 promoter, along with a TWIST1 expression vector (TWIST1) or control vector (Vector). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity and presented as relative luciferase activity. Data are calculated based on three independent biological repeats and statistical significance was assessed by two-tailed Student's t-test. ∗P  < 0.05; ∗∗∗P  < 0.001; ns, not significant. (L).  mIHC showed the expression of DAPI, PHOX2B, TWIST1 and TAC1 in NB primary tissues. (M).  Bar plot quantifying the percentage of TAC1+ TWIST1+ PHOX2B+  cells among total PHOX2B+  malignant cells in individual neuroblastoma tumors. Samples are grouped by MYCN amplification status (MYCN Amp, n = 15 vs MYCN Non-Amp, n = 15). (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)
