Distal metastasis remains a major clinical challenge in neuroblastoma (NB), the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. However, the molecular mechanisms mediating tumor-endothelial crosstalk and NB metastasis remain incompletely understood. By integrating single-cell omics analyses of clinical NB samples with experimental validations, we established the molecular subtypes of NB and identified a C2 subtype marked by MYCN  amplification and dual positivity for TWIST1 and TAC1 expressions. This aggressive tumor subpopulation exhibited enhanced secretion of the neuropeptide substance P (encoded by TAC1), which was regulated by the transcription factor TWIST1. TAC1 signaled to tumor-associated endothelial cells with elevated TACR1 expression, consequently leading to endothelial senescence and disrupted vascular integrity. Remarkably, TAC1 overexpression was sufficient to accelerate NB tumorigenesis, circulating tumor cell (CTC) generation and metastatic progression in vivo.  Clinically, TWIST1+ TAC+  CTCs were significantly enriched in the blood samples of metastatic NB patients compared to the non-metastatic group. As a proof-of-principle study, we further demonstrated that the TACR1 antagonist aprepitant could effectively suppress endothelial senescence, tumorigenesis, and CTC-mediated metastatic progression in vivo , presenting a potential therapeutic strategy for NB patients with TAC1-TACR1 activation.   Keywords Neuroblastoma  TWIST1  TAC1-TACR1  Endothelial senescence  Circulating tumor cell (CTC)  Aprepitant   Data availability To increase the statistical power, we downloaded the publicly available scRNA-seq data from previous study GSE137804 that are publicly accessible at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ . In house scRNA-seq raw data have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive in BIG Data Center, Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences under BioProject HRA014094 (publicly accessible at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/s/sY85n7Bn ).   1 Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB) is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, accounting for approximately 7% of all pediatric malignancies [1 ,2 ]. Clinically, NB exhibits significant tumor heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous regression in low-risk cases to aggressive progression with distant metastasis in high-risk disease [3 ]. Despite advances in multimodal treatment—including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgical resection, and autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplantation—the long-term prognosis for high-risk NB remains unsatisfactory, with a 5-year overall survival rate of only about 50% [4 ]. Recurrence and distant metastasis pose the greatest challenges to improving patient outcomes, as metastatic lesions often develop resistance to conventional therapies and evade immune surveillance [5 ,6 ]. Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying NB metastasis is essential for identifying new therapeutic targets and optimizing clinical management. Amplification of the MYCN oncogene is a defining event in metastatic neuroblastoma (NB), occurring in approximately 20–30% of patients [7 ,8 ]. As a member of the MYC family of oncoproteins, MYCN  exerts broad transcriptional control, regulating up to 15% of genes in the human genome [9 ]. Under physiological conditions, MYCN protein expression is tightly regulated; however, in MYCN-amplified NB, its dysregulation drives aggressive tumor progression. MYCN overexpression activates signaling pathways that promote proliferation, angiogenesis, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), thereby enhancing the metastatic potential of tumor cells [10 ,11 ]. TWIST1, a pivotal transcription factor in the EMT program, has been identified as a direct downstream target of both MYCN and MYC in neuroblastoma [12 ]. Cellular senescence is a biological response to diverse stressors, including microenvironmental perturbations, nutrient deprivation, DNA damage, organellar dysfunction, and aberrant cell signaling [13 ]. This process is characterized by four major hallmarks: stable cell-cycle arrest, a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), macromolecular damage, and metabolic dysregulation [14 ]. Endothelial cells form and maintain the closed vascular network essential for nutrient transport and gas exchange. Under pathological conditions, however, endothelial injury can trigger a senescent phenotype, leading to increased vascular permeability and structural abnormalty [15 ,16 ]. Endothelial senescence contributes to tumor metastasis by directly facilitating tumor cell migration and adhesion through SASP-mediated signaling [17 ,18 ], and by indirectly fostering a premetastatic niche through the recruitment of myeloid cells [19 ]. To date, the molecular mechanisms driving endothelial senescence within the NB tumor microenvironment have not been explored. The neuropeptide substance P (SP, encoded by TAC1) Substance P was first discovered in 1931 by Ulf von Euler and John H. Gaddum [20 ]. SP is predominantly localized within the central and peripheral nervous systems but is also secreted by epithelial cells [21 ]. It exerts its biological functions mainly through G protein-coupled neurokinin receptors (NKRs), NK1R, NK2R, and NK3R, with NK1R (also known as tachykinin receptor 1, TACR1) exhibiting the highest affinity for SP [22 ]. In neuroblastoma, SP has been shown to promote tumor cell proliferation via activation of NK1R [23 ]. Aprepitant is a small-molecule selective antagonist of TACR1 that is clinically approved for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) [24 ]. Whether aprepitant treatment can influence NB progression and treatment remains to be clarified. In this study, we systematically investigated the tumor-endothelial crosstalk mechanism by integrating single-cell transcriptomic profiling of clinical samples with functional validations. We identified the TWIST1–TAC1–TACR1 paracrine signaling between tumor and endothelial vasculature as a critical driver of endothelial senescence and NB metastasis. In vivo , elevated TAC1 expression markedly accelerated tumorigenesis, CTC generation, and metastasis. Furthermore, the TACR1 antagonist aprepitant exhibited significant anti-tumor effects in mouse models. To translate our finding, we demonstrated that the abundance of TWIST1+ TAC1+  CTCs was significantly associated with metastatic progression, serving as potential noninvasive biomarkers for NB diagnosis and treatment.  2 Results 2.1 Single-cell transcriptomic landscape of NB We performed scRNA-seq on 28 samples from 23 NB patients and 4 normal adrenal tissue, including 27 primary NB, 1 neck metastases, 4 normal tissues (Table S1 ). After quality control and batch correction, a total of 260701 single cells were included for the analysis. Using the classical features of different cell clusters, 10 cell types were identified, including adrenal cortex cells (25800; CYP11A1 , CYP11B1  and NR5A1 ), B cells (5612; CD19 , MS4A1  and CD79A ), endothelial cells (17547; PECAM1 ,CDH5  and CLDN5 ), erythrocyte cells (3784; HBB , ALAS2  and SLC25A37 ), fibroblast cells (28389; COL1A1 , COL3A1  and COL6A1 ), myeloid cells (25028; CD14 , C1QA  and FCGR3A ), plasma cells (2520; TNFRSF17 , IGHG1  and IGHA1 ), schwaan cells (5599; S100B , PLP1  and SOX10 ) and T cells (29536; CD3D , CD3E  and CD8A ) (Suppl. Fig. S1A–B ). The proportions of these 10 cell types in different samples, which were shown in Suppl. Fig. S1C . Among these subpopulations, adrenal cortex cells and erythrocyte cells were enriched in normal adrenal tissue samples and immune cells such as B cells, myeloid cells, plamsa and T cells were enriched in primary adrenal tissues (Suppl. Fig. S1D ).  2.2 A unique TWIST1+  TAC1+  subpopulation in MYCN-amplified NB is associated with poor clinical outcome The neuroblast cells expressing CHGA , CHGB , PHOX2B  and TH  (Suppl. Fig. S2A ) were further subclassified and the 10 cell subtypes were found in all patients (Fig. 1  A, Table S2 ). Each cell subtype had its specific transcriptional signatures (Suppl. Fig. S2B ). Most cells were derived from the primary tumor (Suppl. Fig. S2C ). Copy-number variation (CNV) analysis from single-cell transcriptomes was employed to define malignant and non-malignant neuroblast cells by inferCNV (Suppl. Fig. S2D–E ). Based on the differentially expressed genes in each malignant neuroblast cluster in single-cell RNA-Seq level (Table S2 ), we conducted unsupervised clustering analysis in TARGET-NBL cohort and identified three clusters, including 29 cases in cluster 1 (C1), 31 in cluster 2 (C2) and 102 in cluster 3 (C3) (Suppl. Fig. S2F–H , Table S3 ). C2 subtype had significantly inferior over survival and C1 experienced the best over survival (log-rank test, P  = 0.033) (Fig. 1 B). To decipher the underlying mechanisms responsible for different clinical characteristics among the three subtypes, we further investigated their molecular and biological phenotypes. Through performing Jaccard correlation analysis, we assessed distribution of single-cell RNA-Seq identified malignant neuroblast cells among the three subtypes. C2 subtype was observed to show high enrichment for Neuroblast_TAC1 subtype (Fig. 1 C). At the clinical level, we observed that the C2 subtype was primarily associated with patients harboring MYCN amplification. Furthermore, the majority of these patients exhibited high COG risk and were classified as INSS stage 4 (Fig. 1 D). Using published ADRN and MES gene signatures [25 ,26 ], we computed state scores for each tumor and compared them across the C1–C3 taxonomy. Neither ADRN nor MES scores differed significantly among C1, C2, and C3 (Suppl. Fig. S2I ), indicating that our classification captures biological variation beyond the canonical ADRN/MES states. Furthermore, we identified the Neuroblast_TAC1 malignant cell subpopulation, the one most closely resembling the C2 subtype, which exhibited the highest MYCN mRNA expression among all malignant subsets at single-cell resolution (Suppl. Fig. S2J ). Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of genes upregulated in Neuroblast_TAC1 malignant cells compared with other malignant subpopulations revealed significant enrichment in protein folding, neuron spine, and neuron cell-cell adhesion (Fig. 1 E). We also found that several neuropeptide-related genes, notably TAC1 (encoded by the tachykinin precursor 1), TAC3 (encoded by the tachykinin precursor 3), VGF, NPB, and NPW, were distinctly expressed in the Neuroblast_TAC1 subpopulation (Fig. 1 F and Suppl. Fig. S2K ). Moreover, patients with tachykinin precursor score had significantly worse survival than the patients with tachykinin precursor score in TARGET-NBL cohort (Fig. 1 G). We next performed comparative analysis of Neuroblast_TAC1 subpopulation versus other malignant cells to identify key transcription factors (TFs) that were strongly upregulated in Neuroblast_TAC1 subpopulation. Among the significantly enriched TFs, TWIST1 was the top hit and has been reported as being directly regulated by MYCN [12 ] (Fig. 1 H). TWIST1-KD cells exhibited impaired cell proliferation, colony formation assay, migration, and invasion in two NB cell lines SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y (Suppl. Fig. S3A–C ). Conversely, overexpression of TWIST1 (TWIST1-OE) resulted in the upregulation of cell proliferation, colony formation, migration and invasion capabilities in vitro  (Suppl. Fig. S3D–G ). Interestingly, ChIP-seq data analysis revealed a potential binding site for TWIST1 at the TAC1 promoter region in 293T and hESC derived neural crests cells (Fig. 1 I), which was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR analysis in two NB cell lines SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y, suggesting a direct regulation of TAC1 by TWIST1 in our model systems (Fig. 1 J). We also performed promoter dual-luciferase reporter assay using a TAC1 promoter construct containing the predicted TWIST1-binding motif (WT) and a mutant construct with the core TWIST1 motif mutated (MUT). TWIST1-OE significantly increased the luciferase activity driven by the WT TAC1 promoter, whereas this activation was abolished in the MUT promoter, indicating that TWIST1 regulated TAC1 promoter activity in a manner dependent on the intact TWIST1-binding site (Fig. 1 K). The reduction of TACR1 protein was also evident in TWIST1 KD cells by Q-PCR and Western blot (Suppl. Fig. S3H–I ). Finally, we performed mIHC analysis on MYCN Amp and MYCN Non-Amp NB patients to detect PHOX2B+  TWIST1+  TAC1+  malignant cells (Fig. 1 L). The percentage of TAC1+ TWIST1+ PHOX2B+  cells among total PHOX2B+  tumor cells was substantially higher in MYCN-amplified tumors compared with MYCN-non-amplified tumors (Fig. 1 M). Collectively, these results suggested that TWIST1 transcriptionally activated TAC1 expression preferentially in MYCN-amplified NB subpopulation, which exhibited poor clinical outcome.  2.3 TACR1+  endothelial cells exhibit a senescent phenotype We further explored how substance P (TAC1) may influence the tumor microenvironment. Substance P can bind to three distinct G protein-coupled receptors, NK1, NK2, and NK3, which are encoded by the genes TACR1 , TACR2 , and TACR3  [27 ]. Our results indicated that TACR1 mRNA expression was restricted to endothelial cells, whereas malignant cells lacked detectable tachykinin receptors (Fig. 2  A). Single cell omic analysis showed all endothelial cells expressing PECAM1 , ENG , CDH5  and SLCO2A1  and identified 11 endothelial subtypes in all samples, including active capillary cells, tip cells, vein cells, lymphatic endothelial cells, and artery cells (Fig. 2 B, Suppl. Fig. S4A–B  and Table S4 ), and among these subtypes, 2 tip subpopulations, CDKN1A+  vein cells, ACKR1+  vein cells, JUN+  active capillary cells and artery cells were enriched in tumor microenvironment compared to normal tissue (Fig. 2 C). Ligand-receptor pair analysis across various subpopulations revealed that the TAC1-TACR1 and TAC3-TACR1 pairs were enriched in the crosstalk between TAC1+  neuroblastoma cells and two venous endothelial cell subpopulations. (Fig. 2 D). Subsequently, through mIHC, we observed a marked presence of TACR1+  CD31+  endothelial cells in close proximity to these PHOX2B+  TWIST1+  TAC1+  malignant cells, suggesting potential crosstalk between malignant cells and endothelial cells (Fig. 2 E). Furthermore, the C2 subtype patients exhibited significantly higher TAC-TACR1 signaling activity, which was associated with worst overall survival compared to the C1 subtype (Suppl. Fig. S4C–D ). Interestingly, we found that TACR1 was predominantly expressed in two venous endothelial subpopulations: CDKN1A+  and ACKR1+  vein cells (Suppl. Fig. S4E ). Based on its expression levels, all endothelial cells were stratified into TACR1+  and TACR1-  subsets (Suppl. Fig. S4F ). Analysis revealed that 34.1% of cells within the CDKN1A+  venous endothelial subpopulation exhibited TACR1 expression (Suppl. Fig. S4G ). Survival analysis revealed that CDKN1A+  and ACKR1+  venous endothelial cells were associated with poor patient prognosis (Suppl. Fig. S4H ). We further performed a differentially expressed gene analysis and found that compared with TACR1-  endothelial cells, TACR1+  endothelial cells exhibited significant upregulation of the classical cellular senescence markers CDKN1A/p21 (Fig. 2 F). Cellular senescence score and SASP score were significantly upregulated in TACR1+  endothelial cells compared to the TACR1-  subgroup (Fig. 2 G). We further identified a subset of CDKN1A+  TACR1+  CD31+  endothelial cells in NB tumors by mIHC (Fig. 2 H). Consistently, metastatic patients exhibited significantly elevated total CTC numbers compared to the non-metastatic group in NB patients. Notably, TWIST1+  CTCs and TWIST1+  TAC1+  CTCs were detected at very low levels in non-metastatic cases but surged to much higher levels in metastatic patients (Fig. 2 I). We also integrated scRNA-seq data from 11 cancer types to build a comprehensive transcriptional atlas of endothelial cells (Suppl. Fig. S5A–B ). This resource, which comprised 50654 endothelial cells from primary tumor tissue and categorized into 15 transcriptionally distinct subpopulations based on marker gene expression (Suppl. Fig. S5A–C ). TACR1 was notably absent in tumor-associated endothelial cells across these adult solid tumors (Suppl. Fig. S5D ). Together, these results suggested that substance P receptor, TACR1, was localized to venous endothelial cells and was associated with a senescent phenotype in a subset of NB cells.  2.4 TACR1 regulates ROS homeostasis to promote endothelial senescence and loss of endothelial integrity To assess if TACR1 plays a causal role in endothelial senescence, we conducted differential gene analysis between CD31 high patients and CD31 low patients, with an overlapping analysis of signatures distinguishing the TACR1 high patients versus the TACR1 low patients in TARGET-NBL cohort (Fig. 3  A). Interestingly, both CD31 high and TACR1 high patients upregulated genes related to SASP such as CXCL2, CCL19, IL16 and PGF (Fig. 3 B). Both CD31 high and TACR1 high patients upregulated pathways involved in chemokine activity, cellular extravasation, cellular response to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and aging (Fig. 3 C). GSEA analysis revealed significant enrichment of response to reactive oxygen species (Fig. 3 D). To dissect the functional relationship between TACR1 activity, cellular senescence and ROS regulations, we overexpressed TACR1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and stimulated TAC1 (substance P) recombinant protein. This manipulation revealed a significant upregulation of CDKN1A/p21 and p53 in TACR1-overexpressing cells compared to the negative controls (Fig. 3 E–F). Meanwhile, TACR1-OE cells with TAC1 recombinant protein exhibited positive staining for SA-β-galactosidase (β-gal), a canonical marker of cellular senescence (Fig. 3 G). Flow cytometric cell cycle analysis consistently revealed that the G0/G1 phase fraction was significantly increased in TACR1-OE HUVEC cells with TAC1 recombinant protein (Fig. 3 H). There was also a significant upregulation of SASP-related gene expressions, including MMP1 , ICAM1 , CXCL8 , GDF15 , TNFa  and GDF15  (Suppl. Fig. S6A ).  Using the mitoSOX red dye, we found the mitochondrial ROS dramatically increased in TACR1-OE HUVEC cells supplemented with TAC1 recombinant protein (Fig. 3 I). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) analysis was applied to capture the ultrastructural changes of mitochondria in TACR1-OE HUVEC cells with TAC1 recombinant protein demonstrated significantly enlarged and swollen mitochondrial morphology (Fig. 3 J), reduced the ratio of cristae length to outer mitochondria, average membrane cristae length, cristae number per mitochondria and number of mitochondria per field, as compared to control cells (Fig. 3 J). There was also a significant downregulation of cell-cell junction genes, including CDH5 , CLDN5  and TJP1 , as confirmed by qPCR analyses (Fig. 3 K). Compared to control cells, stimulation with TAC1 recombinant protein in TACR1-OE cells significantly reduced the tube-forming capacity of endothelial cells (Fig. 3 L). TACR1-OE HUVEC cells significantly disrupted the structural and functional integrity of endothelial cells and enhanced the cellular senescence of endothelial cells, as evidenced by reduced trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and the endothelial TJP1 and CDKN1A/p21 expression (Fig. 3 M–N). Collectively, these results demonstrated that TAC1-TACR1 activation in endothelial cells can promote mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS accumulation, leading to cellular senescence and endothelial dysfunction.  2.5 Aprepitant suppresses TAC1-TACR1 activation-induced endothelial senescence and dysfunction To experimentally investigate the molecular mechanisms driving endothelial abnormality by TAC1-TACR1 axis, an in vitro  co-culture system was established by co-culturing NB malignant cells or substance P protein with HUVEC (Fig. 4  A). It comprised in four experiment groups: HUVEC (control), HUVEC co-cultured with wild-type SK-N-BE (2) or SH-SY5Y cells, HUVEC co-cultured with TAC1 (substance P) recombinant protein, and HUVEC co-cultured with SK-N-BE (2) or SH-SY5Y cells treated with aprepitant, a drug targeting neurokinin-1 receptor (TACR1) for the treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting [28 ]. Our results demonstrated that co-culture with SK-N-BE (2) or SH-SY5Y cells, or treatment with TAC1 (Substance P) recombinant protein, substantially induced cellular senescence in HUVECs. This was evidenced by elevated expression of p21 and p16 (Fig. 4 B–C), an increased percentage of β-gal-positive cells (Fig. 4 D), a higher G0/G1 phase fraction (Fig. 4 E), downregulated cell cycle-related genes (Suppl. Fig. S7A ) and upregulated SASP-related genes ( Suppl. Fig. S7B ). However, Aprepitant treatment largely reversed this senescent phenotype in endothelial cells ( Fig. 4 B–E and Suppl. Fig. S7A ). We found that exposure to either NB cell lines or TAC1 (Substance P) recombinant protein impaired HUVEC tube formation and TEER, effects that were reversed by aprepitant treatment (Fig. 4 F–G and Suppl. Fig. S7C ). Staining for TJP1 and p21 in HUVEC also demonstrated the effect of malignant cells or recombinant protein SP on the induction of senescence (p21) and the concomitant loss of tight junctions (TJP1) (Fig. 4 H and Suppl. Fig. S7D ). Together, these results suggested that targeting the neurokinin-1 receptor with aprepitant may present a promising therapeutic strategy to counteract endothelial dysfunction by suppressing cellular senescence.  2.6 TAC1 overexpression promotes endothelial senescence and metastatic progression,  and the TACR1 inhibitor aprepitant demonstrates significant anti-tumor efficacy in vivo  To determine the functional role of the TAC1-TACR1 axis in vivo , we first generated TAC1 overexpression (TAC1-OE) SK-N-BE (2) cell lines (Suppl. Fig. S8A ). We established subcutaneous xenograft models with the control tumors (NC), TAC1-OE tumors and TAC1-OE tumors treated with the clinically approved TACR1 antagonist aprepitant. Tumors derived from TAC1-OE cells exhibited a significant increase in both tumor volume and weight compared to those from control cells (Fig. 5  A–C). Notably, aprepitant treatment markedly attenuated TAC1-OE-driven tumor growth, reducing both tumor volume and tumor weight to levels comparable to the NC group (Fig. 5 A–C). Consistent with the metastasis-promoting function of TAC1, we observed a significant increase in CTCs isolated from the blood of mice in the TAC1-OE group compared with the NC group, suggesting substantially enhanced metastatic potential of TAC1-OE tumor cells (Fig. 5 D and Suppl. Fig. S8B ). Strikingly, aprepitant treatment substantially reduced the elevated CTC number observed in the TAC1-OE group (Fig. 5 D and Suppl. Fig. S8B ). mIHC quantification of subcutaneous tumors from the TAC1-OE group exhibited a strong positivity of Cdkn1a+ Cd31+  senescent endothelial population, which was presented at very low levels in control tumors (Fig. 5 E and Suppl. Fig. S8C ). Importantly, aprepitant treatment mitigated this TAC1-OE–associated endothelial senescence phenotype, decreased the abundance of Cdkn1a+ Cd31+  endothelial cells, and partially restored endothelial junctional integrity (Fig. 5 E and Suppl. Fig. S8C ). These data supported that TAC1 promoted endothelial dysfunction and enhanced tumorigenesis in vivo  in a TACR1-dependent manner. Next, to test if TAC1-OE affects the metastatic potential in NB, we performed metastasis assay using tail-vein injections (Fig. 5 F). TAC1-OE cells showed substantially enhanced metastatic outgrowth compared with the control beginning at ∼3 weeks post injection (Fig. 5 G–H). Remarkably, aprepitant significantly suppressed TAC1-OE-driven metastatic progression, reducing tumor burden to a level similar to the control group (Fig. 5 G–H). Consistently, histopathological analysis confirmed these changes in tumor burden (Fig. 5 I and Suppl. Fig. S8D ). The TAC1-OE group exhibited a significantly higher abundance of Cd31+  β-gal+  endothelial cells, whereas the population of Cd31+ Cdh5+  cells was reduced compared to the control (NC) mice. Aprepitant potently rescued the endothelial impairment induced by TAC1-OE. (Fig. 5 J). mIHC assays confirmed the abundance of Cdkn1a+  Cd31+  endothelial cells adjacent to PHOX2B+  TAC1+  malignant cells in the TACR1-OE group (Fig. 5 K and Suppl. Fig. S8E ). Collectively, these data indicated that TAC1 promoted endothelial senescence and vasculature remodeling associated with metastatic progression. Importantly, pharmacologic blockade of TACR1 by aprepitant exhibited potent inhibitory effects on both tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo .   3 Discussion Tumor heterogeneity and plasticity are fundamental drivers of neuroblastoma progression [29 ]. To deconvolute this complexity, we performed a comprehensive molecular characterization using integrative multi-omic analyses at single-cell resolution. This approach revealed three molecular subtypes (C1, C2, and C3) with distinct molecular and clinical features. Notably, the C2 subtype was abundantly detected in patients with MYCN amplification and was associated with poor clinical outcome (Fig. 1 B). C2 subtype exhibited concurrent high expression of both MYCN and TWIST1 (Fig. 1 H) Prior studies have confirmed TWIST1 expression drives a poorly differentiated neuroblastoma phenotype and promotes NB progression and metastasis [30 ]. Consistently, TWIST1 has also been identified as a direct transcriptional target of MYCN, solidifying its role as a key downstream effector [31 ]. In this study, we identified that TWIST1 directly transactivates the expression of a neuropeptide Substance P (encoded by TAC1) in MYCN-amplified NB (Fig. 1 I–K). Thus, a known EMT-related oncogene TWIST1 can exert significant impact on tumor microenvironment by activating tumor-specific TAC1 expression and secretion, subsequently inducing elevated TACR1 signaling in recipient endothelial cells, which promoted tumor growth and metastasis in a positive feedback manner. Interestingly, previous studies have established that in breast cancer, dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons can release substance P to the tumor microenvironment, which induces apoptosis in cancer cells and facilitates the death of TACR1+  malignant cells, leading to the release of single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). These ssRNA molecules subsequently interact with Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) on other cancer cells, ultimately promoting metastasis [32 ]. This finding highlights a direct link between SP and its receptor TLR in cancer progression and suggests that other related pattern recognition receptors may similarly intersect with SP-driven pathways to modulate the tumor microenvironment and metastatic potential, an avenue worthy of further exploration in neuroblastoma and other malignancies. Additional evidence indicates that substance P secretion from DRG neurons can enhance macrophage infiltration via the TAC1–TACR1 axis [33 ]. Surprisingly, we observed that NB tumor cells can hijack the presumably neuronal-specific TAC1 expression. Through a series of clinical and experimental analyses, we revealed that tumor-secreted TAC1 predominantly signaled to TACR1 in tumor-associated endothelial cells and drove endothelial senescence and vascular abnormality, which correlated well with enhanced tumorigenesis, CTC generation and metastasis (Fig. 5 D). Our finding is consistent with a prior seminal study by Henssen, Odersky et al. demonstrating that neuroblastoma cell lines express TACR1 and that pharmacologic inhibition of the tachykinin receptor signaling using clinically available NK1R/TACR1 antagonists aprepitant can reduce neuroblastoma cell viability, induce apoptosis, and suppress tumor burden in xenograft models, supporting TACR1 as a druggable vulnerability in neuroblastoma [34 ]. Furthermore, several studies have found a regulatory role of TAC1-TACR1 signaling in brain tumor and breast cancer progression, suggesting the dysregulation of this pathway is implicated in disease progression of multiple cancer types [32 ,35 ]. In our work, we further provided complementary evidence that TACR1 played a critical role in tumor-associated endothelial senescence that indirectly enhanced metastatic potential, suggesting TAC1–TACR1 signaling can have tumor-promoting effects on both tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment in neuroblastoma development (Fig. 3 ). The findings from our group and other studies revealed that aprepitant may possess potential therapeutic value in suppressing NB progression, which warrants further investigations in the clinical settings. Cellular senescence was first characterized by Hayflick in 1961 [36 ]. It is defined by stable cell cycle arrest triggered by various stressors such as DNA damage, oncogene activation, and replicative exhaustion [37 ]. Cellular senescence is often activated primarily through the p53/p21 and pRB/p16 signaling pathways [38 ]. The TACR1-driven senescent endothelial cells upregulated a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which broadly includes inflammatory chemokines, cytokines, growth factors, and proteases, as well as mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation in certain circumstances [39 ,40 ]. Notably, Gundem, Levine et al. associated ROS with the SBS18 mutational signature in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, reflecting tumor-cell-intrinsic oxidative stress [41 ]. Our study extends this concept by identifying endothelial-specific ROS accumulation as an additional, distinct component of MYCN-driven oxidative stress in the tumor microenvironment. Endothelial cells constitute a selectively permeable barrier that regulates molecular exchange between the blood and peripheral tissues [42 ]; upon senescence induction, this barrier is compromised by the disruption of VE-cadherin and ZO-1, coupled with a marked downregulation of occludin and Claudin-5 [43 ]. How TACR1 signaling impacts endothelial senescence remains unclear. Here, using a combination of TACR1-overexpressing HUVECs, substance P stimulation, and a tumor-endothelial co-culture model, we demonstrated that TACR1 activation markedly induced endothelial cell senescence and disrupted tight junction integrity (Fig. 4 ). Aprepitant, an antagonist of the neurokinin-1 receptor (NK1R/TACR1), is clinically used to manage chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting [44 ]. Beyond its antiemetic role, pharmacological inhibition of TACR1 has been shown to suppress the growth of multiple tumor types, notably including neuroblastoma, gallbladder cancer, glioblastoma and breast cancer [32 ,45–47 ]. Prior work demonstrates that TACR1 expression in neuroblastoma cell lines and provides evidence that TACR1 signaling engages downstream kinase pathways, including SRC/p-SRC, and that pharmacological TACR1 blockade can reduce SRC phosphorylation with concomitant repression of E2F2 and induction of TP53-associated programs, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis in neuroblastoma models [34 ]. Along the line, our work illustrtaed an interesting observation that TACR1 was expressed in tumor-asssociated endothelial cells and faciliated senescence induction and vascular remodeling both in vitro  and in vivo  (Fig. 5 ). These observations suggested that the TAC1–TACR1 axis may operate through dual, context-dependent modalities: a tumor cell–intrinsic pathway reported in cell-line systems (potentially involving SRC-associated signaling) and a paracrine tumor–endothelial crosstalk pathway within the tumor microenvironment that drives endothelial ROS stress, senescence, and barrier dysfunction to facilitate NB metastatic progression. Further mechanistic studies are needed to delineate whether TAC1 protein has any regulatory function on tumor cell itself, and how senescent endothelial cells may feedback on tumor cells to facilitate metastasis. These findings could provide important molecular insights and potential drug targets for devising novel anti-metastasis treatment in NB. We acknowledge several limitations in the present study. Although our TF enrichment analysis identified multiple candidate regulators in Neuroblast_TAC1 cells, we focused on TWIST1 because it showed strong enrichment and it was directly linked to TAC1 transcriptional regulation and downstream functional phenotypes. Nevertheless, other TFs may also contribute to the Neuroblast_TAC1 program and/or MYCN-associated transcriptional networks. In addition, only one metastasis sample was available for single-cell omic analysis, which undoubtably requires further validation in additional clinical samples.  4 Conclusions In conclusion, single-cell multi-omic dissection of primary and metastatic neuroblastoma samples identified distinct NB molecular subtypes. Among them, the C2 subtype was characterized by poor prognosis, MYCN amplification, and high TWIST1 expression. We further demonstrated that TWIST1 directly transactivated the expression of TAC1, the gene encoding substance P, thereby engaging the TAC1-TACR1 signaling axis to mediate tumor-endothelial crosstalk. This tumor-endothelial communication was crucial for vascular remodeling and metastasis, acting through the promotion of endothelial senescence and the disruption of inter-endothelial tight junctions. Remarkably, the TACR1 inhibitor (also known as NK1R antagonists) aprepitant effectively suppressed TACR1-driven endothelial senescence, tumorigenesis, and metastasis in vivo , implicating its therapeutic potential in NB treatment. Importantly, our work provided a potential non-invasive CTC-based biomarker detection technology to pinpoint the highly aggressive NB subtype with elevated TAC1-TACR1 signaling activity, which may require improved therapeutic interventions (Fig. 6  , Working Model). Nevertheless, the implementation of CTC liquid biopsy warrants further clinical validations using a larger cohort of patient samples.  5 Materials and methods 5.1 Ethics approval and consent to participate Fresh NB specimens were collected from Shenzhen Children's Hospital under item number 202301302 and Children's Hospital of Fudan University under item number No. (2020)416. Fresh blood samples of NB patients were collected from the Children's Hospital of Fudan University. All patients provided written informed consent for participation in the study. The collection and utilization of these clinical specimens were sanctioned by the Shenzhen Children's Hospital and Children's Hospital of Fudan University ethical review board.  5.2 Cell culture and treatment All NB cell lines (SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y) were purchased from QuiCell (China) in 2024 with short tandem repeat (STR) multiplex profiling. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were purchased from Biospecies Co., Ltd (Table S6 ). on November 25, 2023. SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y cell lines were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), while HUVECs were maintained in endothelial cell medium (ECM; ScienCell, USA). All cells were incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 . Experimental procedures were performed on cells between passages 3 and 10 post-thawing. Indirect co-culture was carried out using 0.4 μm pore-size Transwell inserts (Corning, NY, USA).  5.3 Small interfering (si) RNA and plasmid transfection TWIST1 and negative control (NC) siRNAs were synthesized by GenePharma (China), and their sequences (5′ to 3′) are provided in Table S7 . Cells were transiently transfected with siRNAs using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol and were harvested 48 h post-transfection.  5.4 Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) and spatial analysis Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) was performed using the PANO 7-plex IHC Assay Kit (Panovue, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. In brief, tissue sections were first incubated at 75 °C for 1 h to enhance adhesion to the slides. Subsequently, samples were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series (100%, 95%, 75% and 50%). Antigen retrieval was carried out in EDTA-based retrieval buffer (pH 9.0; ZSGB-Bio, Beijing, China) using microwave-assisted heating. To minimize nonspecific background, tissue sections were blocked prior to sequential incubation with primary antibodies and horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies. After each round of antibody binding, tyramide signal amplification (TSA) was applied to boost detection sensitivity. Following TSA, sections were incubated with biotinylated anti-rabbit and anti-mouse secondary antibodies, then with HRP-conjugated streptavidin, as specified in the kit protocol (Panovue, Beijing, China). For chromogenic visualization, biotinylated antibodies were developed using streptavidin-alkaline phosphatase, whereas fluorescent detection was achieved using streptavidin-conjugated fluorophores with excitation wavelengths at520, 570, 620, 690, or 780 nm. Multispectral imaging was performed using the Vectra Polaris Automated Quantitative Pathology Imaging System (Akoya Biosciences, Delaware, USA). Spatial analysis of immune and tumor cell distributions, as well as potential cell–cell interactions within the tumor microenvironment, was conducted using HALO image analysis software (Indica Labs, Corrales, NM, USA). This approach enabled high-resolution, multiparametric characterization of the tissue architecture. A complete list of antibodies and their specifications is provided in Table S8 .  5.5 Plasmid transfection and construction of stable cell lines Overexpression plasmids encoding TAC1 and overexpression plasmids encoding TACR1 were obtained from Miaoling Biotechnology (China). Lentiviral vectors were transfected into HEK293T packaging cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Viral supernatants collected 48 h post-transfection, filtered through a 0.45 μm nitrocellulose membrane (MilliporeSigma) to remove cell debris, and used to infect target cells. Following transduction, stable cell lines were established by selecting transduced cells with puromycin (1.0 μg/mL; MilliporeSigma) for 4 consecutive days.  5.6 Cell viability, migration and invasion assay Cell proliferation was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Beyotime, China). Cells were plated at a density of 1000 cells per well in 96-well plates, and the optical density was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad Laboratories, USA) at designated time points. For the migration assay, 8 μm pore transwell inserts (Corning, NY, USA) were placed in 24-well plates with 800 μL of medium containing 10% FBS in the lower chamber, and 200 μL of serum-free medium containing 5 × 10^4 appropriately treated cells was added to the upper chamber, followed by 24 h of incubation. After medium removal, the cells were fixed with methanol and stained with crystal violet solution. For the invasion assay, the insert membranes were pre-coated with Matrigel (Corning, USA) diluted in DMEM. Then, 200 μL of serum-free medium containing 1 × 10^5 appropriately treated cells was added to the upper chamber and cultured for 24 h. After medium removal, the cells were fixed with methanol and stained with crystal violet solution. Microscopic images were captured using an OLYMPUS microscope, and cell quantification was performed using ImageJ software.  5.7 Chromatin Immunoprecipitation-qPCR Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) experiments were performed following the manufacturer's instructions provided with a commercial kit (CST, 9003, USA). Briefly, cells were treated with 1% formaldehyde for crosslinking, followed by nuclear extraction and chromatin fragmentation through sonication after cell lysis. The fragmented chromatin was then diluted in an appropriate buffer and distributed for immunoprecipitation procedures. Following the addition of anti-TWIST1 antibody, samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C under continuous rotation. Antibody-chromatin complexes were subsequently captured using magnetic protein A/G beads.  5.8 Dual luciferase reporter assay Dual luciferase activity was measured using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay Kit (BRK0044, ABclonal, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, transfected adherent cells were washed twice with PBS and lysed with 1 × Passive Luciferase Lysis Buffer at room temperature for 15 min. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 g for 3 min, and supernatants were collected. Firefly luciferase activity was first measured by adding 100 μl of working solution (0.2 mg/ml D-Luciferin) to 20–100 μl of lysate in a white opaque plate, followed by immediate luminescence detection. Subsequently, 100 μl of 1 × Coelenterazine working solution was added to the same reaction to measure Renilla luciferase activity as an internal control. Relative luciferase activity was calculated as: Relative Luciferase Activity = (Firefly luciferase reading of the sample − Firefly luciferase reading of the blank control)/(Renilla luciferase reading of the sample-Renilla luciferase reading of the blank control)  5.9 Senescence-associated β-galactosidase assay To assess cellular senescence, cells from each experimental group were plated in 6-well plates at a density of 2 × 105  cells per well. After 48 h of culture or corresponding treatment, the cells were rinsed with PBS and fixed using the solution provided with the Senescence-associated β-galactosidase Staining Kit (Beyotime, China). Staining was then performed strictly according to the manufacturer's instructions, with incubation at 37 °C (without CO2 ) for 12 h until blue-stained senescent cells were observed under a microscope. Images of at least three randomly selected fields per well were captured using an OLYMPUS inverted microscope, and positively stained cells were quantified using ImageJ software. The senescence level was determined by calculating the percentage of β-galactosidase-positive cells. All experiments were set up with three replicate wells and independently repeated three times.  5.10 Cell cycle analysis For cell cycle assessment, cells from each experimental group were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 2 × 105  cells per well. After 48 h of standard culture or corresponding treatment, cells were collected, washed twice with ice-cold PBS, and fixed in pre-chilled 70% ethanol at 4 °C overnight to stabilize DNA content and integrity. Fixed cells were then peeled and washed twice with PBS to remove residual ethanol. Subsequently, they were treated with RNase A (100 μg/mL) at 37 °C for 30 min to digest RNA and prevent interference with DNA staining. Cells were then stained with propidium iodide (PI, 50 μg/mL) in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min to label nuclear DNA. Flow cytometric analysis was performed using a CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, USA), with a minimum of 10,000 events acquired per sample. Data was analyzed using FlowJo software (v10), and the distribution of cells in the G0/G1, S, and G2/M phases was determined using the Watson algorithm. All experiments were independently repeated in triplicate to ensure reliability and reproducibility of results.  5.11 Western blotting Cells were lysed by RIPA buffer (Beyotime, China) supplemented with 1% protease and phosphatase inhibitors (MCE, USA). Lysates were incubated on ice for 30 min. Following sonication, lysates were centrifuged at 12,000×g  for 15 min at 4 °C. Protein concentrations were determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime, China). Protein was eluted and denatured in SDS loading buffer at 95 °C for 8 min. Equal amounts of protein were resolved on 10% SDS-PAGE gels and subsequently transferred to 0.45 μm PVDF membranes (Merck-Millipore, Germany). Membranes were blocked at room temperature for 15 min using 1 × QuickBlock™ Blocking Buffer (NCM, China), then incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. After washing, membranes were treated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using ECL detection reagents (17046, Zenbio, China) on a ChemiDoc MP imaging system (Bio-Rad, USA). Detailed information on relevant antibodies provided in Table S8 .  5.12 Quantitative real-time PCR Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed to assess the mRNA levels of target genes. Total RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Mini Kit (74106, QIAGEN), and reverse transcription was carried out with the TranScript All-in-One First-Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (with genomic DNA removal) from TransGen Biotech. qRT-PCR amplification was conducted using the PerfectStart Green qPCR SuperMix (TransGen Biotech) on a CFX96 Touch Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad, USA), following the manufacturer's instructions. Gene expression levels were normalized to GAPDH and calculated using the 2^–ΔΔCT method. Data are described as relative mRNA expression levels. The primer sequences used for RT-qPCR are provided in Table S9 .  5.13 Indirect coculture systems For the indirect co-culture system, HUVECs were seeded into 6-well plates (5 × 105  cells/well) in ECM medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Simultaneously, approximately 5 × 105  treated SK-N-BE (2) and SH-SY5Y cells were plated in Transwell inserts (0.4 μm pore size, 6.5 mm diameter; Corning, NY, USA) and maintained for 48 h. In this system, tumor cells were placed in the upper compartment, while HUVECs were cultured in the lower chamber to allow indirect interaction.  5.14 Endothelial barrier permeability Endothelial barrier permeability was evaluated by measuring trans endothelial electrical resistance (TEER). HUVECs were seeded at a density of 5.0 × 104  cells per well onto Transwell polyester membrane inserts (pore size: 0.4 μm; diameter: 6.5 mm; Corning, NY, USA) placed in 24-well culture plates. TEER was recorded using the Millicell® Electrical Resistance System (Millipore, USA). A stable and confluent monolayer was established when TEER readings reached a plateau. Following this, changes in barrier integrity were assessed by monitoring TEER values under different experimental conditions.  5.15 Matrigel tube formation assay For the in vitro  tube formation assay, each well of a 48-well plate was coated with 200 μL of Matrigel (Corning, USA) and allowed to solidify at 37 °C for 30 min. HUVECs (3 × 104  cells in 200 μL) were seeded onto the polymerized Matrigel, with experimental groups including cells alone or with specified treatments. After 6 h of incubation at 37 °C, the cells were stained with Calcein (Beyotime, China) for fluorescence labeling. Tubular structures were visualized using a confocal microscope (Leica, Germany), with images captured from four randomly selected fields per well, and tube node quantification was performed using ImageJ software.  5.16 Flow cytometry analysis The study analyzed tumor tissues from subcutaneous tumors in mouse model using flow cytometry. Tumors tissues were isolated and preserved in cold DMEM medium containing 5% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% GlutaMAX, and 1% penicillin-streptomycin before mechanical mincing. Enzymatic digestion followed at 37 °C for 30 min with a cocktail of 2 mg/ml collagenase IV, 0.2 mg/ml dispase, and 0.1 mg/ml DNase I in supplemented DMEM. The cell suspension was filtered through 40 μm strainers with 10 ml of supplemented DMEM per sample. Myelin removal involved mixing the suspension with 90% isotonic Percoll in 10 × PBS, followed by centrifugation at 800×g  for 20 min. After resuspending the pellet in cold MACS BSA buffer, samples underwent two centrifugation cycles at 300×g  for 5 min at 4 °C, with intermediate resuspension in cold buffer and flow cytometry staining buffer to reach 1,000,000 cells/100 μl. For subcutaneous tumors, samples were incubated at 4 °C for 15 min with with anti-mouse Cdh5 (PE,Thermo fisher, Cat#12-1441-80) and anti-mouse CD31 (Biolegend, Cat#102527). CellEvent Senescence Green (Invitreogen, Cat#C10840) was used to determine the cell senescence. Dead cells were labeled with viobility fixable dye (Miltenyi Biotech, Cat#130-109-816). Data acquisition is used by a MACSQuant Analyzer (Miltenyi Biotech), with analysis performed in Flowlogic software (Miltenyi Biotech).  5.17 Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was conducted in accordance with established histological protocols to evaluate overall tissue morphology. In summary, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections underwent deparaffinization in xylene and were subsequently rehydrated through a graded series of alcohol solutions. The sections were then stained with hematoxylin for a duration of 2 min to visualize cell nuclei, followed by differentiation and blue steps to enhance nuclear contrast. Subsequently, the sections were counterstained with eosin for approximately one to 2 min to delineate cytoplasmic and extracellular matrix components, thereby providing distinct contrast among various tissue structures. Following staining, the sections were dehydrated through a graded alcohol series and cleared in xylene. Finally, the slides were mounted using Entellan® mounting medium (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) and allowed to dry prior to examination under a light microscope. The stained sections were assessed for architectural features, cellular morphology, and potential pathological alterations.  5.18 In vivo tumorigenesis and metastasis assays All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Southern University of Science and Technology. NCG nude mice were purchased from the GemPharmatech (Guangdong, China). Xenograft experiments were divided into two groups: control and TAC1 overexpression. SK-N-BE (2)-vector and SK-N-BE (2)-TAC1-OE cells (1 × 106  per mouse) were subcutaneously injected into the right flank of 6-week-old female NCG mice (18-20 g). Tumor length and width were measured every week, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula: (length × width2 )/2. Aprepitant was administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at 10 mg/kg every other day, starting from day 15 after tumor implantation/inoculation, until the experimental endpoint. For the tail vein metastasis model, mice were allocated into two groups: SK-N-BE (2)-vector and SK-N-BE (2)-TAC1-OE cells A total of 1 × 106  pretreated SK-N-BE (2) cells were administered via tail vein injection into NCG mice. Body metastases were monitored weekly using a small animal fluorescence imaging system following the administration of luciferin (Product #P1043, prepared at a concentration of approximately 33.3 mg/mL, with an injection volume of 100 μL). Tumor development and growth were monitored using bioluminescence imaging following the administration of luciferin. At the endpoint, lungs and liver tissues were collected and fixed in 4% phosphate-buffered neutral formalin. Lung samples were further analyzed by hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining and mIHC. Aprepitant was administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at 10 mg/kg every other day, starting from week 3 after tumor implantation/inoculation, until the experimental endpoint.  5.19 CTCs isolation in mice Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) were isolated from the peripheral blood of mice using a four-stage spiral microfluidic device (Celutriate Chip 1) based on inertial microfluidics [48 ]. This label-free enrichment system separates CTCs from whole blood by exploiting size-dependent inertial focusing and Dean flow effects, effectively depleting hematopoietic cells while retaining larger target cells. Fresh peripheral blood (2 mL) was injected directly into the microfluidic device without pretreatment, reducing sample handling and maintaining cell viability. The sample passed sequentially through four spiral microchannel stages incorporating lateral displacement geometry, where hydrodynamic forces directed cells according to size. This design efficiently separated larger CTCs from smaller blood components, including erythrocytes and leukocytes. The complete enrichment process required only 5 min, demonstrating both rapid processing and high throughput. Reported results showed CTC recovery efficiencies of 52.3-65.8% alongside >99.95% leukocyte depletion, substantially enhancing the purity of isolated CTC populations.  5.20 Sample preparation and scRNA sequencing Four fresh specimens subjected to single-cell sequencing were stored in Tissue Preservation Solution (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China) and placed on ice. After samples were washed 3 times with HBSS, GEXSCOPE™ Tissue Dissociation Solution (Singleton Biotechnologies) was added to each sample. Subsequently, the tissue was finely cut into small pieces with scissors and then digested at 37 °C for 8 min to dissociate the tissue into single cells. The single-cell suspension (1 × 105 cells/mL) was then loaded onto microfluidic devices and scRNA-seq libraries were constructed according to Singleron GEXSCOPE™ protocol by GEXSCOPE™ Single-Cell RNA Library Kit (Singleron Biotechnologies). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with 150 bp paired end reads. Five fresh specimens for 10x Genomics Cell Preparation Guide describes best practices and general protocols for washing, counting and concentrating cells from both abundant and limited cell suspensions (greater than or less than 100000 total cells, respectively) in preparation for use in10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols. Cell viability was measured with Acridine Orange/Propidium Iodide (AO/PI) kit. scRNA-seq libraries were prepared using ChromiumTM Single Cell G Chip and Chromium Single Cell 5’ Library & Gel Bead Kit v2 and sequencing was accomplished on an Illumina NovaSeq6000 System using a paired-end 150 bp.  5.21 Single‐cell transcriptome sequencing collection and data analysis For Singleron single-cell transcriptome sequencing and data preprocessing, the Telescope software (version 1.5.1) was used for the preprocessing of the sequencing reads. Briefly, the reads in FASTQ format were aligned to human genome reference (GRCh38) using STAR [49 ], and then “RNA multi-samples” were used to derive a gene expression matrix for each sample. For 10X Genomics single-cell transcriptome sequencing and data preprocessing, the Cell Ranger Single-Cell toolkit (v7.2.0) was applied to align reads for this case based on the human reference genome GRCh38. Downstream analysis of single-cell data was performed using the Seurat R package [50 ]. First, we removed cells with mitochondrial RNA content exceeding 20%, as well as those with UMI counts below 200 or above 6000. Potential doublets were predicted and filtered using ‘DoubletFinder’ R package [51 ], with a doublet removal rate set at 4% per patient. The analysis was performed using five principal components and a default pN value of 20%. The filtered gene expression matrix for each sample was normalized and scaled using the “NormalizeData” and “ScaleData” functions in Seurat R package. Batch effects across different patients were adjusted using the Harmony R package [52 ], and gene expression matrices from all samples were integrated. Principal component analysis (PCA) was then performed on the adjusted expression matrix, utilizing highly variable genes (HVGs) identified by the “FindVariableFeatures” function. Next, the “RunPCA” function was used to perform the PCA and the “FindNeighbors” function was used to construct a K‐nearest‐neighbor graph. The most representative principal components (PCs) selected based on PCA were used for cluster analysis with the ‘FindCluster’ function to identify different cell types. Those with high PECAM1 and VWF expressions were identified as endothelial cells; those with high CHGA and CHGB expressions as neuroblast cells. Following unsupervised clustering, we performed cell subpopulations based on their specifically expressed marker genes and named each subpopulation according to its most significantly enriched gene. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each subpopulation were identified using the ‘wilcoxauc’ function from the presto R package, assessing significance based on log2-transformed fold changes (log2FC) and P -values. We consider differentially expressed genes with log2FC > 0.3 and P -value <0.05 to have potential biological significance. To elucidate signaling pathways enriched in specific subpopulations, we conducted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the “clusterProfiler” R package [53 ], with P- value <0.05 set as the significance threshold.  5.22 Tissue preference of each cell subpopulation To estimate the tissue preference of each subpopulation, as previously outlined [54 ], we calculated Ro/e values, defined as the ratio of observed cell counts to expected cell counts within each cluster. The expected number of cells per cell cluster in each tissue was obtained from the χ2  test. Ro/e > 1 for a subpopulation in each tissue indicates that the cluster is enriched in that tissue.  5.23 Copy number variation calling The inferCNV R package (inferCNV of the Trinity CTAT Project, provided at https://github.com/broadinstitute/inferCNV ) was used to infer large-scale chromosomal copy number variations in each cell. All other parameters were set to their default values.  5.24 Chip-seq and data analysis All chip-seq data for TWIST1 were downloaded in public database ChIP-Atlas [55 ]. We used IGV to visualize the genomic regions, and the enhancer regions were divided into nonoverlapping windows of different sizes (the windows with reads ≤1/20 of window size were filtered out).  5.25 Unsupervised clustering analysis in TARGET-NBL cohort We used the “wilcoxauc” function in presto R package (version 1.0.0) to identify specifically highly expressed genes of each malignant neuroblast cells that formed the cluster-specific gene signatures, with a |log2(FC)| value of >0.58 and a P  value of <0.05 being set as thresholds. Moreover, mitochondrial genes, ribosomal genes, house-keeping genes and immunoglobulin genes were filtered out. Based on these cluster-specific signatures, R package ConsensusClusterPlus (version 1.58.0) was leveraged to perform unsupervised analysis in the TARGET-NBL cohort. Detailed parameter settings were shown as follows: maximum cluster number (maxK) = 5, number of repeats (reps) = 50, proportion of items to sample (pItem) = 0.8, proportion of features to sample (pFeature) = 1, cluster algorithm (clusterAlg) = “hc” (hierarchical clustering), and distance = “pearson”. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to show the distribution difference of different molecular subtypes determined by unsupervised clustering analysis.  5.26 Jaccard similarity analysis According to the 10 subpopulations of malignant cells and three subtypes in TARGET-NBL, the genes with log (fold change) > 0.3 and P < 0.05 were defined as differentially expressed genes. Jaccard similarity was quantified using the differential genes of each subpopulation. The quantity of Jaccard similarity was the proportion of the genes intersecting the two subpopulations to the genes in union in the two subpopulations.  5.27 Calculation of endothelial infiltration score in TARGET-NBL cohort We used the ‘wilcoxauc’ function to identify the specific genes in Veins_ACKR1 and Veins_CDKN1A subpopulations, then applied deconvolution method to calculate Veins_ACKR1 and Veins_CDKN1A score in each sample of the TARGET-NBL cohort. Endothelial cell infiltration fractions were subsequently quantified each sample using MCPcounter [56 ], followed by comparative analysis of infiltration levels between the high- and low-score groups.  5.28 Bulk RNA sequencing data collection and processing Bulk RNA sequencing transcriptome data of patients with TARGET-NBL and E-MTAB-8248 from ArrayExpress database, and the corresponding clinical data were downloaded from Xena database (https://xena.ucsc.edu/ ). Fragments per kilobase million (FPKM) values were converted to transcripts per kilobase million (TPM) values, and the Ensembl gene IDs were converted to gene symbols concerning the annotation file.  5.29 GO enrichment analysis Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was performed using the enrichGO function in the R package clusterProfiler (v4.0) [57 ]. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified by comparing Neuroblast_TAC1 cells with all other malignant neuroblast subpopulations (one-vs-rest). Genes with logFC >0.3 and P  < 0.05 were used as the input gene list.  5.30 Statistical analysis Comparisons between two groups were performed using two-tailed Student's T-test under the normality assumption. Pearson's correlation was used to measure the correlation between two continuous variables and r  > 0.3 and P  < 0.05 was considered significant. Log-rank test was used for univariate survival analyses and showed as the Kaplan-Meier plot. All statistical analyses and visualization were performed using R or GraphPad Prism. The lines in the middle of the box plot are median and the upper and lower lines indicate 25th and 75th percentiles. P  < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The number of replicates and statistical tests used in figures were shown in corresponding figure legends. title: Focal adhesion kinase and p53 synergistically decrease neuroblastoma cell survival
abstract: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and is responsible for over 15% of pediatric cancer deaths. Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase that is important in many facets of neuroblastoma tumor development and progression. The p53 oncogene, although wild type in most neuroblastomas, lacks significant function as a tumor suppressor in these tumors. Recent reports have found that FAK and p53 interact in some tumor types. We have hypothesized FAK and p53 coordinately control each other's expression and also interact in neuroblastoma. In the present study, we showed that not only do FAK and p53 interact but each one controls the expression of the other. In addition, we also examined the effects of FAK inhibition combined with p53 activation in neuroblastoma and showed that these two, in combination, had a synergistic effect on neuroblastoma cell survival. The findings from this present study help to further our understanding of the regulation of neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and may provide novel therapeutic strategies and targets for neuroblastoma and other pediatric solid tumors.
