It causes approximately 15 % of pediatric cancer-related deaths worldwide [1] . Neural crest–derived sympathetic progenitor cells give rise to this tumor. The disease primarily affects infants and young children, with a median age at diagnosis of 1–2 years [2,3] . The disease displays remarkable biological heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous regression in infants to aggressive, treatment-resistant metastatic disease in older children [4] . Globally, clinicians estimate the incidence at 10.5 cases per million children under 15. Genetic predisposition and environmental factors drive notable geographic variability [5] . Nearly half of neuroblastoma cases are high-risk. They are often characterized by MYCN amplification, 11q deletion, and diploidy, all of which are associated with a poor prognosis [6] . Intensive multimodal therapies yield a 5-year survival rate of less than 50 % [7] . The most common metastatic sites are bone and bone marrow. Resistant tumor cells often persist at these sites [8,9] . Because these challenges, together with therapy-related toxicities, persist, there is an urgent need for better-targeted, less toxic treatments [10] . Immunotherapy has emerged as a promising approach. It leverages the unique immunological landscape of neuroblastoma [11] . Tumor cells typically exhibit low or absent MHC class I expression. This reduces their visibility to cytotoxic CD8 + T cells but may increase susceptibility to natural killer (NK) cell-mediated cytotoxicity [12,13] . Nevertheless, the TME remains profoundly immunosuppressive. It is enriched with regulatory T (Treg) cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), which all hinder effective anti-tumor immune responses [14] . Despite these challenges, neuroblastoma expresses several tumor-associated surface antigens that are amenable to immunotherapeutic targeting [15] . Among them, disialoganglioside GD2 is highly expressed on neuroblastoma cells. It is minimally present on normal tissues, except neurons, melanocytes, and peripheral nerves, making it an ideal target [16] . Additional emerging targets, such as B7-H3 (CD276), L1CAM, and glypican-2 (GPC2), offer further opportunities for multi-antigen targeting strategies [17] . Given its clinical maturity, GD2-directed antibody therapy is discussed in detail in 3.1 . This is followed by emerging antibody, cellular, and immunomodulatory platforms. The use of immunotherapy has shifted neuroblastoma management from purely cytotoxic regimens toward immune-based strategies. Among available approaches, GD2-directed monoclonal antibodies (e.g., dinutuximab and naxitamab) are most clinically validated. They are often integrated into multimodal protocols and frequently paired with immune-stimulatory agents. These therapies have improved outcomes in high-risk disease [17] . Mechanistic details and supporting clinical evidence are reviewed in 3.1 . Despite these gains, anti-GD2 therapy is limited by transient immune activation, antigen-escape variants, and treatment-related neuropathic pain [18] . These challenges have pushed the evolution toward cellular immunotherapy platforms. These new platforms can sustain long-term immune surveillance [19] . Consequently, next-generation approaches such as CAR T-cell therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, tumor vaccines, oncolytic virotherapy, and cytokine-based strategies are under active investigation. Early-phase studies report promising antitumor activity [16] . Key immunotherapeutic mechanisms and representative agents discussed in this review are summarized in  Fig. 1 . This review provides a comprehensive overview of current immunotherapeutic strategies in neuroblastoma, highlighting recent clinical advances, mechanistic insights, resistance mechanisms, and future directions. We underscore the critical need for rational combination therapies, biomarker-driven approaches, and personalized treatment strategies to improve outcomes for children afflicted with this challenging malignancy.  2 Tumor immunology and neuroblastoma Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest–derived sympathetic progenitors and can evade immune elimination through a combination of tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental mechanisms [20,21] . A frequent feature is reduced expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I), which limits recognition by cytotoxic CD8 + T cells [22] . This phenotype has been associated with impaired interferon signaling, including reduced activity of interferon regulatory factors and defects in interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)–driven pathways that normally promote antigen presentation and immune activation [23] . Although loss of MHC-I can increase vulnerability to NK cell cytotoxicity, neuroblastoma often establishes compensatory mechanisms that blunt NK-cell function within the TME [12] . The TME is shaped by bidirectional interactions among tumor cells, stromal components (e.g., fibroblasts, mesenchymal stromal cells, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs)), and immune populations including T cells, NK cells, TAMs, MDSCs, Tregs, and dendritic cells (DCs) [24–26] . Collectively, these interactions promote immune dysfunction and facilitate tumor persistence. Multiple cytokine axes contribute to this suppressive milieu. Neuroblastoma-derived CSF-1 can recruit macrophages and favor M2-like polarization, supporting tumor growth and tissue remodeling [12,24] . CAF-mediated extracellular matrix remodeling and secretion of CXCL12 and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) can further reinforce immune suppression by recruiting suppressive myeloid cells and Tregs, limiting NK-cell activation, and promoting T-cell exhaustion [27] . In parallel, interleukin-10 (IL-10) produced by Tregs and other cells suppresses antigen-presenting cell function and dampens effector T-cell responses [28,29] . MYC-family biology, particularly MYCN amplification, plays a central role in establishing an immunologically cold phenotype. MYCN-amplified tumors are associated with increased expression of immunosuppressive and pro-angiogenic mediators (e.g., IL-10, VEGF, CSF-1, and TGF-β), reduced recruitment of effective antigen-presenting and lymphoid populations, and enrichment of Tregs, MDSCs, and TAMs [30–33] . Rapid tumor expansion can also generate hypoxia, with HIF-1α–dependent programs promoting extracellular matrix changes, angiogenesis, and additional barriers to immune infiltration [34] . MYCN-linked regulation of matrix metalloproteinases further supports invasion and dissemination [35] . By contrast, non-MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas more often exhibit greater immune-cell diversity and a greater representation of effector populations, features associated with improved clinical outcomes in several profiling studies [29,36] . Overall, neuroblastoma commonly suppresses immune surveillance through impaired antigen presentation, inhibitory cytokine networks, and accumulation of suppressive myeloid and regulatory lymphoid programs [36] . Therapeutic strategies that recondition the TME and restore effective innate and adaptive immunity are therefore key priorities for improving responses to immunotherapy [37] .  3 Antibody-based immunotherapies and related modalities 3.1 Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies Building on its high tumor expression and limited distribution in normal tissues, GD2 has become the principal target for antibody-based immunotherapy in neuroblastoma. GD2 is a member of the b-series gangliosides synthesized through altered glycosylation patterns in cancer cells [38] . It exhibits low expression in normal tissues but is widely detected in neoplasms, including neuroblastoma, other neuroectodermal-derived tumors, and sarcomas [39] . Among all cancer types, neuroblastoma shows the highest GD2 expression, which promotes tumor cell adhesion and invasiveness, facilitating metastatic dissemination in human cell models [40] . Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) induce tumor cell death primarily by activating the classical complement pathway [41] . These antibodies target the terminal penta-oligosaccharide of GD2 and exert their anti-neuroblastoma effects through antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) [42] . Beyond immune-mediated mechanisms, anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies may also influence tumor survival pathways: preclinical data suggest downregulation of PI3K/Akt signaling in neuroblastoma cells, and at least one older study indicates a reduction in FAK phosphorylation following GD2-targeted treatment [42] . Neuroblastoma cells are particularly susceptible to ADCC and CMC due to diminished expression of complement-inhibitory proteins [43] . High-risk neuroblastoma responds to GD2-targeted mAbs, although different antibodies vary in efficacy and toxicity profiles [44] . Dinutuximab, a chimeric anti-GD2 mAb, was approved by the FDA in 2015 for combination immunotherapy in pediatric high-risk neuroblastoma [45] . Studies have shown that adding dinutuximab to isotretinoin therapy significantly improves event-free survival (EFS) and OS [46] . Dinutuximab beta (DB), another chimeric IgG1 anti-GD2 mAb, received EMA approval in 2017 for children over 12 months with high-risk neuroblastoma responsive to induction therapy or with relapsed/refractory disease [47] . Naxitamab (DANYELZA®, naxitamab-gqgk), a humanized IgG1 anti-GD2 mAb (hu3F8), received accelerated FDA approval for patients aged one year and older with relapsed or refractory high-risk neuroblastoma involving bone or bone marrow, who have shown at least partial response or stable disease after prior therapy [48] . Recent studies suggest that naxitamab-based chemo-immunotherapy, especially in combination with irinotecan, temozolomide, and GM-CSF, is effective in treating primary chemo-resistant high-risk neuroblastoma, with improved response durability when initiated early [49] . Despite their efficacy, anti-GD2 therapies are associated with a distinct toxicity profile due to on-target binding to GD2 on peripheral nerve fibers. The most common adverse effect is infusion-related nerve pain, attributed to complement activation on nerve components [16,50] . Other frequent infusion reactions include fever, chills, urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension, often requiring premedication with antihistamines, analgesics, and corticosteroids [51,52] . Dinutuximab and dinutuximab beta share similar toxicity profiles, though severity and frequency may vary with dosing and concurrent cytokine therapy [53] . Neuropathic pain is typically most intense during initial infusions and may be complicated by capillary leak syndrome, elevated hepatic transaminases, and electrolyte imbalances, as observed in pediatric trials [54] . Co-infusion with cytokines, particularly interleukin-2, has been linked to increased fever, hypotension, and vascular leak, necessitating regimen adjustments for better tolerability [55] . Management strategies include titrated infusion rates, opioid analgesia, gabapentin for neuropathic pain, and close hemodynamic monitoring [53] . For naxitamab, outpatient administration has shown a similar adverse event spectrum. Trial 201 reported frequent occurrences of tachycardia, cough, hypotension, pain, vomiting, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and nausea. Grade ≥ 3 events such as pain, hypotension, urticaria, and bronchospasm were managed with premedication and monitoring [56] . Another study identified abdominal pain, hypotension, urticaria, and bronchospasm as the most common Grade ≥ 3 adverse events, none of which required treatment discontinuation [57] . Experience from China suggests that both overall and severe adverse reactions decrease over successive cycles, indicating improved tolerability with clinical familiarity [58] . Beyond toxicity, acquired resistance can limit the durability of GD2-directed therapies. Antigen modulation, including GD2 downregulation or loss after therapeutic pressure, has been reported in a subset of post-treatment cases (e.g., ∼15–25 % in some series) and may contribute to relapse by enabling immune escape. The molecular and microenvironmental drivers of antigen escape and broader resistance pathways are discussed in 5.1  and provide a rationale for multi-antigen targeting and biomarker-guided combinations.  3.2 Cytokine Therapy Cytokines are soluble mediators that coordinate immune-cell activation, expansion, and trafficking, and they have been incorporated into neuroblastoma immunotherapy primarily to augment effector function and enhance ADCC [59,60] . The cytokines most commonly used in this setting include interleukin-2 (IL-2) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), whereas interferon-alpha (IFN-α) has been explored more selectively [60] . IL-2 can expand and activate NK cells and T lymphocytes, thereby strengthening ADCC in anti-GD2–based regimens [61] . GM-CSF promotes myeloid differentiation and activation, supporting macrophage- and granulocyte-mediated effector mechanisms that can further amplify ADCC [62,63] . IFN-α may enhance antigen presentation pathways and cytotoxic lymphocyte activity, although its clinical use in neuroblastoma remains less well characterized than that of IL-2 or GM-CSF [15,64] . IL-15 has emerged as a mechanistically attractive alternative to IL-2 because it stimulates NK cells and CD8 + T cells through shared receptor components while potentially reducing some IL-2–associated toxicities and unwanted expansion of regulatory subsets [65] . In preclinical neuroblastoma models, IL-15 has demonstrated antitumor activity and has therefore been prioritized for continued translational evaluation [66,67] . Cytokine signaling also intersects with broader tumor biology; for example, IL-6 and VEGF contribute to inflammatory and angiogenic programs, whereas IFN-γ can promote anti-tumor immune activity in appropriate contexts [68,69] . Engineered cytokine–antibody formats (e.g., immunocytokines) have been investigated to concentrate immune stimulation at the tumor site and intensify cytotoxic effector functions [70,71] . Clinically, the most mature evidence supporting cytokine use comes from regimens combining anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies with IL-2 and/or GM-CSF, which improve survival outcomes in high-risk neuroblastoma and enhance ADCC through activation of innate effector cells [72–74] . In relapsed/refractory disease, cytokines have also been incorporated into chemo-immunotherapy combinations (e.g., with temozolomide and irinotecan) to increase response rates compared with chemotherapy alone in selected settings [75,76] . However, randomized European experiences have reported increased toxicity without clear survival benefit for certain IL-2 schedules, reinforcing the need to optimize dosing, route, and patient selection [46,74,77] . Toxicity remains a major limitation of cytokine therapy, particularly with IL-2, which can cause capillary leak syndrome, fever, hypotension, and related systemic adverse effects [78] . These tolerability constraints, together with the suppressive neuroblastoma microenvironment, motivate continued evaluation of alternative cytokine strategies (e.g., IL-15–based approaches) that aim to preserve immune potentiation while improving safety [65,79] .  3.3 Checkpoint inhibitors ICIs block immune checkpoints, surface proteins that help prevent overactivation of the immune system, thereby enhancing the body's ability to target and destroy tumor cells [80] . The main checkpoints targeted by these drugs are programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) and its ligand PD-L1, as well as cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein-4 (CTLA-4) and its ligands B7–1 and B7–2. These checkpoints regulate the activation of T cells—a type of white blood cell that attacks infected or cancerous cells—and help maintain the body's tolerance to its own tissues. Tumors can manipulate these pathways to evade immune system attack [81,82] . PD-1 is found on the surface of activated T cells, B cells (another type of white blood cell involved in immune responses), and NK cells (cells that target infected or abnormal cells without prior activation). When PD-1 binds to its partners, PD-L1 or PD-L2, it inhibits the immune response [83] . CTLA-4 inhibits the interaction between CD28 and B7 on antigen-presenting cells, thereby reducing T-cell activation. Although these mechanisms are essential for preventing autoimmune reactions, tumors exploit them to foster an environment that suppresses the immune response and supports tumor growth [84,85] . Checkpoint blockade therapy uses monoclonal antibodies to inhibit PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4. This approach has transformed treatment for several adult malignancies, especially those with high tumor mutation burden (TMB) and strong immunogenicity [86] . However, neuroblastoma presents unique ICI therapy challenges. High-risk neuroblastoma usually shows low TMB, lacks classical HLA class I expression, and has minimal or absent PD-L1 on tumor cells. As a result, it is immunologically "cold" [11,87] . PD-L1 is mainly expressed on TAMs, whereas neuroblastoma cells are often PD-L1-negative [88] . High macrophage-derived PD-L1 levels correlate with better survival. In contrast, a PD-1/PD-L1 ratio over 1 links to poor outcomes. This balance between checkpoint expression is clinically relevant. Other immune-modulatory pathways, like SLAMF7 signaling in macrophages, enhance phagocytosis. They are associated with a better prognosis [89] . Pediatric neuroblastoma trials of ICIs have shown modest activity. Nivolumab (anti-PD-1) and atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) are well tolerated. However, they rarely yield objective responses and offer limited benefit in stabilizing disease [90–92] . Similarly, ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) is tolerated but has negligible single-agent efficacy. Patients with immune-related adverse events tend to have better survival. This suggests partial immune activation [93] . These findings emphasize the need for biomarker-enriched trials, given the enrolled patients' low TMB and PD-L1 expression [94] . Preclinical models have studied resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) and strategies to overcome it. Anti-GD2 antibodies can induce increased PD-L1 expression on neuroblastoma cells. This makes cancer cells more sensitive to drugs that block programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and increases the destruction of cancer cells by immune cells, a process known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, in both laboratory studies (in vitro) and living organisms (in vivo) [88] . Combined blockade of CTLA-4 and PD-1, especially with the chemotherapy drug cyclophosphamide or vaccines made from tumor cells, increases the activity of immune cells called effector CD8 + T cells and can lead to complete tumor regression in cancer-prone mouse models [33,95] . These findings underscore the potential of multi-modal approaches to overcome innate resistance in high-risk neuroblastoma. Additionally, PD-L1-positive NK cells in neuroblastoma tumors are highly activated and functionally intact, and their presence independently correlates with favorable outcomes. Their presence suggests that combining ICIs with NK cell–based adoptive transfer may enhance anti-tumor activity by circumventing the limitations of ICI monotherapy [96,97] . Furthermore, dual blockade of TIGIT and PD-L1 in preclinical mouse models has demonstrated superior tumor growth inhibition compared to single-agent treatments [98] .  3.4 Cancer vaccines Vaccines have emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for neuroblastoma, aiming to stimulate the immune system to recognize and eliminate tumor cells by delivering tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) or neoantigens. These approaches may prevent disease recurrence and improve patient survival [99,100] . Given the poor tolerance of pediatric patients to highly toxic treatments, vaccine-based therapy offers a focused method for generating robust antitumor immunity with reduced systemic toxicity [100] . Among immunotherapeutic modalities, DC vaccines have been investigated in neuroblastoma, with early-phase studies demonstrating feasibility and immunologic activity [101,102] . DCs, as professional antigen-presenting cells, bridge innate and adaptive immunity by internalizing antigens from the TME and presenting them to T cells via MHC molecules in secondary lymphoid organs, thereby triggering cytotoxic immune responses [103] . In DC-based vaccines, patient-derived or in vitro–differentiated DCs are loaded with TAAs or neoantigens and reinjected into the patient. This enhances tumor-specific T-cell activation and promotes antitumor immunity with a favorable safety profile [104] . Effective chemokine-directed migration of DCs to the TME is also critical, enabling interaction with other immune cells, including NK cells, and amplifying global immune activation [105,106] . Preclinical and clinical studies have provided growing evidence supporting the feasibility of DC-based vaccination in neuroblastoma and other pediatric solid tumors. Mechanistic experiments demonstrate that DCs derived from defined precursors efficiently prime cytotoxic T cells and orchestrate potent antitumor immune responses, validating their use as professional antigen-presenting platforms [107,108] . Early-phase clinical data indicate that autologous, monocyte-derived DCs pulsed with tumor lysate or tumor-associated antigens are safe and capable of eliciting measurable T-cell responses in children with high-risk neuroblastoma, though objective tumor regression remains uncommon [109] . Broader reviews of pediatric cancer vaccination confirm the immunogenicity of DC platforms but emphasize persistent variability in clinical efficacy and the need to refine antigen selection, DC maturation protocols, and delivery strategies [110,111] . Continued investigation combining DC vaccines with checkpoint blockade or cytokine adjuvants may enhance durability and depth of response in neuroblastoma patients [107] . Recent advances in personalized immunotherapy have focused on neoantigen-directed and mRNA vaccines, often combined with nanotechnology to enhance delivery and immune activation [112,113] . Neoantigens, derived from tumor-specific mutations, are inherently immunogenic due to their lack of central tolerance, making them ideal targets for personalized vaccine design and prompting rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluation of novel vaccine platforms [114,115] . mRNA vaccines encode tumor-specific antigens that are taken up by DCs and processed into MHC-bound peptides, stimulating both humoral and cellular immunity [116] . In neuroblastoma, targets such as GD2 have been successfully addressed using mRNA vaccines, resulting in potent immune responses and tumor regression in preclinical models. However, challenges with vaccine platforms may hinder translation into clinical practice [117] . Nanoparticle-based delivery systems, including lipid nanoparticles and polymers, improve vaccine stability, optimize biodistribution, and facilitate penetration across the blood–brain barrier, enabling effective antigen presentation to brain tumors [118,119] . Despite these promising developments, challenges remain. The immunosuppressive TME, particularly in the central nervous system, and the protective physiology of the blood–brain barrier complicate vaccine delivery and immune activation [104] . Effective chemokine-directed migration of DCs to the TME is also critical, enabling interaction with other immune cells, including NK cells, and amplifying global immune activation [120,121] . Preclinical and clinical data support the potential of DC vaccines in neuroblastoma, although effective delivery and overcoming the immunosuppressive microenvironment remain challenges.  3.5 Oncolytic viruses Clinical activity with oncolytic viruses (OVs) has already been demonstrated in neural crest–derived tumors such as melanoma, where the FDA-approved oncolytic herpes simplex virus (HSV), talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), reduced tumor burden and improved outcomes [122,123] . OVs are broadly classified into naturally occurring viruses with inherent tumor selectivity and genetically modified viruses engineered to enhance tumor tropism and safety. Wild-type OVs, such as reovirus, Newcastle disease virus, and parvovirus, exploit tumor-associated defects in interferon signaling or oncogenic pathways (e.g., Ras) to replicate selectively within cancer cells [124] . Genetic engineering of viral backbones has enabled the expression of tumor-associated antigens (e.g., NY-ESO-1) or adaptor molecules, such as protein A, for antibody-mediated retargeting, thereby increasing specificity for neuroblastoma cells [125] . Several viral vectors have been explored in pediatric solid tumors. Adenovirus (Ad), a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus, is widely used due to its well-characterized biology and amenability to genetic manipulation [126] . HSV-1, a neurotropic virus with an established safety profile, has been extensively studied in brain tumors and is a suitable candidate for neuroblastoma [127,128] . Other OVs under investigation include poliovirus, measles virus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), vaccinia virus (VV), Seneca Valley virus (SVV), Sindbis virus (SINV), Zika virus, and parvoviruses [129] . Beyond viral platform selection, the strength of the preclinical evidence in neuroblastoma is heavily influenced by the model system used [130] . Much of the early efficacy literature relies on immunodeficient xenografts, which are valuable for demonstrating direct oncolysis but systematically underrepresent adaptive immune dynamics central to OV-mediated “in situ vaccination” [131] . Consequently, translation requires greater emphasis on immunocompetent or humanized platforms capable of capturing antigen spreading, interferon-driven antiviral restriction, myeloid reprogramming, and the durability of T- and NK-cell memory responses [132] . In practice, this includes orthotopic or metastatic neuroblastoma models to reflect osteomedullary tropism, longitudinal immune profiling (e.g., intratumoral chemokine induction, TCR clonality expansion, and myeloid polarization), and evaluation of OV performance under clinically relevant constraints such as prior chemotherapy, corticosteroid exposure, and variable baseline anti-viral serostatus [130,133] . A second translational determinant is vector immunogenicity and the kinetics of viral clearance [134] . Systemic delivery is often limited by complement activation, Fc- and scavenger receptor–mediated uptake, and rapid induction of neutralizing antibodies after initial dosing, which can prevent re-dosing and truncate intratumoral replication [135] . These barriers are especially salient in pediatric settings, where repeated administrations may be necessary to sustain immune pressure in metastatic disease [129] . Emerging strategies to mitigate premature clearance include cell-carrier delivery (e.g., MSC- or immune-cell “Trojan horse” approaches), capsid/envelope engineering to reduce antibody binding, transient modulation of innate sensing pathways, and rational scheduling with checkpoint blockade to preserve antitumor immunity while managing excessive anti-viral immunity [136,137] . These design considerations should be incorporated into neuroblastoma-focused OV pipelines alongside standard safety measures (e.g., tumor-selective promoters, microRNA targeting, and attenuation of neurovirulence for neurotropic backbones) [129] . OVs exert antitumor effects through multiple mechanisms: selective replication and tumor cytolysis, induction of immunogenic cell death with release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), disruption of tumor vasculature, and transgene-mediated delivery of therapeutic genes to enhance immunity [138] . Genetic modifications, such as tumor-specific promoters (e.g., hTERT), microRNA binding sites, or targeting of neuroblastoma-specific alterations (MYCN amplification, ALK mutations, p53 inactivation), can improve tumor specificity and reduce off-target toxicity [139,140] . OVs interact closely with innate immunity, particularly NK cells, which present a dual challenge. On one hand, NK cells can prematurely eliminate viral particles and limit replication; on the other hand, they play a critical role in OV-induced antitumor immunity. Recent studies show that combining oHSV with Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-targeted CAR-NK cells or priming NK cells via OV infection enhances tumor clearance in preclinical models [135,141] . A recent neuroblastoma-focused example illustrates how OV “arming” can be leveraged to enhance effector-cell function: an IL-21–secreting oncolytic HSV platform (C021) increased the activity of CAR-NK cells in neuroblastoma models, improving cytotoxic mediator release (e.g., IFN-γ, granzyme B, perforin) and extending survival in xenograft settings compared with non–cytokine-secreting parental virus controls [142] . Such data support the concept that cytokine-armed OVs can simultaneously debulk tumors and recondition the microenvironment to favor innate effector persistence, providing a mechanistic rationale for the co-development of OV–cell therapy in neuroblastoma. Early clinical experience in neuroblastoma has shown encouraging safety and feasibility. The first pediatric report of oncolytic adenovirus therapy involved a six-year-old with stage IV refractory disease who exhibited measurable viral expression in metastatic tumors [143] . To improve systemic delivery and potentially reduce toxicity, autologous mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been used as carriers in the Celyvir system to deliver ICOVIR-5 adenovirus. In a first-in-human, first-in-child trial, the treatment was well tolerated, and in children with refractory neuroblastoma, 2 patients showed disease stabilization (although no confirmed long-term remission has been reported) [144] . Other viruses, such as Pexa-Vec (modified vaccinia virus), were safe but showed limited efficacy in pediatric trials [145] . Seneca Valley Virus NTX-010 was well tolerated but rapidly cleared due to neutralizing antibodies, highlighting the challenge of sustaining viral replication in the clinic [146] . Combination regimens offer promise in overcoming these limitations. Preclinical and translational studies suggest that OVs can be combined with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and, especially, immunotherapy, such as checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4, anti-PD-1/PD-L1), to create an inflammatory TME conducive to T cell infiltration and activation [124] . Given their modifiability, ability to bypass conventional resistance mechanisms, and favorable toxicity profiles, OVs represent a compelling immunotherapeutic modality for neuroblastoma, particularly in combination strategies. 3.5.1 Emerging challenges and future preclinical directions Despite encouraging safety signals, several obstacles still limit the clinical impact of OVs in neuroblastoma. First, durable efficacy is limited by poor intratumoral spread in bulky or fibrotic lesions. It is also challenged by spatially uneven viral replication, especially in metastatic sites like bone marrow [129] . Second, anti-viral immunity can trigger inflammation but may also prematurely end viral replication. This shortens the window for antigen release and cross-priming [147] . Third, neuroblastoma’s immunologically cold biology, especially in MYCN-amplified disease, can weaken antigen presentation and limit effector recruitment. Even when local inflammation occurs, rational combinations remain necessary. These might include OV with checkpoint blockade, cytokine-armed approaches, or antibody- and cell-based therapies [148] . Finally, the field would benefit from using standardized endpoints in preclinical studies. These include immune correlates of response (chemokine induction, antigen spreading, myeloid repolarization), resistance signatures (dominant antiviral over antitumor transcriptional programs, rapid seroconversion, metabolic suppression), and comparisons of dosing and administration (intratumoral/locoregional versus systemic) [124,130] . These priorities create a near-term roadmap for improving neuroblastoma OV data sets and for choosing combination regimens more likely to succeed.    4 Adoptive cell therapy: CAR-T and beyond Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is a transformative strategy in cancer immunotherapy, particularly in hematologic malignancies, enabling T cells to recognize tumor antigens independently of MHC presentation [149,150] . CARs are synthetic receptors composed of a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) domain targeting a tumor-associated antigen, linked to intracellular signaling domains such as CD28 or 4–1BB to promote activation and persistence [151] . In neuroblastoma (NB), GD2 is the most extensively characterized target due to its high, near-universal expression on tumor cells and its minimal presence in normal tissues, offering a favorable therapeutic window [152] . Preclinical models have demonstrated potent anti-tumor activity of GD2-targeting CAR-T cells; for instance, high-affinity GD2 CARs (e.g., E101K mutant) achieved tumor control in xenograft models but were associated with Central Nervous System (CNS) toxicity, highlighting on-target/off-tumor risks [153,154] . To overcome tumor heterogeneity and antigen escape in neuroblastoma, alternative CAR targets such as B7-H3 and L1CAM have been investigated. B7-H3 is broadly expressed in the majority of neuroblastoma tumors, reported in approximately 55–97 % of cases, including some GD2-negative subtypes, and B7-H3-directed CAR-T cells have demonstrated potent preclinical efficacy in pediatric solid tumor models [155,156] . L1CAM has also been explored as a potential CAR-T target in neuroblastoma, although early clinical studies showed limited efficacy and no objective responses. In contrast, early-phase trials using intracerebroventricular or locoregional administration of B7-H3 CAR-T cells in pediatric CNS tumors demonstrated encouraging safety and local antitumor activity. However, low-level B7-H3 expression in certain normal tissues, such as the TRUCKs (fourth-generation CARs), is engineered in the pancreas and liver, raising potential concerns for on-target/off-tumor toxicity with systemic delivery. [157,158] . L1CAM, another promising NB antigen, has been targeted via a glycosylation-specific epitope (CE7); however, a phase I trial reported limited clinical responses, with only one of six low-tumor-burden patients showing regression [159] . MYCN amplification, a hallmark of aggressive NB, suppresses immune signaling and antigen presentation (e.g., L1CAM), contributing to an immunosuppressive microenvironment and reduced CAR-T efficacy [29] . Combination therapy with MYCN inhibitors (e.g., MLN8237) has shown potential to restore antigen expression and enhance CAR-T function, albeit with increased toxicity [158] . Despite success in hematologic cancers, CAR-T therapy in solid tumors faces multiple challenges: poor tumor infiltration due to physical barriers (vasculature, ECM), immunosuppressive TMEs (e.g., MDSCs, Tregs, TAMs, TGF-β, IL-10), and treatment-related toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome [160,161] . Engineering strategies such as C-C chemokine receptor type 2b (CCR2b) and C-X-C chemokine receptor type 2 (CXCR2) expression have improved tumor homing, while interleukin-6 (IL-6) blockade (tocilizumab), corticosteroids, and interleukin-1 (IL-1) inhibitors (e.g., anakinra) help mitigate toxicities [162–164] . To overcome these barriers, next-generation CARs have been developed. TRUCKs (fourth-generation CARs) are engineered to secrete cytokines (e.g., Interleukin 12 (IL-12) and IL-15) upon antigen recognition, reshaping the TME and activating innate immunity, though systemic toxicity remains a concern [162,165] . "Armored CARs are engineered to resist immunosuppression and enhance T cell function by incorporating elements such as PD-1 dominant-negative receptors or cytokine traps (e.g., dnTGF-βRII). Preclinical and early clinical studies have shown promising results [162] . Logic-gated and switchable CARs, such as SynNotch-based platforms, allow context-dependent activation, improving specificity and reducing off-tumor effects [166] . Additional innovations, including CAR-NK platforms, CAR-antibody hybrids, and switch receptors like PD-1/CD28, aim to optimize safety, persistence, and tumor recognition [167,168] . Moreover, targeting novel tumor-associated antigens such as CLDN6, EphA2, VEGFR-2, and LunX expands the therapeutic landscape of CAR-T cells in solid tumors [169–171] . The interplay of cellular and antibody-based immunotherapies in neuroblastoma is summarized in Fig. 1 , which illustrates how CAR-T cells, cytokines, and antibody-dependent mechanisms collectively enhance tumor eradication.  5 Biomarkers, resistance pathways, and combination strategies Immunotherapy has revolutionized the treatment of neuroblastoma, particularly in high-risk disease, yet most patients derive limited clinical benefit [11,172] . Both innate and acquired resistance, driven by tumor-intrinsic features, a suppressive TME, and host immune dynamics, pose significant barriers to durable immune control [173] . Elucidating these complex resistance mechanisms and identifying predictive biomarkers is essential for designing rational combination regimens that improve outcomes in children with neuroblastoma [174] . 5.1 Mechanisms of resistance to immunotherapy in neuroblastoma Tumor heterogeneity and antigen loss drive immunotherapy resistance, especially in treatments needing stable GD2 expression [19,175,176] . The main mechanisms underlying immunotherapy resistance in neuroblastoma are illustrated in  Fig. 2 , highlighting how antigen loss, immune exhaustion, and suppressive cytokines shape an immune-evasive TME. Neuroblastoma cells evade immune recognition by downregulating GD2 through genetic alterations, epigenetic silencing, or adaptive depletion under therapeutic pressure. GD2 downregulation has been observed in approximately 15–25 % of patients following anti-GD2 antibody therapy [177] , driven by transcriptional suppression and enzymatic degradation of ganglioside biosynthesis pathways, notably involving downregulation of ST8SIA1 and B4GALNT1 [178] . Tumor plasticity and subclonal evolution further contribute to antigenic drift. Immunotherapy itself can select for GD2-negative variants. Single-cell sequencing and immunohistochemistry have revealed that relapsed neuroblastomas often contain GD2-low or GD2-negative subpopulations. This shift is associated with lineage transdifferentiation, where tumors adopt a more mesenchymal phenotype, reducing GD2 expression and increasing resistance [98,179] . T-cell exhaustion is another critical barrier to effective immunotherapy. It is characterized by chronic expression of inhibitory receptors, impaired cytokine production, and reduced proliferative capacity [180] . Persistent antigen exposure, TME-mediated suppression, and prolonged cytokine stimulation promote exhaustion. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) frequently express markers such as PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT, indicative of functional impairment [181] . Advanced immune profiling shows that exhausted T cells in neuroblastoma coexpress multiple checkpoints and possess transcriptional signatures distinct from those of adult tumors [13] . This phenotype undermines the efficacy of T-cell–based therapies, including CAR-T cells, as terminally exhausted cells respond poorly to checkpoint blockade and fail to mount robust antitumor responses [182] . Although less prominent than in adult cancers, PD-1/PD-L1 signaling remains significant in neuroblastoma. Elevated expression of CTLA-4, TIGIT, and LAG-3 on T cells and myeloid cells is increasingly observed [180,183] . Inflammatory cytokines often induce this upregulation during immunostimulation or as a feedback response to immunotherapy. Tumor cells exploit these pathways to escape immune surveillance, for example, IFN-γ induces PD-L1 expression, while TGF-β and IL-10 promote CTLA-4 and TIGIT expression on T cells [184] . IL-6, commonly elevated in chronic inflammation, also contributes to PD-L1 induction and expansion of MDSCs [18,185] . Immunosuppressive cells dominate the TME and actively suppress antitumor immunity. Tregs, MDSCs, and M2-polarized TAMs are enriched in high-risk neuroblastoma and correlate with poor response to immunotherapy [186,187] . Tregs inhibit effector T cells via cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β, metabolic suppression via CD39/CD73-mediated adenosine production, and checkpoint ligand expression [11] . MDSCs suppress T and NK cells through arginase-1, reactive oxygen species, and nitric oxide, while promoting Treg expansion and angiogenesis. M2-TAMs contribute to immunosuppressive cytokine secretion, tissue remodeling, and tumor progression [186,188] . Metabolic immunosuppression represents an additional, increasingly recognized resistance axis. It often operates alongside antigen loss and checkpoint-mediated exhaustion [24] . Neuroblastoma-driven depletion of key nutrients, such as tryptophan and arginine, and build-up of suppressive metabolites can directly impair T-cell proliferation, reduce NK-cell cytotoxicity, and promote expansion or dominance of suppressive myeloid programs [189,190] . Notably, polyamine metabolism—linked to aggressive neuroblastoma—can reinforce a cold immune phenotype by promoting suppressive myeloid polarization and limiting effector infiltration [191] . These metabolic constraints can act as upstream resistance determinants. Unless targeted with metabolic modulators, they blunt the benefit of antibodies, checkpoint blockade, and adoptive cellular therapies [190] . Chemokine-guided recruitment, spatial organization, and exosome-mediated signaling together establish a niche that fosters tumor persistence. High densities of these myeloid cells are associated with intrinsic resistance to monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T cell therapies [12] .  5.2 Biomarkers of response and resistance GD2 remains the principal target for immunotherapy in neuroblastoma. However, inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity of GD2 expression significantly influences therapeutic efficacy. Specifically, immunophenotyping studies reveal that a substantial subset of high-risk neuroblastomas exhibit partial or heterogeneous GD2 expression, particularly after exposure to anti-GD2 antibodies or relapse [178] . As a result, GD2-low or negative subsets are associated with treatment failure and poor prognosis. Additionally, lineage plasticity, including mesenchymal transition, can drive GD2-low states and therapy resistance (see 5.1 ) [192] . Beyond GD2 status, immune cell infiltration density and phenotype within neuroblastoma lesions serve as key biomarkers of therapeutic response. Tumors with an "immunologically hot" immune microenvironment, rich in CD8 + T cells, NK cells, and M1-like macrophages, are more likely to respond to immunotherapies, unlike "cold" or immune-excluded tumors [193,194] . To define these features, multiparameter flow cytometry and spatial transcriptomics are employed to derive immune infiltration signatures predictive of response. High baseline or on-treatment infiltration of cytotoxic T cells or activated NK cells correlates with benefit from anti-GD2 antibodies, cytokine modulation, and cell therapies [13] . Conversely, enrichment of Tregs, MDSCs, or M2 TAMs predicts resistance [192] . In addition to cellular markers, cytokine profiles also serve as biomarkers. Elevated levels of TGF-β, IL-10, and C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) are associated with immunosuppression and treatment failure. In contrast, increased IFN-γ, TNF-α, or GM-CSF is associated with therapeutic responses in certain contexts [195] . Another factor informing biomarker-driven stratification is ALK mutation status. ALK-mutant neuroblastomas are more aggressive and exhibit immune evasion features, including impaired antigen presentation, elevated levels of immunosuppressive cytokines, and altered checkpoint expression [196] . These tumors also show changes in TME composition, reduced sensitivity to cytotoxic lymphocytes, and variable responses to targeted and immune therapies [14,193] . Epigenetic modifications further contribute to immune evasion by suppressing immune signaling and antigen expression [197] . Specific patterns, such as H3K27me3, help distinguish between immune-active and immunologically cold neuroblastomas and predict immunotherapy response [196] . Transcriptomic profiling has further delineated gene signatures of immunologically hot or cold phenotypes, enabling predictive modeling based on both tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental features [198] . Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have become central tools for identifying novel biomarkers and potential combination therapy targets. These include metabolic enzymes (e.g., IDO1, ARG1) and chemokine receptors (e.g., CXCR4) that are enriched in resistant tumors. Conversely, widespread expression of anti-tumor chemokines, such as CXCL9 and CXCL10, has been associated with improved therapeutic responses [199,200] . Importantly, the clinical utility of biomarkers depends not only on their biological relevance but also on feasibility, reproducibility, and predictive performance at a decision-making timepoint [201] . For example, ALK mutation status is clinically actionable for selecting ALK inhibitors; however, its value as a stand-alone predictor of immunotherapy benefit remains uncertain, because ALK-driven immune evasion and changes in antigen presentation may not translate into consistent response patterns across immunotherapy modalities [202,203] . Similarly, cytokine “signatures” are often context-dependent: circulating cytokines are influenced by tumor burden, concurrent infections, steroid exposure, and the timing of sampling relative to therapy, which can limit specificity and make fixed thresholds difficult to generalize [204,205] . Accordingly, cytokine panels are more likely to be clinically useful when prospectively standardized (baseline and on-treatment timepoints), combined with cellular readouts (e.g., NK/T-cell activation markers), and validated in independent cohorts [206] . High-dimensional profiling approaches such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics can strengthen biomarker development by resolving intratumoral cellular states, antigen-expression heterogeneity, and the spatial architecture of immune suppression [207] . In practice, these data can inform trial design by: enriching or stratifying patients based on immune phenotype (immune-desert, immune-excluded, inflamed), identifying dominant suppressive programs (e.g., myeloid-driven, TGF-β–rich, adenosine/metabolic) to rationally select combination partners, mapping co-expression of target antigens across tumor subclones to prioritize multi-antigen CAR-T/NK constructs, and defining pharmacodynamic endpoints through on-treatment biopsies that track pathway modulation and immune-cell state transitions [98,208] . Key limitations include inter-tumor heterogeneity, temporal evolution under therapy, sampling bias from single-site biopsies, and analytical variability across platforms; mitigation strategies include multi-region and longitudinal sampling, integration with liquid biopsy (ctDNA/ctRNA) to capture systemic representation, and pre-specified, centralized bioinformatics pipelines to support regulatory-grade reproducibility [24,98] .  5.3 Combination strategies to enhance immunotherapy efficacy The multifaceted resistance of neuroblastoma to immunotherapy necessitates multi-targeted combination approaches. Over the past decade, preclinical and clinical studies have explored combinations of immune therapies with checkpoint inhibitors, targeted agents, and TME modulators to improve outcomes [208] . Meanwhile, cytotoxic therapies remain foundational in treating high-risk neuroblastoma and possess potent immunomodulatory effects [15] . Specifically, chemotherapeutic agents can enhance antitumor immunity by inducing immunogenic cell death, exposing neoantigens, upregulating death receptors (e.g., Fas/CD95 and TRAIL receptors DR4/DR5), and depleting immunosuppressive TME components, such as Tregs and MDSCs [209] . Combining immunotherapies with induction or consolidation chemotherapy has shown synergistic tumor control in preclinical and clinical settings [210] . For instance, anti-GD2 antibodies exhibit enhanced ADCC when combined with agents such as cyclophosphamide and topotecan [211] . Radiotherapy similarly promotes local immune activation, enhances antigen presentation, and induces in situ vaccination, thereby enhancing the efficacy of CAR-T or NK cell therapies [95] . Given the heterogeneity of checkpoint molecules implicated in T-cell exhaustion and resistance, dual or multi-checkpoint blockade has emerged as a promising strategy. In neuroblastoma preclinical models, combining anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 therapy with CTLA-4, LAG-3, or TIGIT inhibitors has demonstrated synergistic antitumor activity. These combinations enhance T-cell reinvigoration, increase cytotoxic lymphocyte infiltration, and prevent or overcome adaptive resistance in both murine and patient-derived xenograft models [212,213] . Targeted therapies and small-molecule inhibitors also modulate neuroblastoma immunogenicity through distinct mechanisms. ALK inhibitors (e.g., crizotinib, lorlatinib) are particularly relevant in ALK-mutated neuroblastomas. Inhibiting ALK signaling can reverse immunosuppressive features of the TME, enhance tumor antigenicity, and increase sensitivity to immune-mediated killing [214] . Other targeted agents, such as EZH2 histone methyltransferase inhibitors, can de-repress immune-activating genes and improve responses to checkpoint blockade [215,216] . Additionally, metabolic interventions are emerging as pragmatic combination partners to counteract tumor-driven immune suppression and to address resistance mechanisms that are not fully reversible by checkpoint blockade alone [217] . A particularly relevant axis in neuroblastoma is polyamine metabolism, in which ornithine decarboxylase (ODC1) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in polyamine biosynthesis [218] . Polyamine abundance can sustain suppressive myeloid phenotypes, constrain cytotoxic lymphocyte fitness, and thereby synergize with antigenic and checkpoint-based resistance pathways [219] . Pharmacologic ODC1 inhibition with difluoromethylornithine (DFMO/eflornithine) reduces polyamine pools and has been proposed to recondition the TME toward improved immune effector function, providing a mechanistic rationale for combining DFMO with antibody- or cell-based immunotherapies (e.g., anti-GD2 regimens, CAR-based platforms) [220] . Clinically, DFMO has also been evaluated as a post-standard-of-care maintenance approach in high-risk neuroblastoma, with externally controlled comparisons suggesting improved event-free and OS, supporting continued investigation of polyamine targeting in risk-adapted, biomarker-informed regimens [221] . A key translational nuance is that tumors may compensate for reduced biosynthesis by increasing polyamine uptake, potentially blunting DFMO’s immunometabolic effects [222] . Recent mechanistic work implicates the polyamine transporter ATP13A3 as a mediator of DFMO-induced polyamine uptake in neuroblastoma, highlighting an actionable resistance mechanism and providing a rationale for dual targeting of polyamine synthesis and transport/uptake in combination strategies [223] . In this context, pairing DFMO with inhibitors of polyamine uptake (or transport-associated vulnerabilities) represents a rational next step to sustain metabolic pressure while immunotherapies drive effector engagement and antigen spreading [214] . Collectively, these combination strategies, spanning cytotoxic agents, checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and metabolic modulators, represent a rational path forward to overcome resistance and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy in neuroblastoma. Future clinical trials incorporating biomarker-driven patient selection and multi-modal regimens will be critical to translating these insights into durable clinical benefit.   6 Clinical trials landscape Recent clinical trials have focused on the immunotherapeutic potential of GD2-targeted strategies in neuroblastoma. This is especially true in high-risk and relapsed cases. Central agents such as naxitamab and dinutuximab are often combined with immune-stimulatory molecules, such as GM-CSF  and β-glucan. These combinations aim to enhance ADCC, improve innate immune activation, and reduce relapse rates. To complement qualitative synthesis, incorporating quantitative efficacy metrics from clinical trials can sharpen cross-study interpretation [224] . Key endpoints in neuroblastoma immunotherapy studies include objective response rate (ORR; the proportion achieving complete or partial response), as well as time-to-event measures such as progression-free survival (PFS), EFS, OS, and, where randomized comparators are used, hazard ratios (HR) summarizing relative treatment effects [225] . For example, the randomized ANBL0032 study (NCT00026312) showed that adding dinutuximab-based immunotherapy to isotretinoin improved 2-year EFS (66 ± 5 % vs. 46 ± 5 %) and 2-year OS (86 ± 4 % vs. 75 ± 5 %). This underscores the value of standardized survival metrics alongside narrative conclusions [226] . Phase I trials have primarily addressed feasibility, pharmacokinetics, and safety. For example, NCT07027748 explored prolonged naxitamab infusion with GM-CSF, irinotecan, and temozolomide. The goal was to synergize immune stimulation and cytotoxicity while minimizing neurotoxicity [227] . NCT05782959 tested BCD-245, a next-generation anti-GD2 antibody with reduced inflammatory side effects [228] . NCT05421897 evaluated a rapid infusion of dinutuximab to reduce hospitalization duration without compromising safety. These studies reflect efforts to optimize delivery and tolerability [229] . Phase II trials have shifted toward efficacy and dosing refinement. NCT06528496 combined reduced-intensity chemotherapy with anti-GD2 and GM-CSF to balance efficacy and toxicity [230] . NCT06013618 assessed naxitamab alone and in combination with chemotherapy in patients with refractory disease [231] . NCT04936529 and NCT06057948 integrated β-glucan, GM-CSF, and OPT-821 vaccine to sustain anti-tumor memory [232,233] . The comprehensive NCT04385277 trial combined dinutuximab, sargramostim, chemotherapy, isotretinoin, and Iobenguane I-123 to target residual disease [234] . Expanding on the diversity of phase II efforts, additional studies such as NCT06574698 and NCT06438614 evaluated naxitamab + GM-CSF with or without ICE chemotherapy in relapsed or soft-tissue–associated neuroblastoma [235,236] . The New Approaches to Neuroblastoma Therapy (NANT) STING protocol (NCT06450041) incorporated NK cells and anti-GD2 therapy to enhance innate-adaptive synergy. NCT05489887 investigated early integration of immunotherapy during induction chemotherapy in newly diagnosed patients [235] . Hybrid phase I/II trials explored novel cellular and molecular combinations. NCT04238819 combined abemaciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor, with chemotherapy and immunotherapy. This approach assessed cell-cycle inhibition alongside immune activation [237] . NCT06948994 evaluated autologous NK cells with anti-GD2 antibodies in both newly diagnosed and relapsed patients [238] . Late-phase trials have begun to assess long-term outcomes. NCT06071897 (phase III) investigates naxitamab + GM-CSF during induction chemotherapy [239] . NCT06047535 (phase IV) evaluates the same combination ± isotretinoin as maintenance therapy post-remission [240] . Overall, the clinical trial landscape reflects a clear evolution. Early feasibility studies have given way to multi-agent regimens integrating immune activation, cytotoxic chemotherapy, and cell-based approaches. Future directions should emphasize sequencing optimization, biomarker-driven patient selection, and long-term management of toxicity. These efforts will be critical to achieving durable, personalized outcomes and advancing toward next-generation immunotherapeutic strategies in pediatric oncology [33,241] . Key quantitative endpoints (e.g., ORR, PFS/EFS, OS, and HR where applicable) are highlighted to facilitate cross-trial comparison. Interpretation of efficacy signals across the neuroblastoma immunotherapy trial landscape should account for common sources of bias [33] . Many studies are early phase (I/II), single-arm, and open-label, with small sample sizes. This can limit precision and increase uncertainty around point estimates (e.g., ORR) and time-to-event outcomes (e.g., PFS/EFS) [242] . Additional risks include selection bias, such as enrolling fitter patients or specific molecular subsets; heterogeneity in prior lines of therapy; variable response-assessment methods and imaging schedules; and reliance on historical controls. Each of these factors can complicate cross-trial comparisons [243,244] . Across modalities, anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody–based regimens currently provide the most mature efficacy evidence. This includes demonstrated survival benefit in randomized settings, such as dinutuximab-based immunotherapy improving EFS and OS in ANBL0032 [245] . By contrast, GD2-targeted cellular therapies, such as CAR-T or CAR-NKT, remain predominantly in early-phase clinical trials. Reported responses should be interpreted cautiously, given limited cohort sizes and shorter follow-up. For example, interim phase I data for GD2-CAR.15 NKT cells reported an ORR of 25 % (3/12) with a disease control rate of 58 % (7/12) [152,245] . Collectively, these data support continued development. They also highlight the need for harmonized endpoints and longer follow-up to enable robust efficacy benchmarking across platforms.  7 Conclusion Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative modality in the treatment of neuroblastoma, shifting from an adjunctive option to a central component of modern pediatric oncology. The success of anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies has catalyzed a wave of innovation, expanding the therapeutic arsenal to include CAR-T cells, OVs, NK cell platforms, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. These approaches collectively aim to overcome immune evasion and establish durable, memory-driven antitumor responses. However, the journey toward universal efficacy is far from complete. Tumor heterogeneity, antigen loss, and immunosuppressive microenvironments continue to challenge the durability of therapy. CAR-T cell therapy, while promising, is constrained by toxicity risks and cost barriers, limiting its accessibility and scalability. The emergence of resistance mechanisms, such as GD2 downregulation, T-cell exhaustion, and suppressive myeloid populations, underscores the need for biomarker-driven personalization. To accelerate biomarker translation, future efforts should move beyond single-marker approaches and adopt AI-enabled, multi-institutional discovery pipelines. Integrating harmonized multi-omic data (bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, spatial profiling, proteomics/metabolomics, and liquid biopsy signals such as ctDNA/ctRNA) with standardized clinical metadata can support the development of interpretable predictors of response, resistance, and toxicity. Where cross-center data sharing is constrained, federated or privacy-preserving learning frameworks can enable model training across institutions while maintaining patient confidentiality. Importantly, candidate signatures should be externally validated and then prospectively embedded into clinical trials as stratification variables, adaptive enrichment criteria, or pre-specified companion diagnostics to ensure clinical utility and reproducibility. Despite rapid scientific progress, the real-world impact of immunotherapy in neuroblastoma will ultimately depend on whether these advances can be implemented equitably across health systems. Substantial global access disparities persist, particularly between high-income countries and low- and middle-income settings, where pediatric oncology capacity may be constrained by a limited specialist workforce, restricted diagnostic infrastructure, and delayed referral pathways. Many contemporary immunotherapies, including anti-GD2 antibodies and cellular therapies, require coordinated multidisciplinary teams and supportive-care capabilities that are not uniformly available, thereby amplifying outcome gaps even when the underlying treatments are clinically effective. Cost and supply-chain complexity are major barriers to equitable access. Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies remain expensive biologics with access often shaped by reimbursement policies, national procurement capacity, and availability of reliable distribution and cold-chain logistics. For CAR-based platforms, barriers extend beyond drug pricing to include manufacturing, quality control, vein-to-vein time, need for specialized inpatient monitoring for toxicities (e.g., CRS and neurotoxicity), and access to intensive care and advanced laboratory monitoring. Collectively, these requirements can limit scalability and delay treatment initiation, especially in low-resource environments where timely delivery is critical for aggressive, high-risk disease. Strategies to improve equity should be considered alongside efficacy-focused innovation. First, broader availability of biosimilars and increased competition in manufacturing for anti-GD2 antibodies could reduce costs and improve supply reliability, particularly if paired with regional production hubs, technology transfer, and streamlined regulatory pathways. Second, implementation-focused optimization, such as standardized supportive-care protocols, toxicity-mitigation approaches, and safe, outpatient-compatible delivery models, may reduce hospitalization burden and make anti-GD2 regimens more feasible across diverse settings. Third, next-generation cellular immunotherapies should prioritize “globally deployable” designs, including universal/adaptor CAR platforms, off-the-shelf allogeneic or CAR-NK products, and simplified manufacturing workflows that reduce reliance on infrastructure while maintaining safety. Finally, equitable implementation requires intentional trial design and policy alignment: inclusion of geographically diverse sites, reporting of feasibility and resource-use endpoints (e.g., time-to-treatment, hospitalization days, supportive-care intensity), and incorporation of health-economic analyses to inform sustainable adoption. Equity-focused trial design should be treated as a core scientific objective rather than a downstream implementation concern. Trials should proactively reduce structural barriers by using pragmatic eligibility criteria, enabling decentralized or hybrid follow-up when feasible, and incorporating capacity-building elements (e.g., standardized biomarker workflows and regional biobanking) to support participation from low-resource settings. In addition to traditional efficacy endpoints, protocols should pre-specify equity and feasibility metrics, such as time-to-treatment, required supportive-care intensity, and assay/monitoring complexity, to clarify real-world deployability. Finally, early alignment with regulators, payers, and manufacturers (including biosimilar or access programs) can shorten the gap between evidence generation and sustainable adoption across diverse health systems. Recent clinical trials reflect a strategic pivot toward combination regimens that integrate immunotherapy with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents. These multi-modal approaches have demonstrated synergistic potential, particularly when guided by predictive biomarkers such as ALK status, immune infiltration profiles, and cytokine signatures. Advances in transcriptomics, epigenetics, and metabolic profiling further enable precise patient stratification and therapeutic tailoring. Looking ahead, the field must prioritize three pillars: rational combination strategies to overcome resistance, biomarker integration for personalized therapy, and explicit reduction of global access disparities by designing lower-toxicity, lower-cost, and more scalable immunotherapy programs, supported by pragmatic implementation strategies, expanded availability in low-resource settings, and platform innovations such as biosimilars and universal/adaptor cellular therapies. Emerging technologies, including universal CAR platforms, nanomedicine, and microbiome-modulating interventions, offer exciting avenues for progress. If these scientific and practical challenges are addressed in parallel, immunotherapy can evolve from a selective innovation into a universally accessible, curative standard of care for children with neuroblastoma. The convergence of biological insight, clinical rigor, and translational innovation will define the next era of pediatric cancer therapy. title: Thiosemicarbazones down-regulate N-Myc expression in neuroblastoma cells via transcriptional and post-translational mechanisms
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is an aggressive childhood cancer in which the transcription factor N-Myc is a key oncogenic driver. Iron-binding ligands such as desferrioxamine (DFO) suppress N-Myc expression, but the mechanism remains unclear. To examine this, we evaluated the clinically trialed thiosemicarbazone, DpC, which showed potent anti-proliferative activity against NB and compared it to DFO. RNA-sequencing revealed DpC elicited transcriptional changes at ~20-fold lower concentrations than DFO. In NB cells, DFO or DpC up-regulated several N-Myc downstream targets, including the metastasis suppressor, NDRG1, and induced NDRG1 nuclear translocation in three NB cell-types. Both agents significantly decreased N-Myc mRNA and protein in p53-mutant cells (Kelly, BE(2)-C), whereas in SH-SY5Y cells (wild-type p53), DFO caused no significant change in N-Myc mRNA or protein. This result together with its marked efficacy at lower concentrations at down-regulating this key oncoprotein, highlighted the superiority of DpC relative to DFO. In SH-SY5Y cells, silencing studies indicated the p53 target, MDM2, maintained N-Myc mRNA following DFO. The loss of N-Myc protein by the ligands was reversed by the proteasome inhibitor, epoxomicin. Considering the role of the proteasome, silencing the ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1), which catalyzes the first step in ubiquitination, implicated a ubiquitin-independent proteasomal process in the activity of DFO and DpC. Collectively, DFO and DpC down-regulate N-Myc in NB cells via combined transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. DpC demonstrated multiple advantageous properties to DFO, and unlike DFO, is known to be orally active in vivo and simple to synthesize, facilitating its administration and economical production.

                  Neuroblastoma (NB) is an aggressive childhood cancer in which the transcription factor N-Myc is a key oncogenic driver. Iron-binding ligands such as desferrioxamine (DFO) suppress N-Myc expression, but the mechanism remains unclear. To examine this, we evaluated the clinically trialed thiosemicarbazone, DpC, which showed potent anti-proliferative activity against NB and compared it to DFO. RNA-sequencing revealed DpC elicited transcriptional changes at ~20-fold lower concentrations than DFO. In NB cells, DFO or DpC up-regulated several N-Myc downstream targets, including the metastasis suppressor, NDRG1, and induced NDRG1 nuclear translocation in three NB cell-types. Both agents significantly decreased N-Myc mRNA and protein in p53-mutant cells (Kelly, BE(2)-C), whereas in SH-SY5Y cells (wild-type p53), DFO caused no significant change in N-Myc mRNA or protein. This result together with its marked efficacy at lower concentrations at down-regulating this key oncoprotein, highlighted the superiority of DpC relative to DFO. In SH-SY5Y cells, silencing studies indicated the p53 target, MDM2, maintained N-Myc mRNA following DFO. The loss of N-Myc protein by the ligands was reversed by the proteasome inhibitor, epoxomicin. Considering the role of the proteasome, silencing the ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1), which catalyzes the first step in ubiquitination, implicated a ubiquitin-independent proteasomal process in the activity of DFO and DpC. Collectively, DFO and DpC down-regulate N-Myc in NB cells via combined transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. DpC demonstrated multiple advantageous properties to DFO, and unlike DFO, is known to be orally active in vivo and simple to synthesize, facilitating its administration and economical production.

Fig. 9   Fig. 10 Schematic of the multiple anti-neoplastic mechanisms of DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC against NB cells. (1) Depletion of cellular iron by the ligands is demonstrated by the up-regulation of the typical iron responsive molecule, the TfR1. (2) KEGG analysis of the RNAseq data demonstrated changes in the p53 signaling pathway were induced by DFO and DpC in SH-SY5Y NB cells with wild-type p53, but not Kelly or BE(2)-C NB cells that possess mutant p53. DFO did not decrease N-Myc  mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells due to the up-regulation of the p53 target MDM2 that stabilizes N-Myc  mRNA [76] . In fact, silencing MDM2  led to sensitization to DFO and a decrease in N-Myc protein. (3) In contrast, the HIF-1 signaling pathway was up-regulated by DFO across all three NB cell-types, with six HIF-1-responsive N-Myc targets, ALDOA , CDKN1A , HES1 , HK2 , PDK1 , and NDRG1 , being uniformly induced in all NB cell-types. These changes contribute to metabolic alteration and reprogramming, with the up-regulation of HK2, ALDOA, and PDK1 potentially accelerating glycolytic flux, contributing to an archetypal Warburg-like effect. This initial compensatory response is overcome by tumor cell killing via  multiple mechanisms [18,21,22,30,32,42] . Considering this, the other HIF-1 responsive N-Myc targets, CDKN1A (p21) and NDRG1, enforce growth arrest and the inhibition of metastasis. (4) NDRG1 was demonstrated to translocate to the nucleus in all NB cell-types, where it interacts with N-Myc protein in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells; (5) A non-ATF3 mediated mechanism was involved in inhibiting N-Myc  mRNA transcription leading to down-regulation of N-Myc protein. (6) The ligand’s ability to down-regulate N-Myc protein was inhibited by the proteasomal inhibitor, epoxomicin, and occurred by an ubiquitin-independent mechanism. The multiple targeting activity of the ligands is beneficial, as it guards against the development of resistance. Centre for Cancer Cell Biology and Drug Discovery, Institute for Biomedicine and Glycomics, Griffith University Gold Coast Queensland 4215 Australia       Neuroblastoma (NB) is an aggressive childhood cancer in which the transcription factor N-Myc is a key oncogenic driver. Iron-binding ligands such as desferrioxamine (DFO) suppress N-Myc expression, but the mechanism remains unclear. To examine this, we evaluated the clinically trialed thiosemicarbazone, DpC, which showed potent anti-proliferative activity against NB and compared it to DFO. RNA-sequencing revealed DpC elicited transcriptional changes at ~20-fold lower concentrations than DFO. In NB cells, DFO or DpC up-regulated several N-Myc downstream targets, including the metastasis suppressor, NDRG1, and induced NDRG1 nuclear translocation in three NB cell-types. Both agents significantly decreased N-Myc  mRNA and protein in p53-mutant cells (Kelly, BE(2)-C), whereas in SH-SY5Y cells (wild-type p53), DFO caused no significant change in N-Myc  mRNA or protein. This result together with its marked efficacy at lower concentrations at down-regulating this key oncoprotein, highlighted the superiority of DpC relative to DFO. In SH-SY5Y cells, silencing studies indicated the p53 target, MDM2, maintained N-Myc  mRNA following DFO. The loss of N-Myc protein by the ligands was reversed by the proteasome inhibitor, epoxomicin. Considering the role of the proteasome, silencing the ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1), which catalyzes the first step in ubiquitination, implicated a ubiquitin-independent proteasomal process in the activity of DFO and DpC. Collectively, DFO and DpC down-regulate N-Myc in NB cells via  combined transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. DpC demonstrated multiple advantageous properties to DFO, and unlike DFO, is known to be orally active in vivo  and simple to synthesize, facilitating its administration and economical production. As such, NB is the most common cancer diagnosed during the first year of life and has been divided into four stages (Ⅰ to Ⅳ), which correlate with survival [2] . Localized disease (stage I) has the best prognosis, whereas widespread disease (stage IV) has the worst [2] . Unfortunately, the prognosis of children with advanced NB remains poor, and new therapeutic approaches are urgently required. Approximately 50 % of high-risk NB patients have amplified MYCN  oncogene, resulting in increased N-Myc oncoprotein that functions as a transcription factor [3] . These increased N-Myc levels are also considered to play an important role in the pathogenesis of NB [4] . The expression of N-Myc is established as a major driver of NB pathogenesis, which is confirmed by the observation that genetic hyper-expression of MYCN  promotes NB development, and may contribute in other cancer-types, including medulloblastoma, neuroendocrine prostate cancer, and pancreatic cancer [3,5–9] . Thus, N-Myc is an attractive molecular target for NB treatment [10] . Studies have revealed that the well-characterized iron chelator, desferrioxamine (DFO;  Fig. 1 A), which has been used for decades to treat iron overload disease [11,17] , effectively inhibits NB growth in vitro , in vivo , and in clinical trials [11–13] . This unusual sensitivity could be related to the altered iron metabolism of NB cells, where iron-loaded ferritin and the avid secretion of ferritin have been reported [14] . In fact, serum ferritin levels have been used as a prognostic marker to assess NB tumor stage and progression [15] . However, treatment with DFO suffers major problems, including: (1)  limited membrane permeability that leads to poor activity after oral administration; (2)  a short serum half-life [16] ; and (3)  DFO requires prolonged subcutaneous infusion (12–24 h/day; 5–7 days/week) to induce significant iron chelation from tissues [17] . These issues highlight the critical need to develop new and improved therapeutic agents that target cellular iron that could result in an effective treatment for NB. Our laboratory designed, developed, and patented the di-2-pyridylketone thiosemicarbazone (DpT) class of iron-binding ligands [18]  as well as their negative control thiosemicarbazones (e.g. , 2-benzoyl pyridine 2-methylthiosemicarbazone; Bp2mT; Fig. 1 B) that cannot bind metal ions and are devoid of biological activity [19,20] . The DpT analogues include the first-generation lead ligand, di-2-pyridylketone 4,4 dimethyl thiosemicarbazone (Dp44mT; Fig. 1 C), and an improved second-generation agent, di-2-pyridylketone 4-cyclohexyl-4-methyl-3-thiosemicarbazone (DpC; Fig. 1 D), that effectively inhibits the proliferation of a broad spectrum of cancer cells in vitro  and in vivo  with marked selectivity versus  normal cell-types [21,22] . The marked anti-cancer activity of these ligands in vitro  and in vivo  and their tolerability has also been reported independently of our laboratory [23–28] . Moreover, unlike DFO, which was never specifically designed as an anti-cancer drug, Dp44mT and DpC were the result of extensive structure-activity relationship studies over twenty years to hone their efficacy and selectivity [18,21] . In fact, these agents were specifically engineered to result in a “double punch” mechanism [29,30] . That is, they incorporated a metal ion-binding moiety that bound intracellular iron and copper that is essential for growth (the first punch), but also resulted in a “second punch” [29,30] . This second punch was mediated by the generation of redox-active complexes with Fe(III) and Cu(II) that led to cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) [29,30] . The high therapeutic potential of DpC was underlined by its appropriate pharmacokinetics [31] , which resulted in its commercialization and a Phase I clinical trial [32] . Further, DpC demonstrated effective anti-tumor activity against a variety of human tumor types in vitro  and in vivo,  including NB when given via  the i.v.  or oral administration route, with good selectivity and high tolerability [33] . Important pharmacological mechanisms of activity of these new thiosemicarbazones included their novel mechanisms in overcoming tamoxifen resistance in breast cancer [34]  and P-glycoprotein (Pgp) resistance via  their ability to target Pgp in lysosomes [35] . Further, Dp44mT and DpC acted to suppress a variety of oncogenic signaling molecules and pathways, including epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) [36] , cellular mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-Met) [37] , the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) and NFĸB pathways [38] , the Wingless (WNT) pathway [39] , and the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) pathway [23,40,41] . At the same time, Dp44mT and DpC up-regulated a number of tumor suppressors e.g. , p53 [42] , mitogen-inducible gene 6 (MIG6) [20] , and the metastasis suppressor, N-Myc downstream regulated gene-1 (NDRG1) [43] . The ability of the thiosemicarbazones to up-regulate the metastasis suppressor, NDRG1, and block metastasis in vivo [23,41]  is significant, as metastasis is the major killer of cancer, leading to 90 % of deaths [44] . Despite advances in immunotherapies, metastatic tumors remain a pernicious nightmare as there are no drugs that specifically inhibit metastasis in the clinics [45] . The up-regulation of NDRG1 occurs by these thiosemicarbazones via  hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF1α)-dependent and -independent mechanisms [43,46]  to suppress oncogenic cellular signaling (e.g ., EGFR, c-Met, etc. ), which leads to the inhibition of metastasis [23,41] . Considering these studies with DFO and DpC, it was previously demonstrated that DFO can lead to the down-regulation of N-Myc  at both the mRNA and protein levels [11] . However, the molecular mechanism of this effect was never elucidated and is important to dissect considering the marked role of N-Myc in NB pathogenesis. Herein, we performed RNA sequencing (RNAseq) using three NB cell-types with both non-amplified and amplified MYCN  to understand the molecular targets involved in the activity of DFO and DpC. Studies to dissect mechanism were then performed to understand the down-regulation of N-Myc  by these agents, which revealed multiple complex mechanisms of its regulation at the mRNA and protein levels, with the ligands inducing a ubiquitin-independent mechanism of proteasomal degradation of N-Myc.  2 Results 2.1 DFO and DpC broadly affect mRNA expression and alter N-Myc mRNA and its downstream target genes While a previous study indicated that DFO could decrease N-Myc  mRNA and protein expression in multiple NB cell-types, the precise mechanism(s) involved were not deciphered [11] .
