Moreover, the activity of more effective iron-binding ligands of the clinically trialed thiosemicarbazone class, such as DpC [22,33,41] , were not examined on N-Myc  mRNA and protein levels. To understand the mechanisms of activity of DFO and DpC on NB cells, initial experiments examined whole-genome RNAseq after a 24 h/37 °C incubation with DFO (100 μM) relative to DpC (5 μM). These RNAseq studies implemented N-Myc  non-amplified SH-SY5Y cells that have two to three N-Myc  copies [47,48] , compared to NB cells with pronounced N-Myc  amplification, namely Kelly and BE(2)-2 cells with 407 and 510 N-Myc  copies, respectively [47,49] . These concentrations of DFO and DpC and the incubation time used were specifically implemented as preliminary studies with these three cell-types resulted in the up-regulation of the iron-responsive molecules, transferrin receptor 1  (TFRC ) and NDRG1 [21,43]  at the mRNA and protein levels. Moreover, these concentrations and incubation times did not result in pronounced cellular death. The higher concentration of DFO relative to DpC was utilized because of the greater hydrophilicity, lower permeability, and anti-proliferative efficacy of DFO [50] versus  the high lipophilicity and anti-proliferative activity of DpC [22] . The RNAseq analysis revealed that there was a significant (p.adj.  < 0.05) differential in the mRNA levels induced by DFO versus  the control and this consisted of 8407 genes in SH-SY5Y NB cells, 6280 genes in Kelly NB cells, and 3110 genes in BE(2)-C NB cells, with 1262 being commonly altered across the three cell-types (Fig. 1 E;  see NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus; accession number GSE291132). Relative to DFO, the effect of DpC induced a significant (p.adj.  < 0.05) differential in the expression of 5156 genes, 4567 genes, and 3620 genes in SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C NB cells, respectively, with 994 being commonly altered between the three cell-types (Fig. 1 E). The heatmap of the overall alterations in gene expression induced by DFO or DpC indicated similarities, but also differences between the three cell-types, with many changes being observed with both treatments (Fig. S-1A ). Comparing the significant (p.adj.  < 0.05) alterations in gene expression induced by DFO and DpC, a high correlation (Pearson’s correlation coefficient r  = 0.86–0.94) was observed between the two ligands in all three NB cell-types (Fig. S-1B-D ). Moreover, the drug-induced changes (p.adj.  < 0.05) in gene expression for DFO or DpC between N-Myc  non-amplified cells (SH-SY5Y) to N-Myc  amplified cells (Kelly and BE(2)-C) were also highly correlated (r  = 0.76–0.86; data not shown. Overall, these data suggested that all the NB cell-types responded similarly to these agents. This was interesting to consider, as the concentration of DpC used was 20-fold lower than DFO, demonstrating the markedly greater chelation efficacy of DpC. Incubation with DFO or DpC in the three cell-types, resulted in the differential expression of 2024–3787 and 2641–3564 genes, respectively, with a log2  fold change > 1 or < −1 relative to the untreated control. Only a minority of these genes (11.2–14.94 %) across the three cell-types had an uncharacterized molecular role using the Functional Annotation tool from the database, DAVID. Using the latter database, genes were then annotated into known biological processes, and the top ten illustrated for SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 1 F), Kelly cells (Fig. 1 G), and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 1 H). This analysis identified the following biological processes were commonly affected across all three cell-types after treatment with either DFO or DpC, these included “cell cycle”, “apoptosis”, “cell division”, and “neurogenesis” in that general order, from highest to lowest number of genes affected (Fig. 1 F-H). Notably, “cell cycle” was consistently identified across all three cell-types in the top four biological processes affected after treatment with DFO or DpC. “Ion transport” was identified in the top ten biological processes differentially regulated by DFO or DpC in all cell-types, except DFO-treated BE(2)-C cells, which again, is in good agreement with the ability of these ligands to avidly bind cellular metal ions [17,22] . Similarly, “differentiation” was also consistently identified as a common biological process that was differentially regulated across all cell-types except in DpC-treated Kelly cells (Fig. 1 F-H). Examining the effect of DFO and DpC in each specific cell-type, nine of the ten biological processes regulated in SH-SY5Y NB cells were the same for each ligand, with “cell cycle”, “differentiation”, and “cell adhesion” being commonly affected and within the top three biological processes (Fig. 1 F). This observation indicates that the two ligands acted similarly on biological processes in SH-SY5Y despite their marked differences in structure (Fig. 1 A, D), permeability, and anti-proliferative efficacy [22] . Moreover, analysis of the activity of DFO and DpC in Kelly NB cells demonstrated seven out of the ten biological processes regulated were the same for both agents, with “transport” and “cell cycle” being commonly affected and within the top three identified Fig. 1 G). The “transport” process dominated, with the number of genes involved being two-fold greater than all other biological processes in Kelly cells. Analyzing BE(2)-C cells, again seven biological processes were the same between DFO and DpC, with the top two processes being different (i.e. , “transcription” and “transcription regulation”) to that observed for SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells (Fig. 1 H). Within the top ten biological processes regulated by DFO and DpC, both “transcription” and “transcription regulation” dominated in BE(2)-C cells, with the number of genes involved being greater than two-fold that observed for all other biological processes (Fig. 1 H). In summary, assessing the effect of DFO and DpC on all three NB cell-types, DAVID function annotation analysis demonstrated that these agents acted similarly on the major biological processes.  2.2 KEGG pathway enrichment analysis in SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C NB cells The differential gene expression in SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C cells for DFO and DpC versus  the Control was further examined by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis [51]  and Ingenuity pathway analysis [52] . The raw data from KEGG analysis for all three cell-types are provided in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE291132), and the top five up-regulated and top five down-regulated KEGG pathways are shown in  Fig. 2 A-C. Examining SH-SY5Y cells, two out of the top five pathways were commonly and significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) up-regulated by DFO and also DpC (i.e. , “cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction” and the “p53 signaling pathway”; Fig. 2 A). Additionally, DFO and DpC acted similarly to significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) down-regulate three KEGG pathways from the top five (i.e. , “cell cycle”, “alcoholism” and “neutrophil extracellular trap formation”; Fig. 2 A). In contrast, three from the top five pathways in SH-SY5Y cells that were significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) up-regulated by DFO (i.e. , “efferocytosis”, HIF1 signaling pathway”, and “neuroactive ligand receptor interaction”) were different than those significantly (p.adj . < 0.05) up-regulated by DpC (i.e. , “ECM-receptor interaction”, “PI3K-AKT signaling pathway” and the “calcium signaling pathway”; Fig. 2 A). Similar alterations were previously identified in MCF-7 breast cancer cells, with a marked increase in the expression of HIF-1 and p53 signaling pathway genes being observed after a 24 h/37 °C incubation with DpC [42]  or DFO [53] . In summary, for SH-SY5Y cells, while DFO and DpC targeted common KEGG pathways (e.g. , the “cell cycle”), there was also evidence for different targeting mechanisms between the two agents, as demonstrated by the different KEGG pathways modulated. In Kelly cells, DFO and DpC had the same effect at significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) up-regulating only one KEGG pathway, namely the “neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathway”, while there were no KEGG pathways commonly down-regulated by DFO and DpC (Fig. 2 B). For DFO or DpC, there was only one KEGG pathway commonly and significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) down-regulated between SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, namely “alcoholism” and “cell cycle”, respectively (Fig. 2 A cf. Fig. 2 B). KEGG pathway analysis of the BE(2)-C cell data demonstrated only one of the top five pathways were commonly shared between DFO and DpC, namely the “MAPK signaling pathway” (Fig. 2 C). Considering KEGG analysis of the RNAseq more broadly across all three NB cell-types, the up-regulation of the “p53 signaling pathway” by DFO and DpC was only observed in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 2 A), and not Kelly (Fig. 2 B) or BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 2 C). As expected from previous gene array and RNA sequencing studies [42,53] , the “HIF1 signaling pathway” was significantly (p.adj.  < 0.05) up-regulated by DFO relative to the control in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 2 A-C). In contrast, it is unclear why DpC did not induce the expression of this pathway, particularly considering its ability to target intracellular iron pools like DFO [17,22] .  2.3 Top ten up- and down-regulated genes in SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C NB cells Further analysis of the RNAseq data utilizing SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C NB cells included identification of the top ten up- and down-regulated genes in response to DFO- and DpC- treated vs. vehicle control-treated cells (    Tables 1–4 ). Assessment of the top ten up-regulated (Table 1 ) and down-regulated genes (Table 2 ) after incubation with DFO in all three NB cell-types indicated no commonly regulated genes between the three cell-types. Many of the genes up-regulated by DFO and DpC in these NB cells were different to those previously identified in human MCF-7 breast cancer cells [42,53] . Surprisingly, the top ten up-regulated genes did not include those well characterized to be differentially regulated after iron depletion, such as the transferrin receptor 1  (TFRC ) or NDRG1 [43] . However, while not being in the top ten, these latter two transcripts were significantly up-regulated for all three cell-types and were used as positive controls for the activity of the ligands in binding cellular iron pools (Fig. 2 D-F). This up-regulation of TfR1  and NDRG1  expression was also confirmed at the protein level by western analyses and confocal microscopy studies detailed below. Examining the top 10 up-regulated (Table 3 ) and down-regulated (Table 4 ) genes after incubation of all cell-types with DpC demonstrated that compared to DFO (Tables 1 and 2 ), bone morphogenic protein 6  (BMP6 ) and cyclic ADP ribose hydrolase  (also known as cluster of differentiation 38 ; CD38 ) were commonly up-regulated and down-regulated, respectively, and only in SH-SY5Y cells (Tables 1–4 ). Paradoxically, BMP6  mRNA levels have been identified as being up-regulated by cellular iron donors (i.e. , ferric ammonium citrate or hemin) in human umbilical endothelial cells [54]  or hepatocytes [55] , which is opposite to the up-regulation observed herein after iron-depletion induced by DFO or DpC. In terms of the top ten genes up-regulated by DpC, the mRNA levels of the metallothionein  gene family members were significantly increased in all NB cell-types (Table 3 ). In fact, in SH-SY5Y cells metallothionein 1 M  was up-regulated, while metallothionein 1E, 1 F, 1 G, 1 H , and 1 M  and metallothionein 1B, 1E, 1 G, 1 H,  and 1 M  were significantly up-regulated in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells, respectively (Table 3 ). Only metallothionein 1 M  was commonly up-regulated in all three cell-types, but members of this gene family were also identified to be up-regulated in MCF-7 cells by DpC (i.e ., MT1B  and MT4 ; [42] ), but also by the chelator 311 (i.e. , MT1X  and MT2A ; [53] ). The metallothionein  family of genes are well known to play roles in the storage and metabolism of metal ions such as copper, zinc, cadmium, etc.  and have been demonstrated to be up-regulated by increased Cu, Cd, and Zn in cells [56,57] . It has been shown that DpC and closely related thiosemicarbazones (e.g ., Dp44mT) bind Cu and Zn, and are likely to disturb the intracellular distribution and concentration of metal ions [22,30,58,59] , and this could lead to the up-regulation of the metallothionein  gene family observed. Further evidence that DpC modulated cellular metal metabolism was evidenced by the significant up-regulation of solute carrier family 30 member 2  (SLC30A2 ), which is a Zn transporter in SH-SY5Y cells (Table 3 ) [60] . This Zn transporter is also significantly up-regulated by DpC in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells, but is not in the top ten alterations in gene expression (GSE291132). Up-regulation of the related gene, SLC30A1 , by DpC has also been identified in MCF-7 cells [42] , and while not being in the top ten genes up-regulated by DpC, it was also significantly increased in all three NB cell-types (GSE291132). In the top ten up-regulated genes, DpC up-regulated the zinc finger-containing transcription factor, early growth response 2  (EGR2 ) in BE(2)-C cells (Table 3 ), while DFO and 311 up-regulated its family member, EGR1 , in MCF-7 cells [53] . Again, this alteration could be related to the modulation of metal metabolism by these well-characterized metal-binding ligands [17,61] . Even though EGR1  was not listed in the top ten up-regulated genes induced by DFO or DpC, EGR1  was significantly up-regulated in all three NB cell-types (GSE291132). While EGR2  was in the top ten up-regulated genes in only DpC-treated BE(2)-C cells, it was also significantly up-regulated by DpC in Kelly and SH-SY5Y cells (GSE291132). Notably, while EGR2  was not in the top ten genes up-regulated by DFO, it was also significantly up-regulated by DFO in SH-SY5Y cells, but not in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells (GSE291132). Regarding the top ten most down-regulated genes in all NB cell-types incubated with DpC, it was notable that mitochondrially encoded tRNA’s  (MT-T’s ) were commonly significantly down-regulated (Table 4 ). In SH-SY5Y and Kelly NB cells, only MT-T cysteine  (MT-TC; Table 4 A) and MT-T tyrosine  (MT-TY; Table 4 B) were significantly altered versus  the control, respectively. In contrast, in BE(2)-C cells, the expression of five MT-T’s  were significantly down-regulated, namely: MT-TS1 , MT-TY, MT-TH, MT-TL2, MT-TC  relative to the control (Table 4 C). Upon further examination, many other MT-T  family members were down-regulated after incubation with DpC in all three NB cell-types (GSE291132). As described above for alterations in the expression of other molecules involved in Zn metabolism, the Zn finger transcription factor, Kruppel-like factor 1  (KLF1 ) [62] , and the Zn-containing enzyme, carboxypeptidase Z  (CPZ ) [63] , were significantly down-regulated by DpC in BE(2)-C cells and Kelly NB cells, respectively. Again, these alterations in expression could be related to the effect of DpC on binding cellular Zn pools [58,59,61] .  2.4 Examination of the expression of selected genes and Sankey diagram analysis A previous study demonstrated that DFO markedly down-regulated the expression at the mRNA and protein levels of the key oncogene, N-Myc  in a variety of NB cell-types [11] . Due to the importance of this molecule in NB pathogenesis, alterations in its expression were also assessed herein (Fig. 2 D-F), as it was not within the top 10 genes up-regulated. As expected, N-Myc  mRNA levels were markedly down-regulated by DFO and DpC relative to the control in Kelly and BE(2)-C NB cells (Fig. 2 E, F). However, in SH-SY5Y cells, only DpC significantly decreased N-Myc  mRNA relative to the control, while DFO slightly increased N-Myc  mRNA (Fig. 2 D). It was also relevant to examine the expression of several genes up-regulated by cellular iron depletion, namely NDRG1  and TFRC [43] , which demonstrated significantly increased expression in all three cell-types (Fig. 2 D-F). These results indicate the successful targeting of intracellular iron pools that leads to the up-regulation of these latter molecules involved in suppressing metastasis and cellular iron uptake, respectively [21,43] . Considering that N-Myc is a major transcription factor that is regulated by cellular iron levels [11] , downstream gene targets of N-Myc were examined using a Sankey diagram ( Fig. 3 ), in an attempt to initially understand the mechanisms of action of DFO and DpC. Between the three cell-types, it was clear that these agents led to different alterations in the expression of N-Myc downstream gene targets. However, overlap in altered expression of N-Myc downstream gene targets by DFO and DpC was also observed across these cell-types (Fig. 3 ). For DFO and DpC, eleven and thirteen N-Myc downstream gene targets, respectively, were identified to be common and overlap across all three cell-types (Fig. 3 ). Heat maps of these common, overlapping genes generated for DFO and DpC in all three cell-types indicate that these two agents generally increased their expression (Fig. S-1E ). Of these, six N-Myc downstream targets namely, ALDOA, CDKN1A, HES1, HK2, NDRG1 , and PDK1  were identified as common between both agents, with all these genes being significantly up-regulated in all three cell-types ( Table 5 ). Further analysis of N-Myc downstream target genes after treatment with DFO demonstrated a significant up-regulation of seventeen ribosome protein  mRNA levels, including eleven ribosomal large subunit  (RPL ) and six ribosomal small subunit  (RPS ) genes in only the Kelly NB cell-type (Fig. 2 ). This was not observed after treatment of any of the cell-types with DpC. The MAPK phosphatases, namely dual specificity phosphatase  (DUSP’s ) mRNAs, were also up-regulated by DFO and DpC in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 3 A, B and GSE291132). Previous gene array studies by our laboratory examining DFO and the structurally-related thiosemicarbazone, Dp44mT, also demonstrated the significant up-regulation of the mRNA levels of DUSP1, 5, 10 , and 16,  in DMS-53 lung carcinoma cells [64] . Another downstream target of N-Myc that was previously shown to be regulated by iron-binding ligands is the transcription co-factor, Cbp/P300 interacting transactivator with Glu/Asp-rich carboxy-terminal domain 2  (CITED2 ) [53] . Herein, CITED2  was only significantly up-regulated by DFO in BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 2 A), while its expression was increased in all three NB cell-types by DpC (Fig. 2 B). The product of this latter gene has been reported as an N-Myc  transcriptional modulator [65] .  2.5 DFO and DpC up-regulate NDRG1 and its association with LSD1 in all three NB cell-types The RNAseq demonstrated that DFO or DpC generally down-regulate N-Myc  mRNA in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 2 D-F), with the Sankey diagram analysis indicating NDRG1  is commonly up-regulated in all cells by these ligands (Fig. 2 ). In agreement with this latter result, previous studies demonstrated that NDRG1 is a downstream target of N-Myc after treatment with DFO or DpC, with NDRG1 being shown to be up-regulated by iron-binding ligands including these compounds [18,43] . Furthermore, N-Myc and the histone demethylase, lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1), form a complex that binds to the NDRG1  promoter to inhibit its transcription [66] . NDRG1 also underwent nuclear translocation [67] , where it may interact with LSD1 and/or N-Myc that are predominantly localized in this organelle [66] . Considering these facts, studies were designed to assess the effect of DFO and DpC on the expression and intracellular distribution of NDRG1 and LSD1 and its role in impacting N-Myc expression ( Fig. 4 ). Initial studies implemented western blotting to examine the protein expression of NDRG1 and LSD1 compared to the TfR1 in SH-SY5Y (Fig. 4 A), Kelly (Fig. S-2A ), and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. S-3A ) after an incubation for 24 h/37 °C with control media or this media containing either the negative control thiosemicarbazone, Bp2mT [19,20]  (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM). The expression of the TfR1 was significantly (p  < 0.001–0.01) up-regulated in all three cell-types by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC relative to the Control and Bp2mT (Fig. 4 A, S-2A, S-3A ), demonstrating these ligands induced cellular iron depletion [26,33,50] . In contrast, none of these agents had any significant (p  > 0.05) effect on LSD1 expression versus  the control (Fig. 4 A, S-2A, S-3A ). On the other hand, NDRG1 was markedly and significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.01) up-regulated by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC relative to the control or Bp2mT in all three cell-types (Fig. 4 A, S-2A, S-3A ). The effect of Dp44mT and DpC was similar and significantly (p  < 0.001–0.01) greater than DFO at up-regulating NDRG1 in all three cell-types. In conclusion, DFO, DpC, and Dp44mT up-regulate TfR1 and NDRG1, while having no significant effect on LSD1 expression in all three cell-types. Considering these latter results, studies were then designed to examine the expression and intracellular distribution of NDRG1, N-Myc, and LSD1 using confocal immunofluorescence microscopy in all cell-types, under the same conditions used for western analysis (Fig. 4 B, C; S-2B, C; S-3B, C ). In these studies, DFO and DpC were used, with DpC being chosen instead of Dp44mT because it demonstrated similar activity and had entered clinical trials [32] . Confocal microscopy of all cell-types (Fig. 4 B, C; S-2B,C; S-3B,C ) demonstrated the response of NDRG1 and LSD1 protein levels to DFO or DpC were analogous to those observed from western blotting. In fact, NDRG1 was markedly and significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.001) up-regulated by DFO and DpC, while LSD1 did not alter in intensity versus  the Control. As also observed for western blotting (Fig. 4 A, S-2A, S-3A ), in all three cell-types, DpC demonstrated significantly (p  < 0.001–0.05) greater activity than DFO (Fig. 4 B, C; S-2B, C; S-3B, C ). The greater activity of DpC in up-regulating NDRG1 can be explained by the more rapid ability of this class of thiosemicarbazones relative to DFO to permeate the plasma membrane and chelate intracellular iron pools [18] . Examining N-Myc  expression in SH-SY5Y cells, there was a marked and significant (p  < 0.001) increase in nuclear N-Myc after incubation with DFO versus  the control (Fig. 4 B). This result in SH-SY5Y cells at the protein level was in agreement with the N-Myc  mRNA levels from RNAseq data after incubation with DFO (Fig. 2 D). In contrast, incubation of SH-SY5Y cells with DpC resulted in a marked and significant (p  < 0.01) decrease in N-Myc protein versus  the control, which again matches the RNAseq results for this agent in the same cell-type (Fig. 2 D). Notably, N-Myc and LSD1 are nuclear proteins [68,69] , while NDRG1 was observed in the nucleus and cytoplasm, with a large proportion being cytosolic (Fig. 4 B, C). In addition to the significant (p  < 0.0001–0.001) increase in overall cellular NDRG1 intensity in Fig. 4 B, C, Plot Profile Analysis using Image J revealed DFO, and particularly DpC, significantly (p  < 0.001–0.01) increased nuclear NDRG1 translocation in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 4 D). Similar results to those in SH-SY5Y cells were also obtained using Kelly and BE(2)-C cells, except DFO acted similarly to DpC in Kelly (Fig. S-2D ) and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. S-3D ), significantly decreasing nuclear N-Myc protein. Since confocal microscopy images are captured using a single lateral focal plane, proteins in a similar cellular location can be co-localized, demonstrating their potential proximity [70] . Due to the nuclear translocation of NDRG1 after incubation with DFO and DpC, there was a significant (p  < 0.001–0.05) increase in co-localization between NDRG1 and N-Myc after DFO, but not for DpC in all three cell-types (Fig. 4 B, S-2B, S-3B ). This co-localization occurs only for DFO because of the pronounced decrease in N-Myc protein observed after DpC (Fig. 4 B, S-2B, S-3B ). Due to nuclear NDRG1 translocation, a significant (p  < 0.0001) increase in co-localization is observed for NDRG1 and LSD1 after incubation in all cell-types with DFO or DpC (Fig. 4 C, S-2C, S-3C ). Considering the confocal microscopy studies using all three cell-types above demonstrating the co-localization between NDRG1 and N-Myc (Fig. 4 B, S-2B, S-3B ), but also LSD1 and NDRG1 (Fig. 4 C, S-2C, S-3C ), further experiments then assessed the interaction of these potential protein partners using co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP; Fig. 4 E, S-2E, S-3E ). This was important to examine, as NDRG1 has been demonstrated to associate with other proteins to effect its function e.g ., mitogen-inducible gene 6 [20]  and protein kinase Cα [39] . In these studies, co-IP was performed using an antibody to immunoprecipitate NDRG1 to assess N-Myc and LSD1 association (Fig. 4 E, S-2E, S-3E ). To validate the interaction and examine the non-specific association of immunoglobulins to the protein, an isotype control antibody (IgG) was also utilized. Western analysis (input) of total cell lysates demonstrated a significant (p  < 0.01) increase of N-Myc protein after incubation with DFO versus  the control. but only in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 4 E). In Kelly and BE(2)-C cells, there was a significant (p  < 0.05) decrease in N-Myc protein with DFO versus  the control (S-2E, S-3E ). In contrast, DpC significantly (p  < 0.05–0.01) decreased N-Myc protein in all NB cell-types (Fig. 4 E, S-2E, S-3E ). As described above for all three NB cell-types (Fig. 4 A-D), NDRG1 was significantly (p  < 0.01–0.0001) increased in the input after incubation with DFO or DpC, while LSD1 did not significantly (p  > 0.05) alter versus  the control (Fig. 4 E, S-2E, S-3E ). Co-IP using an NDRG1 antibody demonstrated significantly (p  < 0.001–0.01) higher association of NDRG1 with N-Myc in DFO- and DpC-treated cells compared to the Control in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells (Figs. S-2E, S-3E ). In contrast, for SH-SY5Y cells, no significant interaction between N-Myc and NDRG1 was identified (Fig. 4 E). Moreover, no LSD1 was detected after NDRG1 was pulled down using anti-NDRG1 antibody in all three cell-types, indicating no association between these proteins (Fig. 4 E, S-2E, S-3E ). Collectively, confocal microscopy demonstrated that DFO and DpC significantly increased the translocation of NDRG1 into the nucleus in all 3 NB cell-types, which then led to pronounced co-localization of NDRG1 and LSD1. Regarding co-localization between NDRG1 and N-Myc, this was significantly increased by DFO, but not DpC. This latter effect was due to the marked decrease in nuclear N-Myc expression by the latter agent. Moreover, co-IP demonstrated association of NDRG1 and N-Myc  in the N-Myc  amplified NB cell-types, Kelly and BE(2)-C [47,49] , but not SH-SY5Y cells that have no N-Myc  amplification. [47,48] .  2.6 Dp44mT and DpC decrease N-Myc mRNA and protein in N-Myc non-amplified and amplified NB cell types, while DFO only had this activity in N-Myc amplified cells The studies above demonstrated the effects of DFO and DpC on the expression of N-Myc and N-Myc downstream effectors in all three NB cell-types (Figs. 2 D-F, 3 ). Considering this, studies were then performed to dissect how these ligands affect N-Myc  mRNA and protein expression using RT-qPCR and western analysis, respectively ( Fig. 5 A-L). In these studies, all three NB cell-types were incubated for 24 h/37 °C with control medium (Control), or this medium containing either the negative control compound, Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM). RT-qPCR demonstrated that Dp44mT demonstrated similar activity to DpC in all three cell-types, with these ligands significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.001) decreasing N-Myc  mRNA versus  the control (Fig. 5 A, E, I). Both Dp44mT and DpC were significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.05) more effective than DFO at down-regulating N-Myc  mRNA (Fig. 5 A, E, I), which probably relates to their markedly greater membrane permeability than DFO [18,22] . In fact, as a function of incubation time, DpC demonstrated superior efficacy to DFO in suppressing N-Myc  mRNA levels (Fig. S-4 ). For example, after a 4 h/37 °C incubation, DpC was 6-fold more effective than DFO at decreasing N-Myc  mRNA in Kelly cells (Fig. S-4 ). Studies then investigated protein levels of the TfR1 and N-Myc. The significant (p  < 0.0001–0.01) up-regulation of TfR1 in all three cell-types incubated with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC (Fig. 5 B, F, J) indicated cellular iron depletion by these agents. The protein level of N-Myc was markedly and significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.01) decreased by Dp44mT and DpC in all NB cell-types (Fig. 5 B, F, J). However, in contrast, DFO exhibited differential activity on N-Myc protein depending on the cell-type assessed (Fig. 5 B, F, J), as observed for the mRNA levels (Fig. 5 A, E, I). Examining SH-SY5Y cells that have non-amplified N-Myc [47] , incubation with DFO resulted in a pronounced and significant (p  < 0.0001) increase in N-Myc protein versus  the control (Fig. 5 B), while DFO had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on N-Myc  mRNA (Fig. 5 A). On the other hand, in N-Myc  amplified Kelly and BE-(2)-C cells, DFO induced a marked and significant (p  < 0.0001–0.001) decrease in N-Myc protein versus  the control, which was similar to that observed for Dp44mT and DpC (Fig. 5 F, J). Further studies were performed to examine the mechanisms involved in why DFO had no effect on N-Myc  mRNA and increased its protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells. In these experiments, SH-SY5Y cells were preincubated for 1 h/37 °C in the presence and absence of the protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide (15 µg/mL), and the incubation continued for 24 h/37 °C with DFO (100 µM) or control media (Fig. 5 C, D, G, H, K, L). For SH-SY5Y cells, in agreement with the RT-qPCR results in Fig. 5 A, DFO alone had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on N-Myc  mRNA versus  the control in the absence of cycloheximide (Fig. 5 C). In contrast, in the presence of cycloheximide, DFO markedly and significantly (p  < 0.01) decreased N-Myc  mRNA relative to cycloheximide alone (Fig. 5 C). This observation suggested new protein synthesis was required to maintain N-Myc  mRNA upon DFO treatment in SH-SY5Y cells, indicating a post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism. Assessing the effect of cycloheximide on protein synthesis in the presence of DFO, the significant (p  < 0.001) increase of N-Myc protein in SH-SY5Y cells in absence of cycloheximide was markedly blocked, resulting in an almost complete loss of N-Myc protein (Fig. 5 D). This latter observation agreed with the ability of DFO to significantly (p  < 0.01) decrease N-Myc  mRNA in the presence of cycloheximide (Fig. 5 C). This effect in SH-SY5Y cells was different from that observed with Kelly and BE(2)-C NB cells, where DFO decreased N-Myc  mRNA in the presence or absence of cycloheximide (Fig. 5 G, K), demonstrating the inhibition of protein synthesis did not affect the marked decrease of N-Myc  mRNA induced by DFO. Moreover, western blot analysis indicated that DFO induced a pronounced and significant (p  < 0.01–0.05) decrease in N-Myc protein in the presence and absence of cycloheximide in Kelly and BE(2)-C NB cells (Fig. 5 H, L). To summarize Fig. 5 , there was a different response in SH-SY5Y cells to DFO in the presence of cycloheximide (Fig. 5 C, D) relative to that obtained with Kelly (Fig. 5 G, H) and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 5 K, L). These data demonstrate a metabolic difference between these cell-types, which suggests new protein synthesis is required to enable the maintenance of N-Myc  mRNA and the up-regulation of N-Myc protein observed for DFO in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 5 B, D). For all cell-types, the thiosemicarbazones substantially reduced N-Myc  mRNA and protein versus  the control.  2.7 The transcriptional repressor of N-Myc, ATF3, is up-regulated by DFO and DpC in all three NB cell-types To understand the mechanism involved in the general marked down-regulation of N-Myc  mRNA after incubation with DFO or DpC we initially investigated the expression of known transcriptional regulators of N-Myc  in the RNAseq data (Table S-1). These included: aldehyde dehydrogenase 18 family member A1 (ALDH18A1) [71] , activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) [72] , E2F transcription factor 2 (E2F2) [73] , pleiomorphic adenoma gene-like-2 (PLAGL2) [74] , and specificity protein 1 (SP1) [75] . From these five regulators, only ATF3  was markedly and significantly (p.adj . < 0.00001) up-regulated (log2 FC: 2.15–5.96) in all three NB cell-types by DFO and also DpC (Table S-1 ). Furthermore, this up-regulation of the transcriptional repressor, ATF3, could potentially down-regulate N-Myc  mRNA. As such, studies then progressed to examining ATF3 protein after a 24 h/37 °C incubation of all cell-types with control medium or this medium containing Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM). As observed in Figure S-5 A-C  for all three NB cell-types, ATF3 protein was significantly (p  < 0.05–0.001) increased by DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC. These results agree with the RNAseq data demonstrating that ATF3  mRNA was markedly and significantly (p.adj.  < 0.00001) up-regulated by DFO and DpC in all three NB cells (Table S-1). Since ATF3 is a transcriptional repressor that inhibits N-Myc  expression [72] , this robust up-regulation of ATF3  mRNA and protein may explain why N-Myc  mRNA and protein was down-regulated by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC in NB cells. However, assessment of the role of ATF3 in drug-induced N-Myc protein down-regulation revealed that the silencing of ATF3  did not rescue the decrease in N-Myc after incubation with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC in BE(2)-C cells (Fig. S-5D ). Similar results were also observed for Kelly cells (data not shown). These data suggest that the drug-induced N-Myc down-regulation in NB cells could be through an ATF3-independent mechanism.  2.8 Silencing NDRG1 does not affect the DFO-induced alterations in N-Myc protein in all three NB cell-types The investigations in Fig. 4 , S-1 and S-2  demonstrated the potential role of NDRG1 in the DFO- and DpC-induced alterations in N-Myc protein expression. Considering the markedly different activity of DFO between N-Myc  non-amplified (SH-SY5Y) and N-Myc  amplified (Kelly and BE(2)-C) cells (Figs. 4 , S-1, S-2, 5 ), this agent was used to explore the role of NDRG1 in the regulation of N-Myc protein. These studies were particularly important to examine considering the association of NDRG1 with N-Myc as indicated by confocal microscopy and co-IP (Fig. 4 B, E, Fig. S-2B, S-2E, Fig. S-3B, S-3E ). Furthermore, the studies in Fig. 5  demonstrated that new protein synthesis was required for the stabilization of N-Myc  mRNA in DFO-treated SH-SY5Y cells. To investigate the role of NDRG1 in regulating N-Myc in all three NB cell-types, NDRG1  was silenced by incubation of NB cells for 24 h/37 °C with either the negative targeting siControl or siNDRG1. This medium was then removed and the cells incubated for 24 h/37 °C in the presence of control medium or this medium containing DFO (100 µM) ( Fig. 6 A-C). For all three NB cell-types, TfR1 expression was used as a positive control for the activity of DFO in terms of depleting cellular iron and was significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.05) up-regulated versus  the control after incubation with the siControl or siNDRG1 (Fig. 6 A-C). This observation indicated that NDRG1  silencing had no appreciable effect on TfR1 expression. In contrast, NDRG1  silencing markedly and significantly (p  < 0.01–0.001) down-regulated NDRG1 after DFO treatment relative to that observed after incubating cells with DFO and the siControl. As demonstrated above (Figs. 4 B, 5 B), DFO increased N-Myc expression in SH-SY5Y cells versus  the Control after incubation with the siControl (Fig. 6 A). However, silencing NDRG1  had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on the ability of DFO to up-regulate N-Myc in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 6 A). Examining Kelly and BE(2)-C cells, DFO markedly down-regulated N-Myc protein versus  the control after siControl treatment, with the silencing of NDRG1  not significantly (p  > 0.05) affecting this DFO-mediated decrease in N-Myc (Fig. 6 B, C). Overall, NDRG1  silencing in all NB cell-types suggested the DFO-induced alterations in N-Myc protein were via  an NDRG1-independent mechanism.  2.9 DFO up-regulates protein levels of p53 and its downstream target, MDM2, only in SH-SY5Y cells The studies in Fig. 5 A, B demonstrated a unique effect of DFO on N-Myc  mRNA and protein in SH-SY5Y cells relative to Kelly (Fig. 5 E, F) and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 5 I, J), which indicates a difference in response between these cell-types. An interesting observation was that DFO had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on N-Myc  mRNA in SY-SY5Y cells, with the addition of cycloheximide inducing a marked decrease in N-Myc  mRNA (Fig. 5 C). This observation suggested new protein synthesis was required to maintain N-Myc  mRNA. Furthermore, investigations using NDRG1  silencing demonstrated the effects of DFO on N-Myc protein were NDRG1-independent (Fig. 6 ). Previous studies have also indicated that the downstream target and feedback regulator of p53, namely murine double minute-2 homolog (MDM2), can directly bind to, and stabilize, N-Myc  mRNA [76] . Considering these latter results and the difference between the cell-types (Fig. 5 ), it is well known that SH-SY5Y cells possess wild-type p53 that is functional in terms of its ability to transcriptionally activate downstream target genes e.g., MDM2 [77] . In contrast, Kelly and BE(2)-C cells have mutant p53 that is not fully functional as a tumor suppressor [77,78] . Furthermore, it has been reported that DFO up-regulates wild-type p53 and MDM2 protein in other cell-types [42,79] . As such, it was hypothesized the new protein synthesized that is required to maintain N-Myc  mRNA in DFO-treated SH-SY5Y cells could be MDM2. To investigate this, studies first assessed the effect of DFO (100 µM) on TfR1, N-Myc, p53 and MDM2 protein in all three NB cell-types after a 24 h/37 °C incubation ( Fig. 7 ). The TfR1 was implemented as a positive control as it is up-regulated by the effect of the iron depletion induced by DFO [80] . Incubation with DFO caused a marked and significant (p  < 0.01–0.05) increase in TfR1 expression in all NB cell-types (Fig. 5 A). As described in Figs. 5  and 6 , DFO significantly (p  < 0.01) increased N-Myc protein in SH-SY5Y cells versus  the control (Fig. 7 A), while significantly (p  < 0.05) decreasing it relative to the control in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 7 B, C). Examining p53 and MDM2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 7 A), both were significantly (p  < 0.001) up-regulated by DFO versus  the control, as previously reported in cell-types with wild-type p53 [42] . In contrast, for Kelly NB cells (Fig. 7 B), DFO has no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on the protein level of p53, while significantly (p  < 0.001) decreasing MDM2 protein, probably because p53 is mutant in this cell-type, and does not transcribe downstream targets [78] . For BE(2)-C cells, DFO significantly (p  < 0.01) increased p53 protein versus  the control, while MDM2 was not detected (Fig. 7 C). This latter observation is probably because this cell-type has mutant p53 that cannot transactivate its downstream targets [78] . Overall, these studies in Fig. 7 A-C demonstrate that DFO leads to MDM2 up-regulation only in SH-SY5Y cells with wild-type p53.  2.10 DFO has no effect on N-Myc mRNA levels under control conditions, but decreases N-Myc mRNA after MDM2 silencing The results in Fig. 7 A-C, supported the hypothesis that up-regulation of MDM2 protein in SH-SY5Y cells could stabilize and maintain N-Myc  mRNA levels after DFO treatment. To further examine this premise, SH-SY5Y cells were preincubated for 24 h/37 °C with an MDM2  silencing construct (siMDM2) or a non-targeting negative control siRNA (siControl). This treatment was removed and the cells then incubated for 24 h/37 °C with DFO (100 µM) in the absence or presence of cycloheximide (15 µg/mL). RT-qPCR was then performed (Fig. 7 D). As demonstrated in Fig. 5 C, DFO alone in the absence of cycloheximide had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on N-Myc  mRNA after siControl treatment versus  the control (Fig. 7 D). While upon the addition of cycloheximide, DFO significantly (p  < 0.0001) decreased N-Myc  mRNA versus  the control incubated with cycloheximide alone (Fig. 5 C). These results indicated that protein synthesis was required to maintain N-Myc  mRNA. In contrast, silencing MDM2  significantly (p  < 0.01) decreased N-Myc  mRNA in the presence of DFO, and this was further enhanced (p  < 0.0001) with the addition of cycloheximide (Fig. 7 D). Collectively, these studies in Fig. 7 A-D demonstrate that DFO only up-regulates MDM2 in SH-SY5Y cell with wild-type p53, and that silencing MDM2  prevents its ability to maintain N-Myc  mRNA in the presence of DFO. These results demonstrate the marked differences in the mechanisms of DFO-induced alterations in N-Myc expression between NB cells with wild-type and mutant p53.  2.11 The proteasomal inhibitor, epoxomicin, prevented the down-regulation of N-Myc mediated by Dp44mT and DpC in three neuroblastoma cell-types The studies above demonstrated N-Myc  mRNA levels are decreased by Dp44mT and DpC in all NB cell-types (Fig. 5 A, E, I) with MDM2 playing a key role in the inability of DFO to decrease N-Myc  mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 7 D). To elucidate the mechanisms of the down-regulation of N-Myc protein induced by the ligands, further investigations considered the role of the proteasome. In fact, N-Myc is rapidly degraded by the proteasomal system with a half-life of 30 min [10] , and no studies have examined the ability of proteasomal inhibitors to block the loss of N-Myc protein induced by these ligands. To dissect why DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC generally result in N-Myc protein down-regulation and if the proteasome is involved, studies initially assessed the ability of well-characterized proteasomal inhibitors to prevent the decrease of N-Myc in all cell-types ( Fig. 8 A-C). Preliminary experiments with the well-known proteasomal inhibitors, MG132 or lactacystin [81,82] , demonstrated poor activity or cytotoxicity using established concentrations [83]  (data not shown). On the other hand, another commonly used potent and selective 20S proteasomal inhibitor, epoxomicin [84] , demonstrated low cytotoxicity and the ability to prevent the down-regulation of cyclin D1 by the ligands that occurs via  proteasomal activity after iron depletion [85] . As such, cyclin D1 expression was used as a positive control to demonstrate effective proteasomal inhibition by epoxomicin in all three cell-types (Fig. 8 A-C). In initial optimization studies, effective proteasomal inhibition was achieved using epoxomicin at 1 µM for SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, while 2 µM was necessary for BE(2)-C cells to prevent the loss of cyclin D1 protein. In these studies, NB cells were incubated for 24 h/37 °C with control media (control), or this media containing either Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM) in the presence or absence of epoxomicin (1 or 2 µM). In the presence and absence of epoxomicin, DFO and DpC resulted in significant (p  < 0.0001–0.05) up-regulation of the positive control for iron depletion, the TfR1, relative to the respective controls (i.e. , control and Bp2mT) in all three cell-types (Fig. 8 A-C). Moreover, the specifically designed negative control thiosemicarbazone, Bp2mT, that does not possess biological activity [19]  had no significant (p  > 0.05) effect on TfR1 protein (Fig. 8 A-C). Similar results were also demonstrated for Dp44mT in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells in the presence and absence of epoxomicin where there was a significant (p  < 0.0001–0.01) increase in TfR1 expression versus  these latter controls (Fig. 8 A, B). In contrast, examining BE(2)-C cells, no significant (p  > 0.05) increase in the TfR1 expression was observed in the presence of epoxomicin (Fig. 8 C). The up-regulation of the TfR1 by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC, in all three cell-types was significantly (p  < 0.001–0.05) suppressed in the presence of epoxomicin relative to its absence, suggesting that proteasomal inhibition suppressed its expression. However, in general, across all three NB cell-types, DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC up-regulated TfR1, as observed in other cells [53] . As another control for iron chelation by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC, cyclin D1 protein expression was also examined, being significantly (p  < 0.0001–0.05) decreased versus  the control or the negative control, Bp2mT, in all cell-types in the absence of epoxomicin (Fig. 8 A-C). In contrast, in the presence of epoxomicin, cyclin D1 levels were markedly and significantly (p  < 0.001–0.01) increased for all treatments, with the ability of DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC to decrease cyclin D1 being ablated. These results indicate epoxomicin prevented proteasomal activity that is responsible for cyclin D1 degradation in the absence and presence of iron-binding ligands. These studies confirmed our previous studies demonstrating other proteasomal inhibitors prevent cyclin D1 loss after iron chelation [85] . Similarly to cyclin D1, in the absence of epoxomicin, there was a significant (p  < 0.0001–0.01) decrease in N-Myc protein in the presence of DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 8 B, C). In contrast, the addition of epoxomicin prevented the inhibitory activity of these ligands and resulted in a marked (p  < 0.0001) increase in N-Myc protein in Kelly and BE(2)-C cells relative to all treatments without epoxomicin (Fig. 8 B, C). Examining SH-SY5Y cells, the effect of epoxomicin on N-Myc protein was more complex than for Kelly and BE(2)-C cells (Fig. 8 A). In the absence of epoxomicin, DFO again induced a marked and significant (p  < 0.0001) increase in N-Myc versus  the control in SH-SY5Y cells, while Dp44mT and DpC resulted in a significant (p  < 0.01) decrease (Fig. 8 A). Epoxomicin prevented the decrease in N-Myc induced by Dp44mT and DpC in SH-SY5Y cells, with both leading to a significant (p  < 0.001–0.01) increase of N-Myc versus  the absence of epoxomicin (Fig. 8 A). In the presence of epoxomicin, N-Myc in SH-SY5Y cells after incubation with the control, Bp2mT, or DFO were significantly (p  < 0.01) decreased relative to the absence of epoxomicin. In summary, epoxomicin, generally prevented the DFO-, Dp44mT-, and DpC-mediated down-regulation of N-Myc and the positive control, cyclin D1. Notably, epoxomicin has markedly prevented the down-regulation of N-Myc protein with Dp44mT and DpC in all cell-types (Fig. 8 A-C). This is despite the marked down-regulation of N-Myc  mRNA levels induced by these ligands (Fig. 5 A, E, I) and is because epoxomicin inhibits proteasomal activity [84] . This inhibition prevents the decrease in N-Myc protein irrespective of the pronounced decrease of its mRNA levels (Fig. 5 A, E, I). This response has also been observed by others using different models and molecules [86] , and is expected, since mRNA and protein levels are regulated separately [87,88] .  2.12 Silencing the ubiquitin-activating enzyme, UBA1, does not fully rescue N-Myc or cyclin D1 down-regulation induced by DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC The results in Fig. 8  indicate the proteasome could play a role in the decrease in N-Myc protein after incubation with DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC. Previous studies demonstrated N-Myc degradation is regulated by a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism via  the proteasome [89] . For other proteins, both ubiquitin-dependent and/or ubiquitin-independent mechanisms of degradation are known [90,91] . Our laboratory reported that cyclin D1 and p21CIP1/WAF1  were degraded in iron-replete cells via  a ubiquitin-dependent process, while after iron depletion, ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation occurred [85,92] . Inhibiting the 20S proteasome using epoxomicin [84]  in Fig. 8  prevented the ability of DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC, to decrease N-Myc. Considering this, inhibition of the 20S subunit by epoxomicin will also result in inhibition of 26S proteasomal activity [93]  required for ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation [93] . As such, this does not differentiate between the ubiquitin-dependent and -independent mechanisms of proteasomal degradation. To suppress ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of N-Myc, NB cells were preincubated for 24 h/37 °C with an siRNA targeting ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1  (UBA1 ) or a non-targeting siRNA (siControl). UBA1 is an E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme that catalyzes the first critical step in ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation [94] . It is well known that inhibiting UBA1 with either chemical inhibitors or UBA1  silencing essentially abolishes new ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation [95,96] . Herein, silencing was the preferred option, as chemical inhibitors suffer more off-target effects [97] . Complete UBA1  silencing is lethal, and experimentally, it is not possible to completely inhibit ubiquitination, as a small amount of turnover occurs via  UBA6-mediated pathways, residual UBA1 activity, or ubiquitin-independent pathways [98,99] . As such, relative controls are required to demonstrate pronounced inhibition of ubiquitination and are included herein. After UBA1  silencing, the media was then removed, and the NB cells incubated for 24 h/37 °C with control medium, or this medium containing Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM) and western analysis performed. Again, TfR1 expression was implemented as a positive control for iron depletion mediated by the ligands after incubation with siControl or siUBA1 ( Fig. 9 A-C). Under both conditions there was a significant (p  < 0.05–0.0001) up-regulation of the TfR1 relative to the control or Bp2mT after incubation of DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 9 A-C), as shown previously (Figs. 4 A, 5 B, F, J, 8 A-C). Silencing of UBA1  in all three NB cell-types resulted in a marked and significant (p  < 0.05–0.001) decrease in UBA1  expression versus  the siControl (Fig. 9 A-C). As implemented in Fig. 8 A-C, cyclin D1 was used as a positive control for inhibition of proteasomal activity [85]  mediated by silencing UBA1 , with its levels being significantly (p  < 0.01–0.001) decreased by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC under siControl conditions versus  the respective control and Bp2mT in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 9 A-C). Upon silencing UBA1 , cyclin D1 was significantly (p  < 0.05–0.01) increased in the control and Bp2mT treatment groups relative to the analogous treatments in the siControl, due to inhibition of ubiquitination. These results were comparable to those observed with epoxomicin treatment (Fig. 8 A-C). However, as observed for the siControl, upon incubation with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC, cyclin D1 protein was significantly (p  < 0.01–0.001) decreased after UBA1  silencing versus  the respective control or Bp2mT (Fig. 9 A-C). This response was different to the effect mediated by epoxomicin, which successfully prevented this decrease in cyclin D1 protein (Fig. 8 A-C). N-Myc responded similarly as cyclin D1 to the drug treatment under siControl and siUBA1 treatment (Fig. 9 A-C). This observation indicated the significantly (p  < 0.01–0.001) decreased N-Myc observed using DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC versus  the respective control or Bp2mT after UBA1  silencing could be due to ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation.   3 Discussion N-Myc is a dominant oncogenic driver of NB [3] . Cellular iron depletion with clinically used DFO suppresses NB growth in vitro  and in vivo [11–13]  and decreases N-Myc  mRNA and protein expression [11] . However, DFO’s limited anti-tumor efficacy, short half-life, and inability to be orally administered and requirement for long subcutaneous or intravenous infusions (12–24 h/day, 5–6 days/week) limits its clinical impact [17] . The thiosemicarbazone, DpC, whose primary targets are cellular iron and copper [29,30] , was specifically designed by structure-activity optimization, displays favorable pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and anti-tumor potency [22,31] . In fact, DpC when administered orally has demonstrated marked anti-cancer activity and good tolerability, with toxicology being examined in a variety of tumor models in vivo , including neuroblastoma [33] , prostate cancer [100] , lung cancer [22] , breast cancer [42] , and pancreatic cancer [41] . The high anti-cancer activity of DpC, tolerability, and appropriate pharmacokinetics led to multi-centre Phase I clinical trials (NCT02688101) in patients with advanced and resistant cancer [32] . Herein, we compare and mechanistically dissect how these ligands regulate N-Myc expression and its downstream networks in NB cells with and without N-Myc  amplification. The ligands demonstrate multi-modal mechanisms of action that are illustrated in  Fig. 10  and are discussed further in the sections below. These multiple mechanisms of activity guard against the development of resistance mechanisms that often occur when using anti-cancer drugs with a single mechanism of action [101,102] . 3.1 Transcriptomic response to iron depletion: Targeting of p53 and HIF-1 signaling RNAseq demonstrated broadly overlapping transcriptional changes with either DFO or DpC after a 24 h incubation of all three NB cell-types. Despite this, some distinct differences in the cellular response between DFO and DpC were identified. For instance, DFO significantly up-regulated seventeen ribosome protein  mRNA levels in only Kelly NB cells, with this not being observed with DpC in any cell-type. On the other hand, only DpC up-regulated metallothionein  gene family members and also the Zn transporter solute carrier family 30 member 2  (SLC30A2 ), likely due to the known ability of thiosemicarbazones to avidly bind cellular copper and zinc [22,30,58,59] . This difference in activity between DFO and DpC is probably related to distinct structural design features and different mechanisms of action. That is, DFO is a hydroxamate-based ligand with hard oxygen donors that results in a strong preference for iron and does not redox cycle to generate ROS [17,103] . This is why DFO is specifically used for the treatment of iron overload disease to target iron. In contrast, through a series of structure-activity relationship studies [32,101,102] , DpC was specifically designed as an anti-cancer drug, a DpT ligand that utilizes soft nitrogen and sulphur donor atoms as its metal ligating sites [22,30] . This leads to different metal-binding interactions, redox potentials, and the different responses relative to DFO observed herein, as DpT thiosemicarbazones effectively bind iron, copper, and zinc. The formation of redox-active copper complexes, and less so, iron complexes of the DpT ligands is particularly critical, as it leads to lysosomal membrane permeabilization, which is key for inducing tumor cell death [104]  and overcoming P-glycoprotein-mediated resistance [19,105]  Data enrichment analyses highlighted “cell-cycle”, “apoptosis”, “cell division”, and “neurogenesis”, which is consistent with the anti-proliferative activity of these ligands [22,30] . The down-regulation of genes involved in the cell cycle by DpC relative to DFO in all three NB cell-types agreed with the greater anti-proliferative efficacy of DpC [106] . This activity is consistent with the ability of iron-binding ligands to decrease the mRNA and protein levels of molecules involved in cell cycle progression, e.g. , cyclin D1 [58,107] . KEGG analysis demonstrated that the p53 signaling pathway was only increased by DFO and DpC in SH-SY5Y NB cells with wild-type p53 (Fig. 10 ), but not Kelly or BE(2)-C NB cells with mutant p53 [77] , supporting previous protein-level observations [79] . Conversely, the HIF-1 signaling pathway was significantly up-regulated by DFO across all three NB cell-types (Fig. 10 ), in line with findings in MCF-7 breast cancer cells [42,53] . Six HIF-1-responsive N-Myc targets [43,108–112] , ALDOA , CDKN1A , HES1 , HK2 , PDK1 , and NDRG1 , were uniformly induced by both DFO and DpC in all NB cell-types.  3.2 Metabolic alterations and reprogramming after ligand treatment Considering the functions of these latter six N-Myc downstream targets, ALDOA  and HK2  encode core glycolytic enzymes [113,114] . Their induction probably reflects HIF-1 binding to hypoxia-responsive elements in their promoters after iron depletion [115,116] , a stress that perturbs many iron-dependent metabolic processes, including ATP production [17,103] . It has been reported that cellular iron depletion by ligands transiently depresses ATP levels, activates adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), and provokes a compensatory surge in glycolytic and mitochondrial flux [103] . The up-regulation of HK2  and ALDOA  probably forms part of this metabolic compensation to iron stress [103] . HIF-1 also elevates PDK1 expression [117] , which phosphorylates and inactivates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that acts as a “gatekeeper” between glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle [118,119] . This latter effect diverts pyruvate from the TCA cycle into aerobic glycolysis as a part of the Warburg effect [118] . Together, the up-regulation of HK2 , ALDOA,  and PDK1  after iron depletion probably accelerates the glycolytic flux that has been observed previously [103] , contributing to an archetypal Warburg-like response (Fig. 10 ). This initial compensatory response to iron depletion mediated by the ligands, is overcome by the induction of tumor killing by multiple mechanisms [18,21,22,30,32] . The other HIF-1 targets identified after cellular iron depletion include both CDKN1A  (p21 ) and NDRG1 , which act in concert and enforce growth arrest and the inhibition of metastasis [43,92,104,120,121]  (Fig. 10 ). NDRG1 is an iron-regulated metastasis suppressor [43,122]  that up-regulates p21 by blocking its NEDD4-dependent ubiquitylation [120] . Furthermore, thiosemicarbazone ligands that up-regulate NDRG1 [123]  are known to inhibit tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in vivo [23,40] . These observations demonstrate that the latter alterations in gene expression could have important functional and clinical consequences. Cellular iron depletion also up-regulates the HIF-1 target, HES1 , which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor [124] , that promotes the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) via  E-cadherin suppression [125,126] . Intriguingly, and in contrast, cellular iron deletion also up-regulates NDRG1 that increases E-cadherin and suppresses the EMT [123] . Hence, a complex regulatory network exists in terms of the regulation of metastasis after cellular iron depletion. This is further supported by the fact that DFO and DpC increase the expression of the metastasis suppressor, KAI1 [127] , in all three NB cell-types and in SH-SY5Y cells, respectively (GEO accession no. GSE291132). These studies reinforce the anti-metastatic profile of these ligands and the clinical significance of their activity, as metastasis is the major killer in cancer, leading to 90 % of cancer deaths [44,128] , and there are no clinically used drugs specifically designed to target or treat it [45,129] .  3.3 Ligand-induced post-translational regulation of N-Myc protein This study demonstrated the proteasome inhibitor, epoxomicin, generally prevented ligand-induced N-Myc protein down-regulation across all NB cell-types, consistent with the known rapid proteasomal turnover of N-Myc [10] . However, silencing UBA1 , the E1 enzyme initiating ubiquitination, did not prevent N-Myc loss following treatment with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC [130] . These findings suggest that N-Myc degradation may be mediated via  a ubiquitin-independent proteasomal pathway (Fig. 10 ), a mechanism previously reported for other proteins [131] . Oxidatively damaged proteins are known to undergo degradation via  the 20S proteasome in a ubiquitin-independent manner [132] . As part of their mechanism of anti-cancer activity, both Dp44mT and DpC become highly redox-active upon chelating iron or copper in cells, generating ROS that contributes to oxidative damage [29,30] .The observed reduction in N-Myc protein levels induced by these latter agents may therefore result from both transcriptional down-regulation of N-Myc  mRNA and oxidative stress-induced protein degradation in all three NB cell-types. Notably, UBA1  silencing also failed to prevent the down-regulation of cyclin D1 by these ligands. This effect is consistent with ubiquitin-independent degradation of cyclin D1 that was identified following iron chelation in other cell-types [85,92] . Further studies are required to confirm the mechanism of ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation observed following ligand treatment. This could involve assessing non-canonical SUMO-dependent proteasomal degradation through the 20S subunit, which is ubiquitin-independent [133] . However, considering the apparent rare substrate-specific nature of the latter process and the redox nature of our compounds, it is known that oxidatively damaged proteins undergo ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation [134] . Hence, it could be important to determine whether scavenging ROS prevents N-Myc loss. This may be achieved by pre-treating cells with permeable pegylated catalase (PEG-Catalase) and pegylated superoxide dismutase (PEG-SOD), which neutralize intracellular hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, respectively [135] . Additionally, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which increases glutathione (GSH) and antagonizes thiosemicarbazone-induced oxidative and anti-proliferative effects [30,136,137] , may attenuate N-Myc down-regulation if oxidative stress is involved. Conversely, depletion of GSH using buthionine sulfoximine (BSO), which enhances oxidative activity and efficacy of thiosemicarbazones [104] , is expected to further promote N-Myc degradation. Collectively, these redox-based strategies can help determine the role of oxidative stress in mediating this proteasomal degradation mechanism.  3.4 Advantages of DpC relative to clinically used DFO N-Myc, the major driver of NB pathogenesis, was markedly down-regulated at both mRNA and protein levels by DpC in all three NB cell types, consistent with prior findings using DFO [11] . While these data demonstrate the marked activity of DpC, a limitation to the generalizability of our study is that it did not consider gender/sex issues. However, this was because the current investigation implemented cells in culture to dissect molecular pharmacological mechanisms. Of note, Dp44mT and DpC were more effective than DFO in reducing N-Myc expression across both N-Myc -amplified and non-amplified cells (Fig. 5 A-L). This difference was most evident in SH-SY5Y cells, where DFO failed to decrease N-Myc  mRNA and protein levels, while the thiosemicarbazones demonstrated pronounced efficacy (Fig. 5 A, B). Considering the failure of DFO to decrease N-Myc  mRNA and protein in SH-SY5Y NB cells, it is known these cells do not possess N-Myc  amplification and express wild-type p53 relative to the Kelly and BE(2)-C cells [77] . For the first time, this investigation demonstrated the downstream target of wild-type p53, namely MDM2, played a role in the inability of DFO to decrease N-Myc  mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells. A previous study indicated MDM2 stabilized N-Myc  mRNA in other NB cell-types by its direct interaction with the 3ꞌ untranslated region, although the effect of drugs on this mechanism had not been investigated [76] . This response was not observed examining DpC-treated SH-SY5Y cells and was probably not due to differential regulation of the p53-MDM2 axis by DFO and DpC. This latter deduction is suggested as both DFO and DpC acted similarly to up-regulate MDM2  mRNA levels in SH-SY5Y cells (p53 wild-type) and not BE(2)-C or Kelly cells (p53 mutant). In fact, in SH-SY5Y cells, the log2  fold-change in MDM2  mRNA levels after incubation with DFO or DpC was 2.17 and 2.32, and the p.adj.  was 1.25E-52 and 3.52E-56, respectively. This conclusion is in line with KEGG pathway analysis, demonstrating p53 signaling was affected similarly by both agents in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 2 A). It can be speculated the differential ligand activity in terms of MDM2-mediated stabilization of N-Myc  mRNA is due to the rapid ability of DpC to down-regulate N-Myc  mRNA versus  that observed with DFO (Fig. S-4 ). The pronounced and rapid decrease in N-Myc  mRNA levels by DpC may prevent binding by MDM2, effectively countering is ability to rescue the loss. This enhanced efficacy of DpC is likely due to its superior lipophilicity and membrane permeability of the DpT class of thiosemicarbazones relative to DFO [18] . This effect is highlighted by the greater activity of DpC at decreasing N-Myc  mRNA than DFO as a function of time (Fig. S-4 ), and is in direct accordance with the markedly more potent anti-proliferative efficacy of the thiosemicarbazones against tumor cells, including multiple NB cell-types [33] .  3.5 Clinical perspectives: advantages of thiosemicarbazones At present, there are no clinically approved, specifically designed drugs that inhibit N-Myc activity [136] . The sole directly acting agent against N-Myc, BGA002, is in an early phase-I trial [138] , while several indirect modulators (e.g. , targeting Aurora-A, BET, Pol-I inhibitors, etc .) have reached phase I/II, with limited but encouraging results.  True clinical effectiveness awaits results from these ongoing and future trials [136] .  Given that DpC has already advanced to Phase I clinical evaluation with favorable adsorption from the gut and pharmacokinetics [32] , these findings position DpC as a promising chemically tractable platform capable of potently down-regulating a major oncogenic driver in NB, namely N-Myc. Furthermore, DpC has been demonstrated in multiple tumor cell-types to lead to synergistic anti-proliferative activity with a variety of standard chemotherapeutics including doxorubicin, celecoxib, gemcitabine, cisplatin, etc. [139,140] . The potential of DpC is confirmed by studies in vivo  in mice against a human NB xenograft where it demonstrated effective activity and tolerability after oral administration in mice [33]  and also against multiple other tumor xenografts [22,41,100] . The fact that DpC is relatively simple and economical to synthesize [32] , indicates marked advantages over many chemotherapies (e.g ., immunotherapies) that are highly expensive and require intravenous administration. While DpC demonstrated reversible muscle pain in its clinical trial [32] , recent studies led to DpC analogues, namely the PPP4pSe series, which totally prevent the oxidation of oxy-myoglobin, which was thought to be responsible for the DpC-induced muscle pain [141] . These new PPP4pSe analogues have been specifically designed to prevent this off-target effect and represent a significant advance over DpC, with demonstrated 3-fold greater selectivity against cancer cells relative to their normal counterparts in preclinical models [141] .   4 Conclusions In summary, this study demonstrates the anti-cancer agent, DpC, effectively suppresses N-Myc expression at both mRNA and protein levels across three NB cell-types, regardless of N-Myc  amplification status. In wild-type p53-expressing SH-SY5Y cells, DFO fails to down-regulate N-Myc due to MDM2-mediated N-Myc  mRNA stabilization (Fig. 10 ). In contrast, DpC overcomes this resistance, highlighting its superior therapeutic potential. Compared to DFO, DpC induces a more rapid reduction in N-Myc  transcript levels as well as a more pronounced decrease in N-Myc protein levels, further supporting its superiority. While the down-regulation of N-Myc  mRNA by the ligands was ATF3-independent, additional studies are required to deduce the precise molecular mechanisms involved. Importantly, both DFO and DpC induce broad gene expression changes, but DpC exhibits potent activity at concentrations 20-fold lower than those of clinically used DFO. Mechanistically, DFO and DpC promote ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation of N-Myc and facilitate nuclear translocation of the metastasis suppressor NDRG1, which interacts with N-Myc following treatment (Fig. 10 ). These findings elucidate the mechanism of action of DpC and underscore its significant advantages over DFO in targeting the central NB oncogenic driver, N-Myc. This study provides a strong rationale for the further development of DpC and its analogues as therapeutic agents for NB.  5 Experimental procedures 5.1 Cell culture The well-characterized human NB cell-types, SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA). The SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Park Institute-1640 (RPMI-1640) medium supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, Bovogen, Victoria, Australia), 1 % penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, Missouri, USA), 1 % sodium pyruvate solution (Sigma-Aldrich), and 1 % non-essential amino acid solution (Sigma-Aldrich). The BE(2)-C cells were cultured in Ham’s F12/MEM (50 % Ham’s F12 and 50 % MEM medium) with the same supplements required for RPMI above.  5.2 Compounds DFO was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. The negative control thiosemicarbazone, Bp2mT [19,20] , and the ligands, Dp44mT and DpC, were synthesized and characterized by established methods [19,20,37,41,142] .  5.3 RNA isolation, sequencing, and analysis NB cells were seeded in a 60 × 15 mm petri dish and allowed to attach overnight. The cells were then incubated for 24 h/37 °C with either control medium or this medium containing Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM). The cells were collected in 1 mL of TRI reagent (Sigma-Aldrich), and RNA was extracted as per  the manufacturer’s instructions. RNAseq was performed using next-generation sequencing (NGS) with Illumina TruSeq technology (Novogene, Hong Kong, China). The raw data (raw readings from the instrument) were first processed using FASTP software to ensure data quality for further analysis. The differential expression analysis was then performed in R (version 4.3.0; Lucent Technologies, USA) using the DESeq2 package. Genes with an adjusted p -value (p. adj. ) ≤ 0.05 found by DESeq2 were assigned as significantly differentially expressed. The KEGG enrichment analysis was performed through R using clusterProfiler package (version 4.3.0; Lucent Technologies, USA) [51] , while the functional annotation tool was implemented from the database, DAVID (davidbioinformatics.nih.gov; accessed November 2024). Data for generating Sankey diagrams were processed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) [52] . The complete dataset can be accessed from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (accession number GSE291132; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). Three separate biological replicates were performed and analyzed.  5.4 Western analysis Cell lysate preparation, protein estimation, and western blotting were performed using standard protocols [39] . The primary antibodies used in this project included those against: N-Myc (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA; Cat. #: 51705 s), LSD1 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: 2139 s), cyclin D1 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: 2978 s), MDM2 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: 86934 s); NDRG1 (1/2500; Abcam, Cambridge, UK: Cat. #: ab37897), p53 (1/500; Abcam, Cat. #: ab26), ATF3 (1/1000; Abcam, Cat#: ab207434); β-actin (1/5000; Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. #: A5441); and TfR1 (1/2500; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat. #: 13–6800). The secondary antibodies utilized were from Sigma-Aldrich: anti-goat (1/5000, Cat.#: A8919), anti-mouse (1/5000, Cat. #: A9044), and anti-rabbit (1/5000, Cat.#: A0545). Blots were imaged using an Azure Sapphire Biomolecular Imager (Azure Biosystems, California, United States). Densitometry of the images was collected using Image Lab (Bio-Rad, California, United States) and analyzed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad, Inc, California, United States).  5.5 Confocal microscopy A 22 × 22 mm cover slip was added into a 6-well plate (Corning) and coated with poly-D -lysine solution (Sigma-Aldrich). Then, 100,000 cells were seeded onto the coverslip and incubated for 24 h/37 °C. The medium was subsequently removed, and the cells fixed by a 10 min incubation with ice-cold 4 % paraformaldehyde followed by 10 min permeabilization using 0.1 % Triton-X 100 in PBS. After permeabilization, the cells were blocked by a 1 h/20 °C incubation with 5 % BSA in PBS/0.3 M glycine and then incubated overnight with primary antibody diluted in 1 % BSA/PBS on an orbital shaker at 200 rpm/4 °C. The primary antibodies used include anti-LSD1 (1/200; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat#: 2139 s), anti-N-Myc (1/400, Cell Signaling Technology, Cat#: 84406 s), and anti-NDRG1 (1/200, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: WH0010397M3). Before the 1 h/20 °C incubation with secondary antibody in 1 % BSA/PBS on an orbital shaker at 200 rpm, the cells were washed using ice-cold 1 % BSA in PBS, 3 times for 10 min each. Then, the secondary antibody was removed by aspiration and washed using ice-cold 1 % BSA in PBS for 4 times for 10 min each. The secondary antibodies used were from Cell Signaling Technology and included anti-rabbit (1/2000, Cat#: 4413 s) and anti-mouse (1/2000, Cat#: 4408 s). Coverslips were subsequently washed 3 times with 1 % BSA/PBS solution and mounted onto a slide using ProLong Gold DAPI mounting solution (Cat. # P36935; Invitrogen, Waltham, MA). The slides were left to dry in a dark room overnight. Confocal/immunofluorescence images were obtained using an Olympus FV3000 confocal microscope (Evident Scientific) with a 100 × objective. Fluorescence intensities and co-localization analysis were quantified using ImageJ software (NIHD). The Pearson correlation coefficient (r ) was calculated using the Image J plugin, JACoP. Further statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad. To maintain uniform samples for the accurate assessment of co-localization, the following measures were implemented during sample preparation and the image acquisition process. These included the use of a consistent number of cells that were seeded on each coverslip per  sample to minimize variation in sample thickness. Additionally, only a cell monolayer was implemented, and within each experiment, all microscope acquisition parameters remained constant.  5.6 Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) Whole cell lysates were prepared using lysis buffer (Pierce IP Lysis Buffer, Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat#: 87788) containing protease inhibitor (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: 11836153001) and Phospho-STOP (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: 4906837001). A well-established co-IP procedure was performed in this study to determine the interactions between target proteins [39] . Briefly, 400 µg of protein from cell lysates was incubated with an antibody against NDRG1 (Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 9485 s), while the respective isotype control antibody (Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 3900 s) was utilized to determine the non-specific binding of immunoglobulins to the protein of interest. Then, the magnetic bead solution (30 mg/mL; Pierce Protein A/G Magnetic Beads; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat#: 10002D) was incubated with the antibody:lysate solution for 1.5 h/4 °C after overnight blocking in 5 % BSA/PBS. The supernatant was removed from the sample after incubation with the magnetic beads followed by five washes using ice-cold PBS. The magnetic beads were then resuspended using 5x loading dye containing 10 % β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich) and the protein was denatured by boiling for 5 min/95 °C. This sample was then used for SDS-PAGE and western blotting as described above. Ten percent (40 µg) of the amount of the proteins used for co-IP was used as the input samples for direct comparison. For subsequent western blotting, the primary antibodies used were anti-LSD1 (1/1000, Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 4218 s), anti-N-Myc (1/1000, Abcam; Cat. #: AB16898).  5.7 cDNA synthesis and qPCR After the extraction of mRNA, as described in 5.3 , the cDNA was synthesized using a cDNA synthesis kit (Promega, Wisconsin). Briefly, 4 µL of DEPC-treated water, 4 µL of reaction buffer with random primer, and 2 µL of enzyme mix were added to prepare a transcription reaction solution. Then, 1 µg of mRNA was added to 10 µL transcription reaction solution, and DEPC-treated water was used to make up the final volume to 20 µL. The cDNA was then synthesized using a PCR machine through a reverse transcription cycle, which included 5 min primer annealing at 25 °C, 60 min extension at 42 °C, and 15 min inactivation at 70 °C. The synthesized cDNA was stored for 24 h/4 °C and then used to perform qPCR to determine the expression level of target genes, including the housekeeping gene, GAPDH . The cDNA was first diluted 1:20 and 2 µL of diluted cDNA was added into the reaction mix, which contained 1x SensiFAST SYBR (Meridian Bioscience, OH), 250 nM forward and reverse primer (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 U/µL RiboSafe RNase inhibitor, and DEPC-treated water to make up the final volume to 20 µL. The system was set at 1 cycle of 10 min for polymerase activation at 95 °C, 40 cycles of 15 s/95 °C for denaturation, 15 s/60 °C for annealing and 15 s/72 °C for extension. During the 40 cycles, the fluorescence reading was recorded at the end of each amplification cycle. The expression level of genes was calculated using the ΔΔCq method. The following primers were utilized: TfR1 : (FW: 5ꞌ-GCTGTTTGGGAATATGGAAGGA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-TGCCTACACCGGATTTTGCA-3ꞌ); N-Myc : (FW: 5ꞌ-GGACACCCTGAGCGATTCA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-GGGAAGGCATCGTTTGAGGA-3ꞌ); and GAPDH : (FW: 5ꞌ-ACCATCTTCCAGGAGCGAGA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-TGCTGATGATCTTGAGGCTGT-3ꞌ).  5.8 Gene knockdown using small interfering RNA (siRNA) A non-targeting negative control siRNA (siControl; Cat.#: 4390843, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was implemented along with a specific siRNA (all at 75 µM) against ATF3  (siATF3; Invitrogen; Cat.#: 4392420, assay ID: s224089), MDM2  (siMDM2; Invitrogen; Cat. #: AM51331, assay ID: Hs00540450), NDRG1  (siNDRG1; Invitrogen; Cat.#: AM16706, assay ID: 135611), and UBA1  (siUBA1; Cat.#: 4390824, assay ID: Hs01031318). The related sequencing and silencing sites of these siRNAs are available from the supplier’s websites. The siRNAs were transfected into NB cells using Lipofectamine RNAiMAXR (Invitrogen; Cat.#: 13778100), with incubation with siRNA/lipofectamine complex in Opti-MEM medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat. #: 31985070) for 24 h/37 °C. Then, the cell lysates were collected, and western blotting was performed as described above.  5.9 Data analysis Statistical analyses of RNAseq data was performed as described above in 5.3 . All other data analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software, San Diego). The two-sample Student’s t- test (independent/unpaired) was performed using at least 3 independent experiments. Statistical significance was set at p  < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation.
