title: ALK regulates macrophage polarization <ce:italic>via</ce:italic> the USP7/SOX9/MFAP2-mediated glycolytic pathway to promote neuroblastoma progression
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is a common pediatric malignancy in which activating mutations of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) drive tumor progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that ALK signaling promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis. Using qRT-PCR, western blot, and co-culture systems, we found that ALK inhibition with lorlatinib reduces lactate production, downregulates M2 markers, and upregulates M1 markers in NB cells and NB mouse models. Mechanistically, Co-IP and ubiquitination assays revealed that ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, which deubiquitinates and stabilizes SOX9. Dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP-qPCR analyses further demonstrated that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter to activate its transcription. Functional assays showed that elevated MFAP2 enhances glycolysis, leading to increased lactate and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which in turn polarizes tumor-associated macrophages toward the pro-tumor M2 phenotype. Importantly, in vivo experiments confirmed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effects of lorlatinib. These findings identify the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a critical regulator of metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in NB, and suggest that targeting this axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB.

For in vitro  experiments, CLB-GE, Kelly, and SH-SY5Y cell lines were selected. (A-B) qRT-PCR and western blot analysis were performed to detect ALK mRNA and pALK/ALK protein expression levels, respectively, in the indicated cell lines. For in vivo  experiments, 3 × 106  Kelly cells were subcutaneously injected into the right posterior flank of BALB/c nude mice to establish an NB model. Starting from day 7 post-inoculation, mice were orally administered the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib (60 mg/kg/day) for three weeks, after which mice were euthanized and tumor tissues were collected. (C) Tumor growth curve. Tumor sizes were measured every three days for three weeks, with day 7 post-inoculation designated as day 0. (D) Representative photographs of harvested tumors. (E) Measurement of tumor weight. (F-G) Lactate level and LDH activity in tumor tissues were detected by commercial kits. (H–I) Levels of immunosuppressive cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β1 in tumor tissues were measured by ELISA. (J-L) qRT-PCR and western blot analysis were used to detect the mRNA and protein expression levels, respectively, of macrophage polarization markers (M1: iNOS, CD86; M2: Arg1, CD206). ⁎⁎  p  < 0.01, ⁎⁎⁎  p  < 0.001 vs  CLB-GE or Kelly or NB.  Fig. 1   Fig. 2 Effects of ALK inhibition on glycolysis and macrophage polarization in vitro . SH-SY5Y or Kelly cells were treated with or without lorlatinib. (A-D) qRT-PCR was performed to detect ALK mRNA expression level, and western blot analysis was conducted to determine ALK and pALK protein expression levels in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells. (E–F) Commercial kits were employed to measure lactate level and LDH activity in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells. (G-L) qRT-PCR and western blot were carried out to assess the mRNA and protein levels of HK2 and PKM2 in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells. Lorlatinib-treated SH-SY5Y or Kelly cells were co-cultured indirectly with THP-1 cells (pretreated with PMA for 24 h to induce macrophage differentiation) at a 1:1 ratio using Transwell chambers. After co-culture, the following assays were performed on THP-1-derived macrophages. (M-N) ELISA was utilized to detect the levels of immunosuppressive factors (IL-10, TGF-β1) and the immune-promoting factor (TNF-α) in macrophages. (O–P) Western blot analysis was performed to examine the protein levels of iNOS, CD86, Arg1, and CD206. ⁎  p  < 0.05, ⁎⁎  p  < 0.01, ⁎⁎⁎  p  < 0.001 vs  Control, ns vs  Control. Neuroblastoma (NB) is a common pediatric malignancy in which activating mutations of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) drive tumor progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that ALK signaling promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis. Using qRT-PCR, western blot, and co-culture systems, we found that ALK inhibition with lorlatinib reduces lactate production, downregulates M2 markers, and upregulates M1 markers in NB cells and NB mouse models. Mechanistically, Co-IP and ubiquitination assays revealed that ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, which deubiquitinates and stabilizes SOX9. Dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP-qPCR analyses further demonstrated that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter to activate its transcription. Functional assays showed that elevated MFAP2 enhances glycolysis, leading to increased lactate and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which in turn polarizes tumor-associated macrophages toward the pro-tumor M2 phenotype. Importantly, in vivo  experiments confirmed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effects of lorlatinib. These findings identify the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a critical regulator of metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in NB, and suggest that targeting this axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB. It accounts for more than 7% of malignancies in patients under 15 years of age and is responsible for approximately 15% of pediatric cancer-related deaths [2] . ALK is one of the most frequently mutated genes in NB [3,4] , and activating mutations, such as ALK-F1174L, have been established as a critical risk factor driving NB progression [5] . Particularly when ALK mutation coexists with MYCN amplification, patients often present with relapsed/refractory disease, rendering clinical treatment exceedingly challenging [6] . Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ALK drives NB progression is of great significance for identifying novel therapeutic targets. Tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in NB progression [7] . Macrophages in the TME, exhibit high plasticity and can be polarized into two distinct states: the M1 phenotype (anti-tumor) and the M2 phenotype (pro-tumor). In NB, tumor-associated macrophages predominantly display an M2-like phenotype, thereby promoting tumor immune evasion, angiogenesis, and metastasis [8] . However, the precise molecular mechanisms by which NB cells regulate macrophage M2 polarization remain largely unclear. Recent studies have revealed that lactate generated from glycolysis can induce macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype [9] . In various tumors, including lung cancer and lymphoma, ALK activation has been demonstrated to significantly enhance glycolytic levels in tumor cells, thereby supporting their malignant phenotypes [10,11] . However, whether ALK regulates macrophage polarization through modulating glycolysis in NB remains unreported. Of note, a recent study has shown that ALK mutation drives NB progression by activating the WNT signaling pathway, and inhibition of the WNT pathway markedly attenuates ALK mutation-induced tumor growth [5] . Moreover, WNT signaling activation has been extensively documented to promote aerobic glycolysis through multiple mechanisms [12] . Based on these findings, we hypothesize that in NB, ALK activation may enhance the glycolytic capacity of tumor cells, and the resulting lactate subsequently induces macrophage M2 polarization. To investigate the upstream molecular mechanisms by which ALK enhance the glycolytic capacity, the transcriptomic dataset GSE228194  (ALK-mutant vs.  ALK-wild-type) was analyzed. Differential expression analysis identified a total of 1917 differentially expressed genes, among which microfibril-associated protein 2 (MFAP2) was one of the most significantly downregulated genes and was further identified as an upstream regulator of glycolysis and macrophage M2 polarization. Moreover, analysis using the GeneMANIA database revealed a co-expression relationship between ALK and MFAP2. Previous studies have reported that MFAP2 is upregulated in various tumors and promotes tumor progression through the WNT signaling-mediated glycolytic pathway [13,14] . However, the role of MFAP2 in NB and its upstream regulatory mechanisms have not yet been reported. To further identify the upstream transcription factors regulating MFAP2, we predicted potential transcription factors of MFAP2 using the hTFtarget database and intersected them with significantly upregulated differentially expressed genes from GSE228194 , as well as the top 1000 glycolysis-related genes from GeneCards, leading to the identification of SRY-box transcription factor 9 (SOX9). In addition, JASPAR database analysis predicted that SOX9 binds to the GCATTGTT sequence within the promoter region of MFAP2. Previous studies have shown that SOX9 expression in NB cells is associated with multiple key biological processes, including migration, invasion, and differentiation [15] . However, the specific function of SOX9 in NB and the mechanisms underlying its upregulation remain unreported. Ubiquitination and deubiquitination of proteins are key mechanisms regulating their stability and activity [16] . Using the Ubibrowser database, we identified the deubiquitinating enzyme USP7 as a potential key regulator of SOX9 stability. Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 7 (USP7) plays important roles in tumorigenesis and immune regulation [17] , and can influence the activity of transcription factors (such as REST and cMyc) through deubiquitination [18] . Previous studies have shown that USP7 promotes glycolysis in tumor cells [19]  and drives NB progression through multiple pathways [20] . Moreover, various USP7 inhibitors have been demonstrated to suppress NB growth [21,22] . Of note, the activity of USP7 is regulated by phosphorylation, which converts USP7 from an inactive to an active state [23] . However, whether ALK activation promotes USP7 phosphorylation, thereby activating its deubiquitinase activity, subsequently enhancing SOX9 protein stability, and ultimately increasing MFAP2 transcription in NB remains to be experimentally validated. Based on the above findings, this study aims to investigate whether ALK activation in NB enhances the deubiquitinating activity of USP7 via  phosphorylation modification, thereby increasing the protein stability of the transcription factor SOX9 and subsequently upregulating MFAP2 transcription. Furthermore, we seek to explore whether MFAP2-mediated glycolysis promotes macrophage M2 polarization, thereby facilitating tumor progression in NB. By elucidating this novel regulatory axis, we hope to provide a theoretical foundation for identifying new therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers for NB.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Animal model establishment and treatment Female BALB/c-nu nude mice (6–8 weeks old, n  = 48) were purchased from Beijing SPF Biotechnology Co., Ltd. All mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle at 21–26 °C and 40–70% humidity, with free access to food and water. After one week of acclimatization, a Kelly cell line stably overexpressing MFAP2 was constructed using a lentiviral vector, and 3 × 106  cells were subcutaneously injected into the right posterior flank of each mouse to establish a NB model. Mice were orally administered lorlatinib at 60 mg/kg/day. Tumor sizes were measured every 3 days using a caliper, and tumor volumes were calculated using the formula: V = length × width2  / 2. After 4 weeks, mice were euthanized, and tumors were harvested, weighed, and photographed. Each group consisted of 6 mice. All experimental protocols have been reviewed and approved by Fujian Medical University (IACUC FJMU 2024-Y-0068).  2.2 Cell culture Human neuroblastoma cell lines SH-SY5Y and Kelly were purchased from Xiamen Yimo Biotechnology Co., Ltd. SH-SY5Y cells were cultured in proprietary medium (IM-H227-1, Yimo). Kelly cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (ZB000BF, Sangon) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (10099141C, Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P1400, Solarbio). Both cell lines were maintained at 37 °C in a 5% CO2  incubator (311, Thermo Scientific). For drug treatment, cells were treated with 10 μmol/L lorlatinib (HY-12215, MCE) for 24 h.  2.3 Lactate level measurement For cell samples, cells from each group were collected, lysed by ultrasonic disruption in distilled water, and centrifuged at 8000 ×g  for 10 min at room temperature. The supernatant was collected for analysis. For tissue samples, tumor tissues were accurately weighed and homogenized in 9 volumes of normal saline (weight: volume = 1:9) on ice using a mechanical homogenizer. The homogenate was centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. Reagents were added according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Lactate Assay Kit (A019-2-1, Nanjing Jiancheng). After thorough mixing, the absorbance was measured at 530 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher Scientific).  2.4 Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level measurement For cell samples, cells from each group were collected and processed according to the manufacturer's instructions of the L-Lactate Dehydrogenase Assay Kit (P0393S, Beyotime). For tissue samples, tumor tissues were accurately weighed and homogenized in 9 volumes of normal saline (weight: volume = 1:9) on ice using a mechanical homogenizer. The homogenate was centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. The assay was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Lactate Dehydrogenase Assay Kit (A020–2, Nanjing Jiancheng). Absorbance was measured at 440 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher) for both sample types.  2.5 Flow cytometry analysis of M1 and M2 macrophage polarization THP-1-derived macrophages were used to assess M1 and M2 polarization following co-culture with Kelly cells. Briefly, THP-1 cells were differentiated into M0 macrophages by treatment with 150 nM phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) for 24 h. Differentiated M0 macrophages were then co-cultured with Kelly cells in Transwell chambers for 24 h. After co-culture, macrophages were harvested and centrifuged. Subsequently, cells were resuspended in 1× Binding Buffer to a density of 1 × 106  cells/mL. The cells were then incubated with 2 μL of PE anti-human CD163 antibody (326,505, Biolegend) and 2 μL of APC anti-human CD86 antibody (374,207, Biolegend) for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. After incubation, the stained cells were analyzed using a flow cytometer (RMNNC-3000, Agilent).  2.6 Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay Cell viability was assessed using the CCK-8 assay. Briefly, cells were adjusted to a density of 1 × 106  cells/mL and seeded into 96-well plates with three replicate wells per group. Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a 5% CO2  incubator until reaching confluence. Then, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution (C0037, Beyotime) was added to each well, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 2 h in the dark. The optical density was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher Scientific).  2.7 Wound healing assay Cell migration was evaluated by a wound healing assay. Briefly, cells were seeded into 6-well plates and cultured to confluence. A linear scratch was created using a 200 μL pipette tip. After washing with PBS to remove detached cells, the medium was replaced with serum-free medium. Wound closure was observed and photographed at 0, 24, and 48 h. Migration distance was measured using ImageJ software.  2.8 Transwell invasion assay Cell invasion was assessed using Matrigel-coated Transwell chambers (356,234, BD Biosciences). Cells were resuspended in serum-free medium (2 × 105  cells/mL) and 100 μL was added to the upper chamber, with 600 μL of 10% FBS-containing medium in the lower chamber. After 24 h of incubation, non-invading cells were removed, and invading cells were fixed, stained with crystal violet, and counted under a microscope. Invasion ability was quantified using ImageJ software.  2.9 Immunofluorescence staining of Ki-67 Ki-67 expression in tumor tissues was detected by immunofluorescence. Briefly, paraffin-embedded tumor sections were dewaxed, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval by microwave heating in antigen retrieval buffer (G1203, Solarbio). After blocking with 3% BSA, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-Ki-67 antibody (ab15580, Abcam; diluted 1:200). Subsequently, sections were incubated with CY3-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (A0516, Beyotime) for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (G1012-100 L, Servicebio). Fluorescence images were captured under a microscope.  2.10 Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) Total RNA was extracted from cells or tissues by RNA extraction solution (G3013, Servicebio), and cDNA was synthesized using PrimeScript RT reagent Kit (RR037Q, Takara). qRT-PCR was performed using TB Green Premix Ex Taq II (RR820Q, Takara) to amplify and measure the relative mRNA expression levels of ALK, iNOS, CD86, Arg1, CD206, HK2, PKM2, MFAP2, TGFBI, ALDH1A3, TCF7L2, SMAD3, SOX9, ETS1, STAT3 and USP7. The 2−ΔΔCT  method was used for data analysis, with β-actin as the reference gene. All primer oligonucleotides were custom-synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Primer sequences are listed in Table 1  .  2.11 Western blot Total proteins were extracted from cells or tissues using RIPA lysis buffer (BL504A, Bio Sharp), and concentrations were determined with a BCA protein assay kit (BL521A, Bio Sharp). Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% skim milk (D8340, Solarbio) for 2 h at ambient temperature, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies targeting the following proteins: SOX9 (1:1000, 55152-1-AP, Proteintech), Arg1 (1:1000, 16001-1-AP, Proteintech), CD206 (1:1000, 18704-1-AP, Proteintech), ETS1 (1:1000, 12118-1-AP, Proteintech), STAT3 (1:1000, 10253-2-AP, Proteintech), TCF7L2 (1:1000, 13838-1-AP, Proteintech), SMAD3 (1:1000, 30130-1-AP, Proteintech), MFAP2 (1:1000, ab231344, Abcam), UB (1:1000, 10201-2-AP, Proteintech), ALK (1:1000, 611551, Biolegend), iNOS (1:1000, 22226-1-AP, Proteintech), CD86 (1:1000, 83523-4-RR, Proteintech), HK2 (1:1000, 22029-1-AP, Proteintech), PKM2 (1:1000, 15822-1-AP, Proteintech), USP7 (1:1000, 26948-1-AP, Proteintech), TGFBI (1:1000, 10188-1-AP, Proteintech), ALDH1A3 (1:1000, 25167-1-AP, Proteintech), and pALK (1:1000, bs-3022P, Bioss). β-actin (1:1000, 66009-1-Ig, Proteintech) served as an internal reference. Following primary antibody incubation, membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies (1:5000, AB0101, AB0102, Abways) for 2 h at 37 °C. Protein signals were visualized using Immobilon Western chemiluminescent HRP substrate (WBKLS0100, Millipore) and captured with a Gel imaging analysis system (ChampChemi 910, SINSAGE). Densitometric analysis of band intensities was performed using ImageJ software.  2.12 Cell transfection Kelly or SH-SY5Y cells were seeded in 6-well plates and cultured to 70–80% confluence. Transfection was performed using Lipo8000™ transfection reagent (C0533, Beyotime) following the manufacturer's instructions. For DNA transfection, 2.5 μg of plasmid DNA (OE-MFAP2, OE-SOX9, OE-USP7, or empty vector) was diluted in 125 μL of Opti-MEM with 4 μL of Lipo8000 per well. The OE plasmids (FH1619, Fenghui) were generated using the pCDH-CMV-MCS-EF1-GFP-Puro backbone vector (HG-VMS0751, Honor). For siRNA transfection, 100 pmol of si-MFAP2 (Sangon Biotech) or negative control siRNA was mixed with 4 μL of Lipo8000 in 125 μL of Opti-MEM, incubated for 20 min at room temperature, and then added to the cells. After 48 h, cells were harvested for downstream assays.  2.13 Lentiviral transduction To establish MFAP2-overexpressing stable cells, Kelly cells were transduced with LV-OE-MFAP2 lentivirus (packaged in pCDH-CMV-MCS-EF1-GFP-Puro vector, HG-VMS0751, Honor). Cells were seeded in 24-well plates at 70% confluence and incubated with 2 μL of virus (1 × 109  PFU/mL) for 24 h. The medium was then replaced with fresh complete medium. Overexpression was confirmed by qRT-PCR and western blot. For stable SOX9 knockdown cells, cells were transduced with sh-SOX9 lentivirus (HG-SH005618, Honor) following the same infection procedure described above. The target shRNA sequences for SOX9 were as follows: sh-SOX9-1, GCATCCTTCAATTTCTGTATA; sh-SOX9-2, CTCCACCTTCACCTACATGAA. Knockdown efficiency was verified by qRT-PCR and western blot.  2.14 Transwell co-culture assay THP-1 cells (1 × 105  cells) were treated with 150 nM PMA for 24 h to induce differentiation into M0 macrophages and seeded into the lower chambers of Transwell plates. An equal number of treated SH-SY5Y or Kelly cells were seeded into the upper chambers. The co-culture system was incubated for 24 h. Subsequently, macrophages in the lower chambers were collected for further detection of macrophage polarization markers.  2.15 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) The levels of IL-10 (E-EL-M0046, Elabscience), TGF-β1 (E-EL-0162, Elabscience), and TNF-α (E-EL-H0109, Elabscience) were measured using commercial ELISA kits. All procedures were performed as per the kit protocols. Absorbance was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher), and cytokine concentrations were calculated from standard curves.  2.16 Dual-luciferase reporter assay The MFAP2 promoter dual-luciferase reporter plasmid was constructed by Tsingke Biotechnology. Cells were seeded in 6-well plates and co-transfected with the reporter plasmid together with either SOX9 overexpression plasmid (OE-SOX9) or negative control (OE-NC) using Lipo8000™ transfection reagent (C0533, Beyotime) when cell density reached 70%–80%. After 24–48 h of transfection, cells were lysed with 500 μL of reporter cell lysis buffer per well, and the supernatant was collected after centrifugation. Firefly luciferase detection reagent (100 μL, measured at 560 nm) and Renilla luciferase detection working solution (100 μL, measured at 465 nm) were added sequentially, and chemiluminescence was measured using a multimode microplate reader (Spark, TECAN) according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime). The ratio of firefly luciferase activity to Renilla luciferase activity was calculated to normalize MFAP2 promoter activity across groups.  2.17 ChIP-qPCR detection of SOX9 binding to the MFAP2 promoter ChIP assay was performed using a Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Kit (P2078, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer's instructions. OE-NC and OE-SOX9 cells were crosslinked with formaldehyde, harvested, lysed, and sonicated. The lysates were incubated with SOX9 antibody (sc-271374, Santa Cruz) overnight at 4 °C, followed by addition of Protein A + G agarose to precipitate the immune complexes. After washing, the complexes were eluted. Following decrosslinking, the samples were digested with Proteinase K, extracted with phenol-chloroform, and precipitated with glycogen to purify the DNA. The purified DNA was used as a template for qPCR with TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (RR820Q, Takara). Fold enrichment was calculated to analyze the enrichment of the MFAP2 promoter.  2.18 Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) detection Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (BL504A, Bio Sharp) supplemented with protease inhibitors (A32955, Thermo Fisher). Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA kit (BL521A, Bio Sharp). For immunoprecipitation, lysates were incubated overnight at 4 °C with Protein A + G magnetic beads pre-coupled with specific antibodies (anti-ALK, anti-SOX9, anti-USP7, or control IgG) using an immunoprecipitation kit (P2179S, Beyotime). After washing, bound proteins were eluted by boiling in 1× SDS loading buffer. For ubiquitination detection, cells were treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 prior to lysis. Immunoprecipitated samples and inputs were analyzed by western blot with indicated antibodies.  2.19 Cycloheximide (CHX) assay for SOX9 protein stability Cells were treated with cycloheximide (CHX, HY-12320, MCE) at a final concentration of 2–3 μg/mL to block de novo  protein synthesis. Cells were harvested at 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 h after CHX treatment, and SOX9 protein expression level was detected by western blot. A protein degradation curve was plotted accordingly.  2.20 Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 statistical software, with standard deviation used to estimate intra-group variability. P  < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A two-tailed, unpaired Student's t -test was used to compare data between two groups, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed for comparing data among multiple groups. Tukey's post-hoc multiple comparisons test was conducted.   3 Results 3.1 ALK inhibition by lorlatinib suppresses glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization in vivo  To characterize the expression pattern of ALK in NB, the expression level of ALK was examined in ALK-positive NB cell lines (CLB-GE, Kelly, and SH-SY5Y). Kelly and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited higher level of ALK mRNA and protein and were therefore selected for subsequent experiments (Fig. 1 A–B ). To investigate the effect of ALK on NB progression in vivo , a nude mouse NB model was established by injection of Kelly cells, and mice were treated with the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib. Lorlatinib treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth rate (Fig. 1 C), reduced tumor volume and weight at the endpoint (Fig. 1 D–E), indicating that ALK inhibition effectively suppresses the tumor progression of NB in vivo . Furthermore, ALK inhibition reduced glycolysis in NB, as evidenced by significantly decreased lactate content (Fig. 1 F) and LDH activity (Fig. 1 G) in tumor tissues following lorlatinib treatment. Given that glycolysis can promote macrophage M2 polarization in the TME [24] , we further examined the expression of immunosuppressive factors and macrophage polarization markers in tumor tissues. Lorlatinib treatment significantly reduced the secretion levels of immunosuppressive factors IL-10 (Fig. 1 H) and TGF-β1 (Fig. 1 I), decreased the mRNA (Fig. 1 J) and protein (Fig. 1 L) expression levels of M2 macrophage markers (Arg1, CD206), and increased the mRNA (Fig. 1 J) and protein (Fig. 1 K) expression levels of M1 macrophage markers (iNOS, CD86) in tumor tissues. These results suggest that ALK inhibition reduces glycolysis and reverses M2 polarization of macrophages in NB progression.  3.2 ALK mediates glycolysis to induce M2 macrophage polarization in vitro  To investigate the regulatory role of ALK inhibition on glycolysis and macrophage polarization in vitro , SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were treated with lorlatinib. Lorlatinib treatment did not significantly alter ALK mRNA expression level in either cell line (Fig. 2 A ), which is expected as lorlatinib inhibits ALK kinase activity rather than its transcription, but effectively reduced ALK phosphorylation level in both SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells (Fig. 2 B–D). Furthermore, lorlatinib treatment significantly decreased lactate production (Fig. 2 E), LDH activity (Fig. 2 F), and the mRNA and protein expression levels of the glycolytic key enzymes HK2 and PKM2 (Fig. 2 G–L) in both cell lines, indicating that inhibition of ALK activity markedly impairs the glycolytic capacity of NB cells. To explore the effect of ALK-inhibited NB cells on macrophage polarization, lorlatinib-treated NB cells were indirectly co-cultured with PMA-differentiated THP-1-derived macrophages (M0 macrophages). Macrophages co-cultured with lorlatinib-treated NB cells exhibited significantly reduced levels of the immunosuppressive factors IL-10 and TGF-β1, as well as decreased protein expression of M2 polarization markers Arg1 and CD206. In contrast, the levels of the pro-inflammatory factor TNF-α and the protein expression of M1 polarization markers iNOS and CD86 were upregulated (Fig. 2 M-P). Consistently, lorlatinib treatment significantly reduced the percentage of M2 (CD163-positive) macrophages (Fig. S1A). To confirm that glycolytic lactate serves as the causal factor for NB cell-triggered M2 macrophage polarization, we performed lactate rescue experiments using lorlatinib-exposed Kelly cells (Fig. S1B-E). Supplementation with exogenous L-lactate (Nala) restored lorlatinib-suppressed IL-10 and TGF-β1 secretion while dampening lorlatinib-upregulated TNF-α release (Fig. S1B–C). Consistently, Nala partially rescued lorlatinib-triggered M1 marker upregulation (iNOS, CD86) and recovered the lorlatinib-reduced expression of M2 markers (Arg1, CD206) (Fig. S1D-E). These results verify glycolytic lactate as the key metabolite mediating ALK-driven M2 macrophage polarization. Taken together, ALK activation enhances glycolysis and lactate production in NB cells to induce M2 macrophage polarization, while ALK inhibition reverses this process.  3.3 ALK upregulates MFAP2 expression to promote glycolysis To explore the key downstream mediators of ALK signaling in NB, we analyzed differentially expressed genes based on the GEO dataset GSE228194 . Volcano plot analysis revealed that MFAP2, TGFBI and ALDH1A3 were significantly downregulated in the ALK MUT (ALK-mutant) group (Fig. S2A). Genemania database further confirmed a strong co-expression relationship between ALK and MFAP2 (Fig. S2B). Notably, analysis of the TARGET Neuroblastoma (NBL) dataset identified a robust positive correlation between MFAP2 expression and glycolysis GSVA score in NB clinical tumor samples (Fig. S2C). To validate whether MFAP2 expression is regulated by ALK activity, we examined MFAP2 level in both in vivo  and in vitro  models after lorlatinib treatment. Lorlatinib treatment remarkably reduced the mRNA and protein levels of MFAP2, TGFBI and ALDH1A3 both in tumor tissues of NB model mice and Kelly cells, with MFAP2 showing the most pronounced alteration. Of note, TGFBI mRNA expression exhibited no significant difference in Kelly cells following lorlatinib intervention (Fig. 3 A–D ). Collectively, these data identify MFAP2 as a direct downstream target of ALK signaling in NB. To explore the biological function of MFAP2 in NB, MFAP2 overexpression (OE-MFAP2) and knockdown (si-MFAP2) were performed in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, respectively. The efficiency of MFAP2 overexpression (Fig. S2D–G) and knockdown (Fig. S2H–K) was validated in each cell line. Compared with the overexpression (OE)-negative control (NC) or siRNA negative control (si-NC) groups, MFAP2 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein levels of the key glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2, whereas MFAP2 knockdown exerted the inhibitory effects (Fig. 3 E–I). Consistently, MFAP2 overexpression significantly increased lactate production and LDH activity, while MFAP2 knockdown markedly suppressed these glycolytic parameters (Fig. 3 J–K). Furthermore, MFAP2 overexpression significantly enhanced NB cell viability (Fig. 3 L), as well as cell invasion (Fig. 3 M–O) and migration (Fig. S2L), whereas MFAP2 knockdown led to significant inhibition of these capacities. Collectively, these results indicate that MFAP2, which is regulated by ALK, potently promotes glycolysis, invasion, and migration in NB cells.  3.4 ALK promotes MFAP2 transcription by upregulating SOX9 To investigate the molecular mechanism by which ALK regulates MFAP2 expression, potential transcription factors mediating this process were screened. A total of 90 putative transcription factors of MFAP2 were retrieved from the hTFtarget database. These were intersected with the significantly upregulated differentially expressed genes (840 genes) from the GEO dataset GSE228194  and the top 1000 glycolysis-related genes obtained from GeneCards, yielding five candidate transcription factors: TCF7L2, SMAD3, SOX9, ETS1, and STAT3 (Fig. S3A). Further bioinformatic analysis based on the TARGET-NBL dataset uncovered a moderate positive correlation between SOX9 expression and M2-type tumor-associated macrophage infiltration (Fig. S3B). The JASPAR database predicted that SOX9 could specifically bind to the GCATTGTT sequence within the MFAP2 promoter region (Fig. S3C–D). Western blot analysis revealed that lorlatinib treatment significantly downregulated the protein levels of STAT3, SOX9, TCF7L2, SMAD3, and ETS1 in Kelly cells, among which SOX9 exhibited the most pronounced reduction (Fig. 4 A–B ). To validate the transcriptional regulation of MFAP2 by SOX9, MFAP2 expression was examined in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells overexpressing SOX9 (the overexpression efficiency was validated in Fig. S3E–H). The results demonstrated that SOX9 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein level of MFAP2 (Fig. 4 C–G). Dual-luciferase reporter assays further confirmed that SOX9 overexpression significantly enhanced the transcriptional activity of the wild-type MFAP2 promoter (PGL3-MFAP2 WT) in both SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, whereas no significant activation was observed with the mutant promoter (PGL3-MFAP2 MUT) (Fig. 4 H). ChIP-qPCR assays also showed that SOX9 directly bound to the MFAP2 promoter region in both NB cell lines, and this binding was significantly enhanced upon SOX9 overexpression (Fig. 4 I). Together, these results indicate that SOX9, as a transcription factor, directly binds to and activates MFAP2 transcription, thereby mediating the regulation of MFAP2 expression by ALK signaling.  3.5 ALK inhibition promotes proteasome-dependent degradation of SOX9 To further investigate the regulatory mechanism of ALK on SOX9, a series of experiments were performed. Co-IP assays showed that there was no direct protein–protein interaction between ALK and SOX9 in SH-SY5Y or Kelly cells (Fig. 5 A ). The effect of lorlatinib treatment on SOX9 protein stability was then assessed using the protein synthesis inhibitor CHX. In SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, SOX9 protein exhibited a relatively slow degradation rate and a long half-life. In contrast, lorlatinib treatment significantly accelerated the degradation of SOX9 and markedly shortened its half-life, indicating that inhibition of ALK activity reduces SOX9 protein stability (Fig. 5 B–D). To determine whether this degradation process is mediated by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, the ubiquitination level of SOX9 was examined, and the proteasome inhibitor MG132 was employed for validation. Co-IP assays revealed that lorlatinib treatment significantly increased the ubiquitination level of SOX9 (Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, MG132 treatment effectively rescued the lorlatinib-induced downregulation of SOX9 protein (Fig. 5 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that inhibition of ALK activity promotes ubiquitination and proteasome-dependent degradation of SOX9, thereby reducing its protein stability. However, the absence of a direct protein interaction between ALK and SOX9 suggests that other intermediary molecules may mediate this regulatory process.  3.6 ALK stabilizes SOX9 through USP7-mediated deubiquitination to promote MFAP2 expression To identify the intermediary molecules mediating the regulatory relationship between ALK and SOX9, the UbiBrowser database was employed to predict potential upstream deubiquitinases of SOX9 (Fig. S4A). Given that USP7 has been reported to promote glycolysis in tumor cells [19] , USP7 was selected as the core candidate molecule. We further used PhosphoSitePlus database to predict multiple phosphorylation modification sites on USP7 (Fig. S4B). Moreover, we assessed the impact of ALK inhibition on total USP7 and phosphorylated USP7 (p-USP7). Western blot results showed that lorlatinib treatment reduced the abundance of both USP7 and p-USP7 in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells (Fig. 6 A ), indicating that ALK kinase activity supports USP7 expression and its phosphorylation modification. Co-IP results confirmed that ALK and USP7 reciprocally formed endogenous protein complexes, and lorlatinib treatment drastically weakened their mutual binding (Fig. 6 B). To verify that this interaction is direct rather than mediated by other intracellular factors, we conducted GST pull-down assays with recombinant proteins, which validated the direct physical binding between ALK and USP7 in vitro  (Fig. 6 B). The endogenous interaction between USP7 and SOX9 was also validated by Co-IP results (Fig. 6 C). To further validate the regulatory effect of USP7 on SOX9, USP7 overexpression was performed in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells. Both the mRNA and protein expression level of USP7 was significantly increased in the OE-USP7 groups, confirming the overexpression efficiency (Fig. 6 D–G). The effect of USP7 overexpression on SOX9 protein stability was then assessed using a CHX chase assay. The results demonstrated that USP7 overexpression significantly slowed the degradation rate of SOX9 and prolonged its protein half-life (Fig. 6 H–I). Furthermore, ubiquitination assays revealed that USP7 overexpression markedly reduced the ubiquitination level of SOX9 (Fig. 6 J–K), indicating that USP7 stabilizes SOX9 protein through deubiquitination. On this basis, the effects of USP7 overexpression on the expression of SOX9 and its downstream target gene MFAP2 were examined. The results showed that USP7 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein levels of SOX9 and MFAP2 (Fig. 6 L–O). To genetically validate the hierarchical ALK-USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 cascade, we performed two sets of rescue/blocking assays presented in Fig. S4C–P. First, SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were treated with lorlatinib alone or lorlatinib combined with USP7 overexpression. USP7 overexpression rescued lorlatinib-triggered downregulation of SOX9 and MFAP2 at both mRNA and protein levels (Fig. S4C–K). We further performed CHX chase assays to evaluate SOX9 protein stability under the same treatment conditions. Lorlatinib notably accelerated SOX9 degradation and shortened its half-life, whereas co-overexpression of USP7 effectively rescued SOX9 protein stability impaired by ALK inhibition (Fig. S4L). These rescue data confirm that USP7 acts downstream of ALK to maintain SOX9 and MFAP2 expression. Next, we carried out epistasis blocking assays in Kelly cells to validate SOX9 as the indispensable downstream effector of USP7. The knockdown efficiency of SOX9 shRNA constructs was verified by qRT-PCR and western blot (Fig. S4Q–S). Compared with OE-NC control, USP7 overexpression significantly elevated intracellular lactate production, upregulated glycolytic genes HK2, PKM2 as well as MFAP2 at both mRNA and protein levels, and increased β-catenin protein expression; however, simultaneous knockdown of SOX9 partially abolished these phenotypes (Fig. S4M–P). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that USP7, as a key intermediary molecule between ALK and SOX9, binds to both proteins, stabilizes SOX9 through deubiquitination, and consequently upregulates MFAP2 expression.  3.7 MFAP2 mediates ALK-induced tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 polarization in vivo  To investigate whether MFAP2 functions as a key downstream effector of ALK signaling in vivo , a Kelly cell line stably overexpressing MFAP2 was established, and a subcutaneous nude mouse model was generated with or without lorlatinib intervention. Compared with the LV-OE-NC group, MFAP2 overexpression (LV-OE-MFAP2 group) significantly accelerated tumor growth (Fig. 7 A ), increased tumor volume and weight (Fig. 7 B–C), and elevated the proportion of Ki-67-positive proliferative cells (Fig. 7 D–E). Moreover, lactate content (Fig. 7 F), the secretion levels of the immunosuppressive factors IL-10 and TGF-β1 (Fig. 7 G–H), as well as the mRNA and protein expression levels of the M2 macrophage markers Arg1 and CD206 (Fig. 7 I–K), were all significantly increased. In contrast, lorlatinib treatment (LV-OE-NC + lorlatinib group) markedly suppressed the above tumor-promoting, glycolysis-promoting, and M2-polarizing effects. Notably, compared with the LV-OE-NC + lorlatinib group, the LV-OE-MFAP2 + lorlatinib group exhibited a partial reversal of these inhibitory effects, as evidenced by significant recoveries in tumor growth, lactate production, immunosuppressive factor secretion, and M2 polarization levels, indicating that MFAP2 overexpression could partially antagonize the anti-tumor effects of ALK inhibition. Conversely, the expression levels of the M1 macrophage markers iNOS and CD86 showed opposite trends (Fig. 7 I–K). In summary, these in vivo  findings demonstrate that MFAP2 significantly promotes NB tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 macrophage polarization. Furthermore, overexpression of MFAP2 partially counteracts the anti-tumor effects of the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib, further confirming that MFAP2 acts as a key downstream effector of ALK signaling and mediates ALK-induced promotion of tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 macrophage polarization in NB.   4 Discussion NB is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, and patients with refractory or relapsed NB have dismal survival rates [25] . Despite recent advances in comprehensive treatment strategies, including targeted therapies, the prognosis for patients with high-risk NB remains poor, particularly for those harboring ALK gene mutations [26] . Targeting the ALK receptor has emerged as one of the most promising and specific therapeutic approaches for NB [27,28] . Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ALK drives NB progression is of great significance for the identification of novel therapeutic targets. In this study, we unveil a previously unrecognized mechanism by which ALK drives NB progression through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 signaling axis, which regulates glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization. Specifically, ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, thereby enhancing the protein stability of SOX9. SOX9, acting as a transcription factor, directly binds to the promoter region of MFAP2 and upregulates its expression. In turn, MFAP2 potentiates the glycolytic capacity of NB cells, leading to increased lactate production and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which induces the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward the M2 phenotype and ultimately accelerates tumor growth. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of ALK with lorlatinib effectively disrupts this signaling cascade, suppresses glycolysis, reverses M2 polarization, and impedes NB progression. ALK is one of the most frequently mutated oncogenes in NB, and its activating mutations serve as critical drivers of NB progression [29] . Multiple studies have elucidated the molecular mechanisms by which ALK promotes NB progression from distinct perspectives. For instance, ALK upregulates POSTN and activates WNT signaling to drive NB progression [5] , and super-enhancer-driven IRF2BP2 regulates the chromatin accessibility of ALK and cooperates with AP-1 to maintain NB cell survival [30] . Clinically, lorlatinib has demonstrated favorable efficacy and safety in patients with ALK-driven relapsed or refractory NB, with a modified response rate of 30% as a single agent in pediatric patients and 63% when combined with chemotherapy [31] . Consistent with these reports, the present study shows that ALK is highly expressed in human NB cells and a nude mouse NB model, and that lorlatinib treatment significantly suppresses the proliferation, migration, and invasion of NB tumor cells. More importantly, we reveal for the first time that ALK regulates glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis, thereby expanding the current understanding of ALK signaling pathways. USP7, a widely expressed deubiquitinating enzyme, exerts pro-tumorigenic effects across multiple cancer types, including breast, pancreatic, gastric, ovarian, and lung cancers [17,32–34] . Previous studies have demonstrated that USP7 stabilizes various substrate proteins, such as c-Myc, p53, and PTEN [35–37] , through deubiquitination, thereby contributing to tumor progression. In NB, high USP7 expression is associated with poor prognosis, and pharmacological inhibition of USP7 effectively suppresses NB cell growth [20] . In the present study, we observed that inhibition of ALK activity markedly reduces the interaction between USP7 and ALK. Furthermore, USP7 overexpression significantly prolongs the half-life of SOX9 protein and decreases its ubiquitination level. Collectively, these findings suggest that ALK stabilizes SOX9 by activating the deubiquitinase activity of USP7, thereby providing novel mechanistic insight into the role of USP7 in NB pathogenesis. SOX9 is a pivotal transcription factor of the SOX family, playing critical roles in various malignancies [38] . In NB, SOX9 has been reported to be associated with cell differentiation, migration, and invasion [15] ; however, its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain largely undefined. In this study, we identified SOX9 as a key transcription factor downstream of the ALK signaling pathway, and demonstrated that its protein stability is regulated by USP7-mediated deubiquitination. Furthermore, using dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChIP-qPCR, we provide the first evidence that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter and activates its transcription. These findings not only link SOX9 to glycolytic metabolism in NB but also offer novel insights into the functional role of SOX9 in tumors. MFAP2 is an essential component of extracellular matrix microfibrils [39]  and has recently garnered increasing attention in cancer research. Previous studies have reported that MFAP2 is upregulated in various malignancies, including oral squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, where it promotes glycolysis and tumor progression by activating the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway [13,40] . Consistent with these published findings, our western blot data in Kelly cells revealed that β-catenin protein levels fluctuated synchronously with glycolytic enzymes HK2, PKM2 and MFAP2 upon USP7 overexpression and SOX9 knockdown (Fig. S4O–P), indirectly supporting that MFAP2 may drive glycolysis via  WNT/β-catenin signaling. However, the expression and function of MFAP2 in NB have not been previously characterized. In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that MFAP2 is a key downstream effector molecule of the ALK signaling pathway, and its expression is positively regulated by the ALK-USP7-SOX9 axis. Functional assays revealed that MFAP2 overexpression significantly enhances glycolytic capacity, proliferative activity, and invasive and migratory abilities of NB cells. More importantly, in vivo  experiments showed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effect of lorlatinib, further confirming that MFAP2 serves as a critical mediator of the pro-tumorigenic function of the ALK signaling pathway. The interplay between tumor cell metabolic reprogramming and immune microenvironment remodeling is a current hotspot in cancer research. Studies have shown that lactate produced by tumor cells can act as a signaling molecule to induce the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward the M2 phenotype, thereby promoting immune evasion [41,42] . In the present study, we validated this mechanism in NB: following lorlatinib-mediated inhibition of ALK activity, lactate production in NB cells was reduced, accompanied by downregulated expression of M2 macrophage markers and upregulated expression of M1 markers in tumor tissues. Furthermore, in vitro  co-culture experiments confirmed that NB cells with suppressed ALK activity induced macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype. Notably, we further performed lactate rescue co-culture assays to provide direct causal evidence: exogenous lactate supplementation largely reversed lorlatinib-triggered M1 shift and restored M2 polarization, verifying glycolytic lactate as the key metabolite mediating ALK-MFAP2 axis-driven macrophage phenotypic remodeling. These findings suggest that ALK not only promotes NB progression through cell-autonomous mechanisms but also reshapes the immune microenvironment via  metabolic reprogramming. From a translational perspective, our results offer insights for improving targeted therapy for ALK-positive high-risk NB. Considering the unsatisfactory sustained efficacy of single-agent lorlatinib in clinics, combinatorial treatment with lorlatinib plus USP7 inhibitors or glycolysis inhibitors may concurrently suppress oncogenic signaling, restrain tumor glycolysis and reverse M2 macrophage-mediated immunosuppression. Such combination strategies are expected to improve therapeutic responses and overcome drug resistance, and warrant further preclinical and clinical investigation. The present study has several limitations. First, only female mice were used for in vivo  assays, and sex-based differences in metabolism and immune response remain unexamined, which will be addressed in future work. Second, we have not conducted dedicated functional experiments to dissect how extracellular MFAP2 triggers Wnt/β-catenin-dependent glycolysis, which requires further investigation in future work. Third, Correlative analyses based on the TARGET-NBL dataset provide preliminary clinical evidence, yet survival analysis of the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 signature awaits validation in future cohorts. In summary, this study reveals for the first time a novel mechanism by which ALK promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization in neuroblastoma through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 signaling axis. This finding not only deepens our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ALK-driven NB progression but also provides a new theoretical basis for targeted therapy of NB. Targeting the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 axis, particularly the combination of ALK inhibitors with glycolysis or USP7 inhibitors, may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB patients. Future studies should further explore the role of this signaling axis in NB resistance and relapse, as well as evaluate its value in clinical prognosis prediction.  5 Conclusion In summary, this study elucidates a previously unrecognized mechanism by which ALK drives NB progression. Mechanistically, ALK signaling stabilizes SOX9 via  USP7-mediated deubiquitination, which transcriptionally upregulates MFAP2. Elevated MFAP2 promotes glycolysis in NB cells and induces M2 macrophage polarization, thereby facilitating tumor growth. Pharmacological inhibition of ALK using lorlatinib disrupts this USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis, suppresses glycolysis, reverses M2 polarization, and attenuates tumorigenesis. Collectively, these findings identify MFAP2 as a critical downstream effector of ALK signaling and establish the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a promising therapeutic target for NB. title: Chromosomal instability degrades developmental phenotypes essential for anti-GD2 immunotherapy outcomes in high-risk neuroblastoma
abstract: High-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NBL) is a pediatric malignancy that arises during sympathoadrenal development and expresses the surface disialoganglioside GD2. Monoclonal anti-GD2 immunotherapy is a mainstay of HR-NBL treatment; however, it is associated with severe toxicities. Genomic correlates of outcomes following multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy are limited. We profile 840 tumors and identify actionable ALK gene fusions in HR-NBL. We leverage fetal sympathoadrenal single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize patients with improved post-multimodality outcomes. We demonstrate that patients with improved outcomes have tumors that upregulate noradrenergic and metabolic phenotypes characteristic of mature sympathoblasts—a fetal sympathoadrenal cell population. We show that loss of these developmental phenotypes is mediated by chromosome 11q loss. Targeted analysis of 19 biopsy pairs identifies significant clonal evolution and accumulation of cell-cycle mutations following multimodality treatment. Collectively, we identify chromosomal instability—specifically 11q loss—as key in degrading developmental phenotypes critical for outcomes following multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy.

(low-risk, intermediate-risk, other neuroblastic histologies), NA-HR-NBL (non-amplified high-risk neuroblastoma); and Amp-HR-NBL (MYCN-amplified high-risk neuroblastoma). (B) Overall survival from diagnosis for MiOncoseq patients. (C) OncoPrint of tumor samples from MiOncoseq. Includes somatic mutations, copy-number alterations, gene fusions, and germline variants. Also included are telomere maintenance mechanisms (TMM), MYCN and ALK alteration status, and scaled TERT expression. Measures of chromosomal instability (CIN) including the whole genome integrity index (wGII), the frequency of large state transitions (LSTs), and alterations of chromosome arm 1p and 11q shown. Ploidy, age at diagnosis, International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) stage, and available sequencing data shown. (D) ALK fusions with protein domains shown. (E) Copy number of chromosome 4 highlighting PHOX2B amplifications. (F–I) CIN measures including total chromosomes and chromosome arms gained or lost relative to baseline ploidy, LST, and wGII. ANOVA and Wilcoxon rank-sum test p  values shown. (J) Heatmap of co-occurrence (orange) and mutual exclusivity (yellow) for frequently altered features in diagnostic HR-NBL.    Figure 2 Designation of high-risk neuroblastoma patients with improved outcomes following treatment regimens containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (A) Overview of the treatment of high-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NBL). (B) The clinical context in which HR-NBL patients received regimens containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy stratified by outcomes. Either multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (MMT-GD2) or chemotherapy given in combination with anti-GD2 immunotherapy (CHEMO-GD2). (C) Patients who received MMT-GD2/CHEMO-GD2 stratified by outcomes. Unknown intervals for MMT-GD2 shown in red. Vertical red line represents minimum follow-up of 18 months.    Figure 3 Genomic and transcriptomic correlates of improved outcomes following treatment regimens containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (A) High-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NBL) patients stratified by outcomes following multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (MMT-GD2) or chemotherapy given in combination with anti-GD2 immunotherapy (CHEMO-GD2). Somatic mutations, copy-number alterations, gene fusions, and germline variants shown. Also included are telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM), MYCN amplification status, and ALK alteration status. Measures of chromosomal instability (CIN) including the whole genome integrity index (wGII), the frequency of large state transitions (LSTs), and gains or losses of chromosome arms and ploidy shown. REM, continued remission; CDC, continued disease control; PRG, progression. (B) Recurrent alterations in HR-NBL stratified by MMT-GD2/CHEMO-GD2 and outcomes. FCGR2A/FCGR3A indicate presence of high-affinity SNPs (rs1801274, rs396991). RAS and P53 refer to the presence of detected alterations in these pathways. (C) TMM stratified by outcomes. (D–G) CIN measures by outcomes. (H) Ploidy by outcomes. (I) MMT-GD2 differentially expressed genes. (J) Gene ontology (GO) enrichment of genes upregulated in MMT-GD2 REM. Representative pathways shown. (K) Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) results for patients with improved outcomes following MMT-GD2. Representative upregulated pathways with a consistent direction of effect shown. Negative log10 of the adjusted p  value shown. (L and M) GSEA of noradrenergic signature in MMT-GD2 (L) and CHEMO-GD2 (M) groups. Normalized enrichment score (NES) and p  value shown. Categorical significance assessed via chi-squared test. Continuous variable significance assessed via ANOVA with subsequent Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. NS, not significant; ∗p  < 0.05, ∗∗p  < 0.01, ∗∗∗p  < 0.001 unless otherwise shown.    Figure 4 Immune populations are prognostic but not associated with improved outcomes following treatment regimens containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (A) Overlap between MMT-GD2 differentially expressed genes and the immune response pathway (GO:0006955). (B and C) Expression of NCR3LG1 (B) and NLRC5 (C) in the SEQC and TARGET cohorts. Significance assessed via ANOVA with subsequent Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. (D) UMAP embedding of the integrated neuroblastoma single-cell atlas. (E) Representative marker genes for each cell type. (F) Total cells for each cell type in the integrated neuroblastoma single-cell atlas. (G) UMAP embedding of all immune cells in the integrated neuroblastoma single-cell atlas. (H) Total cells for each immune cell subtype in the integrated neuroblastoma single-cell atlas. (I) Deconvoluted cell proportions stratified by outcomes following either multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy (MMT-GD2) or chemotherapy given in combination with anti-GD2 immunotherapy (CHEMO-GD2). REM, continued remission; CDC, continued disease control; PRG, progression. (J) Relationship between deconvoluted proportions and either MMT-GD2/CHEMO-GD2 outcomes in MiOncoseq or overall survival (OS) in SEQC/TARGET. The TARGET/SEQC cohorts were subgrouped into high-risk (HR), all (HR + IR/LR), and non-HR patients (IR/LR). GD2 significance determined via Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Significance in the SEQC/TARGET cohorts determined using a log rank test between the top and bottom quartile. Color indicates direction of effect; size proportional to −log10 adjusted p  value. (K and L) OS of SEQC patients: HR + IR/LR (K) and HR (L) stratified by highest and lowest quartile of type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1) proportions. Unadjusted log rank p  value shown.    Figure 5 A developmental sympathoadrenal single-cell atlas and identification of sympathoadrenal phenotypes of noradrenergic differentiation (A and B) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding of the integrated fetal sympathoadrenal single-cell atlas overlaid with cell type (A) and weeks post-conception (B). (C) Representative marker genes for the integrated fetal sympathoadrenal cell atlas. (D and E) UMAP embedding of the integrated fetal sympathoadrenal single-cell atlas overlaid with noradrenergic (D) and mesenchymal (E) scores. (F) Immature and mature sympathoblast gene set derivation. (G) Immature and mature sympathoblast gene set scores for sympathoblasts profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing stratified by weeks post-conception. Means and 99% confidence intervals shown. (H) Pearson correlations between noradrenergic, mesenchymal, mature sympathoblast, and immature sympathoblast gene signature scores within all profiled fetal sympathoadrenal cells. (I) Sympathoblast transcriptional module derivation using high-dimensional weighted gene coexpression analysis (hdWGCNA).
