In addition to the tumor's genetic, cellular, and molecular characteristics, factors such as the patient's age and the stage of the disease influence whether the tumor undergoes spontaneous regression or progresses to metastasis, often rendering it resistant to therapy.1   While low-risk NB can naturally regress or differentiate into benign ganglioneuroblastoma, high-risk NB tends to advance to metastatic spread, with only about 20 % of patients surviving for five years post-diagnosis despite intensive chemotherapy.2  , 3   Various signaling pathways are pivotal in neuroblastoma cell survival, including transcription factors (MYCN, NF-κB, and p53), growth factors (PDGF, IGF, VEGF, and EGF), and protein kinase pathways (AKT, PI3K, FAK, and ALK). The literature highlights several pharmacological inhibitors, gene knockdown studies, and chemotherapeutic agents targeting these survival pathways.4   However, the role of MAPKAPKs in neuroblastoma or other tumors remains largely unexplored. MAPK-activated protein kinase 3 (MAPKAPK3/MK3/3pk), first identified in 1996, belongs to the Ser/Thr protein kinase family and functions as a protein activated by mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs). It is primarily activated by MAPKs such as p38 α/β, ERK1/2, and JNK1/2, and plays a significant role in regulating processes including cytokine production, endocytosis, autophagy,5   interferon therapy, intimal hyperplasia, transcription regulation, inflammation,6   and chromatin remodeling.7   Activation of MAPKs has been observed in over 50 % of cases of lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia, as well as in other types of cancer.8  , 9   Phosphoproteomic studies on neuroblastoma cell lines have demonstrated that ALK drives neuroblastoma progression via JNK signaling.10   Additionally, Marengo et al. reported that the invasiveness and migration of neuroblastoma cells treated with etoposide depend on p38MAPK activity, and its inhibition offers improved control over the invasiveness of stage-IV NB.11   The synthetic retinoid Fenretinide, also known as 4-hydroxyphenyl retinamide (4-HPR), has demonstrated strong anticancer properties through extensive in vitro and in vivo studies, as well as in chemoprevention clinical trials.12  , 13   Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain its cytotoxic effects.14–17   At low concentrations (0.5 μM for 7 days), 4-HPR induces neuronal differentiation in NB SH-SY5Y cells,18  , 19   while at concentrations ranging from 0.01 to 5 μM (over 24 to 72 h), it triggers ceramide- and ROS-mediated apoptosis, highlighting its dose-dependent activity on cancer cells.20   Additionally, 4-HPR has been shown to inhibit focal adhesion kinase (FAK), which supports cancer cell invasion, through high-affinity binding. It also binds with high affinity to the ATP-binding sites of all three JNK isoforms, resulting in their inhibition.21   Despite its promising in vitro cytotoxic effects, 4-HPR's anticancer efficacy in clinical trials has been limited due to poor bioavailability. The need for very high drug doses to achieve therapeutic effects often leads to issues such as gastrointestinal toxicity and reversible nyctalopia, which reduce drug tolerability and patient compliance.22–24   When administered orally at lower doses alongside other drugs, 4-HPR has shown improved efficacy, likely due to either synergistic effects or enhanced drug exposure caused by co-administered agents.23  , 25  , 26   However, low bioavailability remains a concern when 4-HPR is used alone. Moreover, oral formulations require a liquid nutritional supplement carrier and are associated with additional side effects.26   Various nanoformulations have been developed to enhance drug bioavailability, including orally administered PLGA PVP-4HPR millicylinders,27   nano-micellar fenretinide formulations (Bio-nFeR),28   and fenretinide emulsions for intravenous use. Although PLGA PVP-4HPR millicylinders improve the drug release rate, they face challenges such as larger particle size and drug crystallization during release.27   On the other hand, fenretinide emulsions are associated with minimal cases of symptomatic intralipid intolerance.29   In this study, we propose a strategy to address the limitations of the drug and existing nanoformulations by developing human serum albumin (HSA) nanoparticles for drug encapsulation. This approach aims to enhance the drug's solubility, bioavailability, and cytotoxic effects. HSA, the most abundant protein in the human body, is synthesized in the liver, has a molecular weight of 66.5 kDa, and a half-life of approximately 19 days. X-ray structural analysis reveals that HSA is composed of three domains (I, II, and III), each containing two subdomains (Ia, Ib, IIa, IIb, IIIa, and IIIb). These domains are arranged to provide multiple binding sites for both hydrophobic and hydrophilic drugs, as well as metabolic substrates. HSA nanoparticles, produced via a simple desolvation method, are biocompatible and non-immunogenic.30   The therapeutic efficacy of this nanoformulation is demonstrated through effective drug loading, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, disruption of mitochondrial membrane potential and G2/M cell cycle arrest. The drug-loaded nanoparticles also influence the expression of pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic molecular markers, facilitating Bax translocation to mitochondria to induce apoptosis. Bax mitochondrial translocation, regulated by p38 MAPK, has been previously observed under ischemic conditions31   and in other systems.32  , 33   This study is the first to report that the reduction of Bax phosphorylation by MAPKAPK3/3pk promotes its translocation to mitochondria in neuroblastoma, identifying MAPKAPK3 as a kinase responsible for Bax phosphorylation in addition to other previously known kinases.34   Immunoprecipitation studies confirm the interaction between MAPKAPK3 and Bax, while immunocytochemistry imaging shows enhanced Bax migration following exposure to 4HPR-loaded nanoparticles in NB cells. Further investigations are necessary to elucidate the detailed mechanisms underlying these observations. Synthesis of 4HPR loaded HSA nanoparticles HSA nanoparticles were prepared by desolvation method. In 2 % aqueous solution of HSA (pH 8.2), ethanol was added drop wise with continuous stirring at 800 rpm until solution becomes turbid and cross linked with 8 % glutaraldehyde for 14–16 h under continuous stirring (300 rpm). 4HPR loaded HSA nanoparticles were also prepared by the same method. 4-HPR dissolved in ethanol was added drop wise in 2 % HSA solution in 1:5 ratio (drug:HSA). The supernatant is discarded and all the washings are accompanied by pellet resuspension in MQ by bath sonicating for 10 mins. For drug loaded nanoparticles the supernatants are collected for checking drug loading.  Characterization of nanoparticles The attributes like hydrodynamic size (size), zeta potential (net charge) and the heterogeneity of the particle system (polydispersity index aka PDI) provides key information about suitability of the particles for drug delivery application which was accomplished by Zeta sizer Nano ZS (Malvern) (with 100 times dilution of non-lyophilised reaction in MQ). The functional groups and the secondary structures in HSA and its nanocarriers were analysed by a Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy (lyophilized samples) and circular dichroism (CD) spectrophotometer (JASCO J-1500) (similarly diluted liquid sample as for Zeta sizer), respectively. The surface and morphological characterizations of nanoparticles were performed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The purified nanoparticles were drop casted on the carbon-coated Copper grid 300 mesh (S160–3, Agar Scientific) for Transmission Electron Microscopy.  Nanoparticles' drug loading, encapsulation efficiency, stability, and solubility analysis The supernatant from the drug loaded nanoparticles was collected and analysed under UV spectroscopy. Following which, the drug loading efficacy and encapsulation efficiency were calculated using the following formulae. Time- dependent zeta potential analysis in DMEM supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) and PBS was performed to study the stability of the nanoparticles. Saturated solution of 4HPR and 4HPR loaded nanoparticles in PBS (pH 7.4) was prepared to assess the specific solubility at 37 °C for 24 h. In vitro cytotoxicity assay 1 × 104  SH-SY5Y cells per well of a 96-well plate seeded in serum deprived media and treated with different dosage of 4HPR (from 0.5 μM −10 μM) and comparable dosage of 4HPR loaded HSANPs and blank HSANPs for 24 h. The cellular viability was estimated by adding final concentration of 0.45 mg/ml of MTT (in PBS), after 24 h of incubation and incubated for 3 h. OD was measured at 596 nm in Tecan. The IC50  doses of 4HPR and 4HPR loaded HSANPs were calculated using non- linear regression method.  Flow cytometry For all the flow cytometry experiments except cell cycle, 1 × 105  SH-SY5Y cells seeded in serum deprived media; treated with IC50  dose of 4HPR, 4HPR loaded HSANPs, and comparable blank HSANPs, for 24 h. To analyse the mitochondrial membrane potential, treated cells were stained with 10 μM of final concentration of JC-1 dye (ab113850, Abcam) for 30 mins upon the completion of 24 h. Cells were then trypsinized and washed twice with PBS before fluorescence analysis using 494 nm and 518 nm filters for FITC and 496 nm, 566 nm and 576 nm filters for PE. Apoptosis analysis was done using FITC annexin V kit from Invitrogen (V13242). Treated cells were analysed in FACS for their distribution in PE positive and annexin positive region to assess the early and late apoptotic population using similar filters as mentioned earlier. For cell cycle analysis, 1 × 106  cells were synchronized in serum deprived media for 48 h and treated with IC50  doses of 4HPR, blank nanoparticles and drug loaded nanoparticles for 24 h in fresh serum deprived media. After 24 h cells were trypsinized and washed twice with 10 mM PBS and fixed for 2 h; by adding drop wise 70 % chilled ethanol at 4 °C before propidium iodide (PI) staining (0.1 mg/ml final concentration along with 0.2 mg/ml RNAse) for 30 min in dark. The cell cycle distribution based on the PI binding to the DNA was recorded by Flow Cytometer.  Estimation of reactive oxygen species 1 × 104  SH-SY5Y cells were treated with 10 μM 2,7-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFHDA) dye (D6883, Sigma) for 45 min before the treatment of 4HPR loaded HSANPs, blank HSANPs, and 4HPR in phenol free media. Time dependent DCF fluorescence measurement was performed with excitation at 485 nm and emission at 529 nm using Infinite M-plex (Tecan).  Protein isolation and western blotting 4HPR loaded HSANPs, blank HSANPs, and 4HPR at IC50  were used to treat 70 % confluent SH-SY5Y cells. After 24 h, the whole cell protein was isolated using RIPA buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 1 % NP-40, 0.1 % SDS, 5 mM EDTA, 0.5 % Sodium deoxycholate and freshly added proteases inhibitors) and quantified with Bradford reagent (ML106) and prepared in 4× lamellae buffer (CSH protocols), boiled at 95 °C for 10 mins. Denaturing SDS-PAGE was used to resolve the desired protein markers and the bands were transferred using towbin's buffer onto PVDF membrane (0.2 μm) (Bio-Rad Immune-Blot®) with semi-dry SD transfer system (Bio-Rad Technology). The membrane was blocked in 5 % BSA prepared in TBST (50 mM Tris, 150mMNaCl and 0.1 % tween 20) and immune-stained with the (1:1000) dilution of respective primary antibodies for overnight at 4 °C. After 3 washes with TBST for 10 mins, counterstaining of the blot with 1:10000 dilution of HRP tagged secondary antibody is performed at RT for 1.5 h; followed by 3 washes with TBST for 10 mins. The bands on blot were developed by Clarity™ Western ECL substrate (Bio Rad Technology). Beta-actin was taken as endogenous control. Antibodies used: Anti-beta actin, Anti-Bax, Anti-Bcl2, Anti-3pk, Anti-caspase 3 and HRP tagged Anti-Mouse, and HRP tagged Anti-rabbit purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology, USA.  Immunofluorescence Tumor tissues fixed in 4 % formaldehyde were then treated with proteinase K (MB086) (working solution 0.6 units/ml) based solution for 20 mins at 37 °C for antigen retrieval. Next, the sections were permeabilized with 0.1 % TritonX-100 in the TBS followed by the blocking of the sections at room temperature for 30 min using 3 % BSA in TBST (0.1 % triton-x). The sections were then incubated with primary antibody (1:200 in TBST) overnight at 4 °C, then incubated with TRITC tagged secondary antibody (1:500) in 2 % BSA for overnight at 4 °C in dark conditions after washing with 0.1 % TBST (3 washes, 10 mins each). Sections were then washed thrice with 0.1 % TBST and mounted on a glass slide with DAPI for fluorescence analysis.  Bio distribution of nanoparticles All experimental animals used in the present study were complied with the guidelines of the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) and approved by the Institutional Animal Ethical Committee (IAEC) of the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Mohali (IISER, Mohali) and National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute (NABI, Mohali). Six-week-old Balb/C mice were used to study the whole-body biodistribution of nanoparticles with the approval of Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (NABI, Mohali). The mice were sedated with Isoflurane in the IVIS anaesthesia system. With the 6 L min − 1 flow rate of evacuation pump and an Oxygen supply to the anaesthesia chamber 2.5 % isoflurane at a flow rate of 1.5 L min − 1 was run into the chamber. The mice were kept in the sterilized anaesthesia chamber following which administered with 5 mg ml − 1 Indocyanine green (ICG)-tagged HSANPs via intravenous route and sterile PBS in control group. Time dependent biodistribution of nanoparticles was observed and subsequently, the mice were sacrificed. The IVIS Spectrum in vivo imaging system (IVIS Illumina Series-III) was used for both in vivo and ex vivo imaging.  In vivo experiments The xenograft mice model of NB was developed in the nude mice with due ethical clearance from the Institutional animal ethical committee (IAEC) of the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Mohali (IISER, Mohali). The animal studies have been conducted by following CPCSEA (Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals) guidelines. This study is in continuation with the previously published work35   wherein the details of the animal experimental design is mentioned. Present study utilizes the tumor tissues to study the drug mediated new molecular mechanics with the purpose to achieve the maximum advantage from the previously treated tumor samples (n = 3) and reduce the animal sacrifices.35    Statistical analysis All the experimental data with the sample size of 3 (n  = 3) were analysed using appropriate statistical tools ANOVA in Origin pro 8.5 and t-test at a significance level of p  ≤ 0.05.   Results and discussion Characterization of HSA nanoparticles Being a member of the BCS (Bio pharmaceutics Classification System) class IV with a high n-octanol-water partition coefficient of 6.31 logP (hydrophobicity index); the drug is poorly water soluble which lowers its bioavailability.27   Therefore, the entrapment of 4HPR in HSA nanoparticles is used as a strategy to overcome this problem and eventually enhance the therapeutic efficacy of the drug treatment. The mean hydrodynamic size of the prepared blank and 4HPR loaded HSANPs was 131.8 nm (Standard Deviation (SD) 0.40) and 153.1 nm (SD 1.159) with the polydispersity index of 0.107 (SD 0.028) and 0.085 (SD 0.002), respectively (Fig. 1 a ). This narrow distribution of the size along with the PDI value; indicates the homogenous population of the particles system. The zeta potential of the blank and 4HPR loaded HSANPs were found to be −29 mV (SD 0.777) and − 33.2 mV (SD 0.872), respectively (Fig. 1 b). This negative value of zeta potential is attributable to the presence of carboxylic groups on the protein which also implies the stability of the nanoparticles.36   Loading 4HPR into HSA nanoparticles resulted in a marginal increase in the hydrodynamic size of the loaded HSANPs and also increased the negative zeta potential, thereby conferring stability to the nanoformulation in the liquid medium. The drug loading capacity of the 4HPR loaded nanoparticle is calculated to be 13.5 % with the encapsulation efficiency of 80.68 % indicating that a substantial amount of the drug is loaded in HSA nanoparticles making it effective for NB killing compared to the bare drug. The loading capacity of the HSA nanoparticles is comparable with exiting nanoformulations.27  , 29   The morphology of the nanoparticles under transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was confirmed as spherical, which correlated with the size distribution analysis from DLS (Fig. 1 c and d). FTIR spectroscopy of 4HPR represents the characteristics peaks in 1600–1500 cm−1  region due to amide and ring bonds, at 3500 and 3300 (N H stretch, 2° amide respectively), 1629 (C O, strong, amide), 1575 (C C ring stretch), 1543 and 1505 cm−1  (N H bending).37   These characteristic peaks of the 4HPR disappear which could be due to non-covalent/hydrophobic interaction between drug and HSA when encapsulated in HSA nanoparticles. It implies that in the aqueous surrounding drug occupies the hydrophobic crevices in the protein molecule and attaches itself via hydrophobic interaction. It's been reported that there are nine characteristic absorption bands in protein-peptide group.38   Out of these, C O stretching corresponding to Amide I  band (1600–1700 cm−1 ), is the most informative part of the protein in secondary structure determination which is directly associated to the backbone conformations and each of the secondary structure has different C O stretching.39   HSA, comprising with each of the three structurally homologous α-helical domains (I–III) are subdivided into sub-domains A and B.40   FTIR analysis show that there is a significant decrease in intensity of amide-I band (1655 cm−1 ) and amide-II band (1543 cm−1 ) when HSA is converted into blank HSANPs, and this intensity slightly increases upon drug binding (Fig. 2 a ). Also, a change in the peak intensity of amide A band (3500 cm−1 ) is observed. Together, this decrease in the band peaks indicates the decrease in the ά-helical content of the total protein structure upon its conversion into nanoparticles, and non-covalent drug-protein interactions upon drug binding.41   In addition, the circular dichroism spectroscopy shows two characteristic peaks of the α-helical structure in HSA as negative bands at 208 nm, and 222 nm. A significant decrease in helical content in HSA protein was observed upon conversion into blank nanoparticles, while smaller decrease in 4HPR-loaded HSA nanoparticles indicating that trapping of the drug inside the nanoparticles led to changes in its secondary structure. The ά helical content of the blank nanoparticles changed to 56.6 % from 80.12 % present in HSA protein, (Fig. 2 b and c) which aligns with earlier reports that ligand/drug binding alters the secondary structures of HSA.42   The time-dependent zeta potential of nanoparticles was not found to be changed significantly till 72 h when incubated in DMEM medium supplemented with 10 % FBS at 37 °C, inferred as systemic stability of nanoparticles (Fig. 2 d). The specific drug binding pockets for lipophilic drugs; in HSA protein; provides enough space and non-covalent interactions for the entrapped drug to be able to be effective for a longer period of time.43   The aqueous solubility of the drug upon encapsulation in nanoparticles increased by 13.4 times (Fig. 2 e). This is in agreement with literature that 4HPR aqueous solubility increases effectively in the form of nanoformulation.44  , 45   Although, one of the benefits of HSA nanoparticles is that, it does not employ the utilization of extra solubilizers and surfactants as a delivery vehicle27  ; in large quantity to solubilize a highly lipophilic drug which otherwise results in immediate drug release, undesirable for long-acting delivery systems. As nanoparticles enhance the delivery of the hydrophobic drugs, HSA encapsulated 4HPR was found to be delivered inside the cells after 4 h. Images from confocal microscopy shows that rhodamine tagged 4HPR loaded nanoparticles reach the cytoplasm and inside nucleus after 4 h (Fig. 3 a ) which is in accordance with the reports stating the A549 cellular uptake of FITC-DTX-NPs.46   The uptake mechanism of HSA nanoparticles is an energy demanding process and has been reported to be mediated by both caveolae- and clathrin-dependent endocytosis. Reports suggests that use of inhibitors which block both the pathways showed significant reduction in particle uptake. Also reduction in temperature from 37 °C to 4 °C also slowed nanoparticle internalization, attributing uptake to be an energy-dependent process.47    In vitro efficacy studies Drug cytotoxicity studies on SH-SY5Y cells for 24 h revealed enhanced efficacy of 4HPR loaded HSANPs compared to the free drug, whereas blank HSANPs did not show any significant cytotoxicity. The calculated IC50  dose of 4HPR was approximately 10 μM and 4HPR loaded HSANPs showed higher in vitro cytotxicity with IC50  of approximately 6 μM (Fig. 3 b). This also indicates that the nanoparticles lead to more effective killing of cancer cells as compared to the bare drug.  Mechanism of in vitro cytotoxicity ROS is an important facilitator of apoptosis. Study of time dependent ROS using DCFHDA shows a 0.44 % increase in ROS in case of 4HPR loaded nanoparticles, compared to 0.14 % of bare drug, while other groups were non-toxic relatively (Fig. 3 c). Cell cycle data from flow cytometry revealed that 4HPR loaded HSANPs treatment significantly arrested the cell population in G2/M phase as reported in leukemic cells and glioma cells48  , 49   which shows the cytostatic behaviour of drug (Fig. 4 a and b ). JC-1 dye; upon staining of the treated cells show a decrease in J-aggregate/J-monomer ratio (indicative of healthy cells) from 2.65 for cells treated with 4HPR only to 0.68 in case of drug loaded nanoparticles, while control maintained the ratio at 7.2 (Fig. 4 c, d and e). This indicates the proapoptotic nature of the drug; i.e. depolarization of mitochondrial membrane potential; which is further exacerbated by 4HPR loaded nanoparticles.20   Further, increased expression of cleaved caspase-3 in case of drug loaded nanoparticles is responsible for the disruption of cytoskeletal and other structural proteins in the cells. Western blotting showed the significant increase in α II spectrin breakdown products (BDPs) of size 120 kd in treatment group50   (Fig. 4 f-h). Apoptotic assay also indicates the 1.76 times increase in late apoptotic population compared to only drug (Fig. 4 i and j). 4HPR's killing/pro-apoptotic effect is reported to be executed by generating oxidative stress in the cancer cells. ROS is generated in the mitochondria by mitochondrial respiratory chain proteins which leads to disruption of mitochondrial membrane potential, DNA damage and also alters the cellular protein expression to affect cell cycle progression.51    In vivo bio-distribution of 4HPR loaded HSANPs The biodistribution studies of 4HPR loaded HSANPs in BALB/c mice were performed to understand its therapeutic and diagnostic efficacy, toxicity and biocompatibility. The photoluminescence intensity of ICG labelled 4HPR loaded HSANPs was measured at different time points of 0.25 h, 1 h, 3 h, 6 h, and 24 h (Fig. 5 a ) in mice. The ex-vivo bioimaging of vital organs (brain, spleen, kidneys, heart and liver) demonstrated the accumulation of particles in the liver after 24 h represent the hepatic uptake by opsonisation and no visible accumulation in other organs which implies very less cytotoxicity to the vital organs of the nanoparticles.52  , 53   Further analysis of ROI radiant intensity confirmed the similar observation (Fig. 5 b).  Molecular mechanism for apoptosis 4HPR is reported to induce Bax/Bcl2 ratio which eventually leads to Bax mitochondrial translocation by affecting its conformation.54  Fig. 6 a and b  in vitro data shows that treatment with drug loaded nanoparticles; Bax/Bcl2 ratio is significantly increased as compared to control indicating the induction of apoptosis at this dose and not differentiation in SH-SY5Y cancer cells. Expression of Bax increased up to 4.34 times in case of drug loaded nanoparticles which is about 1.56 times more, compared to the 2.78 times increase observed with bare drug treatment. The anti-apoptotic protein Bcl2 was reduced up to 8.33 times which is 3.5 times more reduction in cases of drug loaded nanoparticles as compared to 2.38-fold in case of bare drug treatment only. This significant change in pro-and anti-apoptotic protein expression due to nanoparticle can be attributed to the enhanced drug availability in the aqueous milieu. Literature55   indicates that post-translational modifications,56   regulate Bax translocation to mitochondria during apoptosis. In this study, we investigated the role of Bax phosphorylation in neuroblastoma, particularly its impact on mitochondrial translocation. Previous reports suggest that downregulation of p38 MAPKs and JNK improves the survival outcomes of stage IV neuroblastoma. Here, we specifically targeted the expression of MAPKAPK3/3pk, a downstream marker of the p38/JNK pathway. In vitro analysis revealed that phosphorylated Bax remains localized in the cytoplasm, and exposure to 4HPR-loaded nanoparticles significantly reduced the phosphorylated fraction of Bax (Fig. 6 c and d). This observation aligns with previous findings by Kale et al.,34   leading us to hypothesize that MAPKAPK3/3pk could function as a kinase responsible for Bax phosphorylation. Protein-protein interaction studies using immunoprecipitation demonstrated that MAPKAPK3 binds to Bax, as evidenced by the interaction detected with anti-Bax antibody. However, this interaction was diminished following treatment with 4HPR-loaded nanoparticles (Fig. 6 e and f), suggesting that the phosphorylated form of Bax does not facilitate mitochondrial translocation. Reduced MAPKAPK3 expression, and consequently decreased Bax phosphorylation, promotes Bax translocation to mitochondria, leading to apoptosis. Western analysis with 3pk activator anisomycin also shows that 3pk and bax are related. (Fig. 6 g and h) Immunofluorescence studies in Fig. 6 i and j show Bax mitochondrial translocation as red fluorescence from anti bax TRITC staining. The colocalization coefficient, represented by the Pearson coefficient, was 0.8 for drug-loaded nanoparticles compared to 0.56 for controls, indicating enhanced Bax translocation into mitochondria upon treatment with the nanoparticle formulation. In vivo analysis further corroborated these findings, showing an increased Bax/Bcl2 ratio and downregulation of MAPKAPK3/3pk in treatment group as compared to control animals (Fig. 7 a and b ). Qualitative analysis through immunofluorescence also confirmed apoptosis in tumor tissues, evidenced by enhanced caspase-3 expression (Fig. 7 c and d) and αII-spectrin BDPs (Fig. 7 e and f). Collectively, these observations confirm that 4HPR loaded HSA nanoparticles are effective in both in vitro and in vivo in killing of cancer cells at lower doses thus potentially minimizing the side effects.  Conclusion This study demonstrates that 4HPR, when delivered as a nanoformulation, exhibits significantly enhanced effectiveness in killing neuroblastoma cells by caspase activation and disrupting structural proteins; compared to the bare drug, highlighting the therapeutic potential of drug encapsulated nanoparticles. Further investigation into apoptotic mechanism revealed the influence of Bax phosphorylation, role of MAPKAPK3/3pk and its reduction in Bax migration to mitochondria. While several kinases have been previously implicated in regulating Bax, this study suggests that MAPKAPK3/3pk may represent a novel kinase involved in Bax-mediated apoptosis and provides a new perspective for understanding and potentially targeting Bax regulation to improve therapeutic outcomes in NB. title: MicroOrganoSphere™ technology to advance drug screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine
abstract: Background Neuroblastoma is among the most fatal pediatric solid tumors and high-risk patients face poor survival despite intensive treatment. Genomic profiling alone has not translated into effective treatment stratification for all neuroblastoma patients. Drug screening offers a complementary strategy, but conventional preclinical models are constrained by limited establishment success from low-input material and by timelines often incompatible with diagnostic decision-making. Here, we evaluated MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology, in which tumor cells are encapsulated in Matrigel droplets generated by microfluidic droplet formation, by a head-to-head comparison with the conventional suspension cultures to improve growth and drug testing in neuroblastoma. Methods MOS™ were established from patient-derived tumoroids, freshly dissociated patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumors, PDX-derived tumoroids, and a freshly dissociated patient tumor to compare growth and drug responses with suspension. Results Tumor cell growth in MOS™ was comparable or superior to suspension cultures. MOS™ drug screens were performed at a 2.5-fold lower seeding density compared to suspension, whilst maintaining reliable results with consistent drug sensitivity profiles and screen quality to suspension. Promisingly, drug testing in MOS™ was feasible within 9 days of receiving fresh PDX tumor tissue. Conclusion These results demonstrate in a proof-of-concept setting how MOS™ technology could support the establishment and drug screening of neuroblastoma cultures from low-input samples within clinically relevant timelines. MOS™ technology provides a promising functional platform to accelerate preclinical drug testing in neuroblastoma precision medicine.

Keywords Precision medicine  3D cancer models  Pediatric oncology  Neuroblastoma   Data Availability Supporting imaging and drug screening data is available upon request.   1 Introduction Neuroblastoma, the most prevalent pediatric extra-cranial solid tumor, poses a therapeutic challenge [1] . Current treatment for high-risk patients includes induction chemotherapy, surgery, high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation and radiation therapy followed by consolidation therapy with anti-GD2 antibody treatment and retinoic acid [2] . Despite their rigorous treatment regimen, high risk patients face a 5-year overall survival of 50% [3] . The heterogeneity in clinical response highlights the urgent need for a more effective and targeted approach. Median progression-free survival across high-risk pediatric cancers, including neuroblastoma, has been reported as 116 days [4]  with ranges from 1 to 65 months reported for neuroblastoma patients [5] . This emphasizes the limited clinical window for identification of effective therapeutic strategies. Currently, pediatric precision oncology trials use genome sequencing to identify patient-specific targetable driver mutations to guide clinical decisions [4,6] . Such actionable driver genes are detected in 37–94% of patients, and the clinical benefit from matched targeted therapies remains limited for many patients. This can partly be explained as genetic characterization does not fully capture the disease’s complexity, and epigenetic and microenvironmental factors should also be considered [7,8] . As an alternative screening approach that could overcome these limitations, functional drug testing is increasingly considered to guide treatment [8–14] . In vivo  patient derived xenograft (PDX) models are representative and have been used extensively to study tumor response [15] . However, they are low-throughput, time-consuming and expensive to develop and maintain, as engraftment and stable expansion require approximately 1–11 months, followed by several weeks to assess drug response [9,16–18] . While 2D cell lines are easy to culture, they fail to mimic the tumor's complex architecture [16] . 3D patient-derived tumoroids, that have been established for neuroblastoma [10,18,19] , offer a more promising middle ground with better scalability and lower costs compared to PDX. They more accurately mimic the architecture and physiological responses of solid tumors compared to 2D models [20] . However, tumoroid establishment has several limitations that hinder its clinical implementation for precision medicine: the required large amount of input material, limited success rate, loss of the tumor microenvironment and extended establishment time, typically requiring 3–12 months, after which drug testing typically lasts 5 days [4,9,10,12–14,16,18,20,21] . This often exceeds patients’ progression-free survival [4] . Patients are treated during these extended establishment periods of PDX and tumoroid models, which may limit the representation of the current state of the patient’s tumor. Additionally, in precision oncology programs, treatment strategies are typically discussed in a Molecular Tumor Board, where molecular profiling results become available after a mean turnaround time of 25.4 days. To allow integrated discussion alongside molecular profiling, preclinical models used to guide treatment decisions should ideally provide drug response predictions within a similar timeframe. To shorten establishment timelines, ex vivo  short-term drug screening can be performed on freshly dissociated tumor tissue cultured in suspension. This method has been successfully explored in novel pediatric precision medicine studies [8,9,11,22] , but is limited by the low quantity of available tumor material from minimally invasive procedures used in children, variable viability after dissociation, and the time required to expand sufficient biomass prior to screening. Further optimization is therefore required to improve success rates and reduce the time to screen. MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology can be used to overcome the previously mentioned limitations of ex vivo  screens. MOS™ are droplets generated by microfluidic droplet formation that encapsulate patient-derived tumor cells in Matrigel. MOS™ are automatically and rapidly generated from minimal patient tissue (i.e. low input samples with limited cell numbers) in a high-throughput fashion [23] . Compared to conventional tumoroids, MOS™ require lower input tissue and can be rapidly used for drug screening for personalized medicine. In colorectal cancer, MOS™ responses to chemotherapeutics correlated with clinical outcome [24,25]  and Ding et al . demonstrated that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ∼10 days from small, 18-gauge, biopsies. In addition, MOS™ accurately recapitulate patient samples and their microenvironment [24] , recapitulate the heterogeneity within tumors [25]  and facilitate the testing of immuno-oncology therapies [26] . The feasibility of MOS™ in pediatric solid tumors, with a different developmental origin and tumor biology than adult colorectal cancer, and its performance relative to suspension cultures have not yet been evaluated. If using MOS™ technology in neuroblastoma could reduce the number of cells required per well, it would allow testing of a broader array of therapeutic agents, increasing the throughput of drug screening processes with the same biomass input. In this study, we explore the potential of the MOS™ platform as an alternative to previously optimized suspension cultures for neuroblastoma patient-derived models: patient-derived tumoroids, PDX-derived fresh tumor and tumoroid models, and a fresh patient tumor. We directly compare MOS™ and suspension cultures to assess viability, proliferation and drug sensitivity testing of tumoroids and freshly dissociated samples. Our findings demonstrate how MOS™ technology can support short-term culture and functional drug testing, providing a framework for integrating MOS™ into preclinical testing pipelines for neuroblastoma to overcome some of the key limitations of currently available technologies.  2 Methods Detailed experimental procedures, including model generation, culture conditions, imaging settings and data processing pipelines, are provided in the Supplementary Methods . 2.1 Model generation and culture All cultures were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2 . Tumoroid cultures were passaged twice per week, routinely tested for Mycoplasma and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. 2.1.1 Patient derived tumoroid cultures In brief, three patient-derived tumoroids with distinct molecular backgrounds were selected for outgrowth experiments (Suppl. Table 1 ) and cultured in neuroblastoma organoid medium (NBOM) [10,19] .  2.1.2 PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures Neuroblastoma PDX models were previously established and genetically profiled in the ITCC-P4 consortium [27] . Previously reported comprehensive molecular profiling was used in this study: low coverage whole genome sequencing, whole exome sequencing, DNA methylation profiling and RNA sequencing [22,27] . The dissociation method for the PDX samples and the established PDX tumoroids are previously described [18,22] . In brief, fresh PDX tumors were mechanically dissociated, followed by a two-step enzymatic digestion. Fresh PDX cultures were resuspended and cultured in NBOM, with the exception of NB0026, that was cultured in suspension in TSM for 8 days prior to drug screening. For tumoroid establishment, freshly dissociated cells were cultured until stable growth was observed and human tumor cultures were confirmed by SNP analysis and, subsequently, tumoroids were molecularly profiled [18] .  2.1.3 Patient-derived fresh primary culture A fresh neuroblastoma tumor sample was obtained during surgical resection of a refractory patient through an institutionally approved biobank study at the Princess Máxima Center (PMCLAB2025.660). All procedures were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, with age-appropriate written informed consent from patients and/or parents. Preparation of the tumor pieces was started within 2 h after surgery. The primary tumor sample was dissociated via the Liberase protocol, as described in the Supplementary Methods , and immediately MOS™ were generated, and MOS™ and suspension cultures were plated in NBOM.   2.2 Generation and plating of MicroOrganoSpheres™ MOS™ were generated as previously described [24] . Briefly, dissociated tumor cells from patient-derived tumoroids, PDX and human primary tissue digest were resuspended in ice-cold, growth factor–reduced Matrigel (Corning) at a defined density corresponding to 50 viable tumor cells per MOS™. The cell–Matrigel mixture was kept on ice to prevent premature polymerization. MOS™ were generated using a proprietary droplet-based microfluidic generator, which produces highly uniform Matrigel droplets encapsulating tumor cells. Briefly, the cell–Matrigel suspension was loaded into a temperature-controlled microfluidic system in which pressure-driven flow generates monodisperse droplets in an immiscible oil phase. Generation was performed under cooled conditions to maintain Matrigel in liquid state during droplet formation. Droplet size is defined by the microfluidic geometry and pressure settings, resulting in reproducible MOS™ diameters of 230–250 µm. Following droplet generation, MOS™ were collected and incubated at 37°C for 30 min to allow Matrigel polymerization. After gelation, solidified MOS™ were demulsified by transfer onto a hydrophobic PVDF membrane to separate the oil phase from the aqueous droplets. After 2–3 min, polymerized MOS™ were recovered using pre-warmed NBOM. Recovered MOS™ were counted, centrifuged at 150xg  for 5 min and subsequently resuspended at the appropriate density for plating for downstream applications.  2.3 Plating of MOS™ and suspension cultures For MOS™ cultures, MOS™ were dispensed in a 384-well flat bottom plate (6007460, Perkin Elmer) at a density of 40 MOS™ per well, final cell density: 2000 cells per well in 40 µL. For suspension cultures, 40 µL of single cell suspensions were plated in a flat bottom 384-well tissue culture treated microplate (#3764, Corning). For cell growth experiments ( Fig. 1 ), 2000 cells per well were plated, matching MOS™ conditions. For drug screening ( Fig. 2 ), the suspension cultures were seeded at 5000 cells per well, based on previously optimized conditions for neuroblastoma drug screening [10,18] .  2.4 Microscopy-based cell viability readout and analyses In brief, cell viability was assessed by microscopy using Calcein AM viability dye (Calcein; 0.625 µM; #65–0853–78, ThermoFisher) and Ethidium-Homodimer−2 (EthD; 2.5 µM; #E3599, ThermoFisher). The readout was performed with either ImageXpress® Micro Confocal High-Content Imaging system (IXM, Molecular Devices) or the Thunder Widefield Fluorescence microscope (Thunder, Leica™; Suppl. Table 1 ). Wells without any detected viability (<4%) were excluded from analysis. Image analysis was performed using threshold-based segmentation of live (Calcein-positive) and dead (EthD-positive) objects, after which integrated fluorescence intensities were used for downstream analysis.  2.5 Drug screening In brief, drug screening was performed using libraries of 45–90 compounds. Compounds were tested in duplicate across six concentrations (0.1 nM to 10 µM). DMSO-treated wells served as negative controls and staurosporine-treated wells as positive controls. Cells were incubated with compounds for 72 h in fresh PDX screens and 120 h in PDX-derived tumoroid screens. For MOS™ cultures, viability was determined using the microscopy-based live/dead readout. A t = 0 plate was included to assess growth during the screen. Viability was calculated from the relative live and dead fluorescence signals. For suspension cultures, and for comparison in MOS™ cultures after microscopy, CellTiter-Glo 3D (CTG) was used as a conventional ATP-based viability readout [18] .   3 Results 3.1 Tumor cell growth in MicroOrganoSpheres™ is comparable or superior to growth in conventional suspension culture To assess MOS™ technology for neuroblastoma cells, growth of tumor cells derived from various model systems (patient-derived tumoroid, PDX, patient) was monitored when grown in MOS™ and compared to the conventional growth method: in suspension cultures (Fig. 1 A). Tumor tissue was dissociated into single cells and encapsulated in Matrigel droplets using microfluidic droplet generation. After polymerization and demulsification, MOS™ were cultured under standard conditions in direct comparison with suspension cultures. The optimal cell density for cell growth, determined by microscopic inspection, was identified as 50 cells per MOS™ (Suppl. Fig. 1  A). Microfluidic droplet generation produced uniform MOS™ with a diameter of 230–250 µm. Spheroids in MOS™ did not exceed this size, whereas suspension cultures could form larger spheroids, although reliable diameter quantification in suspension was limited due to partial attachment. Growth was observed using fluorescent-based microscopy, where adapted-threshold based signal intensity of Calcein AM and Ethidium Homodimer, were used to identify and quantify the amount of live and dead objects respectively (Suppl. Fig. 1B -C). Viable biomass of patient-derived tumoroids cultured in MOS™ versus suspension was quantified over eight days. MOS™ cultures could successfully be established from all tested patient-derived tumoroids (n = 3), where a biomass increase was observed over time in all models (Fig. 1 B-C; Suppl. Fig. 2  A). MaxNB067 demonstrated superior biomass expansion in MOS™ cultures compared to suspension, while AMC691B and AMC691T showed comparable growth in both conditions. Interestingly, AMC691B cells formed more defined 3D structures in MOS™ compared to the flatter 2D structures when cultured in suspension (Fig. 1 C). These results show comparable to improved cell growth in MOS™ versus suspension cultures derived from patient-derived tumoroids. Next, MOS™ cultures were established from freshly dissociated PDX-derived tissues. PDX-expanded tumors provide sufficient biomass for larger experiments compared to fresh patient samples, while recapitulating molecular and phenotypic profiles of the patient tumor [28–30] . Parallel MOS™ and suspension cultures were established from four samples and all models showed comparable viability (Fig. 1 D-E; Suppl. Fig. 2B ). One model (NB0276) failed to expand in both conditions, consistent with previous reports describing unsuccessful short-term neuroblastoma cultures due to failed growth after dissociation [18,22] . To determine whether possible benefit was due to the presence of Matrigel in the MOS™ conditions, and not the MOS™ themselves, a control experiment with media enriched with Matrigel was performed. Here, biomass decreased in fresh PDX cultures enriched with 0.5% and 5% Matrigel compared to NBOM (Suppl. Fig. 2  C). These results indicate that MOS™ supports cell growth to a similar extent as suspension in freshly dissociated PDX tissues. Lastly, for one fresh patient tumor that was available, outgrowth was compared in MOS™ versus suspension cultures when established directly from the primary patient material. Cell growth was monitored over 10 days (Fig. 1 F-G). Biomass rapidly increased in MOS™, peaking at day 3, while biomass rapidly decreased in suspension cultures. These results indicate that MOS™ technology enables short-term expansion of fresh patient-derived tumor cells ex vivo . Taken together, these findings demonstrate that MOS™ supports viable growth across diverse neuroblastoma models, including fresh and tumoroid cultures derived from patients and PDXs.  3.2 MicroOrganoSphere™ technology enables reliable drug screening, with in vitro  drug sensitivities consistent with those obtained using suspension cultures albeit requiring less biomass To determine whether MOS™ cultures can be reliably used for drug sensitivity testing, automated drug screening in both MOS™ and suspension culture was performed on three PDX-derived tumoroid models and one freshly dissociated PDX sample (Fig. 1 A). Drug sensitivity of suspension cultures was assessed using CTG-based viability, the conventional method for neuroblastoma tumoroid screens [10] . For MOS™ cultures, drug sensitivity was evaluated using the microscopy-based live/dead ratio quantification (Calcein for viable objects, EthD for dead objects; described in Methods). For each compound tested, six concentrations were screened in duplicate. Between 45 and 90 compounds were tested per sample, based on the available biomass, and vehicle (0.25% DMSO) and staurosporin (10 µM) were included as live and dead control, respectively (Fig. 2 A). Abemaciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor inducing approximately 50% cell death in this model (1 µM), was selected as a representative compound to visualize intermediate drug response between vehicle and positive control. To compare drug screen quality and reproducibility, the coefficient of variation (CV) in vehicle-treated control wells and the inter-replicate correlation were used. Drug screens in MOS™ cultures displayed identical average CVs of 9% in vehicle-treated control wells compared to suspension cultures (Fig. 2 B), which is within the preferred acceptance threshold of 10% [31] . Average inter-replicate correlation (same drug, same concentration, different well in the other plate) was comparable but lower in MOS™ conditions (r = 0.83) versus in suspension (r = 0.92; Suppl. Fig. 3  A). Although MOS™ drug screens were seeded at 2000 cells per well compared to 5000 cells per well in suspension cultures, screen quality metrics were comparable between both conditions. We next explored whether MOS™ drug screens reflected expected genotype-associated drug response patterns. NB0026, the only sample with homozygous TP53 inactivation, showed limited response to the MDM2 inhibitor idasanutlin, whereas the TP53-wild-type samples were sensitive (Fig. 2 C). This is consistent with prior reports, but this descriptive observation could not be statistically evaluated because of the limited cohort size (n = 4) and only one TP53-altered sample was included [32–34] . Similarly, NB0026 harbored an ALK mutation, but due to the limited cohort size, no association between ALK status and ALK inhibitor sensitivity could be assessed (Suppl. Fig. 3B ). Drug response was consistent between MOS™ and suspension cultures for three PDX-derived tumoroids and one freshly dissociated PDX (r = 0.88–0.93; Fig. 2 D-E; Suppl. Fig. 3  C). To assess whether MOS™ conditions affect response of individual compounds, we performed a comparative analysis between MOS™ and suspension screens using Limma [35] ; adjusted p-value > 0.05). No individual compound showed a significantly different response between MOS™ and suspension cultures. Inclusion of the freshly dissociated PDX sample NB0026 indicated the ability to rapidly screen low biomass samples. This sample was briefly cultured in suspension prior to drug screening, which was performed 9 days after tissue receipt in MOS™ and suspension, with a 2.5-fold lower seeding density in MOS™. These results indicate that, under the conditions tested here, MOS™ enables drug screening with comparable drug responses and screening quality compared to suspension cultures at a 2.5-fold lower seeding density. Next to microscopy-based readouts, we used CellTiter-Glo (CTG) luminescent cell viability assay to determine cell viability and subsequent drug response as this is the conventional readout for suspension cultures [18,22] . CTG was performed as a second readout for MOS™ conditions, on the same wells as the microscopy-based readout, to assess drug screen quality using CTG as a readout of MOS™ cultures. Due to low cell numbers in MOS™, CTG readouts were less reliable compared to a microscopy-based readout. The variability in vehicle-treated control wells was too high in the CTG-based readout (CV = 0.35, compared to CV = 0.09 in the microscopy-based readout) and inter-replicate correlation was poor (r = 0.54, compared to r = 0.83 in the microscopy-based readout; Suppl. Fig. 3D ). These results show that for drug screening in MOS™, the microscopy-based readout is a more reproducible and reliable approach compared to CTG. The microscopy-based workflow was fully automated and required comparable time to CTG-based workflows, enabling high-throughput screening. Taken together, these results show that MOS™ technology, combined with a microscopy-based readout, enables reliable drug screening with drug sensitivities and screen quality consistent with conventional suspension cultures, while using a 2.5-fold lower seeding density.   4 Discussion High-risk neuroblastoma remains associated with poor survival despite intense multimodal treatment, and robust biomarkers for treatment stratification are lacking in a substantial subset of patients [1,3] . Functional approaches such as in vitro  drug testing have shown promise in guiding treatment in pediatric cancers [8,9,12,14] , but broader implementation is limited by the large amount of required input material, long turnaround times and low establishment success [10,12–14,16,21,36] . MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology allows for rapid automated ex vivo  testing, with responses to chemotherapy reflecting clinical outcome [24] . Here, we evaluated the potential of MOS™ as an alternative for conventional suspension cultures in neuroblastoma to enable drug screening from limited cell numbers. By this novel direct comparison, we demonstrate that MOS™ technology supports short-term tumor cell growth at least as well as suspension cultures and that drug screening can be performed using fewer cells while maintaining reproducibility and drug sensitivity profiles compared to suspension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MOS™ technology is suitable for standardized drug screening in the rare and understudied pediatric cancer neuroblastoma. Across multiple patient-derived sources, including patient-derived tumoroids, PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures and one freshly dissociated patient tumor, MOS™ supported short-term outgrowth that was comparable or superior to suspension culture. This data demonstrates that MOS™ can maintain neuroblastoma tumor viability even from low-input samples, consistent with previous work showing successful establishment of MOS™ cultures from small 18-gauge biopsies [24] . Although only a single primary patient sample could be included here, this proof-of-concept study supports feasibility for future expansion to larger patient cohorts. As expected, variability in growth of the models was observed, especially for the PDX-derived and freshly dissociated patient tumor. Such variability in growth rates has been previously described and has been associated with partial failure of model development [18,22] . Drug screening in MOS™ was performed at 2000 cells per well compared with 5000 cells per well in suspension cultures, while maintaining comparable reproducibility and consistent drug response profiles. The suspension condition reflected the established neuroblastoma drug screening conditions using 5000 cells per well and a CTG-based viability assessment [18] , whereas MOS™ screening was optimized for lower-input screening combined with a microscopy-based viability readout. Potentially a microscopy-based readout could also improve the quality of suspension drug screens at lower densities. A lower seeding density allows the same number of compounds to be tested with less material, which is particularly relevant for fresh patient samples where material is often limited. While reproducibility of MOS™ drug screens was comparable to suspension and below the preferred acceptance threshold of 10% [31,37] , well-to-well variability could be further reduced by quantifying cell viability at the level of individual MOS™ rather than at the whole-well level, as applied in this study. Recent work has demonstrated that single-MOS™ analyses are feasible and result in high reproducibility (CV ≤ 2.5; [25] ). MOS™ cultures showed a tendency toward slightly reduced drug sensitivity compared to suspension, which might be due to reduced drug penetration into the tumoroids because of the different 3D structure or the presence of Matrigel. Only for the freshly dissociated PDX sample NB0026 the effect could be due to presence of TME, although the trend in this sample is less obvious. Interestingly, the freshly dissociated patient tumor showed rapid growth in MOS™ compared to suspension, where it even decreased in biomass. By testing more samples in the future, it needs to be investigated whether this large advantage of the MOS™ technology is consistent across neuroblastoma subtypes. In a freshly dissociated PDX sample, MOS™ drug screening could be successfully completed within nine days of tissue receipt. Likewise, a fresh patient tumor expanded biomass in the first three days after MOS™ generation, comparable with patient-derived tumoroids and fresh PDX samples that increased biomass. These proof-of-concept experiments in one fresh patient tumor and one fresh PDX drug screen provide initial evidence that MOS™ can support ex vivo  testing of fresh material within a short time frame. This is important, as the long turnaround times that often exceed the median time to progression [4] , have limited the clinical use of patient-derived tumoroids [9,10,12] . Ex vivo  drug screening of fresh tumor tissue shortens turnaround times [11,22] , and the reduced cell input required by MOS™ could further improve feasibility of screening low-input samples. We could not compare drug response in MOS™ with patient response, as this data was not available for these samples. However, previous studies have shown that MOS™ responses correlated with clinical outcome [24,25] , and that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ∼10 days of sample receipt in adult cancers. Although future studies should expand this work, as larger pediatric cohorts will be essential to validate clinical applicability and to correlate drug response with patient outcomes, these findings suggest that MOS™ is suited for drug screening within a clinically relevant time frame, especially for low-input material. Next to MOS™, many complementary 3D ex vivo  modelling approaches are being developed to improve the physiological relevance of in vitro  drug testing [38] . Whole-tissue platforms such as ALTEN preserve intact tumor tissue architecture and multicellular niches by encapsulating primary tissue fragments in alginate hydrogels [39] . These approaches are well suited for studying the native tissue niche and interactions with the tumor micro-environment (TME) but are generally less scalable and allow testing of fewer compounds. In contrast to whole-tissue platforms, patient-derived tumoroids provide high scalability and long-term expansion, making them suitable for compound discovery and biomarker research. However, patient-derived tumoroids require longer establishment times. MOS™, in contrast, is optimized for the rapid generation and short-term expansion of tumor cells from freshly dissociated low-input samples, enabling reproducible and scalable drug sensitivity testing within clinically relevant timelines which is especially useful for guiding clinical decision-making. Successful MOS™ generation depends on the quality and viability of the starting material after mechanical and enzymatic dissociation, which may vary between samples. In addition, MOS™ cultures rely on Matrigel, which introduces an extracellular matrix environment that must be tolerated by tumor cells. In our study, using MOS™ allowed parallel testing up to 90 compounds while maintaining 3D growth conditions. As such, MOS™ is particularly suited for precision medicine applications, where speed is crucial. This study did not investigate tumor TME retention, although previous work has shown that MOS™ can preserve stromal components [24] . Exploring if neuroblastoma MOS™ retain elements of the TME will be an important next step for assessing compound activity in a more patient representative setting. In patient samples where other cell types are present, tumor-specific markers, such as NCAM, B7H3 and L1CAM, could be used to distinguish tumor from non-tumor responses. In addition, MOS™ have been shown to support efficient CAR-T cell infiltration and killing, indicating their potential for immunotherapy testing [26] . In addition, culture conditions such as hypoxia have been proposed to better recapitulate aspects of the neuroblastoma tumor niche [40,41] . While hypoxia was not investigated in the present study, MOS™ cultures can be maintained under controlled oxygen conditions after generation. Finally, it should be noted that ex vivo  drug screening does not capture in vivo  pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic processes. Factors such as plasma protein binding, drug lipophilicity and tissue distribution can influence effective drug exposure at the tumor site and should be considered when translating ex vivo  drug sensitivity results to clinical applications [42–44] . Future studies of neuroblastoma MOS™ screening could include evaluation of TME preservation, testing of immunotherapies, hypoxia culture, and better representing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic processes.  5 Conclusion This proof-of-concept demonstrates that MOS™ technology supports the ex vivo  growth and drug screening of neuroblastoma cells, including low-input samples, within clinically relevant time frames. Future studies should focus on expanding pediatric patient cohorts, assessing clinical applicability and comparing drug response to clinical outcome, to validate MOS™ as a functional precision medicine platform for preclinical drug testing. title: mRNA vaccination using peptide nanoparticles triggers a strong immune response against endogenous GPC2 in a murine neuroblastoma model
abstract: Neuroblastoma is an aggressive pediatric solid tumor that arises during embryonic development and contributes to 15% of cancer-related deaths in children. To date, neither experimental nor clinical trial data on an mRNA vaccine for neuroblastoma have been published, highlighting a significant gap in the anticancer vaccine development pipeline. This study presents the first mRNA vaccine for the treatment of neuroblastoma. We explored the self-assembling peptide RALA for delivering mRNA encoding glypican 2 (GPC2), a potent tumor-associated antigen in neuroblastoma. These data outline rigorous in vitro characterization of vaccine nanoparticle formulations, cellular uptake, and functionality. Immunization of mice with RALA/mGPC2 generated an antigen-specific cellular immune response against GPC2, with significant increases in IFN-γ and IL-2 expression by splenocytes and TNF-α expression by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Immunization delayed tumor development by 10–11 days and reduced tumor volume by 70% compared with unvaccinated controls in a subcutaneous murine model of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma. This work demonstrates the therapeutic potential of the RALA/mGPC2 vaccine for treating neuroblastoma. Additionally, GPC2 is upregulated across multiple adult and pediatric cancer subtypes, establishing this vaccine as an attractive immunotherapy with far-reaching potential.
