Objective Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive malignant tumors in humans, with poor prognosis. The acetylase tumor inhibitor (Pracinostat) has been shown to suppress the growth of various tumors. This study aimed to investigate the effects of Pracinostat on the pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 and to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms through both in vivo and in vitro experiments.  Methods BxPC3 cells were treated with Pracinostat, and cell viability was assessed by CCK-8 assay; the differentially expressed miRNAs in cells before and after pracinostat treatment were screened by high-throughput sequencing, and miR-381–3p was selected as the target gene; the targeting relationship between miR-381–3p and MDM2 was verified by double luciferase reporter gene; the relationship between miR-381–3p, MDM2 and P53 signaling pathways was verified by immunoprecipitation, Western blot and other experiments. Pancreatic tumor models were established in BALB/c nude mice to study the role of pracinostat in vivo.  Results Pracinostat upregulated the expression of miR-381–3p and p53, while downregulating MDM2 expression. It also inhibited the proliferation and migration of pancreatic cancer cells and promoted apoptosis. Treatment with a miR-381–3p inhibitor reversed the effects of Pracinostat. In addition, MDM2 was found to promote the ubiquitination and degradation of p53 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In vivo experiments confirmed that Pracinostat inhibited tumor growth in nude mice.  Conclusion pracinostat activates the p53 signaling pathway by targeting the miR-381–3p/MDM2 axis, thereby inhibiting the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells. These findings provide novel insights and potential therapeutic strategies for pancreatic cancer, and may also provide a reference for the treatment of other malignancies.   Keywords Pancreatic cancer  Pracinostat  MiR-381–3p  MDM2  Degradation of p53 ubiquitination   Data availability The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.   1 Introduction Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a tumor of the digestive system with high malignancy and poor prognosis for survival[1] . Risk factors include smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, and dietary habits[2] .It is expected that by 2025, PC will surpass breast cancer to become the third leading cause of cancer death[3] . Due to the fact that the early clinical symptoms of PC patients are relatively cryptic, the disease course is already in the middle and late stages when local invasion, invasion of adjacent organs or distant tumor metastasis are detected[4] , which leads to a low resectable rate of PC surgery. At the same time, comprehensive treatment measures such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not very satisfactory for the treatment of PC[5] . Therefore, it is urgent to find new drugs for PC. Pracinostat (Pralistat, SB939) is a histone deacetylase inhibitor and an anticancer drug with good pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties[6] . It can inhibit the growth and proliferation of tumor cells, and at the same time has the effect of strengthening the immune system, thus achieving the effect of treating cancer. Pracinostat has been shown to have therapeutic effects on a variety of cancers, including lymphoma[7] , leukemia[8] , breast cancer[9] , lung cancer[10] , etc. However, there are no studies reported on pracinostat in the treatment of PC, so this study will explore the effect of pracinostat on PC progression. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of non-coding single-stranded RNA small molecules cut from precursor single-stranded RNA molecules, which can regulate the translation and stability of specific genes [11] . miRNAs can specifically inhibit or target specific mRNAs and participate in the regulation of important cell signaling pathways such as cell development, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis[12] . In recent years, significant changes in a variety of miRNAs have been found in PC tissues, indicating that miRNAs can directly or indirectly affect PC [13] . In this study, after treating pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 with pracinostat, miRNA sequencing was performed on the samples in an attempt to find non-coding RNA targets for clinical treatment and blocking pancreatic cancer, providing a theoretical basis for the treatment of pancreatic cancer. miR-381–3p has been found to be involved in the occurrence and development of a variety of diseases and to regulate the biological processes of cells, including cell proliferation, apoptosis, migration, invasion and differentiation[14–16] . However, the specific molecular mechanisms by which miR-381–3p regulates pancreatic cell proliferation, apoptosis and migration in PC remain to be studied. Among the downstream regulatory mechanisms of miR-381–3p, it has been found that miR-381–3p can regulate the expression of the downstream molecule p53 by inhibiting its target gene to promote apoptosis of endothelial cells and inhibit proliferation [17] . As a tumor suppressor, p53 is an important regulator of cancer cell homeostasis. It plays a key role in the process of DNA damage, which can block the cell cycle, promote apoptosis, and affect DNA repair[18] . Usually, p53 has low activity, which is due to its interacting protein mouse bi-minute 2 homolog (MDM2) having E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, which can degrade p53 through the proteasome system. MDM2 is a key regulator of proliferation-related pathways and can regulate cell proliferation, apoptosis, and cell cycle by interacting with p53[19] . Studies such as Wang have found that Holliday ligation recognition protein inhibits the expression of p53 by promoting MDM2, which in turn promotes the proliferation, migration, and invasion of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells[20] . Therefore, based on the above research, this study will explore the impact of pracinostat on PC processes by modulating the miR-381–3p/MDM2/p53 axis.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials The BxPC3 cell line was purchased from Punocell Cell Bank. Nude mouse without thymus was purchased from the Animal Experimental Center of Medical University. The Animal Experimental Ethics Committee of Kunming Medical University (Kmmu2020414) provided all necessary approval for these experiments. Clinical samples Adjacent tissue and Pancreatic cancer tissue were obtained from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University. All experiments involving these materials were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (FEY-BG-39–2.0). Each patient gave written consent for the research.  2.2 Reagent The following materials were utilized for this study: Pracinostat (SB939) from Selleck, mimic of miR-381–3p (miR-381–3p mimic) and its negative control (NC mimic), miR-381–3p inhibitor (NC inhibitor) and its negative control (NC inhibitor), MDM2 overexpression plasmid (Guangzhou Borui Bio), LV-miR-381–3p lentivirus (Shanghai Jikai Bio), DMEM medium (Dalian Meilun, MA0212–2), fetal bovine serum (Punocell, 164210), Cell Counting Kit-8 (Dongren Chemical Technology (Shanghai, CK04) one-step TUNEL cell apoptosis in situ detection kit (Shanghai Kaiji, KGA7062), FITC-coupled Annexin-V apoptosis detection kit (BD, 556547), cell cycle detection reagent Kit (biosharp, BL114A), 0.1 % crystal violet aqueous solution (Solarbio, G1064), UltraSensitive SP mouse/rabbit (Fuzhou Maixin, KIT-9720), DAB color development kit (Beijing Zhongshan Bio, ZLI-9019), miRcute miRNA extraction and isolation kit (TIANGEN, DP501), Lipofectamine 3000 transfection kit (Therom, MAN0009872), HA-ub antibody (CST #3936), dual luciferase reporter gene detection kit (MCE, HY-K1013), antibody MDM2 (proteintech, 66511–1-Ig), P53 (proteintech, 60283–2-Ig), CyclinA2 (proteintech, 18202–1-AP), CyclinB1 (proteintech, 55004–1-AP), CyclinD1 (proteintech, 60186–1-Ig), CyclinE1 (proteintech, 11554–1-AP).  2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Cell culture Human pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 was cultured using DMEM (Meilunbio, MA0212–2), adding 10 % fetal bovine serum and 1 % penicillin/streptomycin, and cultured in an incubator at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. The cell morphology was observed using a microscope, and the fluid was changed and passaged routinely. Subsequent transfection cell experiments transfected NC mimic, miR-381–3p mimic, NC inhibitor and miR-381–3p inhibitor with Lipofectamine 3000 to BxPC3. The transfection method was carried out according to the reagent instructions, and the transfection efficiency was detected after transfection 48 h.  2.3.2 Animal experimentation Thirty male BALB/c nude mice aged 6–8 weeks were randomly divided into Control group, pracinostat group, Pracinostat+LV-sh-miR-381–3P group, 10 mice in each group. Bxpc3 cells were injected subcutaneously into the left armpit of nude mice at a dose of 1 × 105 . When the tumor diameter was 0.5 cm, Control group was given normal saline as a control. pracinostat group was administered for 15 days, Pracinostat+LV-sh-miR-381–3P group was administered for 15 days and LV-sh-miR-381–3P lentivirus (1 × 108  UT/50 μL) was injected into nude mice through the tail vein (injected every 3 days). The nude mice were euthanized at 21 days of injection of Bxpc3 cells, and the tumors were weighed and photographed for follow-up experiments.  2.3.3 Tumor tissues collection This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (FEY-BG-39–2.0) and is in line with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments for ethical research involving human subjects. Fifteen pairs of pancreatic cancer and adjacent non-tumor tissues were collected from patients of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University. In addition, written informed consent was obtained from patients for this study.  2.3.4 CCK-8 BxPC3 cells were adjusted to a concentration of 3 × 103  cells/mL and aseptically plated into 96-well plates with 100 μL per well. After 24 h of incubation in a cell culture incubator, the cells were exposed to different doses of pracinostat for 24 and 48 h. Subsequently, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution(Dongren Chemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was added to each well and the plates were further incubated for 2 h. Absorbance was then measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader（BioTek，0284）.  2.3.5 Cell sequencing BxPC3 cells were made into 1 × 105  cells/mL cell suspension and inoculated into 6-well plates, 2 mL per well. The plates were incubated in an incubator for 24 h, and the cells were treated with 0uM and 1uM pracinostat for 24 h the next day. Collected cells were commissioned to Lianchuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. for cell sequencing to analyze differentially expressed miRNAs.  2.3.6 RT-qPCR Extract miRNAs from cell samples, clinical samples, and animal samples using the miRcute miRNA Isolation Kit ((TIANGEN, DP501)), and determine miRNA concentration and purity. Reverse transcription of miRNAs into cDNA using miRNA reverse transcription reagents and qRT-PCR using SYBR Green Master (Roche, Mannheim, Germany). Fluorescence quantitative PCR was performed with U6 or β-actin as an internal reference, and the experiment was repeated at least 3 times. See  Table 1  for primer sequences.  2.3.7 Western blot Cell samples, clinical samples, and animal samples of different groups were treated with RIPA lysate and then the supernatant was centrifuged. The protein concentration was determined by BCA method, and the loading amount was calculated according to the protein concentration. The protein was heat-denatured for 15 min, 10 % SDS-PAGE separator was configured, and 5 % SDS-PAGE concentrate was added to the upper layer. The sample was loaded. After the initial voltage of SDS-PAGE electrophoresis was turned on for 90 v for 20 min, the voltage was adjusted to 110 v and the bottom of the glue was run for 45 min to end the electrophoresis. The electrophoretic gel was neatly cut and gently slowly spread onto the PDVF membrane with a power supply of 250 mA for 65 min and the improved PDVF membrane was taken out with 5 % skim milk and sealed for 2 h. The primary antibody was incubated in the incubation box at 4 °C overnight, and the antibody dilution ratio was 1:2000. The next day, the TBST membrane was washed 3 times, and the corresponding secondary antibody was incubated for 2 h. Imaging was taken with a chemiluminescence instrument imaging system.  2.3.8 Apoptosis and cell cycle were detected by flow cytometry Apoptosis rate was determined using the FITC-conjugated Annexin-V Apoptosis Detection Kit (BD, 556547). Briefly, the digestive juices of the cells after administration were collected to make a cell suspension. Add 1 mL PBS 1000 rpm/min and centrifuge for 5 min, discard the supernatant and add 500uL 1× buffer to resuspend the cells. Add 5 μL FITC and 5 μL PI according to the kit instructions and stain in the dark for 30 min. Apoptosis rate was detected using flow cytometry（BD, FACSCalibur). The cell cycle was determined using the Cell Cycle Detection Kit (biosharp, BL114A). Briefly, the digestive fluid of the cells after administration was collected to make a cell suspension. After collecting the cells, add 1 mL 70 % ethanol to fix the cells overnight. Wash the cells with PBS the next day. Add 500 μL 1X buffer to resuspend the cells. Add 5 μL PI dye for 30 min. Detect the cell cycle with flow cytometry（BD,FACSCalibur).  2.3.9 Transwell detects cell invasion After diluting Matrigel gel with serum-free medium 1:3, add it evenly and slowly to the upper chamber at the bottom of the Transwell chamber, and air dry at 4 ℃. Aspirate the excess liquid from the upper chamber, place the chamber in a 24-well culture plate, and add 500 µL of serum-free medium. After standing for 15 min, aspirate the medium, add 200 µl of cell suspension to the upper chamber, and add 500 µL of complete medium to the lower chamber. Incubate in an incubator at 37 ℃ for 24 h, and remove the cell culture plate. Fix with 4 % paraformaldehyde for 30 min, add crystal violet stain (Solarbio, G1064), and take pictures with a microscope.  2.3.10 Colony formation assay Spread the cell suspension into a petri dish of about 200 cells/mL medium, culture at 37 ℃, 5 % CO2  for 2 weeks, and replace the fresh culture solution every 2 days. When visible clones appear in the petri dish, terminate the culture and discard the culture solution. Fix with 4 % paraformaldehyde for 30 min and add crystal violet dye, wash off the violet dye with running water, and air dry. Calculate the cell clone formation rate.  2.3.11 Cell scratch experiment The cells were cultured into the 6-well plate by drawing a 1 cm straight line across the hole with a marker pen on the back of the 6-well plate with a sterilized ruler. The cells were treated with medicine the next day and scratched with a horizontal line perpendicular to the back of the 6-well plate. The scratched cells were washed with PBS and photographed under the microscope for 0 h. The 6-well plate was placed in a 37 ℃ CO2  incubator for 24 h and photographed under the microscope for 24 h.  2.3.12 Immunohistochemistry The collected animal samples and clinical samples were fixed using 4 % paraformaldehyde, followed by the steps of dehydration, embedding, sectioning, baking, dewaxing, hydration, antigen repair, etc. Next, use 10 % goat serum to seal for 2 h. Incubate the primary antibody at 4 °C overnight, and wash the tablets with PBST 3 times the next day. Incubate the secondary antibody dropwise for 2 h, and color with DAB. Stain the nucleus with hematoxylin, differentiate with 1 % alcohol hydrochloride, dehydrate, seal, and take pictures under a microscope.  2.3.13 Co-immunoprecipitation Collect the cells and purify the protein, dividing the protein into two parts. Add one part of the protein to the 4X loading buffer and boil for 15 min for denaturation as input. Add 1 μg of MDM2 antibody to the other part of the protein and slowly shake and incubate overnight at room temperature. The next day, add the pretreated 10 μL protein A agarose beads to the protein that was incubated overnight with the antibody and slowly shake and incubate for 4 h at room temperature. Centrifuge and retain the pellet and repeat three times. Add the pellet to the 4X loading buffer and boil for 15 min. Detect the MDM2 and P53 proteins with Western blot. The control antibody is IgG.  2.3.14 Double luciferase reporting experiment The possible binding check point on miR-381–3p and MDM2 3 '-UTR was predicted by Starbase website (https://rnasysu.com/encori/ ). Then, the 3′ -UTR sequence containing the binding check point was amplified by PCR and cloned onto the luciferase-expressed reporter gene vector to construct the wild-type (WT) -MDM2 vector and the mutant (Mut) -MDM2 vector. Next, according to the instructions for use of the Lipofectamine TM3000 (Therom, MAN0009872) kit, miR-381–3pmimic, mimic NC and WT-MDM2, Mutu-MDM2 were co-transfected into Bxpc3 cells and cultured for 48 h. Finally, measure luciferase activity according to the instructions for use of the dual luciferase reporter gene detection kit (MCE, HY-K1013).  2.3.15 Tunel Mouse tumor tissue was fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde and washed with PBS, then stained with tunel using Tunel Apoptosis Detection Kit (Shanghai Kaiji, KGA7062) according to the manufacturer's procedure. Then the nucleus was stained with DAPI, and the slides were rinsed and imaged using fluorescence microscopy. Finally, the apoptosis was analyzed using an image analyzer.  2.3.16 Statistical analysis All data were analyzed on GraphPad Prism version 8 software (GraphPad, USA), and the data were repeated 3 times. Multiple comparisons were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance, and pair comparisons were statistically analyzed using T-test. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.    3 Results 3.1 Pracinostat can inhibit the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells First, Bxpc3 cells were treated with 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2.0 μM pracinostat for 24 h and 48 h, respectively. The results showed that pracinostat had a significant inhibitory effect on the viability of Bxpc3 cells ( Fig. 1 A). Subsequent experiments selected 1 μM pracinostat as the experimental conditions (Fig. 1 B). Then, the apoptosis experiment, cell cycle assay, colony formation assay, cell scratch experiment, and Transwell experiment find that compared with the control group, the apoptosis rate of Bxpc3 cells treated with pracinostat was significantly increased, and the cell proliferation and migration ability were significantly weakened, the proportion of cell arrested in the G2/M phase was significantly increased (Fig. 1 C-G). Western blot results showed that compared with the control group, the protein expression levels of P53, P21, and CyclinA1 in Bxpc3 cells treated with pracinostat were significantly increased, while the protein expression levels of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1 were significantly reduced (Fig. 1 H). In summary, pracinostat can inhibit the proliferation and invasion of Bxpc3 cells and promote apoptosis.  3.2 miRNA differential analysis and verification After treatment of Bxpc3 with pracinostat, differential expression analysis of miRNA was performed ( Fig. 2 A-B). Sequencing results showed that, compared with the normal group, there were 1102 differentially expressed miRNAs in the dosing group, of which 566 were up-regulated and 536 were down-regulated. Among them, miR-381–3p was significantly overexpressed. RT-qPCR detected the expression of miR-383–3p in the cell samples and found that the expression of miR-383–3p was consistent with the sequencing results (Fig. 2 C). The expression of miR-383–3p in the clinical samples (n = 15) was detected and it was found that the expression of miR-383–3p was significantly reduced in the cancerous tissue compared to the adjacent tissue (Fig. 2 D).  3.3 Pracinostat can inhibit the vicious biological behavior of Bxpc3 by promoting miR-381–3p After transfection with miR-381–3P inhibitor, Bxpc3 cells were treated with pracinostat. CCK-8 results showed that compared with pracinostat, the miR-381–3P inhibitor group promoted cell proliferation ( Fig. 3 A). Flow cytometry detection of cell apoptosis found that miR-381–3P inhibitor reversed the promoting effect of pracinostat on cell apoptosis (Fig. 3 B). Cell cycle assays also found that compared with pracinostat, the proportion of cell cycle arrest in the G2/M phase was reduced in the miR-381–3P inhibitor group (Fig. 3 C). The results of clone formation, Transwell and scratch experiments showed that miR-381–3P inhibitor reversed the inhibitory effects of pracinostat on clone formation ability, invasion and migration (Fig. 3 D-F). In summary, pracinostat may inhibit the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 by promoting miR-381–3p.  3.4 MiR-381–3p can target MDM2 As a negative regulator of P53, MDM2 plays a regulatory role in many tumors. One of the interesting phenomena is the discovery on the starbase bioinformatics website that miR-381–3p may have the possibility of targeted binding to MDM2. Through dual luciferase reporting experiments, we found that overexpression of miR-381–3p significantly inhibited luciferase activity of the Wt-MDM2 3 'UTR reporter gene vector (P < 0.001), but had no effect on luciferase activity of the Muti-MDM2 3′ UTR reporter gene vector ( Fig. 4 A-B). Further studies found that both interference and overexpression of miR-381–3p affected the mRNA expression level and protein expression level of MDM2 in BxPC3 cells (Fig. 4 C-D).  3.5 MiR-381–3p inhibits pancreatic carcinogenesis by binding to MDM2 This study confirmed that miR-381–3p can bind to MDM2. Subsequently, CCK-8 assay, apoptosis assay, cell cycle analysis, colony formation assay, cell scratch assay, and Transwell assay were performed. The results showed that compared with the control group, transfection with miR-381–3p mimics promoted cell apoptosis and inhibited cell proliferation, colony formation, and invasion. Meanwhile, the proportion of cell arrested in the G2/M phase was significantly increased in the miR-381–3p mimic group. Furthermore, transfection with OE-MDM2 reversed the effects induced by miR-381–3p mimics ( Fig. 5 A-F). Western blot results showed that compared with the Control group, the miR-381–3p minic group upregulated the protein expression levels of P53, P21, and CyclinA. At the same time, miR-381–3p minic reduced the ubiquitination level of P53. Similarly, transfection of OE-MDM2 reversed the effect of miR-381–3p mimics (Fig. 5  G). In conclusion, miR-381–3p inhibits the occurrence of pancreatic cancer through MDM2 binding.  3.6 MDM2 promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of P53 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway In order to further determine whether P53 is regulated by MDM2, co-immunoprecipitation was used to determine the ubiquitination of P53 by MDM2 in BxPC3 cells. The results showed that in the presence of MG132, the interaction between exogenous MDM2 and P53 was significantly enhanced ( Fig. 6 A), and in the presence of MG132, knocking down MDM2 resulted in increased levels of P53 ubiquitination (Fig. 6 B). This result suggests that MDM2 promotes P53 ubiquitination, thereby mediating P53 degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.  3.7 Animal experiments demonstrate that pracinostat affects the progression of pancreatic cancer through miR-381–3p The pancreatic cancer model was established by tumorigenesis in nude mice, and the results of tumor mass and volume detection showed that the administration of pracinostat could significantly inhibit tumor growth compared with the DMSO group; the administration of pracinostat at the same time as the tail vein injection of LV-sh-miR-381–3P chronic disease into the nude mice, the tumor growth increased faster than that of the administration group alone ( Fig. 7 A-C). It is indicated that the inhibition of tumor growth by pracinostat is achieved by promoting the expression level of miR-381–3p. Immunohistochemical results showed that Ki67 expression levels decreased in the pracinostat group, and LV-sh-miR-381–3P could reverse the effect of pracinostat ( Fig. 8 D); Tunel test results showed that compared with the Control group, the tumor tissue apoptosis in the pracinostat group increased, while LV-sh-miR-381–3P was able to inhibit the effect of pracinostat (Fig. 7 E); Western blot test results showed that compared with the Control group, pracinostat upregulated the expression of P53, P21, CyclinA1, and P53, and reduced the expression levels of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, At the same time, Western blot showed that pracinostat reduced the ubiquitination level of P53 (Fig. 7 F). Compared with the pracinostat group, transfection of LV-sh-miR-381–3P reversed the effect of pracinostat (Fig. 7 F).   4 Discussion PC tumor is a very lethal and aggressive malignancy, ranked first among asymptomatic cancers, accounting for 5 % of cancer-related deaths[21] . The factors that cause PC include hereditary oncogene variants, age, blood type, microbiota, obesity, etc[22] . Therefore, exploring the mechanism of PC occurrence and development can help to find effective therapeutic drugs and provide targets for early diagnosis of PC. Pracinostat is an effective anti-cancer drug that has been revealed to have therapeutic effects in a variety of cancers. For example, Lian et al. found that Pracinostat can slow down the progression of breast cancer and improve the immunotherapy effect of breast cancer[23] . The study by Chen et al. also shows that Pracinostat can promote apoptosis by inhibiting the proliferation, migration and invasion of glioma cells, thereby alleviating the progression of glioma[24] . However, there is no research report on the treatment of PC by Pracinostat. In this study, we explore the effect of Pracinostat on the progression of PC. We found that Pracinostat treatment can promote the expression of CyclinA1, a cell cycle-related protein, and inhibit the expression of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, while reducing the proliferation, migration and invasion ability of BxPC3 cells, and improving apoptosis. In addition, Pracinostat treatment can also promote the apoptosis of tumor tissues in vivo and inhibit the growth of tumors. This suggests that Pracinostat has the effect of inhibiting the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells, and Pracinostat treatment may be a new method to alleviate the progression of PC. Pracinostat can inhibit the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells, but the specific mechanism by which it alleviates PC progression is not yet clear. In recent years, studies have found that many miRNAs are involved in the process of PC occurrence and affect various stages of pancreatic injury. For example, the study of Jingyang et al. showed that miR-320b can inhibit the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells by targeting negative regulation of FOXM1[25] ; while the study of Zhang et al. found that miR-132 can promote the proliferation, invasion and migration of pancreatic cancer cells by inhibiting the expression of the tumor suppressor gene PTEN, thereby exacerbating the development of PC[26] . In this study, we first found that miR-381–3p was less expressed in PC and Bxpc3 cells through bioletter analysis and miRNA expression differentiation analysis of Bxpc3 cells. In addition, miR-381–3p has been widely studied in a variety of cancers. For example, the study of Shang et al. found that miR-381–3p can inhibit the proliferation and metastasis of cervical cancer cells by down-regulating FGF7, and induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, thereby alleviating the progression of cervical cancer[27] . The study of Sun et al. showed that miR-381–3p can reduce the proliferation level of bladder cancer cells by inhibiting RAB2A, activate apoptosis, and then inhibit the development of bladder cancer[28] . However, the specific link between miR-381–3p and PC is unclear. Therefore, our study mainly focused on miR-381–3p. We also found that the expression of miR-381–3p was highest in Bxpc3 cells after administration of pracinostat. MiR-381–3p inhibitors can partially reverse the effect of pracinostat, promote the proliferation, migration and invasion of BxPC3 cells, and reduce apoptosis. This suggests that the inhibitory effect of pracinostat on pancreatic cancer cells is achieved by upregulating miR-381–3p. This experiment demonstrates that miR-381–3p can target and negatively regulate the expression of MDM2, which is likely to be an important mechanism for miR-381–3p to interfere with the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells. MDM2, a ubiquitin ligase, mainly regulates cell cycle, apoptosis, proliferation, differentiation and transformation functions[29] . MDM2 is highly expressed in many tumors, such as retinoblastoma, as well as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and is considered to be one of the important factors in the occurrence and development of tumors. Previous studies have shown that overexpression of MDM2 can promote the proliferation of retinoblastoma cells, inhibit apoptosis, and then promote the development of retinoblastoma[30] . At the same time, inhibition of MDM2 can effectively inhibit the proliferation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells, promote apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and inhibit the growth of nasopharyngeal carcinoma[31] . In our study, overexpression of miR-381–3p can inhibit the expression of MDM2, while overexpression of MDM2 can effectively up-regulate the expression of cycle-related proteins CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, and down-regulate the expression of CyclinA1, thereby promoting the proliferation, migration and invasion of Bxpc3 cells, and inhibiting apoptosis. Therefore, the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells is positively correlated with the expression of MDM2, and inhibiting MDM2 expression by up-regulating miR-381–3p may be one of the ways to alleviate the process of PC. It is well known that MDM2 is a major negative regulator of p53 and can interact with p53 to form a stable complex. When MDM2 binds to p53, MDM2 not only prevents the transcriptional activation of p53, but also promotes the degradation of p53 through ubiquitination[32] . Mutations and/or inactivation of p53, a major regulator of anti-proliferative function, are critical for tumorigenesis[33] . External stimulation-induced p53 activation inhibits the proliferation of cancer cells because it promotes the expression of a range of related proteins, thereby inducing apoptosis and cell cycle arrest[34,35] . MDM2/p53 axis has been widely studied in the regulation of cancer process. For example, oryzine activates p53 by inhibiting MDM2, thereby inducing neuroblastoma cell apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and inhibiting the progression of neuroblastoma[36] . Knockdown of RPS27a can inhibit MDM2-mediated p53 ubiquitination and degradation, promote apoptosis and G1 phase arrest of lung adenocarcinoma cells, inhibit cell proliferation, and alleviate the process of lung adenocarcinoma[29] . This study also found that MDM2 can promote P53 ubiquitination and mediate p53 degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. The above results suggest that the inhibitory effect of miR-381–3p on malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells and PC is achieved by mediating the MDM2/p53 axis. Overall, our study found that Pracinostat can increase the targeted binding effect of miR-381–3p to MDM2 by upregulating the expression of miR-381–3p, thereby inhibiting the binding of MDM2 to P53, thereby inhibiting the ubiquitination degradation of P53, further activating p53, thereby inhibiting the proliferation, migration and invasion of Bxpc3 cells, promoting apoptosis and cycle arrest, thereby alleviating the process of PC(Fig. 8 ). Our results suggest that Pracinostat may be an effective therapeutic agent for PC. title: The key vulnerabilities and therapeutic opportunities in the USP7-p53/MDM2 axis in cancer
abstract: The MDM2/MDMX-p53 circuitry is essential for controlling the development, apoptosis, immune response, angiogenesis, senescence, cell cycle progression, and proliferation of cancer cells. Research has demonstrated that USP7 exerts strong control over p53, MDM2, and MDMX stability, with multiple mediator proteins influencing the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis to modify p53 expression level and function. In cases where p53 is of the wild type (Wt-p53) in tumors, inhibiting USP7 promotes the degradation of MDM2/MDMX, leading to the activation of p53 signaling. This, in turn, results in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Hence, targeting USP7 presents a promising avenue for cancer therapy. Targeting USP7 in tumors that harbor mutant p53 (Mut-p53) is unlikely and remains largely unexplored due to the existence of numerous USP7 targets that function independently of p53. Considering that Mut-p53 exhibits resistance to degradation by MDM2 and other E3 ligases and also shares the same signaling pathways as Wt-p53, it is reasonable to suggest that USP7 may play a role in stabilizing Mut-p53. However, there is still much to be done in this area. If the hypothesis is correct, USP7 may be a potent target in cancers containing both Wt-p53 and Mut-p53.

The MDM2/MDMX-p53 circuitry is essential for controlling the development, apoptosis, immune response, angiogenesis, senescence, cell cycle progression, and proliferation of cancer cells. Research has demonstrated that USP7 exerts strong control over p53, MDM2, and MDMX stability, with multiple mediator proteins influencing the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis to modify p53 expression level and function. In cases where p53 is of the wild type (Wt-p53) in tumors, inhibiting USP7 promotes the degradation of MDM2/MDMX, leading to the activation of p53 signaling. This, in turn, results in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Hence, targeting USP7 presents a promising avenue for cancer therapy. Targeting USP7 in tumors that harbor mutant p53 (Mut-p53) is unlikely and remains largely unexplored due to the existence of numerous USP7 targets that function independently of p53. Considering that Mut-p53 exhibits resistance to degradation by MDM2 and other E3 ligases and also shares the same signaling pathways as Wt-p53, it is reasonable to suggest that USP7 may play a role in stabilizing Mut-p53. However, there is still much to be done in this area. If the hypothesis is correct, USP7 may be a potent target in cancers containing both Wt-p53 and Mut-p53.
