Results Upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity and p53 and c-Jun expression in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells Caspases-3/7 play a critical role in the execution phase of apoptosis. The enzymes are normally expressed as inactive pro-enzymes, but can be activated via proteolysis in apoptotic signaling cascades. Activation of caspases-3/7 results in the cleavage of PARP, a DNA repair enzyme. To assess caspase-3/7 activity in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, two assays were employed. Proteolytic cleavage of full-length PARP into two fragments of 89 and 24 kDa serves as a sign for caspase-3/7 activation and apoptosis. Expression and proteolysis of PARP in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y cells were analyzed by Western blotting using an antibody that recognized the full-length protein of 113 kDa and the major truncated fragment of PARP. In addition, we measured the processing of the artificial caspase-3/7 substrate, CaspaseGlo-Substrate, which generated a light-emitting compound following proteolysis. The cells were cultured for 24 h in medium containing 1% fetal calf serum to reduce the concentration of growth factors in the medium that may block apoptosis and function as survival factors (Van Golen and Feldman, 2000 ). Under these conditions, no significant upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity was detected (data not shown). The cells were incubated with different concentrations of arsenite for 8 h and assessed for caspase-3/7 activity. Fig. 1  A, B show that incubation of the cells with 5 μM arsenite triggers an upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. This activity was detectable after 4–6 h of incubation, depending on the caspase-3/7 assay used (Fig. 1 C, D) and was highest after 8 h of stimulation. Thus, all following experiments have been performed with an arsenite concentration of 5 μM and an incubation period of 8 h. It is well documented that arsenite triggers a signaling cascade involving the activation of protein kinases and transcription factors. In particular, the stimulation of stress-activated protein kinases, c-Jun N-terminal protein kinases (JNK) and p38 and the activation of the transcription factor c-Jun have been reported (Namgung and Xia, 2000; Wong et al., 2005 ). In addition, several reports connected arsenite-induced cell death of fibroblasts, gastric cancer cells, and cortical neurons with an upregulation of p53 expression (Jiang et al., 2001; Wong et al., 2005 ). Western blot experiments revealed that expression of both c-Jun and p53 is stimulated in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells (Fig. 1 E).  The upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity and expression of c-Jun and p53 in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells is attenuated following preincubation with NAC It has been reported that arsenite executes its cytotoxic effect via the generation of oxidative stress (Miller et al., 2002; Gupta et al., 2003 ). Therefore, we preincubated the cells with the thiol-containing antioxidant/radical scavenger NAC before we stimulated the cells with arsenite. Fig. 2  A, B show that upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y cells was significantly reduced when the cells had been preincubated with NAC. Next, we analyzed the expression of p53 and c-Jun in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells that had been pretreated with NAC. Fig. 2 C shows that this compound significantly reduced p53 expression and almost abolished c-Jun expression resulting from arsenite treatment, suggesting that the generation of oxidative stress is responsible for the upregulation of both c-Jun and p53 expression. However, this experiment could not clarify whether an upregulation of either c-Jun or p53 expression or both is necessary for the enhanced caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells.  Expression of a truncated mutant of p53 or knockdown of p53 reduces caspase-3/7 activity and chromatin fragmentation in arsenite-treated human neuroblastoma cells To directly address the question whether p53 is required for the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-stimulated neuroblastoma cells, we expressed a truncated mutant of p53, termed p53DD, in SH-SY5Y cells via lentiviral gene transfer. This p53 mutant retains the C-terminal portion of p53 including the oligomerization domain, but lacks the transactivation and DNA-binding domains (Gottlieb et al., 1994 ). In addition, p53DD contains a FLAG epitope for immunological detection. A schematic representation of p53 and p53DD is depicted in Fig. 3  A. p53DD is able to oligomerize with wild-type p53, leading to the formation of inactive oligomers between p53DD and wild-type p53 (Gottlieb et al., 1994 ). Cellular proteins of mock-infected SH-SY5Y cells or SH-SY5Y cells infected with a p53DD encoding lentivirus were fractionated by SDS-PAGE. The truncated p53 protein was identified by Western blot analysis using antibodies targeting the FLAG epitope. Fig. 3 B shows that the p53 mutant was synthesized as expected. Next, the functional implication of p53DD expression was assessed. Fig. 3 C, D show that expression of p53DD significantly reduced caspase-3/7 activity in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells that had been stimulated with arsenite, indicating that expression of p53 is required for arsenite-induced cell death in these cells. The induction of programmed cell death by arsenite was confirmed by analyzing the fragmentation of the chromatin in apoptotic nuclei by transferring dUTP-TMR to the free 3′ ends of fragmented DNA (TUNEL assay). Fig. 3 E shows that p53DD significantly attenuates the arsenite-induced chromatin fragmentation in neuroblastoma cells. To corroborate the results obtained with the mutant p53, we expressed a p53-specific shRNA in neuroblastoma cells using lentiviral gene transfer. The provirus also contained a second transcription unit that encoded for enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) under the control of the CMV promoter/enhancer. Expression of EGFP was used as a control to monitor successful infection, expression of HDAC1 was used as a loading control. SH-SY5Y cells were either infected with a lentivirus that did not encode for an shRNA (mock) or infected with a lentivirus encoding an shRNA directed against p53. Fig. 4  B, C show that caspase-3/7 activity was significantly reduced in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y cells expressing a p53-specific shRNA. In addition, expression of a p53-specific shRNA significantly reduced the number of cells with fragmented chromatin following arsenite treatment (Fig. 4 D). Together, these data indicate that p53 is responsible for the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity and the fragmentation of chromatin in arsenite-stimulated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells.  Nutlin-3 induces p53-dependent cell death in neuroblastoma cells SH-SY5Y cells express a wild-type form of p53 (Nakamura et al., 2007 ). Nevertheless, the function of p53 in neuroblastoma cells has been questioned due to a proposed cytoplasmic location of p53. Our results clearly show that p53 is required to induce caspase-3/7 activity and DNA fragmentation in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. To support this conclusion, we directly analyzed p53-dependent caspase-3/7 activation using nutlin-3–stimulated SH-SY5Y cells. Nutlin-3 is a cis -imidazoline compound that binds to the E3 ubiquitin ligase mouse double minute (MDM2) and abrogates the interaction between p53 and MDM2. As a result, the degradation of p53 is attenuated (Vassilev et al., 2004 ). Nutlin-3 has been used to treat a variety of cancers, including neuroblastoma (Van Maerken et al., 2006 ). Fig. 5  A shows that expression of p53 is upregulated in nutlin-3–treated neuroblastoma cells. Treatment of the cells with nutlin-3 triggered an upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells that was not blocked by preincubation of the cells with NAC (Fig. 5 B). Likewise, expression of p53 in nutlin-3–stimulated cells was not attenuated following incubation with NAC (Fig. 5 A). However, expression of the p53DD mutant abrogated caspase-3/7–dependent proteolysis of PARP (Fig. 5 C), and the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in nutlin-3–stimulated neuroblastoma cells (Fig. 5 D). Likewise, knockdown of p53 via expression of a p53-specific shRNA in the cells significantly reduced caspase-3/7 activity in nutlin-3–treated cells (Fig. 5 E). These data were confirmed by analyzing the fragmentation of the chromatin. Expression of p53DD or expression of a p53-specific shRNA significantly reduced the number of cells with fragmented chromatin in neuroblastoma cells (Fig. 5 F, G).  Betulinic acid induces p53-independent cell death in neuroblastoma cells Betulinic acid (BA) is a pentacyclic triterpene that has been shown to induce apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells independently of p53 (Fulda and Debatin, 2000 ). Fig. 6  A shows that betulinic acid-induced caspase-3/7 activity was not significantly reduced in neuroblastoma cells that expressed p53DD, thus confirming the previously published data. Likeweise, betulinic acid-induced chromatin fragmentation was not attenuated by p53DD (Fig. 6 B).  p53 is transcriptionally active in arsenite and nutlin-3–stimulated neuroblastoma cells p53 is a sequence-specific transcription factor that acts directly or indirectly to change the gene expression pattern of the cells. It is thought that the biological functions of p53 are largely mediated through transactivation of specific p53-responsive genes, although a transcription-independent function of p53 has been proposed (Vaseva and Moll, 2009 ). We directly measured p53-regulated transcription in arsenite or nutlin-3–treated neuroblastoma cells using a chromatin-embedded p53-responsive reporter gene containing four copies of the p53 responsive element BS2 derived from the human PUMA promoter. This reporter has recently been used to show that p53-dependent transcription is essential for camptothecin-induced neuronal death (Uo et al., 2007 ). A schematic depiction of the integrated provirus encoding the p53-responsive luciferase expression unit is shown in Fig. 7  A, including the sequence of the wild-type BS2 and a mutated version of this element. Fig. 7 B shows that transcription of the reporter gene is significantly activated in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells. However, mutation of the p53 binding site abolished the effect of arsenite on reporter gene transcription. Likewise, stimulation of the cells with nutlin-3 induced an upregulation of p53-dependent transcription, as depicted in Fig. 7 C. Thus, we conclude that both arsenite and nutlin-3 treatment enhanced p53-mediated transcription in neuroblastoma cells.  Expression of a dominant-negative mutant of c-Jun or knockdown of c-Jun do not reduce caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-treated human neuroblastoma cells To assess the role of c-Jun in the regulation of cell death in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells, we chose a dominant-negative approach. The modular structure of dominant-negative mutant of c-Jun, c-JunΔN, lacking the N-terminal regulatory region and transcriptional activation domain, is depicted in Fig. 8  A. The mutant c-JunΔN contains c-Jun residues from amino acid 188 to amino acid 331 and a triple FLAG tag on the N-terminus. The dominant-negative mutant fails to activate transcription because of the lack of the transcriptional activation domain. Rather, the dominant-negative mutant inhibits DNA-binding of the wild-type c-Jun by blocking the cognate sites for DNA-binding. The biological activity of this mutant has been demonstrated (Steinmüller and Thiel, 2003 ). Expression of c-JunΔN was confirmed in SH-SY5Y cells infected with a c-JunΔN encoding lentivirus (Fig. 8 B). Next, we assessed the biological function of c-JunΔN expression on the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells. Fig. 8 C shows that caspase-3/7 activity was upregulated in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells in the presence or absence of c-JunΔN, suggesting that c-Jun is not part of the signaling cascade connecting arsenite stimulation with caspase-3/7 activation. Likewise, arsenite-induced chromatin fragmentation was not attenuated in neuroblastoma cells expressing c-JunΔN (Fig. 8 D, E). As a control for c-Jun–induced caspase-3/7 activation, we expressed a constitutively active mutant of MAP3 kinase mitogen-activated/extracellular signal responsive kinase kinase (MEK) kinase-1 (MEKK1) in SH-SY5Y cells. Fig. 8 F shows that a FLAG-tagged version of this truncated mutant termed MEKK1Δ was expressed in SH-SY5Y cells as expected, leading to an upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity. Expression of the dominant-negative mutant of c-Jun, c-JunΔN, almost completely blocked this upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in MEKK1Δ-expressing neuroblastoma cells (Fig. 8 G), indicating that MEKK1Δ exerts its effects on caspase-3/7 activation via activation of c-Jun. To confirm the previous results, we expressed a c-Jun–specific shRNA in SH-SY5Y cells using lentiviral gene transfer. As a control, cells were infected with a lentivirus that did not encode for an shRNA (mock). The cells were left untreated or stimulated with arsenite. Nuclear extracts were prepared and analyzed for c-Jun immunoreactivity. In SH-SY5Y cells expressing a c-Jun–specific shRNA, arsenite-induced upregulation of c-Jun was blocked (Fig. 9  A). Expression of HDAC1 was used as a loading control. Cellular extracts were prepared and analyzed for EGFP expression. Fig. 9 A shows that EGFP was expressed independently of arsenite stimulation. Next, we used SH-SY5Y cells expressing the c-Jun–specific shRNAs to assess the role of c-Jun in the signaling cascade leading to enhanced caspase-3/7 activity following arsenite stimulation. Fig. 9 B, C show that caspase-3/7 activity was not significantly reduced in arsenite-treated SH-SY5Y cells expressing a c-Jun–specific shRNA. In addition, arsenite-induced fragmentation of chromatin was not attenuated in SH-SY5Y cells expressing a c-Jun–specific shRNA. Together, these data indicate that the upregulation of c-Jun expression is not an essential part in the signaling cascade that leads to enhanced caspase-3/7 activity and programmed cell death in arsenite-stimulated SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells.  Arsenite-induced caspase-3/7 activation in neuroblastoma cells does not require JNK Activation of c-Jun requires phosphorylation by JNK. Using phospho-specific antibodies, we show that c-Jun is phosphorylated in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells. As a control, we treated the cells with ceramide, a lipid known to activate JNK (Fig. 10  A). However, treatment of the cells with the JNK inhibitor SP600125 did not reduce caspase-3/7 activity in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells (Fig. 10 B), indicating that JNK is not required for the arsenite-induced induction of caspase-3/7. In contrast, reduced caspase-3/7 activity was measured in ceramide-stimulated neuroblastoma cells in the presence of SP600125 (Fig. 10 C).   Discussion Elucidating of the cytotoxic mechanism of arsenite will provide the basis for understanding the chemotherapeutic potential of this compound. Caspases play critical roles in many apoptotic signaling cascades, leading to the proteolysis of hundreds of substrates (Lüthi and Martin, 2007 ). The objective of this study was to determine the molecular mechanism of arsenite-induced caspase-3/7 activation in neuroblastoma cells. In contrast to a previously published hypothesis (Karlsson et al., 2004 ), we show here that p53 plays an important role in the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity in neuroblastoma cells following treatment with arsenite. Although the hypothesis of Karlsson et al. (2004) is based on the comparison of different neuroblastoma cell lines, our conclusion is supported by experiments that directly interfered with the biological function of p53 using two methods. First, we expressed a truncated p53 that functioned as dominant-negative mutant. Second, p53 levels were reduced as a result of expression of a p53-specific shRNA. In both cases, the upregulation of caspase-3/7 activity and the fragmentation of chromatin in arsenite-treated neuroblastoma cells was attenuated. The transcription factor p53 is one of the most commonly mutated proteins in human cancer. Mutated p53 is unable to inhibit cell growth in response to stress, thus triggering tumor development. In contrast to many other cancers, the p53 protein is rarely mutated in human neuroblastoma. Nevertheless, early studies reported an inactivation of p53 in neuroblastoma cells due to cytoplasmic sequestration as a result of hyperubiquitylation (Becker et al., 2007 ). However, several recent reports described a predominant nuclear localization of p53 in neuroblastoma cells (Chen et al., 2007 ). In addition, wild-type p53 was fully functional in neuroblastoma cell lines showing an intact downstream transcriptional response following irradiation and DNA damage (Chen et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2007 ). To confirm the biological function of p53 in neuroblastoma cells, we investigated programmed cell death induced by nutlin-3. Nutlin-3 is a cis -imidazoline compound that binds to the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 and prevents the interaction between p53 and MDM2 (Vassilev et al., 2004 ). MDM2 binds and ubiquitinates p53, leading to its proteasomal degradation. As a result of nutlin-3 treatment, the degradation of p53 is blocked, and p53 signaling events are activated. Treatment of neuroblastoma cell lines with nutlin-3 showed that nutlin-3–mediated MDM2 inhibition sensitized the cells to chemotherapy-induced apoptotic cell death (Barbieri et al., 2006 ). The authors suggested that nutlin-3 may be used as an adjuvant to chemotherapy of neuroblastoma. Here, we confirmed that nutlin-3 activates caspases-3/7 in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells as reported (Ribas et al., 2006 ) and showed that caspase-3/7 activation and chromatin fragmentation was prevented in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells expressing either a dominant-negative–truncated p53 mutant or a p53-specific shRNA. In contrast, caspase-3/7 activation and DNA fragmentation induced by stimulation of neuroblastoma cells with the natural pentacyclic triterpenoid betulinic acid was not suppressed by either p53DD expression of knockdown of p53, underlining the specificity of the approach. Together, these results show that both arsenite and nutlin-3–regulated caspase-3/7 activation and DNA fragmentation in neuroblastoma cells require p53. These data are in accordance with new therapeutic strategies of neuroblastoma cells using nutlin-3 to sensitize the cells for chemotherapeutic treatment involving doxorubicin, cisplatin, and etoposide (Wagner and Danks, 2009; Wolter et al., 2010 ). p53 is a sequence-specific transcription factor. Thus, “the ability to activate transcription remains key to p53's modus operandi” (Vousden and Prives, 2009 ). However, a transcription-independent function of p53, involving the mitochondria, has been proposed (Vaseva and Moll, 2009 ). In addition, a recent report showed that arsenite induces p53 translocation to mitochondria (Watcharasit et al., 2008 ). However, no experiments were performed in this study to prove that this translocation has a functional impact. In addition, the authors used an arsenite concentration of 50 μM for their experiments, making a comparison to our results difficult. We directly showed that arsenite and nutlin-3 increased the transcription of a p53-sensitive reporter gene in neuroblastoma cells, suggesting that p53 regulates caspase-3/7 activity via a transcriptional mechanism. Furthermore, the experiments involving expression of p53DD exclude a mechanism involving targeting of p53 to the mitochondria, as this apoptotic pathway requires mostly monomeric p53 and is not blocked by p53DD (Vaseva and Moll, 2009 ). These results are in agreement with a recent published study underlining the importance of transcriptionally active p53 in cultured cortical neurons treated with either campthothecin or nutlin-3 (Uo et al., 2007 ). Arsenite-treatment has been reported to induce oxidative stress in various cell types (Chen et al., 1998; Miller et al., 2002; Gupta et al., 2003 ). Arsenite forms a complex with glutathione, leading to the rapid oxidation of glutathione and the disruption of the cellular redox status. The formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) induces oxidative DNA damage including DNA strand breaks in arsenite-treated cells that may trigger an upregulation of p53 expression. Thus, p53 is a redox-sensitive transcription factor (Liu et al., 2008 ). Overproduction of reactive oxygen species may additionally activate stress-activated protein kinases such as JNK, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of c-Jun. Accordingly, JNK and c-Jun activation have been connected with arsenite-induced cell death (Huang et al., 1999; Namgung and Xia, 2000; Davison et al., 2004 ). Our results show that arsenite-induced caspase-3/7 activation and chromatin fragmentation occurs independently of JNK and c-Jun in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, indicating that cell-type–specific variations play a role in arsenite-triggered apoptotic signal transduction. In contrast, c-Jun was required for the cell-death pathway induced by forced expression of a constitutively active MEKK1 in SH-SY5Y cells. In summary, we have shown that caspase-3/7 activation and chromatin fragmentation in either arsenite or nutlin-3 stimulated human neuroblastoma cells requires p53. A causal relationship between p53 activation and caspase-3/7 upregulation could be demonstrated in experiments involving expression of a dominant-negative mutant of p53 or knockdown of p53 expression via RNAi. The data provide evidence that p53 works via a transcriptional mechanisms and not via targeting to the mitochondria. c-Jun expression is also upregulated in arsenite-treated human neuroblastoma cells. However, a causal link between c-Jun expression and caspase-3/7 activity was not demonstrated.   Acknowledgments We thank Moshe Oren for plasmid pLXSNp53DD and Richard S. title: Dihydroartemisinin inhibits NSCLC by targeting MDM2/c-Myc axis independent of p53
abstract: The antimalarial agent Dihydroartemisinin (DHA) has significant potential for drug repurposing for cancer therapy including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, its underlying anti-tumor mechanisms remain to be elucidated. In this study, we demonstrated that DHA suppressed the mouse double minute 2 (MDM2) in A549 and H1299 cells, whereas MDM2 overexpression effectively restored DHA’s inhibition on both NSCLC cell lines. We showed that DHA acted via phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) and Janus kinase (JAK)/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling pathways to inhibit MDM2 expression. Being an established MDM2 target, p53 was significantly upregulated in p53 wild-type A549 cells upon DHA treatment both in vitro and in vivo; however, the mediating role of MDM2 in DHA’s suppression on NSCLC is independent of p53 since DHA-treated si-p53 A549 cells had comparable colony formation capacity compared with that of si-Control. The anti-tumor effects of DHA bypass p53 was further implicated using H1299, a cell line which is MDM2-overexpressed but p53-null. Instead, c-Myc was observed to mediate the effects of DHA/MDM2 axis as co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) analysis showed the direct protein interaction between MDM2 and c-Myc, both were substantially reduced upon DHA treatment. Furthermore, c-Myc overexpression effectively restored DHA’s suppression on proliferation, and DHA’s induction on apoptosis of A549 and H1299 cells. Finally, immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis showed that in vivo administration of DHA substantially reduced both MDM2 and c-Myc expression in xenograft murine models. Taken together, our results demonstrated that DHA inhibits NSCLC by targeting MDM2/c-Myc axis independent of p53.

Laboratory Medicine Teaching and Research Section The Second Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University Hefei 230601 China       Graphical abstract       The antimalarial agent Dihydroartemisinin (DHA) has significant potential for drug repurposing for cancer therapy including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, its underlying anti-tumor mechanisms remain to be elucidated. In this study, we demonstrated that DHA suppressed the mouse double minute 2 (MDM2) in A549 and H1299 cells, whereas MDM2  overexpression effectively restored DHA’s inhibition on both NSCLC cell lines. We showed that DHA acted via  phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) and Janus kinase (JAK)/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling pathways to inhibit MDM2 expression. Being an established MDM2 target, p53 was significantly upregulated in p53 wild-type A549 cells upon DHA treatment both in vitro  and in vivo ; however, the mediating role of MDM2 in DHA’s suppression on NSCLC is independent of p53 since DHA-treated si-p53 A549 cells had comparable colony formation capacity compared with that of si-Control. The anti-tumor effects of DHA bypass p53 was further implicated using H1299, a cell line which is MDM2-overexpressed but p53-null. Instead, c-Myc was observed to mediate the effects of DHA/MDM2 axis as co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) analysis showed the direct protein interaction between MDM2 and c-Myc, both were substantially reduced upon DHA treatment. Furthermore, c-Myc  overexpression effectively restored DHA’s suppression on proliferation, and DHA’s induction on apoptosis of A549 and H1299 cells. Finally, immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis showed that in vivo  administration of DHA substantially reduced both MDM2 and c-Myc expression in xenograft murine models. Taken together, our results demonstrated that DHA inhibits NSCLC by targeting MDM2/c-Myc axis independent of p53. However, it remains the leading cause of cancer death, with almost 2.5 million new cases (12.4 %) and an estimated 1.8 million deaths (18.7 %) in 2022 [1 ]. Lung cancer is histologically categorized into non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), wherein the former comprises ∼85 % of all cases [2 ]. Being a treatment option for NSCLC, traditional Chinese medicine, especially Chinese herbs and herbal extracts have attracted considerable attention due to their potential benefits of anticancer activity to be weighed against the minimal side-effects. In recent years, Dihydroartemisinin (DHA), a globally recognized antimalarial drug with high efficacy and safety, has exhibited anticancer potential in a variety of malignancies including NSCLC [3 ]. DHA is one of the most pharmacologically relevant derivatives of artemisinin, the active component isolated from Chinese Traditional Herbs Artemisia annua by Tu’s team at 1972 [4 ]. DHA is synthesized by the reduction of lactone group to hemiacetal group at the C-10 of artemisinin, both are sesquiterpene lactones characterized by a special peroxide group as the pharmacophore. Hemoglobin uptake and digestion of malarial parasites lead to release of excessive free redox-active heme and free ferrous iron (Fe2+ ), which subsequently activate artemisinin and its derivatives by cleavage of the endoperoxide bridge within this group. Activated artemisinin or DHA either prevent the formation of hemozoin by alkylating heme, or directly alkylate and inactivate biomacromolecule targets by the generation of copious amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [4 ,5 ]. Multiple anticancer effects of DHA have been reported including inhibition of proliferation, metastasis and angiogenesis, and promotion of apoptosis, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and autophagy [6 ,7 ]. DHA has also been reported to suppress several signaling pathways such as the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT), Janus kinase2 (JAK2)/Signal transducer and activator of transcription3 (STAT3), and NF-κ B signaling [3 ]. It is to be noted that compared with normal cells, cancer cells produce higher basal levels of ROS which contribute to oncogenesis by increasing cancer metabolism and growth, and inhibiting antioxidants [8 ]. DHA treatment may induce excessive production of ROS to render DNA damage and eventually causing cell death of cancer cells [9–12 ]. However, the anticancer mechanism of DHA remains to be fully elucidated although numerous reports have indicated that DHA could be a potential candidate for cancer treatment. MDM2 (murine double minute 2) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase acts by targeting various substrates for ubiquitylation, thereby promoting proteasome-dependent degradation [13 ]. It has been widely recognized that MDM2 is an oncoprotein since it targets principally the tumor suppressor protein p53. MDM2 is in fact the best documented negative regulator of p53 by promoting ubiquitylation and proteasome-dependent degradation of p53. MDM2 overexpression was observed in various tumors, therefore favoring uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor formation by quenching the activity of p53 [14 ]. On the other hand, ample evidence has suggested that MDM2 also has multiple p53-independent oncogenic effects that are involved in DNA repair, cell proliferation, and genomic instability [15 ,16 ]. MDM2 was shown to exert oncogenic effects by directly or indirectly upregulating c-Myc, the grand orchestrator of cancer growth and immune evasion in hematologic malignancies [17 ,18 ]. Thus, MDM2 is a key regulator fueling tumorigenesis and a promising drug target for cancer therapy. In this study, we investigated the underlying mechanisms of DHA’s antitumor effects in NSCLC, especially its inhibition on MDM2 and the engagement of p53 in tumor-suppressive activity of DHA. Our results showed that DHA inhibits NSCLC by targeting MDM2/c-Myc axis independent of p53.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Reagents and media RPMI 1640 culture medium was acquired from Biochannel (Nanjing, China). Cell migration (%) was calculated as: [(0 h wound area − 24/48 h wound area)/0 h wound area] × 100 %.  2.9 Transwell invasion assay Wild-type A549 and H1299 cells were pretreated with DMSO, NAC (5 mM), or IC50  DHA in the presence or absence of NAC for 24 h. The DMSO-treated and si-Control groups were set as 100 %, and relative invasion rate (%) was calculated as (experimental group/DMSO or si-Control group) × 100 %.  2.10 Cell apoptosis assay Wild-type, c-Myc-overexpressed and mock transfected A549 and H1299 cells were left untreated or treated with DMSO or IC50  DHA for 24 h. Next, 20 μL protein A/G-coupled magnetic beads were added and incubated at 4 °C with rotation and the isolated beads were washed thrice with lysis buffer, resuspended in 40 μL 1 × loading buffer and boiled at 100 °C for 10 min. Samples including input control were validated via  Western blotting assay as described above.  2.13 Statistical analysis Quantitative evaluations of experimental results including Western blotting, transwell and wound healing assays were conducted using ImageJ software (version 1.8.0). Results are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Two-tailed Student’s t -test was used to compare two groups for independent samples and comparison of means of were employed by analysis of variance (ANOVA). All statistical analyses were performed by utilizing IBM SPSS Statistics (version 22.0). For determining the IC50  values of DHA on A549 and H1299 cell lines, cells were exposed to a gradient concentration of DHA, and IC50  was calculated via Probit regression analysis in SPSS. A threshold of P  < 0.05 was used to define statistically significant differences.   3 Results 3.1 DHA inhibits growth, migration and invasion of NSCLC cells in a way partially dependent on ROS Concentration gradients of DHA (0, 5, 10, 25, 50 and 100 μM) were used to treat NSCLC cell lines A549 and H1299 for 24 h, and CCK-8 and colony formation assays were performed to assess reproductive cell survival of both cell lines. As shown in Fig. 1  A, DHA acted in a concentration dependent manner to inhibit cell growth of both A549 and H1299 cells. DHA’s IC50  concentrations for A549 and H1299 cells were 30.57 μM and 12.95 μM, and thus in the following experiments 30.00 μM and 15.00 μM were selected as working concentrations for the two cell lines, respectively (Fig. 1 A). The colony formation assay further confirmed DHA’s suppression on the growth of NSCLC cells. DHA treatment reduced the tumor colony by more than 50 % and 90 % for A549 (P  < 0.001) and H1299 (P  < 0.0001) cells, respectively (Fig. 1 B). Flow cytometric detection of Annexin V/PI double staining cells showed that the total apoptosis including early (FITC+ /PI− ) and late (FITC+ /PI+ ) apoptotic cells were 70.44 ± 1.69 (%) and 16.19 ± 0.29 (%) (P <  0.0001) for DHA treated and untreated A549 cells (Fig. 1 C), and 34.50 ± 0.79 (%) and 8.21 ± 1.18 (%) (P <  0.0001) for the corresponding H1299 cells (Fig. 1 D), respectively. Next, wound healing assay showed that the migration ability of DHA-treated A549 and H1299 cells were markedly decreased at 24 h (both P  < 0.01) and 48 h (P <  0.001, P <  0.0001) compared with that of the control groups (Fig. 1 E and F). Similarly, the transwell assay (with Matrigel) showed that DHA treatment significantly reduced invasion ability of A549 and H1299 cells (both P  < 0.0001, Fig. 1 G). It has been well established that the excessive production of cytotoxic ROS is one of the mechanisms behind the anti-tumor and antimalarial effects of DHA. Thus, being an antioxidant-scavenger of ROS, NAC was used to explore whether DHA’s anti-tumor effects are derived from ROS-dependent mechanisms. We observed an approximately 60 % inhibition of DHA on the cell viability of both A549 and H1299 cells and 10 % restoration in the presence of NAC, as compared to DHA treatment only (P <  0.0001, P <  0.01) (Fig. 1 H and I). However, NAC had no significant effects on restoring DHA’s suppression on the migration (Fig. 1 E and F) and invasion (Fig. 1 G) of A549 and H1299 cells. Taken together, these results demonstrated that DHA inhibited growth, migration and invasion of NSCLC cells in a way partially dependent on ROS.  3.2 MDM2 inhibition is involved in DHA’s effects on NSCLC To further explore the underlying anti-tumor mechanisms of DHA, we evaluated the roles of MDM2 in mediating DHA’s effects against NSCLC since DHA was observed to down-regulated MDM2 in human hepatoma cells [19 ]. MDM2 amplification has been detected in many human malignancies including NSCLC, and MDM2 overexpression is associated with tumor progression of NSCLC [20 ]. Firstly, si-RNA-mediated MDM2  knockdown in A549 and H1299 cells dramatically reduced the tumor colony formation by approximately 50 % and 80 % for A549 (P  < 0. 01) and H1299 (P  < 0.001) cells, respectively (Fig. 2  A and B). Also, the in vitro  wound healing assay indicated that si-MDM2 A549 and H1299 cells had significantly slower wound closure than that of mock controls both at 24 h (P  < 0.0001, P  < 0.001) and 48 h (both P  < 0.001) (Fig. 2 C). Similarly, the Matrigel invasion assay showed that the number of invasive A549 and H1299 cells in the si-MDM2 group were significantly less than that in the si-Control group (both P  < 0.0001) (Fig. 2 D). These results confirmed the oncogenic role of MDM2, which may represent a potential therapeutic target in NSCLC. Of note, DHA treatment substantially suppressed MDM2 levels both in A549 (P  < 0.01) and H1299 (P  < 0.05) cells (Fig. 2 E). To verify MDM2′s role in mediating the anti-tumor effects of DHA in NSCLC, MDM2  overexpression in both A549 and H1299 cells were performed and its protective role against DHA inhibition was investigated. MDM2  overexpression effectively counteracted DHA’s suppression on MDM2 level (P  < 0.001, P  < 0.05) (Fig. 2 F) and, more importantly, substantially restored DHA’s inhibition on the proliferation of both A549 and H1299 cells (both P  < 0.05) at 24, 48 and 72 h post-treatment (Fig. 2 G). Collectively, these findings supported that MDM2 inhibition was involved in DHA’s anti-tumor effects on NSCLC.  3.3 DHA acts via PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT3 signaling pathways to inhibit MDM2 expression We first asked whether ROS is involved in mediating DHA’s inhibition on MDM2 since DHA inhibits growth of NSCLC cells in a way partially dependent on ROS. As shown in Fig. 3  A, the ROS scavenger NAC per se  had no influence on MDM2 expression. Also, addition of NAC did not significantly abrogate DHA’s inhibition on MDM2 expression both in A549 and H1299 cells. To further explore whether the intracellular signaling cascades are involved in transducing DHA’s suppressive effects on MDM2 expression, PI3K/AKT, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/extracellular signal regulated protein kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2), and JAK/STAT3 pathways were observed for their influence by DHA. The Western blotting results showed that the phosphorylated levels of AKT (p-AKT) and p-STAT3 (all P  < 0.05) but not p-ERK1/2 were substantially decreased in DHA treated A549 and H1299 cells as compared with that of DMSO-treated controls (Fig. 3 B). Next, MK 2206 dihydrochloride, a potent and selective allosteric AKT inhibitor, and Stattic, a nonpeptidic small molecule selectively inhibit the activation and function of the STAT3 SH2 domain, were used to verify the two signaling pathways involved in MDM2 expression. As expected, the targeted inhibition of AKT and STAT3 by MK 2206 and Stattic resulted in significantly reduced expression of MDM2 both in A549 (P  < 0.01, P  < 0.05) and H1299 (both P  < 0.05) cells (Fig. 3 C and D). Taken together, these findings strongly suggested that DHA acts via  PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT3 signaling pathways to inhibit MDM2 expression.  3.4 The mediating role of MDM2 in DHA’s effects on NSCLC is independent of p53 It is widely accepted that the focus on MDM2 can be attributed to its ability to bind and inhibit the activity of p53, therefore MDM2 dysregulation in tumors favoring uncontrolled cell proliferation. However, the findings presented in Results 3.2 had suggested that the mediating role of MDM2 in DHA’s suppressive effects on NSCLC was independent of p53 as the cell line H1299 is MDM2-overexpressed but p53-null (Fig. 2 E). However, p53 was significantly upregulated in p53 wild-type A549 cells upon DHA treatment (P  < 0.001), along with the downregulation of MDM2 (P  < 0.01) (Fig. 2 E). Furthermore, siRNA-mediated MDM2  knockdown led to markedly increasement of p53 expression in A549 cells, as compared with si-Control (Fig. 2 A). Likewise, IHC analysis of the tissue sections from DHA-treated, A549-innoculated tumor-bearing mice showed a substantial increase of p53 expression compared with that from DMSO-treated, subcutaneous xenografts (Fig. 4  A). Therefore, to test the involvement of p53 in mediating the effects of DHA-MDM2 axis, p53  knockdown was conducted by small RNA interference to investigate DHA’s inhibitory effects on A549 cells (Fig. 4 B). CCK-8 and the colony formation assays showed that the DHA-treated si-p53 A549 cells had comparable cell viability (Fig. 4 C) and tumor colony counting (Fig. 4 D) compared with that of si-Controls. Thus, these results suggested that the mediating role of MDM2 in DHA’s effects on NSCLC is independent of p53.  3.5 MDM2/c-Myc axis is involved in mediating DHA’s effects on NSCLC To further elucidate the mechanistic model in which intermolecular interactions between MDM2 and its downstream molecule, several p53-independent targets of MDM2 including B7-H3 (CD276) [21 ], E2F1 [22 ], and c-Myc [18 ] were explored for their possible involvement in DHA/MDM2 axis in NSCLC. Compared with si-Control, si-MDM2 had no influence on B7-H3 expression in both A549 and H1299 cells. Also, si-MDM2 had no effects on E2F1 in H1299 cells, although it generated significant downregulation of E2F1 in A549 cells (P  < 0.05). In contrast, si-MDM2 led to substantially reduced expression of c-Myc both in A549 (P  < 0.01) and H1299 (P  < 0.05) cells (Fig. 5  A). To further investigate whether c-Myc is involved in mediating the effects of DHA/MDM2 axis, Co-IP assay was conducted to identify physiologically relevant protein–protein interactions between MDM2 and c-Myc in DHA treated NSCLC cells. To avoid p53 interference, we selected H1299 cells to perform Co-IP analysis. The protein A/G-coupled magnetic nanoparticles were employed to capture specific antibodies against MDM2 or c-Myc, which was used as Co-IP bait to bind target protein in cell lysates of H1299 cells treated or left untreated with IC50  DHA. The input fraction collected beforehand ensured the quality of starting sample materials used for the Co-IP analyses. The Co-IP results showed that MDM2 and c-Myc were pulled out from the cell lysates, by mutually using the corresponding specific antibodies as bait proteins. Of note, the immunoprecipitated MDM2 and c-Myc protein substantially reduced in the cell lysates from DHA-treated H1299 cells as compared with that from control group (Fig. 5 B). Thus, these findings suggested the direct protein interactions between MDM2 and c-Myc, and the inhibitory effects of both MDM2 and c-Myc by DHA treatment of NSCLC cells. Being a proto-oncogene, MDM2  is recognized to encode an E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase that mediates ubiquitination of p53 and other proteins for degradation. On the other hand, MDM2 was also reported to generate protective effects against proteasome-dependent degradation by competing with other E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase to prevent binding, ubiquitination and degradation of specific target by the competitor [23 ]. Therefore, si-MDM2 in combination with proteasome inhibitor MG132 were used to detect MDM2′s effects on c-Myc. The results showed that MG132 treatment led to substantially increasement of MDM2, suggesting that MDM2 per se  was degraded by ubiquitin–proteasome pathway. However, with the dynamic change of MDM2 level upon si-RNA-mediated MDM2  knockdown, MG 132 treatment, and the integrated interventions, c-Myc protein significantly upregulated or downregulated in keeping with MDM2 both in A549 and H1299 cells (Fig. 5 C). These results strongly indicated that regulation of c-Myc by MDM2 is likely to be protective and thus facilitates the function of both genes in NSCLC oncogenesis. Finally, to verify the roles of c-Myc in mediating the action of DHA/MDM2 axis, c-Myc  overexpression, which could effectively counteracted DHA’s suppression on the protein, was conducted to observe its reverse effects on DHA inhibition (Fig. 5 D). As shown in Fig. 5 E and F, c-Myc  overexpression effectively restored DHA’s suppression on the proliferation of A549 and H1299 cells (both P  < 0.05) (Fig. 5 E), and DHA’s induction of apoptosis on both cell lines (P  < 0.0001, P  < 0.05) (Fig. 5 F). Taken together, these results highlight the involvement of MDM2/c-Myc axis in mediating DHA’s anti-tumor effects in NSCLC.  3.6 DHA suppresses MDM2 and c-Myc expression in xenograft murine model We have previously shown that DHA inhibits NSCLC tumor growth in the xenograft murine model developed by subcutaneous injection of A549 cells into BALB/c Nude mice [7 ]. Here we further performed IHC analysis to verify DHA’s in vivo  inhibition on MDM2 and c-Myc in tumor-bearing mice. As shown in Fig. 6  , in vivo  administration of DHA (50 mg/kg) reproduced its suppression on MDM2 and c-Myc, since both staining densities were substantially reduced in pathological sections from experimental mice compared with that from DMSO treated xenografts. Thus, these findings further reinforce the critical involvement of MDM2/c-Myc axis in mediating DHA’s anti-tumor effects in NSCLC and support both molecules as promising targets in NSCLC therapy.   4 Discussion Being an antimalarial drug with low toxicity and known safety, DHA has received increasing attention in recent years for its anticancer activity which was reported to act through various molecular mechanisms. In this study, we have provided further evidence that DHA exerts therapeutic effects on NSCLC by inhibiting growth of NSCLC cells in a way partially dependent on ROS. We observed an approximately 60 % inhibition of DHA on the cell viability of both A549 and H1299 cells and 10 % restoration in the presence of NAC, however; NAC had no significant effects on restoring DHA’s suppression on the migration and invasion of both cell lines. These results are consistent with previous observations that artesunate (ART) and DHA mediated inhibition of proliferation as well as promotion of apoptosis in NSCLC A549 cells were partly reversed by NAC [12 ]. These findings lead us to conclude that DHA acts, at least in part, in a ROS-independent manner to suppress NSCLC. It is worth mentioning that the generation and elimination of ROS under physiological conditions are delicately balanced, whereas cancer cells have moderate increase of ROS which plays important roles in oncogenesis and cancer progression [24 ]. However, DHA-induced overproduction of ROS, exactly as it exerts effects as antimalarial drugs, may cause cancer cell death once beyond a threshold of cytotoxicity. The traditional anticancer modalities such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy also rely on ROS accumulation to cause cytotoxic oxidative stress [25 ]. Thus, ROS is a key regulator in determining cell fate and DHA represents a new anticancer agent by promoting ROS outbreak in NSCLC. Additional molecular mechanisms may be involved in DHA’s inhibitory effects on NSCLC since we observed only an approximately 10 % restoration of DHA inhibition on the cell viability of both A549 and H1299 cells in the presence of NAC. Our data indicated the role of MDM2 in mediating DHA’s effects on NSCLC. However, p53 is not involved in the DHA-MDM2 action axis although p53 was upregulated upon in vitro  and in vivo  DHA treatment and MDM2  knockdown in A549 cells. In the two cellular contexts, A549 and H1299 cells are p53  wild-type and p53 -null, respectively. Upon DHA treatment, p53  knockdown in A549 cells generated comparable cell viability and tumor colonies with that of si-Control. It has been reported that DHA’s antitumor effects against hepatoma cells were mediated by inhibiting cell proliferation and inducing G1-phase arrest. Furthermore, treatment of hepatoma HepG2 cells with DHA resulted in a dose-dependent increase of p53 and a decrease of MDM2 expression; however, whether MDM2-p53 axis is involved in DHA’s effects in hepatoma cells was not explored in this study [19 ]. While p53 signaling constitutes a complex cellular stress response network playing its role as a tumor suppressor, MDM2 is generally believed to function as a critical regulator for restraining p53 activity by facilitating its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation [26 ]. However, accumulated evidence has suggested that MDM2 is likewise engaged in a complex network to optimize multiple regulatory mechanisms, and thus may exert certain p53-independent functions [27 ]. It has been previously observed that drug-protein adducts of DHA with transferrin (DHA-TF) enhance tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) induced apoptosis in a p53-independent and ROS-dependent manner in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) [28 ]. Hence, being an important target for cancer therapy, low-molecular-weight compounds and peptides including DHA that inhibit MDM2 may have different putative targets beyond p53 that requires further studies. Previous study has shown that MDM2 stabilizes c-Myc mRNA to upregulate its expression, and targets MDM2-cMyc axis to overcome drug resistance in xenograft multiple myeloma mouse model, irrespective of p53 tumor suppressor status [18 ]. MDM2 was also observed to regulate MYCN mRNA stabilization and translation in human neuroblastoma cells [29 ]. Our further findings elucidate the mechanistic model in which intermolecular interactions between MDM2 and c-Myc, which are involved in mediating the effects of DHA/MDM2 axis in NSCLC cells. Furthermore, the immunoprecipitated MDM2 and c-Myc proteins substantially reduced in the cell lysates from DHA-treated NSCLC cells. Abundant evidence has indicated that MDM2, an E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase, has p53-independent activities that act either through ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (UPP)-mediated degradation of target proteins or by competing with other E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase to protect against degradation [14 ,23 ]. By using of MG132, our findings demonstrated that MDM2 per se  is degraded by UPP proteolytic pathway. Of note, the immunoprecipitated c-Myc synchronized with the dynamic change of MDM2 level upon si-RNA-mediated MDM2  knockdown, MG 132 treatment, and the integrated interventions. This strongly suggests that MDM2-mediated regulation of c-Myc may be protective and thus contribute to the oncogenic properties of both genes in NSCLC. We further showed that c-Myc overexpression effectively restored DHA’s suppression on the proliferation of A549 and H1299 cells, and DHA’s induction of apoptosis on both cell lines. It is to be noted that c-Myc has also been proved to be the target of DHA treatment in colorectal cancer (CRC) as DHA significantly increased c-Myc protein degradation and hence reduced its expression in the late-stage CRC [30 ]. Taken together, these results highlight the involvement of MDM2/c-Myc axis in mediating DHA’s anti-tumor effects in NSCLC. However, clearly further studies are required to fully elucidate the role of MDM2-mediated stablization rather than ubiquitination of c-Myc in its function regulation. Studies in a variety of neoplastic settings have demonstrated inhibition of STAT3 and AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) phosphorylation and their involvement in the antitumor effects of DHA [31–34 ]. We have observed the phosphorylated levels of AKT and STAT3 but not ERK1/2 are substantially decreased in DHA treated A549 and H1299 cells as compared with that of DMSO-treated controls. We therefore used AKT inhibitor MK 2206 dihydrochloride and STAT3 activation inhibitor Stattic to verify the two signaling pathways involved in mediating DHA’s suppression on MDM2 expression. The targeted inhibition of AKT and STAT3 by MK 2206 and Stattic resulted in proportionally reduced expression of MDM2 both in A549 and H1299 cells. Thus, these findings strongly suggested that DHA acts via  PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT3 signaling pathways to inhibit MDM2 expression. It is also to be noted that in vivo  administration of DHA in cyclophosphamide (CTX) immunosuppressive mice model promoted splenic immune cell proliferation and accumulation by promoting a cascade reaction of the phosphorylation of MAPK and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), and the relevant cell cycle signaling [35 ]. A possible explanation is that DHA enhanced antitumor activity of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes by inhibiting the production of transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) [36 ] and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) [37 ] in many tumors. It is therefore not surprising that DHA has opposite effects on cancer cells and immune cells since it has subtle regulation on the number and function of T cell subsets such as CD8+  cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) [6 ]. More in-depth studies may determine the exact mechanisms of DHA enhancing T cell activation and cellular immunity and shifting of cytokine profile in favor of antitumor immunity. In summary, we have identified MDM2/c-Myc axis as the target of DHA which exerts anti-tumor effects in NSCLC. DHA acts via  PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT3 signaling cascades to inhibit MDM2, which has direct interaction and positive regulation on c-Myc. This study unlocks the regulatory network of both oncogenes, MDM2 and c-Myc, and supports a model of DHA suppression in NSCLC via  MDM2/c-Myc axis independent of p53 (Fig. 7  ). title: The p53 Codon 72 Pro/Pro Genotype Identifies Poor-Prognosis Neuroblastoma Patients: Correlation with Reduced Apoptosis and Enhanced Senescence by the p53-72P Isoform
abstract: The p53 gene is rarely mutated in neuroblastoma, but codon 72 polymorphism that modulates its proapoptotic activity might influence cancer risk and clinical outcome. We investigated whether this polymorphism affects neuroblastoma risk and disease outcome and assessed the biologic effects of the p53-72R and p53-72P isoforms in p53-null cells. Comparison of 288 healthy subjects and 286 neuroblastoma patients revealed that the p53-72 polymorphism had no significant impact on the risk of developing neuroblastoma; however, patients with the Pro/Pro genotype had a shorter survival than those with the Arg/Arg or the Arg/Pro genotypes even in the stage 3 and 4 subgroup without MYCN amplification. By Cox regression analysis, the p53 Pro/Pro genotype seems to be an independent marker of poor prognosis (hazard ratio = 2.74; 95% confidence interval = 1.14–6.55, P = .014) together with clinical stage, MYCN status, and age at diagnosis. In vitro, p53-72P was less effective than p53-72R in inducing apoptosis and inhibiting survival of p53-null LAN-1 cells treated with etoposide, topotecan, or ionizing radiation but not taxol. By contrast, p53-72P was more effective in promoting p21-dependent accelerated senescence, alone or in the presence of etoposide. Thus, the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype might be a marker of poor outcome independent of MYCN amplification, possibly improving risk stratification. Moreover, the lower apoptosis and the enhanced accelerated senescence by the p53-72P isoform in response to DNA damage suggest that patients with neuroblastoma with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype may benefit from therapeutic protocols that do not rely only on cytotoxic drugs that function, in part, through p53 activation.

All rights reserved 1522-8002/12/$25.00 DOI 10.1593/neo.12594     Abstract     The p53 gene is rarely mutated in neuroblastoma, but codon 72 polymorphism that modulates its proapoptotic activity might influence cancer risk and clinical outcome. We investigated whether this polymorphism affects neuroblastoma risk and disease outcome and assessed the biologic effects of the p53-72R and p53-72P isoforms in p53-null cells. Comparison of 288 healthy subjects and 286 neuroblastoma patients revealed that the p53-72 polymorphism had no significant impact on the risk of developing neuroblastoma; however, patients with the Pro/ Pro genotype had a shorter survival than those with the Arg/Arg or the Arg/Pro genotypes even in the stage 3 and 4 subgroup without MYCN amplification. By Cox regression analysis, the p53 Pro/Pro genotype seems to be an independent marker of poor prognosis (hazard ratio = 2.74; 95% confidence interval = 1.14-6.55, P = .014) together with clinical stage, MYCN status, and age at diagnosis. In vitro, p53-72P was less effective than p53-72R in inducing apoptosis and inhibiting survival of p53-null LAN-1 cells treated with etoposide, topotecan, or ionizing radiation but not taxol. By contrast, p53-72P was more effective in promoting p21-dependent accelerated senescence, alone or in the presence of etoposide. Thus, the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype might be a marker of poor outcome in­dependent of MYCN amplification, possibly improving risk stratification. Moreover, the lower apoptosis and the enhanced accelerated senescence by the p53-72P isoform in response to DNA damage suggest that patients with neuroblastoma with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype may benefit from therapeutic protocols that do not rely only on cytotoxic drugs that function, in part, through p53 activation.   Neoplasia (2012) 14, 634–643     Introduction   Neuroblastoma (NB) is a childhood solid tumor that accounts for 8% to 10% of all childhood cancers and for ~15% of all deaths be­cause of pediatric malignancies [1]. NB arises from neuroectodermal precursor cells of the neural crest, and therefore, tumors can develop anywhere in the sympathetic nervous system [1]. Clinically, NB is remarkably heterogeneous: age at diagnosis [2], clinical stage (based on the International Neuroblastoma Staging System [3]), and tumor histology [4] are the most important variables for predicting disease risk and selecting appropriate therapeutic protocols. Children older than 18 months, with tumor at advanced stage (3 or 4) or with un­favorable histologic findings have an adverse outcome despite intensive multimodal treatments such as high-dose myeloablative chemotherapy followed by rescue with autologous bone marrow [5]. Clinical hetero­geneity correlates with several genetic abnormalities whose detection in tumor cells has further improved risk stratification [5]. V-myc myelocytomatosis viral-related oncogene NB-derived (MYCN) onco­gene amplification [6], hemizygous deletions of chromosomal region 1p36 [7], and unbalanced gain of 17q regions [8] are the most common genomic aberrations in NB. MYCN amplification occurs in ~20% of cases and represents the most powerful marker of poor outcome [9]. In contrast to other malignancies, only 2% to 3% of NBs have mutations of the p53 gene [10]. p53 is a tumor suppressor gene that encodes for a nuclear phosphoprotein, which, on activation, regulates many biologic processes such as cell cycle checkpoints, apoptosis, and cellular senes­cence [11]. Impairment of such processes has important implications for clinical behavior and response to therapy of tumors with nonfunc­tional p53 [12]. p53 also activates the transcription of the murine dou­ble minute (MDM2) gene that encodes for the major negative regulator of p53 [13]. In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in identifying and assessing the frequency of gene variants (polymorphisms) as a tool to predict interindividual cancer risk and response to cancer therapies [14].   A polymorphism is defined as a DNA sequence change that occurs in a significant proportion (>1%) of a large population [15]. The most common type of genetic variation is a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). For the p53 gene, an SNP has been identified at codon 72 within exon 4 causing an Arg>Pro substitution [16]. The p53-72R isoform seems to be more potent than the p53-72P isoform in induc­ing apoptosis, and increased mitochondrial localization and reduced affinity of the p53-72R isoform for the p53 inhibitor iASPP are among the proposed mechanisms that may be responsible for such an effect [17,18].   In this study, we compared the frequency of the p53 codon 72 Arg/ Arg, Arg/Pro, and Pro/Pro genotypes in 288 control subjects and 286 newly diagnosed NBs and correlated these frequencies with clinical­biologic variables such as age at diagnosis, primary tumor site, clinical stage, and MYCN amplification. We report here that patients with the Pro/Pro genotype, including those with normal MYCN status and advanced disease stages, seem to have a shorter 5-year survival than those with the Arg/Pro or Arg/Arg genotype.   The more aggressive disease of patients with NB with the Pro/Pro genotype correlated with lower apoptosis and enhanced survival of cytotoxic drug or ionizing radiation (IR)–treated p53-null LAN-1 cells expressing the p53-72P compared with the p53-72R isoform. By con­trast, expression of the p53-72P isoform, alone or in the presence of a low concentration of etoposide, induced an increase in senescent cells.   Together, these findings suggest that, although relatively rare, the p53 codon 72 Pro/Pro genotype might identify a subgroup of patients with NB with aggressive disease independently of the status of other markers predictive of poor outcome. Moreover, patients with this genotype may respond less efficiently to treatments that induce DNA damage and increased p53 expression/activity and may benefit from therapeutic protocols that include cytotoxic drugs with p53-independent mechanisms of action.   Materials and Methods   Subjects   Two hundred eighty-six patients with NB (258 Italian patients, most of whom were previously included to assess the frequency of the MDM2 SNP-309 polymorphism [19] and 28 British patients) were selected for the analysis of the p53 codon 72 genotype. Their clinical and biologic characteristics are listed in Table W1. Tumor DNA was analyzed in each patient, whereas peripheral blood DNA was also genotyped in 40 cases to confirm that polymorphism fre­quency did not reflect somatic mutation. Selection criteria were lack of previous treatments and availability of adequate amount of DNA. Tumor DNA was used because peripheral blood lymphocytes are not always readily attainable from patients with NB. Institutional written informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians of patients with NB. The study underwent ethical review and approval according to local institutional guidelines.   Controls   The p53 codon 72 genotype was also evaluated in peripheral blood DNA of 288 healthy individuals from anonymous blood donors randomly selected during a 5-year period (2000-2005) at several Northern Italy Blood Banks and from control subjects stored at the “Oncology Institute of Veneto,” Padova, Italy. Their age ranged from 25 to 60 years (median, 45 years) and the male-to-female ratio was approximately 46% to 54%.   NB Cell Lines DNA   DNA from NB-69, NBL-W, NBL-S, BE1N, TR14, NGP, NB1691, and LS NB cell lines was from Dr Tweddle’s laboratory, whereas DNA from RN-GA, SH-EP, SK-, GI-CAN, and SK-NBE2 cell lines was from Dr Raschellà’s laboratory. DNA from LAN-5, HTLA-230, GI-CAN, SH-SY5Y, IMR32, LAN-1, and SK-N-AS cell lines was obtained using QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) (Table W2).   p53 Codon 72 Genotyping   The p53 DNA segment for codon 72 genotype was amplified by polymerase chin reaction (PCR) using 150 ng of DNA and a pair of forward (5'-TTGCCGTCCCAAGCAATGGATGA-3') and reverse (5'-TCTGGGAAGGGACAGAAGATGAC-3') primers that gener­ated a 199-bp DNA product. DNA amplification was done as follows: 95°C for 1 minute, 60°C for 1 minute, and 72°C for 2 minutes for 40 cycles. PCR products were separated by electrophoresis in 1% agarose gel with ethidium bromide, extracted using a PCR purification kit (Roche Diagnostics GmbH, Mannheim, Germany), and each frag­ment was sequenced from both ends on an ABI PRISM 377 DNA Sequencer using the ABI PRISM Big Dye Terminator (PE Biosystem, Foster City, CA). Thirty tumor and control DNA were independently resequenced to confirm the genotype’s accuracy.   Statistical Analysis   The frequencies of p53 polymorphism at codon 72 were cross­tabulated in patients with NB versus healthy controls using a two-sided Fisher exact test. The frequencies of p53 polymorphism at codon 72 in patients with NB versus known prognostic factors were also cross­tabulated using the Fisher exact test to evaluate the significance of the association.   Clinical-pathologic variables were categorized as follows: age at diag­nosis (<18 vs =18 months) [2], primary site (adrenal vs nonadrenal), clinical stage according to the International Neuroblastoma Staging System [3] (stage 1, 2, and 4 S vs 3 and 4), and MYCN status (single copy vs amplified).   Five-year overall survival curves on the basis of the p53 genotype at codon 72 in all patients with NB or in subgroups defined on the basis of established prognostic factors were calculated according to Kaplan and Meier [20], and the statistical significance of the differ­ences was assessed using log-rank test. Cox multiple regression anal­ysis [21] was carried out, including clinical stage, MYCN status, age at diagnosis, and p53 polymorphism as covariates. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < .05 was considered statistically significant. The analyses were carried out using the software package SPSS 11.0 for Windows (SPSS, Inc, Chicago, IL). The Hardy-Weinberg equilib­rium was assessed by .2 test.   Plasmids   p53-72R-ERTAM and p53-72P-ERTAM were generated as follows: the p53-72R and p53-72P coding sequences were amplified by reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction from total RNA of ACN and NBL-S cells, respectively. Sense primer (5'GTTAACATGGAG­GAGCCGCA-3')containsa5'-flapping HpaIsiteflanked by theATG, and antisense primer (5'GGATCCGTCTGAGTCAGGC-3')containsa 5'-flapping BamHI and a mutated p53 stop codon. The ligand-binding domain of the mutated (Gly525Arg) tamoxifen-responsive murine estrogen receptor (ER) was obtained by BamHI/EcoRI digestion of the .uORF-C/EBPa-ERTAM vector [22]. Each PCR product and the digested ERTAM fragment were subcloned into the HpaI/EcoRI– digested MigRI vector.   Cells Cultures and Retroviral and Lentiviral Infections   p53-null human NB cell line LAN-1 [23] was cultured in Dulbecco modified Eagle medium with Glutamax (Invitrogen-GIBCO, Carlsbad, CA) supplemented by 10% fetal bovine serum and penicillin and strep­tomycin (100 µg/ml each) at 37°C, 5% CO2. For retroviral infections, Phoenix cells were transiently transfected with the indicated plasmids. The infectious supernatant was collected 48 hours later and was used to infect (a 48-hour procedure) LAN-1 cells. Twenty-four hours later, infected cells were sorted (EPICS Profile Analyzer; Coulter, Hialeah, FL) for green florescent protein (GFP) expression and maintained in culture as described [24].   For lentiviral infections, 293T cells were cotransfected with p21shRNA pLKO.1 (20 µg) and the packaging plasmids pCMVd8.2 (10 µg) and pCMV-VSVG (15 µg) using the calcium phosphate transfection kit (Invitrogen). Lentiviral stocks were harvested 48 hours later, centrifuged for 5 minutes at 3000 rpm, aliquoted, and stored at -80°C. Lentiviral titers were determined by transduction of 3 × 104 293T cells with serial dilutions of the viral stocks in 24-well plates sup­plemented with puromycin (2 µg/ml). Then, LAN-1-p53-72R-ER or LAN-1-p53-72P-ER plated at a cell density of 2 × 104 cells per well and transduced with a multiplicity of infection of 10 using one round of cosedimentation and incubation. Lentivirally transduced cells were selected in the presence of puromycin (2 µg/ml).     Protein Analysis   Cell lysates from 5 × 105 cells were suspended in 50 µlof2× Laemmli lysis buffer (BioRad, Richmond, CA) and boiled for 10 min­utes. For Western blot analysis, 20 µl (equivalent to 200,000 cells) was resolved by 10% SDS-PAGE, transferred to nitrocellulose membranes, and blotted with the indicated antibodies: anti-p53 (DO-1, sc-126; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA), anti–phospho Ser-15 p53 (no. 07-388; Cell Signaling), anti–ß-actin (sc-47778; Santa Cruz Bio­technology), anti-p21 (DF10; Calbiochem, San Diego, CA), and anti-MDM2 (no. 0P46; Calbiochem). Secondary antibodies were peroxidase labeled, and peroxidase was detected with Enhanced Chemiluminescence Kit (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech, Little Chalfont, United Kingdom).   Irradiation Treatment   Cells were irradiated with different x-ray doses (20, 40, and 80 cGy) using a Gilardoni x-ray generator (Gilardoni SpA, Mandello del Lario, Lecco, Italy). Irradiation times varied from 15 to 30 seconds depending on the dose. After irradiation, medium was changed, and cells were kept at 37°C in the incubator for 24 hours. Subsequently, cells were plated for colony formation assays or used for flow cytometric measurements carried out after an additional 48 hours (72 hours after irradiation).   Flow Cytometry Analysis   Cells were harvested, and pellets were washed twice with PBS and diluted in 2× Nicoletti solution (0.1% Na citrate, 0.1% Triton X-100, 50 µg/ml propidium iodide) for 5 minutes before the analyses. Samples were analyzed by flow cytometry using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA). For each sample, at least 2 × 104 cells were analyzed. Cell cycle distribution and hypodiploid DNA content were calculated by Cell Quest software (BD Biosciences). Statistical significance (P) was calculated by two-tailed Student’s t test.   Confocal Immunofluorescence   LAN-1 (parental and p53-ER–derivative) cells were plated on Culture Slides (BD Falcon) and, 36 hours later, treated with 250 nM 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (4-HT). After 2 hours, cells were washed twice this PBS, fixed with ice-cold methanol for 20 minutes, permeabilized in 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS (5 minutes), washed twice with PBS, and blocked in 1% bovine serum albumin/PBS for 30 minutes at room temperature.   Slides were stained with an anti-p53 monoclonal antibody (PAb 1801; Calbiochem) diluted 1:80 in 5% milk–Tris-buffered saline and Tween 20, incubated for 1 hour at room temperature. After a 30-minute incubation at room temperature with antirabbit Alexa Fluor 555 conjugate (A-21428; Invitrogen) diluted 1:300 in 5% milk– Tris-buffered saline and Tween 20, slides were washed three times in PBS and rinsed in water. For nuclei staining, Hoechst 33258 was added in the last PBS wash. As control, LAN-1 cells were stained in the absence of the anti-p53 antibody. Cells were visualized by Leica TCS SP2 confocal laser scanner microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany) using a 40× oil immersion objective, and images were analyzed with Leica software.   Colony Assay   Parental, p53-72R-ER, and p53-72P-ER–derivative LAN-1 cells were seeded at 3 × 105 cells per well in six-well plates. The following day, cells were treated with etoposide (5, 10 or 20 µM) or taxol (2 µM). After 3 hours, cells were washed and seeded (5 × 103, 1×104, 2×104 cells perplate)insix-wellplateswithorwithout 4-HT (250 nM). After 7 days, plates were stained with Crystal violet, and colonies were counted.   SA-ß-gal Staining Assay   The staining for SA-ß-galactosidase activity was performed as described [25]. Briefly, cells were seeded in 24-well plates and treated with 4-HT alone (250 nM, 48 hours) when 80% confluent or with 4-HT and etoposide (25 nM etoposide for 3 hours and then 250 nM 4-HT for 48 hours) when 50% confluent. At the end of the treatment, cells were washed in PBS and fixed in 2% formaldehyde/0.2% glutar­aldehyde. Cells were then washed and incubated at 37°C for 4 hours with fresh SA-ß-gal staining solution (1 mg of 5-bromo-4-chloro-3­indolyl-ß-D-galactoside per milliliter, 40 mM citric acid/sodium phosphate [pH 6.0], 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 5 mM potassium ferricyanide).   Real-time PCR Expression Analyses   For real-time quantitative PCR, total RNA was isolated from p53­72R-ER-and p53-72P-ER-LAN-1 cells using the RNeasy Mini kit (Qiagen). RNA was treated for 1 hour at 37°C with DNase-RNase free (Roche Applied Science, Mannheim, Germany), which was then deactivated for 15 minutes at 65°C. Four micrograms of total mRNA was reverse-transcribed using SuperScript III Reverse Transcriptase kit (Invitrogen), and the resulting complementary DNA was used as a PCR template. All reactions were done in triplicate, and total RNA was extracted from two separate experiments.   Primer pairs of analyzed genes (MDM2:FW5'-caagttactgtgtatcagg­caggg-3',RV5'-tctgttgcaatgtgatggaagg-3'; BAX:FW 5'-ggagcgg­cggtgatggac-3',RV5'-ggcccctgtcttcatgatctgc-3'; NOXA:FW5'­cagagctggaagtcgagtgtg-3',RV5'-gttcctgagcagaagagtttgg-3'; PERP:FW 5'-cccgtgaagtacacccagacc-3',RV 5'-gcccacccaaagccgtagg-3'; PAI-1:FW 5'-aagactcccttccccgactc-3',RV 5'-cacagagacagtgctgccgt-3'; p21:FW5'­cctgcccaagctctaccttcc-3',RV 5'-ggtccacatggtcttcctctgc-3'; HPRT:FW 5'-agactttgctttccttggtcagg-3',RV 5'-gtctggcttatatccaacacttcg-3') were de­signed using Beacon Design software (Premier Biosoft International, Palo Alto, CA). Real-time quantitative PCR was performed using GoTaq qPCR Master Mix (Promega, Madison, WI) on a MyIQ thermocycler (BioRad) and quantified using MyIQ software (BioRad) that analyzes the Ct value of real-time PCR data with the ..Ct method. HPRT, a house­keeping gene with constant expression, was used as an internal control to normalize input complementary DNA.   Results   Frequency and Association with Poor-Prognosis Predictors of p53-72 Genotypes   Genotype frequencies at codon 72 of p53 (Arg/Arg, Arg/Pro, and Pro/Pro) and other genetic and clinical characteristics of patients with NB included in this study are summarized in Table W1. The geno­type frequencies in all groups were within the Hardy-Weinberg equi­librium. The frequency of the Pro/Pro genotype in tumor DNA was not significantly different from that of peripheral blood samples of control subjects (3.8% vs 6.6%, P = .190); no statistical significance was also noted if the comparison was limited to the Italian control and NB cohorts (not shown). In 40 cases tested, peripheral blood and tumor DNA genotypes were identical indicating that polymorphism frequency did not reflect somatic mutation or loss of heterozygosity/copy number gains which are uncommon in NB for region 17p13 [26], the chromo­somallocationofthe p53 gene. In an attempt to validate independently the frequency of the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype in a larger cohort of patients with NB, we searched the dbGaP database (http://www.ncbi. nlm.nih.gov/gap), which contains the data set of Wang et al. [27] with 1627 patients with NB and 3254 genetically matched disease-free con­trols. However, data for the p53-72 SNP (rs1042522) were not available because the array platforms used in the Wang et al. data set (Illumina HumanHap550v3.0, HumanHap550v1.1, and Human610_Quadv1_B) do not assay the rs1042522 SNP.   Of interest, the frequency of the Pro/Pro genotype was low (1/20, 5%) also in human NB cell lines (Table W2). We then assessed whether the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype was associated with predictors of poor outcome such as advanced clinical stage (3 and 4), age at diag­nosis 18 months or older, adrenal primary site, and MYCN ampli­fication (Table 1). A statistically significant association of the Pro/Pro genotype with age 18 months or older (P = .031) was noted; although not statistically significant, the Pro/Pro genotype was more represented in patients with unfavorable stage (3 and 4), and seemed to be inversely associated with MYCN amplification (Table 1). In particular, of the seven patients with stage 4 disease with the Pro/Pro genotype, only one had MYCN amplification.   Effect of p53-72 Genotypes on Survival   Cumulative Kaplan-Meier 5-year overall survival of patients with NB with the Pro/Pro genotype was shorter than that of patients with the Arg/Arg (P = .042, log-rank test) or the Arg/Pro genotype (P =.003, log-rank test). Because survival of patients with the Arg/Arg and the Arg/Pro genotype was undistinguishable, we decided to combine these two groups and compare to the Pro/Pro group in all the analyses. As shown in Figure 1A, patients with the Pro/Pro genotype had a shorter survival that those with the Arg/Arg and Arg/Pro genotypes (P =.014, log-rank test). Moreover, in the NB subgroup with normal MYCN status, patients with the Pro/Pro genotype had a shorter overall survival than those with the Arg/Arg and Arg/Pro genotypes (P = .005, log-rank test; Figure 1B). In this subgroup, overall survival of patients with the Pro/Pro genotype was also shorter when limiting the analysis to those either at stage 3 and 4 or at stage 4 only (P =.008 and P = .003, re­spectively, log-rank test; Figure 1, C and D). We also observed a shorter overall survival in patients with the Pro/Pro genotype in the subgroups at stage 4, with age 18 months or older, and with normal MYCN status (P = .013; Figure W1). The p53 Codon 72 Polymorphism Is an Independent Prognostic Factor   Because the p53 codon 72 Pro/Pro genotype was associated with a shorter overall survival, we asked whether it might represent an inde­pendent factor distinct from other common NB prognostic indicators such as clinical stage, MYCN status, and age at diagnosis. Thus, we carried out a Cox multiple regression analysis for overall survival that included stage, MYCN status, age at diagnosis, and p53 codon 72 geno­types as covariates. Interestingly, the hazard ratio between Pro/Pro and Arg/Arg or Arg/Pro genotypes was significant (2.74; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.14-6.55, P = .024; Table 2), suggesting that the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype may represent an additional independent prognostic marker in NB.   Biologic Effects of p53-72R and p53-72P in NB Cells   To address potential mechanisms associated with the more aggressive disease in patients with NB with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype, we es­tablished p53-null LAN-1 derivative cell lines expressing the tamoxifen (4-HT)-regulated p53 72R-ER or p53 72P-ER isoform (Figure W2) and assessed whether their activation modulates differentially the effects of cytotoxic drugs or IR on apoptosis, survival, and senescence.   For the experiments assessing the effects of cytotoxic drugs on apop­tosis and survival, we selected etoposide and topotecan because they are used to treat patients with NB and function, in part, through DNA damage-dependent p53 activation and also taxol because its mechanism of action is p53 independent [28,29].
