Discussion   Genetic characteristics associated with tumor initiation and/or progres­sion and predictive of clinical outcome are a subject of intense investi­gation. Several recent studies have analyzed the relation between the polymorphism of p53 codon 72 and cancer development, disease pro­gression, response to chemotherapy, and overall survival. In several studies, the p53-72Arg/Arg genotype was associated with increased risk for breast [30,31], gastric [32], ovary [33], oral [34], skin cancer [35], and sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma [36]. On the contrary, other studies have demonstrated an association between the Pro/Pro geno­type and increased risk for non–small cell lung [37], nasopharyngeal [38,39], thyroid [40], and skin cancer [41]. The reasons for these dis­crepancies might depend on methodological differences in the studies (laboratory and statistical analyses, selection of patients, and control subjects) and/or true geographic and ethnic variations. Instead, more consistent results were obtained when assessing the correlation between p53 codon 72 allelic variants and tumor progression, patients’ response to chemotherapy, and overall survival [42–45]. In these studies, patients with the Pro/Pro genotype had a worse outcome than those with the Arg/Arg genotype, probably reflecting different biologic properties of the two p53 variants. The p53-72R isoform has been shown to be more effective of the 72P isoform in inducing apoptosis, a difference possibly explained by its more efficient mitochondrial localization and/or re­duced affinity for iASPP, a member of the ASPP family which inhibits the transactivating and apoptotic functions of p53 [17,18].   Thus, we analyzed the frequency of p53-72 genotypes in DNA sam­ples of patients with NB and their association with disease extent and clinical outcome. Because the p53 gene is rarely mutated in NB, it is conceivable that the expression of a p53 isoform with reduced proapop­totic activity may have a negative impact on cancer risk and clinical outcome. Although there was no association between any of the p53 codon 72 genotypes and risk to develop NB, patients with the p53­72 Pro/Pro genotype had a shorter overall survival compared to those with the Arg/Arg and Arg/Pro genotypes. Of interest, overall survival of patients with the Arg/Arg and the Arg/Pro genotypes was undistin­guishable; this observation is consistent with a number of possibilities (which can be tested experimentally) such as functional dominance of the p53-72R over the p53-72P isoform or unequal levels of isoform expression when both p53-72 alleles are present.   Although caution is necessary because of the groups’ small size, a decrease in overall survival in patients with the Pro/Pro genotype was also observed in the subgroup with no MYCN amplification, includ­ing patients at stages 3 and 4 or at stage 4 only. These findings are intriguing and potentially important because amplification of MYCN is the most common and reliable marker of poor outcome, especially in infants (children <1 year at diagnosis) with stage 4 disease [46]. Nevertheless, a substantial part of older children with stage 4 NB has a dismal outcome despite the absence of MYCN amplification [47]. In these patients, the genetic trait(s) responsible for tumor aggressiveness are still under investigation [47]. The association of the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype with shorter overall survival in the subgroup of patients with stage 3 and 4 disease without MYCN amplification raises the possibility that it may be one of the factors promoting tumor aggressiveness in stage 4 disease with normal MYCN status. That the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype might be a marker of poor outcome in NB is further sup­ported by the results of the Cox multiple regression analysis, which sug­gest the independence of this polymorphism from other commonly used prognostic indicators such as clinical stage, age at diagnosis, and MYCN status. Consistent with these data, of 20 NB cell lines examined, the only one with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype is the NBL-S line, which has an aggressive behavior in mice and normal MYCN status [48], although the half-life of N-myc protein in NBL-S cells is longer than normal [48].   Experiments carried out using etoposide, topotecan, or IR-treated p53-null LAN-1 derivative cell lines expressing the 4-HT–regulated p53-72R-ER or p53-72P-ER isoform support the hypothesis that NB cells from patients with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype exhibit an increased survival and a reduced propensity to undergo apoptosis. However, in the p53-72-ER-LAN-1 cell lines treated with taxol, a drug with p53-independent mechanism of action [27,28], the effects of the two p53 isoforms were essentially undistinguishable. Based on these data, it is reasonable to speculate that patients with NB with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype may benefit more from co-treatment with drugs that induce DNA damage and increase p53 expression (e.g., topoisomerase I or II inhibitors or IR) and drugs with p53­independent mechanisms of action.   Of interest, p53-72P was more effective than p53-72R in promot­ing the appearance of senescent (ß-gal–positive) cells in vitro.Al­though it is unknown whether enhanced senescence would also be associated with activation of p53 in NB with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype, it is conceivable that undergoing p53-dependent accelerated senescence rather than apoptosis may allow some NB cells to escape cytotoxic drug–induced killing through cell-autonomous and/or para­crine mechanisms [49,50].   In summary, although relatively rare, the p53 codon 72 Pro/Pro genotype might be relevant for improving risk stratification and, per­haps, selecting more personalized therapeutic protocols. In light of the results of this pilot study, further investigations in a larger num­ber of patients and in mouse models of NB are warranted to validate the impact of this p53 polymorphism as a prognostic marker and modulator of chemotherapy sensitivity. The p53 gene is rarely mutated in neuroblastoma, but codon 72 polymorphism that modulates its proapoptotic activity might influence cancer risk and clinical outcome. We investigated whether this polymorphism affects neuroblastoma risk and disease outcome and assessed the biologic effects of the p53-72R and p53-72P isoforms in p53-null cells. Comparison of 288 healthy subjects and 286 neuroblastoma patients revealed that the p53-72 polymorphism had no significant impact on the risk of developing neuroblastoma; however, patients with the Pro/Pro genotype had a shorter survival than those with the Arg/Arg or the Arg/Pro genotypes even in the stage 3 and 4 subgroup without MYCN amplification. By Cox regression analysis, the p53 Pro/Pro genotype seems to be an independent marker of poor prognosis (hazard ratio = 2.74; 95% confidence interval = 1.14–6.55, P  = .014) together with clinical stage, MYCN status, and age at diagnosis. In vitro , p53-72P was less effective than p53-72R in inducing apoptosis and inhibiting survival of p53-null LAN-1 cells treated with etoposide, topotecan, or ionizing radiation but not taxol. By contrast, p53-72P was more effective in promoting p21-dependent accelerated senescence, alone or in the presence of etoposide. Thus, the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype might be a marker of poor outcome independent of MYCN amplification, possibly improving risk stratification. Moreover, the lower apoptosis and the enhanced accelerated senescence by the p53-72P isoform in response to DNA damage suggest that patients with neuroblastoma with the p53-72 Pro/Pro genotype may benefit from therapeutic protocols that do not rely only on cytotoxic drugs that function, in part, through p53 activation. title: Biogenic synthesis of Au<ce:glyph name=sbnd></ce:glyph>Ag nanocomposite using <ce:italic>Moullava spicata</ce:italic>: mechanistic insights into <ce:italic>p53</ce:italic>-independent cancer cell apoptosis and enhanced diabetic wound healing
abstract: Diabetic wounds and cancer are complex pathological conditions driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired cellular regulation, necessitating multifunctional therapeutic strategies. This study aimed to develop plant-mediated AuAg nanocomposites using Moullava spicata (MLSPI) and to evaluate their mechanistic role in anticancer and diabetic wound healing applications in an animal model. Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposites were synthesized through a green reduction process using MLSPI stem extract as both a reducing and stabilizing agent. Comprehensive physicochemical characterizations were conducted via UV–Visible spectroscopy, zeta potential, DLS, FTIR, XRD, TEM, SAED, SEM, and EDS. In vitro anticancer mechanisms were investigated through MTT assay, apoptosis analysis, and Western blotting in SH-SY5Y cells to assess cytotoxicity and p53/MDM2 pathway modulation. In vivo diabetic wound healing efficacy was evaluated by wound contraction, tensile strength, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and histopathological analysis. Spectroscopic analysis confirmed nanocomposite formation with a red shift from 266 to 275 nm. DLS revealed a mean hydrodynamic size of 177.4 ± 38.7 nm with zeta potential of −38.3 mV, indicating a good colloidal stability. XRD confirmed crystalline face-centered cubic structures of Au and Ag, while microscopy (TEM/SEM) showed predominantly spherical nanoparticles. EDS confirmed elemental composition. The nanocomposite exhibited moderate cytotoxicity (IC₅₀ = 108.73 μg/mL) compared to Cisplatin (9.77 μg/mL). Mechanistically, apoptosis was associated with an increased late-apoptotic cell population and reduced expression of p53 and MDM2 proteins, suggesting modulation of apoptotic signaling pathways. In diabetic wounds, nanocomposite markedly improved wound contraction, tensile strength, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis, while reducing inflammatory infiltration, particularly at higher dose. Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposites exerted dual therapeutic effects through oxidative stress-mediated apoptosis and enhanced tissue regeneration.

Fig. 1 Characterization of MLSPI extract and Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC (a)  UV–Visible absorption spectra of the MLSPI stem extract exhibited a characteristic absorption peak at 266 nm, indicating the presence of intrinsic chromophoric phytoconstituents. The synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC displayed a red-shifted absorption maximum at 275 nm, suggesting the involvement of these biomolecules in nanoparticle synthesis and stabilization. In addition, broad SPR bands were observed at approximately 430 nm and 535 nm, corresponding to Ag and Au nanoparticles, respectively, thereby supporting the formation of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC. (b)  FTIR spectra of MLSPI extract (reported by Patil et al. (2025)) and synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC, showing notable shifts in functional groups, including O H stretching (3336.04 to 3353.52 cm−1 ) and C O stretching (1612.65 to 1726.84 cm−1 ), indicating involvement of biomolecules in nanoparticle synthesis and stabilization. (c)  DLS analysis of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showing mean hydrodynamic diameter (177.4 ± 38.7 nm), mode size (162.6 nm), and Z -average diameter (187.9 nm), suggesting a moderately broad size distribution. (d)  Zeta potential analysis of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showed a surface charge of −38.3 mV with electrophoretic mobility of −0.000296 cm2 /V·s, which indicating strong electrostatic repulsion and high colloidal stability. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)  Fig. 1   Fig. 2 Characterization of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposite. (a)  XRD pattern showing sharp diffraction peaks, with prominent reflections at 38.99°, 67.61°, 76.81°, and 85.83° which are the (111), (220), (311), and (222) planes of fcc structures of Au and Ag, in agreement with JCPDS 04–0784 and 04–0783. (b–d)  SEM images illustrating predominantly spherical nanoparticles along with some irregular morphologies, indicating the formation of heterogeneous nanostructures. (e)  EDS spectrum confirming the elemental composition, showing the presence of C (51.93 ± 1.36%), O (31.49 ± 2.65%), N (0.35 ± 1.05%), Ag (9.60 ± 1.13%), and Au (6.63 ± 1.15%) in mass percentage.  Fig. 2   Fig. 3 TEM and elemental characterization of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposite (a–g)  TEM images of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showing predominantly spherical nanoparticles with slight irregular morphology, indicating uniform nucleation with minor anisotropic growth. (h)  SAED pattern exhibiting a mixed structural nature with distinct diffraction spots superimposed on a diffuse halo, suggesting the coexistence of amorphous and crystalline phases. (i)  EDS spectrum confirming the elemental composition of the nanocomposite, including C, O, Ag, and Au, along with minor traces of Cl and Cu. (j)  The electron image of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC used for elemental mapping analysis. (k)  EDS elemental mapping overlay demonstrating the spatial distribution of elements within the nanocomposite. (l–q)  Individual elemental mapping images showing the distribution of: (l)  Ag, (m)  Au, (n)  C, (o)  O, (p)  Cu, and (q)  Cl, which may confirm the presence of bioorganic layers surrounding the nanoparticles.  Fig. 3   Fig. 4 Cytotoxic and apoptosis-inducing effects of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC in SH-SY5Y cells. (a)  MTT assay showing dose-dependent cytotoxicity of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC, with cell viability decreasing from 94.32 ± 1.6585% at 6.25 μg/mL to 56.75 ± 0.2745% at 100 μg/mL, compared with the standard drug. Cisplatin exhibited higher cytotoxicity, reducing cell viability from 58.47 ± 0.6978% to 11.42 ± 1.0930% over the same concentration range, with an IC₅₀ of 9.775 μ g/mL, while Au– Ag– MLSPI–NC depicted an IC₅₀ of 108.733 μ g/mL. The statistical analysis revealed extremely significant differences (****p  < 0.0001, ***p  < 0.001) at all tested concentrations compared to the standard. (b–g)  Flow cytometric analysis of apoptosis: (b, c)  control cells showing predominantly viable population; (d, e)  Cisplatin-treated cells demonstrating increased apoptotic population; (f, g)  Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated cells exhibiting a marked reduction in viable cells (22.14 ± 0.61%) compared to control and a significant increase in late apoptotic/dead cells (54.98 ± 0.34% vs.  32.45 ± 0.51%), with minimal early apoptosis. The elevated debris fraction (22.70 ± 0.62%) in treated cells indicates extensive cellular damage. Population profile plots reveal a shift toward higher Annexin V expression, confirming enhanced apoptosis. (h)  Western blot analysis of apoptotic regulatory proteins showing expression levels of p53  and MDM2 in SH-SY5Y cells across different treatments: (i) control, (ii) Cisplatin, and (iii) Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC, with β -actin choose as an internal loading control. Bharati Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University) Pune MS 411030 India       Diabetic wounds and cancer are complex pathological conditions driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired cellular regulation, necessitating multifunctional therapeutic strategies. This study aimed to develop plant-mediated Au Ag nanocomposites using Moullava spicata  (MLSPI) and to evaluate their mechanistic role in anticancer and diabetic wound healing applications in an animal model. Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposites were synthesized through a green reduction process using MLSPI stem extract as both a reducing and stabilizing agent. Comprehensive physicochemical characterizations were conducted via  UV–Visible spectroscopy, zeta potential, DLS, FTIR, XRD, TEM, SAED, SEM, and EDS. In vitro  anticancer mechanisms were investigated through MTT assay, apoptosis analysis, and Western blotting in SH-SY5Y cells to assess cytotoxicity and p53 /MDM2 pathway modulation. In vivo  diabetic wound healing efficacy was evaluated by wound contraction, tensile strength, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and histopathological analysis. Spectroscopic analysis confirmed nanocomposite formation with a red shift from 266 to 275 nm. DLS revealed a mean hydrodynamic size of 177.4 ± 38.7 nm with zeta potential of −38.3 mV, indicating a good colloidal stability. XRD confirmed crystalline face-centered cubic structures of Au and Ag, while microscopy (TEM/SEM) showed predominantly spherical nanoparticles. EDS confirmed elemental composition. The nanocomposite exhibited moderate cytotoxicity (IC₅₀ = 108.73 μg/mL) compared to Cisplatin (9.77 μg/mL). Mechanistically, apoptosis was associated with an increased late-apoptotic cell population and reduced expression of p53  and MDM2 proteins, suggesting modulation of apoptotic signaling pathways. In diabetic wounds, nanocomposite markedly improved wound contraction, tensile strength, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis, while reducing inflammatory infiltration, particularly at higher dose. Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposites exerted dual therapeutic effects through oxidative stress-mediated apoptosis and enhanced tissue regeneration. In the field of nanotechnology, inorganic nanoparticles, including metals and metal oxides, exhibit properties such as hydrophilicity, non-toxicity, and biocompatibility, which support their use in drug delivery, imaging, and diagnostics [2] . Among metallic nanostructures, gold (AuNPs) and silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have gained considerable attention in biomedical research as multifunctional delivery platforms owing to their unique physicochemical properties, ease of surface modification, intrinsic therapeutic activities, and broad range of applications [3] . AuNPs have been extensively studied for their outstanding biocompatibility and adaptable surface chemistry, which enable effective drug conjugation. Consequently, they are widely employed in drug delivery and bioimaging, chemical sensing, where they utilize their distinctive plasmonic properties and easy surface functionalization to improve diagnostic and therapeutic results [4] . Moreover, AuNPs have emerged as versatile agents in cancer treatment because of their particular physicochemical properties and multifunctional capabilities [5] . Their small size and tunable surface characteristics enable them to accumulate in the tumor microenvironment and act as targeted delivery vehicles for therapeutic agents, thereby improving treatment specificity and efficacy [6] . In addition, AuNPs exhibit strong optical properties, particularly surface plasmon resonance, which enables them to absorb light and convert it into heat, leading to photothermal destruction of tumor cells upon irradiation [7] . Furthermore, AuNPs act as effective radiosensitizers because of their high atomic number, which enhances radiation absorption and promotes secondary electron generation and localized damage to cancer cells during radiotherapy [8,9] . They also contribute to multimodal cancer therapy by serving as platforms for simultaneous imaging, drug delivery, and therapeutic interventions, improving both diagnosis and treatment outcomes [9] . Collectively, these properties make AuNPs a promising nanoplatform for targeted, minimally invasive, and highly efficient especially for cancer therapy. Whereas, AgNPs are distinguished by their ability to combat a broad spectrum of pathogens, including multidrug-resistant ones, making them useful in both wound care and medical device applications [10] . Particularly, in diabetic wound healing, AgNPs play a crucial role in overcoming impaired healing conditions such as chronic inflammation, persistent infection, and poor angiogenesis. Their antibacterial mechanism entails the breakdown of microbial cell membranes, resulting in the leakage of intracellular contents and subsequent cell death, which is particularly important in diabetic wounds prone to infection [11,12] . AgNPs further induce oxidative stress in pathogens through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, resulting in damage to lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids [12] . Controlled release of Ag+  ions enhance antibacterial activity by interacting with thiol groups of enzymes and disrupting cellular respiration [11] . Additionally, AgNPs inhibit DNA replication and protein synthesis, thereby preventing microbial proliferation in chronic diabetic wounds [12] . This facilitates targeted therapeutic drug delivery to tumor and diabetic wound sites, enhancing anticancer efficacy while promoting localized tissue regeneration, angiogenesis, and infection control, while minimizing systemic toxicity and side effects [5] . AgNPs and AuNPs nanoparticles exhibit distinct yet complementary therapeutic roles in biomedical application, particularly in diabetic wound healing and cancer application. AgNPs are predominantly preferred for diabetic wound healing owing to their potent antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties, whereas AuNPs are more suitable for cancer applications owing to their superior biocompatibility, surface functionalization, and capability for targeted drug delivery and photothermal therapy. This multifunctional profile renders them highly promising nanoplatforms for the combined treatment of wound healing and cancer. Therefore, integration of Au and Ag nanoparticles into a single bimetallic nanocomposite system offers significant advantages over their respective monometallic interactions between two metals. Au Ag nanocomposites combine the strong antimicrobial and cytotoxic properties of Ag with the superior biocompatibility, stability, and surface functionalization-capability of Au, resulting in enhanced overall therapeutic performance. Studies have reported that bimetallic systems exhibit improved biological activity because their components can act through multiple mechanisms simultaneously, thereby enhancing efficacy and reducing the likelihood of resistance development [13] . In particular, Au Ag nanocomposites demonstrate enhanced anticancer activity and improved drug delivery efficiency due to improved cellular uptake, stability, and controlled-release behavior compared with individual nanoparticles [14] . Furthermore, experimental evidence indicates that Ag Au nanocomposites exhibit superior antitumor efficacy owing to the combined effects of ROS generation from silver and the plasmonic and targeting properties of gold [15] . Similarly, bimetallic core–shell or hybrid Au Ag nanoparticles have been shown to possess enhanced antibacterial, antidiabetic, and anticancer activities compared to single-metal systems, highlighting the importance of interactions in improving multifunctional biomedical performance [16] . The incorporation of both Au and Ag into a single nanocomposite leads to improved physicochemical properties, enhanced biological activity, and multifunctionality, making these systems highly promising for advanced biomedical applications. Moullava spicata  (MLSPI) (syn. Wagatea spicata ; Caesalpinia spicata ), commonly known as Vakeri or Waghati, is an endemic scandent shrub belonging to the family Caesalpiniaceae  found in moist deciduous forests of India, particularly in Goa, Karnataka, and Maharashtra. It is characterized by 1–2 pinnate leaves with 5–6 pairs of distinct leaflets, a prickly rachis, scarlet, pubescent flowers arranged in spikes, and tomentose pods, with flowering and fruiting occurring from November to April [17] . Traditionally, its roots are used in the treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis and pneumonia, while the bark and roots are employed for managing skin diseases and diabetic wounds, and the leaves are used to treat skin infections, chicken pox, and inflammation in lactating women, owing to its abundance of bioactive phytochemicals namely flavonoids, phenolics, tannins, and terpenoids, which also facilitate nanoparticle synthesis [18–20] . Considering these attributes, the plant was selected to investigate its anticancer and diabetic wound healing activity, which remains largely unexplored, with limited literature available, and the stem extract was specifically employed for the green synthesis of Ag-Au-NC to improve therapeutic efficacy. Therefore, this study aims to develop a multifunctional Au Ag nanocomposite system derived from MLSPI, a relatively underexplored medicinal plant with an effective therapeutic potential, for anticancer and diabetic wound-healing applications. In brief, stem extract of MLSPI, rich in flavonoids, phenolics, terpenoids, and tannins, was utilized as bioreducing and stabilizing agents for the eco-friendly synthesis of Au Ag nanocomposites, thereby integrating the advantages of both metals into a single platform. Furthermore, the synthesized nanocomposite was designed to exploit the effects of AuNPs and AgNPs, imparting enhanced therapeutic properties. The resulting Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposite was envisaged to function both as a bioactive therapeutic system and a potential targeted drug-delivery platform. Comprehensive evaluations were performed, including physicochemical characterization through UV–Visible spectroscopy, polydispersity index (PDI), particle-size distribution, zeta potential analysis, dynamic light scattering (DLS), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), selected area electron diffraction (SAED), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Biological assessments comprised cytotoxicity evaluation using the MTT cell assay against SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, apoptosis analysis, and Western blotting studies. In addition, safety and therapeutic efficacy were examined through acute dermal toxicity studies and in vivo  wound healing investigations, including wound-contraction analysis, tensile strength measurement of healed skin, and histopathological examination. As a result, the Au–Ag–MLSPI nanocomposite (Au–Ag–MLSPI-NC) exhibited enhanced biological activity, increased cytotoxicity, and improved wound-healing potential. Therefore, MLSPI-mediated Au Ag nanocomposites may serve as an effective candidate for the development of advanced nanotheranostic systems, highlighting the unexplored biomedical potential of this plant.  2 Experimental work 2.1 Materials All chemicals, compounds and reagents used in the current investigation were of analytical grade and without further process purification. Silver nitrate (AgNO₃) and chloroauric acid (HAuCl₄) were procured from Loba Chemie Private Ltd., Mumbai, India. Fetal bovine serum (FBS), MTT reagent, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), HEPES, NaCl, MgCl₂, EDTA, Tris, glycine, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) were obtained from HiMedia Laboratories Private Ltd., Mumbai, India. Muse™ Annexin V & Dead Cell Reagent and Mini Blot Module were purchased from Merck Millipore (USA) and Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific (USA), respectively. Nonidet P-40, dithiothreitol (DTT), and Laemmli sample buffer were procured from SRL (Sisco Research Laboratories), India. SureCast™ reagents including SureCast™ Acrylamide (40%), SureCast™ APS, and SureCast™ TEMED were received from Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA. HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were purchased from Genei Laboratories Pvt. Ltd., Bengaluru, India. For in vivo  studies, alloxan monohydrate was procured from SRL (India), while ketamine and xylazine were obtained from Neon Laboratories Ltd., India. Soframycin cream (Sanofi India Ltd.) was used as the standard drug for in vivo  wound healing activity. Formalin (10% neutral buffered formalin) and xylene for histological processing were obtained from Merck Life Science Private. Ltd., India.  2.2 Plant collection, authentication and extraction of MLSPI The stem material of MLSPI was obtained in mid-January from coordinates 17.7189° N latitude and 73.3969° E longitude, located in Konkan belt region (Western Ghats foothills), Maharashtra, India. Dr. V. B. Shimpale, a professor (Department of Botany), New College in Kolhapur, verified the authenticity of the gathered plant samples. A voucher specimen (Herbarium No. CBP 01) was prepared and deposited in the departmental herbarium on 22/08/2023 for future reference purpose. The collected stems were thoroughly cleaned to remove soil, dust, and other adhering impurities, followed by drying under appropriate conditions. The dried plant material was then coarsely powdered. Extraction was carried out using a Soxhlet apparatus with 95% ethanol as the solvent. The extraction process was continued until complete exhaustion of the plant material. The obtained stem extract yielded an extractive value of 14.95% (w /w).  2.3 Synthesis of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC were synthesized through a green reduction method using MLSPI stem extract as both a reducing and stabilizing agent. A 1% (w /v ) MLSPI stem extract was prepared in distilled water (Milli-Q) and filtered to remove suspended particulate matter. The extract was initially homogenized using a magnetic stirrer (REMI 2MLH) at 1000 rpm for 15 min. For the synthesis of AgNPs, 1 mL of 1 mM AgNO₃ aqueous solution was added to prepared extract while stirring constantly [18] . The mixture was stirred for 10 min, subsequently heated to boiling for 1 min in a sealed container. The reaction mixture was subsequently incubated at 25 ± 1 °C for 75 min to facilitate the reduction of Ag+  ions, considered by characteristic color change (typically yellowish to brown), confirming the formation of AgNPs. For the formation of Au Ag nanocomposite, 1 mL of 1 mM HAuCl₄ solution was slowly added to preformed AgNP suspension under constant stirring [21] . The resulted reaction mixture was maintained under continuous stirring for an additional 20 min and then kept undisturbed at ambient temperature overnight to allow complete biogenic reduction of Au3+  ions onto the AgNPs, resulting in the formation of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC. The synthesized Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC were purified by centrifugation (REMI PR-24) at 10,000 rpm for continuous 20 min, followed by three washes with distilled water (DW) to remove unreacted constituents, and then redispersed for further characterization and biological evaluations.  2.4 Characterization of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC The synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC was comprehensively characterized using multiple analytical techniques to confirm its formation, structural properties, morphology, and surface chemistry. The preliminary confirmation of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC synthesis was performed using UV–Visible (Shimadzu - UV-1800) spectroscopy, where characteristic surface plasmon resonance (SPR) peaks corresponding to AuNPs and AgNPs were monitored over an appropriate wavelength range, indicating the successful formation of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC bimetallic nanostructures. The hydrodynamic particle size distribution, PDI, and surface charge (zeta potential), which are crucial variables behavior governing stability and dispersion, were determined using DLS analysis with HORIBA Scientific SZ-100 instrument (Japan). Functional groups responsible for the synthesis and stabilization of Au–Ag-MLSPI-NC were identified using FTIR in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode (Bruker, Japan), recorded over a spectral range of 500–4100 cm−1 . The crystalline structure, phase purity, and lattice characteristics of the synthesized Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC were investigated through XRD analysis with a D2 Phaser (Bruker Ltd., Germany), providing information regarding the formation of metallic phases and possible alloying behavior. The average crystallite size of the Ag Au nanoparticles was estimated using the Debye–Scherrer equation. The detailed morphology, particle size, and dispersion pattern of the nanocomposite were further examined using TEM (JEOL JEM 2100 Plus, Japan), while the corresponding SAED patterns were used to confirm the structural arrangement and crystalline nature. In addition, surface morphology and topographical features were analyzed using SEM (JEOL JSM-IT 200), and elemental composition along with the presence of gold and silver in the nanocomposite was confirmed with EDS coupled with the SEM system. Together, these analytical techniques provided comprehensive insight into the physicochemical properties, structural integrity, and the successful synthesis of the Au–Ag–MLSPI-NC.  2.5 MTT assay of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC against neuroblastoma cell SH-SY5Y The cytotoxicity of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC against human SH-SY5Y cells was assessed using the MTT assay. Briefly, SH-SY5Y cells were propagated in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and then seeded into 96-well plates at a density maintained with 1.0 × 105  cells/mL (100 μL per well). After incubation for 24 h at 37 ± 1 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂ to allow cellular attachment, SH-SY5Y cells were treated with different concentration of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC (6.25, 12.5, 25, 50 and 100 μg/mL) and further re-incubated for 24 h. This was followed by the addition of 20 μL of MTT solution (2 mg/mL) to each well containing MEM without phenol red. The plates were then incubated for 2 h to allow the formation of formazan crystals [22] . The resulting crystals were then dissolved (using an appropriate solvent such as DMSO), a microplate reader was used to measure absorbance at 540 nm. Cell survival was expressed as a percentage compared to untreated control cells that were not treated.  2.6 Apoptosis assay of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC against SH-SY5Y cell lines SH-SY5Y cells were cultured according to previously established standard protocols [23] . The LD₅₀ concentration of Au–Ag–MLSPI-NC (108.733 μg/mL) was used to treat SH-SY5Y cells, which were then further incubated for the next 24 h at 37 ± 1 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂. The control group comprised untreated cells maintained under identical conditions. Following treatment, the cells were transferred to 12 × 75 mm polystyrene tubes. For fixation, a minimum of 1 × 104  cells was employed for each sample. After centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 5 min, the supernatant was gently removed while ensuring the integrity of the cell pellet, which was visible at the tube's bottom. Subsequently, 100 μL of Muse™ Annexin V and Dead Cell Reagent were added to each well. After gently mixing the samples using a medium-speed vortex for three to five seconds, the sample were incubated at ambient temperature in dark condition for 20 min. Following incubation, the cells were analyzed using a flow cytometer, and data were collected using Muse flow cytometry software. Muse FCS 3.0 software was used to quantify apoptosis after gating the cells relative to untreated controls.  2.7 Western blotting analysis of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC SH-SY5Y cells was cultured under standard conditions and maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 ± 1 °C with 5% CO₂. Upon reaching the desired confluence, cells were treated with the LD₅₀ concentrations of the test compounds, Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC (108.733 μg/mL) and Cisplatin (9.775 μg/mL), for continuous 24 h. Untreated cells maintained under identical conditions functioned as the negative control. Following treatment, cells were thoroughly washed twice with TBS and gently scraped utilizing a pre-chilled cell scraper. The harvested cells were transferred into pre-cooled microcentrifuge tubes followed by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting pellets were resuspended in ice-cold TOTEX buffer (1 mL per 4 × 106  cells; containing 350 mM NaCl, 20 mM HEPES, 1% Nonidet P-40, 20% glycerol, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 mM MgCl₂, and 0.1% PMSF) and incubated with constant stirring for 30 min at 4 °C. The samples were sonicated three times for 10–15 s each to ensure complete cell lysis and reduce viscosity. Following centrifugation at a constant speed 16,000g  for 20 min at 4 ± 0.5 °C, the supernatant containing soluble proteins was gently collected and maintained on ice. Protein concentrations were estimated using a standard protein assay, and aliquots were stored at −20 °C until further use. For electrophoresis, 20 μg of total protein from each sample was combined with an equal volume of 2× Laemmli sample buffer, heated at 95 °C for 5 min, and briefly centrifuged before gel loading. Protein samples were fractionated using SDS–PAGE using 10% resolving gels and 5% stacking gels prepared using SureCast™ reagents, according to the manufacturer's guidelines. Electrophoresis was conducted in a running buffer (25 mM Tris, 192 mM glycine, 0.1% SDS, pH 8.3) at an initial voltage of 70 V until dye front penetrated resolving gel, thereafter continuing until the dye front migrated to approximately 5 cm above the bottom of the gel (around 1–1.5 h). Following separation, the gels were carefully extracted and quickly washed with distilled water. Proteins were then transferred to nitrocellulose membranes using a Mini Blot Module (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) at 10 V for 60 min, in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Following transfer, membranes were washed with TBST (TBS supplemented with 0.1% Tween-20) and incubated with 5% BSA in TBST for 1 h at ambient temperature. The membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the designated primary antibodies, then washed there to five times with TBST. Thereafter, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at ambient temperature and washed similarly with TBST. Protein bands were detected using the Promega ECL Western Blotting Substrate in accordance with the manufacturer's guidelines. Chemiluminescent signals were acquired using a ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad, USA), and densitometric analysis was performed using appropriate image analysis software.  2.8 Acute dermal toxicity (ADT) of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC The acute dermal toxicity and skin irritation potential of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC were assessed in accordance with OECD 404 guidelines, using Wistar rats weighing 250–300 g [18] . The animals were acclimated under conventional laboratory settings before the experiment. For the study, a specific area of dorsal skin was shaved and cleaned 24 h before application. A measured amount of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC was administered topically to the exposed skin and secured with a semi-occlusive bandage for 24 h. After removal of the dressing, the application site was gently cleaned, and the animals were observed at regular intervals for signs of erythema, edema, or any other dermal reactions for up to 14 days. The severity of skin irritation was scored according to the OECD 404 grading scale, and the results were used to assess the dermal safety profile of the Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC.  2.9 Wound healing activity of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC The wound healing potential of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC was evaluated using a diabetic excision animal wound model in rats. Diabetes was induced in overnight-fasted rats by intraperitoneal administration of alloxan monohydrate at a dose of 100 mg/kg body weight [18] . Following confirmation of hyperglycemia, the selected rats were anesthetized with a mixture of xylazine and ketamine. The dorsal fur was shaved, and the exposed skin was disinfected with 70% alcohol. A full-thickness circular excision wound was then created under aseptic conditions. The selected rat animals were randomly picked and distributed in four groups, each consisting of six rats, and the study was carried out for 21 days. Group I served as the diabetic control, Group II (standard) received topical application with the formulation Soframycin cream, Group III was treated with 3% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC, and Group IV received 5% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC. The respective treatments were applied topically once daily to the wound area, and wound healing was assessed by measuring wound contraction at predetermined time intervals (0, 7, 14, and 21 days). The wound area was traced onto transparent sheets and calculated, finally, the percentage of wound contraction was calculated relative to the initial wound size (Eq. (1)  ). By the conclusion of the research period, the tensile strength of the healed skin was evaluated utilizing a continuous water-flow method, which measures the force required to break the wound tissue, thereby indicating the quality and strength of the repaired tissue.(1) % of wound contraction = Initial wound size − Specific  day  wound size   Initial wound size   ∗ 100    At the end of the 21-day treatment period, a histopathological evaluation of wound tissues was performed to assess the quality of tissue regeneration. The animals were sacrificed, and skin samples from the wound area, including a margin of the surrounding normal tissue, were carefully excised. The obtained tissues were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin, dehydrated through a graded alcohol series, cleared in xylene, and embedded in paraffin. Thereafter, thin sections were prepared using a microtome (approximately 5 μm thick), which were then stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Key histological criteria, including collagen deposition, re-epithelialization, fibroblast proliferation, neovascularization, and inflammatory cell infiltration, were assessed by examining stained tissue under light microscope. The findings were compared among the different treatment groups to determine the extent and quality of wound healing induced by the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC. In between, on the 7th day after the final dose administration of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC, biochemical parameters, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and Interleukin-6 (IL-6) were evaluated using standard diagnostic kits [18] .  2.10 Statistical analysis GraphPad Prism was used for statistical analysis. In vivo  tests included six animals per group (n  = 6), with six independent readings recorded for each parameter. All in vitro  procedures, including apoptosis and western blotting analysis, were performed in triplicate (n  = 3). The proportion of wound contraction was calculated by using ImageJ for wound area analysis. Using appropriate image-analysis software, densitometric analysis of protein expression levels was carried out for western blotting and normalized to internal controls. Muse FCS 3.0 software was used to analyze flow-cytometric apoptosis data. The mean ± standard deviation (SD) was used to represent all data. Tukey's post-hoc multiple comparison test was used after one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to assess statistical significance across groups. A p -value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC characterization 3.1.1 UV–visible spectral analysis of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC UV–visible spectroscopic analysis was performed to characterize MLSPI and Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC formulation. The spectrum of MLSPI showed a characteristic absorption peak at 266 nm, indicating the presence of its intrinsic chromophoric functional groups (Fig. 1 a ) [24] . In contrast, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC formulation exhibited a slight red shift, with an absorption peak at 275 nm (Fig. 1 a). In addition to the UV absorption band, broad and low-intensity absorption features were observed at the regions of 405–455 nm and 520–560 nm. These bands corresponded to the characteristic SPR of Ag and Au NPs, respectively. The Ag-related SPR band appears as a broad feature centered at ∼430 nm (Fig. 1 a), while the Au-related SPR band is seen as a weak and broadened absorption around ∼535 nm [25,26] . The broadness and reduced intensity of these SPR bands may be due to the formation of Au Ag nanocomposite system, particle size distribution, possible electronic interactions between the two metallic components and phytochemical capping. The Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showed a slight red shift, this shift in the absorption maximum and SPR bands may suggests the successful formation of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC and possible interactions between MLSPI and the Au Ag NPs. The observed change in wavelength may be attributed to surface plasmon resonance effects and electronic interactions, confirming the conjugation and stabilization of MLSPI within the Au Ag nanostructure.  3.1.2 FTIR spectra of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC The FTIR spectrum of MLSPI stem extract reported by Patil et al. (2025) [18] , showed a broad band at 3336 cm−1  corresponding to O Hstretch  of phenolic/alcoholic groups, band at 2857 and 2924 cm−1  due to aliphatic C Hstretch , and prominent peak at 1612 cm−1  indicating C Ostretch  (Fig. 1 b). Additional bands at 1030 cm−1  and 1213 cm−1  were attributed to cyclic C Ostretch  and C Hbend , respectively, confirming the presence of ester or ether functional groups [18] . In contrast, the FTIR spectrum of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC revealed distinct absorption bands corresponding to key functional groups derived from MLSPI plant extract. A broad peak at 3353.52 cm−1  was noted for O Hstretch  vibrations, confirming the presence of O H groups from phenolic or alcoholic constituents (Fig. 1 b). A comparison of the FTIR spectra of MLSPI stem extract reported by Patil et al. (2025) with that of the synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC revealed noticeable shifts in the frequencies of key functional groups. These findings are consistent with previous reports [27] , confirming the role of plant-derived biomolecules in nanoparticle synthesis.  3.1.3 DLS particle size analysis and PDI determination of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC DLS analysis of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC revealed a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 177.4 ± 38.7 nm, indicating a moderately broad particle size distribution. Typically, nanoparticles smaller than 200 nm are generally considered appropriate for therapeutic applications owing to increased permeability and retention (EPR) effects and improved cellular absorption [28] . The high negative zeta potential value indicates strong electrostatic repulsion among the nanoparticles, which contributes to excellent colloidal stability by preventing aggregation [30] . Typically, zeta potential values greater than −30 mV are considered indicative of highly stable nanoparticle systems [30] . The negative surface charge observed in present the study can be attributed to the adsorption of negatively charged biomolecules, such as phenolic and carboxylate groups, from the MLSPI plant extract onto the nanoparticle surface, which may act as stabilizing and capping agents. Furthermore, the measured electrophoretic mobility value may support the observed zeta potential and may confirms the uniform movement of charged particles under an applied electric field. These findings suggest that the synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC possesses good physicochemical stability, making it suitable for biomedical and drug delivery applications.  3.1.5 XRD analysis of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC Fig. 2 a  exhibited prominent diffraction peaks at 27.51°, 32.11°, and 46.55°, along with characteristic reflections at 38.99°, 67.61°, 76.81°, and 85.83°. The diffraction peaks at 38.99°, 67.61°, 76.81°, and 85.83° were indexed to the (111), (220), (311), and (222) crystallographic planes of the face-centered cubic (fcc) structure of Au Ag nanoparticles, consistent with JCPDS card numbers 04-0783 (Ag) and 04–0784 (Au). The overlapping nature of these reflections indicates the formation of a bimetallic Au Ag nanocomposite, while slight shifts in peak positions relative to standard values may be attributed to lattice strain, nanoscale effects, and alloying interactions between Au and Ag atoms. The average crystallite size calculated using the Debye–Scherrer equation was approximately 10–11 nm, confirming the formation of highly crystalline nanoparticles within the nanometer range.  3.1.6 Surface morphology analysis using SEM and EDS of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC SEM analysis showed that the synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC exhibited predominantly spherical morphologies along with some irregular shaped structure. It was selected as a clinically established platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent and a widely used positive control for neuroblastoma studies. The result demonstrated concentration-dependent increase in cell inhibition for both treatments. Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showed significant cytotoxic effects, with cell viability decreasing from 94.32 ± 1.6585% at 6.25 μg/mL to 56.75 ± 0.2745% at 100 μg/mL comparing with Cisplatin as standard drug (Fig. 4 a ). The standard drug exhibited cytotoxicity with cell viability decreasing from 58.47 ± 0.6978% at 6.25 μg/mL to 11.42 ± 1.0930% at 100 μg/mL, with an IC₅₀ value of 9.775 μg/mL. Statistical analysis revealed extremely significant differences (****p  < 0.0001, ***p  < 0.001) at all tested concentrations compared to the standard. The IC₅₀ value of Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC was found to be 108.733 μg/mL, suggesting comparable cytotoxic activity against SH-SY5Y cells. The Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC displayed a dose-dependent but comparatively milder inhibitory effect on neuroblastoma cell proliferation. Previous investigations have shown that Au and Ag nanoparticles induce cytotoxicity in neuronal cells such as SH-SY5Y via  mechanisms involving mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and disruption of cellular metabolism [32,33] . Although several studies have investigated the anticancer activity of Au Ag bimetallic nanoparticles against various cancer cell lines, direct studies involving SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells remain unavailable or extremely limited. However, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC exhibited an IC₅₀ value of 108.73 μg/mL against SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, indicating moderate cytotoxic activity. A previous study by Katifelis et al. demonstrated that Ag/Au bimetallic nanoparticles synthesized using tryptophan exhibited pronounced anticancer activity against HCT116, 4 T1, and HUH7 cancer cell lines, with approximately 50% growth inhibition observed at concentrations of about 20–30 μg/mL and cell viability decreasing to less than 10% at 50 μg/mL for certain cell lines [34] . The comparatively higher IC₅₀ value observed for Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC suggests lower cytotoxic potency under the present experimental conditions. The observed differences may be attributed to variations in cancer cell type, nanoparticle composition, particle size, synthesis strategy, surface chemistry, phytochemical capping, cellular uptake, and experimental conditions. Notably, integration of Au and Ag nanomaterials has been reported to amplify both therapeutic efficacy and cytotoxic effects, highlighting need for precise dosage optimization in biomedical uses [35] . In this context, the present findings emphasize neurotoxic possibilities attributed with the Ag Au complexes and reinforce necessity for comprehensive toxicity evaluation during their development for clinical or experimental purposes. The anticancer activity observed in the present study should be considered preliminary, although the synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC demonstrated measurable growth-inhibitory effects against SH-SY5Y cells. Further studies are required to enhance therapeutic efficacy through optimization of nanoparticle formulation, surface functionalization, targeted delivery strategies, and evaluation in advanced biological models. Additionally, the absence of MLSPI extract, AuNP, and AgNP control groups limits the ability to determine the individual contributions of each component and to conclusively establish any potential synergistic effects associated with the Au Ag nanocomposite system.  3.3 Apoptosis assay of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC Apoptosis analysis reveals a pronounced cytotoxic effect of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC treatment compared with the control and standard treatment. In untreated cells, the majority remained viable (65.83 ± 0.49%), whereas exposure to the Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC markedly reduced the viable cell population to 22.14 ± 0.61%, indicating a substantial loss of viability (Table 1  ). Correspondingly, the proportion of late apoptotic/dead cells increased from 3.30 ± 0.12% in the control to 54.98 ± 0.34% following treatment, contributing to a significant increase in the total apoptotic cells (33.05 ± 0.51% vs.  54.63 ± 0.68%). Interestingly, early apoptotic cells were minimal in both groups (0.72 ± 0.07% vs.  0.06 ± 0.01%), suggesting that the treated cells rapidly progressed to late apoptosis or secondary necrosis rather than accumulating in the early apoptotic phase. Additionally, the elevated debris fraction in the treated group (22.70 ± 0.62% compared with 0.99 ± 0.09% in control) further supports extensive cellular breakdown (Fig. 4 b–g). Moreover, the population profile demonstrates a significant shift of cells toward higher Annexin V expression, indicating increased apoptotic activity and reduced viability following treatment (Fig. 4  c, e  and g ). Figs. 4 b–4 g show representative images from three independent experiments. These findings indicate that Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC induces strong cytotoxicity primarily through late-stage apoptotic pathways. While the underlying mechanisms were not directly investigated in the present study, the observed effects may be associated with cellular stress responses commonly reported for bimetallic Au Ag nanomaterials. Further studies are required to elucidate the precise molecular mechanisms involved.  3.4 Western blotting analysis of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC Western blotting was performed to determine expression levels of p53 , MDM2, and β -actin chosen as loading control in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells treated with Cisplatin and Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC, relative to untreated control cells (Fig. 4 h). The results (Table 2  ) revealed that p53  expression increased markedly in cells treated with Cisplatin (relative ratio: 1.58) compared to the control (1.12), indicating activation of the p53 -mediated stress response. In contrast, treatment with Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC resulted in a lower p53  expression level (relative ratio: 0.69) compared with the control, suggesting lower induction of cellular stress. Similarly, MDM2 expression, which is a downstream negative regulator of p53 , showed an opposite trend. MDM2 expression decreased in Cisplatin-treated cells (relative ratio: 0.82) and was further downregulated in Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC-treated cells (relative ratio: 0.45) compared with the control (1.18), implying reduced p53 -MDM2 feedback activation in response to Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC treatment. The Western blot image Fig. 4 h confirmed these findings, with visibly enhanced p53  bands and diminished MDM2 expression in Cisplatin-treated cells, while Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC treatment resulted in lower intensities of both p53  and MDM2 bands compared to control. Overall, the Western blot results demonstrated. That Cisplatin treatment markedly upregulated p53  expression in SH-SY5Y cells, consistent with its well-established role as a DNA-damaging agent that activates the p53 -dependent apoptotic pathway. This was accompanied by a moderate reduction in MDM2 expression, reflecting the suppression of p53 's negative feedback loop under strong stress conditions. In contrast, cells treated with Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC may showed downregulated expression of both p53  and MDM2, indicating a comparatively lower induction of DNA damage or oxidative stress. The reduced p53 /β -actin ratio (0.69) and MDM2/β -actin ratio (0.45) suggest that Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC may help maintain cellular homeostasis without triggering significant apoptotic signaling. These results imply that Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC are comparable cytotoxic toward neuronal cells compared to Cisplatin. The concomitant downregulation of p53  and MDM2 may suggests modulation of the p53 –MDM2 feedback axis, potentially contributing to the nanoparticles' cytoprotective or stress-attenuating properties. These findings indicate that Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC exert a milder cellular response in SH-SY5Y cells compared to Cisplatin, highlighting their potential as a biocompatible nanotherapeutic candidate with reduced genotoxic potential. The present study demonstrates that the bimetallic Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC exerts measurable cytotoxic and apoptotic effects on SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells, although the extent and underlying mechanism of action differ markedly from those of the standard chemotherapeutic agent, Cisplatin. Notably, the variations observed between the MTT assay, apoptosis analysis, and Western blot results can be attributed to the distinct cellular endpoints and biochemical processes assessed by each method. MTT assay results revealed a concentration dependent especially reduction in cell viability following treatment with Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC; however, the cytotoxic effect was moderate compared to Cisplatin, as indicated by the higher IC₅₀ value. This apparent discrepancy is consistent with previous reports indicating that nanoparticle-induced cytotoxicity may be underestimated by metabolic assays, as mitochondrial activity can persist in cells undergoing apoptosis. Although AgNPs have been reported to induce oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in previous studies [36] , these parameters were not directly assessed in the present study. Therefore, MTT-based measurements may overestimate cell viability when compared with direct apoptosis assays. In contrast, apoptosis analysis in current proposed study demonstrated a substantial increase in late apoptotic and dead cell populations following nanocomposite treatment. The predominance of late apoptosis, coupled with minimal early apoptotic cells, may suggests a rapid progression of cells toward advanced apoptotic or secondary necrotic stages. Similar findings have been reported in SH-SY5Y cells exposed to AgNPs, where apoptosis is mediated through mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress pathways, leading to accelerated cell death progression [37] . Furthermore, nanoparticle-induced oxidative stress has been identified as a key driver of apoptosis via  disruption of intracellular redox balance and induction of peroxidation [32] . These observations may suggest that apoptosis induced by the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposite occurs via p53 -independent mechanisms. Supporting this, previous studies have shown that nanoparticles can induce intrinsic apoptotic pathways through mitochondrial dysfunction in a p53 -independent manner [38] , often associated with downstream events such as cytochrome C release and caspase activation. Additionally, AgNPs have been reported to modulate multiple signaling pathways, including suppression of survival signals and induction of ROS-mediated damage, leading to apoptosis without necessarily activating classical DNA damage responses [39] . The observed downregulation of both p53  and MDM2 in the present study further may supports the hypothesis that Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC induces a milder, non-genotoxic cellular stress response compared to Cisplatin. The substantial increase in cellular debris observed following treatment provides further evidence of extensive membrane damage and late-stage apoptosis or secondary necrosis. Nanoparticles are commonly known to interact directly with cellular membranes due to their high surface reactivity, resulting in structural disruption and loss of cellular integrity. This mode of action differs fundamentally from that of conventional chemotherapeutic agents, which primarily target nuclear DNA. Taken together, these findings highlight a fundamental difference in the mechanism of action between Cisplatin and Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC. While Cisplatin induces strong cytotoxicity through DNA damage and activation of p53 -dependent apoptosis, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposite may appear to exert its effects through oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and membrane disruption, leading to p53 -independent apoptotic pathways as per earlier described literature. Such mechanisms may offer advantages in reducing genotoxic side effects while still achieving effective tumor cell killing. At the end, the integration of metabolic, apoptotic, and molecular analyses indicates that Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC induces significant apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells primarily through non-genotoxic mechanisms. The observed discrepancies among assays underscore importance of employing multiple complementary approaches to accurately assess nanoparticle cytotoxicity. These final outcomes may support potential of bimetallic Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposites as an effective candidate for safer and targeted nanotherapeutic applications, particularly in neuronal systems where minimizing DNA damage is critical. The present study did not directly evaluate reactive oxygen species generation, mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane damage, or caspase activation. Consequently, although previous literature suggests that Au Ag nanomaterials may induce apoptosis through these mechanisms, the mechanistic insights provided here remain preliminary and require further experimental validation.  3.5 Acute dermal toxicity of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NPs The acute dermal toxicity of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC was evaluated, and no mortality or treatment-related adverse effects were observed during the study period. The treated animals showed no signs of skin irritation, including erythema or edema, at the site of application. Body weight, food intake, and general behavior remained normal and comparable to those of the control group. Additionally, no gross pathological abnormalities were detected in the major organs. These findings indicate that Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC exhibits no apparent dermal toxicity and possesses good biocompatibility following acute exposure. The results suggest that Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC is safe for topical application; however, further long-term toxicity studies are recommended to confirm its safety profile.  3.6 Wound healing activity of Au-Ag-MLSPI-NC The extent of wound healing was determined by estimating the percentage of wound contraction on days 1, 7, 14, and 21 (Table 3  ). In the diabetic control group, wound healing was markedly delayed, as evidenced by minimal contraction throughout the study period, reaching only 31.17 ± 1.94% by day 21. This delayed healing is characteristic of diabetic conditions, where hyperglycemia impairs normal tissue repair mechanisms. In contrast, the standard-treated group (Soframycin cream) showed a significantly higher rate of wound closure, achieving 81.10 ± 3.88% contraction at the end of the treatment period. Treatment with Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC resulted in a marked and dose-dependent improvement in wound healing. The 3% formulation demonstrated progressive contraction from 1.51 ± 0.13% (day 1) to 70.58 ± 3.70% (day 21). Similarly, the 5% formulation showed enhanced activity, with wound contraction increasing from 2.07 ± 0.42% (day 1) to 74.33 ± 4.12% (day 21). Both treatment groups showed highly statistically significant differences (p  < 0.0001) when compared with the control animal group at all time points. Notably, the enhanced wound contraction observed in the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated groups indicate a substantial improvement in delayed diabetic wound healing, particularly during the proliferative phase (days 7–14), where a sharp increase in contraction was observed. The tensile strength of healed skin, an important indicator of collagen maturation and tissue integrity, is presented in Table 4  . The control group showed lowest tensile strength (388 ± 12.01 g/cm2 ), indicating poor healing quality. In diabetic conditions, reduced tensile strength reflects impaired collagen synthesis and weak tissue remodeling. The standard-treated group exhibited the highest tensile strength (589 ± 14.85 g/cm2 ), confirming effective restoration of tissue integrity. Both nanoparticle-treated groups showed significant improvement compared with the control. The 3% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC group demonstrated a tensile strength of 490 ± 14.52 g/cm2 , while the 5% formulation further increased it to 520 ± 13.65 g/cm2 , indicating enhanced collagen deposition and improved tissue remodeling. The increase in tensile strength in the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated groups suggest improved collagen organization and cross-linking despite the diabetic condition, highlighting the ability of the formulation to partially restore the impaired healing process. Thus, Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC holds an effective therapeutic system for treatment of diabetic wounds. In vivo  estimation of TNF-α  levels in blood samples was performed using a standard calibration curve with concentrations ranging from 0 to 2000 pg/mL. Based on the standard curve, the TNF-α  concentration of the control sample was found to be 325.76 ± 3.78 pg/mL. In comparison, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC showed a higher TNF-α concentration of 501.54 ± 5.54 pg/mL on day 7, indicating activation of the inflammatory phase of wound healing. The increased TNF-α  level in the treated sample indicates a notable inflammatory response, suggesting that the formulation may influence cytokine production in vivo . These findings highlight the importance of TNF-α  as biomarker for evaluating inflammation and the biological effect of the developed Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC system. Moreover, the in vivo  estimation of IL-6 levels in blood samples was performed using a standard calibration curve with concentrations ranging from 0 to 8000 pg/mL. By considering the calibration, the IL-6 concentration of control was estimated to be 298.51 ± 4.09 pg/mL on 7th day of treatment. In comparison, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC exhibited a higher IL-6 concentration of 485.56 ± 5.45 pg/mL. The increased IL-6 level in the treated sample indicates an elevated inflammatory response, suggesting that the formulation may significantly influence cytokine production in vivo . These findings highlight the importance of IL-6 concentration as a key biomarker for evaluating inflammatory status and the biological activity of the developed Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC system. The elevated levels of pro-inflammatory markers IL-6 and TNF-α observed in Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC group indicate an active inflammatory phase, which is crucial for initiating the wound healing process. This early cytokine response helps in immune cell recruitment, debris clearance, and activation of repair mechanisms [40] . Thus, the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC formulation appears to support and enhance the initial stages of wound healing. The present study demonstrates that Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC significantly enhances wound healing in an animal model, as evidenced by increased wound contraction and improved tensile strength. Diabetic wounds are characterized by excessive production of ROS, diminished growth factor activity, and impaired fibroblast function, all of which contribute to chronic non-healing wounds [41] . The significant improvement observed in Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated groups suggests that the nanocomposite effectively counteracts these diabetes-associated impairments. The accelerated wound contraction observed in Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated groups may be attributed to enhanced fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, and re-epithelialization. AgNPs are well known for their broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, which prevents wound infection and reduces prolonged inflammation, thereby promoting faster healing [42] . Additionally, AgNPs have been reported to stimulate keratinocyte migration and angiogenesis, which are critical for wound closure [43] . This is particularly crucial in diabetic wounds, which are highly susceptible to microbial infections due to compromised immune responses. AuNPs, on the other hand, support wound healing by stimulating cell proliferation, promoting angiogenesis, and facilitating tissue regeneration. In diabetic conditions, where angiogenesis is severely impaired, AuNPs may help restore vascularization by stimulating endothelial cell growth and improving blood supply to the affected wound site. Recent studies have demonstrated that biopolymer-based AuNPs significantly improve in vitro  wound healing and cellular migration, supporting their role in tissue repair [44] . The combination of Au and Ag nanoparticles in the present formulation likely may enhances these biological effects, leading to improved healing outcomes. The dose-dependent increase in wound contraction, particularly in the 5% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC group, suggests that a higher nanocomposite concentration improves therapeutic efficacy, possibly through increased bioavailability at the wound site. Similar findings have been reported where nanoparticle-loaded hydrogels and topical formulations significantly accelerated wound closure compared to untreated controls [45] . The near-comparable performance of the 5% formulation to the standard treatment indicates its potential to overcome delayed wound closure typically observed in diabetic conditions. Tensile strength results further may validate the healing potential of the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC. Increased tensile strength indicates enhanced collagen maturation, cross-linking, and extracellular matrix remodeling. In diabetic wounds, collagen deposition is often disorganized and insufficient; however, the observed increase in tensile strength suggests that Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC improves collagen quality and structural integrity of the repaired tissue. Metallic nanoparticles have been shown to improve collagen deposition and tissue organization, leading to stronger and more resilient healed tissue [46] . Moreover, recent advancements in green-synthesized nanoparticle systems highlight their reduced toxicity and improved biocompatibility, making them suitable for biomedical uses. Studies have demonstrated that plant-mediated or biopolymer-assisted nanoparticle formulations significantly enhance wound healing while minimizing adverse effects [47] . Although the Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC formulation did not surpass the standard drug completely, it exhibited substantial wound healing activity, particularly at higher concentrations. These outcomes are especially significant in the context of diabetic wound management, where delayed healing remains a major clinical challenge. The observed effects may be due to combined anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and pro-regenerative properties of nanocomposite.  3.7 Histopathological study Histopathological investigation of wound tissue samples from different treatment groups was performed on day 21 to assess the extent of tissue regeneration, inflammatory response, collagen deposition, and re-epithelialization. In the control group (Group I), tissue sections revealed incomplete re-epithelialization, persistent inflammatory cell infiltration, and poorly organized collagen fibers. The dermal layer appeared disrupted with sparse fibroblast proliferation and minimal neovascularization, indicating delayed wound healing typically associated with diabetic conditions. The standard-treated group (Group II; Soframycin cream) showed well-formed epithelial layers with complete re-epithelialization, dense and well-organized collagen fibers, and marked fibroblast proliferation. Minimal inflammatory cell infiltration and prominent neovascularization were observed, indicating effective wound repair and tissue remodeling. In the 3% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated group (Group III), histological sections demonstrated moderate to complete re-epithelialization, with improved collagen deposition and better organization compared with the control. A reduction in inflammatory cells and increased fibroblast activity was noted (Fig. 5  ). Moderate neovascularization was evident, suggesting enhanced progression through proliferative phase of wound healing. 5% Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC-treated group (Group IV) exhibited near-complete re-epithelialization with a well-defined epidermal layer, along with densely packed and well-aligned collagen fibers. Significant fibroblast proliferation and enhanced angiogenesis were observed, accompanied by minimal inflammatory infiltration. The overall tissue architecture closely resembled that of the standard-treated group, indicating substantial improvement in diabetic wound healing. Histopathological findings correlate well with the wound contraction and tensile strength data. Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC treatment, particularly at 5%, markedly improved tissue regeneration, collagen maturation, and angiogenesis while reducing inflammation, thereby accelerating wound healing in diabetic conditions.   4 Conclusion The present study demonstrates that the green-synthesized Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC nanocomposite possesses stable physicochemical characteristics and significant multifunctional biological activity. The observed cytotoxic and apoptotic effects highlight its therapeutic potential. The nanocomposite induced moderate cytotoxicity in neuroblastoma cells, where apoptosis was predominantly associated with a p53 -independent pathway, may indicating activation of alternative cell death signaling cascades possibly involving ROS generation and intrinsic mitochondrial dysfunction rather than classical DNA damage response pathways; however, the precise molecular mechanisms responsible for these effects remain to be elucidated. In diabetic wound models, the nanocomposite significantly accelerated healing by modulating key biological processes, including suppression of excessive inflammatory signaling, enhancement of fibroblast proliferation, stimulation of angiogenesis, and promotion of extracellular matrix remodeling and collagen maturation. Collectively, these effects suggest regulation of the inflammatory–proliferative phase transition through restoration of redox balance and improvement of the cellular regenerative microenvironment. However, the present study is limited by lack of detailed mechanistic validation at the molecular signaling level, insufficient in vivo  toxicological profiling, and the absence of pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies. Moreover, the observed anticancer efficacy remains moderate compared to conventional chemotherapeutics, indicating the need for optimization of nanoparticle design and targeting efficiency. Future research should focus on elucidating ROS-mediated signaling pathways, mitochondrial apoptotic mechanisms, and angiogenic regulatory networks underlying the observed effects. Advanced in vivo  studies, surface functionalization strategies for targeted delivery, long-term safety evaluation, and translational optimization will be essential to establish Au–Ag–MLSPI–NC as a potential nanotheranostic platform for cancer therapy and diabetic wound management. Prof. Jadhav's energetic vision bridges green chemistry with modern drug delivery, reflecting his commitment to shaping the future of pharmaceutics and addressing global healthcare challenges with creativity and purpose. His research expertise lies in nanotechnology-driven drug delivery, medicinal chemistry, and novel therapeutic systems. He has made significant contributions to the development of nanocarriers, PLAROsomes, liposomes, and nanoemulsions aimed at improving stability, bioavailability, and therapeutic efficacy of drugs in cancer, inflammatory, and pulmonary diseases. Dr. Bhinge's work spans green synthesis of metal and bimetallic nanoparticles, phytochemical-based therapeutic formulations, and multifunctional nanomaterials with applications in anticancer therapy, rheumatoid arthritis management, and antimicrobial treatments. His research has also extended into biogenic nanotransferosomal vesicles, functional biopolymers, and drug delivery scaffolds, reflecting an interdisciplinary approach that bridges pharmaceutical chemistry with biomedical innovation. With numerous publications in reputed journals, active collaborations, and translational research projects, Dr. Bhinge continues to advance pharmaceutical sciences through innovative nanomedicine strategies and sustainable drug delivery approaches. His academic and research contributions reflect a strong commitment to developing next-generation therapeutic platforms to address pressing healthcare challenges. He has played a pivotal role in the development and expansion of Bharati Vidyapeeth as a premier institution of higher education and research. With extensive experience in pharmaceutical sciences and biomedical research, his scholarly contributions encompass drug delivery systems, natural product research, pharmaceutical technology, and pharmacological investigations. title: Hydroxytyrosol's effect on the expression of apoptosis and oxidative stress related genes in BE (2)-C neuroblastoma cell line
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is defined as a type of tumor that involves the autonomic nervous system. Oxidative stress (OxS) resulted from dopamine (DA) oxidation and the reduction of antioxidant enzyme activity is the main reason for the initiation and progression of NB. The aim of this study was the evaluation of the protective effects of Hydroxytyrosol (HT) against OxS induced by H2O2. In the present in vitro study, the OxS condition was induced by H2O2 treatment of BE (2)-C cells; then, the cells were treated by several concentrations of HT and Vitamin C (VC). Next, the expression levels of genes related to OxS and apoptosis were measured through the RT-qPCR method. Subsequently, the activity of catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) was determined via enzyme colorimetric assay. Finally, the level of malondialdehyde (MDA) was measured by the Thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) assay. HT treatment leads to a significantly decreased the expression level of Bax, caspase-3, and p53 (p < 0.05); as well, the expression levels of Nrf-2, SOD, Bcl-2, PPAR-γ, CAT, and GPx were increased at a significant manner (p < 0.05). Moreover, HT treatment led to a remarkable increase in the enzyme activity of CAT, SOD, and GPx (p < 0.001). Finally, the MDA levels were significantly reduced (p < 0.001) in BE (2)-C cells after HT treatment. The findings suggest that HT could have neuroprotective effects by enhancing various enzymatic and molecular pathways to increase the cellular antioxidant defense. Additionally, HT reduced the expression of the P53 gene and blocked the apoptotic signaling pathways by suppressing Bax and caspase-3. However, further animal models studies are needed to approve the beneficial effects of HT.

Department of Biochemistry Lorestan University of Medical Sciences Khorramabad Iran       Edited by Jormay Lim Neuroblastoma (NB) is defined as a type of tumor that involves the autonomic nervous system. Oxidative stress (OxS) resulted from dopamine (DA) oxidation and the reduction of antioxidant enzyme activity is the main reason for the initiation and progression of NB. The aim of this study was the evaluation of the protective effects of Hydroxytyrosol (HT) against OxS induced by H2 O2 . In the present in vitro study, the OxS condition was induced by H2 O2  treatment of BE (2)-C cells; then, the cells were treated by several concentrations of HT and Vitamin C (VC). Next, the expression levels of genes related to OxS and apoptosis were measured through the RT-qPCR method. Subsequently, the activity of catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) was determined via enzyme colorimetric assay. Finally, the level of malondialdehyde (MDA) was measured by the Thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) assay. HT treatment leads to a significantly decreased the expression level of Bax, caspase-3, and p53 (p  < 0.05); as well, the expression levels of Nrf-2, SOD, Bcl-2, PPAR-γ, CAT, and GPx were increased at a significant manner (p < 0.05). Moreover, HT treatment led to a remarkable increase in the enzyme activity of CAT, SOD, and GPx (p  < 0.001). Finally, the MDA levels were significantly reduced (p < 0.001) in BE (2)-C cells after HT treatment. The findings suggest that HT could have neuroprotective effects by enhancing various enzymatic and molecular pathways to increase the cellular antioxidant defense. Additionally, HT reduced the expression of the P53 gene and blocked the apoptotic signaling pathways by suppressing Bax and caspase-3. However, further animal models studies are needed to approve the beneficial effects of HT.
