In kids, the NB has a high prevalence after leukemia and brain cancer; actually, NB is responsible for 15–20 % of child mortality in all pediatric tumor mortalities (Shawraba et al., 2021 ). Almost all patients who suffer from NB have a high level of dopamine (DA); in the cytosol, the monoamine oxidase enzyme causes DA oxidation, however, it may be occurring by some nonenzymatic mechanisms (Magalingam et al., 2022 ). The oxidized DA could participate in reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2011 ). Previously, it has been shown that DA treated NB cells (SH-SY5Y) induces the expression of apoptosis-related genes including caspase-3 and p53 that finally leads to blockage of cell cycle (Ouazia et al., 2015 ; Mansour-Ghanaei et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, it seems that treating NB cells by an antioxidant agent and then treatment with DA could stop the activation of caspase-9. These findings suggest that apotosis induced in NB cells by pile-up DA is ROS-dependent, the neuronal degeneration is facilitated through oxidative stress (OxS) (Ouazia et al., 2015 ; Babaei et al., 2019 ). The findings of mechanisms of the neurodegenerative disorder are expanded by focusing on neurodegenerative disturbance pathogenesis, including excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases (Gay et al., 2018 ; Moghaddam Ahmadi et al., 2021 ). OxS plays an important role in the beginning and progress of these complications. There are two factors involved in inducing cellular OxS: First, ROS excessive formation and second decreased activity of cellular antioxidant enzymes (Balmus et al., 2016 ). In the OxS situation, the body cells must maintain a stable state of homeostasis through some enzymes, for instance, superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT). Actually, these enzymes have a key function in converting ROS to H2 O and O2  that are more stable and harmless products (Rahal et al., 2014 ; Hassanipour et al., 2020 ). It has been well documented that neuronal over formation of ROS is the most important reason for the initiation and progression of neurodegenerative disease (Luca et al., 2015 ). Nowadays, various compounds are used to reduce cellular OxS. A series of them are polyphenols; these compounds are plant metabolites that have numerous hydroxyl groups on one or more aromatic rings by different bioactivities including neuroprotective effects. Therefore, it is essential to study the antioxidant effects of polyphenols in neuronal protection. Oliva oil, which is rich in phenolic compounds, has several beneficial effects on OxS status, it seems that these effects are related to phenolic compounds. Hydroxytyrosol (HT) with IUPAC name 4-(2-Hydroxyethyl)-1,2-benzenediol and chemical formula C8 H10 O3 , is known as an important phenolic compound that has high antioxidant activity (Bertelli et al., 2020 ). The leaves and oil of the olive are rich in HT, it has well environmental stability and high tissue absorption (Wang et al., 2019 ). The HT has a wide range of positive features including anti-inflammatory, anti-atherogenic, and anti-thrombotic effects. In vitro investigations have been shown that in addition to the antioxidant functions, HT has beneficial effects against endothelial dysfunction and lipid profiles disorders (El-Azem et al., 2019 ). Consequently, it could be very effective in the neuronal disturbance. Moreover, HT could have anti-tumor effects, because it can interact with several factors that are involved in regulating the cell cycle and apoptosis pathways (Elmaksoud et al., 2021 ; Aghajanzadeh et al., 2021 ). In the current study, we evaluated the HT effects on improving cellular oxidation status in BE (2)-C cells. In beginning, we induced the OxS situation by H2 O2  treatment; then, the cells were treated with HT and Vitamin C (VC); the VC treated cells were considered as the positive control. Next, a panel of genes' expression that is related to cellular apoptosis and oxidation status was evaluated. In continue, the activity of antioxidant enzymes was measured. Lastly, the level of malondialdehyde (MDA) as a lipid peroxidation index was determined.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials BE (2)-C cell line obtained from Pasteur Institute (Iran Biological Resource Center, Pasteur Institute, Tehran, Iran). HT (H4229), Thiazolyl Blue Tetrazolium Blue (MTT) (M2128) powder, and phosphate buffer saline (PBS) (SLBJ2117V) tablets were achieved from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Acid ascorbic (CAS 50-81-7), Hydrogen peroxide 30 % (H2 O2 ) (107209), and dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) (K44917952) were obtained from Merck (Merck, Germany). Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) (1791923) high glucose media, Trypsin/EDTA 0.25 % (1726653), and Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) (42Q7363K) were obtained from Gibco (Maryland, USA).  2.2 Cell culture The neuroblastoma cell line (BE (2)-C) cultured in DMEM high glucose medium supplemented with 10 % FBS with Trypsin/EDTA 0.25 % antibiotics and were incubated at standard conditions i.e. temperature 37 °C, humidity 95 %, and 5 % CO2 .  2.3 Assessment of cell viability by MTT assay In order to evaluate the cell toxicity of HT, MTT assay was done; in brief, the BE (2)-C cells (104  cells/well) were seeded in a 96-well plate in triplicate. Then, they were incubated with several concentrations (0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 μM) of HT for 24, 48, and 72 h; the old media was removed, and then, the fresh media containing 2 mg/ml MTT (3-(4,5-Dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2, 5-Diphenyltetrazolium Bromide) solution were added and incubated for an additional 4 h at 37 °C. Subsequently, the media were removed and 200 μl DMSO plus 25 μl Sorenson glycine buffer were added. Next, the 96-wells plate was gently shaken (15 min), and lastly, optical density (OD) in each well was assessed at 570 nm by a 96 well-plates reader (Labsystems, Finland) (Hemmati-Dinarvand et al., 2022 ). The suitable concentrations of H2 O2  (400 μM) and VC (50 μM) were selected based on previous literature (Aquilano et al., 2009 ).  2.4 Total RNA extraction and Real-time RT-PCR The total RNA was extracted by the TRIzol method, according to the manufacturer's datasheet (Hemmati-Dinarvand et al., 2022 ). Then, the concentration of total extracted RNA was measured via the NanoDrop Spectrophotometer and its quality was assessed by using gel electrophoresis. The complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized via the Takara cDNA synthesis kit (Takara, Japan) in which extracted RNA was converted into cDNA; accordingly, we normalized the concentration of all RNA extracted samples at 500 ng/μl; then, synthesis of cDNA was done with 2 μl (1000 ng/μl) of extracted RNA samples. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) was implemented using SYBR green (Prime Script RT Master Mix, Takara) by using 1 μl of each cDNA samples in the 15 μl final volume and MIC PCR (BioMolecular System, Australia). All reactions have been done in triplicate. The sequence of primers used is shown in Table 1  . The analysis of raw data was performed by the 2-∆∆Ct  method, and the GAPDH gene was considered an internal control (Hemmati-Dinarvand et al., 2022 ).  2.5 Measurement of cellular antioxidant enzymes activity To determine the activity of antioxidant enzymes including SOD, CAT, and GPx, we applied the Colorimetric Assay Kits (KIAZIST Life Sciences, Tehran, Iran). The treatment groups were organized as follows: untreated cells (control); treated cells with H2 O2  (400 μM) (2 h incubated), HT (25 μM) (24 h incubated) + H2 O2  (400 μM) (2 h incubated), HT (50 μM) (24 h incubated) + H2 O2  (400 μM) (2 h incubated), HT (100 μM) (24 h incubated) + H2 O2  (400 μM) (2 h incubated), and VC (50 μM) (24 h incubated) + H2 O2  (400 μM) (2 h incubated). In brief, 5 × 106  cells were seeded for each T75 flask; the seeded cells were incubated in the incubator situation as mentioned above to reach 80–90 % confluency. Then, we prepared the specimens; the cells were trypsinized and centrifuged, the supernatant was removed, and the lysis buffer was added. Afterward, the cells were incubated at 4 °C for 20 min. Then, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min. The supernatants were stored at −80 °C until use. Finally, the measurement of antioxidant enzymes activities, SOD (unit/mg protein), GPx (unit/mg protein)and Catalase (unit/mg protein), were determined according to instruction of the manufacturer of commercial kits (Kiazist, Iran).  2.6 Evaluation of cellular oxidation status Lipid peroxidation as an index of cellular oxidation status, was assessed via the MDA assay. The levels of MDA were determined in each treatment group according to the method described previously (Mohammadi et al., 2021 ). Actually, the MDA was measured by the thiobarbituric acid-reactive substances (TBARs) manner. Briefly, 100 ml of prepared specimens were added to 0.9 ml of deionized water in a sterile falcon. Then, 0.5 ml of thiobarbituric acid reagent (0.67 g of 2-thiobarbituric acid dissolved in 100 ml of distilled water with the addition of 0.5 g of NaOH and 100 ml of glacial acetic acid) was added to each sample. Subsequently, the obtained mixture was heated for 60 min in a boiling water bath. After reaching Lab temperature, each sample was centrifuged at 5000 ×g  for 15 min. Lastly, the OD of samples was determined via a 96-well Plates Reader (Labsystems, Finland) at 534 nm. MDA levels were assessed by the molar absorption coefficient of MDA (1.56 × 105  M).  2.7 Statistical analysis The statistical analysis of the obtained data was performed by an unpaired t -test or one-way ANOVA by Rest (v 7.00) software. Data obtained from three or more independent experiments were expressed as mean ± SD. A p  < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.   3 Results 3.1 HT cytotoxicity To assess the safe dose and time of HT, the BE (2)-C cells were treated with different dosages of HT for 24, 48, and 72 h. Accordingly, the IC50  values for HT treatment, 24 h' time and concentrations of 25 μM, 50 μM, and 100 μM were selected for treatment of cells (Fig. 1  ).  3.2 HT significantly decreased apoptosis-related genes and increased antioxidant-related genes expression The p53, Bax, caspase-3, PPAR-γ, Nrf-2, Bcl-2, SOD, CAT, and GPx gene expressions in BE (2)-C cells were assessed. The assessed genes were under treatment with HT (25, 50, and 100 μM), and VC (50 μM) for 24 h followed by H2 O2  (400 μM)-induced oxidative stress situation for 2 h. The results of treated groups were compared to non-treated (control) group. The results showed that the gene expression levels of Bax (p  = 0.014) and caspase-3 (p  = 0.027) were significantly decreased in each 25, 50, and 100 μM treated by HT. Additionally, a significant elevation of Bax and caspase-3 genes expression in H2 O2 -treated group in compare to control group was observed. (Fig. 2 A and B ); moreover, the expression levels of p53 gene were markedly decreased at 25 and 50 μM of HT, but it was remarkably increased at 100 μM dosage of HT, as well, the Nrf-2 and SOD were markedly decreased during treatment by H2 O2  in compare to control group (Fig. 3 A ). On the other hand, the expression levels of Nrf-2 and SOD were significantly increased at all three concentrations of HT (Fig. 3  B and C); nevertheless, the followed gene expressions were markedly increased: The Bcl-2 at 50 μM, PPAR-γ at 100 μM, CAT at 25 and 100 μM, as well, GPx at 50 and 100 and CAT at 25 and 100 μM dosage of HT; however, the expression levels of CAT and GPx were significantly decreased after treatment with H2 O2  in compare to control group (Fig. 4 A-D ).  3.3 Cellular antioxidant status improvement by HT treatment To evaluate cellular antioxidant status, the activity of CAT, GPx, and SOD enzymes were assessed. The findings showed that treatment of BE (2)-C cells with H2 O2  leads to a decrease in enzyme activity compared to the control (non-treated) group, significantly (p  = 0.004). Additionally, HT-treated cells (25, 50, and 100 μM) increased the activity of GPx and SOD, markedly (p  < 0.001); as well, the activity of CAT was significantly increased at HT-concentrations of 25 and 50 μM in compare to untreated cells. Moreover, the findings obtained from Vitamin C (VC)-treated cells showed that VC leads to increased activity of enzymes in which GPx and SOD activity were statically significant compared with the control group (p  < 0.001) (Fig. 5 A-C ).  3.4 Measurement of the MDA levels In order to the evaluate the cellular oxidation situation, the levels of MDA after treating the BE (2)-C cells H2 O2  (400 μM), VC (50 μM), and HT (25, 50, and 100 μM) were measured and then, the obtained results were compared to non-treated group. The level of MDA in H2 O2  treated cells was increased in compared to the control group, significantly (p < 0.001). The results indicated that HT at all three concentrations and VC treated led to decreased levels of MDA, but these changes were not significant statistically (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 6  ).   4 Discussion OxS has an important role in the initiation and progression of neurodegenerative complications. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) degrade biological molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, eventually, it leading to cell death through apoptosis or necrosis. Therefore, the removal of excess ROS or inhibition of ROS formation can be effective in preventing oxidative cell death (Singh et al., 2019 ). In the current study, the HT effects on the expression of apoptosis and OxS related genes in BE (2)-C Neuroblastoma cells were assessed. HT led to upregulation of p53, BCL-2, and downregulation of Bax and caspase-3.It has been also reported that HT has the anti-apoptotic effects on epithelial and tumor cells (Meek, 2009 ). P53 is known as an important factor to regulate the Bcl-2 gene family that have a key role in trigger of apoptosis (Sjöström-Mattson et al., 2009 ). We observed that upregulation of p53 was in accordance to decreased in pro-apoptotic genes (Bax and caspase-3) and increased anti-apoptotic genes i.e. Bcl-2. Mohan V et al., observed that elevation of the p53 gene leads to overexpression of caspase-3 and triggers of apoptosis in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells (Mohan et al., 2016 ). In line with our results, Polager S et al., reported that OxS induction by free radicals could lead to upregulation of the P53 gene and activation of this protein (Polager and Ginsberg, 2009 ). Furthermore, Kalaiselvan and Dewapriya in the separate studies showed that HT protects cells against oxidative agents by reducing intracellular oxidants, reducing Bax expression, and increasing Bcl-2 expression (Kalaiselvan et al., 2016 ; Dewapriya et al., 2013 ). Kitsati et al., have shown that H2 O2  by increasing cellular Fe2+  leads to the activation of MAPK signaling, p38, and caspase-3 proteins, and finally apoptosis occurs. However, HT via a covering of Fe2+  could insert protective effects against H2 O2  damages (Kitsati et al., 2016 ). On the other hand, the findings showed that treatment of cells with HT leads to a significant increase in the expression of anti-oxidant-related genes including Nrf-2, PPAR-γ, CAT, SOD, and GPx. Due to the fact that increasing the activity of an enzyme is directly related to increasing its gene expression, the obtained results showed that the activity of CAT, GPx, and SOD undertreatment with HT and VC were enhanced, considerably; H2 O2  treated cells led to a significant decrease in the activity of CAT, GPx, and SOD. Furthermore, the level of MDA as an oxidation status index during treatment with HT and VC was decreased but not significantly. However, H2 O2  treatment leads to a remarkable increase in MDA. The Nrf-2 signaling is a major regulator pathway against OxS that has a key role to modulate the expression of numerous antioxidant genes. Thus, it plays an important role in regulating cellular redox mode. Under normal homeostatic conditions, the Nrf-2 transcription factor in the cytoplasm is inhibited by Keap1. Upon exposure to ROS, the Nrf-2 factor is cleaved from the Keap1 inhibitor and transported into the nucleus, where it binds to the ARE in the promoter region of its encoding genes. Induces the production of antioxidant enzymes such as CAT, SOD, and GPx and phase II enzymes such as HO-1, NQO-1, and GCL, which play an important role in the fight against ROS (Kim et al., 2018 ). Formerly, the dynamic changes in the Nrf-2 signaling pathway have been reported in neurodegenerative diseases. Also, it has been observed that HT, as a direct antioxidant, induces the production of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes in several cell lines including endothelial and HepG-2 cell lines (Bao et al., 2017 ). Based on the inverse relationship between cellular oxidant-antioxidant content, it seems logical to infer that MDA levels decrease with increasing cell antioxidant content. Funakohi et al. reported that HT via the Nrf-2/HO-1 pathway has protective effects against OHDA-6-induced oxidative stress in the SH-SYS5 cell line. Actually, HT activates its transcriptional activity by increasing Nrf-2 expression in a dose-dependent manner that leads to increased expression of HO-1 and inhibits the production of ROS in the SH-SYS5 cell line (Funakohi-Tago et al., 2018 ). Zhu et al. studied human retinal pigment epithelial cells (ARPE-19) under acrolein-induced oxidative stress, they found that HT could increase the transport of Nrf-2 to the nucleus that leading to increased expression of downstream genes including HO-1, NQO-1, GCL, CAT, SOD, and GPx (Zhu et al., 2010 ). PPARγ was initially recognized as a key regulator of transcription in adipogenesis but has been shown that play greater roles in other biologically related processes, such as infection and inflammation. PPARγ activation reduces the inflammatory response and improves cognitive impairment associated with many neurodegenerative disorders (Zolezzi et al., 2013 ). Additionally, it has a negative regulator of oxidative stress and suppresses several pro-inflammatory factors, such as NF-κB, STAT-6, AP-1, COX-2, and iNOS. Also, PPARγ promotes the expression of several antioxidant genes such as HO-1, CAT, GPX, and SOD. It has been suggested that there is a cross-regulation between the Nrf-2 and PPARγ to enhance each other expression. Moreover, it seems that these two pathways are linked by a positive feedback loop that maintains the simultaneous expression of transcription factors and antioxidant genes (Collino et al., 2006 ).  5 Conclusion The results of the current study showed that HT could protect the neuroblastoma cells against OxS by enhancing various enzymatic and molecular pathways including increasing the expression of Nrf-2 and PPARγ genes to enhance the cellular antioxidant defense. It has the potential to increase antioxidant capacity in H2 O2 -induced stressed cells. Additionally, HT could reduce the expression of the P53 gene and block the apoptotic signaling pathways by suppressing Bax and caspase-3.  Ethics approval and consent to participate Not applicable. title: STK33 as the functional substrate of miR-454-3p for suppression and apoptosis in neuroblastoma
abstract: miR-454-3p has been reported to be a tumor-suppressive microRNA (miRNA) in multiple cancer types. We identified the kinase STK33 mRNA, which is a high-risk factor for survival in neuroblastoma (NB) patients, as being a substrate of miR-454-3p in NB. Even though STK33 is an attractive target for several cancers, the development of inhibitors of STK33 has been challenging. For the various cell lines tested, we demonstrated reduced growth and viability with the miR-454-3p mimic. From among the candidate NB-associated miRNAs, miR-454-3p mimic and its antagonist had the most profound effect on STK33 mRNA and protein-level changes. Under various conditions of growth and external stress for the cells, the RNA levels for miR-454-3p and STK33 also negatively correlated. Luciferase reporter assays demonstrated STK33 as a substrate for miR-454-3p, and recombinant versions of STK33 resistant to miR-454-3p significantly blunted the suppressive effect of the miR-454-3p and established STK33 as the major functional substrate of miR-454-3p. Overexpression of miR-454-3p or knockdown of STK33 mRNA promoted autophagy and at the same time, increased the apoptotic markers in the tested NB cells, indicating a mechanism for the suppressive effect of the agents. Given the difficult-to-drug targets such as STK33 and the recent successes in RNA delivery methods for cancer treatment, it is thought that targeting cancer cells with a suppressive miRNA such as miR-454-3p for STK33-dependent cancer types may be an alternative means of NB therapy.

Research Article  STK33 as the functional substrate of miR-454-3p for suppression and apoptosis in neuroblastoma Dongkwan Yoo  Sichen Wu  Seunghyuk Choi  Sung-Oh Huh ⁎   Ali Sadra ⁎   Department of Pharmacology, College of Medicine, Institute of Natural Medicine, Hallym University, Chuncheon, Gangwon State, Republic of Korea Department of Pharmacology, College of Medicine, Institute of Natural Medicine, Hallym University Chuncheon Gangwon State Republic of Korea  Department of Pharmacology, College of Medicine, Institute of Natural Medicine, Hallym University, Chuncheon, Gangwon State, Republic of Korea  ⁎ Correspondence:      miR-454-3p has been reported to be a tumor-suppressive microRNA (miRNA) in multiple cancer types. We identified the kinase STK33 mRNA, which is a high-risk factor for survival in neuroblastoma (NB) patients, as being a substrate of miR-454-3p in NB. Even though STK33 is an attractive target for several cancers, the development of inhibitors of STK33 has been challenging. For the various cell lines tested, we demonstrated reduced growth and viability with the miR-454-3p mimic. From among the candidate NB-associated miRNAs, miR-454-3p mimic and its antagonist had the most profound effect on STK33 mRNA and protein-level changes. Under various conditions of growth and external stress for the cells, the RNA levels for miR-454-3p and STK33 also negatively correlated. Luciferase reporter assays demonstrated STK33 as a substrate for miR-454-3p, and recombinant versions of STK33 resistant to miR-454-3p significantly blunted the suppressive effect of the miR-454-3p and established STK33 as the major functional substrate of miR-454-3p. Overexpression of miR-454-3p or knockdown of STK33 mRNA promoted autophagy and at the same time, increased the apoptotic markers in the tested NB cells, indicating a mechanism for the suppressive effect of the agents. Given the difficult-to-drug targets such as STK33 and the recent successes in RNA delivery methods for cancer treatment, it is thought that targeting cancer cells with a suppressive miRNA such as miR-454-3p for STK33-dependent cancer types may be an alternative means of NB therapy. INTRODUCTION Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric cancer that originates from the sympathetic arm of the nervous system. The cancer cells are neuroblasts from lymph nodes, bone marrow, and other organs, but specifically form outside of the cranium. NB also represents 15% of death from pediatric cancers (Lundberg et al., 2022; Monclair et al., 2009 ). The therapies for NB involve surgery, radiation treatment, and regimens of chemotherapy, whose success depends on the risk categories, with the stage 4 and 4s, representing metastatic cancer and stage 4 having the highest risk and worst outcome (Zhong et al., 2018 ). Most recently, there has been an interest in obtaining messenger RNA (mRNA) signatures for NB cases for better addressing their prognosis and treatment options (Zhong et al., 2018 ). The focus has also been on characterizing the function of various RNA-interacting proteins and regulatory RNA in NB (Bishayee et al., 2022; Schulte et al., 2010 ). MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a group of RNA species that do not code for protein and are involved in numerous essential functions for normal physiology. They have also been implicated in various states of pathology, such as tumor development (Bartel, 2018 ). miRNAs function by regulating the half-life of their target mRNA; this is mainly by antisense base-pairing to specific nucleotides in the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR) of their target, driving subsequent degradation and/or translation block of the bound mRNA (Behm-Ansmant et al., 2006; Eichhorn et al., 2014 ). It should be mentioned that binding to the 5′ untranslated region or open-reading frames of mRNAs can occur for some miRNAs (Bai et al., 2023 ). For tumors, there are also extensive 3′ UTR changes through alternative polyadenylation that produce mRNA transcripts of varying 3′ UTR lengths, making the prediction of miRNA-binding sites for tumor targets more difficult (Tian and Manley, 2017 ). From a recent estimate, there are approximately 2,300 species of mature miRNA in human cells (Alles et al., 2019 ), and most await characterization. We performed a search in the miRNA databases and the current literature for NB-associated miRNA either upregulated or downregulated in NB tissue. From this search, miR-454-3p was found to be downregulated in multiple cancer types and has also been reported to be a tumor suppressor (An et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022; Zuo et al., 2019 ). Besides being directly tumor suppressive, miR-454-3p can be downregulated for the benefit of tumor microenvironment, such as in the pituitary adenomas, allowing increased levels of extracellular TNF-α for bone destruction and invasiveness (Zhu et al., 2021 ). In this study, we confirmed the tumor-suppressive behavior of miR-454-3p in NB cells and sought to identify the growth-modulating substrates of this miRNA in these cells. From the predicted substrates of miR-454-3p, serine/threonine kinase STK33 was chosen for further study as STK33 displays relatively high expression in certain NB samples and also has a highly unfavorable survival characteristic for NB patients. Via a luciferase reporter assay in both cancer and noncancer cells, we confirmed the interaction of miR-454-3p with the STK33 3′ UTR motif. The changes in RNA levels for miR-454-3p and STK33 in NB under varying conditions of stress or growth also negatively correlated as would be predicted for miR-454-3p modulating the native levels of STK33 in these cells. From functional addback experiments, STK33 mRNA also seemed to be the major tumor-suppressive target of miR-454-3p. In these cells, the introduced recombinant STK33, designed with its mRNA in not having an available 3′ UTR, blocked the potency of the miR-454-3p mimic. STK33 is a priority target for therapeutic intervention in multiple cancers, even though for KRAS-dependent cancer cells, STK33’s role has been controversial; specifically, the kinase inhibitors used in those studies proved to be ineffective with inhibitors blocking the kinase function of the target (Luo et al., 2012; Scholl et al., 2009 ); however, the effort of discovery and testing of additional small-molecule inhibitors for STK33 continues, possibly targeting the nonkinase parts of the protein (Tran et al., 2023; Vala et al., 2024 ). We propose that using a miRNA therapeutic may prove to be more effective for an STK33 block as it has the attractive characteristics of being less likely for the tumor to develop resistance (Diener et al., 2022; Szczepanek et al., 2022 ) and the recent success of nanoparticle mediated in delivery of RNA for cancer therapy (Dowdy, 2017; Mirón-Barroso et al., 2022 ).  MATERIALS AND METHODS Statistical Survival Analysis of NB and Other Cancer Patients Survival analyses were obtained from the R2 database for the 3 published patient cohorts (http://r2.amc.nl ): the Sequencing Quality Control NB patient dataset that includes 498 patients, the NRC NB dataset includes 283 patients with primary untreated NB tumors, and the NB KOCAK dataset includes 649 patients. Information from the R2 database is listed in  Table 1 . Patient survival analyses were performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, also performed in the R2 database (http://r2.amc.nl ), and the statistical significance of the difference between groups was determined by t-tests with P  < .001 considered statistically significant.  Transfection of shRNA, siRNA, miRNAs, Overexpression, and Control Vectors Transfection was performed according to the Lipofectamine-3000 manufacturer’s protocol. The cells were seeded in 6-well or 96-well cell culture plates in a growth medium without antibiotics. Lipofectamine-3000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was diluted in either Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium medium with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and mixed with the shRNA and siRNA oligo or the vector construct and P3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The transfection complex was then mixed with media containing the cells. After 6 hours, the cells were supplemented with fresh complete media and incubated for various times according to the experiment. The hsa-miR-454-3p miRNA mimics, antagonists, and negative controls (NCs) were purchased from Gene Pharma (China). Silencer siRNAs for STK33 and siRNA control (AccuTarget Negative Control siRNA) were synthesized by Bioneer (Republic of Korea). miRNA and siRNA used for the experiments are listed in  Table 2 . shRNA for STK33 was purchased from Vector Builder (China) (Table 2 ). Qiagen Human Allstars for viability were purchased from Qiagen (Germany).  Cell Culture and Reagents Human NB cells (SK-N-DZ, SK-N-AS, IMR-32, SK-N-SH, and SH-SY5Y) and HEK-293 were purchased from American Type Culture Collection and Korea Cell Line Bank (Republic of Korea). SK-N-DZ, SK-N-AS, SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y, and HEK-293 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco BRL, Invitrogen) with 10% (FBS; Gibco BRL, Invitrogen) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco BRL, Invitrogen). IMR-32 cells were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. SK-N-DZ and SK-N-AS were neuroblasts that were isolated from the brain metastases of 2-year-old and 6-year-old White female patients with NB, respectively. All cells were incubated in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO2  and ambient air. The cell lines used were periodically checked for mycoplasma infection using the Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit (American Type Culture Collection), and no cells were infected. Other than the cell culture reagents listed above, the chemicals and the reagents were purchased from the following: insulin, Alpha Diagnostic International; FGF2, Thermo Fisher Scientific; acridine orange (AO), heparin, tunicamycin, Millipore Sigma; doxycycline, Clontech Takara. The primary antibody vendors are listed in  Table 3 . Secondary antibody vendors were goat antirabbit HRP, Invitrogen; goat antimouse HRP, Fortis Life Sciences.  Viability Assays NB cells were seeded in a 96-well plate at a density of 3 × 104  cells/well and after drug treatment or transfection, the assay was performed using Quanti-MAX WST-8 Cell Viability Assay Kit reagent (Biomax). Fluorescence (relative fluorescence units/absorbance at 570 nm) was measured, and viability histograms were plotted using GraphPad Prism 9.5 software (GraphPad). All the experiments were conducted 3 times for reproducibility.  Western Blotting Human NB cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 0.3 × 106  cells per well. After treatment, the cells were lysed on ice with radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate, and 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Cell Signaling Technology). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 4°C for 20 minutes at 13,500 rpm, and the supernatants were collected. Protein concentrations were measured using the Bradford assay (BioRad). Equal protein amounts were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis using 12% to 15% reducing gels, then transferred to 0.45-µm polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (Millipore Sigma). Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk (Japan) in Tris-Buffered Saline + Tween 20 (TBST) (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.6, and 0.1% Tween 20) for 1 hour at room temperature. They were then incubated overnight at 4°C with the primary antibody, followed by washing with TBST for 10 minutes for 3 times. The membranes were subsequently incubated with the appropriate secondary antibody at room temperature for 2 hours and washed again with TBST. Protein bands were visualized using Immobilon Forte Western HRP Substrates (Millipore Sigma), with detection performed either by film or using the FUSION FX-Western Blot & Chemi Imaging System (Vilber Lourmat). Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase served as the internal control. Densitometric analysis of the Western blot bands was conducted using ImageJ software (NIH, nih.gov , USA). Antibodies used for Western blotting are listed in Table 3 . All the experiments were conducted 2 or more times for reproducibility.  Quantitative Real-Time PCR Total RNA, including miRNA, was extracted from NB cells by Direct-Zol RNA Miniprep Plus (Zymo Research), from which Complementary DNA(cDNA) was made using the ReverTra Ace qPCR RT Master Mix with gDNA Remover (TOYOBO), miRNA 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Vazyme), and levels of target message RNA were detected and quantified with AccuPower Greenstar qPCR kit (Bioneer). miRNA Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix was made according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Human glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and U6 were used as the internal control. All the experiments were performed 2 or more times for assay reproducibility. Primers in qPCR are listed in  Table 4 .  Luciferase Reporter Assay DNA fragments of the wild-type (WT) 3′ UTR containing predicted target sites (410-417) of miR-454-3p were amplified from human genomic DNA. The amplified WT 3′ UTR was inserted downstream of firefly luciferase coding sequences into dual-luciferase reporter (Promega), a vector that contains both firefly and Renilla luciferase cDNAs under the control of separate promoter/terminator systems, to generate the STK33-WT reporter. Mutant reporter (STK33-mut1) with mutations of the seed sequences at each predicted target site was generated using site-directed mutagenesis kit. SK-N-DZ or HEK-293 cells were cotransfected with the specified luciferase reporters (0.8 ng/μL) and oligoes (miR-454-3p mimic or control oligo, 100 nM). Luciferase activities were measured after 72 hours, and the effect of miR-454-3p was determined using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System (Promega). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity in order to evaluate the assayed miRNAs.  Bioinformatics Analysis of miRNA For miRNA target prediction, 3 popular public databases, Targetscan Human 8.0 (https://www.targetscan.org/vert_80/ ), miRTarBase 9.0 (https://dian‌alab.e-ce.uth.gr/tarbasev9), and miRDB (https://mirdb.org/mirdb/index.html ) were used and cross-checked.  Cell Apoptosis Detection by Flow Cytometry Cell apoptosis was performed by Dead Cell Apoptosis Kits with Annexin V for Flow Cytometry (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. NB cells were transfected with the miRNA mimics, siSTK33, or doxycycline-inducible shSTK33 vector. Flow cytometry on the Annexin V-stained cells was performed using a FACS Calibur II flow cytometer (Becton Dickinson), and their data were analyzed with Flowing software (Turku Bioscience).  AO Staining Human NB cells were seeded in 12-well plates at 0.1 × 106  cells per well. After treatment with miR-454-3p, siSTK33, or doxycycline for inducible shSTK33 cell lines, cells were stained with 2.5 μM AO solution (Sigma-Aldrich) in culture medium at 37°C for 30 minutes. Cells were washed with a complete medium twice. Then, fluorescence images were acquired and analyzed on a confocal system (Carl Zeiss).  Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were via GraphPad Prism 9.5 (GraphPad). Data are presented as mean ± SEM with the 2-tailed Student’s t-test for comparing the means of 2 groups. Data with P  < .05 were considered to be statistically significant.   RESULTS STK33 is upregulated in late-stage NB, impacting survival; miR-454-3p directly interacts and reduces STK33 RNA levels in NB cells. Previous studies have shown that STK33 is highly expressed in various cancer tissues, such as colon cancer (Zhang et al., 2019 ) and hepatocellular carcinoma (Yang et al., 2016 ), having been demonstrated to have a significant impact on cancer cell survival. For NB, STK33’s role has not been elaborated. For NB patients, they are typically categorized into low-, intermediate-, or high-risk groups, depending on both clinical and biological factors (Pinto et al., 2023 ). Key determinants include the clinical stage of the disease and specific genetic markers with the International Neuroblastoma Staging System and the presence of MYCN Proto-Oncogene(MYCN) amplification (Table 1 ). From 3 NB patient cohorts (SEQC, n  = 498; KOCAK, n  = 476; NRC, n  = 276), STK33 RNA message is highly upregulated in NB late stages (stages 3 and 4) in the R2 cancer database (Supplementary Fig. S1A ). In the same samples, cells that carry a MYCN amplification are also high in STK33 expression (Supplementary Fig. S1B ). Amplification of the MYCN proto-oncogene is strongly associated with aggressive disease (Irwin and Goldsmith, 2024 ). The STK33 mRNA expression also strongly correlates with patient survival in all 3 of the NB patient cohorts (Supplementary Fig. S1C ). STK33 protein is readily detected in 5 NB cell lines SK-N-DZ, SK-N-AS, IMR-32, SH-SY5Y, and SK-N-SH ( Fig. 1 A). miRNAs regulate over 30% of human genes and are being extensively studied for their crucial roles in cancer biology (Sassen et al., 2008 ). We hypothesized that certain miRNAs might regulate the expression of STK33 in NB, thereby influencing potentially NB progression. Using Targetscan, miRTarBase, and miRDB miRNA databases, 2 nonbinding miRNAs and 3 potentially binding miRNAs against STK33 mRNA were selected for analysis (Table 2 ). We selected SK-N-AS and SK-N-DZ for our initial screening of various miRNA mimics and antagonists as these express medium and high levels of native STK33 protein, respectively. To investigate whether these miRNAs regulate STK33 expression, we transfected SK-N-DZ and SK-N-AS cells with miRNA mimics and antagonists for each miRNA, along with NC. Antagonists of miR-130a-3p, miR-301b-3p, and miR-454-3p resulted in upregulation of STK33 expression. However, miR-454-3p mimics/antagonist pair had the most effect in changing the STK33 protein levels in both cell lines (Fig. 1 B). Our findings indicate that miR-454-3p has 1 functional binding site on the 3′ UTR of human STK33 mRNA (Fig. 1 C). To map and confirm direct binding and suppression of STK33 RNA message by miR-454-3p, assays with luciferase reporters carrying either the WT or mutated (Mut) putative binding site in the STK33 3′ UTR were performed (Table 2 ), and they confirmed miR-454-3p suppressing STK33 RNA carrying the STK33 3′ UTR in both SK-N-DZ cancer and HEK-293 noncancer cells (Fig. 1 D). Transfection of the miR-454-3p mimic significantly increased the miR-454-3p qPCR signal; the mimic also significantly reduced the STK33 mRNA levels in the transfected cells (Fig. 1 E). These data collectively suggest that miR-454-3p directly binds to STK33 and regulates its expression in NB cells. miR-454-3p Mimic or STK33 Knockdown Suppresses Cell Viability In Vitro Previous studies have suggested that miR-454-3p may act as a tumor suppressor in various cancers (Liao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023 ). To check for viability changes when having reduced STK33 levels in these cells, 3 oligoes of siSTK33 were tested for STK33 RNA message reductions via qPCR (Supplementary Fig. S2 A), and viability changes in NB cell lines and HEK-293 cells (Supplementary Fig. S2 B) and siSTK33#2 displayed maximal potency. A positive control oligo mix (Qiagen Human Allstarss) was also used in the viability assay from a commercial vendor. Five NB cell lines were then evaluated to determine viability changes for silencing STK33 or introducing additional miR-454-3p. For both the STK33 knockdown or added miR-454-3p, there were significant viability losses in all of the cell lines tested. These NB cell lines represented both MYCN-amplified and not-amplified cells (Bishayee et al., 2022 ) ( Fig. 2 A). To evaluate the time course of miR-454-3p mimic and inhibitor viability changes on NB cells, the cultured cells were assayed every 24 hours for up to 96 hours for viability changes according to treatment. Each data point had an NC and was time-matched (Fig. 2 B and C). A viability augmentation was seen with the miR-454-3p inhibitor under basal conditions. The miR-454-3p inhibitor had a lesser of the growth-modulatory effect compared with the miR-454-3p mimic, possibly for the basal cells already having relative low levels of native miR-454-3p. The viability decreases were in a time-dependent fashion in both cell lines with the miR-454-3p mimic. To confirm the specificity of siSTK33#2, a functional addback of tagged of STK33 was performed. The addback STK33 recombinants were N-terminal FLAG or C-terminal HA-tagged, each carrying a silent mutation as not to bind to siSTK33#2 oligo (N-FLAG STK33* and C-HA STK33* designation) and allowing STK33 protein to be expressed. The expression of the tagged recombinants was confirmed by Western blots as well (Fig. 2 D). The viability loss of siSTK33 was reversible by the recombinant STK33 addbacks, indicating that the siSTK33#2 was properly targeting STK33 and was not off-target (Fig. 2 E). With siSTK33#2, compared with NC oligoes, there was also a time-dependent decrease in the viability of each treated cell line (Fig. 2 F).  Native STK33 RNA and Protein Changes Mirror Those of the Native miR-454-3p To determine whether regulation of native STK33 RNA changes in the cell is linked to changes in the availability of native miR-454-3p and vice versa, the SK-N-DZ and SK-N-AS cells were treated with external growth factors FGF2 or insulin or stressors of serum starvation or inducer of endoplasmic reticulum stress, tunicamycin (Brewer and Diehl, 2000 ). FGF2 is a major protumor factor in NB (Akl et al., 2016; Beenken and Mohammadi, 2009; Korc and Friesel, 2009; Powers et al., 2000 ), and insulin can promote the proliferation and survival of NB cells (Meyer et al., 2007 ). Previous studies have indicated that starvation can block S-phase entry of the cell cycle and trigger significant apoptosis in various NB cells (Beierle et al., 2002; Duan et al., 2001 ). Also, previous studies have shown that tunicamycin induces stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and promotes apoptosis in cancer cells (Banerjee et al., 2024 ). When assayed for STK33 RNA and miR-454-3p-level changes, the different conditions of available selective growth factor and stress resulted in changes that were direct mirror images of each other, presenting a strong negative correlation ( Fig. 3A ). The protein-level changes for STK33 also closely matched its RNA changes (Fig. 3B ).  STK33 Can Reverse the Suppression of miR-454-3p Mimic To assess whether the inhibitory function of miR-454-3p is ultimately due to a reduction of STK33 protein levels, we cotransfected the 2 cell lines with miR-454-3p in the absence or presence of tagged versions of STK33 vector. The vectors of STK33 expressed full-length STK33, tagged either at STK33 N-terminus or C-terminus, but having no available 3′ UTR for the miRNA mimic to bind, making them true functional addbacks. We already knew these constructs were functional for their STK33 activity as they reversed the siSTK33 knockdown (shown above that they allowed a functional addback even in the presence of siSTK33 oligoes) (“N-FLAG STK33*” and “C-HA STK33*” designation, silently mutated as not to bind to siSTK33#2 oligo) (Fig. 3C ). For both cell lines, the added STK33 recombinants nearly reversed the inhibition of miR-454-3p mimic (Fig. 3D ). This indicated that STK33 protein is the major functional substrate of miR-454-3p in these cancer cells in terms of viability recovery.  miR-454-3p Induces Autophagy Flux Through the Inhibition of STK33 in NB Cell Autophagy is an intracellular housekeeping mechanism for maintaining cell homeostasis (Debnath et al., 2023 ), and with increased cellular stress, its levels increase, but sometimes to the overall detriment of the cell. Given its importance in cellular health and given the known role of autophagy in cancer progression, each external modulation of the cancer cell was assayed for changes in the levels of autophagy, as there have also been several studies on the use of autophagy flux as a therapeutic strategy for NB (Han et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2018; Pham et al., 2018 ). Recent studies investigated the role of STK33 in regulating autophagy in cancer, as STK33 depletion in renal cell carcinoma cells inhibited autophagy by activating The mammalian target of rapamycin/unc-51-like kinase 1 signaling pathway (Li et al., 2023 ). These findings suggest that STK33 may be an important target for the regulation of autophagy in various cancers, but its role in NB has not been explored. Hence, the effects of either miR-454-3p mimic or STK33 knockdown on the autophagy levels in the NB cells were measured and compared. Either the miR-454-3p mimic or STK33 knockdown caused a significant increase in the accumulation of LC3-II and a decrease of p62 under basal conditions ( Fig. 4 A and B). To verify whether the observed changes were due to increased autophagic flux and not due to a block in late autophagy, we treated the same cells with bafilomycin A1 (Baf) in the presence or absence of miR-454-3p and siSTK33 transfection. Baf is a lysosomal V-ATPase inhibitor, an end-phase autophagy inhibitor, that prevents autophagosome-lysosome fusion. In the presence of a true increase in autophagy flux, the increases in the presence of Baf for LC3-II would persist. Indeed, in the presence of Baf, miR-454-3p mimic or siSTK33 still led to increases in LC3-II accumulation over the cells treated with Baf only; this indicated that the autophagic flux was increased by either miR-454-3p or siSTK33 treatment (Supplementary Fig. S3 A and B). A number of cells were also tested with a doxycycline (Doxy)-inducible suppressive hair-loop STK33 (shSTK33) construct, which allowed knockdown of STK33 with doxycycline (cells not induced by Doxy were used as NC) (Supplementary Fig. S4A  and B). Similar to the above, changes in the markers of autophagy were studied for the inducible shSTK33 cells in the presence or absence of Baf. We first performed AO staining of the cells, a method that stains for acidic vesicular organelles in the cellular cytoplasm with a shift from green to red fluorescent organelles under a fluorescence microscope (Supplementary Fig. S4C ). We also had LC3-II and p62 changes monitored with the knockdown of STK33, similar to the above experiments with the miR-454-3p mimic or siSTK33. These experiments suggested that the knockdown of STK33 in the 2 cell lines also induces autophagy through the inhibition of STK33 in NB cells. This was similar to miR-454-3p mimic or siSTK33 also inducing autophagy in the NB cells.  miR-454-3p Mimic, Similar to siSTK33, Increases the Markers of Apoptosis in the NB Cells To further validate that either STK33 knockdown or treatment with miR-454-3p mimic induces apoptosis in NB cells, we transfected the NB cells with the miR-454-3p mimic or siSTK33 oligos or induced a knockdown of STK33 with the doxycycline induction with the shSTK33 vector. These were performed alongside their respective control groups. The cells were then assayed via Western blotting for changes in their apoptotic markers. A group of cells were also assayed for changes in the binding of Annexin V at their cell surface, which is a measure of phosphatidylserine appearance at the cell surface, a marker of apoptosis (Lin et al., 2023 ) (Chen et al., 2023 ). miR-454-3p mimic or siSTK33 led to increased levels of cleaved caspase 3 and Bax, while the levels of their antiapoptosis marker Bcl-2 were reduced ( Fig. 5 A and B). Quantitative bar graph results of protein expression from the Western blot analyses are also provided (Supplementary Fig. S5 ). These were similar to doxycycline-induced shSTK33 in the same NB cell lines with increased levels of cleaved caspase 3 and Bax and reduced levels of Bcl-2 (Supplementary Fig. S4D ). In addition, the levels of the Annexin V binding were increased in those cells (Fig. 5 C and D). Cleaved caspase 3, along with Bax and Bcl-2, and increased levels of cell-surface Annexin V binding served to indicate increased levels of apoptosis in the treated cells. These results confirm that the suppression of native STK33 upregulated the levels of apoptosis markers in NB cells, in line with the findings of viability suppression shown. These findings suggest that STK33 and miR-454-3p exhibit opposing roles and are part of a system of control using 1 species and not the other in the given metabolic and growth scenario for the cell. This relationship highlights the potential of targeting STK33 with miR-454-3p RNA in future studies for therapeutic intervention in NB. A summary of the processes of regulation of STK33 RNA block/stability with miR-454-3p mimic, leading to increased levels of the markers of autophagy and apoptosis, is shown graphically ( Fig. 6 ).   DISCUSSION Treatment with small-molecule inhibitors, as best documented for kinase inhibitors, can lead to relapse, which is a major source of cancer-related mortality (Pucci et al., 2024 ). Using the case of STK33, a serine/threonine kinase, its reduction of activity may be best addressed by introducing miR-454-3p for NB cancer therapy. miRNAs block whole pathways (Diener et al., 2022; Szczepanek et al., 2022 ), and they are usually 20 to 25 nucleotides in length, but as RNA, they are highly charged and prone to degradation outside of the cell. Until recently, their targeted delivery of even modified RNA with improved serum stability had been challenging. Advances in delivery methods using nanoparticles have allowed effective targeted delivery of RNA species to the tumor (Bartel, 2018; Eichhorn et al., 2014 ). For these therapeutics, the macromolecules are endocytosed by target cells, have reduced clearance by the kidneys, do not manifest toxicity, and are not overly immunogenic (Dowdy, 2017; Mirón-Barroso et al., 2022 ). Suppression with a miRNA in cancer cells may also be an attractive means of therapy for cells that develop resistance: this could be in the form of overexpression of multidrug resistance genes, and these are less likely with RNA therapy. Two recent examples of miRNA therapy include the case of miRNA Let7b given in combination with paclitaxel, sizably reducing multidrug resistance gene expression and leading to tumor death in drug-resistant ovarian cancer cells (Gandham et al., 2022 ). The other example is miR-101-5P that made the HER2+ breast cancer cells more sensitive to trastuzumab and lapatinib (Normann et al., 2021 ). With the approach of replenishing downregulated or lost tumor suppressor miRNAs having an inhibitory effect on cell proliferation, invasion, or behaviors such as angiogenesis, it is thought that the therapeutic miRNA is blocking the translation of protumor genes or mRNA. The miRNA mimics are the form of oligonucleotides used for miRNA introduction to the cells and were also used for miR-454-3p in our study. The oligonucleotides are chemically synthesized as double-stranded RNA duplexes (Garofalo and Croce, 2011; Ors-Kumoglu et al., 2019 ), having a “guide strand,” which is the sequence of miRNA it mimics, and a “passenger strand,” being partially or completely complementary to the “guide strand” (Henry et al., 2011 ). These miRNA mimics, once inside the cell, guide their target mRNA into the RNA-induced silencing complex, leading to a translational block or mRNA degradation (Shah et al., 2016 ). miR-454-3p has been reported to downmodulate the neuronal differentiation 1 (NEUROD1) mRNA in NB with interaction also confirmed by luciferase reporter assays (Zhang et al., 2022 ). NEUROD1 is a known transcription factor implicated in neuronal differentiation and maturation. It is upregulated in NB samples and can also promote migration and proliferation in NB cells (Lu et al., 2022 ). To our knowledge, our work is the first reporting of the miR-454-3p with STK33 mRNA. We have also shown that overexpression of STK33 can overcome the suppressive effect of miR-454-3p in our assays, indicating that STK33 is the dominant substrate of miR-454-3p. In addition, the RNA levels for STK33 and miR-454-3p negatively correlate under different growth and stress conditions for the cell. We also demonstrated direct interaction of STK33 mRNA 3′ UTR with miR-454-3p via luciferase reporter assays. As for any possible link between STK33, NEUROD1, and miR-454-3p, it requires further analysis. With respect to the specific targets of STK33, as there are 538 kinases in the human genome (Alonso et al., 2004; Manning et al., 2002 ), STK33 is a relatively recent discovery and poorly understood in its functions in cancer and other cells (part of a group of “dark kinases”) (Berginski et al., 2021; Ku et al., 2024 ). However, a number of interesting findings about STK33 expression and function have already been made. STK33 is evolutionarily conserved in higher species, is expressed in a number of normal tissues, including the testis, and is required for sperm development in mice (Martins et al., 2018 ). There is also elevated STK33 expression in various cancers. STK33 has been reported to reduce p53 tumor suppressor expression in large-cell lung cancer (Wang et al., 2015 ) and bind and stabilize c-Myc oncogene in hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (Yang et al., 2016 ). STK33 has also been reported to interact with HSP90 chaperone, with HSP90 facilitating the interaction with HIF-1α hypoxia-response transcription factor and stabilizing the STK33 protein levels (Azoitei et al., 2012 ). However, there have been recent controversies on the role of STK33 in cancer as inhibitors blocking its kinase activity were shown to be ineffective for KRAS-dependent cancer cells (Luo et al., 2012; Scholl et al., 2009 ); despite this, another set of inhibitors have shown efficacy in cancer cells (Tran et al., 2023; Vala et al., 2024 ). miR-454-3p has been documented to bind to more than 30 targets inside various cancer cells (An et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022; Zuo et al., 2019 ). For most of these cancers, miR-454-3p is heavily downregulated, and it binds and suppresses a large number of different types of RNA, including a number of proto-oncogenes such as c-Met. Some are expressed in NB. Whether they are all suppressed by miR-454-3p in NB, it remains to be tested. miR-454-3p is also bound by a number of RNA sponges in the form of long noncoding RNA, thus lowering the functional levels of miR-454-3p. From this list of miR-454-3p binders, binding to STK33 RNA message is unique. For STK33 being a significant tumor promoter and drug target, our work provides the functional link between a tumor suppressor and its target a tumor promoter in NB cells. We also demonstrate that STK33 is able to reverse the suppression of miR-454-3p, establishing it as the major functional target of miR-454-3p. In the broader scheme of RNA-based therapeutics, in recent years, with the endocytosis-based delivery systems for RNA, the first siRNA-based therapeutic molecule was approved in the United States by the regulatory agency in 2018, and there is anticipation for a number of phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials succeeding for various indications including cancer (Chakraborty et al., 2017; Hanna et al., 2019 ). There has also been a sizable increase in research on validating new RNA targets, which will feed into the aforementioned clinical efforts. As the performance of the delivery methods also improves, the coming together of the technologies could improve the practicality of RNA-based treatments for cancer. title: Fluoride induces apoptosis via inhibiting SIRT1 activity to activate mitochondrial p53 pathway in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells
abstract: There has been a great concern about the neurotoxicity of fluoride since it can pass through the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in the brain. It has been suggested that apoptosis plays a vital role in neurotoxicity of fluoride. However, whether p53-mediated apoptotic pathway is involved is still unclear. Our results showed that apoptosis was induced after treatment with 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Exposure to 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h significantly upregulated the levels of p53 and apoptosis-related proteins including PUMA, cytochrome c (cyto c), cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP, whereas downregulated Bcl-2 in SH-SY5Y cells. Meanwhile, fluoride increased p53 nuclear translocation, cyto c release from mitochondria to cytoplasm and mitochondrial translocation of Bax in SH-SY5Y cells. Fluoride-induced increases of apoptotic rates and apoptosis-related protein levels were significantly attenuated by inhibiting p53 transcriptional activity with pifithrin-α. In addition, fluoride inhibited the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 and increased p53 (acetyl K382) level in SH-SY5Y cells. Apoptosis and upregulation of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP and p53 (acetyl K382) induced by fluoride could be ameliorated by SIRT1 overexpression or its activator resveratrol in SH-SY5Y cells. Taken together, our study demonstrates that fluoride induces apoptosis by inhibiting the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 to activate mitochondrial p53 pathway in SH-SY5Y cells, which depends on p53 transcriptional activity. Thus, SIRT1 may be a promising target to protect against neurotoxicity induced by fluoride.

Department of Occupational and Environmental Health School of Public Health Tongji Medical College Huazhong University of Science and Technology 13 Hangkong Road Wuhan Hubei 430030 PR China       There has been a great concern about the neurotoxicity of fluoride since it can pass through the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in the brain. It has been suggested that apoptosis plays a vital role in neurotoxicity of fluoride. However, whether p53-mediated apoptotic pathway is involved is still unclear. Our results showed that apoptosis was induced after treatment with 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Exposure to 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h significantly upregulated the levels of p53 and apoptosis-related proteins including PUMA, cytochrome c  (cyto c ), cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP, whereas downregulated Bcl-2 in SH-SY5Y cells. Meanwhile, fluoride increased p53 nuclear translocation, cyto c  release from mitochondria to cytoplasm and mitochondrial translocation of Bax in SH-SY5Y cells. Fluoride-induced increases of apoptotic rates and apoptosis-related protein levels were significantly attenuated by inhibiting p53 transcriptional activity with pifithrin-α. In addition, fluoride inhibited the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 and increased p53 (acetyl K382) level in SH-SY5Y cells. Apoptosis and upregulation of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP and p53 (acetyl K382) induced by fluoride could be ameliorated by SIRT1 overexpression or its activator resveratrol in SH-SY5Y cells. Taken together, our study demonstrates that fluoride induces apoptosis by inhibiting the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 to activate mitochondrial p53 pathway in SH-SY5Y cells, which depends on p53 transcriptional activity. Thus, SIRT1 may be a promising target to protect against neurotoxicity induced by fluoride.
