Although it is protective against dental caries and osteoporosis in trace concentrations, long-term exposure to high levels of fluoride causes detrimental effects, such as endemic fluorosis. It has been found that people living in high-fluoride areas not only suffered from dental and skeletal fluorosis but also had defective functions in other systems, including brain (Perumal et al., 2013 ; Xiong et al., 2007 ). Since fluoride can cross the blood-brain barrier, it could be accumulated in the important regions of the brain to affect the central nervous system (CNS) (Mullenix et al., 1995 ). The detrimental effects of fluoride on CNS have been reported in both epidemiological and animal studies. Various epidemiological studies demonstrated that the IQ scores of children living in high-fluoride areas were significantly lower than those of children in low-fluoride areas, and there was an inverse dose-response relationship between fluoride levels in urine or serum and IQ scores (Choi et al., 2012 ; Ding et al., 2011 ; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Exposure of rats to various concentrations of fluoride not only resulted in impairment of learning and memory abilities (Dong et al., 2015 ; Zhu et al., 2017 ), but also led to structural and functional brain damage (Akinrinade et al., 2015 ; Lou et al., 2013 ; Niu et al., 2015 ). Moreover, in vitro studies have shown that fluoride induced toxicity in various nerve cells such as primary rat hippocampal neurons (Zhang et al., 2007 ), BV2 microglial cells (Chen et al., 2017 ; Yan et al., 2013 ), neuron-like rat pheochromocytoma PC12 cells (Wu et al., 2015 ) and human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells (Niu et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2011 ). In addition to oxidative stress (Basha and Madhusudhan, 2010 ; Chouhan et al., 2010 ; Flora et al., 2009 ), lipid peroxidation (Basha and Madhusudhan, 2010 ; Bharti and Srivastava, 2009 ; Shanthakumari et al., 2004 ), decrease of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Dong et al., 2015 ; Liu et al., 2010 ; Shan et al., 2004 ), cell cycle arrest (Zhang et al., 2008 ), and alteration of ERK1/2 (Liu et al., 2010 ), cumulative evidences support a role of apoptosis in fluoride-induced neurotoxicity. Apoptosis was induced in primary rat hippocampal neurons (Zhang et al., 2007 ), PC12 cells (Wu et al., 2015 ) and SH-SY5Y cells (Xu et al., 2011 ) after exposure to 20, 40 and 80 mg/L of sodium fluoride (NaF) for 24 h. Consistently, Liu et al. (2011)  found that exposure to excessive NaF (50 mg/L) induced apoptosis in rat brains as well as in SH-SY5Y cells. The mechanisms of apoptosis have been associated with enhanced oxidative stress (Wu et al., 2015 ; Zhang et al., 2007 ), activation of Fas/Fas-L (Xu et al., 2011 ) and JNK signaling pathways (Liu et al., 2011 ). It is not clear, however, whether p53-mediated apoptotic pathway is involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis. The tumor repressor p53 plays a key role in cell cycle arrest, cell senescence, DNA repair, inhibition of tumor angiogenesis, as well as apoptosis (Evan and Vousden, 2001 ; Li et al., 2012 ). To further uncover the molecular mechanisms of apoptosis induced by fluoride, we investigated the mitochondrial p53 pathway in SH-SY5Y cells. p53 has been found to promote apoptosis via both transcription-dependent and transcription-independent pathways (Schuler and Green, 2001 ). p53 transcription-dependent apoptosis is mediated through transcriptional activation of pro-apoptotic genes such as Bax , PUMA  and NOXA . p53 transcription-independent apoptosis is triggered by translocation of p53 from cytoplasm to mitochondria and then interaction of p53 with anti-apoptotic BCL (B Cell Lymphoma) proteins (Yi and Luo, 2010 ). Both pathways contribute to oligomerization of pro-apoptotic proteins in the mitochondria, which could induce mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and the release of cytochrome c  (cyto c ) from mitochondria. Cyto c  then activates caspase-3, the critical executioner of apoptosis, which cleaves PARP. Cleaved PARP is an important marker of apoptosis. The amount, stability and activity of p53 can be regulated by post-translational modifications including phosphorylation, ubiquitination and acetylation (Appella and Anderson, 2001 ; Xu, 2003 ). p53 can be acetylated to promote its transcriptional activity (Tang et al., 2008 ). SIRT1, an NAD+ -dependent deacetylase, has been shown to regulate cell death/survival, cell growth and senescence, inflammation, metabolism and stress response (Sosnowska et al., 2017 ). p53 has been identified as the first non-histone substrate of SIRT1. SIRT1 deacetylates p53 at lysine 382 to decrease nuclear translocation of p53 and thus inhibit p53-mediated transactivation (Han et al., 2008 ; Langley et al., 2002 ; Vaziri et al., 2001 ). As a cell line of human origin, SH-SY5Y cells which were thrice cloned from SK-N-SH cell line possess stem cell properties and numerous characteristics of human neurons (Dayem et al., 2014 ; Presgraves et al., 2003 ). Therefore, SH-SY5Y cells have been widely used as an in vitro model to evaluate neurotoxicity of various agents (Cheung et al., 2009 ; Jang et al., 2016 ; Lee et al., 2005 ). In the present study, we investigated whether SIRT1/p53 pathway was involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. Our study suggested that fluoride induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, which is mainly caused by decreasing the activities of SIRT1 to increase p53 (acetyl K382), thus promoting nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity of p53 to activate mitochondrial p53 apoptotic pathway. Our study suggested that SIRT1 might be a promising target to protect against fluoride-induced neurotoxicity.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials NaF, pifithrin-α (PFT) and resveratrol (RSV) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, MO, USA). Antibodies specific to SIRT1, PARP, cleaved caspase-3, p53 and Bax were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Beverly, MA, USA). Anti-acetyl p53 (K382) and alexa 488-conjugated anti-mouse antibodies were purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, MA, USA). Anti-PUMA and Bcl-2 antibodies were purchased from Proteintech Group (Wuhan, China). Anti-cyto c , β -actin and GAPDH antibodies were purchased from Bioworld Technology (St Louis Park, MN, USA). Horse-radish peroxidase-conjugated (HRP) anti-rabbit and anti-mouse secondary antibodies were purchased from Wuhan promoter Biological Co. Ltd. (Wuhan, China).  2.2 Cell culture, treatment and transfection Human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells were purchased from American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA). Cells were cultured in an incubator at 37 °C with a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2  in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium/Ham's F-12 (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). Exponentially growing cells were exposed to 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h. Untreated cells were used as control. Cells were transfected with adenovirus encoding SIRT1 (Vigene Bioscience, Jinan, China).  2.3 Cell viability assay Cells were seeded into 96-well plates (6000 cells/well) and cell viability was measured by Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo, Kumamoto, Japan) following the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well at the end of exposure, and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for an additional 2 h. The optical density at 450 nm was measured using a multidetection microplate reader (Model, Synergy 2; BioTek Instruments Inc., Winooski, VT, USA).  2.4 Morphology of apoptotic cell The morphological changes of apoptotic cells were observed by Hoechst 33342 (Sigma) staining. Cells grown on glass coverslips were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min before staining with Hoechst 33342 (2.5 μg/mL) in dark at 37 °C for 15 min. The coverslips were mounted onto glass slides and subsequently viewed under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).  2.5 Annexin V–FITC/propidium iodide assay The percentages of cells undergoing apoptosis were examined by Annexin V–FITC/propidium iodide (PI) assay (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) under the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, cells were harvested at the end of treatment. Then 1 × 105  cells were stained with Annexin V-FITC and PI (5 μL each) in dark for 15 min. Stained cells were then examined by a flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and the percentages of apoptotic cells were analyzed by ModFit software (Verity Software House, Topsham, ME, USA).  2.6 Western blot Cells were lysed using radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) supplemented with phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (Beyotime). Proteins were quantitated using Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.) and separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis gel. After incubation with antibodies, the immune complexes were detected with ECL reagents (Advansta Inc., Menlo Park, CA, USA) and scanned using a GeneGnome chemiluminescent imaging system (Syngene, Frederick, MD, USA). The band intensities were analyzed using Quantity One software.  2.7 SIRT1 deacetylase activity SIRT1 deacetylase activity was determined using SIRT1 Assay Kit (Sigma) under the manufacturer's instructions. In addition, 1 μM trichostatin A was added to the reaction according to Li et al. (2008) . Nuclear proteins were extracted with CeLytic NuCLEAR Extraction Kit (Sigma). The fluorescence intensity was measured at excitation/emission wavelengths of 340/440 nm with a fluorescent microplate reader (Model, Synergy 2; BioTek Instruments Inc.)  2.8 Confocal microscopy At the end of exposure, SH-SY5Y cells cultured on coverslips were incubated with 0.2 μM Mito Tracker® Red CMXRos (Yeasen, Shanghai, China) at 37 °C for 30 min. Then cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, and permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 before blocking with 10% goat serum for 1 h. Cells were then incubated with primary mouse monoclonal antibodies (p53, Bax and cyto c ) at 4 °C overnight, followed by incubation with Alexa 488-conjugated anti-mouse secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Subsequently, cell nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 before mounting, and then fluorescent signals were imaged under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus).  2.9 Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 18.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by One-way ANOVA with Student-Newman-Keuls test, and differences between two groups were tested by independent Student's t -test. Data were presented as the means ± standard deviation (SD) from three independent experiments. Difference was considered statistically significant at P  < .05 and statistically highly significant at P  < .01.   3 Results 3.1 Fluoride induces apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells To investigate if fluoride induces apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, CCK-8 assay was first carried out to determine the concentrations of NaF to treat SH-SY5Y cells. Cells were treated with NaF at 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 80 mg/L for 24 h and then cell viability was examined. When cells were exposed to 40, 50, 60 and 80 mg/L of NaF, cell viabilities were significantly reduced (84.84%, 70.76%, 52.31% and 34.31% as compared with that of untreated cells, respectively, P  < .01) (Fig. 1  ). 80 mg/L has been commonly used as the highest dose in neurotoxicity study of fluoride in different cells. Since the viability of the cells exposed to 80 mg/L of NaF was <50%, we used 60 mg/L as the maximum dose in the following study. SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h, and unexposed cells were taken as control. Compared with control, NaF not only reduced cell numbers but also caused morphologic changes including cell rounding and floating (Fig. 2 A ). Hoechst 33342 staining revealed that 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF caused nuclear fragmentation and condensation (Fig. 2 B). Annexin V–FITC/PI assay showed that both of the early and total apoptotic rates of the cells exposed to 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF were significantly increased (P  < .05) (Fig. 2 C and D). All of the results suggested that fluoride induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, which may significantly contribute to fluoride-induced toxicity in these cells.  3.2 Mitochondrial p53 pathway is involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells To investigate the role of mitochondrial p53 pathway in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, cells were exposed to 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h. Whole cell lysates were extracted and the expression levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP, p53, PUMA, Bax, Bcl-2 and cyto c  were measured by Western blot. As shown in Fig. 3 A , NaF significantly upregulated the protein levels of cleaved caspase-3 at 40 and 60 mg/L and cleaved PARP at 60 mg/L compared with control (P  < .05 or P  < .01). Meanwhile, NaF significantly increased the protein levels of p53 at 40 and 60 mg/L, and PUMA and cyto c  at 60 mg/L, whereas significantly downregulated Bcl-2 protein level at 60 mg/L, compared with control (P  < .05) (Fig. 3 B). Although there was no significant change in the protein level of Bax after NaF treatment, immunofluorescent staining displayed that Bax translocated to mitochondria after treatment with 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF (Fig. 4  ). Notably, the nuclear translocation of p53 was also significantly enhanced by 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF, and cyto c  were released from mitochondria to cytoplasm in the cells exposed to 60 mg/L of NaF (Fig. 4 ). These evidences indicated that fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells was associated with mitochondrial p53 pathway, which is dependent on the transcriptional activity of p53.  3.3 Inhibition of p53 transcriptional activity blocks fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells PFT is a specific inhibitor of p53 transcriptional activity. To further confirm that mitochondrial p53 pathway was involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, we pretreated the cells with 10 μM PFT for 1 h before exposure to 60 mg/L of NaF for 24 h. As shown in Fig. 5 A , PFT significantly reduced total apoptotic rate of SH-SY5Y cells treated with NaF (P  < .05). The increased levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP, p53, PUMA and cyto c  induced by NaF were also ameliorated by PFT (Fig. 5 B), which were in accord with the results of flow cytometry (Fig. 5 A). These results further verified that p53 transcription-dependent pathway was involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells.  3.4 SIRT1 deacetylase activity is decreased in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells As a deacetylase of p53, SIRT1 can bind to and deacetylate p53 on lysine 382, thereby suppressing p53-mediated transactivation of pro-apoptotic genes and subsequently preventing apoptosis. To investigate whether SIRT1 was involved in regulation of mitochondrial p53 pathway as an upstream signaling molecule, SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to NaF at 20, 40 and 60 mg/L for 24 h, and the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 was detected by SIRT1 Assay Kit and expression of SIRT1 and p53 (acetyl K382) were measured by Western blot. NaF significantly reduced the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 to 45.8% at 60 mg/L as compared with control but only slightly increased the protein level of SIRT1 at 40 and 60 mg/L (1.25 and 1.28 fold, respectively, P  < .05) (Fig. 6 A ). Meanwhile, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF significantly upregulated p53 (acetyl K382) level (P  < .05) (Fig. 6 B). These results suggested that fluoride could inhibit the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 to upregulate acetylation of p53.  3.5 Overexpression of SIRT1 or pretreatment with RSV attenuates fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells To further understand the role of SIRT1 in fluoride-induced apoptosis, SH-SY5Y cells were transfected with adenovirus encoding SIRT1 for 24 h or pretreated with a specific SIRT1 activator, RSV (20 μM) for 2 h. Cells were then treated with 60 mg/L of NaF for an additional 24 h. The apoptotic rates of the cells were detected by flow cytometry and the protein levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP, p53 (acetyl K382) and p53 were measured by Western blot. As shown in Fig. 7 A , apoptosis of SH-SY5Y cells induced by NaF was significantly decreased by overexpression of SIRT1 (P  < .05). Meanwhile, upregulation of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP and p53 (acetyl K382) by NaF were significantly attenuated by SIRT1 overexpression (P  < .05) (Fig. 7 B) or pretreatment with RSV (P  < .05) (Fig. 8  ). These evidences indicated that SIRT1 has a protective role against fluoride-induced apoptosis via modulating mitochondrial p53 pathway in SH-SY5Y cells.   4 Discussion Ingestion of groundwater with high concentrations of fluoride is the predominant source of human exposure to fluoride. It has been reported that the maximum concentrations of fluoride in groundwater reached up to 30–50 mg/L (Barbier et al., 2010 ), which were close to the doses used in our study. Therefore, the concentrations of fluoride in the study are supposed to be environmentally relevant. Moreover, the concentrations of 20, 40 and 80 mg/L of NaF have been frequently used in previous studies to treat various cell lines including primary rat hippocampal neurons (Wu et al., 2015 ), PC12 cells (Zhang et al., 2007 ) and SH-SY5Y cells (Xu et al., 2011 ). Since our study showed that the viability of the cells treated with 80 mg/L of NaF was <50%, we used 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF to treat SH-SY5Y cells in the present study. Apoptosis, a genetically controlled form of cell death, is characterized by cell shrinkage, chromosomal condensation and fragmentation (Orrenius et al., 2003 ). Our results showed that fluoride induced morphological changes of SH-SY5Y cells. Upregulation of apoptotic rates and the levels of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP in the cells exposed to fluoride further indicated that fluoride could induce apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. These results provided evidence that apoptosis might contribute to the reduction of cell viability induced by fluoride. Our results are consistent with previous studies which showed that fluoride elicited neural cytotoxicity via induction of apoptosis. According to Zhang et al. (2007) , after 24 h of exposure to 40 and 80 mg/L of NaF, the percentages of apoptosis in primary rat hippocampal neurons were significantly increased. Liu et al. (2011)  showed that exposure to excessive fluoride (50 ppm) induced apoptosis in both rat brains and SH-SY5Y cells. Although p53 is an important mediator of apoptosis, whether p53 apoptotic pathway was involved in fluoride-induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells was previously not clear. Our results demonstrated that the protein levels of p53, PUMA and cyto c  were significantly upregulated whereas the level of Bcl-2 was downregulated after exposure to 60 mg/L of NaF. Moreover, immunofluorescent staining showed that 60 mg/L of NaF significantly induced nuclear translocation of p53 and mitochondrial release of cyto c , and 20, 40 and 60 mg/L of NaF significantly induced Bax translocation from cytoplasm to mitochondria. These results suggested that apoptosis caused by fluoride was dependent on the induction and activation of p53, and p53 transcription-dependent pathway played a leading role in this process. This notion was further confirmed by pretreating SH-SY5Y cells with PFT, a specific inhibitor of p53 transcriptional activity. To the best of our knowledge, there has been no report about the involvement of p53 pathway in fluoride-induced neurotoxicity, and the mechanisms were mainly attributed to changes in the expression of apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins or other apoptosis-related pathways. Lou et al. (2014)  found that exposure to 10 and 50 mg/L of NaF for 6 months significantly elevated the expression of Bax while decreased the expression of Bcl-2 in the cortices of rat brains. The same results were also observed in the neurons of rat brain after exposure to 60 and 120 ppm of NaF for 10 weeks (Yan et al., 2016 ). Another study demonstrated that exposure to excessive fluoride (50 ppm) induced apoptosis in both rat brains at 6 months as well as in SH-SY5Y cells at 24 h via activating JNK phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2011 ). Xu et al. (2011)  showed that exposure to 40 and 80 mg/L of NaF for 24 h induced apoptosis via Fas/Fas-L pathway in SH-SY5Y cells. Therefore, our findings likely provide a new target to prevent or treat fluoride-induced neurotoxicity. As a deacetylase of p53, SIRT1 could reduce p53 acetylation, thereby blocking its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity (Han et al., 2008 ). In our study, the deacetylase activity of SIRT1 was significantly decreased (45.8% of control) in fluoride-induced apoptotic cells. However, expression of SIRT1 protein was only slightly increased (1.2–1.5 fold of control) after exposure to fluoride. Generally, upregulation of SIRT1 in response to stress is possibly a compensatory mechanism to restore cellular functions and homeostasis. Therefore, we speculated that SIRT1 level was increased as an insufficient protective response to fluoride treatment. The phenomenon that declined SIRT1 deacetylase activity was accompanied by a slight increase in the protein level was also reported in the frontal and temporal cortices of patients with dementia with Lewy bodies (Singh et al., 2017 ) and MRC-5 fibroblasts stimulated with TNF-α for 6 h (Chu et al., 2017 ). In our study, apoptosis and the levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP and p53 (acetyl K382) induced by fluoride were significantly decreased by SIRT1 overexpression in SH-SY5Y cells, indicating that SIRT1 could relieve fluoride-induced apoptosis via inhibiting mitochondrial p53 signaling pathway. A similar phenomenon was recently reported by Suzuki et al. (2017)  who demonstrated that SIRT1 downregulated p53 acetylation to mitigate fluoride-induced mitochondrial damage and apoptosis in ameloblast cells. In addition, we found that there was no significant change in p53 protein level in fluoride-treated cells after overexpression of SIRT1, indicating that SIRT1 inactivates p53 via deacetylation at K382 but not through downregulation of p53 protein to reduce its transcriptional activity. RSV is a polyphenolic SIRT1 activating compound mainly found in the skin of grapes. Howitz et al. (2003)  showed that RSV significantly increased SIRT1 activity through an allosteric interaction, resulting in the increase of SIRT1 affinity for both NAD+  and the acetylated substrate. In the present study, the levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP and p53 (acetyl K382) induced by fluoride were also significantly ameliorated by pretreatment with RSV. These results further confirmed that SIRT1 could act as an upstream signal regulator of p53 pathway to attenuate fluoride-induced apoptosis. However, in contrast to SIRT1 overexpression, pretreatment with RSV significantly downregulated p53 protein level that was induced by fluoride. Possible explanation is that RSV has other functions such as anti-oxidation and anti-aging (Li et al., 2012 ; Yu et al., 2012 ), which may trigger different signaling pathways to regulate the expression of p53.  5 Conclusions Our results showed that fluoride induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells, which is caused by decreasing the activities of p53 deacetylase SIRT1, and thereby increasing nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity of p53 to activate mitochondrial p53 pathway. RSV, a natural SIRT1 inducer, may provide a more convenient and effective method to prevent fluoride-induced neurotoxicity.  Conflicts of interest None. title: HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 suppresses miR-22 to induce growth inhibition and apoptosis <ce:italic>via</ce:italic> p53-independent PTEN activation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells
abstract: Here we report a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor named DWP0016, which exhibits anti-neuroblastoma potential in vitro. DWP0016 effectively inhibited proliferation of neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells at submicromolar levels but did not affect the growth of normal cells. Flowcytometry analysis showed DWP0016 arrested cell cycle at G1 phase and induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently. Western-blotting results showed DWP0016 induced significant increase of histone H3 acetylation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Molecular mechanistic studies suggested that DWP0016 activated p21Cip/WAF1, p27/KIP1 and caspase-3, -9 which facilitated to contribute the cell cycle and apoptosis. Besides, DWP0016 activated tumor suppressor PTEN to inhibit the PI3K/Akt cell signal pathway. Intensive investigations showed down-regulation of miR-22 by DWP0016 stimulated the activity of PTEN promoter and then enhanced PTEN at both transcription and protein expression level. SiRNA silencing results suggested knockdown of PTEN sufficiently blocked cell growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. Conclusively, our results showed DWP0016 was a promising candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with its PTEN and microRNA regulations mechanisms.

HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 suppresses miR-22 to induce growth inhibition and apoptosis via  p53-independent PTEN activation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells Hui Jin a  c   Lifeng Liu a   Weiping Deng a   Yanhua Lu a   Jianhui Tian b   Hegeng Li b  ⁎⁎   Jianwen Liu a  ⁎   a State Key Laboratory of Bioreactor Engineering, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Chemical Biology, School of pharmacy, East China University of Science and Technology, Shanghai 200237, China State Key Laboratory of Bioreactor Engineering, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Chemical Biology, School of pharmacy, East China University of Science and Technology Shanghai 200237 China   b Department of Oncology, Longhua Hospital, Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, National Clinical Research Centre for Traditional Chinese Medicine and Oncology, Shanghai 200032, China Department of Oncology, Longhua Hospital, Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, National Clinical Research Centre for Traditional Chinese Medicine and Oncology Shanghai 200032 China   c School of Life Sciences and Technology, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China School of Life Sciences and Technology, Tongji University Shanghai 200092 China   ⁎ Corresponding author at: East China University of Science and Technology, #268, 130 Meilong Road, Shanghai 200237, China. Tel.: +86 21 64252044; fax: +86 21 64252044.  ⁎⁎ Corresponding author.      Here we report a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor named DWP0016, which exhibits anti-neuroblastoma potential in vitro . DWP0016 effectively inhibited proliferation of neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells at submicromolar levels but did not affect the growth of normal cells. Flowcytometry analysis showed DWP0016 arrested cell cycle at G1  phase and induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently. Western-blotting results showed DWP0016 induced significant increase of histone H3 acetylation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Molecular mechanistic studies suggested that DWP0016 activated p21Cip/WAF1 , p27/KIP1   and caspase-3, -9 which facilitated to contribute the cell cycle and apoptosis. Besides, DWP0016 activated tumor suppressor PTEN to inhibit the PI3K/Akt cell signal pathway. Intensive investigations showed down-regulation of miR-22 by DWP0016 stimulated the activity of PTEN promoter and then enhanced PTEN at both transcription and protein expression level. SiRNA silencing results suggested knockdown of PTEN sufficiently blocked cell growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. Conclusively, our results showed DWP0016 was a promising candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with its PTEN and microRNA regulations mechanisms.   Keywords HDAC inhibitor  Apoptosis  miR-22  PTEN  PI3K/Akt pathway    1 Introduction Neuroblastomas are the most common solid brain tumor occurring in children, which accounts for 8–10% of all pediatric malignancies [1] . For more than 30 years, neuroblastoma has remained one of the most challenging malignant tumors for both clinicians and basic scientists though novel gene-regulation therapeutic approaches emerging [2] . Most neuroblastomas are initially chemo- and radiosensitive, but when recurrent, are resistant with 25% of stage 4 patients over 1 year of age being long term survivors. An important mechanism of intrinsic chemoresistance in many tumor cells is an abnormality in the p53 tumor suppressor gene pathway [3,4] . Previously several studies screening for p53 mutations have shown that p53 mutations in neuroblastoma tumors and cell lines are rare. Acquired p53 mutations in the treatment progress possibly determine multidrug sensitivity in neuroblastoma [5–9] . These studies suggest that targeting other genes beyond p53 maybe a novel therapeutic approach for effective neuroblastoma treatment. The tumor suppressor gene phosphatase and tensin homolog deleted on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is regarded as the most potential target for cancer treatment besides p53. Previous work has demonstrated several layers of crosstalk between p53 and PTEN, which twisted the PTEN-p53 tumor suppressor network [10–12] . PTEN plays a role not only in inducing cell cycle arrest and programming apoptosis, but also in other aspects of cell physiology, including the regulation of cell adhesion, for highly acidic substrates, migration, and differentiation. PTEN is down-regulated in many poorly differentiated cancers, including neuroblastoma [13] . Besides, PTEN inhibits PI3K/Akt cell signal pathway by counteracting with the action of PI3K through dephosphorylating the D-3 position of polyphosphoinositides [14] . PI3K/Akt pathway is commonly overactive reducing apoptosis and allowing proliferation in many cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as brain cancers [15] . Previous reports showed PI3K/Akt pathway involved in the biology of neuroblastoma and the chemotherapy-induced apoptosis in neuroblastoma [16,17] . However, the understanding about the regulations balance between p53, PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway in the biology of neuroblastoma remained largely unknown. MicroRNAs are small 19–24 bp long non-coding RNAs which function primarily to down-regulate gene expression in all metazoan eukaryotes. The microRNAs specifically interact with target mRNAs through base pairing, which made miRNAs play important roles in the pathogenesis of different human diseases [18–20] . Increasing work reported regulations on microRNA to targets tumor genes were reasonable and practicable for carcinoma treatment, including lung cancer, colon cancer, and neuroblastoma [21–25] . A new microRNA-22 (miR-22) is screened out to directly bind to a specific site on PTEN 3′UTR, which resulting in PTEN down-regulation while suppression of miR-22 led to PTEN activation. Interestingly, other reports showed reverse conclusions that over-expression of miR-22 was able to activate PTEN [26,27,28,29] . These debates suggest the complicated interactions between miR-22 and PTEN, which may facilitate to shed a light for PTEN regulations and thus cancer treatment. Histone deacetylases inhibitors (HDACi) emerge as the most potent anti-cancer agents in recent years. HDACi are a class of compounds that interfered with the function of histone deacetylases (HDACs) [30–32] . Inhibition of HDACs by HDACi results in histone hyper-acetylation, which lead to growth inhibition of carcinoma cells, cell cycle block, apoptosis in vitro  and in vivo [33] . A variety of HDACis as potent cancer therapeutic agents have entered preclinical and clinical trials aimed at both solid and liquid tumors [34–36] . Companied with the prominent anti-tumor effects of HDACi, more and more new HDAC inhibitors are synthetized for better performance and more applications. Besides, detailed knowledge of mechanisms controlling proliferation and differentiation on HDAC regulations with HDAC inhibitor may lead to a better understanding for the treatment especially for malignancy such as neuroblastoma. In this study, we evaluated the antitumor potential in neuroblastoma of a synthesized HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 (Patent No. 201110030648). DWP0016 effectively inhibited the cell proliferation in neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y and other carcinoma cell lines. DWP0016 arrested cell cycle at G1  phase and induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. Regulations on p21Cip/WAF1 , p27/KIP1   and caspase-3 and -9 are associated with the cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016. DWP0016 up-regulated the activity of PTEN promoter, transcription and protein expression level of PTEN in SH-SY5Y cells. The activation of PTEN by DWP0016 was attributed to the suppression of miR-22 and thus led to inhibition on PI3K/Akt pathway. These findings suggest that DWP0016 down-regulates miR-22 to activate PTEN, which contributes to the antitumor efficacy in neuroblastoma. Conclusively, DWP0016 is a potent candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with its PTEN activation mechanism.  2 Methods and materials 2.1 Chemicals DWP0016, {(E )-3-(2-benzyl-5-(2-(piperidin-1-yl) ethyl)-2,3,4,5-tetrahydro-1H -pyrido [4,3-b]indol-8-yl)-N -hydroxyacrylamide}, was shown in Fig. 1  . The structure of DWP0016 was confirmed by the analysis of its 1 H NMR, 13 C NMR and MS spectra. Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) was used as positive drug. The precursors were purchased from Ambion (USA).  2.2 Cell lines and cell culture Cell lines were purchased from Cell Bank of Type Culture Collection of Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China), including human colorectal carcinoma cells (HCT-8), gastric carcinoma cells (MKN-45), human neuroblastoma cells (SH-SY5Y), human neuroblastoma cells (SK-N-SH), human neuroblastoma cells (IMR-32). Human neurons (HN) were purchased from Sciencell Research Laboratories (USA). HCT-8 and MKN-45 cells were maintained in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum. SH-SY5Y, SK-N-SH, IMR-32 cells were grown in DMEM:F12 (1:1) with 10% fetal calf serum. HN cells were maintained in Neuronal Medium (Sciencell). Penicillin (100 U/mL) and streptomycin (100 U/mL) were added to all kinds of medium. Cells were incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 95% air and 5% CO2 .  2.3 Cell viability assay 3-(4,5-Dimethyl-thiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT, Sigma) assay was performed to assess viable cell numbers after drug exposure as described previously [37] . Briefly, cells in 96-well plates were incubated with DWP0016 at 0.156, 0.3125, 0.625, 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10 μM for 48 h at 37 °C. After exposure, MTT was added and absorbance values were collected in an Automated Microplate Reader (Multiskan Ex, Finland) at 570 nm using a reference at 630 nm. The values were converted to cell numbers according to a standard growth curve of the relevant cell line. The concentration, which reduced cell numbers to 50% relative to DMSO treated cells, was calculated as IC50  by using a Bliss assay.  2.4 Flow cytometric analysis of cellular DNA content The cellular DNA content analysis was performed as described previously [38] . Briefly, cells were incubated with DWP0016 at the concentration of 0.5, 1, 2 μM for 48 h. Then harvested, treated and untreated cells were fixed with 70% ice-cold ethanol and were kept at −20 °C overnight. Fixed cells were centrifuged, washed and resuspended in PBS containing in concentration of 50 μg/mL of propidium iodide (PI, P4170, Sigma) and 100 μg/mL of DNase-free RNase at 37 °C for 30 min as previously reported. Cell cycle was analyzed by using cell cytometer (FACScan, Becton Dickinson) and Cell Quest Pro software.  2.5 Flow cytometric analysis of apoptosis and necrosis Apoptosis assessment was performed by using an Annexin-V/FITC apoptosis detection kit (Invitrogen, USA) as described previously [39] . Briefly, cells were incubated with DWP0016 at the concentration of 0.5, 1, 2 μM for 48 h. Harvested cells were stained with Annexin-V/FITC and PI in binding buffer for 15 min at room temperature in the dark as previously reported. The samples were analyzed by FACScan flow cytometry (Becton Dickinson, USA) to determine the percentage of cells displaying FITC and PI staining.  2.6 Determination of caspase activity The assay was performed with a caspase activity kit (Promega) as described previously [40] . Briefly, cells were treated with DWP0016 at the concentration of 0.5, 1, 2 μM for 48 h. After treatment, cells were collected and resuspended in 50 mM Tris–HCl [pH = 7.4], 1 mM EDTA, and 10 mM ethyleneglycol-tetraacetic acid (EGTA) as previously described. Cell lysates were clarified and clear lysates were incubated with 100 μM of enzyme specific colorigenic substrates at 37 °C for 1 h. The activity of caspase-3, -8 and -9 was described as the cleavage of colorimetric substrate by measuring the absorbance of 405 nm.  2.7 Real-time quantitative reverse transcription-PCR analysis Total RNA was isolated from cells treated with DWP0016 by using a RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen, UK) according to the manufacturer's recommendations. Real-time PCR was performed by using SYBR Green Supermix Reverse in Transcription System (Takara, Japan) with 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). Primers were obtained from Shanghai Sangon Biological Engineering Technology & Services Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). The sequences of used primers were as follows. For PTEN, ATT CCC AGT CAG AGG CGC TAT (forward) and TGT GCT GCC CTT CTG TTC AAG (reverse). For p21, TCC CAA ACG CAA AGA CTG (forward) and AGG GTT TGC GTT TCT GAG (reverse). For p27, CTG CCC TCC CCA GTC TCT CT (forward) and CAA GCA CCT CGG ATT TT (reverse); for PI3K, AGG TTC ATG TGC TGG ATA CT (forward) and TGG GCT CCT TTA CTA ATC TC (reverse); for Akt ACG ATG AAT GAG GTG TCT GT (forward) and TCT GCT ACG GTG AAG TTG TT (reverse). Primers for GAPDH as reference gene were GGT CGG AGT CAA CGG ATT TG (forward) and ATG AGC CCC AGC CTT CTC CAT (reverse). Primers for miR-22 were GCA CAT GCG AAT AAG CTG CCA GTT GAA GAA (forward) and GAC GAC C CA GTT ATC AGT CCG TTT GGA A (reverse); primers for U6 as reference gene were CGC TTC GGC AGC ACA TAT ACT AAA ATT GGA AC and GCT TCA CGA ATT TGC GTG TCA TCC T TG C (reverse). The PCR products were verified by melting curve analysis and by sequencing.  2.8 Cell transfection Cells were seeded in 96-well or 6-well plates before transient transfection as described previously [41] . At indicated time points, cells were transfected with PTEN specific siRNA, pre-miR-22 or vehicle by using Lipofectamine™ 2000 Transfection Reagent (Introvigen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Then the cells were treated with DWP0016 in the concentration of 0.5, 1, 2 μM and the control were treated with medium in equal volume for 48 h. SiRNAs were synthesized by Introvigen and targeted the following cDNA sequences: for PTEN, 5′-GTA TAG AGC GTG CAG ATA A-3′; for p53, 5′-GCA TCT TAT CCG AGT GGA A-3′. SH-SY5Y cells with transient transfection siRNA were harvested for MTT assay, cell cycle analysis assay and apoptosis assay.  2.9 Luciferase assay Cells were seeded in 96-well plates before being transfected by using Lipofectamine™ 2000 Transfection Reagent (Introvigen) as described previously [42] . Then cells were transfected with PTEN promoter plasmid or vehicles. The PTEN promoter plasmid was kindly given by PhD Nadav Bar et al. [27] . Promoter activity was measured by using a dual luciferase Reporter Assay System (Promega). Relative luciferase activity was analyzed by using a Turner Designs TD20/20 Luminometer (Sunnyvale). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to the activity of the renilla luciferase control. Extracts from at least three independent transfection experiments were assayed in triplicate. The results are shown as means ± SD.  2.10 Western blot analysis SH-SY5Y cells were treated with DWP0016 at concentration of 0.5, 1, 2 μM for 48 h. Protein was abstracted and Western blotting was performed as previously described [43] . Protein concentrations of cell lysates were determined using the Bradford method. Briefly, certain quantized proteins were separated in SDS-PAGE and then were transferred to PVDF membrane. After blocked at room temperature, membranes were incubated with different primary antibodies before visualized and photographed. The antibodies used in the experiments were: anti-PTEN, anti-PI3K, anti-PI3K-phospho-p85, anti-AktSer473 , anti-phosphor-AktSer473 , anti-p21Cip/WAF1 , anti-p27/KIP1  , anti-p53, anti-acetylated-histone H3 and anti-β-actin which were obtained from Santa Cruz. Antibodies of total histone H3 and cleaved PARP were obtained from Cell Signaling Technology.  2.11 Statistical analysis All in vitro  experiments were performed in triplicate and were repeated at least three times. The results presented as mean values ± SD. Statistical significance was performed by using Student t test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) test where appropriate. The significance level was set as *P  < 0.05, **P  < 0.01 and ***P  < 0.001.   3 Results 3.1 DWP0016 effectively inhibited proliferation in five carcinoma cell lines including SH-SY5Y cells but not affect the growth in normal human neurons As results showed in Fig. 2 A–E , DWP0016 exhibited an effectively dose-dependent cell proliferation inhibition against multiple human carcinoma cell lines, including MKN-45, HCT-8 and neuroblastoma cells SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 cells. The calculated IC50 s were much more potent than those of SAHA (Table 1  ). The lowest IC50  was 0.569 μM, which against SH-SY5Y cells. The IC50 s of SAHA against SH-SY5Y cells was 3.951 μM, which was almost 7 times as high as that of DWP0016. Importantly, DWP0016 did not affect the growth in human neurons HN while the IC50  against the cell line was far beyond the effective dose of carcinoma cell lines (Fig. 2 F), which indicated that DWP0016 did not induce significant cytotoxicity in normal cells. These findings suggested DWP0016 effectively inhibited the proliferation in SH-SY5Y cells without general cytotoxicity in normal cells.  3.2 DWP0016 induced G1  phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells As cell cycle analysis results showed, DWP0016 induced a significant G1  accumulation and S and G2  depletion dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 3 A) . With treatment of DWP0016 at the concentration of 1.0 μM, 69.39% cells were blocked at G1  phase, and the proportion was 54.23% in the control, which generated statistical significances compared to that of control (P  < 0.05). As the concentration rose to 2.0 μM, the portion of cells blocking in G1  phase was 72.51% consistently (P  < 0.001). The results suggested the G1  phase proportion of gated SH-SY5Y cells with DWP0016 treatment ascended dose-dependently (Fig. 3 B). Then Annexin-V/FITC staining was performed to detect the apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells with DWP0016 treatment. The data exhibited that DWP0016 induced apoptotic death in these tumor cells dose-dependently (Fig. 3 C). As the results showed in Fig. 3 D, the total apoptosis induced was 15.13% with DWP0016 treatment at the concentration of 0.5 μM, which generated statistical significances compared to that of control (P  < 0.05). The total percentage of apoptotic cells was 33.86% with DWP0016 at the concentration up to 1.0 μM. As the concentration rose to 2.0 μM, the total apoptotic cell proportion was 51.24% consistently (P  < 0.001). The entire necrosis exhibiting in separate up-left quadrant suggested DWP0016 did not induce apparent necrosis in SH-SY5Y cells. These results suggested that DWP0016 induced dose-dependent apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells.  3.3 DWP0016 up-regulated the mRNA level and protein expression of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1  dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells To explore cell cycle arrest molecular mechanisms, we examined the mRNA level and protein expression of G1  cell cycle negative regulators p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1 . Real-time PCR results showed that both mRNA level of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1  were up regulated dose-dependently with DWP0016 exposure (Fig. 4 A) . With treatment of DWP0016 at the concentration of 1.0 μM, the mRNA level of p21 raised to 5.12 fold of that in the control (P  < 0.01). The mRNA level of p27 ascended to 3.02 fold of that in the control, which also generated significant difference to the control (P  < 0.01). As the concentration rose to 2.0 μM, the mRNA level of p21 was 7.27 fold and that of p27 was 5.98 fold compared to that in the control (P  < 0.001). Then we investigated the protein expression of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1 . Expectedly, the protein expression of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1  was promoted dose-dependently with DWP0016 treatment consistently (Fig. 4 B). These results suggested DWP0016 enhanced the transcription and protein expression of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1 , which were associated with the G1  cell cycle induced by DWP0016.  3.4 DWP0016 stimulated caspase activity and induced cleaved PARP expression To investigate whether the induced apoptosis were associated with caspases activation, we examined the activity of caspase-3, -8 and -9 in DWP0016-treated SH-SY5Y cells. We found that DWP0016 significantly activated the activity of caspase-3 and -9 dose-dependently, but not affected that of caspase-8 (Fig. 4 C). With DWP0016 treatment at the concentration of 0.5 μM, the activity of caspase-3 was up-regulated to 116.27% compared to control. As the concentration rose to 1.0 μM, the activity of caspase-3 was promoted to 242.57% compared to control. The activity of caspase-9 was activated with DWP0016 treatment dose-dependently as the up-regulation on caspase-3. DWP0016 did not affect the activity of caspase-8 as no statistical significance between the treated vs  the control (P  > 0.05). We also observed caspase-specific degradation of PARP in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently manner (Fig. 4 D) with DWP0016 treatment consistently. These results showed that both the activity of caspase-3 and caspase-9 were activated with DWP0016. Caspase-3 and caspase-9 activation involved in the apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells.  3.5 DWP0016 induce histone H3 hyper-acetylation in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently The protein expression of total histone H3 and acetylated-H3 in SH-SY5Y cells were investigated by performing Western blotting. As shown in Fig. 5 A , neither DWP0016 nor SAHA affected the expression of total histone H3. Noticeably, an ascending protein expression of acetylated-histone H3 were both observed in DWP0016 and SAHA-treated samples dose-dependently, which confirmed hyper-acetylation induction efficacy of DWP0016 and SAHA. The protein expression was more pronounced in DWP0016-treated samples. The densitometry results were consistent to the protein expression (Fig. 5 B). These results suggested that DWP0016 induced more remarkable histone-H3 acetylation in neuroblastoma cells than SAHA, which was consistent to the better proliferation inhibition in SH-SY5Y cells than SAHA.  3.6 DWP0016 activated PTEN to inhibit PI3K/Akt pathway in SH-SY5Y cells To assess whether DWP0016 affected the mRNA level and expression of PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway, real-time PCR assay was performed to detect the mRNA level of PI3K, Akt and PTEN. The results suggested that DWP0016 did not affect the mRNA level of PI3K nor that of Akt, but significantly up regulated the mRNA level of PTEN in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6 A) . At concentration of 1.0 μM, DWP0016 elevated the mRNA level of PTEN to18.38 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.01). As concentration rose to 2.0 μM, the mRNA level was up regulated to 69.25 fold compared to the untreated (P  < 0.001). Then we investigated the protein expression of PI3K, phosphorylation form of PI3K (p-P85), Aktser473 , phosphorylation form of Aktser473  (p-Aktser473 ), p53 and PTEN. As shown in Fig. 6 B, DWP0016 augmented the protein expression of PTEN dose-dependently. In contrast, the protein expression of p-p85 and p-Akt significantly declined while the expression of PI3K and Akt were not affected. Interestingly, the protein expression of p53 was not affected with DWP0016 at concentrations as indicated. Dual-luciferases report assay results suggested DWP0016 activated the activity of PTEN promoter dose-dependently (Fig. 6 C) dose-dependently. These results showed DWP0016 up-regulated PTEN to inhibit PI3K/Akt pathway without p53 interference in SH-SY5Y cells.  3.7 DWP0016 down-regulated miR-22 to up-regulate PTEN mRNA level and protein expression Intensive investigations were performed to explore the regulation mechanism of PTEN. Firstly, we identified one miR-22 recognition element within 3′-UTR of human PTEN gene (Fig. 6 D), which is highly conserved among vertebrates (www.Targetscan.org ). We then performed real-time PCR to determine the level of miR-22 in SH-SY5Y cells with DWP0016 at concentrations as indicated. As shown in Fig. 6 E, DWP0016 decreased the level of miR-22 in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently. With DWP0016 treatment at concentration of 0.5 μM, the level of miR-22 shrank to 0.598 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.05). At concentration of 1.0 μM, DWP0016 decreased the level of miR-22 to 0.375 fold of the control (P  < 0.01). As concentration rose to 2.0 μM, the level of miR-22 shrank to 0.127 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.01) in SH-SY5Y cells. We investigate the mRNA level of PTEN in transiently transfected SH-SY5Y cells with miRNA-specific precursor (pre-miR-22) exposed to DWP0016. As shown in Fig. 6 F, the mRNA level of PTEN was decreased to 0.612 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.01) with pre-miR-22. With DWP0016 treatment at concentration of 1.0 μM, the mRNA level of PTEN increased to 7.895 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.01) in pre-miR-22-transfected SH-SY5Y cells. Without pre-miR-22, DWP0016 elevated the mRNA level of PTEN to18.38 fold to the untreated (P  < 0.01). We then detected the protein expression of PTEN in transfected SH-SY5Y cells. Expectedly, the protein expression was consistent to the mRNA level regulations, which confirmed the regulation on PTEN by DWP0016 (Fig. 6 G). These results suggested that down-regulations of miR-22 by DWP0016 facilitated the activation of PTEN in SH-SY5Y cells.  3.8 Knock down of PTEN but not p53 sufficiently blocked the cell growth, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis caused by DWP0016 A siRNA assay specific to knock down PTEN was performed to verify the role of PTEN in DWP0016-treated cells. We examined the protein expression of PI3K, p-PI3K, Akt, p-Akt and PTEN in PTEN silenced SH-SY5Y cells by DWP0016 exposure or not. The expression of PTEN was negative in PTEN silenced cells regardless of DWP0016 treatment. The expression of PI3K, p-PI3K, Akt, and p-Akt were not affected (Fig. 7 A) , which confirmed the inhibition of PI3K/Akt pathway was through PTEN activation. As the results shown (Fig. 7 B), at concentration of DWP0016 in 1.0 μM, the cell viability in SHSY5Y cells with PTEN siRNA was 95.17% which made no statistical difference to the control (P  > 0.05). In contrast, the cell viability without siRNA by the DWP0016 treated was 24.91% (P  < 0.001). Additionally, the G1  of cell cycle distributions arrest caused by DWP0016 was blocked by PTEN siRNA, which made no statistical difference between the untreated and the treated with siRNA (P  > 0.05) (Fig. 7 C). Moreover, the total apoptosis was 5.02% with PTEN siRNA whereas the value was 48.49% (P  < 0.001) without siRNA (Fig. 7 D). As the results shown (Fig. 7 E), at concentration of DWP0016 in 1.0 μM, the cell viability in SHSY5Y cells with p53 siRNA was 56.31% which made statistical difference to the control (P  < 0.05). Meanwhile, the total apoptosis was 22.46% with p53 siRNA which also made statistical difference to the control (P  < 0.001). These results exhibited that knock-down of p53 did not sufficiently block effects induced by DWP0016 treatment. Instead, knock-down of PTEN sufficiently blocked the cell growth inhibition, cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 treatment. In other words, p53-independent PTEN was required for the efficacy of DWP0016 and PTEN was a crucial target gene for DWP0016.   4 Discussion In this study, we evaluated a HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 inhibited the tumor growth of neuroblastoma in vitro . DWP0016 induced G1  phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in SH-SYS5Y cells, which were associated to regulations on p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1  and caspases-3 and -9. Down-regulation of miR-22 by DWP0016 activated PTEN in promoter, mRNA and protein expression level. As shown in Fig. 8  , DWP0016 up regulated PTEN to inhibit PI3K/Akt pathway and finally induced the growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. Neuroblastomas are the most common brain tumor and characterized as a fatal malignancy tumor for children. Its clinical heterogeneity, from spontaneous regression in infants to relentless progression in older children, makes the effects of traditional chemotherapies are limited. Focusing on novel targets and approach enhanced the therapeutic effects for the treatments [2]  while required chemo-resistant risk exists. Explorations on more safe and potent approaches make epigenetic regulation agents such as HDAC inhibitor be regarded as promising candidates for neuroblastoma treatments. Their efficacy has been widely recognized as Vorinostat (SAHA) in 2006 and Romidepsin (FK228) in 2009 which were separately licensed to treat CTCL [44] . Guided by the antitumor efficacy of HDAC inhibitor, different HDAC inhibitors are used to treat neuroblastoma [45,46] . However, the effects and involved molecular mechanisms remained largely unknown. The results (Fig. 2 A–E) showed HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 effectively inhibited the cell growth in 3 neuroblastoma cell lines (SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y and IMR-32) and another 2 carcinoma cell lines (MKN-45 and HCT-8) dose dependently. The lowest IC50  was against SH-SY5Y cells which suggested the potential of DWP0016 in neuroblastoma treatments (Table 1 ). Importantly, the results indicated that DWP0016 did not induce significant cytotoxicity in normal cells (Fig. 2 F). The flow cytometry analysis suggested DWP0016 induced G1  cell cycle arrest and apoptosis dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 3 A–D). Molecular mechanisms studies showed DWP0016 up regulated the mRNA level and expressions level of p21Cip/WAF1  and p27kip1  dose-dependently, which contributed to G1  cell cycle arrest (Fig. 4 A and B). Caspases activity (Fig. 4 C) and cleaved PARP protein expression (Fig. 4 D) suggested the activation of caspase-3 and caspase-9 involved in the apoptosis caused with DWP0016 treatment. Both cell cycle arrest and apoptosis contributed the growth inhibition caused by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells, which made DWP0016 more potent. As HDAC inhibitor induced histone hyper-acetylation to exhibit anti-tumor efficacy and less side-effects, we detected the acetylation of histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells. Previous reported showed DWP0016 was more effective to inhibit HDAC enzyme activity than SAHA in U251 glioblastoma cells [47] , which led the more obvious acetylated-H3 in DWP0016 treated groups than that of SAHA. Expectedly, the results showed DWP0016 induced much more remarkable acetylated-histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells than SAHA (Fig. 5 A and B) as in U251 cells. These results are also consistent to previous reports about other HDAC inhibitors [37,48] . We notice that the viability of cells with DWP0016 at the concentration of 1.0 μM was not lower than that of cells with SAHA at the concentration of 5.0 μM though the expression of acetylated-H3 with DWP0016 was more makeable. In our conditions, it was enough for DWP0016 to induce hyper-acetylation of histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells at the concentrations as indicated, which facilitated the growth inhibition. As doses became higher, other mechanisms might involve in the effects of HDAC inhibitors such as cell cycle arrest, apoptosis and other regulations beyond hyper-acetylation of histone H3. These need further investigations and the explorations were on our agenda. After all, all these results suggest HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 is a potent HDAC inhibitor to treat neuroblastoma with its proliferation inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induction efficacy. One paper examined the gene status of tumor suppressor PTEN in 106 tumors from patients with neuroblastoma and found PTEN was rarely mutated but 100% of tumors expressed PTEN protein [49] . Interestingly, we found both the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN are up-regulated dose-dependently with DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 6 A and B). As activation of PTEN inhibited PI3K/Akt pathway, we found DWP0016 significantly down regulated the protein expression of p-PI3K and p-Akt. These results were consistent to studies with certain HDAC inhibitors about the regulations on PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway in other carcinoma cells [50–52] . Previous reports showed promotion of PTEN-p53 physical association and the recruitment of the PTEN-p53 complex to the p53 binding sites in the PTEN promoter, leading to PTEN transcriptional activation [53,54] . Effective acetylation of histone H3 makes the structure of chromatin relatively loose and then facilitates gene transcription and expression [30,31] , which contributes to the molecular regulations of most HDAC inhibitor. Further investigations showed the protein expression of p53 was not affected with DWP0016 (Fig. 6 B), regardless of the wild-type p53 status in SH-SY5Y cells. The effects on p53 were consistent to the effects with DWP0016 in another wild-type p53 harboring glioblastoma cell line U-87 reported but not U251 cells by us [37,47] . However, DWP0016 induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells but not in U-87 cells. Considering the PTEN mutant status in U-87 cells [55]  but PTEN wild-type status in SH-SY5Y cells, the differences might due to PTEN status between cell lines. Besides, p53-independent PTEN activation induced by DWP0016 attenuated the required chemo-resistant possibility due to effects on p53. Our novel findings suggest that activating PTEN is practicable to exhibit antitumor potential in neuroblastoma with a HDAC inhibitor such as DWP0016. Intensive investigations suggested DWP0016 activated the activity of PTEN promoter dose-dependently (Fig. 6 C) by performing a dual-luciferases report assay. Interestingly, the activity of PTEN promoter with DWP0016 treatment of 4 μM was lower than that of 2 μM though still higher than the control (Fig. 6 C). In our conditions, DWP0016 activated PTEN expression at certain concentrations (<2 μM) which was enough sensitive to SH-SY5Y cells and other tumor cell lines listed in this research. These observations indicated the possibility that higher concentration of DWP0016 might exhibit different effects on PTEN which remained another issue. Previous studies reported the activity of PTEN promoter could be regulated by multiple factors besides p53 such as Egr-1 [56] , Tat [57] , and CBF-1 [58] etc . Recent reports show epigenetic regulations such as methylation and microRNAs also play important roles in the regulations on PTEN promoter. Accumulating evidence reveals that microRNAs involved in the regulations of PTEN, which shed a light in PTEN regulations. According to the studies, PTEN was found to be regulated by multiple miRs including miR-21 [59] , miR-494 [60] , miR-222 [61] , miR-214 [62]  and 26a [63]  in different reports. Though multiple miRNAs could regulate PTEN expression, the regulations between gene-miRNA may be specific and depend on diverse upstream signaling pathways. miR-22 is a novel micro-oncogene and downregulates PTEN levels acting directly through a specific site on PTEN 3′UTR, which facilitated to associate with tumor suppression function of PTEN. The reason why PTEN was affected by miR-22 was due to an important regulatory element in their promoters. Reversely, one paper showed miR-22 is a tumor-suppressing microRNA and overexpression of miR-22 activated PTEN signaling [26–29] . The controversial reports about PTEN and miR-22 need more identification, especially for cancer treatments. We investigated miR-22 level in DWP0016-treated SH-SY5Y cells and found DWP0016 down-regulated the level of miR-22 dose-dependently (Fig. 6 E). As shown in Fig. 6 F and G, pre-miR-22 down-regulated the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN. Regardless the down-regulation of PTEN with pre-miR-22, DWP0016 up-regulated the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN (Fig. 6 F and G). Then we performed a siRNA assay to identify the role of PTEN in DWP0016-treated SH-SY5Y cells. As the siRNA results shown in Fig. 7 A–F, silencing PTEN but not p53 sufficiently blocked the cell growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings suggested that PTEN was required for the antitumor efficacy of DWP0016. There are reports about other HDAC inhibitors such as trichostatin A (TSA) affected microRNA expression to facilitate apoptosis in different carcinoma cells especially in chemoresistant tumor cells [64–66] . Our studies first report that HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 was able to down-regulate miR-22 in neuroblastoma. In this study, our novel findings identified miR-22 suppressed PTEN in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. Besides, associated to the suppression of miR-22 with PTEN, our studies suggested that DWP0016 suppressed miR-22 to activate PTEN in SH-SY5Y cells, which highlighted the unique mechanisms of DWP0016. How DWP0016 down-regulated miR-22 remained unknown. Further studies about DWP0016 may shed more light on these subjects. In conclusion, we reported that DWP0016 induced tumor growth inhibition in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. DWP0016 arrested cell cycle, induced apoptosis dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells. Suppression of miR-22 by DWP0016 activated PTEN promoter activity, transcription and protein expression, which inhibited PI3K/Akt pathway. Our findings suggest DWP0016 is a promising antitumor candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with PTEN and microRNA regulations. title: Chemotherapy-Induced Apoptosis in a Transgenic Model of Neuroblastoma Proceeds Through <ce:italic>p53</ce:italic> Induction
abstract: Chemoresistance in neuroblastoma is a significant issue complicating treatment of this common pediatric solid tumor. MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas are infrequently mutated at p53 and are chemosensitive at diagnosis but acquire p53 mutations and chemoresistance with relapse. Paradoxically, Myc-driven transformation is thought to require apoptotic blockade. We used the TH-MYCN transgenic murine model to examine the role of p53-driven apoptosis on neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and the response to chemotherapy. Tumors formed with high penetrance and low latency in p53-haploinsufficient TH-MYCN mice. Cyclophosphamide (CPM) induced a complete remission in p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors, mirroring the sensitivity of childhood neuroblastoma to this agent. Treated tumors showed a prominent proliferation block, induction of p53 protein, and massive apoptosis proceeding through induction of the Bcl-2 homology domain-3-only proteins PUMA and Bim, leading to the activation of Bax and cleavage of caspase-3 and -9. Apoptosis induced by CPM was reduced in p53-haploinsufficient tumors. Treatment of MYCN-expressing human neuroblastoma cell lines with CPM induced apoptosis that was suppressible by siRNA to p53. Taken together, the results indicate that the p53 pathway plays a significant role in opposing MYCN-driven oncogenesis in a mouse model of neuroblastoma and that basal inactivation of the pathway is achieved in progressing tumors. This, in part, explains the striking sensitivity of such tumors to chemotoxic agents that induce p53-dependent apoptosis and is consistent with clinical observations that therapy-associated mutations in p53 are a likely contributor to the biology of tumors at relapse and secondarily mediate resistance to therapy.

All rights reserved 1522-8002/08/$25.00 DOI 10.1593/neo.08778     Introduction   Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of child­hood [1]. The proto-oncogene MYCN is amplified in one third of neuroblastomas and is associated with high-risk disease and poor sur­vival [1–5]. The ability of Myc proteins to induce malignant transfor­mation is limited by coordinate induction of both proliferation and apoptosis [6–8]. Consequently, mutations of p53 are common in sev­eral Myc-driven malignancies at diagnosis and enhance oncogenesis.   In neuroblastoma, genetic defects in the p53 pathway function (mutation in p53 or p14ARF, amplification of MDM2) are rare at di­agnosis but are present in cell lines established from patients treated with prolonged therapy [9–12]. In the absence of such mutations, am­plification of MYCN in newly diagnosed neuroblastomas is typically associated with epigenetic abnormalities that impair apoptosis: silenc­ing of caspase-8 or overexpression of the antiapoptotic proteins Bcl-2 and survivin [13–15]. These events are independently associated with poor outcome in neuroblastoma and represent potential mechanisms contributing to malignant progression [13,15,16].   Despite such defects in apoptotic signaling, newly diagnosed neuro­blastoma tumors typically respond to chemotherapeutics such as cyclo­phosphamide (CPM) irrespective of risk group, suggesting that epigenetic regulation of apoptotic pathways is either insufficient to block apoptosis in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy or is not initially present at diagnosis [17,18]. Because virtually all patients respond to initial therapy, outcome in this disease is mainly determined by the like­lihood of relapse, with high-risk patients (including tumors that show amplification of MYCN ) frequently relapsing with drug-resistant tu­mors [10,19].   The TH-MYCN model shows that coordinate mutation of p53 is not required for MYCN-driven oncogenesis in neuroblastoma, mirroring the situation in human high-risk tumors. It follows that apoptosis is functionally suppressed by other means. However, this presents a paradox in that MYCN-driven murine neuroblastomas retain exquisite sensitivity to chemotherapeutics, which exert their effects through induction of apoptosis. To examine this question, we sought to determine whether the p53 pathway was active or in­active in TH-MYCN and whether induction of the pathway occurred in response to chemotherapy.   TH-MYCN is a native neuroblastoma model in which tumorigene­sis is driven by targeted expression of a TH-MYCN transgene in the neural crest of transgenic mice [20]. These animals develop an aggres­sive malignancy that is morphologically, genetically, and clinically sim­ilar to human high-risk MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma [21,22]. We show that p53 haploinsufficiency enhances the effect of MYCN-driven transformation in neuroblastoma, that basal p53 pathway function and apoptosis are suppressed in such tumors (in contrast to in vitro observations), that haploinsufficiency amplifies the effect of MYCN on transformation in neuroblastoma, and that the chemoresponse of effective agents such as CPM requires intact p53-driven apopto­sis. Mechanistically, CPM induces p53 and activates a variety of p53 targets critical to apoptosis, including PUMA, Bim, Bax, caspase-3, caspase-9, and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP). The in vivo re­sponse of TH-MYCN–driven tumors to CPM is similar to that ob­served in cultured human cell lines treated with CPM. In three cell lines with equivalent levels of p53 protein but increasing levels of Mycn, the apoptotic response to CPM correlated with the induction of p53 and could be blocked by siRNA to p53.   Taken together, these data document the activity in murine tu­mors of a frontline chemotherapeutic agent used in children with newly diagnosed neuroblastoma and add to evidence validating mice transgenic for TH-MYCN as a preclinical platform for developmental therapeutics. Furthermore, these observations highlight the utility of mice transgenic for TH-MYCN as a preclinical model in which to delineate the kinetics and details of apoptotic signaling in response to CPM. The induction and functional activation of p53 in these tumors reinforce the importance of p53 signaling in the therapeutic response to cytotoxic chemotherapy. These observations are also con­sistent with clinical data that cytotoxic chemotherapy selects for loss of p53 function, that recurrence in neuroblastoma is subsequently driven by p53 mutation, and that p53 mutation in relapsed tumors contributes secondarily to therapeutic resistance [10,23,24].   Materials and Methods   Cell Culture and Treatments   SHEP, SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y, and Kelly neuroblastoma cell lines were obtained from the University of California at San Francisco. Cells were grown in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium with 10% FBS at 37°C. 4-Hydroxyperocyclophosphamide (4OH-CPM) was obtained from Susan Ludeman (University of North Carolina) and was dissolved at 20 mg/ml in water. For in vivo therapy, CPM from the University of California at San Francisco Clinical Pharmacy was dissolved at 1 mg/ml.   Proliferation and Apoptosis Assays   Cell growth and proliferation were assessed by soluble tetrazolium (WST-1; Roche, Indianapolis, IN). Necrosis and apoptosis were assessed using a Cell Death Detection ELISA (Roche) that detects intracellular or released nucleosomal H2b DNA. Values were cor­rected for vehicle (DMSO). Cells were plated and assayed at 6 to 24 hours using a Synergy HT-1 spectrophotometer (Biotek, Winooski, VT). Percent toxicity was standardized using Triton X-100 as a positive control (0-100 mM).   Immunoblot Analysis and Antibodies   Cells were suspended in nondenaturing lysis buffer (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA) with 0.5% SDS. Lysates were sonicated and cleared at 14,000g at 4°C. Protein content was assayed by the BCA method (Pierce, Rockford, IL), and 20 to 40 µgofprotein was analyzed on 4% to 12% gradient denaturing gels (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). Membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with pri­mary antibodies [cleaved caspase-3 (9664; Cell Signaling Technology), caspase-9 (9508; Cell Signaling Technology), p53 (9282; Cell Signal­ing Technology), Bim (4582; Cell Signaling Technology), Bax (2772; Cell Signaling Technology), PARP (9542; Cell Signaling Technology), PUMA (4976; Cell Signaling Technology), and ß-tubulin (05-661; Upstate, Billerica, MA)] and visualized using HRP-conjugated second­ary antibodies (Calbiochem, Gibbstown, NJ) and ECL-Plus reagents.   Immunohistochemistry   For frozen sections, mice were killed after therapy, and tumors were embedded in Tissue-Tex O.C.T. compound (Sakura, Torrance, CA), cooled at -80°C (24 hours), sectioned at 4-µmthickness, mounted on Superfrost slides (Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA), and placed in 70% ethanol (1 hour at 4°C). Slides were washed three times with wash buffer (Dako, Carpinteria, CA), treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide (for 10 minutes), rewashed, blocked with casein (for 10 minutes), and incubated with caspase-3 antibody (CST 9664) at a dilution of 1:100 at room temperature in a humidi­fied chamber (for 2 hours). Slides were rewashed three times and in­cubated with rabbit Envision+ secondary antibody (Dako) at room temperature in a humidified chamber (for 30 minutes) treated with Dako DAB+ complex (for 4 minutes), rinsed with water, counter­stained with Gills modified hematoxylin (American Master Tech, Lodi, CA), dehydrated, and mounted for analysis. Paraffin-embedded tissues were cut and mounted, deparaffinized with xylene through graded alcohol to water, and then placed in PBS. Heat-induced epi­tope retrieval was performed at 120°C in citrate buffer at pH 6.0, fol­lowed by treatment in 3% peroxide (for 20 minutes). Washing and antibody incubations were as previously mentioned. Ki-67 staining in paraffinized sections was performed using a Ki-67 rat primary anti­body (M7249; Dako) in a 3-hour incubation followed by process­ing as previously mentioned. Development was with streptavidin HRP (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ) at a dilution of 1:100 for 1 hour at room temperature.   In Vivo Therapy in TH-MYCN Transgenic Mice   TH-MYCN mice were maintained in hemizygotic matings as pre­viously described [20]. Hemizygous TH-MYCN were serially crossed to p53+/- mice (FVBN) [25] and E2F1-luciferase mice (FVBN) [26] for more than four generations to re-establish tumor penetrance in the 129X1/SvJ strain. A similar approach was used in luciferase crosses. For the analysis of the in vivo effects of CPM on tumor growth in mice transgenic for TH-MYCN (in strain 129X1/SvJ), a tumor intervention design was implemented. The assay end point was tumor mass. In par­allel experiments, tumor response and progression were confirmed using luciferase bioimaging of TH-MYCN/E2F1-Luc doubly trans­genic animals, in which a luciferase signal is emitted from proliferating tumor tissue and is a surrogate indicator of Mycn activity. Animals (seven per arm) with palpable tumors (approximately 60 days of life) were treated three times per week with intraperitoneal injections of CPM (150 mg/kg in 100 µl of saline) or vehicle (saline) and were then killed. In parallel, animals (three per arm) were followed by noninvasive imaging, using the Xenogen IVIS Lumina system (Caliper Life Sciences, Hopkinton, MA) with a background bioluminescence setting of 38,000 photons/sec per square centimeters. At sacrifice, tumors were imaged, excised, measured, weighed, and snap-frozen for further analysis. Lysates were prepared for immunoblot analysis as pre­viously mentioned, except that tumors were initially homogenized in TBS with protease inhibitors (Compleat; Roche, Inc.) before lysis. Significance analysis was performed using the Student’s t test. All ani­mals were handled in accordance with institutional guidelines for safe and ethical treatment of mice.   Results   Effect of p53 Heterozygosity on Neuroblastoma Tumor Formation in Mice Transgenic for TH-MYCN   Given the critical role of p53 in regulating myc-driven onco­genesis, we sought to evaluate induction of apoptosis by p53 in spontaneously growing neuroblastoma tumors originating within a native murine background. We therefore used the well-characterized TH-MYCN neuroblastoma model in which tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)–mediated overexpression of MYCN is targeted to the periph­eral neural crest [20]. This model faithfully recapitulates high-risk human neuroblastoma tumorigenesis by all major clinicopathologic criteria. To evaluate the effect of p53 dysfunction on TH-MYCN– driven neuroblastoma tumor formation, we introduced TH-MYCN into a p53-deficient background by serial crosses against animals with an inactivated germ line p53 allele [25]. Tumors arose in doubly transgenic animals with higher penetrance and reduced latency (Figure 1A). The initial anatomic appearance of these tumors was similar to that of p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors (Figure 1B), but end-stage tumors were larger and were characterized by a higher density of proliferating neuroblasts and lower levels of apoptosis and necrosis on histologic analysis (Figure 1, C and D). Taken together, the data imply that, in neuroblastoma tumor progression, inactiva­tion of p53 could enhance MYCN oncogenicity, at least in part by decoupling the growth-stimulatory activity of MYCN from its ability to concurrently drive apoptosis. Cyclophosphamide Inhibits Tumor Proliferation and Stimulates Apoptosis In Vivo   To analyze the effect of CPM on apoptosis, necrosis, and prolifera­tion, we treated a cohort of transgenic animals with early, established tumors, sacrificing animals at several time points within 24 hours of CPM treatment. Tumors showed no changes in vascularity (data not shown) and exhibited no obvious cellular or structural changes (observable apoptosis or necrosis) in response to CPM treatment (Fig­ure W1, A–C). In vehicle-treated tumors, immunoreactivity for the proliferation marker Ki-67 was positive in most nuclei (Figure 3, A and B). In response to CPM, Ki-67 labeling decreased dramatically even by 24 hours (Figure 3C). Whereas control tumors had negligible staining for the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 3D), high levels of cleaved caspase-3 were observed 3 and 6 hours after treatment with CPM (Figure 3, E and F ). A wave of apoptosis throughout the tumor was demonstrated at low power (Figure 3, H–J ), with maximal staining visible at 6 hours after treatment. At 24 hours, apoptotic stain­ing was associated with foci of necrosis (Figure 3J, inset). Significantly, levels of apoptosis induced by similar treatment of p53-haplodeficient tumors with CPM were minimal, as assessed by immunostaining for cleaved caspase-3 (Figure W2). No significant differences in apoptosis were seen by immunohistologic analysis in vehicle-treated p53+/- versus p53+/+ tumors (data not shown).   Apoptosis in Tumors Treated with Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Is Driven by p53   To evaluate apoptotic signaling in response to CPM, we treated a cohort of early tumor-bearing transgenic animals and assessed levels of key apoptotic proteins by immunoblot (Figure 4A). In contrast to basal apoptotic activity detectable by immunoblot analysis of cul­tured neuroblastoma cell lines, activation of the p53 pathway and caspase-3 cleavage were minimal in vehicle-treated tumors, consistent with the low-level caspase-3 staining seen in Figure 4. Rapid induc­tion of p53 was observed at 3 hours after treatment with CPM, with a peak at 6 hours after treatment (Figure 4A). Cleaved caspase-3 and -9 were maximal at 6 hours after treatment and were sustained dur­ing a 12-hour period. These data indicate that basal apoptotic activity in spontaneously progressing TH-MYCN neuroblastomas is minimal but that p53-driven apoptosis is intact and can be strongly induced in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy.   CPM Treatment of Murine Neuroblastoma Activates Apoptosis   PUMA and Bim are Bcl-2 homology 3 (BH3)–only proteins, proapoptotic components of the mitochondrial cell death pathway, and are critical effectors of p53-induced apoptosis in Myc protein– driven tumors [27]. In response to CPM treatment, PUMA was strongly induced in vivo, peaking at 3 hours and dissipating by 12 hours (Figure 4A). Bax, a downstream target of PUMA and a criti­cal effector of myc-induced mitochondrial apoptosis, was strongly expressed (Figure 4B). Bim, a BH3-only protein necessary for apop­tosis in myc-driven lymphoma, was induced prominently. Cleavage of caspases-3 and -9 (Figure 4A)and PARP (Figure4B) occurred concurrently, indicating high levels of apoptosis. Taken together, these findings indicate that the proapoptotic effect of CPM proceeds through the intrinsic p53 regulatory pathway of BH3 proteins, im­plicating PUMA, Bax, and Bim as key effectors of p53 function in primary murine neuroblastoma tumors.
