(McCarty et al., 2011 ) Neurotoxic effects are concentration-dependent, often showing a biphasic pattern in which low concentrations alter neurotrophic hormone levels, while higher, sustained concentrations are directly cytotoxic and trigger apoptotic cell death (Bathina and Das, 2015 ; Ogura et al., 2014 ). Prolonged arsenic exposure may lead to severe adverse health effects, including metabolic disorders (e.g., diabetes), malignancies, skin pigmentation abnormalities, and cognitive impairments (Ratnaike, 2003 ). The inherent toxicity of arsenic, a naturally occurring metalloid present in groundwater and the food chain, is primarily attributed to its inorganic forms, such as arsenite and arsenate (Tchounwou et al., 2012 ). Arsenate can disrupt the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) backbone due to its structural similarity to phosphate, which leads to its erroneous incorporation in place of phosphate (Singh and Giri, 2018 ). In addition, arsenite binds to sulfur-containing enzymes and proteins, impairing their function (Tchounwou et al., 2012 ). Beyond these direct molecular interactions, arsenic also exerts adverse effects mediated by excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and the activation of epigenetic modifications, which collectively alter the expression and function of key hormones and enzymes (Tchounwou et al., 2012 ). This disruption of the neuroendocrine axis highlights how environmental toxins like arsenic can impair critical hormonal signaling pathways, such as that of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which is essential for neuronal maintenance and survival (Elsayed and Foo, 2025a ). Furthermore, arsenic-induced cellular stress frequently converges on the mitochondrial (intrinsic) apoptotic pathway (Yen et al., 2012 ). Understanding this pathway is essential for the present work, as it provides the mechanistic context in which survival signals and stress responses determine cell fate. Upon arsenic exposure, DNA damage activates tumor protein 53 (p53), which promotes pro-apoptotic signaling while suppressing the anti-apoptotic function of B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2). This imbalance favors mitochondrial cytochrome c  release, leading to activation of caspase-9 and subsequent cleavage of caspase-3 (Mustafa et al., 2024 ; Shen and White, 2001 ; Ninomiya et al., 2014 ). Activated caspase-3 cleaves poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), a hallmark event of apoptosis that disrupts DNA repair and promotes DNA fragmentation, thereby driving cells toward programmed death and contributing to neurodegeneration (Chaitanya et al., 2010 ). Under normal conditions, sustained Bcl-2 expression attenuates this cascade; however, suppression of survival growth signaling reduces Bcl-2's protective role, thereby amplifying caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage (Puig et al., 2001 ; Zhang et al., 2012 ). Accumulating evidence indicates that arsenic can interfere with critical pro-survival signaling cascades, particularly those regulated by growth factor pathways (Szymkowicz et al., 2017 ; Ahmed et al., 2013 ). One of the key growth factors involved in neuronal survival is IGF-1, a neurotrophic hormone pivotal for maintaining normal brain function (Wrigley et al., 2017 ). This hormone enhances neuronal survival and growth primarily through the activation of the Ras/Raf/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling cascades (Fig. 1  ). Clinical correlational evidence supports the neuroprotective role of IGF-1. For instance, a two-year prospective study reported a positive association between increased IGF-1 levels and better neurological and memory function in Parkinson's disease patients (Pellecchia et al., 2014 ). Furthermore, direct in vivo evidence from intervention studies indicates that early IGF-1 administration promotes functional recovery after intracranial hemorrhage and improves neuronal performance (Nowrangi et al., 2019 ). IGF-1/AKT signaling modulates multiple checkpoints in the apoptotic cascade (Ghorbani et al., 2015 ). By activating Murine double minute 2 (MDM2), IGF-1/AKT reduces p53 stability and thereby suppresses stress-induced apoptosis (Fig. 2  ). Moreover, AKT promotes the upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins, including Bcl-2, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c  release and consequently prevents caspase-3 activation (Liu et al., 2020 ). During disease development, the equilibrium between pro-survival members of the Bcl-2 protein family and pro-apoptotic members shifts toward the pro-apoptotic factors, making neurons more vulnerable to programmed cell death and elevating the risk of neuronal loss (Callens et al., 2021 ; Kudo et al., 2012 ; Cen et al., 2021 ; Kirkin et al., 2004 ). In addition, AKT preserves DNA integrity and genomic stability by inhibiting the activation of the key executioner enzyme caspase-3. This inhibition prevents caspase-3–mediated cleavage of PARP, a critical event in apoptotic cell death and DNA fragmentation (Ghorbani et al., 2015 ; Jeong et al., 2008 ). Interestingly, the insulin and IGF-1 signaling pathways share significant structural homology, particularly in their substrate-binding domains, leading to the activation of common downstream pathways, such as the PI3K/AKT and Ras/Raf/MAPK cascades (Higashi et al., 2013 ). Although insulin has been shown to protect against arsenic toxicity (Niyomchan et al., 2015 ), the specific role of IGF-1 and its downstream mechanism involving the AKT/p53/Bcl-2 axis in counteracting arsenic-induced neurotoxicity remains entirely unexplored. For this investigation, the human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line was selected based on its established relevance in neurotoxicology studies, its capacity to differentiate into neuron-like cells, and its well-characterized IGF-1/PI3K/AKT signaling response (Wisessaowapak et al., 2024 ; Guan et al., 2023 ). The preservation of neuronal integrity is essential for maintaining cognitive function and neural circuitry, underscoring the importance of identifying mechanisms to counteract neurotoxic insults (Elsayed and Foo, 2025a ; Gazerani, 2025 ). This study is the first to investigate whether IGF-1 confers neuroprotection by rescuing AKT signaling to modulate key apoptotic regulators and DNA fragmentation in arsenic-exposed neuronal cells.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Cell culture Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line (ATCC, USA) was cultured in a complete medium containing an equal mix of Ham's F12 and Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), along with 100 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 mM l -glutamine (all from Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Cells were maintained under controlled incubation conditions at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ atmosphere. Retinoic acid (RA) was used to induce differentiation of SH-SY5Y cells where indicated. Cells were treated with sodium arsenite (NaAsO₂) in the absence or presence of human IGF-1. All compounds (RA, NaAsO₂, IGF-1) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich, USA.  2.2 Treatment To best address distinct research questions, SH-SY5Y cells were used in two optimized states: a differentiated, neuron-like state was induced with RA to provide a more physiologically relevant model for investigating IGF-1/AKT signaling (Niyomchan et al., 2015 ). Conversely, for apoptosis studies, undifferentiated cells were used to prevent the potential confounding influence of RA's inherent pro-survival effects (Kovalevich and Langford, 2013 ). The IGF-1 concentration (10 ng/mL) and treatment durations, 15 min for acute signaling analysis and 30 min as a pre-treatment for protection assays, were selected based on well-established protocols proven to robustly activate AKT phosphorylation and confer neuroprotection in neuronal models (Niyomchan et al., 2015 ; Wisessaowapak et al., 2024 ; Kovalevich and Langford, 2013 ; Humbert et al., 2002 ; Mookherjee et al., 2007 ). This dosage and timing were further confirmed in the pilot studies, which demonstrated reliable AKT activation under serum-free conditions, validating their suitability for assessing the pathway's protective role against apoptosis. First, to determine the impact of arsenic on neuronal apoptosis and the potential protective effect of IGF-1, undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells were seeded in 60 mm dishes, cultured in a standard growth medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 mM l -glutamine, and allowed to reach ∼90 % confluence. Cells were then pretreated with or without IGF-1 (10 ng/mL) for 30 min, followed by exposure to various concentrations of NaAsO₂ (0, 10, 20, or 50 μM) for 24 h. Moreover, to evaluate the impact of arsenic on IGF-1/AKT signaling and the protective effect of IGF-1 treatment on this pathway, SH-SY5Y cells were seeded in 60-mm dishes and allowed to adhere until ∼50% confluent. Cell differentiation was induced by switching to low-serum medium (1% FBS) supplemented with 10 μM RA for three days, and morphological changes were monitored. Subsequently, the differentiation medium was replaced, and the cells were treated with graded concentrations of NaAsO₂ at 0 (control), 1, 5, and 10 μM for 3 days to assess the effects of sustained arsenic exposure on neuronal function. Notably, the 5 μM concentration, equivalent to ∼375 parts per billion (ppb), reflects levels reported in highly contaminated regions and has been associated with an increased risk of neurological disorders (Wasserman et al., 2004 ). After 3 days of induction with NaAsO₂, the medium was replaced with serum-free medium for 2 h, followed by stimulation with 10 ng/mL IGF-1 for 15 min to compare treated and untreated cells. IGF-1 was administered after arsenic exposure to assess its ability to rescue IGF-1/AKT signaling and thereby promote cell growth and differentiation (Niyomchan et al., 2015 ; Wisessaowapak et al., 2024 ; Kovalevich and Langford, 2013 ; Humbert et al., 2002 ; Mookherjee et al., 2007 ). Furthermore, IGF-1 was administered in a serum-free medium to eliminate the influence of other growth factors that could independently activate the AKT pathway. This ensured that any observed AKT activation was exclusively due to IGF-1 stimulation (Zhou et al., 2013 ). In addition, the rationale for employing different concentration ranges of NaAsO₂ in differentiated versus undifferentiated cells is twofold. First, the lower concentrations (1–10 μM) used in differentiated, neuron-like cells are intended to model sustained, environmentally relevant exposure levels that impair neurotrophic signaling over time. Second, the higher concentrations (10–50 μM) used in undifferentiated cells are standard for efficiently inducing a robust apoptotic response within the 24-h timeframe of the apoptosis assays, allowing for clear quantification of cell death and the protective effects of IGF-1 (Wisessaowapak et al., 2024 ; Guan et al., 2023 ; Kovalevich and Langford, 2013 ; Humbert et al., 2002 ; Mookherjee et al., 2007 ).  2.3 Cell lysate preparation Following treatment, the culture medium was aspirated, and adherent cells were rinsed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) prior to lysis. Chemical lysis was performed using a commercially sourced lysis buffer composed of 10 mM Tris (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.5% NP-40, 0.2 mM Na₃VO₄, 10 mM NaF, 0.1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), 100 nM okadaic acid, and a protease inhibitor cocktail (Calbiochem, Germany). The cells were subsequently scraped from the culture surface, and the lysates were transferred to microcentrifuge tubes. The samples underwent three short pulses of sonication and were then centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The final supernatant was aspirated, aliquoted into sterile tubes, and preserved at −80 °C for further analysis (Peach et al., 2015 ).  2.4 Protein concentration determination Protein levels were quantified using the Bradford colorimetric assay. This method is based on the color change of Coomassie blue dye from red (protonated form) to blue (anionic form) upon binding with specific amino acids, including alanine, leucine, arginine, histidine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine (Kielkopf et al., 2020 ). The absorbance at 595 nm was measured to quantify the color change. A serial dilution of bovine serum albumin (BSA) was conducted in triplicate to establish a calibration curve, with 20 μL of each dilution dispensed into a microplate. Protein samples were prepared by diluting 1 μL of each test sample with 19 μL of deionized water, and the preparation was performed in triplicate. Subsequently, 200 μL of Bradford reagent (diluted 1:4) was introduced to each well containing BSA standards and protein samples. The absorbance at 595 nm was quantified using a UV–visible spectrophotometer. The protein concentration of each sample was interpolated from a BSA standard curve.  2.5 Immunoblotting Prior to immunoblotting, protein samples were prepared by mixing cell lysates with an equal volume of 2× Laemmli buffer containing 10% β-mercaptoethanol. The mixtures were then heat-denatured at 95 °C for 5 min to reduce and solubilize the proteins. Subsequently, protein separation was achieved by electrophoresis on a 7.5% SDS-polyacrylamide gel (SDS-PAGE; Bio-Rad, UK) using 20–30 μg of total protein per lane. Following SDS-PAGE, proteins were electrotransferred onto nitrocellulose membranes at 100 V for 1 h. Membrane blocking was performed for 1 h under constant agitation at ambient temperature using a solution of 5% (w /v ) non-fat dry milk prepared in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST). Thereafter, the membranes were subjected to an overnight incubation at 4 °C with gentle shaking in the presence of primary antibodies diluted in the aforementioned blocking buffer. Immunoblotting was performed using the following primary antibodies: rabbit antibodies against total AKT (#4691, 1:2000), phospho-Thr308-AKT (pThr308-AKT, #9275, 1:2000), phospho-Ser473-AKT (pSer473-AKT, #9271, 1:4000), p53 (#2527, 1:2000), and cleaved caspase-3 (#9661, 1:1000), all from Cell Signaling Technology (USA); and mouse antibodies against Bcl-2 (#15071, 1:1000) from Cell Signaling Technology (USA) and PARP (clone 4C10-5, Cat. No. 556494, 1:4000) from BD Biosciences (USA). These membranes were then incubated for 2 h in 5% non-fat dry milk prepared in TBST, followed by incubation with appropriate horseradish peroxidase-linked secondary antibodies (anti-mouse or anti-rabbit) to enhance band visualization. Enhanced chemiluminescence (GE Healthcare, UK) was utilized to visualize protein bands. The chemiluminescent signal was identified and measured utilizing the Chemidoc™ Touch Imaging system (Bio-Rad, UK) in conjunction with Lab™ Touch software and the Image Lab program (Bio-Rad, UK). Afterward, the nitrocellulose membranes were incubated in stripping buffer (62.5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 6.8), 2% SDS, 50 mM β-mercaptoethanol) to enable reprobing for β-actin (#A5316, 1:10,000, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), followed by three washes with TBST. Each immunoblot signal was quantified and normalized to the β-actin signal.  2.6 Flow cytometry For flow cytometric analysis, undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells were seeded in 100-mm culture dishes and allowed to adhere overnight. A subset of cells was pretreated with IGF-1 (10 ng/mL) for 30 min prior to NaAsO₂ exposure (0, 20, or 50 μM) for 24 h, enabling comparison between IGF-1–pretreated and non-pretreated groups. After treatments, the medium from each plate was collected in 15 mL tubes. Cells were detached using 1 mL of trypsin for a few minutes, resuspended in the collected medium, and centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in 300 μL of PBS, after which 700 μL of ice-cold 100% ethanol was slowly added to achieve fixation. Fixed cells were incubated at 4 °C for 1 h or stored at −20 °C for future use. Post-incubation, the cells were centrifuged again at 2000 rpm for 5 min, washed with PBS, and centrifuged for the final time. Cell apoptosis was quantified by flow cytometric analysis of the sub-G1 population (Wlodkowic et al., 2009 ). Following ethanol fixation and washing, which permeabilizes all cellular membranes, cells were stained with propidium iodide (PI), a DNA-intercalating fluorescent dye. The sub-G1 peak represents cells with fractional (hypodiploid) DNA content, resulting from the endonucleolytic cleavage of DNA during apoptosis (Riccardi and Nicoletti, 2006 ). Briefly, 0.5 mL PI solution was added to stain cellular DNA. The PI solution consisted of 10 mL PBS, 50 μL of 10 mg/mL PI, and 4 μL of 1.25 mg/mL RNAse (DNAse-free) to prevent DNA degradation. Analysis was performed within 1 h of staining, and the sub-G1 peak, indicative of cells with fractional DNA content, was quantified.  2.7 Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were conducted as follows: for flow cytometry experiments and Western blot densitometry, comparisons among arsenic-treated groups (concentration–response) were analyzed by one-way ANOVA. Comparisons involving both arsenic concentration and IGF-1 treatment (arsenic × IGF-1 interaction) were analyzed by two-way ANOVA. Both were followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. All analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software Inc., CA, USA), with statistical significance set at p  < 0.05.   3 Results 3.1 Arsenic triggers apoptotic signaling in SH-SY5Y cells by inducing PARP cleavage and upregulating p53 and Bcl-2 Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate whether arsenic exposure induces neuronal cell death as a mechanism of arsenic neurotoxicity. Levels of critical apoptosis-regulating proteins, including PARP, p53, and Bcl-2, were assessed in undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells exposed to varying concentrations of arsenic (Fig. 3  ). The results demonstrated that 24-h arsenic treatment induced a significant, concentration-dependent increase in PARP cleavage, as evidenced by the appearance of the ∼89 kDa fragment, with concentrations of 20 and 50 μM showing a greater effect relative to the control (Fig. 3 A). The appearance of this ∼89 kDa fragment is a direct consequence of caspase-3-mediated cleavage of full-length PARP (∼113 kDa) and serves as a characteristic biochemical marker of ongoing apoptosis (Mu et al., 2019 ). In addition, arsenic exposure induced a concentration-dependent increase in the protein expression levels of p53 and Bcl-2. Significant upregulation of p53 was detected at 20 and 50 μM (Fig. 3 B). In contrast, Bcl-2 expression was significantly increased only at 50 μM (Fig. 3 C), suggesting a potential compensatory survival response that is ultimately overwhelmed by the strong pro-apoptotic signals. These results demonstrate that arsenic promotes apoptotic signaling in SH-SY5Y cells, with potency escalating at higher concentrations (Fig. 3 D-F).  3.2 Arsenic exposure induces DNA fragmentation associated with apoptosis, as measured by flow cytometry Flow cytometry was employed to quantify the sub-G1 cell population, a measure of DNA fragmentation that serves as a marker of apoptosis, to determine if arsenic exposure induces apoptotic cell death. Undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to 0, 20, and 50 μM NaAsO₂ for 24 h, followed by trypsinization and PI staining. Representative flow cytometry histograms illustrate the cell cycle distribution, with the sub-G1 population (apoptotic cells) identified by gate P3 (Fig. 4 A ). Quantitative analysis revealed a significant increase in the sub-G1 population in cells treated with 20 and 50 μM NaAsO₂ compared to untreated controls (Fig. 4 B). These findings indicate that arsenic exposure induces DNA fragmentation characteristic of neuronal apoptosis, thereby providing evidence for its role in arsenic-mediated neurotoxicity.  3.3 Arsenic exposure impairs basal AKT phosphorylation in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells To investigate the potential impairment of IGF-1/AKT signaling by arsenic, neuronally differentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to increasing concentrations of NaAsO₂ (1, 5, and 10 μM). The activation status of the AKT pathway was assessed by immunoblotting for total AKT and its phosphorylation at Thr308 (pT308-AKT) and Ser473 (pS473-AKT) (Fig. 5  ). A decrease in total AKT levels was observed at the higher NaAsO₂ concentrations (5 and 10 μM) (Fig. 5 A). Moreover, arsenic exposure resulted in a concentration-dependent reduction of basal AKT phosphorylation at both Thr308 (Fig. 5 B) and Ser473 (Fig. 5 C). Collectively, these findings indicate that arsenic impairs the basal IGF-1/AKT signaling pathway in a concentration-dependent manner.  3.4 IGF-1 pretreatment attenuates arsenic-induced PARP cleavage and p53 expression The neuroprotective role of IGF-1 in mitigating arsenic-induced apoptosis was determined by Western blot analysis (Fig. 6  ). Pretreating cells with IGF-1 (10 ng/mL) for 30 min prior to arsenic exposure markedly attenuated arsenic-induced PARP cleavage, with the reduction observed in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 6 A). This reduction was significant in cells pretreated with IGF-1 compared to arsenic-treated cells without IGF-1, particularly at arsenic concentrations of 10, 20, and 50 μM (Fig. 6 C). Additionally, IGF-1 pretreatment for 30 min also attenuated the arsenic-induced upregulation of p53 levels. A significant reduction was observed at arsenic concentrations of 20 and 50 μM in cells that had been pretreated with IGF-1 (Fig. 6 B), and this effect was further validated through quantitative analysis (Fig. 6 D). These observations demonstrate that IGF-1 alleviates arsenic-induced apoptotic damage in the neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y cells.  3.5 IGF-1 suppresses arsenic-mediated caspase-3 activation and modulates Bcl-2 levels The impact of arsenic exposure on apoptosis was evaluated by assessing caspase-3 activation, as indicated by its cleaved form, and Bcl-2 expression. Caspase-3 activation entails proteolytic cleavage of the inactive 32 kDa proenzyme into 17–20 kDa and 10 kDa fragments, which subsequently dimerize to generate the active enzyme (Porter and Jänicke, 1999 ). Pretreatment with IGF-1 (10 ng/mL) for 30 min significantly attenuated the upregulation of cleaved caspase-3 induced by 50 μM NaAsO₂ (Fig. 7 A, C ). Furthermore, IGF-1 pretreatment reduced the protein level of the anti-apoptotic regulator Bcl-2, with the effect being most significant at the 50 μM NaAsO₂ concentration (Fig. 7 B, D). This reduction in Bcl-2 suggests that IGF-1 pretreatment restores apoptotic equilibrium, alleviating the cell's need for a heightened compensatory anti-apoptotic response. Collectively, these results demonstrate the protective role of IGF-1 in mitigating arsenic-mediated apoptosis in human SH-SY5Y cells.  3.6 IGF-1 protects against arsenic-induced DNA fragmentation associated with apoptosis To evaluate the neuroprotective role of IGF-1 in response to arsenic-induced genotoxicity, cellular apoptosis was assessed by flow cytometry through quantification of the sub-G1 population. SH-SY5Y cells, pretreated with 10 ng/mL IGF-1 for 30 min prior to a 24-h exposure to 20 or 50 μM NaAsO₂, were stained with PI for DNA content analysis. As previously established, arsenic exposure significantly increased the sub-G1 population, indicating DNA fragmentation and apoptosis (Fig. 4 ). In contrast, IGF-1 pretreatment significantly reduced the proportion of cells in the sub-G1 phase at both arsenic concentrations (Fig. 8 A, B ). These results demonstrate that IGF-1 elicits a neuroprotective effect by attenuating arsenic-induced DNA fragmentation and subsequent apoptotic cell death.  3.7 IGF-1-mediated restoration of AKT signaling following arsenic exposure To evaluate IGF-1's capacity to restore AKT signaling following arsenic exposure, differentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to NaAsO₂ for 3 days, followed by a 15-minute stimulation with IGF-1 (10 ng/mL). As shown in Fig. 9 A , IGF-1 treatment increased the levels of phosphorylated AKT (at Ser473 and Thr308) and total AKT. Quantitative analysis confirmed that IGF-1 post-treatment significantly rescued the arsenic-induced suppression of total AKT expression, with a notable increase observed at 5 and 10 μM NaAsO₂ (Fig. 9 B). Collectively, these results indicate that IGF-1 effectively counteracts the arsenic-induced impairment of AKT signaling in human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells.   4 Discussion This study provides the first mechanistic evidence that IGF-1 confers robust neuroprotection against arsenic-induced neuronal apoptosis by reactivating the impaired PI3K/AKT pathway, rebalancing apoptotic regulators, and preventing DNA fragmentation. While the detrimental impacts of arsenic on the nervous system are well-documented, strategies for pharmacological intervention remain limited (Tyler and Allan, 2014 ; Elsayed and Foo, 2025b ; Ganie et al., 2024 ). To date, this is the first report to delineate the protective role of IGF-1 against arsenic-induced neurotoxicity, specifically via AKT-mediated modulation of PARP, p53, Bcl-2, caspase-3, and DNA fragmentation. The integrity of the IGF-1/PI3K/AKT axis is fundamental to neuronal survival (Wrigley et al., 2017 ; Pellecchia et al., 2014 ). This study establishes that arsenic exposure directly disrupts this critical pro-survival pathway. In neuronally differentiated SH-SY5Y cells, which provide a more mature model for signaling studies, a significant, concentration-dependent reduction was observed in the phosphorylation of AKT at both Thr308 and Ser473 residues (Fig. 5 ). This finding is consistent with previous reports of arsenic impairing insulin signaling and extends this paradigm to the closely related IGF-1 pathway (Niyomchan et al., 2018 ). The concentration at which this inhibition became significant (5 μM) is environmentally relevant, corresponding to levels found in highly contaminated regions (Wasserman et al., 2004 ), thereby enhancing the physiological significance of the findings. Crucially, post-exposure treatment with IGF-1 effectively restored AKT phosphorylation as well as total AKT levels (Fig. 9 ). This rescue effect underscores the potential of IGF-1 to counteract the fundamental signaling defect induced by arsenic, positioning the reactivation of AKT as a central mechanism of protection. To determine the functional consequences of AKT inhibition, the intrinsic apoptotic pathway was investigated. In undifferentiated SH-SY5Y cells, chosen to avoid the confounding pro-survival effects of the differentiating agent, arsenic exposure potently induced apoptosis. This was evidenced by a concentration-dependent increase in key apoptotic markers, including stabilization of the tumor suppressor p53, cleavage of the DNA repair enzyme PARP, and a compensatory rise in the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 (Fig. 3 ). The upregulation of Bcl-2 is particularly noteworthy, as it reflects not an effective pro-survival signal but rather a failed compensatory response to severe apoptotic stress, ultimately overridden by the robust activation of pro-apoptotic factors such as p53 and caspase-3 (Callens et al., 2021 ; Kudo et al., 2012 ; Cen et al., 2021 ; Kirkin et al., 2004 ). Furthermore, the observed DNA fragmentation, quantified by an increased sub-G1 population, confirms the activation of the apoptotic cascade (Fig. 4 ). The most significant novel contribution of this work lies in demonstrating that IGF-1 pretreatment effectively attenuates this entire apoptotic cascade. IGF-1 signaling downregulated the protein expression of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP, and diminished p53 stabilization (Figs. 6 and 7 ). The mechanism underlying p53 reduction can be directly linked to AKT reactivation. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , AKT phosphorylates and activates MDM2, which promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of p53. Thus, by restoring AKT activity, IGF-1 enhances p53 turnover, thereby suppressing its pro-apoptotic transcriptional program (Ghorbani et al., 2015 ; Werner et al., 2016 ). Furthermore, the observed downregulation of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP cleavage signifies a direct blockade of the apoptotic cascade downstream of p53 (Mustafa et al., 2024 ; Shen and White, 2001 ). This inhibition is a logical consequence of upstream AKT-mediated restoration of mitochondrial integrity, which prevents the initiation of the caspase cascade and subsequent PARP cleavage (Chaitanya et al., 2010 ; Gottlob et al., 2001 ). In addition, the observed decrease in Bcl-2 levels following IGF-1 treatment is a strong indicator of successful cytoprotection (Fig. 7 ). Critically, this reduction should not be interpreted as a loss of pro-survival signaling. Instead, it signifies a restoration of cellular homeostasis and apoptotic equilibrium (Callens et al., 2021 ; Kudo et al., 2012 ; Cen et al., 2021 ; Kirkin et al., 2004 ). By alleviating the primary apoptotic insult via AKT reactivation, IGF-1 removes the trigger for a sustained compensatory response, thereby allowing Bcl-2 expression to return to its basal, homeostatic level. While insulin, a structurally and functionally related hormone, has also been shown to activate the PI3K/AKT pathway and protect against arsenic toxicity (Niyomchan et al., 2015 ), this study delineates a more specific and comprehensive neuroprotective role for IGF-1. Unlike insulin, IGF-1 is a primary neurotrophic factor with distinct receptor distribution and signaling dynamics in the brain (Kleinridders, 2016 ). The study's findings demonstrate that IGF-1 not only reactivates AKT but also, through this pathway, orchestrates a coordinated protective response: it downregulates the tumor suppressor p53, stabilizes the compensatory increase in Bcl-2, and ultimately suppresses activation of the executioner caspase-3 and the cleavage of its substrate PARP. This integrated regulation of the AKT/p53/Bcl-2/caspase-3/PARP axis presents a mechanism that may be uniquely potent in the neuronal context for counteracting arsenic-induced apoptosis and DNA fragmentation, extending beyond the general pro-survival effects shared with insulin signaling. Consistent with this interpretation, IGF-1 pretreatment resulted in a significant reduction of DNA fragmentation, as shown by a decreased sub-G1 population in flow cytometric analysis (Fig. 8 ). This finding directly links the IGF-1/AKT-mediated suppression of the apoptotic machinery to the preservation of genomic integrity (Ghorbani et al., 2015 ; Jeong et al., 2008 ). The flow cytometry analysis, based on a total sample size of n  = 4 (two independent experiments conducted in duplicate), provides evidence of DNA fragmentation, a hallmark of apoptosis. Nevertheless, future studies with larger replicate numbers are warranted to enhance statistical robustness. The collective data support a coherent model wherein arsenic-triggered neurotoxicity stems from AKT pathway suppression, leading to cellular apoptosis. Nonetheless, IGF-1 intervention reactivates AKT, orchestrating a protective response that culminates in p53 degradation, inhibition of caspase activity, prevention of PARP cleavage, reduced DNA fragmentation, and enhanced cell survival (Fig. 10  ). Despite the compelling evidence, certain limitations of this study should be acknowledged. The use of an in vitro SH-SY5Y model, while ideal for mechanistic dissection, cannot fully recapitulate the complexity of the intact brain. Future investigations should validate these findings in vivo using animal models of arsenic exposure. Additionally, measuring intracellular arsenic concentrations would help establish a more precise correlation between exposure concentration and phenotypic effects. Furthermore, the therapeutic translation of IGF-1 faces the significant challenge of its oncogenic potential in peripheral tissues (Cao et al., 2012 ). Therefore, the development of targeted delivery strategies, such as safe nano-encapsulation and intranasal administration, will be essential to harness its neuroprotective benefits while minimizing systemic risks (Elsayed and Foo, 2025b ). Finally, exploring whether arsenic directly impacts IGF-1 receptor expression or binding represents an important direction for future research. Overall, the study's findings elucidate a previously unexplored neuroprotective role for IGF-1 against arsenic-induced toxicity. Mechanistically, the protection is associated with the restoration of the PI3K/AKT signaling axis, which rebalances key apoptotic regulators, including p53, caspase-3, PARP, and DNA fragmentation. Consequently, these results elucidate key molecular mechanisms underlying arsenic-induced neurotoxicity, while simultaneously highlighting the prospective therapeutic value of the IGF-1/AKT axis in counteracting the associated neuronal apoptosis.  5 Conclusions This study establishes a novel neuroprotective role for insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) against arsenic-induced toxicity in human neuronal cells. This study demonstrates that arsenic exposure disrupts neuronal homeostasis by potently inhibiting the pro-survival IGF-1/PI3K/AKT pathway, thereby triggering the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This was evidenced by a significant reduction in AKT phosphorylation, concomitant upregulation of p53, activation of caspase-3, cleavage of PARP, and a compensatory increase in Bcl-2, culminating in extensive DNA fragmentation and cell death. The central and novel finding is that IGF-1 pretreatment effectively counteracts this cascade by reactivating AKT signaling. In this protective mechanism, AKT acts as a critical negative regulator of the tumor suppressor p53. This reactivation serves as a master regulatory switch, orchestrating a coordinated protective response as it facilitates p53 degradation, suppresses caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage, and significantly reduces DNA fragmentation and apoptosis. Furthermore, IGF-1 treatment abolishes the arsenic-induced compensatory surge in Bcl-2, which serves as a key indicator of the reestablished apoptotic equilibrium and the return to cellular homeostasis. The observed decrease in Bcl-2 levels following IGF-1 treatment is interpreted as a restoration of apoptotic equilibrium, where diminished cellular stress reduces the need for heightened anti-apoptotic defenses. This is the first report to comprehensively delineate IGF-1's efficacy in mitigating arsenic-specific neurotoxicity and apoptosis through the AKT pathway in a neuronal model. The findings underscore the critical interplay between pro-survival and pro-apoptotic pathways and strongly suggest that enhancing IGF-1 signaling represents a promising therapeutic strategy to prevent arsenic-related neuronal damage. Translation of these findings requires validation in in vivo models to ascertain the therapeutic potential of modulating the IGF-1/AKT pathway for neuroprotective interventions. title: Syrbactin class proteasome inhibitor-induced apoptosis and autophagy occurs in association with p53 accumulation and Akt/PKB activation in neuroblastoma
abstract: Syrbactins belong to a new class of proteasome inhibitors which include syringolins and glidobactins. These small molecules are structurally distinct from other, well-established proteasome inhibitors, and bind the eukaryotic 20S proteasome by a novel mechanism. In this study, we examined the effects of syringolin A (SylA) and glidobactin A (GlbA) as well as two synthetic SylA-analogs (SylA-PEG and SylA-LIP) in human neuroblastoma (SK-N-SH), human multiple myeloma (MM1.S, MM1.RL, and U266), and human ovarian cancer (SKOV-3) cells. While all four syrbactins inhibited cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, GlbA was most potent in both dexamethasone-sensitive MM1.S cells (IC50: 0.004μM) and dexamethasone-resistant MM1.RL cells (IC50: 0.005μM). Syrbactins also inhibited the chymotrypsin-like proteasome activity in a dose-dependent fashion, and GlbA was most effective in SK-N-SH cells (IC50: 0.015μM). The GlbA-promoted inhibition of proteasomal activity in SK-N-SH cells resulted in the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and tumor suppressor protein p53 and led to apoptotic cell death in a time-dependent manner. GlbA treatment also promoted the activation of Akt/PKB via phosphorylation at residue Ser473 and induced autophagy as judged by the presence of the lipidated form of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) and autophagosomes. Collectively, our data suggest that syrbactins belong to a new and effective proteasome inhibitor class which promotes cell death. Proteasome inhibition is a promising strategy for targeted anticancer therapy and syrbactins are a new class of inhibitors which provide a structural platform for the development of novel, proteasome inhibitor-based drug therapeutics.

Graphical abstract Syrbactins: Novel proteasome inhibitor class inhibits cancer cells and induces apoptosis and autophagy.     Syrbactins belong to a new class of proteasome inhibitors which include syringolins and glidobactins. These small molecules are structurally distinct from other, well-established proteasome inhibitors, and bind the eukaryotic 20S proteasome by a novel mechanism. In this study, we examined the effects of syringolin A (SylA) and glidobactin A (GlbA) as well as two synthetic SylA-analogs (SylA-PEG and SylA-LIP) in human neuroblastoma (SK-N-SH), human multiple myeloma (MM1.S, MM1.RL, and U266), and human ovarian cancer (SKOV-3) cells. While all four syrbactins inhibited cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, GlbA was most potent in both dexamethasone-sensitive MM1.S cells (IC50 : 0.004 μM) and dexamethasone-resistant MM1.RL cells (IC50 : 0.005 μM). Syrbactins also inhibited the chymotrypsin-like proteasome activity in a dose-dependent fashion, and GlbA was most effective in SK-N-SH cells (IC50 : 0.015 μM). The GlbA-promoted inhibition of proteasomal activity in SK-N-SH cells resulted in the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and tumor suppressor protein p53 and led to apoptotic cell death in a time-dependent manner. GlbA treatment also promoted the activation of Akt/PKB via phosphorylation at residue Ser473  and induced autophagy as judged by the presence of the lipidated form of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) and autophagosomes. Collectively, our data suggest that syrbactins belong to a new and effective proteasome inhibitor class which promotes cell death. Proteasome inhibition is a promising strategy for targeted anticancer therapy and syrbactins are a new class of inhibitors which provide a structural platform for the development of novel, proteasome inhibitor-based drug therapeutics.   Keywords Apoptosis  Autophagy  Neuroblastoma  Proteasome inhibitors  Syrbactins    1 Introduction The human proteasome is a multi-protein complex that is responsible for the degradation of a large number of proteins that regulate cell division, proliferation, and apoptosis [1,2] . Proteasome inhibitors cause selective apoptosis of malignant cells in cell culture and pre-clinical models and represent a new family of anti-neoplastic agents [3–6] . Most prominently, bortezomib (Velcade® , formerly known as PS-341) is the first proteasome inhibitor approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of refractory and/or relapsed multiple myeloma (MM) and mantle cell lymphoma. The potential efficacy of bortezomib alone and in combination with chemotherapeutic or biologically targeted drugs is currently evaluated in several adult cancer clinical trials and a small number of pediatric cancer trials (e.g ., neuroblastoma) [7,8] . For example, bortezomib was recently approved for the treatment of newly diagnosed myeloma in combination with melphalan and prednisone. Despite the undisputable success with bortezomib, issues regarding bortezomib resistance, inhibitor specificity, and toxicity-associated adverse effects have emerged [9] . Therefore, other, structurally distinct proteasome inhibitors are desirable to expand the existing drug platform and to generate novel types of proteasome inhibitors which may also become useful in the treatment of bortezomib-resistant tumors. We have recently reported the discovery of a new proteasome inhibitor class, the syrbactins, which bind the eukaryotic proteasome by a novel mechanism [10] . Syrbactins, including syringolin A (SylA) and glidobactin A (GlbA) (Fig. 1  ), are small molecule natural products which are structurally distinct from known proteasome inhibitors [4,11] . While SylA is produced by the plant pathogen Pseudomonas syringae  pv. syringae  (Pss ), GlbA is produced by an unknown species of the order Burkholderiales [12,13] . Remarkably, despite their difference in origin, the structural cores of SylA and GlbA are nearly identical and consist of a 12-membered ring system; however, GlbA contains a lipophilic tail which is missing in SylA (Fig. 1 ). The crystal structures of both SylA and GlbA in complex with the yeast proteasome revealed a novel mechanism of covalent, irreversible binding to the catalytic subunits of the proteasome with strongest affinity for the β5 subunit conferring chymotrypsin-like proteolytic activity [10,14] . Prior to this discovery, we found that SylA inhibits cell proliferation and induces apoptosis in human neuroblastoma and ovarian cancer cells [15] , thus suggesting that the observed apoptosis was linked to SylA-mediated proteasome inhibition. To further explore the biological function of syrbactins and their potential as novel drug therapeutics, this study examined the effects of four syrbactins (SylA, GlbA, and two synthetic SylA-analogs; SylA-PEG and SylA-LIP) on cellular proliferation and proteasome activity of cancer cells, including human neuroblastoma (NB), drug-sensitive/resistant multiple myeloma cells, and ovarian cancer cells. For direct comparison, the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib was included. We further examined the role of GlbA in the induction and regulation of apoptosis and autophagy. The results provide a strong rationale for the further exploration of this new proteasome inhibitor class and suggest that syrbactins are potential drug candidates for cancer therapy.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Purification and synthesis of syrbactins Syringolin A (SylA) and glidobactin A (GlbA) were isolated from their biological sources as described [12,16,17] . Lyophilized SylA was dissolved in sterile water and lyophilized GlbA was dissolved in sterile DMSO. Synthetic SylA (used in Fig. 2  ) and SylA-LIP were synthesized as previously described [18]  and dissolved in DMSO. SylA-PEG was synthesized from synthetic SylA by coupling of the corresponding amino PEG residue to its C-terminal carboxylic moiety.  2.2 Mammalian cell cultures and reagents The following panel of chemosensitive and chemoresistant cancer cell lines was used in this study. The human NB cell line SK-N-SH (N/S-type, MYCN -non-amplified, p53 wild type) was established from the bone marrow of a 4-year-old female patient and obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) [19] . NB cell line SK-N-BE(2c) (I-type, MYCN -amplified, p53 mutant) was derived from the bone marrow of a 2-year-old male patient with progressive NB following treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy and was provided by B. Spengler (Fordham University) [20] . Cell lines MM1.S and MM1.RL derived from the parent cell line MM.1, which was established from peripheral blood of a multiple myeloma patient who had become resistant to steroid-based therapy. MM1.S and MM.1RL are sensitive and resistant to dexamethasone, respectively. Together, they provide critical information about disease progression, development of drug resistance, and are useful in the discovery of new therapeutics. U266 is an IL-6 producing cell line isolated from the peripheral blood of a male myeloma patient. All myeloma cells were provided by N. Krett (Northwestern University) [21] . The human ovarian cancer cell line SKOV-3 (p53 deficient, constitutively activated PI3-K and Akt/PKB), which is resistant to several cytotoxic drugs, was provided by B. Warn-Cramer (Cancer Research Center of Hawaii) [22,23] . Cells were seeded 18–24 h before syrbactin or bortezomib treatments and analyzed after 24–72 h. Bortezomib was purchased from LC Laboratories (Woburn, MA, USA). The PI3 kinase inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA) also inhibits autophagic sequestration [24–26]  and was from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Lipofectamine 2000 was used for cell transfections according to the manufacturer's protocol (Invitrogen).  2.3 Cell proliferation assay The CellTiter 96 Aqueous One solution Cell Proliferation Assay (2-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-5-(3-carboxymethoxyphenyl)-2-(4-sulfophenyl)-2H-tetrazolium, inner salt; MTS) (Promega, San Luis Obispo, CA, USA) measures metabolic cell activity and was used to indirectly determine the viability of cells after 48 h treatment with SylA, GlbA, SylA-PEG, SylA-LIP or bortezomib at indicated concentrations by measuring the absorbance at 450 nm using a PerkinElmer HTS7000 Plus bioassay reader. In addition, the viability of cells was determined by counting cells using a light microscope and hemacytometer in the presence of trypan blue for exclusion of dead cells. Cytotoxicity was measured by detecting specific proteases released from damaged membranes using the Cytotox-Glo kit (Promega).  2.4 In vivo proteasome inhibition assay The cell culture-based proteasome Glo™ inhibition assay was performed as previously described [10] . Solid white 96-well microtiter cell culture plates were seeded with cells as indicated and treated with syrbactin or bortezomib. Proteasome inhibition was measured using the proteasome Glo™ reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions (Promega). In brief, cancer cells were treated with SylA, GlbA, SylA-PEG, SylA-LIP or bortezomib at different concentrations as indicated and incubated for 2 h, followed by incubation for 15 min with 100 μl of proteasome Glo™ reagent, containing the bioluminescent substrate Suc-LLVY-aminoluciferin. Luminescence was then measured with a Dynex MLX luminometer.  2.5 Western blot analysis For Western blot analysis, NB cells were seeded in 6-well cell culture plates. After 24 h, cells were incubated for 3 h with 3-MA (7.44 mM) when indicated, followed by GlbA (0.25 μM) treatment for 24 h or 0, 6, 12, 18, and 24 h for time-course experiments. Cell lysates were analyzed by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and electro transfer to PVDF Immobilon-P membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) as previously reported [10] . The primary antibodies were microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) and ubiquitin rabbit whole serum (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA), tumor suppressor protein p53 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA), and PARP, total Akt/PKB, phospho-Akt/PKB (Ser473 ), and α-tubulin (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA). Secondary HRP-antibodies were from GE Healthcare (Piscataway, NJ, USA). After washing the blot with deionized water, proteins were detected using the ECL Plus reagents (Amersham Biosciences, Piscataway, NJ, USA) and Kodak BioMax XAR film (Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). Membranes were stripped at 50 °C for 30 min with ECL stripping buffer (62.5 mM Tris–HCl, pH 6.7, 2% SDS, 100 mM 2-mercaptoethanol) and sequentially probed. Bands were quantified using a Bio-Rad Multi Imager and Quantity One Quantitation Software (Bio-Rad).  2.6 Microscopy Light micrographs were taken after 24 and 48 h treatment at 10× magnification using an inverted Leica DM IL digital microscope. For visualization of endogenous LC3-II accumulation, SK-N-SH cells were treated with GlbA (0.1 μM) or vehicle (DMSO) for 24 h, followed by fixation and permeabilization in ice-cold methanol. Fixed cells were washed and incubated with LC3B antibody (Cell Signaling Technology) followed by incubation with Alexa-Fluor 488 secondary antibody (Molecular Probes, Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). ToPro-3 was included to visualize nuclei and slides were mounted using Prolong Gold®  mounting medium (Molecular Probes). For GFP-LC3 overexpression studies, SK-N-SH cells were transfected with 0.8 μg pEGFP-LC3 plasmid and prepared as described above. For co-localization studies, transfected cells were incubated with anti-ubiquitin (Cell Signaling Technology) and Alexa-Fluor 594 secondary antibody (Molecular Probes). Samples were analyzed by confocal laser scanning microscope (Leica TCS SP-5 AOBS) at 63× magnification.   3 Results 3.1 Syrbactins inhibit the proliferation of cancer cells To examine whether the syrbactins inhibit cell proliferation, GlbA, SylA, and two synthetic SylA-analogs (SylA-PEG and SylA-LIP) were analyzed in parallel (Fig. 1 ). Bortezomib was included as a control for comparison as this drug represents an established proteasome inhibitor that has proven effective in the clinical setting in the treatment of patients with relapsed and/or refractory MM. Human neuroblastoma cells SK-N-SH, human multiple myeloma cells MM1.S, MM1.RL and U266 as well as human ovarian cancer cells SKOV-3 were treated with syrbactins at different concentrations, and the cell viability was determined using the MTS assay as described in Material and Methods. As shown in Fig. 2 A, GlbA most effectively reduced the viability of all tested cell lines in a dose-dependent manner. GlbA was most effective in cell lines MM1.S and MM1.RL with IC50  values of 0.004 μM and 0.005 μM, respectively, and the least effective in SKOV-3 cells with an IC50  of 0.852 μM (Supplement Table 1 ). SylA also inhibited the cell proliferation but at significantly higher, mid micromolar concentrations as previously shown [10,15] . To determine whether the differences in activity might be due to the lipophilic moiety of GlbA which is absent in the natural form of SylA, we also tested two synthetic SylA-analogs, SylA-PEG and SylA-LIP, bearing pegylated and lipidated tails, respectively (Fig. 1 C and D). Remarkably, SylA-LIP, but not SylA-PEG, was effective in all tested cell lines and most pronounced in MM cell lines (MM1.S, MM1.RL, and U266) with IC50  values of 0.026 μM, 0.033 μM, and 0.076 μM, respectively. In comparison, bortezomib was most effective in MM1.S and MM1.RL cells (IC50  values: 0.0024 μM and 0.003 μM, respectively) and the least effective in SKOV-3 cells (IC50 : 0.0399 μM). Collectively, the results presented in Fig. 2 A (summarized in Supplement Table 1 ) suggest that syrbactins exhibit anti-proliferative activity but at varying concentrations. At higher concentrations, GlbA, SylA-LIP, and bortezomib also induced cytotoxicity in all cell lines as the number of viable cells was lower than at the beginning of the experiments (T  = 0). Overall, GlbA was the most effective syrbactin and killed MM cells in a fashion comparable to bortezomib. A significant difference between SylA and SylA-LIP was observed, suggesting that the lipophilic moiety of SylA-LIP improves its anti-proliferative activity by over a 1000-fold (for example, in MM1.RL cells).  3.2 Syrbactins inhibit the proteasomal activity of cancer cells We next tested if the four syrbactins GlbA, SylA, SylA-PEG, and SylA-LIP inhibit the proteasomal activity in metabolically active cancer cells (SK-N-SH, MM1.S, MM1.RL, U266, and SKOV-3) using a cell culture-based proteasome inhibition assay that measures the degradation of a luminogenic substrate (Suc-LLVY-aminoluciferin) specific for the chymotryptic-like proteolytic activity of the proteasome. As shown in Fig. 2 B, GlbA inhibited the proteasomal activity of all cell lines in a dose-dependent manner. SK-N-SH cells were most sensitive to GlbA treatment with an IC50  of 0.015 μM (Supplement Table 2 ). SylA also inhibited the proteasome activity of all tested cell lines in a dose-dependent manner, but at significantly higher (∼45–300-fold) concentrations than GlbA. While SylA-LIP, and less so SylA-PEG, improved their respective activities compared to SylA, they exhibited lower activities compared to GlbA. Bortezomib inhibited all cell lines in a dose-dependent manner with IC50  values in the low nanomolar range, except for SKOV-3 cells where the IC50  was about 10-fold higher and thus comparable to GlbA. Together, the data suggest that GlbA is the most potent syrbactin with highest anti-proteasomal activity in SK-N-SH cells.  3.3 Syrbactin treatment leads to accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins in neuroblastoma cells Ubiquitin is a highly conserved 76-amino acid protein, and proteins that are recognized by the 26S proteasome are typically conjugated to a poly-ubiquitin chain before degradation. We therefore hypothesized that proteasome inhibition should lead to the accumulation of cellular proteins that are ubiquitinated. Since the GlbA-mediated proteasome inhibition was most potent in NB cells, we next analyzed cell lysates of GlbA-treated or vehicle-treated control SK-N-SH cells by Western blot using a rabbit serum which recognizes ubiquitinated proteins. GlbA-treated cells showed a marked increase in ubiquitinated cellular proteins compared to untreated control cells (Fig. 3 A ). We previously observed that SylA treatment also leads to the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins [10] ; however, GlbA induced comparable effects at a 100-fold lower concentration (Fig. 3 A). These results are in support of our observation that syrbactins inhibit the proteasome in metabolically active cells, and that GlbA is a more potent inhibitor than SylA.  3.4 Syrbactins induce apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells Previous studies have shown that inhibition of ubiquitin-mediated degradation of proteins through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway leads to the onset of apoptosis. Therefore, we determined whether syrbactin-promoted cell death involved the induction of apoptosis. SK-N-SH and SK-N-BE(2c) cells were treated with GlbA for various times over a 24-h period. First, we probed cell lysates for the presence of PARP cleavage, which is indicative of apoptosis [27] . As shown in Fig. 3 B, GlbA-treated cells contained cleaved PARP (89 kDa) within 12 h of drug treatment, while only non-cleaved PARP (116 kDa) was detected at earlier time points and in control cells. The tumor suppressor protein p53 is regulated by proteasome degradation and plays a key role during apoptosis. Therefore, we next focused our attention at total levels of p53 in cell lysates. The accumulation of p53 was detected in GlbA-treated cell lysates within 12 h of treatment (Fig. 3 B). In addition to p53, we also examined the presence and activation of Akt/PKB, a well-characterized anti-apoptotic protein kinase. GlbA induced Ser473  phosphorylation of Akt/PKB within 18 h of treatment (Fig. 3 B), suggesting that GlbA activates Akt/PKB and thus exhibits an opposing effect which may counteract apoptosis. The trypan blue exclusion assay confirmed that within 18 h of GlbA treatment there was a loss of membrane integrity and viability in SK-N-SH cells (Fig. 3 C). Interestingly, GlbA did not affect the viability of SK-N-BE (2c) cells within the 24-h period (Fig. 3 C), despite the presence of PARP cleavage. Treatment with GlbA also induced morphological changes in NB cells (Fig. 4 A ). While untreated SK-N-SH control cells were triangular-shaped, GlbA-treated cells appeared rounded and partially detached from the culture plates at 24 h, with more extensive morphological changes at 48 h. These morphological changes are characteristic for cells that undergo apoptosis. To further explore our observations, we analyzed GlbA-treated SK-N-SH cells with or without 3-methyladenine (3-MA), an inhibitor of PI3-kinase [24–26] , and probed cell lysates after 24 h for the presence of PARP cleavage. As shown in Fig. 4 B, GlbA-treated cells contained large quantities of cleaved PARP (89 kDa), while only non-cleaved PARP (116 kDa) was detected in control cells. Interestingly, the presence of 3-MA partially prevented the cleavage of PARP. GlbA treatment led to a strong accumulation of p53 in cellular lysates compared to control cells and 3-MA partially reduced this accumulation (Fig. 4 B). While the total Akt/PKB protein levels did not significantly change, we noted an increase of Ser473 -phosphorylated Akt/PKB in response to GlbA treatment. This phosphorylation of Ser473  was prevented by co-treatment with 3-MA (Fig. 4 B). Together, the results support the time-course experiments of Fig. 3 B and suggest that GlbA induces p53 accumulation and promotes apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells, but also activates Akt/PKB, and this activation can be prevented by treatment with 3-MA.  3.5 Syrbactins-induced proteasome inhibition promotes autophagy in neuroblastoma cells Proteasome degradation and autophagy are the two main proteolytic pathways used by cells to degrade cellular proteins. Since the treatment of cells with 3-MA results in the inhibition of autophagy [28]  and 3-MA reduces the effects of GlbA treatment (Fig. 4 ), we were curious to determine whether syrbactins induce autophagy. To test this hypothesis, we probed GlbA-treated SK-N-SH cells for the presence of native microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) protein. Untreated control cells primarily contain non-lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-I; 18 kDa), while autophagic cells accumulate a lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II; 16 kDa), which associates with autophagic vacuoles (autophagosomes) and thus presents a reliable marker of autophagy [29] . As illustrated in Fig. 5 A , we found that GlbA-treated cells accumulated native LC3-II when compared to untreated control cells and the co-treatment of cells with 3-MA reverted the GlbA-induced formation of LC3-II. The lipidation of LC3-I into LC3-II occurred within 12–18 h of GlbA treatment in SK-N-SH cells, but not SK-N-BE(2c) cells (Fig. 3 B). The formation of distinct autophagosomes was also detected by immunofluorescence in GlbA-treated SK-N-SH cells as represented by green puncta which were absent from untreated control cells (Fig. 5 B). Consistent with these findings, cells transfected with a GFP-LC3 construct exhibited a transition of the GFP-LC3 signals from a diffuse cytoplasmic pattern to a punctated membrane pattern following the treatment with GlbA (Fig. 6 A ), suggesting the localization of LC3 to autophagosomes. Similar GFP-LC3 puncta were observed in the presence of rapamycin, an mTOR inhibitor that has been shown to induce autophagy. We also found by confocal microscopic analysis that these autophagosome representing GFP-LC3 puncta co-localize with ubiquitinated aggregates (Fig. 6 B) and similar observations were made by others in GFP-LC3-expressing prostate cancer cells in response to bortezomib [30] . Together, these experiments suggest that GlbA, in addition to inducing apoptosis, also promotes autophagy. Moreover, autophagy could participate in the clearance of ubiquitinated protein aggregates which have accumulated in response to proteasome inhibition.   4 Discussion The proteasome has recently been recognized as a target for anticancer therapy. Numerous studies successfully showed that proteasome inhibitors preferentially kill cancer cells and induce apoptosis without affecting non-transformed cells [31] . The most prominent inhibitor, bortezomib, has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma, and three second generation proteasome inhibitors, carfilzomib (PR-171), salinosporamide A (NPI-0052), and CEP-18770 are in phase I and phase II clinical trials [9,32,33] . Remarkably, a number of proteasome inhibitors are natural products including lactacystin, epoxomicin, salinosporamide A, eponemycin, tyropeptin A, and TMC-95, and six major families based on the chemical mechanism have been identified [4] . We have recently made the discovery of a seventh class of proteasome inhibitors, the syrbactins, which are structurally distinct natural products that bind the proteasome by a unique mechanism [4,10,11] . Syrbactins so far include the syringolins and glidobactins. Although they share similar structural features, they differ in their macrocyclic lactam core structure and exocyclic side chain. We recently described the total synthesis of SylA and also of SylB, one of several minor metabolites produced by the plant pathogen Pss [18] . SylB has strong structural similarity to SylA and differs from SylA only by the substitution of the SylA 3,4-dehydrolysine residue with a lysine moiety, which results in an alternative scaffold structure with less ring strain [18] . While more distinct, glidobactins are structurally related to syringolins (Fig. 1 ) and have been discovered in the late 1980s [34–36] , however, the mode of action was not recognized until recently [10] . In our previous work, we showed that in vitro , GlbA is the most potent syrbactin proteasome inhibitor identified so far and is 15-fold more active than SylA for the chymotryptic and the tryptic proteasome activity. In contrast, GlbA did not inhibit the caspase-like activity while SylA and SylB moderately affected this activity and this observation was confirmed by co-crystallization [10,18] . As anticipated, the rationally designed syringolin A-based lipophilic derivative (SylA-LIP; Fig. 1 D) proved to be about 100-fold more potent than SylA in its ability to inhibit the chymotryptic activity of the proteasome in vitro [18] . In this report, we confirmed our previous in vitro  findings with SylA and provide strong evidence that GlbA, and also SylA-LIP inhibit cell proliferation and proteasomal activity at significantly lower concentrations than SylA when applied to intact, metabolically active cancer cells. Using a cell-based proteasome activity assay, we observed that GlbA was up to 300-fold more active than SylA depending on the cell type with highest/lowest activities in SK-N-SH cells and U266 cells, respectively. SylA-LIP was up to 48-fold more active than SylA with highest/lowest activities in SKOV-3 and MM1.RL, respectively (Supplement Table 2 ). Interestingly, SylA and SylA-PEG had little effect on cell viability but inhibited the proteasomal activity. This observation suggests that SylA and SylA-PEG do not easily pass the cell membrane which remains intact when exposed to the MTS assay reagents. In contrast, cells exposed to the proteasome assay reagents are permeablized at the end of the 2-h incubation period. Therefore, it is possible that in the proteasome assay, SylA and SylA-PEG do not enter the cell during the 2-h incubation period but after cell permeabilization. Indeed, proteasome activity experiments in which GlbA- and SylA-treated cells were washed (in order to remove the inhibitor) after a 2, 12 or 24-h incubation period (before permeabilization) confirmed that lipophilic GlbA enters cells more readily during the incubation period than hydrophilic SylA (Supplement Fig. 1 ). Similarly, this may explain why SylA-PEG was effective in the proteasome assay but not in the cell viability assay. We further examined these effects by analyzing whole cell lysates from GlbA-treated and untreated cells by Western blot analysis. To study signaling proteins that are regulated towards the beginning of apoptosis, we treated SK-N-SH cells for designated times up to 24 h, since longer treatment at 48 h typically resulted in a non-specific, total degradation of cellular proteins. Western blot analyses revealed that GlbA induced PARP cleavage, a typical marker for apoptosis, and led to p53 accumulation, a protein known to be involved in the induction of apoptosis. These findings were consistent with our previous study on SylA treatment of cancer cells [10,15] . While GlbA treatment had little effect on total Akt/PKB protein levels, the phosphorylation of Akt/PKB at residue Ser473  increased significantly, thus suggesting the activation of Akt/PKB. Interestingly, co-treatment with 3-MA reduced or prevented the GlbA-induced cellular effects (Fig. 4 ). In addition, co-treatment with 3-MA attenuated the cytotoxic effects of GlbA (Supplement Fig. 2 ). GlbA also increased the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) as well as the number of autophagosomes in GlbA-treated cells, indicating the onset of autophagy. Together, these findings suggest that GlbA-mediated inhibition of proteasomal degradation activates both apoptosis and autophagy. Inhibition of autophagy decreased the cytotoxic effects of GlbA and decreased PARP cleavage after 24 h, supporting a pro-apoptotic role of autophagy during GlbA induced proteasome inhibition. Conversely, the onset of autophagy may be a compensatory mechanism in response to GlbA-induced proteasome inhibition, as observed by the co-localization of ubiquitin with LC3-containing autophagosomes. Indeed, Ding et al. suggested that autophagy is likely activated in response to endoplasmic reticulum stress caused by misfolded proteins during proteasome inhibition [30] . The PI3K/Akt signaling has been associated with both anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic responses [37–39]  and, similar to our observation, bortezomib was found to activate Akt/PKB in vitro  and in treated prostate cancer tissues [40] . In our study, the 3-MA effect on Akt/PKB activation during GlbA treatment supports a pro-apoptotic role for Akt/PKB, however, Akt/PKB activation may also occur as a compensatory response to the induction of apoptosis. The results clearly show that GlbA is able to induce both apoptosis and autophagy in neuroblastoma cells. However, it is not clear whether the induction of autophagy is a pro-survival or pro-cell death response. In summary, our study introduces a new class of proteasome inhibitors, the syrbactins, and provides evidence for their use as anti-proliferative agents that exhibit apoptotic properties. Although bortezomib is a successful drug that is used in the treatment of MM and currently evaluated in clinical trials for effectiveness in other types of cancer, novel proteasome inhibitors are needed due to the occurrence of toxicities and the development of potential drug resistance associated with prolonged treatments. Proteasome inhibitors are also known to sensitize chemoresistant cells, further underlining their importance of this new class of therapeutics. Therefore, the newly discovered syrbactin class of proteasome inhibitors should be further studied and developed into a therapeutic agent that may be used for combination treatments or as second-line therapy in bortezomib-resistant tumors. title: Facilitation of 9,10-phenanthrenequinone-elicited neuroblastoma cell apoptosis by NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1
abstract: 9,10-Phenanthrenequinone (PQ), a major quinone component in diesel exhaust particles, is considered to provoke damage of respiratory and vascular cells through highly producing reactive oxygen species (ROS), but little is known about its pathophysiological role in neuronal cell damage. In this study, we found that incubation with 1,2-naphthoquinone, 1,4-naphthoquinone and PQ, major quinone components in diesel exhausts, provokes apoptosis of human neuroblastoma cell lines. SK-N-SH cell treatment with a lethal concentration of PQ facilitated ROS production within 6 h. The treatment also promoted formation of 8-hydroxy-deoxyguanosine, p53 activation, elevation of Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, lowering of mitochondrial membrane potential, and resultant activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3, inferring that ROS production, DNA damage and mitochondrial dysfunction are crucial processes of the PQ-triggered SK-N-SH cell apoptosis. The PQ treatment of SK-N-SH cells elevated the level of 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE), a cytotoxic reactive aldehyde generated from lipid peroxidation. The treatment with PQ and HNE also decreased cellular levels of total and reduced glutathiones, and the damage elicited by HNE was ameliorated and deteriorated by pretreating with cell-permeable glutathione analog and the depletor, respectively. Moreover, the treatment with PQ and HNE decreased the proteasomal proteolytic activities, suggesting a contribution of decrease in the antioxidant abilities to the ROS-mediated neuroblastoma cell apoptosis. Our comparative analyses of 17 cells showed a positive correlation between the PQ reductase and NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1) activities. In addition, overexpression and knockdown of NQO1 augmented and lowered, respectively, the ROS production through PQ redox-cycling and the quinone toxicity. Furthermore, the treatment with PQ and HNE up-regulated the NQO1 expression. Taken together, PQ exposure produces large amounts of ROS in neuroblastoma cells via NQO1 up-regulation and resultant acceleration of its redox-cycling, followed by activation of the ROS-dependent apoptotic mechanism.

Laboratory of Biochemistry Gifu Pharmaceutical University 1-25-4 Daigaku-nishi Gifu 501-1196 Japan       9,10-Phenanthrenequinone (PQ), a major quinone component in diesel exhaust particles, is considered to provoke damage of respiratory and vascular cells through highly producing reactive oxygen species (ROS), but little is known about its pathophysiological role in neuronal cell damage. In this study, we found that incubation with 1,2-naphthoquinone, 1,4-naphthoquinone and PQ, major quinone components in diesel exhausts, provokes apoptosis of human neuroblastoma cell lines. SK-N-SH cell treatment with a lethal concentration of PQ facilitated ROS production within 6 h. The treatment also promoted formation of 8-hydroxy-deoxyguanosine, p53 activation, elevation of Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, lowering of mitochondrial membrane potential, and resultant activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3, inferring that ROS production, DNA damage and mitochondrial dysfunction are crucial processes of the PQ-triggered SK-N-SH cell apoptosis. The PQ treatment of SK-N-SH cells elevated the level of 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE), a cytotoxic reactive aldehyde generated from lipid peroxidation. The treatment with PQ and HNE also decreased cellular levels of total and reduced glutathiones, and the damage elicited by HNE was ameliorated and deteriorated by pretreating with cell-permeable glutathione analog and the depletor, respectively. Moreover, the treatment with PQ and HNE decreased the proteasomal proteolytic activities, suggesting a contribution of decrease in the antioxidant abilities to the ROS-mediated neuroblastoma cell apoptosis. Our comparative analyses of 17 cells showed a positive correlation between the PQ reductase and NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1) activities. In addition, overexpression and knockdown of NQO1 augmented and lowered, respectively, the ROS production through PQ redox-cycling and the quinone toxicity. Furthermore, the treatment with PQ and HNE up-regulated the NQO1 expression. Taken together, PQ exposure produces large amounts of ROS in neuroblastoma cells via NQO1 up-regulation and resultant acceleration of its redox-cycling, followed by activation of the ROS-dependent apoptotic mechanism. Owing to its small size (less than 10-μm diameter), DEP inhaled is speculated to be capable of easily passing from the respiratory tract into the circulation, and thereby exerting its injurious actions in various organs. Although the lung is one of the most preferentially targeted organs on inhalation of the particle [1,2] , cerebral nerve and cardiovascular systems are also regarded as potential targets in case-crossover and exposure studies conducted to evaluate the association with air pollutants [3,4] . In experiments using isolated rat brain capillaries, it is found that DEP alters blood-brain barrier function through oxidative stress and proinflammatory cytokine production [5] . Based on the report, exposure to DEP at its low concentrations less than 5 μg/mL appears to alter the expression and transport activity of the key transporter, P-glycoprotein. On the other hand, fetal exposure of mice to the particle affects the emotional behaviors associated with the serotonergic and dopaminergic systems in the mouse brain [6] . These findings have suggested that low concentrations of DEP elicit encephalic damages in addition to onset and exacerbation of cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, other animal experiments revealed that exposure to urban pollution induces inflammatory and stress protein brain responses and Alzheimer's disease-like pathologic alterations [7,8] . In addition, upon cell-based experiments, treatment with DEP was shown to selectively elicit damage in dopaminergic neurons through the phagocytic activation of microglial NADPH oxidase and consequent oxidative insult [9] . These findings would thus raise concern about severe cranial nerve disorders associated with chronic exposure to DEP. DEP consists of carbonaceous nuclei and a vast number of organic components such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, nitroaromatic hydrocarbons, heterocyclics, aldehydes and quinones [10,11] . Among the components, the abundant and potent toxicants are 9,10-phenanthrenequinone (PQ), 1,2-naphthoquinone (1,2-NQ) and 1,4-NQ (Fig. 1  ), whose cytolethal effects are mainly attributed to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) via the redox-cycles and the subsequent ROS-dependent pathways [12–14] , closely mimicking the toxic mechanisms of DEP [15] . Therefore, it is suggested that the three quinones play crucial roles in pathogenic mechanisms triggered by DEP. Of the three cytotoxic quinones, one of the most extensively studied is a tricyclic quinone PQ, which is highly produced during biological and photo-oxidative reactions of phenanthrene [16] . The ROS production caused by PQ is assumed to be mediated by its redox-cycling, which is initiated by two-electron reduction of the quinone into its hydroquinone 9,10-dihydroxyphenanthrene by some NADPH-dependent reductases [12] . The resultant hydroquinone is rapidly converted into its semiquinone radical through the nonenzymatic dispropotionation with PQ and then followed by regenerating PQ, in parallel with the ROS generation from molecular oxygen. Thus, exposure to small amount of PQ is thought to excessively generate ROS and to consequently cause severe health hazards. Literature revealed contributions of cytochrome P450 reductase and carbonyl reductase (CBR) 1 in the redox-cycling of PQ [12,17] . In addition, we previously showed that CBR4 [18] , l -xylulose reductase (XR) [19]  and two members (AKR1C3 and AKR1B10) in the aldo-keto reductase (AKR) superfamily [20,21]  participate in acceleration of the redox-cycling and consequently activate the ROS-dependent apoptotic signaling. NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1) is well accepted as a superoxide anion scavenger that protects from cytotoxicity elicited by ROS [22,23] . The enzyme is reported to convert quinones into their corresponding hydroquinones in a NADPH-linked two-electron reduction [24,25] , which is, however, the same as that in initial step of the redox-cycling of PQ catalyzed by the above oxidoreductases. Therefore, NQO1 is assumed to be involved in the PQ-mediated redox-cycling, which leads to the cytotoxicity of PQ.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials PQ was obtained from Nacalai tesque (Kyoto, Japan); naphthalene, 1,2-NQ and 1,4-NQ were from Tokyo Chemical Industry (Tokyo, Japan); and phenanthrene, 2-hexenal and 2-nonenal were from Wako Pure Chemical Industries (Osaka, Japan).
