Introduction As an acute cerebrovascular disorder, stroke is currently the third leading reason for death worldwide and a serious long-term disability.1   During the past few years, the absolute number of stroke events, stroke prevalence, stroke disability, and death has been increasing.2   The common type involves ischemic stroke (IS), accounting for about 70–80 % of total stroke cases, attributed to insufficient blood supply to the brain parenchyma.3   As is known, reperfusion is an effective therapy for restoring blood flow and improving brain function. Nevertheless, it has been reported that ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) can trigger multiple cellular responses in the brain, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis.4,5   Furthermore, after the cerebral blood supply is restored, the surviving neurons are also challenged by secondary oxygen stress. In particular, excessive lipid peroxidation accumulation could result in iron-dependent ferroptosis in neurons.6   Currently, the primary treatments for IS are thrombolytic therapy and thrombectomy,7,8   which are limited in their effectiveness. In addition, inappropriate therapeutic modalities can cause extra damage and often experience sensorimotor dysfunction.9   Hence, searching for more effective stroke treatment options is a pressing clinical need. Recently, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has shown unique advantages in the treatment of IS. Increasing evidence has confirmed the neuroprotective properties of TCM in IS, such as anti-inflammation, anti-oxidative stress, and anti-ferroptosis.10   Unfortunately, research on the intrinsic mechanism of TCM in treating IS remains insufficiently in-depth. Naringin, a citrus bioflavonoid extracted from citrus plants, is used in treating diverse diseases.11,12   Several reports have confirmed the significant potential of Naringin in preventing and treating I/R injury.13   For example, earlier studies have shown that Naringin could improve neurological damage in cerebral I/R injury rats by reducing catalase activity and decreasing peroxidation.14   Furthermore, the Naringin-rich rhizome peel has been reported to prevent ischemia-caused neuronal cell death in mouse brain via inhibiting inflammatory processes.15   Meanwhile, Naringin protected brain against I/R damage in rats by repressing endoplasmic reticulum stress.16   Yet, the mechanism by which Naringin alleviates cerebral I/R injury is far from being addressed. As a newly recognized form of programmed cell death, ferroptosis is typically recognized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and excessive oxidative stress.17   Moreover, convincing evidence has suggested that ferroptosis is the cause of reperfusion injury. Widely existed in brain tissues, iron is an important component of the brain. Increased serum iron storage was associated with poor clinical outcomes in AIS patients,18   and iron chelation or depletion could relieve I/R-evoked brain injury.19   It has been reported that some TCMs, like Rhein and Galangin, could protect against cerebral I/R damage via blocking ferroptosis.20,21   Of note, Naringin could ameliorate diabetic cardiac autonomic neuropathy by regulating the NRF2/GPX4 pathway involved in ferroptosis.22   However, it is still unclear whether Naringin can act on ferroptosis in AIS Network pharmacology is a novel strategy for discovering relationships between diseases, targets, and drugs, and assists in understanding the effects of drugs on biological networks.23,24   Herein, in order to whether Naringin possess a neuro-protective impact against brain injury by regulating ferroptosis, the network pharmacology analyzed the targets of Naringin. Our analysis found that tumor protein p53 (TP53) was a vital target gene for Naringin in treating AIS via ferroptosis. TP53 is frequently mutated in cancer and executes its diverse function in tumor suppression. Early studies have established that TP53 could respond to many cellular stresses to modulate gene expression, thereby inducing cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, DNA repair, or alteration in metabolism.25   Interestingly, it has been reported that high TP53 expression can mediate nerve cell apoptosis and have a negative impact on cerebral I/R. TP53 silencing could relieve brain I/R damage by regulating ferroptosis.26   In this study, we aimed to explore whether the regulation effects of Naringin on ferroptosis relieve cerebral I/R injury via targeting TP53.  Materials and methods Cell culture and treatments Under a humidified atmosphere of 5 % CO2  at 37˚C, human neuroblastoma cell lines (SK-N-SH cells, CL-0214; Procell, Wuhan, China) were grown in the Specific medium (CM-0214, Procell). To build the OGD/R model, SK-N-SH cells at 60–70 % confluence were incubated with serum-free and glucose-free MEM medium. Then, these cells were placed in the anaerobic chamber (1 % O2 , 94 % N2 , and 5 % CO2 ) for 2 h at 37℃ to induce in vitro  ischemia. After that, these cells were cultured in MEM medium with 10 % FBS at 37℃ with 95 % air, 5 % CO2  for reoxygenation for 12 h. The control groups were maintained in a complete culture medium under normal conditions. To identify the effects of Naringin on SK-N-SH cells, cells were treated with various doses of Naringin (purity ≥ 98 %, HY-N0153, MedChemExpress, Princeton, NJ, USA) for 24 h.  Counting kit (CCK-8) assay In brief, SK-N-SH cells were harvested in a 96-well plate at a density of 3 × 103  cells per well, followed by treatment with a series of concentrations of Naringin for 24 h. Then, 10 μL CCK-8 solution (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was added for at least 4 h at 37℃, the optical density at 450 nm, which was indicative of a positive association with cell viability, was estimated by using a microplate reader.   ELISA SK-N-SH cell culture medium was collected. Then, secretion of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β in the supernatant was measured by commercial ELISA kits (PT512, PI326, PI301, Beyotime). Flow cytometry for cell apoptosis Following a 24-h incubation period of SK-N-SH cells with Naringin or without, the cells were subjected to trypsin digestion and centrifugation. Then, the cells were washed with PBS and re-suspended in a binding buffer. After that, the reconstituted cells were dual-stained with Annexin V-FITC and PI (Beyotime) for a duration of 15–20 min. Finally, samples were detected through a flow cytometer within 1 h.  Reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection In short, 3 × 105  SK-N-SH cells were incubated with 2’,7’-dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA, in HBSS) (MedChemExpress) with a final concentration of 10 µM for 30 min at 37˚C away from light. After washing and re-suspended in HBSS, the fluorescence intensity was examined using flow cytometry.  Measurement of malondialdehyde (MDA), and glutathione (GSH) Concisely, SK-N-SH cells were harvested and lysed after treatment. Then, the assessment of MDA and GSH levels in cell extract was conducted based on kits (S0131S, Beyotime; ab239709, Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA)  Assessment of intracellular Fe2+  For intracellular ferrous iron (Fe2+ ) content, 1 × 106  SK-N-SH cells were harvested and homogenized with PBS. In the supernatant, Fe2+  level was determined using Cell Total Iron Colorimetric Assay Kit (EEA009, Invitrogen, Paisley Scotland, UK) and analyzed using a microplate reader.  Western blot SK-N-SH cells were lysed with RIPA buffer for 30 min. After quantification using BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime), approximately 30 μg of protein was mixed with loading buffer and incubated at 100˚C for 5 min. Then, the denatured protein samples were separated by 10 % SDS-PAGE gel, transferred on PVDF membranes, blocked with 5 % skim milk, and probed with primary antibodies at 4˚C overnight: TP53 (10442–1-AP, 1:5000, Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA), SLC7A11 (26864–1-AP, 1:1000, Proteintech), and GAPDH (60004–1-lg, 1:200000, Proteintech). Subsequently, the membranes were incubated with corresponding secondary antibody at 37˚C for 2 h. Finally, signals were detected with ECL reagent.  Collection of targets of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis Targets of Naringin were collected from the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD) (https://ctdbase.org/ ) curated and inferred gene-disease associations and SwissTargetPrediction (www. swisstargetprediction.ch) applied to conduct ligand-based target prediction for bioactive small molecules. Targets of AIS and ferroptosis were respectively collected from Genecards databases.  Construction of PPI networks A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network of intersecting targets was built and visualized using STRING database (https://string-db.org/ ) and Cytoscape. CytoHubba and MCODE plug-ins screened Hub genes and modules in the target genes, respectively. The parameters of CytoHubba were set as core genes = top 10 nodes ranked by degree and maximal clique centrality (MCC).  KEGG analysis KEGG is a bioinformatics resource for mining significantly altered metabolic pathways enriched in the gene list. Additionally, the chart of KEGG enrichment analysis was drawn using the SangerBox online tool (http://sangerbox.com/home.html ).  Molecular docking AutoDock Tools (AutoDock Vina 1.1.2 with the default binding free energy scoring function) molecularly docks core components to core targets, calculates the binding properties of Naringin ligands to target proteins, and visualizes the docked conformations based on Discovery Studio. For TP53, the size of gird Box was set to size_x = 63.6555555556, size_y = 52.4222222222, and size_z = 48.6777777778, and the coordinates of center were set to center_x = -24.227, center_y = 20.195, and center_z = -7.749.  Cell transfection In general, 20 nM of TP53 small interference RNA (si-TP53, sense: 5’-UGCGUGUGGAGUAUUUGGAUG-3’, antisense: 5’-UGGUACAGUCAGAGCCAACCUC-3’) or non-targeting siRNA (si-NC) from OriGene (Wuxi, China) was transfected into SK-N-SH cells using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) for 48 h. For TP53 overexpression, the sequence of TP53 cDNA (NM_000546) was cloned into pcDNA vector to construct pcDNA-TP53 (termed oe-TP53). After that, 6 μg of oe-TP53 or oe-NC (pcDNA3.1 empty vector) were transfected into cells for 48 h. After the measurement of transfection efficiency, the corresponding treatment was conducted for these cells.  Statistical analysis In this research, all values are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) with P  < 0.05 indicating statistically significant. Statistical analyses involved were conducted using GraphPad Prism7. Group comparison was performed using Student’s t -test or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s tests.   Results Naringin relieved OGD/R-mediated SK-N-SH cell viability inhibition Firstly, 2D structure of Naringin was shown in  Fig. 1 A. Subsequently, to identify direct cytotoxic effects of Naringin on neuroblastoma SK-N-SH cells, cells were stimulated with various concentrations of Naringin (0, 1, 5, and 10 μM) for 24 h. Results displayed that Naringin exposure had no significant effect on SK-N-SH cell activity (Fig. 1 B). Therefore, 5 μM and 10 μM Naringin were selected for the subsequent experiments. To induce Acute ischemic stroke in vitro , SK-N-SH cells were subjected to OGD/R. Subsequently, to further assess the efficacy of Naringin on OGD/R-injured SK-N-SH cells, cell viability was determined using CCK-8 assay. As displayed in Fig. 1 C, SK-N-SH cell viability was significantly suppressed after suffering from OGD/R treatment, which was abolished with increased doses of Naringin. Together, these data suggested that OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell viability repression was ameliorated after Naringin treatment.  Naringin reduced OGD/R-induced inflammation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis Furthermore, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1Β secretions were apparently induced in SK-N-SH cells underwent OGD/R, which was apparently attenuated after 5 μM or 10 μM Naringin treatment ( Fig. 2 A-2C). Moreover, OGD/R-induced promotion of cell apoptotic percentage was weakened via 5 μM or 10 μM Naringin exposure (Fig. 2 D). Beyond that, 5 μM or 10 μM Naringin stimulation could effectively attenuate the positive effects of OGD/R on oxidative stress, as evidenced by reduced ROS level ( Fig. 3 A) and MDA level (Fig. 3 B), and increased GSH level (Fig. 3 C). In terms of ferroptosis, OGD/R-evoked intracellular Fe+  level promotion was evidently overturned after 5 μM or 10 μM Naringin administration (Fig. 3 D). It has been reported that SLC7A11 could counter cellular oxidative stress-induced cell death, containing ferroptosis.27   Therefore, the expression of SLC7A11 was further determined. As shown in Fig. 3 E, OGD/R resulted in an obvious reduction in SLC7A11 protein level, which was abolished after 5 μM or 10 μM Naringin treatment. Collectively, OGD/R-triggered cell injury was partly receded via Naringin exposure.  Core target screening of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis Next, 272 Naringin target genes from two sources, containing 183 from CTD database and 100 from the SwissTarget prediction, were provided. Moreover, GeneCards offered 6606 acute ischemic stroke (AIS) target genes and 1467 ferroptosis target genes. Then, intersection analysis identified 64 common genes ( Fig. 4 A), which were utilized to further probe mechanisms whereby Naringin ameliorates AIS by modulating ferroptosis. Then, a PPI network was established for the top 10 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) based on the String database (Fig. 4 B). Subsequently, the top 10 hub genes were selected in the CytoHubba plug-in using the MCC algorithm and node degree, including NFKB1, PTGS2, STAT3, JUN, ALB, IL6, AKT1, IL1B, TNF, TP53 (Fig. 4 C). Among them, TP53 was enriched in Apoptosis, MAPK signaling pathway, Neurotrophin signaling pathway, PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Mitophagy-animal, and ferroptosis, according to the KEGG analysis (Fig. 4 D). Overall, TP53 plays a vital role in AIS treatment by Naringin through modulation of ferroptosis.  Molecular docking analysis Furthermore, docking interaction between Naringin and TP53 was analyzed via PyMOL software ( Figs. 5 A and 5 B). Then, the biomolecular interaction of Naringin and TP53 was predicted by using PyMOL system. The predicated docking was displayed in Fig. 5 C, and the 2D schematic diagram was presented in Fig. 5 D. Beyond that, western blot results exhibited that TP53 was markedly increased in SK-N-SH cells after OGD/R treatment, whereas these effects were gradually abolished along with the increased concentrations of Naringin (Fig. 5 E). Altogether, these findings suggested that TP53 was a potential target of Naringin. Naringin blocked OGD/R-evoked cell injury by regulating TP53 Functionally, TP53 knockdown could relieve the repression of OGD/R on cell viability, and TP53 overexpression could abolish the promotion of Naringin on cell viability in OGD/R-treated SK-N-SH cells ( Fig. 6 A). Moreover, OGD/R-induced TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β secretions were partly mitigated by TP53 silencing. Meanwhile, Naringin stimulation-mediated inflammatory response inhibition in OGD/R-disposed SK-N-SH cells was effectively overturned through TP53 upregulation, as evidenced by enhanced TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels (Fig. 6 B-6D). Beyond that, increased apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells caused by OGD/R was distinctly constrained by TP53 deficiency, and the forced expression of TP53 could partially abrogate the negative effects of Naringin on OGD/R-triggered cell apoptosis (Fig. 6 E). In parallel, OGD/R-induced oxidative stress and ferroptosis were also overturned via TP53 downregulation, as described by lower ROS and MDA, higher GSH, and reduced Fe+  level. Meanwhile, the protective effect of Naringin against OGD/R-caused oxidative stress and ferroptosis was significantly reversed by elevated TP53 upregulation, accompanied by increased ROS and MDA, decreased GSH, and enhanced Fe+  level ( Fig. 7 A-7D). In addition, TP53 silencing could improve SLC7A11 protein level, and overexpressing TP53 could ameliorate the positive role of Naringin on SLC7A11 protein level in OGD/R-disposed SK-N-SH cells (Fig. 7 E). All these results indicated that Naringin treatment could ameliorate OGD/R-induced cell injury by targeting TP53.    Discussion Recently, many TMCs have received increasing attention as a probable neuroprotective effect on the treatment of some nervous system diseases, containing cerebral I/R injury.28   Owing to the efficacy and few side effects, TCM represents an important area of focus cerebral I/R therapy. Cerebral I/R injury is one of the common complications of IS, often attributed to restoration of blood flow during thrombolysis or surgical treatment.29   In general, reperfusion provides an effective way to treat AIS, whereas the elevated ROS and inflammation, after reperfusion intensify tissue injury and neuronal death.30   Considering the irreversible I/R injuries, cell death represents a stabilizing indicator for I/R injury. Therefore, clarifying the mechanism of neuronal death after IS may be an effective neuroprotective strategy.31,32   As a distinct form of programmed cell death, ferroptosis is triggered by excessive iron and ROS.33   Increasing evidence has suggested that ferroptosis inhibition protects I/R-induced brain tissue damage.6,34   Notably, multiple experimental studies have presented that TMCs are associated with ferroptosis. For example, Galangin could repress ferroptosis and attenuate cerebral I/R injury by upregulating SLC7A11 and indirectly increasing GPX4 expression.21   Beyond that, Baicalein exerts neuro-protective effects in cerebral I/R through enhancing GPX4 expression and suppressing ferroptosis.35   Naringin is a naturally occurring flavonoid widely presented in citrus fruit and grapefruits.36   Some studies indicated the neuroprotective function of Naringin on neurological disorders,37   containing cerebral I/R.13   It has been reported that Naringin could mitigate cerebral I/R damage in rats through hindering endoplasmic reticulum stress.16   Apart from that, Naringin could protect HT22 cells against OGD/R injury by blocking oxidative stress and inflammatory response via the activation of SIRT1/FOXO1 signaling.38   In addition, much experimental evidence has indicated that Naringin could alleviate myocardial or intestinal I/R injury by repressing ferroptosis via targeting different signaling axis.39,40   Therefore, we hypothesized that Naringin could alleviate cerebral I/R damage by modulating ferroptosis. Herein, we initially found that Naringin had no significant impact on normal SK-N-SH cell viability, implying that Naringin had few side effects on nerve cells. Then, our data exhibited that OGD/R could impair SK-N-SH cell viability, while Naringin abolished these effects with its dosage increase. Functionally, OGD/R-induced inflammation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis were partially overturned after Naringin exposure. It has been reported that SLC7A11 is an important component of the cystine/glutamate reverse transporter and its suppression could cause ferroptosis mainly through ROS accumulation in some diseases.41,42   Herein, our data displayed that Naringin could improve SLC7A11 content, suggesting that Naringin could weaken OGD/R-induced cell damage via inhibiting ferroptosis. However, mechanism by which Naringin suppresses ferroptosis during AIS is still obscure. Network pharmacological analysis is a promising approach for predicting new drugs or disease-specific targets.43,44   Meanwhile, its downstream analysis, molecular docking, could accelerate drug design and screening by predicting affinity binding modes through ligand-receptor interactions.45   Herein, according to PPI network analysis of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis targets, 10 targets with the highest degree values, containing NFKB1, PTGS2, STAT3, JUN, ALB, IL6, AKT1, IL1B, TNF, and TP53, were acquired. After that, target-related enrichment analyses of KEGG pathways found that TP53 is enriched in ferroptosis. Subsequently, molecular docking simulation validated the binding ability between TP53 and Naringin, implying stable ligand-protein interactions. As a tumor suppressor, TP53 could hinder cancer cells through repressing cell cycle progression and boosting apoptosis.46,47   It has been reported that TP53 could reduce cystine uptake by repressing SLC7A11 expression, thereby resulting in Lipid peroxidation accumulation and increased ferroptosis.48   Further studies have suggested that TP53 deficiency could ameliorate cerebral I/R damage by regulating ferroptosis and apoptosis.26,49   Herein, our data confirmed that TP53 knockdown could dampen OGD/R-triggered SK-N-SH cell injury and ferroptosis. Meanwhile, overexpressing TP53 could partly abrogate the repression of Naringin on OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell damage and ferroptosis. These observations supported the neuroprotective effects of Naringin on OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell damage via suppressing TP53-SLC7A11-mediated ferroptosis. The current work was limited to in vitro  research, and in further work, in vivo  studies will utilize animal models to validate the novel mechanism of AIS.  Conclusion In summary, this study employed network pharmacology and molecular docking techniques to elucidate that the bioactive components of Naringin exhibit multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway characteristics in treatment of OGD/R-induced cell damage. Moreover, these findings outlined that Naringin may effectively attenuate OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell inflammation, apoptosis, and oxidative stress via targeting TP53/SLC7A11-mediated ferroptosis, providing an available preclinical basis for further investigation of Naringin in anti-AIS treatment. While our findings propose a novel phytotherapeutic strategy for AIS, clinical translation requires further validation through in vivo studies and human trials. title: Advances and challenges in therapeutic resistant biomarkers of neuroblastoma: A comprehensive review
abstract: Therapeutic resistance is one of the significant challenges in Neuroblastoma. Owing to its molecular diversity, the therapeutic resistance mechanisms of Neuroblastoma are highly complicated. The traditional chemo and radio therapeutics fail to provide adequate solutions to the treatment resistance, demanding in-depth research to improvise the existing prognostic and therapeutic regimens. To address this knowledge gap, several investigations are being employed, such as unravelling the molecular signalling mechanisms involved in drug resistance at genomics and proteomics levels, development of biomarkers for assessing the therapeutic success, development of novel drug targets for cancer stem cells, targeted immunotherapy and combination therapies. This review collates the ongoing research efforts to address the challenges faced in Neuroblastoma treatment resistance and uncovers the importance of transitioning biomarker discoveries into clinical practice.

Fig. 1 Characteristics of NB and biomarkers with prognostic, diagnostic, and therapeutic utility in NB. NB develops from immature nerve cells found in several body areas, most commonly in the adrenal glands, neck, chest, or spinal cord. NB is characterised by various genetic, epigenetic, and interaction factors. Biomarkers are molecules that can be measured in the blood, urine, or tumour tissue and help diagnose and monitor NB progression.  Fig. 1   Fig. 2 Exhibits the cross-interactions of various signalling pathways in NB. The red colour indicates different inhibitors targeted against these pathways. Crizotinib and Loratinib are used against ALK mutations. Rigosertib, Cobimetinib, and Binimetinib are targeted against RAS/MAPK signalling, while AZO6918 and GNF-4256 are targeted against TRK. In developmental signalling, FPN, XAV939, GANT61, and JARID1B are used to treat Neuroblastoma. No Title of the paper Summary References   1 CD133 expression and MYCN amplification induce chemoresistance and reduce average survival time in paediatric neuroblastoma (2018) The study analysed the role of CD133+ cells in NB, which makes them chemoresistant. CD133+ expression and MYCN amplification can be used to predict disease outcomes. [149 ]  2 Verteporfin induces apoptosis and reduces the stem cell-like properties in Neuroblastoma tumour-initiating cells through inhibition of the YAP/ TAZ pathway (2021) The study explores the role of targeting the YAP/TAZ pathway in NB. They found that Verteporfin, an inhibitor of the YAP/TAZ complex, effectively targets YAP/TAZ in Tumour-Initiating Cells from High-Risk Neuroblastoma patients, suppressing the expression of YAP/TAZ, CD133+, and CD44 stem cell populations. It also reduces drug resistance and causes apoptosis. It can be used as first-line therapy along with a combination of standard chemotherapy to advance treatment effects and prevent relapse in NB. [150 ]  3 A Phase I: New Approaches to Neuroblastoma Therapy Study of Buthionine Sulfoximine and Melphalan with Autologous Stem Cells for Recurrent/Refractory High-Risk Neuroblastoma (2016) The study evaluated the role of Buthionine Sulfoximine and Melphalan with Autologous Stem Cells in treating recurrent and high-risk NB. [151 ]  4 Significance of hematopoietic surface antigen CD34 in neuroblastoma prognosis and the genetic landscape of CD34 expressing neuroblastoma CSCs (2021) The study found the role of CD34 in NB. It analysed the hematopoietic surface antigen CD34 levels in NB cells and their relevance to disease progression, evolution, and clinical outcomes. CD34 positivity in NB patients corresponds to advanced disease stage and disease evolution, and it is attributed to poor survival in N-MYC-amplified high-risk patients. [152 ]  5 Transition to a mesenchymal state in neuroblastoma confers resistance to the anti-GD2 antibody via reduced expression of ST8SIA1 (2022) The study analysed the association of ST8SIA1 and GD2 expression in mesenchymal and adrenergic neuroblastoma. They found that reduced GD2 expression in neuroblastoma is linked to the mesenchymal cell state and a forced adrenergic-to-mesenchymal transition, leading to downregulation of GD2 and resistance to anti-GD2 antibodies. Inhibition of EZH2 restored GD2 surface expression and sensitivity to anti-GD2 antibodies. This implies that susceptibility to anti-GD2 immunotherapies is mainly determined by developmental lineage, which may help enhance treatment results for patients with advanced neuroblastoma. [153 ]  6 JARID1B Expression Plays a Critical Role in Chemoresistance and Stem Cell-like Phenotype of Neuroblastoma Cells (2015) The study found the role of JARID1B, which is involved in stemness and drug resistance in NB. JARID1B overexpression promotes stem cell-like characteristics and drug resistance in NB, observed in both MYCN amplification and non-amplified NB cell lines. Suppression of JARID1B expression results in the downregulation of the Notch/Jagged signalling pathway. This correlation implies that targeting JARID1B might be a promising therapeutic strategy for combating malignant NB. [154 ]  7 Molecular and functional analysis of anchorage-independent, treatment-evasive neuroblastoma tumorspheres with enhanced malignant properties: A possible explanation for radio-therapy resistance (2018) The study explored the role of Anchorage-dependent and independent tumorspheres contributing to radioresistance in NB. [155 ]  8 Wnt pathway activity confers chemoresistance to cancer stem-like cells in a neuroblastoma cell line (2012) The study identifies the role of Wnt signalling and its effect in conferring chemoresistance in cancer stem cells in NB. The study showed that Wnt-related genes were differentially expressed in CD133+ cells compared to CD133-negative cells, with and without DOX treatment. DOX treatment significantly suppressed Wnt pathway activity in CD133-negative cells. β-catenin and p-GSK3β expression were more significant in DOX-treated and untreated CD133+ cells. Wnt inhibitors decreased the proportion of living cells in CD133+ cells, indicating that chemoresistance may be caused by elevated Wnt pathway activity. [156 ]  9 Chemoresistance, Cancer Stem Cells, and miRNA Influences: The Case for Neuroblastoma (2015) The review collates the impact of miRNAs on NB and cancer stem cell chemoresistance, which can be used to develop therapeutic regimes. The miR-17-92 and miR-21 are the most pivotal and upregulated, while let-7 and miR-9 are found to be downregulated in NB. [157 ]  10 Cancer stem cells in neuroblastoma therapy resistance (2017) The review emphasises the role of induced CSCs in NB progression, developing drug resistance and relapse in NB. Various signalling (Notch, STAT3, Wnt) and molecular markers such as ALDH and CD133 are being used to characterise the NB CSCs [158 ]  11 Cancer stem cells in Neuroblastoma: Expanding the therapeutic frontier (2019) The review focuses on various molecular markers, such as CD114, CD133, and CD44, essential in CSC progression and survival in NB. Evidence from patient-derived tumours and NB cell lines suggests that targeting various CSC-associated pathways would be an excellent therapeutic outcome for NB. [159 ]  12 Therapy resistance in Neuroblastoma: Mechanism and reversal strategies (2023) The article focuses on the mechanism behind therapy resistance and various reversal strategies used to combat therapy resistance in NB. Tideglusib is one of the drugs that has the potency to inhibit GSK-3β and CSC populations and help overcome therapy resistance in NB. [160 ]  13 Multidrug Resistance and Cancer Stem Cells in Neuroblastoma and Hepatoblastoma (2013) The review summarises the association between Multidrug resistance and CSC in NB and hepatoblastoma. Multidrug resistance occurs due to various factors, such as alterations in DNA repair, decreased drug uptake, and increased efflux, such as the ATP binding cassette. The association of CSC with multidrug resistance makes it even more difficult for the treatment regimes in NB. [161 ]  14 Mesenchymal Stromal Cells in Neuroblastoma: Exploring Crosstalk and Therapeutic Implications (2021) The review provides extensive information on the role of Mesenchymal Stromal cells (MSCs) in NB. MSCs are found to be involved in chemoresistance in NB in high-risk patients. Some studies have shown that MSCs protect NB cells from chemotherapy-induced apoptosis via the signalling pathway STAT3, which aids drug resistance and cell survival in NB. [162 ]  15 Mechanisms involved in selecting and maintaining neuroblastoma cancer stem cell populations and perspectives for therapeutic targeting (2021) The review explores the potential therapeutic strategies and challenges involved in therapy resistance and disease progression in NB. CD133+ NB cells exhibit multipotency and self-renewal capacity and aid in chemoresistance. CD44, a transmembrane glycoprotein, helps mediate cellular attachment and interactions and helps in tumour formation in NB CSCs.  In mouse studies, tumourigenic properties in NB are enriched due to the higher expression of CD24+ /CD34+ enriched NB populations in bone marrow NB metastases.
