Sri Ramachandra Faculty of Clinical Research Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research Chennai 600116 India   1 These authors contributed equally to this work      Therapeutic resistance is one of the significant challenges in Neuroblastoma. Owing to its molecular diversity, the therapeutic resistance mechanisms of Neuroblastoma are highly complicated. The traditional chemo and radio therapeutics fail to provide adequate solutions to the treatment resistance, demanding in-depth research to improvise the existing prognostic and therapeutic regimens. To address this knowledge gap, several investigations are being employed, such as unravelling the molecular signalling mechanisms involved in drug resistance at genomics and proteomics levels, development of biomarkers for assessing the therapeutic success, development of novel drug targets for cancer stem cells, targeted immunotherapy and combination therapies. This review collates the ongoing research efforts to address the challenges faced in Neuroblastoma treatment resistance and uncovers the importance of transitioning biomarker discoveries into clinical practice.   Keywords Neuroblastoma  Biomarkers  Chemotherapy resistance  Radiotherapy resistance  Immunotherapy resistance  Targeted therapy resistance  Cancer stem cell resistance   Data availability No data was used for the research described in the article.   1 Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB) is the prevailing solid tumour outside the skull, primarily affecting kids under five, with a peak incidence in infants and the third most common cancer in children [1 ]. NB, a paediatric cancer, originates from neural crest cells, which are embryonic cells with the potential to develop into various tissues, including the adrenal glands atop the kidneys and nervous system [2 ,3 ]. Besides that, it can also manifest in sympathetic nerve ganglia in nerve tissue along the spine, chest, abdomen, or pelvis. NB exhibits a wide range of clinical behaviours, from spontaneous healing to uncontrollable aggressive growth and metastasis. The NB tumour can infiltrate surrounding tissues and, in advanced stages, spread to distant organs such as the bones, liver, and bone marrow [4 ]. The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC) uses histological factors to classify peripheral neuroblastic tumours based on the Schwannian degree of stromal development, the neuroblastic cell morphology and maturity, the mitosis-karyorrhexis index (MKI), and other factors to determine favourable and unfavourable subgroups [5 ]. The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System (INRG) classifier has the following factors for NB classification: ploidy, gain or loss of function in chromosome 11, histologic category, grade of differentiation, MYCN status, patients' age at diagnosis (children under 18 months old have low prognosis). This eventually results in 16 categories of NB as low risk (>85 %), intermediate risk (≥50 % to ≤75 %), and high risk (<50 %) [6 ]. Prognosis in NB depends on age, disease stage, and genes. Younger patients and those with localised tumours have a better prognosis [7 ]. Unfortunately, treating NB can be challenging in advanced stages, affecting overall survival rates. Therefore, it is imperative to comprehend the intricate biology of NB and develop targeted therapeutic approaches, given its high prevalence in paediatric cancers. Molecular biomarkers are crucial in early detection, diagnosis, treatment and prognostic indicators of NB. Genetic testing, gene expression profiling, and molecular imaging can identify specific genetic and molecular abnormalities associated with NB [7 ,8 ]. As NB is a heterogeneous disease with variable clinical outcomes, molecular biomarkers help stratify patients into varied risk categories. This risk stratification guides physicians in tailoring treatment modalities conforming to the severity of the disease [9 ]. Alterations in genes such as MYCN (N-Myc) are associated with poor prognosis in NB [10 ]. Investigating the tumour's molecular profile helps predict the likelihood of disease progression and survival. Fig. 1   depicts the known characteristics and biomarkers for diagnosing the disease. Vanillylmandelic acid, catecholamines and homovanillic acid are the gold-standard urinary tumour markers that detect NB [11 ]. Molecular-based biomarkers include MYCN, ALK and chromosomal deletions in 11q and 1p [12 ]. PHOX2B is a homeodomain crucial for the nervous system development. Alterations in this gene lead to congenital central hypoventilation syndrome. It was observed that PHOX2A is used as a specific marker for identifying minimal residual disease in NB patients. This gene is considered a very sensitive and specific marker for NB compared to detecting the levels of GD2 synthase and TH. Stutterheim et al. observed PHOX2B in 94 % of bone marrow samples, which is favourable for NB, and it was found to be of greater sensitivity in detecting NB in clinical samples [13 ]. UCHL1 is a good prognostic marker in detecting NB since UCHL1 is responsible for the differentiation of neurons. It was observed that higher levels of UCHL1 are related to good clinical outcomes and better survival in NB. When Retinoic acid (RA) is given, UCHL1 helps promote neuronal differentiation, whereas when UCHL1 is inhibited, there is a significant drop in RA differentiation. In NB, UCHL1 also aids in RA growth arrest while inhibiting UCHL1 leads to growth arrest, indicating the dual role of UCHL1 in proliferation and differentiation [14 ]. NB tends to express higher levels of GD2, which is a glycolipid antigen. In normal tissues, levels of GD2 are minimal, making it advantageous for immunotherapeutic methods. In high-risk NB, anti-GD2 antibodies are effective in improving the survival rate. Hence, GD2 can be used as a specific biomarker [15 ]. Hussein et al. used a multi-omics approach to find novel biomarkers that can be used to treat NB. In ninety-nine NB patients, high-throughput data analysis such as miRNA-seq, methylation status and mRNA-seq has been done, and it was found that MYCN, POU2F2, hsa-miR-1305, hsa-miR-421 and SPI1 are suitable and specific potential markers which can be used for targeting NB [16 ]. In addition, recent studies have shown that non-coding RNAs (ncRNA) such as MEG63, NBAT-1, FOXD3-AS1 and miRNAs such as miR-558 and miR-137 are involved in the NB tumour progression and epigenetic regulation. Targeting these would be a promising therapeutic strategy in treating NB [17 ]. The discovery of many advanced biomarkers, which can improve diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic decisions, has provided specifics about tumour behaviour and clinical outcomes. The NB biomarkers employed in clinical practices are a) amplification of MYCN oncogene correlated with higher risk and worse prognosis, b) segmental chromosomal alterations in chromosomes 1p, 11q, and 17q associated with poor survival outcomes, c) immunotherapy response to surface antigen, anti-GD2, such as dinutuximab are currently incorporated in the NB treatment modalities for high-risk patients, which is crucial in determining the survival probabilities and prognostics of NB patients, d) circulating tumour DNA, conferring insights on heterogeneity, NB progression, and response to various treatments; however, its efficacy as a biomarker or in therapeutics is still under investigation, e) quantifying the presence of biochemical metabolites like catecholamines, f) mutations in ALK genes, g) epigenetic modifications like DNA methylation could be associated with risk stratification and survival [9 ]. However, other conundrums also come together to defy these advances in discovering NB-specific biomarkers. The major challenge itself is the heterogeneity of the NB, making the diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutics difficult across all sub-categories. The aforementioned biomarkers lack predictive power in guiding treatment decisions as well as predicting therapy resistance [18 ]. This review aims to highlight the therapeutics strategies available for NB and discuss the resistance developed in NB against different types of treatment strategies. Further, it comprehensively discusses the signalling targets identified so far that can be explored as marker &/or targets for breaking therapy resistance.  2 Therapeutics against neuroblastoma Conventional treatments for NB include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Surgery aims to eliminate the primary tumour, while chemotherapy and radiation target the remaining cancer cells [11 ]. Immunotherapy, a promising avenue in NB treatment, involves stimulating the invulnerable surrounding system to recognise and destroy cancer cells [19 ]. Additionally, targeted therapies could be employed based on the specific genetic alterations that interfere with specific molecular pathways in NB progression. For instance, identifying tumours with ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) mutations may guide using ALK inhibitors as part of the treatment regimen [20 ]. It is well established that Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) levels are upregulated in NB, which leads to significant resistance in p53-dependent apoptosis. However, COX-2 inhibitors like Indomethacin, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent, have demonstrated great potential in treating NB by significantly increasing the cytotoxic effects and chemosensitivity. Experimental studies suggest that Indomethacin can be a promising drug for treating human cancers, including NB, by interfering with the synthesis of prostaglandins and reducing Aβ42 levels [21 ]. Therapeutic outcomes for paediatric cancer, including NB, are enhanced by investing in the investigation of novel therapies and clinical trials. Thus, molecular biomarkers can monitor the response to various therapies by employing molecular imaging techniques such as positron emission tomography (PET). PET can evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment by measuring the tumour's metabolic activity. Gradual changes observed in the tumour's molecular profile with time during the course of therapy can help tailor the therapeutic strategies, thereby reducing the after-effects. Understanding NB's molecular profiles can pave the way for a personalised treatment that could differentiate aggressive and dormant presentations of the disease [22 ]. Intensive multimodal clinical therapy (IMCT) combines multiple treatment modalities to address various aspects of NB. Based on each patient's profile and disease risk category, combination therapies may be subjected to variation. Conventional treatments are limited in efficacy, especially in advanced cases [23 ]. Radiotherapy effectively controls the disease, particularly when the adrenal medulla is involved [24 ,25 ]. More recent research has focused on targeted therapies, including small-molecule inhibitors, epigenetic and noncoding-RNA treatments, and cell-based immunologic therapies, which promise to improve clinical outcomes [26 ,27 ]. However, the selection of therapy type and the presence of metastases are essential factors in determining the treatment outcome [28 ]. Therapeutic resistance in NB refers to the reduced efficacy of therapies, such as chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, in suppressing and eradicating the cancer cells. NB exhibits resistance to various treatment modalities, a significant challenge in managing the disease. Therapeutic-resistant biomarkers in NB include autophagy, long non-coding RNAs, extracellular vesicles, ATP-binding cassette transporters, microRNAs and cancer stem cells [18 ]. Specific microRNAs, such as those associated with MYCN amplification, differentiation, dissemination, and chemo-resistance, have been identified as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets [29 ]. Other potential biomarkers include CD44, MYCN, neuron-specific enolase, ferritin, vanillylmandelic acid:homovanillic acid ratio, Trk-A, lactate dehydrogenase, chromosome 1p, DNA index, and multidrug resistance [29 ]. The resistance to cytotoxic drugs in NB can be acquired during therapy due to the expansion of tumour cells with stable genetic or epigenetic alterations [30 ]. The diverse cell populations within the tumour, each with different genetic and molecular characteristics, contribute to therapeutic resistance. This heterogeneity can make eradicating all cancer cells with a single treatment approach challenging. NB, a highly heterogeneous cancer, exhibits reversible adaptive plasticity, allowing cells to switch between adhered and sphere-forming phenotypes associated with chemoresistance [5 ]. This plasticity is further complicated by treatment-resistant clones, identified through whole-exome sequencing of cell-free DNA [6 ]. These clones, including cancer stem cells, are crucial in therapy resistance and tumour evolution [7 ]. Some cancer cells may acquire additional mutations that confer resistance to therapies during treatment. The genetics of NB have explored different non-random genetic events, such as the loss of function and gain of function of alleles on the short and long arms of multiple chromosomes associated with tumour suppression and the progression of the disease, MYCN oncogene amplification, and aberrations in the normal diploid chromosomal content [20 ,31 ]. The hyper-diploid DNA index and absence of MYCN amplification are the clonal markers for the disease evolution and beneficial prognostic factors of NB. The emergence of resistant clones during disease evolution can lead to treatment failure. Additionally, the diversity in NB cell identity, influenced by unique transcriptional circuitries, adds complexity to developing resistance [8 ]. Advanced treatment modalities for traditional therapy-resistant NB include antibody-drug conjugates (ADC), radiation combined with multimodal immunotherapy, radiolabelled somatostatin analogues, etc. ADCs are used widely in the treatment of various solid tumours [32 ]. In NB, LGALS3BP, ALK, and GPC2 targeting ADCs are proven effective in the pre-clinical models [33 ,34 ]. hu14.18-IL2, the anti-GD2 conjugate ADC is showing promising effects in clinical trials [35 ]. Wayne L Furman has done a detailed review on immunotherapy in NB [36 ]. However, owing to the heterogeneity and plasticity nature of NB, along with intricacies in drug efflux mechanisms and the tumour microenvironment (TME), poses a significant challenge for developing ADCs specific to NB [37 ]. Moreover, clinical trials of these therapeutic modalities are still under investigation in treating paediatric tumours. Combining immunotherapy with high-dose radiation therapy (HDRT) is one multimodal therapy developed to increase the efficacy of such treatments. Traditional radiation therapy is often used for treating metastatic NB. Radiation therapy is known to modulate the immune microenvironment in cancers. However, radiation resistance usually arises in NB, leading to exploring other options. When combined with immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., anti-PD-1 or anti-CTLA-4), the immune system is activated to recognise and eliminate tumour cells more efficiently [38 ]. Studies in NB mice models demonstrate that HDRT and PD-1 interfere with NB growth, inducing immune response by enhancing CD8+  T lymphocyte infiltration [39 ]. Radiolabelled somatostatin analogues have emerged as an innovative therapeutic approach for NB, particularly in patients resistant to conventional therapies. NB, especially in their more aggressive forms, often express somatostatin receptors (SSTRs), which can be exploited for targeted therapy. Radiolabelled somatostatin analogues, such as 177 Lu-DOTATATE or 90 Y-DOTATOC, bind to SSTRs on the surface of NB cells, delivering targeted radiation to tumour cells while sparing surrounding healthy tissues [40 ]. This targeted approach is beneficial in minimising systemic toxicity, a common challenge in NB treatment. Despite the promise of these innovative therapies, several challenges remain. The heterogeneity of NB at the molecular and cellular levels contributes to the complexity of treatment resistance. Tumour evolution under selective pressure from therapies can give rise to the formation of resistant clones, necessitating the need for adaptive therapeutic strategies. Moreover, the TME, characterised by immune suppression and stromal support, poses additional hurdles in achieving sustained therapeutic success [18 ].  3 Chemotherapy resistance Chemotherapy is a standard treatment for NB and may involve a combination of drugs. Common drugs include vincristine, cisplatin, carboplatin, etoposide, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide. The current chemotherapy approach towards NB can be classified as induction and high-dose chemotherapy. Induction chemotherapy aims to mitigate the tumour burden and is often combined with surgery. In high-dose chemotherapy, treatment is usually accompanied by stem cell transplantation. Drug resistance, both intrinsic and acquired, is the problem faced in treating all types of cancers. In NB, drug resistance is one of the significant challenges faced in therapy response [18 ]. Chemoresistance in NB has been attributed to alterations in proteins implicated in several cellular signalling pathways (Refer to Table 1  ). The genes, proteins, and miRNAs listed in Table 1  have been altered in expression levels, and the clinical significance of these alterations has to be further probed. Identifying molecular pathways and biomolecules altered during the resistance process may help generate useful biomarkers for drug resistance in NB. Listed below are some of the critical molecular pathways and biomolecules altered in drug resistance in NB: 3.1 ABC superfamily Increased drug resistance in cancer cells is closely linked to the elevated expression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter proteins. Notably, the essential ABC proteins involved in drug resistance are the P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1) and the multi-drug resistance protein (MRP) family. The involvement of P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1) in chemoresistance has been extensively investigated across various cancers. P-gp, belonging to the ABC transmembrane transporter family, is notorious for expelling multiple molecules from the cell, including chemotherapeutic agents. In 1991, Chan et al. proposed P-glycoprotein as a potential biomarker for resistance in NB. Their study demonstrated that pre-treatment expression levels of P-gp could predict the efficacy of therapy in non-localised NB [41 ]. The MDR1 gene, encoding P-gp, was upregulated in human NB tissue samples and doxorubicin-resistant NB cells. Additionally, amplification of the 7q21 gene locus, primarily responsible for coding MDR genes, was observed [42 ]. P-glycoprotein overexpression is crucial in conferring resistance to multiple chemotherapy drugs in NB. Inhibition of P-gp in vincristine-resistant NB cells significantly reduced the drug resistance [43 ]. However, studies also indicate that acquiring this resistance and the associated malignant behaviour in NB cells can occur independently of P-gp [44 ]. The MRP family falls under subtype C of the ABC superfamily, with MRP1-9 being extensively studied for their role in drug resistance across various cancers. Numerous inhibitors targeting MRPs have been developed to modulate their function and reverse chemoresistance. In NB tissue samples, MRP1, MRP4, and MRP5 exhibit overexpression [42 ,45 ]. This overexpression of MRP1 shows a significant correlation with N-MYC expression and is frequently linked to therapy failure in NB [46 ]. A comprehensive review by Marina et al. delves into the role of MRP1 in NB biology and drug resistance [47 ]. In NB xenograft mouse models, the inhibition of MRP using probenecid has been shown to retain the chemotherapeutic drug [131-I]MIBG effectively. The study also identifies MRP1 and MRP4 as the routes of excretion for [131-I]MIBG. Combining [131-I]MIBG with MRP inhibitors presents a promising approach to mitigate chemoresistance in NB patients [48 ].  3.2 Apoptosis pathway Alteration in the p53 gene plays a vital role in chemoresistance across several cancers [49 ]. Despite the lower prevalence of p53 mutations in NB, mutated or non-functional p53 strongly correlates with chemoresistance in this context. In NB cell line studies conducted in vitro, it has been observed that NB cells with a TP53 wild-type phenotype exhibit a more favourable response to anti-cancer drugs such as doxorubicin and vincristine, as compared to cells with a mutant phenotype [50 ]. The loss of p53 function is evident in NB cells selected for resistance to chemotherapy drugs, particularly those induced by heavy metals. NB cell lines carrying the p53 M135 mutation demonstrate heightened resistance to chemotherapy drugs such as doxorubicin, vincristine, and cisplatin compared to the parental cell lines [51 ]. The p53 pathway can activate the NF-kB signalling via the MEK/ERK axis, which helps regulate the response of NB towards chemotherapy drugs like doxorubicin. This pathway induces apoptosis in NB cells, thereby improving the effectiveness of the chemotherapy. The study is critical because MEK/ERK inhibitors, developed as anti-cancer agents, can hinder the chemotherapeutic effects of conventional drugs like doxorubicin by inhibiting these proteins [52 ]. Furthermore, multiple crucial proteins in the apoptotic pathway have been implicated in chemoresistance in NB. Elevated expression of the apoptosis regulators Mcl1 and Bcl2 was observed in human NB tissue samples. Gene modulations targeting Mcl1 in NB cell lines unveiled its involvement in multidrug resistance, while alterations to the Bcl2 gene did not impact drug resistance [53 ,54 ]. Notably, a decrease in Bcl2 expression and a corresponding reduction in doxorubicin resistance was observed in NB cell lines where Tissue Factor (TF) had been knocked down, indicating the role of Bcl2 in doxorubicin resistance in NB [55 ].  3.3 Wnt signalling pathway & CSCs Gene expression profiling in two doxorubicin-resistant cell lines and a parental cell line revealed a high expression of the WNT signalling pathway mediator Frizzled 1 (FZD1). Downregulation of FZD1 greatly enhanced the sensitivity of the cells to the chemo drugs. RNA analysis in patient samples also revealed a high expression of FZD1 post-chemotherapy, indicating its role in chemoresistance [56 ]. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) exhibit inherent resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. However, current research has shifted its focus towards exploring acquired genetic alterations in non-stem cancer cells, transforming them into induced cancer stem cells (iCSCs) following radiochemotherapy. To effectively address therapy resistance and achieve successful treatment of NB, it is imperative to develop advanced therapeutic strategies targeting pre-existing CSCs [57 ]. CD133 is expressed generally by the neural progenitor cells. Research conducted on doxorubicin-resistant NB cells has shown an increased presence of CD133+ cells, indicating a potential association with drug resistance. Furthermore, these doxorubicin-resistant NB cells exhibited heightened activity in the Wnt signalling pathway. This heightened activity was characterised by elevated expressions of β-catenin and phosphorylated GSK beta (p-GSK beta) [58 ].  3.4 PI3k/Akt pathway The inhibition of PI3K/Akt has been identified as a strategy to enhance sensitivity to chemo drugs and represents a potential therapeutic target [46 ]. Despite the activation of Akt protein by various factors in doxorubicin-resistant NB cells, studies indicate that inhibiting Akt does not impact the chemoresistance observed in these cells. Overexpression of embryonic stem cell-expressed Ras (eRas) in NB cell lines induced multidrug resistance through the Akt signalling pathway [59 ]. ROCK inhibition in NB cell lines showed increased cell proliferation and chemoresistance to cisplatin [60 ]. Cisplatin-resistant cells exhibited a notably heightened amino acid metabolism compared to cisplatin-sensitive cells, with autophagy playing a pivotal role in this process [48 ]. In NB, cells resistant to doxorubicin and etoposide, increased levels of reduced glutathione and elevated catalase activity were observed. This combination protects cancer cells from membrane lipoperoxidation and avert cell death [61 ].  3.5 Angiogenesis pathway In-silico  gene expression analysis reported that the expression of angiogenesis-associated genes significantly varies between chemosensitive and chemoresistant NB cells. Consecutively, in vitro and in vivo research show a transition towards pro-angiogenic features in chemoresistant NB models. Albeit a change in the expression pattern of pro-angiogenic genes in these cell lines, there is no similarity in the overexpressed genes, pointing to context-dependent changes [68 ]. In NB mouse models, up-regulation of HIF-1α significantly contributed to the anti-angiogenic therapies, and suppressing HIF-1α potentiated the effects of the anti-angiogenic drugs in a mouse model [69 ].  3.6 Cathepsin family Cathepsins, a family of lysosomal proteases, have been extensively studied for their role in chemoresistance in NB. Cathepsin L (CTSL) induced chemoresistance in NB by upregulating the expression of MDR proteins and interfering with autophagy levels. In both in vitro and in vivo settings, inhibiting CTSL and chemotherapy drugs resulted in a significant reversal of chemoresistance in NB [70 ]. Similarly, studies involving MYCN overexpressed NB cell lines revealed increased expression of Cathepsin D (CTSD). Silencing CTSD was shown to reverse chemoresistance to doxorubicin significantly [71 ].  3.7 DNA repair pathway Single-cell RNA sequencing in drug-sensitive parental cells and etoposide and cisplatin-resistant NB cells revealed upregulation in DNA repair mechanisms of genes like BARD1, BRCA1, and PARP1 [72 ]. Studies report alterations in DNA methylation status in chemoresistant NB cells, and combining epigenetic modifiers with chemotherapy drugs has been shown to reverse such resistant epigenetic modifications significantly [73 ].  3.8 Genetic & epigenetic pathways Investigating genetic and epigenetic modifications in chemoresistant NB models has identified potential biomarker candidates. Telomerase function contributes to radiation resistance in NB, while chemoresistance depends on the specific anti-cancer drugs and the model used for the study [74 ]. In approximately 25 % of high-risk NB, the Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres (ALT) mechanism maintains the telomere length. Patient-derived xenograft models of ALT NB demonstrate high resistance to temozolomide and irinotecan, mediated through the constitutive activation of the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein [75 ]. In NB cell lines, an upregulation in the C282Y variant of the cellular iron uptake protein HFE was observed, associated with increased p16INK4A protein expression and resistance to drugs like Temodar and geldanamycin. The HFE variants are prevalent in up to 10 % of Caucasians [76 ]. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in CYP genes regulate drug resistance in NB. Polymorphisms in CYP3A5 and NQO1 affect vincristine resistance in NB [77 ]. In Italian patients with high-risk NB, identifying rs907187 SNPs in the PARP1 gene is associated with the potential failure of induction chemotherapy [78 ]. Few studies have been conducted on the function of micro-RNAs and cancer stem cells in NB chemoresistance, as described in Table 2  .   4 Radiation therapy resistance Having established the critical role of chemotherapy in the multifaceted treatment landscape of NB, it is essential to pivot towards the significance and prevalence of radiotherapy in addressing this complex paediatric cancer. Radiation therapy is often employed in NB after surgery or in cases where complete tumour removal is not possible, aiming to target and destroy cancer cells. However, the mechanisms underlying radiation resistance in NB still need to be fully understood, and there is a scarcity of studies identifying radiation resistance markers in this context. In genetically engineered NB mouse models with MYC-N-driven alterations, the loss of p53 function resulted in resistance to ionising radiation. Microarray analysis of isolated cells revealed increased expression of proteins regulating glutathione metabolism in this scenario [84 ,85 ]. Conversely, in radioresistant variants of human NB IMR 32 cells, there was an increase in the p53 gene. The authors proposed that downstream targets of p53 might act as regulators in this context, although further studies are required for confirmation [86 ]. Studies conducted on human NB cell lines exposed to low linear energy transfer (LET) radiation doses showed a time-dependent regulation of the apoptosis machinery, indicating a potential impact on radiosensitivity in NB [87 ]. Low miR-145 levels were observed in radioresistant NB cells, and the autophagy marker LC3 expression was proportional to miR-145 expression, suggesting autophagy's role in radioresistance in NB [88 ]. In addition, high telomerase activity was found in radioresistant NB cells, and inhibiting this activity significantly altered radio-resistance, similar to chemoresistance [74 ] Understanding resistance mechanisms is crucial to enhance the effectiveness of radiotherapy in treating NB.  5 Immunotherapy resistance The microenvironment surrounding NB tumours involves a complex interaction of biomarkers that plays a key role in developing drug resistance and immune evasion [89 ]. Studies discovering the mechanisms of immune invasion, evasion and unwinding the dynamics within the microenvironment highlight the importance of studying immunotherapy as a potential therapeutic option for NB [90 ]. The TME regulates immune evasion and influences the efficacy of immune responses. This understanding of immune evasion within the TME to exploring immunotherapy highlights the need for interventions that activate the body's immune system against NB [91 ,92 ]. ESTIMATE algorithm identified prognostic genes negatively correlated with MYCN amplification in TME, including ARHGAP15, ABCA9, CCL19, SLAMF8, and CD1C. These genes are associated with T-cell activation, regulation of lymphocyte activation, leukocyte migration, and cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions [93 ]. A positive correlation was observed between immune exhaustion and cytotoxic activity in a subset of MYCN-NA NB tumours. This suggests potential benefits from FDA-approved therapies targeting immune checkpoints CTLA4 and PDCD1 (PD1) for high-risk NB patients [89 ]. TME promotes tumour drug resistance, delving into the biochemical and molecular mechanisms, such as hypoglycemia, reactive oxygen species, and hypoxia in general [94 ,95 ]. Hypoxia, immune suppression, and interactions with surrounding cells contribute to resistance in NB [96 ]. Transcriptomic analyses using Machine Learning identified seven hypoxia-related genes associated with telomeric activation and hypoxia-related immunosuppression in untreated NB tumours [97 ]. NB cells may evade the immune system by expressing immune checkpoint molecules like PD-L1, limiting the efficacy of immunotherapy. Immunotherapy, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibodies targeting markers like GD2, has shown promise in treating NB [90 ]. Dinutuximab, a monoclonal antibody against GD2, has been utilised in some cases, although resistance to immunotherapy can be influenced by the TME and immune escape mechanisms [98 ]. Discerning the relationship of TME, including the extracellular matrix, stromal cells, and immune cells, is crucial for comprehending tumour progression [99 ]. The TME in NB, characterised by reduced T and NK cell infiltration and immune evasion tactics, may contribute to resistance [91 ,100–103 ]. Factors such as low tumour mutation burden, downregulated MHC-I, and the gut microbiome further complicate responses to immune checkpoint blockade [104 ]. Exosomes implicated in metastasis and resistance to immunotherapy in high-risk NB may be targeted with small molecule inhibitors [105 ]. As investigations into the TME of NB have progressed, significant research is being made to shed light on the intricate cellular and molecular processes in tumour growth. Transitioning from exploring TME paves the way for discovering targeted therapies that exploit this knowledge to develop more effective treatments for NB.  6 Targeted therapy resistance – developmental signalling pathways Abnormal activation of developmental signalling such as Notch, Wnt, Hippo and Hedgehog pathways and resistance mechanisms highlights NB progression's complex interplay. Targeting these pathways, including Wnt inhibition, Notch antagonism, and ALK inhibitors, emerges as a promising therapeutic approach [106–108 ]. Fig. 2   depicts the intricate communications of different signalling pathways in NB. Additionally, insights into RA signalling, Hippo/YAP pathway modulation, and epigenetic regulation through BET proteins offer potential avenues for overcoming resistance. Table 3   compiles the various therapeutic targets involved in therapeutic resistance and their phases in clinical trials. 6.1 Wnt signalling Deregulated β-catenin signalling can lead to malignant transformation even in high-risk NBs without MYCN amplification. This activation results in the transactivation of MYC and various other target genes, promoting malignant phenotype. Studies by Liu, et al analysed the effects of activated Wnt signalling in NB, revealing higher MYC and β-catenin expression levels in NB cell lines without MYCN amplification. Additionally, expression profile studies in primary NBs demonstrated abnormal β-catenin-TCF transcriptional activity and elevated expression of WNT ligands in high-risk NBs without MYCN amplification [109 ,110 ]. Targeting the Wnt signalling pathway using specific inhibitors like XAV939 showed enhanced sensitivity to doxorubicin in NB cell lines. Targeting the Wnt signalling pathway, using particular inhibitors like XAV939 or silencing using RNA interference showed improved sensitivity to doxorubicin in NB cell lines [111 ].  6.2 Notch signalling Notch and c-kit are emerging molecules in cancer research. Lithium chloride (LiCl), by inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase 3-β activity, enhances the immunoreactivity of Notch 1, c-kit, Delta1 and Jagged 1. The study emphasises the potential roles of these signalling pathways in cancer [112 ]. Furthermore, the Delta-Notch pathway activation in NB, regulated by the MSX1 homeobox transcriptional factor, is implicated in angiogenesis. Notch signalling antagonists, such as γ-secretase inhibitors (GSIs), lower angiogenesis and reduce tumour viability [110 ]. NB cells can differentiate when treated with RA. Resistance to RA is a common observation in NB, limiting its clinical utility. Gain-of-function genetic studies identify a link between Mastermind-like 3 (MAML3) and RA signalling. MAML3 is a transcriptional coactivator for NOTCH, and its expression leads to the loss of activation of a group of RA target genes, promoting resistance. Moreover, RA-independent functions of MAML3, including activating IGF1R and downstream AKT signalling, contribute to increased proliferation. Understanding the resistance mechanisms to RA may provide insights into potential therapeutic strategies [113 ].  6.3 Hippo/Yes-Associated Protein (YAP) Signalling The highly conserved Hippo/Yes-Associated Protein (YAP) signalling pathway plays a crucial role in regulating various biological processes, including the regulation of tissue regeneration and self-renewal of stem cells [114 ]. In NB, YAP and TAZ activation correlates with adverse prognostic features. High-risk NB tumours with increased genomic alterations show elevated transcriptional activity of YAP [115 ]. Targeting YAP with inhibitors like Peptide 17 has demonstrated potential in preventing tumour growth and improving chemotherapy response. Additionally, the BH3-only protein Harakiri (HRK), inhibited by YAP, acts as a tumour suppressor and suggests the dual inhibition of MEK and YAP as therapeutic targets in RAS-hyperactivated NBs [116 ]. The pre-mRNA processing factor 19 (Prp19) is associated with high-risk markers in NB, promoting invasion, migration, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition by regulating YAP expression [117 ].  6.4 Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) Signalling and its Suppression The Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signalling pathway, crucial for early embryonic development, stem cell renewal, and various cancers, has been explored in NB [118 ]. Kruppel-like factor 9 (KLF9) has been associated with favourable prognosis in NB, and its expression negatively correlates with SHH signalling. Advanced-stage NBs exhibit lower KLF9 expression, confirming its role in suppressing NB growth and progression [119 ]. GANT61, a GLI inhibitor targeting the SHH pathway, reduces the in vivo growth of high-risk NB lacking MYCN amplification [120 ].  6.5 ALK Inhibition and Resistance Mechanisms Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) is considered to be the target of gene modifications in familial and sporadic NB. Crizotinib, an ALK inhibitor, shows effectiveness against specific ALK mutations but has limitations [121 ]. Lorlatinib, a third-generation ALK inhibitor, is being investigated for relapsed NB, implicating ALK inhibitor resistance. NF1 loss-of-function mutations in NB may involve MEK inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy [122 ]. Combining ALK inhibitors with chemotherapy improves outcomes. The complex genetic heterogeneity of NB, including MYCN amplification and ALK mutations, poses challenges in developing targeted therapies [123 ].  6.6 Receptor Tyrosine Kinase (RTK)/PI3K Pathway The dysregulation of apoptotic pathways, specifically the Receptor Tyrosine Kinase (RTK)/PhosphoInositide 3-Kinase (PI3K) pathway, impacts NB development. Targeting the insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor and PI3K signalling axis using specific antibodies against IGF-1R and PI3K inhibitors reduces cell proliferation and sensitises NB cells to chemotherapy. Down-regulation of IGF-1R/PI3K downstream signalling targets and apoptosis are observed in embryonal tumour cells treated with PI3K inhibitors [124 ]. The AKT inhibitor Hu7691 effectively inhibits NB cell growth and promotes cell differentiation, showing promise in clinical trials. The activation of the AKT pathway, linked to a poor prognosis in NB, suggests that AKT inhibitors may offer therapeutic benefits [125 ]. Regorafenib, an FDA-approved diphenyl urea multikinase inhibitor, has shown significant anti-tumour activity in preclinical models, inhibiting various kinases, including TIE-2, PDGFRβ, RET, FGFR1, BRAF, RAF1, VEGFR1–3, and p38 MAPK kinases implicated as surface receptors and intracellular signalling pathways [126 ]. PIK75, a targeted inhibitor of PI3K p110a and R1507, an IGF-1R-specific antibody, decreased cell proliferation in NB cell lines. PIK75 exhibited a wide-ranging anti-proliferative influence, whereas R1507 enhanced the sensitivity of NB cells to chemotherapy [124 ].  6.7 BET proteins and epigenetic regulation BET proteins, epigenetic regulators controlling gene expression, play a role in oncogenesis. BET protein Inhibitors such as GSK1324726A (I-BET726) effectively inhibit cell proliferation and induce cell death in NB cell lines regardless of MYCN expression levels. Gene expression analysis reveals that BET inhibition influences apoptosis and N-Myc-driven pathways. BET inhibitors, like I-BET726, are promising therapeutic agents in NB regardless of MYCN expression level [127 ].  6.8 TrK Inhibitors and Resistance The neurotrophin receptor family member TrK is associated with high-risk NB and poor survival. TrK inhibitors, including GNF-4256 and AZD6918, slow xenograft tumour growth. Combining TrK inhibitors with chemotherapy yields significantly better outcomes. The dysregulation of TrK contributes to drug resistance, angiogenesis, and metastasis in NB [110 ]. Unravelling the complex signalling pathways implicated in NB and their role in therapy resistance is crucial for formulating a comprehensive strategy. This knowledge will aid in identifying and surmounting resistance mechanisms, ultimately enhancing treatment outcomes.   7 Neuroblastoma cancer stem cells in therapeutic resistance NB exhibits heterogeneous clinical behaviour, ranging from relapse to malignant transformation and resistance to chemotherapy. This resistance is predominantly attributed to CSCs, a subgroup within the tumour with stem cell-like properties having self-renewal and differentiating capabilities. Identifying CSC markers and specific genes for therapeutic targeting in NB is challenging as it contributes to heterogeneity, acquiring fast genetic rearrangements, drug resistance and poor outcomes, increasing the risk of tumour progression and recurrence. CD133, FZD6, LGR5, and ALDH are tumour-initiating surface markers inversely correlated with overall survival in NB patients [132–134 ]. A genotype analysis in neural cancer stem cells shows a gain of function mutation in the region 16p13 and is associated with the expression of CD133 [135 ]. Targeted inhibition of CD133 in NB cells hampers NB differentiation. It increases the sensitivity to the drug treatment channelised by regulating several signalling pathways, such as MAPK, ERK, JNK, and PI3K/AKT [132 ,136 ]. Elevated levels of LGR5+ CSCs in IMCT-resistant cells drive oncogenesis, and its inhibition promotes apoptosis through activation of the MEK/ERK pathway [137 ]. Inhibition of the surface receptor, FZD6, interferes with the formation of neurospheres [138 ]. Similarly, suppression of ALDH decreases the formation of neurospheres and is associated with RA tolerance [139 ]. MRP1 is a direct transcriptional target of MYCN in NB, and its activation leads to elevated levels of expression of MPR1 accompanied by drug resistance and increased MRP1-mediated drug efflux. MYCN maintains stemness in NB CSCs, enhancing their plasticity and chemoresistance [140 ]. B cell-specific Moloney murine leukaemia virus Integration site 1 (BMI1) is a polycomb family of proteins, also an oncoprotein, critical in multiple cellular processes like differentiation, senescence, stem cell self-renewal, and drug resistance, which inflicts NB progression [141–143 ]. High expression of BMI1 contributes to therapy resistance by regulating signalling molecules like cyclin E1, KIF1β, and TSLC1. Inhibition of BMI1 by the inhibitor PTC596 induces ferroptosis, increases cytotoxicities, and decreases the EMT transition and stemness of multi-drug resistant NB cells [144 ]. Developmental signalling pathways like Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and TGF-β may contribute to the stemness phenotype of CSCs in NB. Targeting CSC pathways is challenging as they are highly therapy-resistant. POU5F1 is implicated in stemness and tumourigenesis by interacting with members of other pathways like TGF-β, Notch, and Wnt. These pathways are up-regulated, inducing cell proliferation in neurospheres, indicating its potential as a new therapeutic target [145 ]. The transcription factor SLC34A2 plays a regulatory role in the stemness of NB. It exhibits elevated expression in NB-derived spheroids and is inversely correlated with overall and relapse-free survival. SLC34A2 directly interacts with the promoter of MIR25 and targets Wnt signalling antagonist glycogen synthesis kinase 3β (Gsk3β). This suggests that SLC34A2 promotes stemness by facilitating miR-25/Gsk3β-mediated activation of the Wnt signalling pathway in NB cells [146 ]. JARID1B, identified as an oncogene, functions as a histone lysine demethylase, negatively impacting NB survival rates. Its overexpression promotes stem cell-like characteristics and drug resistance in NB, observed in both MYCN amplification and non-amplified NB cell lines. Suppression of JARID1B expression results in the down-regulation of the Notch/Jagged signalling pathway. This correlation implies that targeting JARID1B might be a promising therapeutic strategy for combating malignant NB. The positive association between JARID1B and Notch signalling further suggests the potential efficacy of this combination as a therapeutic target [147 ]. Induced telomerase activity also directly contributes to the proliferation of CSCs. Inhibiting the telomerase activity with Imetelstat interferes with the self-renewing capability of CSCs. Recent studies explore the various signalling targets in conjunction with TME for addressing the NB-CSCs' therapy resistance [97 ]. However, the resistance mechanism of CSCs could be induced or acquired, which is attributed to different intrinsic and extrinsic reactions and clonal evolution [148 ]. Table 4   synthesises the research carried out on NB-CSCs and therapeutic resistance. Identifying the novel regulators that could inhibit CSC growth or sensitise the resistance mechanism offers promising therapeutic targets and provides insights into the intricacies of NB-CSC resistance mechanisms. This investigation aspect could lead to the development of better markers for prognosis/diagnosis of therapeutic resistance.  8 Conclusion and future perspectives A childhood cancer, NB arises from immature precursor nerve cells in various body regions. In the comprehensive landscape of NB treatment, surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy stand as pivotal pillars, each contributing to the multifaceted approach aimed at tackling this challenging malignancy. However, the tumour's inherent resistance to these multimodal therapeutics (IMCT) adds a layer of complexity to the clinical scenario. In the field of NB research, it is imperative to focus on identifying biomarkers for therapeutic resistance. Our review highlights the significant efforts made to apprehend the mechanisms of resistance. It emphasises the need to redirect attention towards identifying robust molecular signatures that can serve as reliable markers of treatment resistance. We propose a paradigm shift in the scientific community to recognise the untapped potential within the well-explored resistance pathways, identifying molecular signatures for developing biomarkers. Through a comprehensive study of these investigations carried out so far, the identification and application of biomarkers in therapeutic resistance will prove indispensable not only in diagnosis and prognosis but also in the development of personalised and effective therapeutic interventions. So, developing therapeutic-resistant biomarkers in NB is challenging. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, refined radiation protocols, and potent chemotherapy regimens, resistance biomarkers in NB continue to evade complete explanation. Understanding the molecular intricacies of NB's ability to evade treatment is crucial in identifying resistance biomarkers and developing targeted therapies. Recent studies have shown the promising value of liquid biopsy, a non-invasive way to detect biomarkers of therapeutic resistance in NB by analysing circulating tumour cells, cell-free DNA, and exosomes in the blood of cancer patients and its significance in monitoring the therapy response [12 ,164 ,165 ]. Furthermore, single-cell sequencing can identify resistance biomarkers and monitor therapy response in NB. Advancements in sequencing technology can reveal the genetic heterogeneity of NB tumours, leading to more precise diagnostic markers. Integrating genetic, proteomic, and metabolic markers into comprehensive panels can improve the accuracy of predicting treatment success. Assimilating such data at various molecular levels can provide a comprehensive outlook on the response to the therapeutics of NB. Fig. 3   outlines the experimental approaches for developing multimodal therapy-resistant biomarkers in NB. In addition, incorporating advanced imaging techniques, such as functional MRI, dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging, and positron emission tomography (PET), can shed light on the functional aspects of the tumour's therapeutic response. These imaging modalities may offer early indications of treatment efficacy, facilitating timely adjustments to the therapeutic regimen. Another promising approach for treating NB is immunotherapy, which utilises the body's immune system to combat cancer. Recent studies have shown its effectiveness in NB therapeutics. However, developing immunotherapy-resistant biomarkers is a significant challenge as uncovering the dynamics of the immune microenvironment and immune escape needs to be addressed. Future therapeutic markers may guide the selection of targeted therapies tailored to specific molecular vulnerabilities. Combining targeted agents with conventional treatments or immunotherapies based on individualised biomarker profiles may enhance treatment efficacy and prevent relapse. So, monitoring dynamic changes in molecular biomarkers during treatment can help identify early signs of resistance with combinatorial therapeutics. Adaptive treatment strategies, guided by real-time biomarker assessments, may mitigate the development of drug resistance. In parallel, adopting Machine Language and Artificial Intelligence for data integration and analysis can process large-scale omics data and clinical information, identifying intricate patterns associated with treatment outcomes and resistance. Such algorithms may assist clinicians in issuing personalised treatment based on a patient's unique biomarker profile. Amalgamating advanced technologies holds immense promise in advancing NB management and improving the overall prognosis for affected individuals. title: XPO1 inhibition with selinexor synergizes with proteasome inhibition in neuroblastoma by targeting nuclear export of IkB
abstract: Across many cancer types in adults, upregulation of the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic transport protein Exportin-1 (XPO1) correlates with poor outcome and responsiveness to selinexor, an FDA-approved XPO1 inhibitor. Similar data are emerging in childhood cancers, for which selinexor is being evaluated in early phase clinical studies. Using proteomic profiling of primary tumor material from patients with high-risk neuroblastoma, as well as gene expression profiling from independent cohorts, we have demonstrated that XPO1 overexpression correlates with poor patient prognosis. Neuroblastoma cell lines are also sensitive to selinexor in the low nanomolar range. Based on these findings and knowledge that bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor, blocks degradation of XPO1 cargo proteins, we hypothesized that combination treatment with selinexor and bortezomib would synergistically inhibit neuroblastoma cellular proliferation. We observed that selinexor promoted nuclear retention of IkB and that bortezomib augmented the ability of selinexor to induce cell-cycle arrest and cell death by apoptosis. This synergy was abrogated through siRNA knockdown of IkB. The synergistic effect of combining selinexor and bortezomib in vitro provides rationale for further investigation of this combination treatment for patients with high-risk neuroblastoma.
