Approximately 15% of childhood cancer-related deaths are due to NB [3] . High-risk NB (HR-NB) constitutes nearly 40% of all cases. Despite comprehensive treatment, the five-year overall survival rate for HR-NB remains under 50% [4] . Critically, even with anti-GD2 immunotherapy, nearly half of treated patients still relapse [5] , and it remains prohibitive for most families in China [6] . Induction chemotherapy plays a pivotal role in reducing tumor burden and enabling subsequent treatments, with patient response during this phase closely correlating with prognosis in HR-NB [7,8] . However, most current chemotherapeutic agents for NB primarily exert their anti-tumor effects through apoptosis, which may promote the development of chemotherapeutic drug resistance, leading to minimal residual disease(MRD) and increasing the risk of relapse [9] . Therefore, there is an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies that can overcome resistance and enhance treatment efficacy in HR-NB. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of cell death characterized by lipid peroxidation [10] . Increasing evidence has demonstrated that ferroptosis has emerged as a promising strategy for the treatment of drug-resistant tumors [11] . During NB treatment, spontaneous phenotypic transition toward a mesenchymal-like state has been observed. These mesenchymal cells exhibit strong drug resistance and are considered a major source of MRD and tumor recurrence [12] . Drug-resistant tumor cells across multiple cancer types converge toward a similar mesenchymal phenotype and rely on GPX4 to maintain redox homeostasis. Inhibition of GPX4 effectively triggers ferroptosis and prevents tumor regeneration [13,14] . Moreover, MYCN amplification, a hallmark high-risk feature of NB, has been reported to confer ferroptosis vulnerability. MYCN-amplified NB cells exhibit iron-dependent features, including upregulation of TFRC, increased labile iron pool, and heightened sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers [15,16] . Besides, MYCN-amplified NB cells show a strong dependence on cysteine, and its rapid consumption during tumor proliferation promotes lipid peroxidation, further enhancing ferroptosis sensitivity [16] . Additionally, over 50% of HR-NB patients present with bone marrow metastasis at diagnosis [17] . Conventional induction chemotherapeutic agents, such as cisplatin, vincristine, and etoposide, exert minimal effects on NB-derived bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), leaving metastatic lesions largely unaffected and ultimately contributing to tumor relapse. Conversely, ferroptosis inducers selectively eliminate NB-BMSCs while sparing normal BMSCs [18] . Collectively, these findings suggest ferroptosis could be a promising therapeutic avenue for NB. However, most ferroptosis inducers(such as Erastin, RSL3) are still in preclinical stage [19] . Identifying clinically available ferroptosis inducers may offer a cost-effective strategy to improve HR-NB outcomes. Arsenic trioxide (ATO), the main active component of traditional Chinese medicinal preparations “Pi-shuang”, exhibits broad antitumor activity, including DNA demethylation, cell-cycle arrest, and restoring the function of TP53 harboring structural mutations [20–22] . Clinically, ATO is widely used in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) by targeting the disease-causing promyelocytic leukemia-retinoic acid receptor alpha (PML-RARα) oncoprotein. However, resistance to ATO can develop in some APL patients, often due to mutations in the PML B-box-2 structure or in the unrearranged PML allele [23,24] . Beyond APL, ATO has also been investigated in other malignancies. In our previous clinical trial, we was the first to demonstrate that combining ATO with conventional chemotherapy significantly improved the complete remission rate in patients with HR-NB [25] . Furthermore, we administered ATO in combination with a cyclophosphamide/topotecan-based salvage chemotherapy regimen to patients with relapsed/refractory HR-NB, achieving favorable efficacy and tolerability [26] . Building on these encouraging clinical outcomes, we aimed to further investigate the mechanisms underlying ATO's anti-NB effects. In our previous studies, we found ATO could trigger ferroptosis in NB cells [27,28] . Nevertheless, the precise molecular mechanism of ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB still remains unclear. In this study, utilizing three NB cell lines (SK-N-AS, SK-N-BE(2), and SH-SY5Y), we demonstrate that ATO exerts antitumor activity by inducing ferroptosis through suppressing the transcription factor USF1, thereby disrupting the transcriptional regulation of GPX4. This is accompanied by the accumulation of ROS, Fe2+ , and malondialdehyde, and a marked decrease in glutathione levels. Hence, our findings provide a mechanistic rationale for the broader application of ATO in the treatment of HR-NB.  2 Methods 2.1 Cells culture and reagents The NB cell lines SK-N-AS, SK-N-BE(2) and SH-SY5Y were obtained from the Sun Yat-sen University(Guangzhou, China). Cells were cultured with DMEM (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Wuhan Pu-nuo-sai Life Technology Co. Ltd., China) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco, USA) at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 . ATO(Cat#202673, 99.995% purity) was purchased from Sigma(St. Louis, MA, USA). Deferoxamine(DFO)(S5742, 99.91% purity), ferrostatin-1(Fer-1)(S7243 99.98% purity), MG132(S2619 99.52% purity) and TLK199(S9698, 99.10% purity) were obtained from Selleck (Texas, USA).  2.2 Cell viability assay We carried out the CCK8 assay and cell flow cytometry for the NB cell viability assay. For CCK8 assay, cells were plated into 96-well plates and grew overnight. NB cells were then exposed to different concentrations of ATO for 24 h. After drug administration, 100 μL of medium containing 10% CCK-8 reagent (APExBIO, Houston, TX, USA) was added to each well and incubated for 2 h in the dark, and plates were read at 450 nm. Besides, the combination index (CI) was calculated according to the Chou-Talalay method [29]  and CalcuSyn software. For flow cytometry, cells were incubated with different concentrations of ATO for 24 h. After treatment, live/dead staining was performed using Fixable Viability Stain 780 (BD Pharmingen) and the cells were incubated in the dark for 15 min. Cell viability was determined using flow cytometry.  2.3 Colony formation assay Approximately 1000 cells per well were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight. Cells were cultured for 12 days with medium refreshed every three days, followed by exposure to the indicated concentrations of ATO for an additional 2 days. Cells were rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and incubated with crystal violet solution (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 10 min. Colonies were photographed and quantified using ImageJ software.  2.4 Wound healing assays Cells were plated in 6-well plates and cultured until confluent monolayers formed. A scratch was created using a 1-ml pipette tip, and cells were plated with PBS to remove debris. Cells were subsequently exposed to different concentrations of ATO, and images were acquired at 0 and 48 h using the microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan). Cell migration into the wound area was quantified using ImageJ software.  2.5 Reactive oxygen species measurement Cells were seeded in 6-well plates and and grew overnight. The next day, the cells were incubated with ATO for 16 h, collected, resuspended in serum-free medium containing 10 μM DCFH-DA(Beyotime, Shanghai, China), and incubated for 30 min. Following staining, the cells were washed and the fluorescence intensity was evaluated with flow cytometry. Additionally, Reactive oxygen species(ROS) levels in lentivirus-infected cells were assessed using the dihydroethidium fluorescent probe(Beyotime, Shanghai, China) as the lentiviral vectors expressed green fluorescent protein.  2.6 Cellular iron measurement Cellular iron levels were assessed using FerroOrange(Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan). Cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and grew overnight, followed by ATO treatment for 16 h. Subsequently, cells were cultured with 0.5 μM FerroOrange for 30 min. After staining, the cells were washed and was analyzed by flow cytometry.  2.7 Glutathione assay Cellular Glutathione(GSH) concentration was measured using the GSH assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, Nanjing, China). After ATO treatment, the cells were lysed, and the supernatants were incubated with dithiodinitrobenzoic acid to generate a yellow chromophore. Absorbance was read at 405 nm. GSH content was normalized to protein concentration (μg/mg protein).  2.8 Malondialdehyde assay Malondialdehyde (MDA) were measured using the MDA assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). After ATO treatment, cells seeded in 6-cm dishes were collected and lysed by sonication. The supernatant was mixed with thiobarbituric acid, and plates were read at 532 nm. MDA content was standardized based on protein concentration (μmol/mg protein).  2.9 Bioinformatics analysis Proteomics analyses were performed by the Jingjie PTM BioLab (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd. The data were deposited in the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB)(OMIX011827). Different expressed proteins(DEPs) were defined as those with a P  value <0.05 and log2  |FC| > 0.585. Protein-Protein interaction (PPI) network were obtained from STRING database(https://string-db.org ) and computed for hub genes using the maximal clique centrality (MCC) method in CytoHubba. Cellular dependency data was obtained from the DepMap Public 22Q4 and Achilled DRIVE Marcotte datasetes using the DepMap (https://depmap.org/portal/ ). Cistrome DB (http://cistrome.org/db/# ) utilized to predict potential transcription factors and ChIP-Seq data acquisition. Correlations between genes was analyzed using data from TARGET-NB cohort accessed through cBioportal (http://www.cbioportal.org ).  2.10 Cell transfection For siRNA transfection, siRNAs were purchased from Gentlegen Biotechnology (Suzhou, China). When the cell reached 30–50% confluence, transfection was conducted wtih CALNP™ RNAi in vitro reagent (D-Nano Therapeutics, Beijing, China) according to the instruction manuals. The siRNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table S1. For lentiviral infection, USF1-overexpressing lentivirus or negative control vectors (Hanheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) were supplemented into the medium in the presence of polybrene to improve infection efficiency. The cells were selected in medium containing puromycin to obtain stably transduced populations.  2.11 Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction(qRT-PCR) Total RNA was isolated using the RNA-Quick Purification Kit (GOONIE, Guangzhou, China). cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Novizan Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China). qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Novizan Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China) on a Roche LightCycler system (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). GAPDH was used as the internal control, and relative gene expression was calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCT method. The primers are listed in the Supplementary Table S2.  2.12 Western blotting NB cells were collected, and total proteins were extracted using lysis buffer (CoWin Bioscience, Beijing, China). Protein concentrations were quantified with the Bicinchoninic Acid Assay kit (CoWin Bioscience). Equivalent protein quantities were separated and subsequently transferred onto PVDF membranes, trimmed based on the molecular weights of the target proteins. The PVDF Membrane was blocked for 30 min with rapid blocking buffer (Epizyme, Shanghai, China), incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, and subsequently with secondary antibodies. The primary antibodies used were as follows: β-tubulin (11,400, GB152667–100, Servicebio), GAPDH (11,000, GB12002, Servicebio), GPX4 (11,000, #59735, Cell Signaling Technology), and USF1 (11,000, A20903, Abclonal).  2.13 Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by PCR (ChIP-PCR) ChIP assays was performed using the SimpleChIP® Enzymatic Chromatin IP Kit(MagneticBeads) (Cell Signaling Technology). Cells were cultured in 15 cm dishes grown to approximately 70–80% confluence and fixed with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature, and subjected to glycine. After washing with cold PBS, the cells were scrapedin PBS containing protease inhibitors on ice and then pelleted by centrifugation. Chromatin was digested with micrococcal nuclease to yield fragments of approximately 150–900 bp. The lysates were incubated separately with specific antibodies (negative control: normal rabbit IgG; USF1 antibody: sc-101,197, Santa Cruz) and immunocomplexes were captured using magnetic beads. Cross-links were reversed, and DNA was purified for subsequent PCR analysis. Primer sequences are provided in the Supplementary Table S3. Thermocycling conditions were as follows: 95 °C for 30 s, 65 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s for 40 cycles. PCR products were resolved on agarose gels, and bands were visualized using a gel documentation system.  2.14 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism. Data are expressed as mean ± SD from independent experiments(n =3). Comparisons between two groups were performed using a two-tailed independent t -test, while multiple-group comparisons were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test. P  values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.   3 Results 3.1 ATO inhibits cell viability, proliferation, and migration while promotes ferroptosis of NB cells To evaluate the cytotoxic effects of ATO on NB cells, we assessed cell viability using the CCK-8 assay and flow cytometry (FVS780 staining). Three NB cell lines with distinct characteristics were used in this study: SK-N-AS (retinoic acid-resistant, non-MYCN-amplified, MES subtype), SK-N-BE(2) (MYCN-amplified, ADRN subtype), and SH-SY5Y (non-MYCN-amplified, ADRN subtype) [30,31] .We found that ATO could exert killing effect on NB cells in a dose-dependent manner(Fig. 1 A-1 B ). The 24 h IC50  of ATO were 48.51 μM for SK-N-AS, 12.39 μM for SK-N-BE(2), and 10.53 μM for SH-SY5Y. In addition, ATO significantly inhibited cell migration and colony-forming ability, as shown in Fig. 1 C and Fig. 1 D. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ATO exhibits remarkable antitumor activity in NB cells. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying ATO-induced cell death, rescue experiments were conducted using various regulated cell death (RCD) inhibitors. ATO-induced cell death was partially reversed by DFO (a ferroptosis inhibior), but not by necrostatin-1 (Nec-1, necroptosis inhibitor)and Z -VAD-FMK (Z-VAD, pan-caspase inhibitor). Notably, Fer-1, another ferroptosis inhibitor, also failed to alleviate the reduction in cell viability(Fig. 1 E). Ferroptosis is primarily characterized by intracellular iron overload, elevated ROS and increased lipid peroxidation [11,32] . To further verify that ATO induces ferroptosis in NB cells, we assessed several ferroptosis related markers, including intracellular ROS, Fe2+ , GSH and MDA. ATO promoted the accumulation of total ROS(Fig. 1 F) in NB cells. Using the FerroOrange fluorescent probe, we further confirmed a marked elevation of intracellular Fe2+  in ATO-treated cells (Fig. 1 G). Consistent with ferroptotic processes, GSH levels were substantially reduced in NB cells following ATO treatment (Fig. 1 H). Additionally, ATO increased MDA level in NB cells(Fig. 1 I), indicating enhanced lipid peroxidation. Taken together, these results demonstrate ATO promotes ferroptosis in NB cells.  3.2 ATO induced ferroptosis by modulating GPX4 transcription To further explore the mechanism underlying the anti-NB effect of ATO, we performed proteomic analyses on ATO-treated SK-N-AS cells. A total of 501 proteins were up-regulated and 767 proteins was down-regulated in the ATO-treated group compared with the control group. KEGG analysis showed enrichment of the ferroptosis pathway. In addition, we observed enrichment of the PI3K-AKT and cell cycle pathways, both of which have been implicated in the antitumor effects of ATO in previous studies (Fig. 2 A ). GO analysis revealed the top-ranked terms within each category, among which the biological process “iron-sulfur cluster assembly” was notably enriched, a process closely associated with ferroptosis [33,34] (Fig. 2 B). Furthermore, GSEA demonstrated activation of the ferroptosis in ATO-treated cells(Fig. 2 C). To further pinpoint key ferroptosis-related targets of ATO, the PPI network was constructed to evaluate ferroptosis-related DEPs. Eight ferroptosis-related DEPs showed differential expression after ATO treatment, with GPX4 was identified as the central node(Fig. 2 D), consistent with its established role in ferroptosis. Proteomic analysis revealed that the GPX4, a key anti-ferroptotic protein, was significantly downregulated following ATO treatment(log2 FC =−0.88). We next sought to elucidate the mechanism by which ATO regulates GPX4 expression. As illustrated in Fig. 2 E, ATO dose-dependently inhibited GPX4 mRNA level. We next assessed GPX4 expression in the presence of MG132, a proteasome inhibitor. Western blotting analysis showed that ATO reduced GPX4 protein levels, and this reduction was not rescued by MG132(Fig. 2 F), indicating that ATO regulates GPX4 primarily at the transcriptional level rather than through post-translational mechanisms. The dependence of NB cell lines on GPX4 ranked among the highest across pan-cancer analyses, placing sixth in CRISPR/Cas9 screening data and first in RNAi data in the DepMap database (Fig. 3 A )This confirms that GPX4 is indispensable for NB cell survival and further reveals that NB is among the tumor types showing the highest GPX4 dependency in pan-cancer analyses, supporting the rationale for targeting GPX4 in NB. To further evaluate the role of GPX4 in NB cells, we established GPX4 knockdown cell lines using siRNA. qPCR and western blot analyses confirmed GPX4 inhibition(Fig. 3 B-3 C). The data showed that GPX4 knockdown significantly increased intracellular ROS, Fe2+ , MDA while reducing GSH levels(Fig. 3 D-G) in NB cell. Moreover, the siGPX4+ATO group did not showed statistically significant differences in these ferroptosis-related indicators compared with the siGPX4 group. Taken together, these findings indicated GPX4 is a key mediator of ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB cells.  3.3 ATO triggers ferroptosis via targeting the USF1/GPX4 axis in NB cells In our previous experiments, we demonstrated that ATO suppresses GPX4 expression at the transcription level rather than through ubiquitin-mediated degradation, thereby triggering ferroptosis in NB cells. To further identify transcription factors involved in ATO-mediated regulation of GPX4, we first predicted potential upstream transcription factors using multiple transcription factor databases and selected those present in at least two databases. These candidates were then intersected with DEPs identified by proteomic profiling of ATO-treated NB cells(Fig. 4   A). Overlapping factors were further screened by manual evaluation of expression patterns together with supporting evidence from the literature. Three transcription factors were ultimately selected for siRNA knockdown in NB cell lines. As shown in Fig. 4 B, NFIC knockdown did not alter GPX4 mRNA levels in any of the three cell lines. ZNF148 silencing upregulated GPX4 mRNA in SK-N-AS cells but decreased it in the other cell lines, suggesting that the regulatory relationship between ZNF148 and GPX4 might be cell line–specific. Notably, USF1 knockdown consistently reduced GPX4 mRNA levels across all three NB cell lines. This experimental evidence is in line with our earlier transcription factor prediction analysis, in which Cistrome DB identified USF1 as one of the putative upstream regulators of GPX4 (Fig. 4 C). In addition, JASPAR motif analysis revealed predicted USF1 binding sites within the GPX4 promoter region (Fig. 4 D). To further substantiate the potential regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4, we next performed co-expression analysis of the candidate transcription factors and GPX4 using the TARGET-NB dataset. This analysis revealed a positive correlation between USF1 and GPX4 expression (Fig. 4 E). Moreover, proteomic profiling of ATO-treated SK-N-AS cells demonstrated that both USF1 and GPX4 were downregulated after treatment (Fig. 4 F), providing additional support for a functional association between USF1 and GPX4. Given these findings, we next examined whether ATO directly regulates USF1 expression. To validate the proteomic findings, we examined USF1 expression following ATO treatment. As shown in Fig. 4 G–4H, ATO markedly reduced USF1 mRNA and protein levels in NB cells. We next investigated whether USF1 directly contributes to GPX4 regulation and ferroptosis. In NB cells, USF1 silencing reduced GPX4 protein expression (Fig. 4 I). In addition, USF1 knockdown significantly increased intracellular ROS (Fig. 4  J), Fe2+  (Fig. 4  K), and MDA (Fig. 4  M) levels, while reducing GSH levels (Fig. 4  L). These results demonstrated that USF1 is closely associated with ferroptosis and that USF1 silencing promotes ferroptotic phenotypes in NB cells. GPX4 expression was substantially higher in OUSF1 cells than in ONC cells(Fig. 5   A), consistent with the regulatory relationship observed in USF1-knockdown experiments. Notably, although ATO treatment reduced GPX4 expression in both groups, the extent of reduction was substantially smaller in OUSF1 cells than in ONC cells(Fig. 5  A), indicating that USF1 overexpression confers resistance to ATO-induced GPX4 downregulation. We next examined ferroptosis-related markers in USF1-overexpressing cells. Under basal conditions, USF1 overexpression reduced intracellular Fe2+  and MDA levels while increasing GSH levels (Fig. 5 C–5E), consistent with an attenuation of ferroptotic stress. The effects on ROS varied across cell lines: in SH-SY5Y cell line, OUSF1 cells did not show significantly lower basal ROS compared with ONC cells, however, the ATO-induced increase in ROS was markedly blunted in OUSF1 cells across all NB lines (Fig. 5 B). Similarly, the ATO-induced changes in Fe2+ , MDA, and GSH were also substantially mitigated in OUSF1 cells relative to ONC cells (Fig. 5 C–5E). Collectively, these results indicate that USF1 overexpression partially protects NB cells from ATO-induced ferroptosis. Given the consistent regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4 at both the transcriptional and functional levels, we subsequently investigated whether USF1 directly binds to GPX4 promoter. Public ChIP-seq data from Cistrome DB revealed a prominent USF1-binding peak in the GPX4 promoter region in SK-N-SH, a non–MYCN-amplified NB cell line (Fig. 5 F). Consistent with this observation, ChIP-PCR analysis performed in the MYCN-amplified SK-N-BE(2) cell line experimentally validated this interaction by confirming the direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter(Fig. 5 G). Overall, our data demonstrate that ATO drives ferroptosis in NB cells via the USF1/GPX4 axis.  3.4 ATO and TLK-199 synergistically enhance Ferroptosis in NB cells In GPX4-independent ferroptosis pathways, targeting the SMURF2/GSTP1 regulatory axis or inhibiting GSTP1 enzymatic activity has been reported to markedly enhance tumor cell sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers [35] . TLK199, also known as Ezatiostat, is an oral GSTP1 inhibitor, has previously entered phase II clinical trials for myelodysplastic syndrome [36] . Because MYCN amplification is a well-recognized high-risk factor in HR-NB and has been reported to sensitize NB cell to ferroptosis [16] , we selected SK-N-BE(2), a MYCN-amplified cell line, for further investigation. We first evaluated whether ATO and TLK199 exerted synergistic antitumor effects using the Chou–Talalay method. The CI values were <1 across all three concentration combinations, indicating synergistic cytotoxicity between ATO and TLK199(Fig. 6 A-B ). Further analysis confirmed that the combination treatment induced stronger ferroptotic responses than either agent alone, characterized by greater increases in intracellular ROS(Fig. 6 C), Fe2+ (Fig. 6 D), and MDA levels(Fig. 6 F), together with more pronounced reduction in GSH levels(Fig. 6 E). Notably, TLK199 alone exhibied minimal cytotoxicity, whereas its combination with ATO significantly enhanced NB cell death. These findings suggest that ATO may potentiate the antitumor efficacy of low-toxicity ferroptosis inducers such as TLK199 by the amplifying the ferroptotic process.   4 Discussion Despite advances in therapeutic strategies, the clinical management of HR-NB remains challenging, with limited survival benefits and high rates of long-term relapse [4] . The survival rate of patients with relapsed HR-NB is unsatisfactory [37] , highlighting an urgent need for novel therapeutic approaches. Ferroptosis is emerging as an attractive therapeutic strategy for drug-resistant tumors [13] . However, the development of effective ferroptosis inducers has been impeded by unfavorable pharmacokinetic properties, limiting their clinical translation [19] . Although some drug components or drug derivatives have also been shown to induce ferroptosis in other tumor cells, their transition to mature clinical practice remains distant [38–40] . Moreover, pediatric medication requires even greater caution. Therefore, identifying clinically approved agents capable of inducing ferroptosis may provide an opportunity to accelerate clinical implementation in NB treatment. ATO not only possesses antitumor activity but also has extensive clinical application experience in pediatric patients, along with favorable safety and cost-effectiveness [21] . Moreover, the exploration of its integration with emerging technologies such as nanomedicine has opened up broad prospects for its potential application across multiple malignancies [41] . In our previous multicenter clinical trials, the combination of ATO and chemotherapy significantly improved treatment outcomes in HR-NB and demonstrated encouraging efficacy in relapsed or refractory cases, with a favorable safety profile [26,42] . However, the precise molecular mechanisms through which ATO exerts its effects in NB remain incompletely understood. Omics analyses of SK-N-BE(2) cells [28]  and SK-N-AS cells in this study revealed that DEPs following ATO treatment were enriched in ferroptosis pathways. In addition, rescue experiments using multiple RCD inhibitors showed that only the ferroptosis inhibitor DFO was able to restore the viability of NB cells after ATO treatment, suggesting that ferroptosis constitutes one of the major cell death mechanisms underlying the antitumor effects of ATO in NB cells. Consistently, we observed that ATO increased intracellular ROS while decreasing GSH levels. These findings were in agreement with previous observations in other cell types, including human pulmonary fibroblasts and spermatogenic cells [43,44] . Additionally, ATO elevated intracellular Fe2+  levels and increased the accumulation of the MDA, further supporting ferroptosis as a key mechanism underlying its antitumor activity. As a key regulator of ferroptosis, GPX4 inactivation leads to lipid peroxide accumulation [45] . Data from the DEPMAP database confirmed that NB cells exhibit high GPX4 dependency across cancers. Cross-validation using both CRISPR/Cas9 and RNAi approaches minimized potential false-positive results from single-platform analyses, further underscoring the critical role of GPX4 in NB cell survival. In this study, we demonstrated that ATO suppresses GPX4 at both the transcriptional and protein levels. Moreover, GPX4 knockdown induced ferroptosis in NB cells, and its combination with ATO did not further enhance ferroptosis-associated biochemical changes. These results further established GPX4 as a key intermediary in ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB cells, providing a possible explanation for why Fer-1 cannot rescue ATO-induced cell death. Although radical trapping antioxidants (RTAs) such as Fer-1 can quench lipid radicals in the downstream autoxidation phase, their late-stage action may be inadequate to counter lipid damage under the persistent upstream oxidative pressure, such as GPX4 or GSH insufficiency [46] . Iron chelators such as DFO reduce the labile iron pool and suppress iron-driven oxidative processes, including the Fenton reaction and the activity of iron-dependent enzymes, thereby preventing the initiation and amplification of lipid peroxidation [47] . These mechanistic distinctions may explain the differential rescue effects observed in our study. USF1, the member of the bHLH-Zip transcription factor family, participates in various cellular processes. Elevated expression of USF1 correlates with unfavorable prognosis [48–52]  and has been implicated in drug resistance and immune evasion in multiple cancers [50] . Beyond oncology, USF1 is also involved in non-cancerous diseases, including nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, where it activates CYBA transcription and subsequently promotes NADPH-derived ROS production and lipid accumulation [53] . However, the relationship between USF1 and ferroptosis remains poorly understood. To date, only one study in prostate cancer has reported that USF1 binds to the BEX1 promoter to enhance its transcription, thereby increasing ferroptosis resistance and promoting tumor progression, although no direct association between USF1 and GPX4 was discussed [54] . In this study, co-expression analysis using the publicly available TARGET-NB microarray dataset revealed a positive correlation between USF1 and GPX4 expression. We further demonstrated that ATO downregulated USF1, whereas siRNA-mediated USF1 silencing induced ferroptosis in NB cell lines. Conversely, USF1 overexpression upregulated GPX4 expression and rescued ATO-induced ferroptotic phenotypes, supporting a regulatory role for ATO in modulating the USF1/GPX4 axis. Finally, evidence from public ChIP-Seq datasets together with our ChIP-PCR experiments further substantiated the direct regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4: the Cistrome database revealed USF1 binding peaks within the GPX4 promoter region in SK-N-SH cells, and our ChIP-PCR assays confirmed direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter in SK-N-BE(2) cells. Technical constraints related to transfection and cell viability under our experimental conditions prevented us from obtaining reliable luciferase reporter assay results. Nevertheless, gene expression analyses, gain- and loss-of-function studies, rescue experiments, and ChIP-based validation together provide strong evidence supporting ATO's regulatory effect on the USF1/GPX4 signaling axis in NB cells. In 2017, Van Groningen et al. defined two NB cell states, adrenergic (ADRN) and MES cells, which differ in morphology, biology, and treatment response, yet remain interconvertible [55–57] . MES cells display greater chemoresistance and are enriched in relapsed and refractory NB [12] , and MES-associated transcripts are more frequently detected in patients with poor outcomes [58] . These observations indicate that NB cell plasticity may allow tumor cells to evade therapeutic pressure, as ADRN cells can transition toward a MES, drug-resistant phenotype under genetic alterations(e.g., ARID1A mutations) or treatment stress [59–61] . Notably, across multiple tumor types, mesenchymal and therapy-resistant cancer cells exhibit a marked dependence on GPX4 to eliminate lipid peroxides, rendering them vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition [13,62] . In this study, we demonstrated that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via USF1/GPX4 axis, thereby mediating its antitumor effects. This mechanism may help explain the clinical benefits of ATO observed in our previous study, particularly in relapsed or refractory NB, and supports its potential application to target MES-like, therapy-resistant NB cells. Further investigation of this therapeutic strategy is warranted. Retinoic acid(RA)–mediated differentiation is a conventional component of consolidation therapy for HR-NB. However, Cardona et al. demonstrated that differentiated NB cell lines acquire resistance to ferroptosis following RA-induced differentiation. This resistance is attributed to increased cystine uptake and the resulting elevation of intracellular cysteine levels, which collectively strengthen the ferroptosis-resistant phenotype of differentiated NB cells. Therefore, ferroptosis-inducing agents may be more effective when administered prior to the RA-induced differentiation phase, consistent with the potential application of ATO during the induction chemotherapy stage in patients with HR-NB. This study preliminarily explored the potential of ATO combined with other drugs to induce ferroptosis. TLK199 alone exhibited minimal cytotoxicity to NB cells, but when combined with ATO, the two drugs synergistically enhanced cell death and related ferroptosis phenotypes, suggesting the potential of ATO in combination with other drugs to induce ferroptosis in NB cells. However, the mechanism underlying the observed synergy remains to be fully explored. Future studies will systematically screen ATO combination drugs, explore the molecular mechanisms, and assess their in vivo effects. Besides, our previously conducted clinical studies have confirmed the clinical potential of ATO for NB treatment. In a non-randomized, multicenter clinical trial, ATO combined with chemotherapy showed a significantly higher objective response rate (86.36% vs. 46.16%, p  = 0.020) compared to traditional chemotherapy in children with stage 4/M NB [25] . Additionally, in a study on relapsed/refractory high-risk NB patients, ATO combined with cyclophosphamide/ topotecan (CT regimen) demonstrated an objective response rate of 54.5% and a disease control rate of 63.6%, with minimal systemic toxicity [26] . These results further support ATO's potential for improving outcomes in both newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory NB patients. So, due to the clinical data already available and in line with the 3Rs principle (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), we did not conduct animal experiments in this study. Moving forward, in future studies focused on ATO in NB, we plan to further investigate its mechanisms and therapeutic efficacy, particularly in combination with other ferroptosis inducers or nanomaterial-based approaches, and explore the specific mechanisms in clinical samples from relapsed and drug-resistant patients, using animal and PDX models. In summary, our findings demonstrated that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via USF1/GPX4 axis, thereby exerting a potent antitumor effect (Fig. 7  ). Considering ATO's established clinical application and the emerging relevance of ferroptosis in NB therapy, our study provides a strong rationale for further assessment of ATO for HR-NB treatment. title: Investigation of anticancer mechanism of oleuropein via cell cycle and apoptotic pathways in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells
abstract: Neuroblastoma is one of the most common types of pediatric tumors that can spread quickly in neuronal tissues. Oleuropein which is active compound of olive leaves, belongs to polyphenols group and has antioxidant, anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory, anti-hypertensive and anti-carcinogenic effects. The aim of the study is to determine the therapeutic effects of oleuropein on cell proliferation, invasion, colony formation, cell cycle and apoptotic mechanisms in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line under in vitro conditions. The effect of oleuropein on cell viability was determined by XTT method. 84 cell cycle control and 84 apoptosis related genes were evaluated by RT-PCR. Effects of oleuropein on apoptosis were researched by TUNEL assay. Protein expressions were determined by western blot analysis. Effects of oleuropein on cell invasion, colony formation and migration were detected by matrigel-chamber, colony formation assay and wound-healing assay, respectively. IC50 value of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cells was detected as 350μM at 48th hours. It is determined that oleuropein causes cell cycle arrest by down-regulating of CylinD1,CylinD2,CyclinD3,CDK4,CDK6 and up-regulating of p53 and CDKN2A, CDKN2B, CDKN1A gene expressions. Oleuropein also induces apoptosis by inhibiting of Bcl-2 and activating of Bax,caspase-9 and caspase-3 gene expressions. Apoptotic cell ratio was found 36.4±3.27% in oleuropein dose group. Oleuropein decreased invasion in SH-SY5Y cells and suppressed colony numbers in ratio of 53.6±4.71%.Our results demonstrated that oleuropein can be a therapeutic agent in the treatment of neuroblastoma.

Neuroblastoma is one of the most common types of pediatric tumors that can spread quickly in neuronal tissues. Oleuropein which is active compound of olive leaves, belongs to polyphenols group and has antioxidant, anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory, anti-hypertensive and anti-carcinogenic effects. The aim of the study is to determine the therapeutic effects of oleuropein on cell proliferation, invasion, colony formation, cell cycle and apoptotic mechanisms in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line under in vitro  conditions. The effect of oleuropein on cell viability was determined by XTT method. 84 cell cycle control and 84 apoptosis related genes were evaluated by RT-PCR. Effects of oleuropein on apoptosis were researched by TUNEL assay. Protein expressions were determined by western blot analysis. Effects of oleuropein on cell invasion, colony formation and migration were detected by matrigel-chamber, colony formation assay and wound-healing assay, respectively. IC50  value of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cells was detected as 350 μM at 48th hours. It is determined that oleuropein causes cell cycle arrest by down-regulating of CylinD1 ,CylinD2 ,CyclinD3 ,CDK4 ,CDK6  and up-regulating of p53  and CDKN2A , CDKN2B , CDKN1A  gene expressions. Oleuropein also induces apoptosis by inhibiting of Bcl-2  and activating of Bax ,caspase-9  and caspase-3  gene expressions. Apoptotic cell ratio was found 36.4 ± 3.27% in oleuropein dose group. Oleuropein decreased invasion in SH-SY5Y cells and suppressed colony numbers in ratio of 53.6 ± 4.71%.Our results demonstrated that oleuropein can be a therapeutic agent in the treatment of neuroblastoma.   Abbreviations NB Neuroblastoma   OLE Oleuropein   XTT [2,3-Bis-(2-methoxy-4-Nitro-5-Sulfophenyl)-2H-Tetrazolium-5-Carboxanilide]   TUNEL mediated deoxyuridine triphosphate (dUTP)-digoxigenin nick-end labeling   CDK Cyclin dependent kinase   DMSO dimethylsulfoxide   HT Hydroxytyrosol    Keywords Neuroblastoma  Oleuropein  Cell cycle  Apoptosis    1 Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric tumor of the autonomic nervous system and originated from precursor cell derived from the neural-crest tissues (Brodeur, 2003; Maris, 2010 ).  NB is the most frequent common extra-cranial solid tumor in early childhood malignancies and is responsible from approximately 15% of all pediatric cancer deaths. Despite extensive treatment for neuroblastoma, high stage NB tumors have poor prognosis with 20% to 40% overall survival (Brodeur, 2003; Maris, 2010; Maris et al., 2007 ). NB is a highly heterogeneous disease both biologically and clinically; thus, therapeutic approaches to NB depend on the stage of the disease, age and biological prognostic factors (Maris et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2011 ).  In view of these cases, studies about effective and novel class agents should be carried out or new treatment strategies are needed for neuroblastoma. Reported large epidemiological studies in several countries demonstrated that Mediterranean region has a significantly reduced all-cause mortality rate (Grosso et al., 2013 ).  The Mediterranean diet is associated with decreased incidence of cardiovascular diseases, cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. The protective effects were attributed to rich fruits, vegetables, whole grains and olive products, which have powerfully antioxidants and biologically active compounds (Renaud et al., 1995 ).  Mediterranean diet includes high consumption of olive products have a plenty source of polyphenols such as oleuropein (OLE) and its derivates, including hydroxytyrosol (HT), which have strong free radicals scavenging activities and inhibitory effects to chemical oxidation of LDL (Stupans et al., 2002; Visioli et al., 1998b ). Oleuropein, belongs to the secoiridoids, a group coumarin-like compounds, is the precursor of olive oil secoiridoids and is abundantly present in the olive leaves and fruit (Gikasa et al., 2007; Servili et al., 2009 ).  Previous in vivo  and in vitro  studies reported that oleuropein has a wide variety of biological activities such as anti-microbial (Bisignano et al., 1999 ), anti-viral (Lee-Huang et al., 2003 ),  antioxidant (De la Puerta et al., 2001 ),  anti-hypertansive (Khayyal et al., 2002 ), anti-atherogenic (Carluccio et al., 2003 ),  hepatoprotective (Domitrović et al., 2012 ),  neuroprotective (Bazoti et al., 2006 ), anti-inflammatory (Visioli et al., 1998a ), anti-aging (Katsiki et al., 2007 ) and anti-diabetic (Al-Azzawie and Alhamdani, 2006 ).  Additionally, anti-carcinogenic effects of oleuropein and its effective mechanisms were demonstrated that in a variety of cancer cell types such as glioblastoma (Tunca et al., 2012 ),  cervical cancer (Yao et al., 2014 ), breast cancer (Han et al., 2009; Sepporta et al., 2014 ),  prostate cancer (Acquaviva et al., 2012 ) thyroid cancer (Bulotta et al., 2013 ) colon cancer (Corona et al., 2007 ),  lung cancer (Mao et al., 2012 ) and leukemia (Fabiani et al., 2011 ).  The aim of this study is to determine the anticancer effect of oleuropein on SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells in vitro  conditions and elucidate underlying molecular mechanism of oleuropein and explore its therapeutic activity. In this context, the effects of oleuropein on apoptosis and cell cycle control genes, invasion, migration and colony formation were evaluated in this study.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Chemicals Trizol was purchased from Invitrogen, Oleuropein, trypan blue solution, hoechst, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 2-amino-2-(hydroxymethyl)-1,3-propanediol (TRIS) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Chemical Company (USA). USA. The other chemicals were purchased from Biological Industries such as RPMI-1640 medium, penicillin/streptomycin mixture, phosphate buffered saline (PBS), fetal bovine heat-inactivated serum (FBS), XTT reagent-cell proliferation kit. Transcriptor first strand cDNA synthesis kit was purchased from Roche Diagnostics, Germany.  2.2 Cell culture In this study, a human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y(ATCC®-: CRL-2266 ™) was used as model cell line. Cells were cultured in DMEM-Ham's F12 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 20 units/ml penicillin and 20 μg/ml streptomycin, and maintained in a humidified atmosphere of 95% air and 5% CO2 at 37 °C. SH-SY5Y cells were treated with 25 μM, 40 μM, 50 μM, 75 μM, 100 μM, 150 μM, 175 μM, 200 μM, 250 μM, 300 μM, 350 μM, 400 μM, 500 μM, 700 μM and 800 μM oleuropein during 72 h, considering a time and dose dependent manner.  2.3 Cell Viability assay Cell viability assays and determination of IC50  dose of OLE in SH-SY5Ycells were performed by using trypan blue dye exclusion test and XTT [2,3-Bis-(2-methoxy-4-Nitro-5-Sulfophenyl)-2H-Tetrazolium-5-Carboxanilide] assay according to manufacturers' instruction. OLE was dissolved in dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) and the final concentration of DMSO did not exceed 0.1%. SH-SY5Ycells were seeded in 96-well plates at a number of 1 × 104  cells/well. After 24 h of incubation, the cells were treated with various concentrations of OLE and incubated for 24, 48 and 72 h. Then using XTT mixture as recommended by supplier assessed cell viability. Formazan formation was quantified spectrophotometrically at 450 nM (reference wavelength 630 nM) using a microplate reader. Viability was calculated using the background-corrected absorbance as follows:Viability %  = A  of experiment well / A  of control well × 100      2.4 RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis and Real-time PCR (RT-PCR) Total RNA was isolated from the cells exposed to IC50  dose of OLE and control cells with TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) according to manufacturer instructions. Complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis was performed on the total RNAs using a Transcriptor First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Roche Diagnostics, Germany), according to the manufacturers' instructions. Quantitative RNA expression analysis of 84 key genes for both cell cycle regulation and apoptosis (programmed cell death) were conducted separately by using array 96 well microplates (Qiagen RT2  Profiler PCR Array, Catalog no: 330,231 PAHS-020ZA, PAHS-012ZA) at Step One Plus Real-Time PCR (Applied Biosystems). Names of these genes are given in S1 Table and S2 Table.  2.5 Western blotting Protein expression levels of CCND1 and BCL2 were determined by Western blotting with Beta-actin as housekeeping. Briefly, total protein was extracted from the SH-SY5Y cells and dose groups using RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris pH 8, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS) supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktails. Next, aliquots containing 100 μg of protein were stacked on 4% polyacrylamide gels and separated 8.5% sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto PVDF membrane. The membrane was blocked with 1% skimmed milk, washed with TBST buffer three times, and incubated overnight at 4 °C with rabbit anti-CCND1, anti-BCL2 antibody (1:1000, Santa Cruz) and goat anti-Beta-actin (1:500, Santa Cruz). And then, the membrane was washed with TBST and incubated with anti-rabbit or goat lgG-HRP secondary antibody (1:5000, Santa Cruz). Proteins were detected using Super Signal West Pico Chemiluminescent Substrate (Pierce, Rockford, IL, USA), and bands were visualized and recorded using “Image J” image analysis software.  2.6 TUNEL assay The apoptotic effects of OLE in SH-SY5Ycells were determined using the transferase mediated deoxyuridine triphosphate (dUTP)-digoxigenin nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assay. The control and dose group of SH-SY5Ycells were fixed with 4% (w /v ) paraformaldehyde and processed by using a commercial kit (In Situ Cell Death Detection Kit, Roche, Germany) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were stained with hoechst dye and imaged in a fluorescent microscope. The data were expressed as a percentage of the area of TUNEL-positive cells in 10 random fields.  2.7 Cell invasion assay Invasion activities of control and dose groups of SH-SY5Ycells were determined according to the BioCoatMatrigel Invasion Chamber guide (BD Biosciences). The cells with serum-free DMEM-F12 medium were seeded at a density of 2x105 cells/well onto the upper chambers of Matrigel-coated filter inserts and serum-containing DMEM-F12 medium (500 μL) was added to the lower chambers. Then the cells were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. After of incubation, filter inserts were removed from the wells. The cells on the upper surface of the filter were wiped with a cotton swab. Filters were fixed with methanol for 10 min and stained with crystal violet. The cells invaded the lower surface of the filter were counted under a light microscope. Each experiment was repeated three times. % Invasion was calculated using control and matrigel membran cell count as follows:% Invasion = The number of cells in matrigel matrix basement membrane The number of cells in control membrane  × 100 .      2.8 Colony assay For colony formation analysis, SH-SY5Y cells were digested with trypsin, counted using trypan blue dye exclusion test and seeded in six-well plates at a density of 103 cells per well. The medium was changed every 3 days for 10 days until visible colonies formed. Colonies were fixed methanol for 10 min and stained with crystal violet.  2.9 Wound-Healing Assay The control and dose group cells were plated at 106  cells per well of 60 × 15 mm style cell culture dishes and grown overnight at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The 80% confluent control group and dose group cells were treated with 350 μM OLE after a straight line scratch was made on a confluent monolayer of cells using a sterile 200 μl plastic pipette tip. To remove debris and smooth the edge of the scratch, the cells was washed with 2 ml serum-free DMEM-Ham's F12. Images of the SH-SY5Y cell proliferation were taken at 0 h 16 h, 24 h and 48 h after the scratch. The scratch assay was performed in triplicate.  2.10 Statistical analysis The analysis of the findings has been achieved with the ΔΔCT method and quantitated with a computer program. The comparison of the groups has been performed with “Volcano Plot” analysis, from “RT2 Profiles™PCR Array Data Analysis”, which is assessed statistically using the “Student t test”. Moreover, statistical analyses have been evaluated with the SPSS 17.0 statistical analysis program (p < 0.05 is significant statistically).   3 Results 3.1 Anti-proliferative effect of OLE in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells Anti-proliferative activity of OLE in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line was determined by XTT assay. As shown in Fig. 1  , OLE inhibited the cell viability of neuroblastoma cells time- and dose-dependent manner and IC50  dose of OLE in SH-SY5Y cell line was found to be 350 μM in the 48th hour.  3.2 Gene expression analysis with RT-PCR After total RNA isolation and cDNA synthesis from control and dose group cells were performed, the expression of genes was studied on Real Time PCR. The effects of OLE in SH-SY5Y cell lines on cell cycle and gene expression in the apoptosis pathways were analised. Genes analyzed are represented in S1 Table and S2 Table. Analysis of gene expression changes in control and dose groups was performed with the specific analysis “Volcano Plot”. It was observed that oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cell line caused a significant increase in the cell cycle related gene expressions of CDKN2A , CDKN2B , CDKN1A , p53 , GADD45A  and a significant decrease in the cell cycle related gene expressions of CCND1 , CCND2 , CCND3 , CDK4 , CDK6 , and WEE1  (Table 1  , p < 0.05). No significant change was observed in other genes. Furthermore, It was observed that oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cell line caused a significant increase in the apoptosis related gene expressions of BAX , BAD , BID , DFFA , CASPASE-1 , CASPASE-3 , CASPASE-9 , CASPASE-8 , P53  and a significant decrease in the apoptosis related gene expressions of Bcl-2, (Table 1 , p < 0.05). No significant change was observed in other genes.  3.3 Effects of OLE on protein expression changes in SH-SY5Y cells Based on the results obtained by RT-PCR, CCND1 and BCL2 protein expression was analyzed by Western blotting in OLE treated cells and these results were compared with the levels of protein in untreated cells. It was noticed that there was a decrease in CCND1 and BCL2 protein expressions, in the oleuropein treatment group cells, compared with the control group cells (Fig. 2  ).  3.4 Apoptotic effect of OLE in SH-SY5Y cells To evaluate the apoptotic effect of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cell line, the TUNEL method was used. A notable increase in apoptotic cells was observed in the OLE treatment group, compared with the control group (Fig. 3 A ). Apoptosis data of the four group in SH-SY5Y cells were shown as follows respectively: Control groups 8 ± 1.02% and OLE dose groups 36.4 ± 3.27% (Fig. 3 B).  3.5 OLE exhibits anti-invasive potential in SH-SY5Y cells According to the results of matrigel invasion chamber assay, the cell invasion was significantly inhibited in the OLE treatment groups, compared with the control groups (Fig. 4 A ). Invasion data of the four groups in SH-SY5Y cell line were shown as follows respectively: Control groups (74.66 ± 2.7) % and OLE dose groups (41.46 ± 2.04) % (Fig. 4 B).  3.6 OLE decreases colony formation of SH-SY5Y cells Using colony formation assay performed colony formation analysis. It was observed that colony formation decreased in the OLE treated group, compared with the control groups in the SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 5 A ). Colony formation data of the four groups in SH-SY5Y cell line were shown as follows respectively: Control groups 41 ± 2 and OLE dose group's 19 ± 1 (Fig. 5 B). Colony formation test results demonstrate that colony numbers in dose group were suppressed in a ratio of 53.6 ± 4.71%.  3.7 OLE decreases migration of SH-SY5Y cells Effects of OLE on cell migration were detected by wound-healing assay. According to results, OLE reduced cell migration in SH-SY5Y cells, compared with the control group. 0, 16 h and 24 h images were given in Fig. 6  .   4 Discussion In recent years, anti-carcinogenic effects of different bioactive food components and their therapeutic activities have become phenomenon in cancer treatment researches. Oleuropein is main phenolic component of olive leaves and extra virgin olive oil and its biological activities and pharmacological effects have been demonstrated (Omar, 2010; Barbaro et al., 2014 ).  In the present study, we aimed to determine the therapeutic effects of oleuropein on cell proliferation, invasion, migration, colony formation, cell cycle and apoptotic mechanisms in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells under in vitro conditions. Although different studies about oleuropein and its anti-cancer effects were studied in various cancer types, this study presents first relation between oleuropein and neuroblastoma. According to our results, cyctotoxic effects of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line were detected in time and dose dependant manner by XTT method and IC50  dose of oleuropein was detected as 350 μM at 48th ours. Cardeno et al. reported that 400 μM oleuropein significantly reduced cell viability in HT-29 colon cancer cell line and inhibits proliferation cels through downregulation of HIF-1α  (Cárdeno et al., 2013 ).  Antiproliferative effect of oleuropein in LNCaP and DU145 prostate cancer cell lines were reported (Acquaviva et al., 2012 ). In another study, dose-dependent cytotoxic effects of oleuropein in breast cancer MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells and the normal MCF-10 A cells were analyzed. They indicated that while MCF-10 showed only marginal sensitivity even when challenged with high doses of oleuropein, both breast cancer cell lines exhibited significant sensitivity and reparted IC50  for MCF-7 amd MDA-MB-231 cells were 110 and 160 μM, respectively (Elamin et al., 2013 ).  In this study, anticancer mechanism of oleuropein was elucidated by analyzing the expression of 84 key genes for both cell cycle regulation and apoptosis separately in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line. The expression changes of these genes related to cell cycle and apoptosis play a significant role in cancer and they can be therapeutic targets for treatment strategies. According to our results, a significant decrease in the mRNA expressions of CCND1 , CCND2 , CCND3 , CDK4  and CDK6  genes and an increase in the expression of p53 , CDKN2A , CDKN2B  and CDKN1A  genes were observed in the oleuropein treatment group cells compared with the control gruop cells. Cyclins, cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs) and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors are important in the mechanism of the cell cycle control and have key roles in cancer developments. CCND1 is an important G1-S checkpoint regulater in cell cycle and promotes tumor growth in various cancer types via overexpression or amplification. In differentiated mammalian cells, cyclin/CDK complexes are involved in regulation of cell cycle transitions and one them is cyclin D/CDK4/CDK6 for G1 progression (Paternot et al., 2010; Musgrove et al., 2011 ).  CDK4 activity is deregulated in many human tumors and critical for different oncogenic transformation process (Paternot et al., 2010 ).  Knockdown of the CCND1/CDK4 or CCND1/CDK6 complexes cause pRB pathway inhibition and E2F transcriptional activity (Molenaar et al., 2008 ).  In a previous study demonstrated that CCND1 , CDK4  and CDK6  gene expressions are overexpressed in neuroblastoma cases compared to other cancer types including lung, cervix, ovary, prostate, breast cancers etc. Furthermore it is remarked that CCND1 and CDK4 activity contribute to the undifferentiated phenotype in neuoblastoma (Musgrove et al., 2011 ). Rader et al. supported CCND1/CDK4/CDK6 overexpressions in different neuroblastoma cell lines including SH-SH5Y cells compared with different cancer cell types by western blot analysis. In the same study, it is demonstrated that CDK4 mRNA expression in high-risk patients is higher than in low-risk patients. They also reported that copy number gain of CDK4 (5.1%), CDK6 (15.7%), and CCND1 (19.5%) in cohort of 375 high-risk patients (Rader et al., 2013 ).  These data showed that the new therapeutic agents which target this overexpressed CCND1/CKD4/6 pathway should be developed for neuroblastoma treatment. According to our results, CCND1 , CCND2 , CCND3 , CDK4 , CDK6  mRNA expressions were downregulated and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors CDKNA2A , CDKN2B , CDKN1A  were upregulated by oleuropein treatment. CCND1 protein expression was also analyzed by western blot technique in this study. Two tumor suppressor genes the CDKN2A  and CDKN2B  have a crucial role in cell cycle progression and are considered to be targets for tumor inactivation. These inhibitors regulate CDK activity ve induce the supression of cell cycle. Some reports suggested that oleuropein induces G1  arrest in several cell line such as MCF-7 and A549 (Han et al., 2009; Mao et al., 2012 ).  However, it is reported that oleuropein induced accumulation of cells in G2/M phase of the cell cycle in the cervical cells (Yao et al., 2014 ).  Elamin et al., demonstrated that oleuropein inhibited breast cancer cell proliferation by delaying the cell cycle at S phase and and downregulating NF-kB and cyclin D1 but activating p21(CDKN1A) (Elamin et al., 2013 ).  Our results suggested that oleuropein is inducing G1/S cell cycle arrest in neuroblastoma cells. Increased p53 mRNA expression in oleuropein treated group cells are also supporting G1/S arrest. Based on the mentioned information and results, oleuropein may be a novel strategic agent for neuroblastoma treatment, especially by suppressing overexpressed CCND1/CDK4/CDK6 pathway members in cell cycle. These results suggest that oleuropein caused G1/S cell cycle arrest due to the changes in these genes which played an important role in the cell cycle progression in neuroblastoma. p53 is a transcription factor that controls cell cycle control and programmed cell death (Struckhoff et al., 2010 ).  P53 reduces genetic instability and allows DNA repair before progressing through the cell cycle and in case of failed repair p53 induce apoptosis for eliminating aberrant cells (Taylor et al., 1999 ).  The apoptosis mechanism in the cell has complex and sophisticated and occurs via extrinsic and intrinsic signalling pathways (Igney and Krammer, 2002 ).  The proapoptotic activity of p53 is due to its transactivation abilities through the transactivation of target genes related to apoptosis, can directly stimulates transcription of apoptosis related genes (Fridman and Lowe, 2003; Hassan et al., 2012 ). P53  gene is mediated apoptosis via the ability to control transcription of proapoptotic members of Bcl-2 family members (Fridman and Lowe, 2003 ).  According to our results mRNA expression of p53  is increased in oleuropein dose group cells. At the same time, proapoptotic genes Bax , Bid  and Bad  mRNA expression is increased, Bcl-2 antiapoptotic gene mRNA expression is decreased in the oleuropein treated cells. Bcl-2 protein expression change was also showed in current study. Furthermore, increased caspase-9 and caspase-3 expression in oleuropein dose group and insignificant expression of extrinsic pathway related genes demonstrated that oleuropein is inducing apoptosis in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells via mitochondrial pathway. In the present study, oleuropein and its apoptotic effects on SH-SY5Y cells were confirmed by TUNEL assay. According to our TUNEL assay results study showed that apoptosis was induced on oleuropein dose cells at the ratio of 36 ± 3.27% compared with control cells 8 ± 1.02%. According to the results, apoptotic cell ratio increased approximately 30% in SH-SY5Y cells with oleuropein treatment. In the previous study, Hassan et al. observed similar results in 200 μM oleuropein treated MCF-7 breast cancer cells and they reported that oleuropein induced apoptosis in breast cancer cells via p53 pathway. They also demonstrated that oleuropein is significantly up-regulating Bax  and down-regulating Bcl-2  expression in breast cancer cells (Hassan et al., 2012 ).  Yao et al. reported that oleuropein induce apoptosis in HeLa cervical cancer cells via mitochondrial apoptotic cascade associated with activation of c-Jun. NH2 -terminal kinase (Yao et al., 2014 ).  Chimento et al. showed that oleuropein and its derivative hydroxytyrosol activate GPER/GRP30- dependent pathways leading to apoptosis of ER-negative SKBR3 breast cancer cells (Chimento et al., 2014 ).  Samet et al. demonstrated that olive leaf extract induces apoptosis in human chronic myelogenous leukemia K562 cells (Samet et al., 2014 ).  Other reports suggested that oleuropein stimulates apoptosis and inhibits proliferation by ERK and Akt activation in thyroid cancer cells (Bulotta et al., 2013 ),  by ERK 1/2 activation in MCF-7 breast cancer cells (Sirianni et al., 2010 ).  Cell migration and invasion are crucial steps in various physiological processes such as morphogenesis, neurogenesis, angiogenesis, wound healing and inflammation (Bozzuto et al., 2010 ).  Invasion and migration are critical events of tumor progression and tumor recurrence (Lavictoire et al., 2003 ).  According to matrigel-chamber results, the invasion of neuroblastoma cells was reduced in the oleuropein treated group, compared to the normal group. While % invasion was found 74.66% in control group, % invasion of oleuropein dose treated group was found 41.46%. Colony formation test results demonstrate that colony numbers in dose group were suppressed in a ratio of 53.6 ± 4.71%. Furthermore, wound-healing results are supporting these positive effects of oleuropein on cell migration inhibition. These results suggest that oleuropein reduced cell invasion, migration and colony formation capacity in neuroblastoma cells. In previous in vivo  study demonstrated that oleuropein inhibits tumor growth and metastases in nude mice with MCF-7 human breast tumor xenografts (Sepporta et al., 2014 ).  Mao et al. showed effects of oleuropein on migration in A549 lung carcinoma cell migration by wound-healing test (Mao et al., 2012 ).  Hassan et al. demonstrated that oleuropein induces anti-metastatic effects in breast cancer cells by modulating expressions of matrix metalloproteinase MMP-2  and MMP-9  and expressions of their inhibitors TIMPs  (Hassan et al., 2012 ).  In another study, it is reported that oleuropein inhibits cell migration and invasion in LN-18, RPMI-7951, T-47D tumor cell lines (Hamdi and Castellon, 2005 ).  In conclusion, many in vitro  and in vivo  researches on bioactive components, novel agents and biomarker molecules that have been investigated in cancer treatment, focus on specifically inducing apoptosis and cell cycle arrest in cancer cells. Failure to obtain satisfactory results in treatment approaches in neural origin tumors, has led to the need to study the details of oncogenesis and molecular underlying mechanisms of these tumors. Therefore, novel biological and chemical agents can be developed and in neuroblastoma progression and treatment. Our results show that, oleuropein inhibits cell proliferation by inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptotic mechanisms and also decreases invasion, migration and colony formation in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line. We presented the effect mechanisms related to apoptosis, cell cycle arrest and invasion of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. Oleuropein may be a candidate agent for treatment of neuroblastoma as a single agent or in combination with other drugs, components or molecules. Thus, more detailed studies in vitro  and in vivo  animal models should be designed to investigate a safe dose with the best effects of oleuropein.  Conflict of interest None. title: The small molecule inhibitor YK-4-279 disrupts mitotic progression of neuroblastoma cells, overcomes drug resistance and synergizes with inhibitors of mitosis
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a biologically and clinically heterogeneous pediatric malignancy that includes a high-risk subset for which new therapeutic agents are urgently required. As well as MYCN amplification, activating point mutations of ALK and NRAS are associated with high-risk and relapsing neuroblastoma. As both ALK and RAS signal through the MEK/ERK pathway, we sought to evaluate two previously reported inhibitors of ETS-related transcription factors, which are transcriptional mediators of the Ras-MEK/ERK pathway in other cancers. Here we show that YK-4-279 suppressed growth and triggered apoptosis in nine neuroblastoma cell lines, while BRD32048, another ETV1 inhibitor, was ineffective. These results suggest that YK-4-279 acts independently of ETS-related transcription factors. Further analysis reveals that YK-4-279 induces mitotic arrest in prometaphase, resulting in subsequent cell death. Mechanistically, we show that YK-4-279 inhibits the formation of kinetochore microtubules, with treated cells showing a broad range of abnormalities including multipolar, fragmented and unseparated spindles, together leading to disrupted progression through mitosis. Notably, YK-4-279 does not affect microtubule acetylation, unlike the conventional mitotic poisons paclitaxel and vincristine. Consistent with this, we demonstrate that YK-4-279 overcomes vincristine-induced resistance in two neuroblastoma cell-line models. Furthermore, combinations of YK-4-279 with vincristine, paclitaxel or the Aurora kinase A inhibitor MLN8237/Alisertib show strong synergy, particularly at low doses. Thus, YK-4-279 could potentially be used as a single-agent or in combination therapies for the treatment of high-risk and relapsing neuroblastoma, as well as other cancers.

Real-time cell growth analysis following BRD32048 treatment using Incucyte Zoom live cell imaging. Phase confluence of cells is plotted over time. (A)  BRD32048 treatment of neuroblastoma lines, (B)  YK-4-279 treatment of neuroblastoma lines, (C)  Normal human non-cancer cell lines treated with YK-4-279. Live cell imaging was carried out in 96-well plates in three technical replicates (n = 3; mean ± SD).  Fig. 1   Fig. 2 Enantiomer-specific YK-4-279 inhibition of neuroblastoma cell lines. (A)  Nine neuroblastoma cell lines and two non-cancerous cell lines were further screened by MTT based cell proliferation assay to determine YK-4-279 sensitivity and IC50  values. (B)  Dose-response curves of YK-4-279(S) enantiomer on neuroblastoma cell lines. (C)  Activity of the YK-4-279(R) enantiomer on neuroblastoma cell lines. All MTT assays were carried out in three independent biological replicates each having three technical replicates (n = 3; mean ± SD). (D)  Immunoblotting of SK-N-AS and GIMEN cells to assess effects on EGF-induced MEK/ERK signaling. Cells were treated with YK-4-279 or Trametinib for 4 h, and then PBS or EGF for a further 10 min before assessing ERK phosphorylation.  Fig. 2   Fig. 3 YK-4-279 induces mitotic arrest and apoptosis in neuroblastoma cell lines. (A)  Propidium-iodide based cell cycle analysis of YK-4-279 treated cells using flow cytometry. Cells were treated for 24 h with 0.5× and 1xIC50  concentrations. Cell cycle analysis was carried out in three independent biological replicates. (B)  SK-N-AS, GIMEN and NF-730 were treated with DMSO (D) or two doses of YK-4-279 for 24 h and protein lysates harvested. Blots were probed for several cell cycle and cell death markers. All neuroblastoma cell lines showed increase of phospho-histone H3 (Ser10(pHH3), cleaved PARP and active caspase-3. Actin was used as a loading control. (C)  Flow cytometry with triple staining for phospho-histone H3 (Ser10) (mitotic cells). Dot plot showing DNA content (X-axis) against phospho-histone H3 (Y-axis). Quantification bar graphs of percentage mitotic cells (right side). Data shown as mean ± SD of three technical replicates. (D)  Zombie live/dead cell marker versus phospho-histone H3(Ser10). Cells synchronized using double-thymidine block were treated with YK-4-279 for 24 h after release. Cells were stained with Zombie dye followed by phospho-histone H3 (Ser10) after fixation and permeabilization and subsequently with propidium iodide. Dot plots of phospho-histone H3 positive cells against dead cells. Q1 and Q2 represent percentage dead cells (Q1 and Q2) negative or positive for phospho-histone H3, respectively. Data shown as mean ± SD of three technical replicates. **P  < 0.01, ***P  < 0.001. Unpaired Student t-test was used to assess the significance of difference between the control and treated samples.  Fig. 3   Fig. 4 Disruption of mitosis induced by YK-4-279. (A)  Four neuroblastoma cell lines, SK-N-AS, GIMEN, SK-N-BE(2)-C and SH-SY5Y were treated DMSO or with 1 μM YK-4-279 (5 μM was used for GIMEN). Prior to treatment cells were synchronized by standard double thymidine block protocol. Immediately after release, cells were treated with YK-4-279 for six hours. The graph shows the percentage of cells at distinct phases of mitosis, which were scored based on chromatin organization, in three independent replicates (n > 25). (B)  SK-N-AS, GIMEN, SK-N-BE(2)-C and SH-SY5Y representative mitotic structures (Red: microtubules, Green: chromosomes) from three independent replicates. Diverse microtubule organization is evident from the images. All DMSO treated cells showed typical metaphase equatorial plates and progressed through mitosis and segregated chromosomes within the nine-minute time frame, whereas YK-4-279 cells were mostly stuck at prometaphase. (C)  Static images of four live neuroblastoma cell lines. The range of abnormalities include fragmented (SK-N-AS), unseparated (GIMEN) and multipolar spindles (SK-N-BE(2)-C and SH-SY5Y) (Red: microtubules, Green: chromosomes). Images shown were representative of three independent replicates (n > 25). See also videos in Supplementary information. (D)  Confocal microscopy showing immunofluorescent localization of Eg5 (pink) in YK-4-279-treated GIMEN cells. Chromatin is stained with DAPI (blue). (D)  SK-N-ASr VCR20  and Kellyr VCR10  lysates were prepared 24 h after treatment with 2× IC50  concentrations of vincristine, paclitaxel and YK-4-279. Blots were probed for mitotic and apoptotic markers, demonstrating unimpaired efficacy of YK-4-279.  Fig. 5   Fig. 6 YK-4-279 synergizes with mitotic inhibitors. (A)  GIMEN cells line were treated either singly, or with combinations of YK-4-279 and vincristine, and the MTT proliferation assay was carried out after 72 h. Cancer Epigenetics Laboratory School of Cellular and Molecular Medicine Biomedical Sciences Building University Walk, University of Bristol Bristol BS8 1TD UK       Neuroblastoma is a biologically and clinically heterogeneous pediatric malignancy that includes a high-risk subset for which new therapeutic agents are urgently required. As well as MYCN  amplification, activating point mutations of ALK  and NRAS  are associated with high-risk and relapsing neuroblastoma. As both ALK and RAS signal through the MEK/ERK pathway, we sought to evaluate two previously reported inhibitors of ETS-related transcription factors, which are transcriptional mediators of the Ras-MEK/ERK pathway in other cancers. Here we show that YK-4-279 suppressed growth and triggered apoptosis in nine neuroblastoma cell lines, while BRD32048, another ETV1 inhibitor, was ineffective. These results suggest that YK-4-279 acts independently of ETS-related transcription factors. Further analysis reveals that YK-4-279 induces mitotic arrest in prometaphase, resulting in subsequent cell death. Mechanistically, we show that YK-4-279 inhibits the formation of kinetochore microtubules, with treated cells showing a broad range of abnormalities including multipolar, fragmented and unseparated spindles, together leading to disrupted progression through mitosis. Notably, YK-4-279 does not affect microtubule acetylation, unlike the conventional mitotic poisons paclitaxel and vincristine. Consistent with this, we demonstrate that YK-4-279 overcomes vincristine-induced resistance in two neuroblastoma cell-line models. Furthermore, combinations of YK-4-279 with vincristine, paclitaxel or the Aurora kinase A inhibitor MLN8237/Alisertib show strong synergy, particularly at low doses. Thus, YK-4-279 could potentially be used as a single-agent or in combination therapies for the treatment of high-risk and relapsing neuroblastoma, as well as other cancers.
